answer: A permanent scar of tough collagen
choices: A permanent scar of tough collagen
A cluster of the missing macrophages
A shrunken half-limb missing its foot
A blister that reopened the wound
context: This 2013 experiment (Godwin, Pinto & Rosenthal) pinned regeneration on the immune system: with macrophages depleted before amputation, the stump healed like a mammal wound, capping itself in thick mature type-I collagen instead of forming a blastema. The macrophages fully returned within about two weeks, but by then the window had closed and no limb grew. Their early inflammatory signals are the switch between scar-free regrowth and scarring. Source: Godwin, Pinto & Rosenthal, "Macrophages are required for adult salamander limb regeneration," PNAS 2013 (https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1300290110).

question: When the axolotl genome was sequenced in 2018, it broke a record as the largest ever assembled and hid a genuine shock: one gene long thought essential to build every other vertebrate simply was not there. Which gene had gone missing?
answer: Pax3, with a cousin gene covering its job
choices: Pax3, with a cousin gene covering its job
Sox2, replaced by an ancient viral insert
Hox13, the limb-tip patterning master
Myf5, the muscle-founder switch gene
context: At about 32 gigabases, over ten times the human genome and roughly 19 Gb of repetitive junk-like DNA, the axolotl genome needed a purpose-built assembler (MARVEL). The find that stunned developmental biologists: Pax3, considered indispensable in all other vertebrates, is absent, and its close relative Pax7 has taken over its role. Mutating Pax7 in axolotls reproduces the very defects mice suffer when they lose Pax3. Source: Nowoshilow et al., "The axolotl genome and the evolution of key tissue formation regulators," Nature 2018 (https://www.nature.com/articles/nature25458).

question: Only on the tropical island of Madagascar, off the east coast of Africa, does one strange lemur creep through the trees after dark. It has huge round yellow eyes for the night, big leathery ears that swivel toward the tiniest sound, and one long bony middle finger it uses to tap for grubs under the bark. It is the largest nocturnal primate on Earth. Which lemur is it?
answer: the aye-aye
choices: the aye-aye
the slow loris
the tarsier
the sugar glider
context: The aye-aye (Daubentonia madagascariensis) runs about 15 inches of body with a bushy tail even longer than that, weighing roughly 4-6 pounds. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aye-aye

question: The aye-aye is a strange, big-eyed nocturnal primate that lives in the rainforests of Madagascar. It hunts by percussive foraging, a trick found in no other primate on Earth: at night it taps a tree trunk with its skinny middle finger up to eight times a second and listens hard with huge bat-like ears pressed close to the wood. What is the aye-aye actually sensing beneath the bark as it taps?
answer: a hollow echo where a grub tunnel runs
choices: a hollow echo where a grub tunnel runs
sap rising through the trunk
the scent of insect eggs
the tree's own heartbeat
context: Tap-scanning fills between 5 and 41 percent of the aye-aye's foraging time; it listens for the hollow echo that betrays a grub tunnel hidden under the bark. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aye-aye

question: The aye-aye is a nocturnal primate of Madagascar that finds hidden beetle grubs by tapping tree bark up to eight times a second with its skinny middle finger and listening for the echo. As it taps a branch, tall bony ridges inside its oversized bat-like ears go to work on the faint sound coming back through the wood. What do those inner ear ridges do to that echo?
answer: focus and funnel it toward the eardrum
choices: focus and funnel it toward the eardrum
split it into two delayed signals
cancel out its own tapping noise
amplify only the highest frequencies
context: The ridges work like a lens, funneling the faint echo of the aye-aye's own taps and the movement of larvae under the bark, so it can pinpoint prey it cannot see. Source: https://factanimal.com/aye-aye/

question: The aye-aye is a nocturnal primate of Madagascar that hunts by tapping tree bark and listening for hollow echoes where a beetle grub tunnels deep in the wood. Once the aye-aye hears such a hollow, it drops its ear from the trunk and gnaws through the hard bark with its two long front teeth. Those incisors do something no other primate's front teeth do. What is strange about them?
answer: they never stop growing for its whole life
choices: they never stop growing for its whole life
they are coated in venom
they glow to lure insects
they fall out and regrow yearly
context: These rodent-like, ever-growing incisors are unique among primates and are the reason early naturalists mistook the aye-aye for a rodent. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aye-aye

question: The aye-aye taps wood, listens for a grub, chisels a hole, then fishes the larva out with a thin finger. On other continents an entirely different creature does this exact job with its beak. Why did a primate evolve to fill that role on Madagascar?
answer: the island has no woodpeckers
choices: the island has no woodpeckers
its grub prey burrow too deep for any beak
Madagascar's birds are all fruit-eaters
the island's woodpeckers went extinct long ago
context: Madagascar has no woodpeckers, so the aye-aye evolved to fill that empty niche, doing with a wiry middle finger the exact job a woodpecker's beak does elsewhere. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aye-aye  (Legend.)

question: The aye-aye of Madagascar is a nocturnal primate that hunts by tapping tree bark, listening for hollow beetle-grub tunnels underneath, and then gnawing a hole through the wood. To fish the fat larva out of the winding tunnel, it uses an unusually long, wiry middle finger. That skinny probing finger works because its middle knuckle carries a joint found in no other primate hand. Which kind of joint is it?
answer: a ball-and-socket joint
choices: a ball-and-socket joint
a fused rigid joint
a double-hinged joint
a sliding cartilage pad
context: The ball-and-socket knuckle joint is the only one of its kind in a primate hand, letting the middle finger rotate freely as it hooks a grub. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aye-aye

question: In 2019 researchers solved a puzzle about the aye-aye: its real fingers are so specialized for fishing grubs out of bark that they can't do one everyday job -- grip a branch to hold on. Yet it climbs just fine. How does it manage?
answer: a whole extra thumb of bone and cartilage grew just for gripping
choices: a whole extra thumb of bone and cartilage grew just for gripping
its long claws hook over the branch and lock in place
its long bushy tail coils around the branch like a fifth limb
its hind feet grip while its hands stay free to work
context: NC State researchers Adam Hartstone-Rose and Edwin Dickinson found the aye-aye has a hidden sixth digit, a 'pseudothumb' with its own fingerprint. Hartstone-Rose: 'It has both a bone and cartilaginous extension and three distinct muscles that move it.' Source: https://news.ncsu.edu/2019/10/aye-aye-extra-finger/  (Legend.)

question: A near-hairless wild pig roams the Indonesian island of Sulawesi. Local people named it the pig-deer because the male's strange tusks reminded them of a deer's antlers. Which animal is this?
answer: the babirusa
choices: the babirusa
the warthog
the Malayan tapir
the collared peccary
context: 'Babirusa' comes straight from Indonesian 'babi rusa' — literally 'pig-deer.' It is a wild pig of Sulawesi and a few nearby islands (the Togian, Sula, and Buru islands), and its near-hairless grey body only adds to the odd look. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babirusa

question: The babirusa is a strange, nearly hairless wild pig that lives in the swampy rainforests of the Indonesian island of Sulawesi. The male grows two pairs of upper canine tusks that keep curving as he ages. These upper canines do something no other pig on Earth does with its teeth. Where do those upper canines end up as the boar grows old?
answer: piercing up through the skin on top of its snout
choices: piercing up through the skin on top of its snout
jutting sideways past its fleshy cheeks
curving down below its lower jaw
fusing into a single bony ridge along its back
context: The male's upper canines don't exit the mouth at all — they grow straight UP, pushing through the skin on top of the snout, then curve backward over the face toward the forehead. It is one of the strangest sets of teeth in the animal kingdom. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babirusa  (Legend.)

question: In the forests of Sulawesi, Indonesia, lives a strange wild pig called the babirusa. The name means 'pig-deer' in Malay because of the bizarre bony tusks curling out of the male's face. Most photos show the two famous upper tusks that pierce straight up through the top of his snout and curl back over his forehead — but the male babirusa actually carries four tusks in all. What is the second pair?
answer: a lower pair of canines that also curve upward
choices: a lower pair of canines that also curve upward
a hidden pair rooted deep in the throat
a spare pair that only grow in old age
a pair of flat grinding tusks at the back
context: The male has FOUR tusks: the famous upper pair that pierces the snout, plus a lower pair of canines that also sweep upward. In dominance fights the lower tusks work as offensive weapons while the snout-tusks act more like defensive guards. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babirusa

question: The babirusa, a wild pig from the island of Sulawesi in Indonesia, is famous for the male's four strange tusks — two upper canines that pierce right through the top of his snout and curl back like horns. Those upper tusks never stop growing throughout his life, and unlike most tusks, they cannot be worn down against food. On an old male that never grinds his down, the endless tusk can, in rare cases, do something grim to the babirusa. What?
answer: it curls round and grows into the animal's own skull
choices: it curls round and grows into the animal's own skull
it snaps off and blinds one of its eyes
it locks the animal's jaw permanently shut
it splits the tip of the snout clean in two
context: Because the tusks never stop growing, an unworn one can, in rare cases, keep arcing until it curls round and penetrates the animal's own skull — a creature that literally grows its teeth through its face and, occasionally, back into its own head. Source: https://blogs.ucl.ac.uk/museums/2016/08/12/specimen-of-the-week-252-the-babirusa-skull/  (Legend.)

question: In the deep ocean twilight, a small fish about 15 centimeters long hangs perfectly motionless. The whole top of its head is a transparent, fluid-filled dome you can see straight through. What is this fish called?
answer: The barreleye
choices: The barreleye
The blobfish
The anglerfish
The viperfish
context: The barreleye (Macropinna microstoma) has a see-through dome covering the top of its skull. Despite its otherworldly, alien-looking head, it is only about 15 cm (6 inches) long. Source: MBARI animal page (mbari.org/animal/barreleye-fish); Robison & Reisenbichler 2008, Copeia.  (Legend.)

question: Look inside the barreleye's clear glass-like dome and you find two glowing green tubes — its real eyes. Instead of looking forward like yours, in their resting position these tubular eyes point in one surprising direction. Where do they aim?
answer: Straight up through the transparent skull
choices: Straight up through the transparent skull
Straight down toward the seafloor
Out to the left and right sides
Backward toward its own tail
context: The tubular green eyes point straight UP through the see-through skull to spot prey silhouetted against the faint light drifting down from far above. Source: MBARI news; Robison & Reisenbichler 2008.  (Legend.)

question: On the front of the barreleye's 'face' sit two dark spots exactly where a fish's eyes would normally be — so the first divers to see one were fooled. But the barreleye's real eyes are the green tubes tucked up inside its dome. So what are the two dark spots on its face actually?
answer: Nostrils — smell organs
choices: Nostrils — smell organs
A second pair of backup eyes
Light-producing lures
Openings to its gills
context: The two dark spots that look like eyes are actually nares — the fish's nostrils, its smell organs. The real eyes are the green tubes hidden inside the transparent dome. Source: MBARI animal page; Wikipedia (Macropinna).

question: The barreleye's tubular eyes normally aim straight up. Scientists were long stumped by a puzzle: how could a fish that only looks upward ever guide food into its own tiny mouth below? In 2008, MBARI (the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute) revealed the trick. What can those eyes do?
answer: Rotate forward inside the dome to follow food down
choices: Rotate forward inside the dome to follow food down
Detach and float free to chase prey
Shoot a beam of light onto the mouth
Grow a third eye near the jaw
context: MBARI solved the decades-old paradox in 2008: the tubular eyes can rotate forward inside the transparent dome, swiveling like binoculars to follow prey down to the mouth. Source: Robison & Reisenbichler 2008, Copeia 2008(4):780-784; MBARI news.  (Legend.)

question: Scientists at MBARI (the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute) found that a barreleye cannot just swivel its eyes forward on their own. Its eyes reach the forward-pointing position only when the fish's whole body makes one specific move. What must the barreleye do to swing them forward?
answer: Roll its whole body from horizontal to vertical
choices: Roll its whole body from horizontal to vertical
Beat its tail hard three times
Drift into a shaft of brighter light
Press its snout against the prey
context: Robison and Reisenbichler watched a live specimen rotate its tubular eyes from pointing up to pointing forward as it tipped its body from horizontal to vertical to feed — the eyes turn as the whole fish rolls upright, so the eye rotation is coupled to the body's roll rather than happening on its own. Source: ScienceDaily 2009; Robison & Reisenbichler 2008.

question: The barreleye lives in the ocean's 'twilight zone,' roughly 600 to 800 meters down, where sunlight fades toward total darkness. To survive there it barely swims at all — instead it hangs almost perfectly still in the water. How does it hold its position so precisely?
answer: With large flat fins making tiny adjustments
choices: With large flat fins making tiny adjustments
By anchoring to rocks with a sticky foot
By filling a float sac with gas
By clinging to passing jellyfish
context: The barreleye hovers almost motionless around 600-800 meters (2,000-2,600 feet) down, using large flat fins to hold position with tiny, precise adjustments. Source: MBARI animal page; ScienceDaily 2009.

question: Researchers think the barreleye is a thief. It hovers beneath a siphonophore — a colonial drifter trailing stinging tentacles over 10 meters long — and picks off small animals already snared there. Its stomach even held jelly fragments. But those tentacles sting; what lets the barreleye raid them safely?
answer: The clear dome shields its eyes from the stinging cells
choices: The clear dome shields its eyes from the stinging cells
A slime coat that neutralizes the venom
It only strikes when the siphonophore sleeps
Thick scales armor-plate its whole body
context: Researchers think the barreleye hovers beneath a siphonophore and picks off small animals already trapped in its stinging tentacles; the transparent dome is thought to shield its delicate eyes from the stinging cells. Captured specimens had jelly fragments in their stomachs. Source: MBARI news; ScienceDaily 2009; Robison & Reisenbichler 2008.

question: W. M. Chapman described the barreleye in 1939, yet for 65 years every drawing of it left the top of the head blank — no artist had ever seen the transparent dome intact until MBARI (the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute) filmed a live one in 2004. Why did those decades of net-caught specimens never show the dome?
answer: The fragile dome collapsed or tore off as nets hauled the fish up
choices: The fragile dome collapsed or tore off as nets hauled the fish up
The dome turns cloudy and opaque the moment the fish dies
The dome dissolves in the preservative used to store specimens
The dome retracts inside the skull whenever the fish is startled
context: Described in 1939 by W. M. Chapman, the barreleye was known only from net-caught specimens whose fragile transparent dome arrived collapsed or torn away — so old drawings left it out entirely. MBARI's ROVs captured the first footage of a living barreleye with its dome intact in 2004, 65 years later. Source: Wikipedia (Macropinna); MBARI news; Robison & Reisenbichler 2008.  (Legend.)

question: In the streams of Central American rainforests, a slim green lizard called the basilisk gets scared, rears up on its two back legs, and sprints across the open water without ever sinking in. The trick reminds people of a famous scene from the Bible in which Jesus walked across the Sea of Galilee. From that scene the lizard picked up a nickname. What is that nickname?
answer: the Jesus Christ lizard
choices: the Jesus Christ lizard
the water dragon
the mangrove skater
the pond skimmer
context: The basilisk (genus Basiliscus) of Central and South American rainforest streams dashes across the surface of a pond or stream on its hind legs without sinking, so it looks like it is running on top of the water — hence the 'Jesus Christ lizard' nickname. Source: National Geographic — Green basilisk lizard.  (Legend.)

question: In the Central American rainforest, a basilisk lizard sits basking on a thin branch high above a stream. A hunting snake starts sliding silently up the same trunk toward it. There is no other branch to leap to, no ground to sprint on, and no room left on the branch to back away. Basilisks are famous for running across water, but this one is stuck up in the sky. What does the cornered basilisk do to escape the snake?
answer: drops straight down out of the tree into the water
choices: drops straight down out of the tree into the water
clamps flat and motionless against the bark
wedges itself into a hollow in the trunk
spreads its ribs into a gliding flap
context: A startled basilisk bolts for the nearest water — and it will even drop straight down out of a tree into the water below to flee, then sprint or swim away, leaving a land predator stranded. Source: Wikipedia — Common basilisk; National Geographic — Green basilisk lizard.

question: The basilisk lizard of Central America is nicknamed the Jesus Christ lizard because it can rear up and sprint on top of a stream. A young lizard is small and light, and it dashes clear across the water for 10 to 20 meters (33-66 ft) before slowing down. A full-grown adult, several times heavier, tries the very same crossing. Weight matters when you are staying on top of the surface. How far does the heavy adult get before it sinks in?
answer: only a few meters
choices: only a few meters
the same 10 to 20 meters
roughly 50 meters
the full width — an adult never sinks
context: Only the light young pull it off well: juvenile basilisks can sprint 10 to 20 m (33-66 ft) across open water, while heavy adults manage only a few meters before their weight breaks them through the surface and they sink. Source: Wikipedia — Common basilisk; Biology Insights.

question: A basilisk lizard of Central America — the 'Jesus Christ lizard' — flees across a pond by sprinting on top of the water. Each foot slaps down and pushes off again before the surface can give way, so the whole run is a blur. If the lizard slowed for even a heartbeat, a foot would break through and it would sink. How many times per second do a sprinting basilisk's feet hit the water?
answer: up to about 20 times
choices: up to about 20 times
about 3 times
about 100 times
about 500 times
context: A basilisk running on water takes up to 20 footsteps per second, slapping so fast that each foot pushes off before the water can close over it. Source: Biology Insights — How Basilisk Lizard Feet Enable Running on Water; National Geographic.

question: Scientists calculated whether a person could ever run across a lake the way a basilisk lizard sprints across a pond. The answer comes down to leg power alone. To slap the water fast enough to hold up an average person's body weight, how much more muscle would that person need than they actually have?
answer: about 15 times as much
choices: about 15 times as much
about twice as much
about a tenth more
no more than they already have
context: Glasheen and McMahon calculated that to hold up our weight a human would have to slap the water faster than 30 m/s, needing roughly 15 times the muscle power a person actually has — so no human can do it. Source: Glasheen & McMahon 1996, Nature 380:340-342, as summarized in water-running scaling literature.  (Legend.)

question: Off the cold coast of Scotland, a diver hangs still in the green sea while an enormous shark the length of a school bus glides straight at him, mouth hanging wide open. It is a basking shark, the second-largest fish in the world — an eating machine, but one built only for the tiny drifting sea creatures called plankton. What does this basking shark actually do to a person in the water?
answer: Nothing at all -- it is a harmless giant
choices: Nothing at all -- it is a harmless giant
Delivers a crushing, bone-breaking bite
Wraps and squeezes prey like a python
Stings with venom-tipped fin spurs
context: The basking shark (Cetorhinus maximus) is completely harmless to people; despite its huge size and gaping mouth it is a gentle, non-aggressive giant. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basking_shark

question: The basking shark is the second-biggest fish alive on Earth today, beaten only by the whale shark. It grows past 33 feet long — longer than a school bus — and weighs several tons. It cruises slowly through cold ocean water with its enormous mouth held wide open like a scoop. With a mouth that huge, what does this giant fish actually feed on?
answer: Tiny drifting plankton
choices: Tiny drifting plankton
Seals hauled out on rocks
Schools of tuna and mackerel
Other sharks its own size
context: For all its size, the basking shark eats nothing but tiny plankton -- straining out copepods and other minute animals from the seawater. Source: https://www.marlin.ac.uk/species/detail/1438

question: A single 5-metre basking shark strains up to 500 tons of seawater an hour to sieve out its plankton. The whale shark and megamouth both work their throats to pump and gulp water across the filter. How does the basking shark drive all that water through its gills?
answer: It simply swims forward with its mouth open
choices: It simply swims forward with its mouth open
It gulps and spits water like a bellows
It suctions prey in with a piston throat
It fans water inward with its huge pectoral fins
context: The basking shark is a passive ram filter-feeder: unlike the megamouth and whale sharks it does no pumping or sucking, relying only on the water it forces through its gills just by swimming forward at about 2 knots. A single 5-metre shark can filter up to 500 tons of seawater an hour this way. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basking_shark

question: The basking shark is a giant plankton-eating fish that can grow past 33 feet long. It cruises slowly through cold ocean water with its cavernous mouth held wide open. Seawater pours in — full of tiny drifting shrimp-like creatures called copepods — and as the shark keeps swimming, the copepods stay behind inside its throat while the water flows on out through the gills. What piece of gear inside its mouth catches the food?
answer: Dark, bristle-like gill rakers
choices: Dark, bristle-like gill rakers
A sticky mucus net in the throat
Rows of small hooked teeth
A muscular grinding gizzard
context: The basking shark strains plankton with dark, comb-like gill rakers on its gill arches; they catch the food while the water passes on through the gills. Its actual teeth are tiny (5-6 mm), useless for feeding. Source: https://asknature.org/strategy/specialized-gills-filter-plankton/

question: In 1977 the Japanese trawler Zuiyo-maru, fishing off New Zealand, hauled a rotting carcass up in its nets — a small head on a 1.5-metre neck with four flipper-like limbs. The crew photographed and measured it as a plesiosaur, a long-necked marine reptile everyone thought had died out with the dinosaurs, then dumped the body back overboard. Scientists later tested tissue samples the crew had kept. What did those tests reveal the carcass to be?
answer: A decayed basking shark
choices: A decayed basking shark
A true surviving plesiosaur
A giant deep-sea squid
An unknown long-necked seal
context: A rotting basking shark loses its lower jaw, gills and fins first, leaving a 'head' on a long 'neck' -- so decayed ones repeatedly get mistaken for plesiosaurs (a 'pseudo-plesiosaur'). Amino-acid tests on saved Zuiyo-maru tissue showed it was a dead basking shark. Legend. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zuiyo-maru_carcass

question: For decades naturalists thought the basking shark passed the lean winter by sinking to the seabed and hibernating, its filter idle. David Sims recalculated the true energetic cost of ram-filtering and found the animal actually lives on a knife-edge. What did his numbers reveal it does instead?
answer: Keeps feeding on any patch dense enough, and just abandons thin water
choices: Keeps feeding on any patch dense enough, and just abandons thin water
Buries itself deep in the seafloor sediment until the spring bloom returns
Switches to hunting and gulping small schooling fish once copepods thin out
Drops its whole metabolism near zero and coasts along on stored liver oil
context: Sims's threshold-foraging work put a real energy budget on the giant filter. Pushing that cavernous mouth through the water creates enormous drag, so filtering only pays off above a plankton density of roughly 0.5 grams per cubic metre; below that the shark burns more energy than it gains and stops feeding, moving on to hunt richer water. Because that break-even threshold is lower than anyone expected, the shark never needs to hibernate -- it can profit on plankton year-round wherever the water is thick enough. Source: Sims 1999 & Sims et al. 2003, 'Threshold foraging behaviour of basking sharks on zooplankton: life on an energetic knife-edge?' (PMC1690094); CORDIS/Nature, 'UK study disproves basking shark hibernation myth.'

question: Off County Clare, Ireland, drones filmed something no one had ever recorded for this species. Up to two dozen mature basking sharks slowly wheeled nose-to-tail, gently rolling belly-up and brushing fin to body as they turned. What were the sharks doing in that stacked, doughnut-shaped ring?
answer: Courting -- each sizing up many possible mates at once
choices: Courting -- each sizing up many possible mates at once
Herding a drifting plankton swarm into one richer patch
Settling a dominance order by jostling for the ring's centre
Basking in the sun-warmed surface before a long deep dive
context: David Sims and colleagues assembled underwater and aerial footage from 2016 to 2021 to describe this 'torus': groups of 6 to 23 mature sharks, equal males and females, circling in a ring 17 to 39 metres across and stacked in layers down to about 16 metres deep, with gentle fin-to-body touching and belly-rolling. Sims called it a slow-motion speed-dating event, where each shark can assess many potential partners at once -- the first courtship behaviour ever documented for the basking shark. Source: Sims et al., Journal of Fish Biology, 2022, 'Circles in the sea' (PubMed 36073958; PMC9826005); phys.org, 'Mysterious circling behavior of basking sharks explained.'

question: The bald eagle is a big dark-brown raptor with a snow-white head and yellow feet, the national bird of the United States. It nests in tall trees along lakes and rivers and hunts fish for a living. On a rocky shore an eagle drops from the air, pins a fresh-caught fish under its yellow talons, and leans down to feed. What is the shape of the beak it tears the flesh with?
answer: A downward-curving hook
choices: A downward-curving hook
A flat sieve like a comb
A slim hollow straw
A hard chisel point
context: A raptor's hooked upper bill lets it tear flesh from prey the talons hold pinned — the shape follows a meat-eater's diet. Source: raptor.umn.edu/about-us/news/what-makes-raptor-part-1-hooked-beaks

question: A woodpecker is a stout forest bird with a stiff tail that props it upright against a tree trunk. It hammers away at the bark, listening for the faint chewing of grubs and beetle larvae tunneling deep under the surface. Then it drills straight in to pull them out. To reach that hidden meat, its bill has to punch through solid wood without shattering. What is its bill shaped like?
answer: A hard, straight chisel
choices: A hard, straight chisel
A curved tearing hook
A flat scooping spoon
A stretchy fishing net
context: A woodpecker's straight, hard bill works like a chisel, drilling into wood to reach insects hidden under bark. Source: calacademy.org/explore-science/woodpecker-inspiration

question: A hummingbird is a tiny bird whose wings blur so fast — dozens of beats each second — that it can hover in one spot in midair. In a summer garden it darts up to a long tube-shaped trumpet flower and holds itself still on the wing, then reaches deep down inside the flower to sip the sugary nectar pooled at the very bottom. What is its bill shaped like to reach so far in?
answer: A slender needle
choices: A slender needle
A broad flat spoon
A hooked tearing blade
A blunt cracking wedge
context: A hummingbird's slender, needle-like bill is built to reach down inside deep tube-shaped flowers for nectar. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sword-billed_hummingbird

question: The brown pelican dives from high above the sea, folds its wings back, and slams beak-first into the water to catch fish. Its long floppy throat pouch hangs under its bill and looks like a shabby afterthought. Yet in one plunge-dive that stretchy pouch scoops up more water and fish than the whole bird's own body weighs. About how much water does the pouch hold when it's full?
answer: About 3 gallons
choices: About 3 gallons
About 1 gallon
About 6 gallons
About a half gallon
context: The pelican's gular pouch can hold about 3 gallons (11 liters) of water and fish, then drains the water out before the bird swallows the catch. Source: seaworld.org/animals/facts/birds/brown-pelican/

question: A roseate spoonbill — a tall pink wading bird whose flat bill is shaped like a soup spoon — walks slowly through a shallow lagoon. It holds the bill a little open under the water and sweeps it steadily from side to side. The muddy water is too cloudy to see through. When a shrimp brushes between the two halves of the bill, the bird snaps them shut in an instant. Which sense tells the spoonbill the exact moment to snap?
answer: Touch
choices: Touch
Sight
Smell
Hearing
context: The spoonbill holds its flat bill slightly open and sweeps it through mud, snapping shut the instant it feels a shrimp or small fish — it hunts by touch, not by sight. Source: nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/news/bold-bizarre-and-brilliant-8-fascinating-facts-about-roseate-spoonbill

question: A flamingo wades into a salty lake, then bends its long neck so its head is completely upside-down under the water. It drags its curved bill backward through the shallows, and comb-like ridges inside the bill strain out tiny brine shrimp and salty algae. Here is the strange part: baby flamingos hatch grey, not pink, so the famous color has to come from somewhere. Something in that shrimpy food does what to the grown bird?
answer: Turns its feathers pink
choices: Turns its feathers pink
Makes it grow taller
Sharpens its eyesight
Curls its long neck
context: Comb-like ridges called lamellae strain out brine shrimp and algae; pigments in that food are what turn a flamingo pink. Source: nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/news/why-are-flamingos-pink-and-other-flamingo-facts

question: In the pine forests of the northern world lives a small stubby finch that eats almost nothing but conifer seeds. The problem is that a pine or spruce cone keeps each seed locked tight between two closed woody scales. A finch with an ordinary straight, pointed bill cannot force those scales apart at all. This little finch has a special bill that pries a scale open every time. What is different about its bill?
answer: Bill tips that cross past each other for leverage
choices: Bill tips that cross past each other for leverage
A hooked upper bill for tearing
A comb of ridges lining the bill
A pouch under the lower bill
context: The crossbill's upper and lower bill tips cross past each other; jammed between two cone scales, the crossed tips give the leverage to pry a scale apart, and the tongue lifts out the seed. Legend-flagged as one of the ladder's vivid handles. Source: allaboutbirds.org/news/craig-benkmans-40-year-fascination-with-crossbills-and-conifers/

question: Crossbills are small forest finches with an odd beak: the upper and lower tips cross past each other like a pair of scissors, perfect for prying open pine and spruce cones to reach the seeds inside. On one spruce tree in the northern woods, two different crossbill species can feed side by side and never compete for the same cones. What single trait sorts each species onto its own kind of cones?
answer: The size of its bill
choices: The size of its bill
The color of its feathers
The time of day it feeds
The height it perches at
context: The small-billed white-winged crossbill works tiny spruce and tamarack cones, while the heavier-billed red crossbill breaks into big pine cones — bill size sorts the birds onto different cones on the same tree. Source: allaboutbirds.org/news/craig-benkmans-40-year-fascination-with-crossbills-and-conifers/

question: On the Galapagos Islands off the coast of Ecuador, the young English naturalist Charles Darwin found a group of closely related little birds — later called Darwin's finches. Their beaks came in wildly different shapes across the islands, from heavy and blunt to fine and pointed, and no two islands had quite the same set. What single thing does each bird's beak shape track?
answer: The food that bird eats
choices: The food that bird eats
The color of its mate
The island's rainfall
The song it sings
context: Give one island a dozen foods and evolution carves a dozen bills — Darwin's finches are closely related species whose bills scale from nut-cracker to insect-tweezer, with only about six genes explaining nearly half the variation in beak size. Source: news.ucsc.edu/2023/10/darwin-finches/

question: Falcons like the peregrine hunt by stooping — diving from high in the sky at over 200 miles an hour to slam into birds in mid-air. Once a falcon has knocked its prey down, it uses a tool that hawks and eagles do not have: an extra sharp notch along the upper edge of its hooked beak, called the tomial tooth. The falcon fits the prey's neck into that notch and bites down hard. What does the bite do?
answer: Severs the spinal cord for a fast kill
choices: Severs the spinal cord for a fast kill
Crushes the prey's skull
Punctures a lung to slow it
Snaps a wing so it cannot flee
context: The tomial tooth lets a falcon sever a prey's spinal cord for a quick kill — a feature hawks and eagles do not have. Source: birdsandblooms.com/birding/bird-species/birds-of-prey/falcon-vs-hawk/

question: High in the misty cloud forests of the Andes mountains darts a tiny hummingbird called the sword-billed hummingbird. Its needle-thin bill is 8 to 12 cm long — the only bird in the world whose bill is longer than the rest of its body. The extreme length lets it drink from deep tube-shaped flowers no other hummingbird can reach. But the bill is so absurdly long that the bird cannot use it for one everyday grooming job. It has to do that job with its feet instead. Which job?
answer: Preening its feathers
choices: Preening its feathers
Scratching an itchy head
Wiping mud off its face
Fluffing its throat patch
context: The sword-billed hummingbird's bill is too long to preen with, so the bird scratches and cleans itself using its feet. Legend-flagged as a vivid handle. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sword-billed_hummingbird

question: The toucan of the South American rainforest is famous for its enormous, brightly colored beak — nearly a third the length of its whole body. In 2009 the Canadian biologist Glenn Tattersall pointed a thermal camera at a live toucan to test a hunch about that oversized beak. Besides handling fruit, what hidden second job did his heat-vision footage reveal the huge bill actually does?
answer: Dumps body heat like a radiator
choices: Dumps body heat like a radiator
Stores fat for the dry season
Amplifies the bird's call
Filters mud from its water
context: Tattersall's infrared study found the toucan pumps blood into its bill to dump body heat, making it one of the largest thermal 'windows' in the animal kingdom — rivaling an elephant's ears. Legend-flagged. Source: science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1175553

question: Daphne Major is a small volcanic islet in the Galápagos Islands where the biologists Peter and Rosemary Grant spent decades measuring the beaks of every finch they could catch. In 1977 a hard drought hit the island, and by the next year about 85 percent of the medium ground finches were dead — but the die-off was not random. The soft seeds ran out first, leaving only the toughest, hardest seeds behind. The Grants found the survivors shared one trait of the beak. Which beak did the drought favor?
answer: The biggest, strongest beaks
choices: The biggest, strongest beaks
The smallest, lightest beaks
The most sharply hooked beaks
The most brightly colored beaks
context: The drought left mostly large, tough Tribulus seeds; birds with the biggest, strongest beaks could crack them and survived, so the survivors shared that one trait — natural selection acting in a single dry year. Legend-flagged. Source: knowledge.carolina.com/discipline/life-science/biology/evolution-of-the-galapagos-finch/

question: On Daphne Major the 1977 drought had favored the biggest beaks. When a second harsh drought hit in 2004, a bigger rival species had arrived and was hogging the large seeds. This time the medium ground finches that survived carried the opposite beak. Which one?
answer: The smallest beaks, better on the seeds left over
choices: The smallest beaks, better on the seeds left over
The biggest beaks, same as the 1977 winners
The longest beaks, for probing cactus flowers
The most hooked beaks, for tearing tough husks
context: Same island, same species as the famous 1977 result -- but the OPPOSITE winner. A population of the much larger LARGE ground finch had colonized Daphne Major and monopolized the big, hard seeds, so during the 2004-2005 drought the medium ground finches with SMALLER beaks (better at the small seeds left over) survived and the big-beaked ones died. This is a textbook case of 'character displacement' caught in real time, and selection against the large-beak type was fierce (selection coefficient s = 0.59). Lamichhaney and colleagues later traced the shift to the HMGA2 gene: birds carrying two copies of the small-beak variant (HMGA2*S) survived far better. Source: Lamichhaney et al. 2016, 'A beak size locus in Darwin's finches facilitated character displacement during a drought,' Science, Apr 22 2016 (PubMed 27102486; Princeton/Uppsala/ScienceDaily coverage), corroborated across multiple outlets.  (Legend.)

question: A crossbill's bill is not just crossed but handed: each bird's lower tip bends fixed to the left or the right for life, so it can only work a cone from one side. Craig Benkman found red crossbills split almost exactly 50/50 between the two. What keeps that even balance?
answer: Whichever type is rarer finds more untouched cones, so it thrives
choices: Whichever type is rarer finds more untouched cones, so it thrives
Chicks copy the crossing direction of the parent that feeds them
The crossing direction flips to match each new cone crop
Left and right tips wear down at exactly the same rate
context: A crossbill's crossed tip is 'handed' -- it crosses either to the left ('sinistral') or the right ('dextral'), fixed for life, forcing the bird to attack cones from one direction. Lefties and righties literally walk around a cone in opposite directions and pry from opposite sides. Craig Benkman found red crossbills occur in a roughly 1:1 ratio and argued it is held there by negative frequency-dependent selection: whichever morph is rarer has more un-worked cones available, so it does better, which pulls the ratio back toward even. (White-winged crossbills are skewed ~3:1 toward right-crossing.) Source: Craig Benkman's work and Springer, 'Are the ratios of bill crossing morphs in crossbills the result of frequency-dependent selection?' (Evolutionary Ecology); Scottish Wildlife Trust, Montana Public Radio, Bootstrap Analysis coverage, corroborated across sources.  (Legend.)

question: The North American beaver is a big flat-tailed rodent that fells whole trees with its front teeth and dams a woodland stream up into a pond. Those two upper front teeth are enormous chisels the beaver uses to gnaw through wood all day long. Look closely at them and you'll notice an unexpected color no other pet or wild rodent seems to have. What color are a beaver's front teeth?
answer: Bright orange
choices: Bright orange
Pale white
Jet black
Dull gray
context: A beaver's incisors are famously orange because the outer enamel is packed with iron instead of the ordinary magnesium in most animal teeth. The iron makes them harder and more acid-resistant, so they resist decay without brushing. Source: https://scienceinsights.org/why-are-beaver-teeth-orange-its-iron-in-the-enamel/

question: A beaver is a big flat-tailed rodent that lives in forest streams and ponds. It spends its whole life gnawing down hard tree trunks — cutting whole trees to build dams and lodges. Its four front teeth are chisels of bright orange enamel. You would think all that wood-chewing would wear those teeth down to painful stubs in a single year. Yet an old beaver still chomps as well as a young one. How does it keep chewing wood for a lifetime?
answer: Its teeth never stop growing
choices: Its teeth never stop growing
It grows a fresh set each spring
It swaps to back molars for wood
It softens the wood with saliva first
context: A beaver's incisors grow continuously, so it must gnaw constantly to wear them down. New tooth forms at the root as fast as the tip wears away, keeping a chisel edge for life. Source: https://a-z-animals.com/blog/beaver-teeth-everything-you-need-to-know/

question: At the edge of a woodland pond sits a big dome of piled mud and sticks. It is called a lodge, and inside it a beaver family — parents and their kits — eats, sleeps, and raises the young. A hungry fox prowls the bank, sniffing all around, but can't get inside to reach them. Where did the beavers put the front door so land predators cannot follow them home?
answer: Underwater, entered by diving
choices: Underwater, entered by diving
On the roof, reached by climbing
Behind a wall of thorns
Facing away, hidden in reeds
context: A beaver builds its lodge with an entrance underwater, so a fox or wolf cannot follow it inside. The dam floods a safe moat around the home, and the family enters by diving. Source: https://a-z-animals.com/articles/ecosystem-engineers-how-beavers-build-wetlands-that-help-fight-climate-change/

question: The North American beaver uses its two big upper front teeth as chisels to cut down whole trees. Iron-hard enamel — the same tough stuff coating the outside of your own teeth — sits only on the front face of each of those incisors. The softer inner material behind it, called dentin, is exposed at the back of the tooth and wears away faster with every bite. What does that lopsided wear do to the tooth as the beaver keeps gnawing?
answer: Grinds it into a fresh chisel edge
choices: Grinds it into a fresh chisel edge
Splits it down the middle
Curls the tip back into the mouth
Dulls it into a flat stub
context: Because the hard iron enamel wears slower than the soft dentin behind it, every bite grinds the tooth back into a sharp chisel edge. The beaver's teeth sharpen themselves. Source: https://scienceinsights.org/why-are-beaver-teeth-orange-its-iron-in-the-enamel/

question: The North American beaver spends much of its life underwater, gliding through the murky pond it built to keep foxes and coyotes on land. It dives with its eyes wide open, yet it still sees clearly and its eyes stay unhurt by all the mud and grit. What piece of built-in gear lets a beaver swim like that?
answer: A see-through third eyelid
choices: A see-through third eyelid
A ring of tiny scales
An oily protective film
A pair of bony eye-shields
context: A beaver has a transparent third eyelid that slides across each eye like built-in swim goggles, letting it see clearly underwater while keeping the water out. Source: https://forthriverstrust.org/mammals-week-anatomy-of-a-beaver/

question: A beaver — a stocky brown rodent that builds dams and lodges in North American ponds — is swimming quietly across its own pond at dusk. Suddenly a shadow passes overhead: maybe an owl, maybe a coyote on the shore. In a flash the beaver brings its broad, flat, leathery tail down hard on the surface with a loud crack that echoes across the water. The tail already helps it steer as a rudder while swimming, but that slap is doing another job. What is the slap for?
answer: Warning the colony of danger
choices: Warning the colony of danger
Stunning fish to eat
Splashing mud onto the dam
Cooling itself in summer heat
context: A beaver's flat scaly tail is a Swiss-army tool: a rudder for steering while swimming, and an alarm. When danger appears, the beaver slaps it hard on the water with a loud crack to warn the whole colony. Source: https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/castoreum/

question: In the fall, a North American beaver spends its evenings dragging leafy branches down to the bottom of its pond, where it builds an underwater larder of winter food. It clamps a branch tight in its four huge orange front teeth and dives, staying under the water for many minutes at a time before surfacing for a breath. Somehow it can swim and work with its mouth full without water pouring down its throat and drowning it. What lets it do that?
answer: Its lips close behind the front teeth
choices: Its lips close behind the front teeth
It blocks its throat with its tongue
It swims with the branch held in a paw
It keeps the branch pinched above water
context: Before diving, a beaver seals itself shut: valve-like muscles clamp the nostrils and ears closed, and its lips close BEHIND the front teeth, so it can carry a branch underwater without swallowing water. It can stay under for about 15 minutes. Source: https://beaversinengland.com/beaver-biology/beaver-biology-2/

question: Deep in the wet boreal forests of Wood Buffalo National Park in northern Canada, several beaver families have been stacking sticks and mud together for generations. Their work grew into a single beaver dam so enormous that in 2007 a Canadian researcher named Jean Thie spotted it while scanning satellite images from space. It is now the largest beaver dam on Earth. Stretched end to end, how long is that dam?
answer: About 800 meters, eight football fields
choices: About 800 meters, eight football fields
About 80 meters, one football field
About 8 kilometers across a valley
About 8 meters, a garden hedge
context: The largest known beaver dam stretches about 800 meters, the length of eight football fields, hidden in Wood Buffalo National Park. It was so big it showed up on satellite imagery in 2007. Source: https://parks.canada.ca/pn-np/nt/woodbuffalo/nature/beaver_gallery  (Legend.)

question: A shaggy, black, cat-sized mammal prowls the rainforest canopy of South and Southeast Asia. The strangest thing hits your nose before your eyes: it smells like hot buttered popcorn. Keepers nicknamed it the 'bearcat,' though it is really a cousin of the civets. What is this popcorn-smelling tree-dweller?
answer: The binturong
choices: The binturong
The red panda
The kinkajou
The fossa
context: The binturong (Arctictis binturong) is a viverrid — a relative of the civets — not a bear and not a cat, despite its 'bearcat' nickname. Its genus name Arctictis is Greek for 'bear-weasel.' It really does smell strongly of hot buttered popcorn. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binturong ; https://today.duke.edu/2016/04/popcorn-scented-binturong

question: The binturong is a shaggy black tree-dwelling mammal of Southeast Asian rainforests, sometimes called a bearcat. Zookeepers and villagers who lived near them all noticed the same odd thing: the animal has a strong scent that smells like something you'd sniff in a kitchen. Chemists expected the source to be some exotic new civet compound, but a 2016 study at Duke University found a molecule people had been smelling at home for years. Which food shares the binturong's signature scent molecule?
answer: Popcorn and cooked jasmine rice
choices: Popcorn and cooked jasmine rice
Fresh-cut cucumber and melon rind
Ripe banana and pear skin
Roasted coffee and dark chocolate
context: The compound is 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline (2-AP) — the very same molecule that makes popcorn and cooked jasmine rice smell the way they do. Greene et al. (2016) found it in every binturong urine sample they tested. Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27056047/ ; https://today.duke.edu/2016/04/popcorn-scented-binturong

question: Here was the puzzle for the Duke researchers. In popcorn, that buttery-smelling molecule forms only under high cooking heat, when sugars and amino acids react together. Lead scientist Christine Drea asked how a binturong makes a cooking smell without ever cooking. Where do they think the compound comes from?
answer: Bacteria living on the animal's skin, fur, or gut make it as the urine passes
choices: Bacteria living on the animal's skin, fur, or gut make it as the urine passes
A special heat-producing gland warms the urine to 'cook' it
The animal eats fermenting fruit that already contains it
Its liver synthesizes the finished molecule directly
context: In popcorn, 2-AP forms through the Maillard reaction — sugars and amino acids reacting under high heat. A binturong never gets that hot, so Christine Drea asked, 'How does this animal make a cooking smell, but without cooking?' The team believes microbes on the binturong's skin, fur, or gut produce the compound as the urine passes. Source: https://today.duke.edu/2016/04/popcorn-scented-binturong

question: High in a Southeast Asian rainforest canopy lives the binturong, a shaggy black tree-dwelling mammal with a long, grabbing prehensile tail. When it wants to leave a tree, it does something almost no other climbing mammal can pull off — it walks headfirst straight down the trunk without slipping, its claws gripping the bark the whole way. A squirrel or a cat coming down a tree usually has to slide, twist, or leap. What lets the binturong pull off a headfirst descent?
answer: Its hind ankles rotate a full 180 degrees to keep the claws hooked
choices: Its hind ankles rotate a full 180 degrees to keep the claws hooked
Suction pads on the soles of its feet grip the bark
It descends by hanging from its tail and letting go in stages
Backward-curving spines along its belly catch the trunk
context: The binturong can rotate its hind ankles a full 180 degrees, so its claws stay hooked into the bark even while it climbs down a trunk head-first — a trick most tree mammals can't manage. It also has a fully prehensile tail it uses as a fifth limb to anchor and balance in the trees. Source: https://a-z-animals.com/animals/binturong/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binturong

question: The blanket octopus is a small, flashy octopus of the tropical open ocean. The female trails long shimmering sheets of webbing from her arms like a cape. Most octopuses hide in rocky reef crevices by day and crawl the seafloor at night. The blanket octopus does neither. It never touches a rock or a grain of sand in its entire life — no dens, no bottom. Where does this octopus spend all of that life instead?
answer: Drifting in the open blue ocean, far above any bottom
choices: Drifting in the open blue ocean, far above any bottom
Clinging to floating rafts of drifting seaweed at the surface
Riding on the backs of large drifting jellyfish
Hovering in the warm water just above deep-sea vents
context: The blanket octopus is pelagic — it lives in the open ocean far from any reef or seafloor, drifting through tropical and subtropical waters from the surface down to about 250 meters. Most octopuses are bottom-dwellers, which makes this open-water lifestyle unusual. Source: https://octonation.com/octopedia/blanket-octopus/

question: Out in the open tropical ocean, a hungry tuna closes in on a female blanket octopus — a soft, shell-less octopus that drifts near the surface with wide sheets of iridescent purple webbing strung between her long arms. There is no shell to hide in, no coral reef to duck behind, and no sandy bottom to flee toward. She has only that webbing to save herself. What does she do with it?
answer: Snaps it open like a giant iridescent cape to look enormous and terrifying
choices: Snaps it open like a giant iridescent cape to look enormous and terrifying
Wraps herself into a tight armored ball
Catches the current with it to outrun the tuna
Scoops the tuna into it like a net and eats it
context: The female unfurls a huge iridescent 'blanket' — sheets of webbing strung between her arms — and spreads it so she suddenly looks enormous and scary, ballooning out to intimidate tuna, sailfish and even sharks. Source: https://octonation.com/fun-facts-about-the-female-blanket-octopus/

question: The blanket octopus drifts through warm open ocean, the female flaring wide sheets of purple webbing between her long arms like a floating cape. She swims right up to a Portuguese man o' war — a drifting jelly-like creature whose long stinging tentacles carry venom strong enough to kill a swimmer. Rather than fleeing the danger, the octopus rips pieces off. What does she do with the stolen stinging tentacles?
answer: Holds the stinging tentacles in its arms as venomous whips
choices: Holds the stinging tentacles in its arms as venomous whips
Eats them to absorb the venom into its own skin
Weaves them into its blanket for extra color
Uses them as bait to lure fish closer
context: Legendary. The blanket octopus tears pieces off the man o' war's deadly tentacles and holds them in its arms like whips, using the stolen stingers as weapons to attack prey and fend off predators. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blanket_octopus

question: The blanket octopus is a soft, shell-less octopus that drifts through the open ocean trailing wide sheets of shimmering webbing between her long arms. A full-grown female can stretch about 2 meters across — roughly the height of a doorway. The male of the very same species is one of the tiniest creatures in the whole animal kingdom, so much smaller than his mate that for centuries no one saw them together. What everyday object is the male about the size of?
answer: A walnut
choices: A walnut
A grape
A paperclip
A thumbtack
context: Legendary. The blanket octopus shows one of the most extreme size gaps in the animal kingdom: the female can reach about 2 meters (6.6 ft), while the male is only about 2.4 cm — roughly the size of a walnut. Source: https://www.iflscience.com/the-blanket-octopus-has-the-most-extreme-sexual-dimorphism-in-the-animal-kingdom-80008

question: In the blanket octopus, the female is a giant — up to two metres of drifting purple webbing — while the male is barely the size of a walnut and rarely seen. The tiny male fills one specialized arm called the hectocotylus with his packet of sperm. When it is finally time to mate with the huge female, what does he do with that specialized arm?
answer: He detaches it and hands the whole arm over to her
choices: He detaches it and hands the whole arm over to her
He wraps it around her mantle and holds on for days
He uses it to fight off rival males nearby
He plants it on the seafloor for her to find later
context: Legendary. The tiny male mates by handing over a whole detachable arm — the hectocotylus — which he packs with sperm and gives to the female; the male almost certainly dies shortly after. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blanket_octopus

question: In the blanket octopus, the female can stretch to about 2 meters while the male is only about the size of a walnut — one of the most extreme size differences in the whole animal kingdom. For centuries, scientists knew this male existed only from dead specimens dragged up in trawl nets and picked out of plankton samples. No one had ever watched a living adult male out in the ocean. When did scientists finally observe a live adult male blanket octopus for the first time?
answer: In 2002, off Australia's Great Barrier Reef
choices: In 2002, off Australia's Great Barrier Reef
In 1902, in a European aquarium
In the 1850s, during a deep-sea dredging voyage
In the 1970s, from a research submarine
context: The dwarf male was such a puzzle that no living one was seen until 2002, when Mark Norman and colleagues found the world's first live adult male off Australia's Great Barrier Reef, calling it 'the world's most sexually size-dimorphic large animal.' Source: https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/00288330.2002.9517126

question: In the 1820s, naturalists cut open female blanket octopuses and argonauts. They kept finding a strange squirming thread inside. Georges Cuvier named it Hectocotylus octopodis and called it a brand-new animal. Decades later, biologists studied whole dwarf males. What did that thread actually turn out to be?
answer: The dwarf male's own detachable arm, left behind after mating
choices: The dwarf male's own detachable arm, left behind after mating
A parasitic ribbon-worm that feeds on octopus eggs
A coiled string of the female's own unfertilized eggs
A stinging thread stripped from a Portuguese man o' war
context: One of biology's great mistaken-identity blunders. Cuvier described the severed hectocotylus as its own parasitic worm species. In the 1840s Albert von Kolliker (examining both argonaut and blanket-octopus specimens) and Heinrich Muller -- who found whole dwarf males whose enlarged arm dropped off when touched -- proved the "worm" was really the male's own detached mating arm. Source: OctoNation, "How Male Argonauts Taught Scientists About Octopus Sex"; Wikipedia "Hectocotylus"; Della Chiaje/Cuvier historical record.  (Legend.)

question: Blanket octopuses tear stinging tentacles from the Portuguese man o' war and brandish them as living weapons. Only tiny males and small immature females are ever discovered holding one. No octopus longer than about seven centimeters carries one. Why does the borrowed stinger drop out of the arsenal once a blanket octopus grows past that size?
answer: A bigger octopus's larger suckers can't grip the narrow stinger without tearing it
choices: A bigger octopus's larger suckers can't grip the narrow stinger without tearing it
Larger octopuses lose their immunity to the man o' war's venom as they mature
The stinger's venom breaks down too fast to be useful on a slow-moving adult
Bigger octopuses can no longer swim close enough to a man o' war to harvest one
context: Individuals longer than about 7 cm have never been seen carrying the tentacles -- their larger suckers likely can't grip the narrow stingers without injury. The borrowed weapon gives the small males a "size refuge," which researchers propose may itself have pushed females to grow enormous while males stayed miniature. Source: Norman, Paul, Finn & Tregenza 2002, "First encounter with a live male blanket octopus," NZ J. Marine & Freshwater Research 36:733-736; citing Jones 1963 and Thomas 1977.

question: The blobfish became famous online as 'the saddest fish in the world' — a droopy, sagging pink blob photographed on the deck of a fishing boat with what looks like a permanently frowning face. But the blobfish actually lives about a kilometre deep in the cold seas off Australia, where crushing water pressure holds its jelly-soft body in normal shape. Yanked to the surface, that body collapses. Down at home a kilometre deep, a living blobfish actually looks like:
answer: a normal blunt-headed pink fish with big black eyes
choices: a normal blunt-headed pink fish with big black eyes
a translucent jelly with glowing blue veins
a spiny grey lump bristling with venom quills
a flat ribbon of skin with no eyes at all
context: The famous melted-face look only appears at the surface: built for crushing deep-sea pressure, the blobfish's body relaxes and collapses in our thin air 'much like a washed-up jellyfish.' At depth it is an ordinary-looking pink fish with feathery fins. Source: BBC Science Focus, 'The blobfish: a bloated guide to the world's ugliest animal' (sciencefocus.com).  (Legend.)

question: The blobfish lives on the deep-sea floor a kilometre down off Australia and New Zealand, where the water pressure is a hundred times what you feel at the beach. When a fisherman's trawl net drags one up and hauls it all the way to the boat deck, its body sags on the surface into the famous drooping, gooey mess — the internet-famous 'saddest fish' face. Which change up here on deck turned a firm deep-sea fish into slop?
answer: the crushing squeeze its body needed suddenly vanished
choices: the crushing squeeze its body needed suddenly vanished
the sunlight burned and blistered its skin
the warm surface water boiled its blood
the thin surface air poisoned its gills
context: At home the blobfish lives where water presses on it 60 to 120 times harder than air presses on us at the surface. A body engineered against that crushing squeeze simply falls apart once the pressure is gone. Source: Wikipedia, Psychrolutes marcidus (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychrolutes_marcidus).

question: The blobfish is a deep-sea fish that lives a kilometre down in the cold dark water off Australia and New Zealand. Its body is mostly floppy jelly — almost no muscle and barely any bone — because chasing prey around would burn precious energy the food-poor deep can't spare. So how does this lazy pink blob manage to eat at all?
answer: it gulps whatever edible scraps drift right past its mouth
choices: it gulps whatever edible scraps drift right past its mouth
it filters mud through long comb-like teeth
it lures prey with a glowing lure on its head
it scrapes algae off rocks with a rasping tongue
context: Strong bones and big muscles cost energy the food-poor deep can't spare, so the blobfish hovers nearly motionless and swallows small crustaceans, sea snails, and drifting scraps, 'whatever passes right in front of them.' As one expert put it, 'Being lazy is a survival strategy.' Source: BBC Science Focus (sciencefocus.com); Australian Museum, fathead / Mr Blobby page.

question: In 2013 the Ugly Animal Preservation Society, a British comedy group, ran an online vote for the 'World's Ugliest Animal.' The winner was the blobfish, a deep-sea fish that collapses into a droopy pink blob when hauled up out of the crushing pressure it needs to hold its shape. The mournful photo that everyone shares is one particular museum specimen, kept at Australia's national fish collection and nicknamed Mr Blobby. What made Mr Blobby's face droop even sadder than a freshly caught blobfish?
answer: preserving him in alcohol tightened his skin and shrank his nose
choices: preserving him in alcohol tightened his skin and shrank his nose
years drying out in a display jar cracked and slackened his face
the trawl net's crushing haul mangled his features on the way up
a rare skin disease had melted his features before capture
context: 'Mr Blobby' (specimen AMS I.42771-001) was netted by trawl on the 2003 NORFANZ expedition on the Norfolk Ridge northwest of New Zealand. Preserving him in alcohol tightened his skin and shrank his nose, exaggerating the sad droopy look, and a tiny parasitic copepod was found clinging to his mouth. Source: Australian Museum, 'Blobfish (aka Mr Blobby)' (australian.museum); Wikipedia, Ugly Animal Preservation Society.  (Legend.)

question: The blue dragon (Glaucus atlanticus) is a tiny sea slug no bigger than your thumb, striped in dazzling silver and electric blue. It lives out in the wide open tropical ocean, never touching land, reef, or bottom. It has no shell to weight it down and no fins to swim with. Yet somehow it stays at the very surface of the sea its whole life. How does the blue dragon ride there?
answer: Belly-up, floating upside down
choices: Belly-up, floating upside down
Clinging to a rock with one foot
Buried in the sandy seabed
Riding on a sea turtle's shell
context: The blue dragon floats upside down at the very surface, belly toward the sky, drifting at the mercy of the wind and currents with almost no power to swim on its own. Source: https://www.australiangeographic.com.au/fact-file/fact-file-blue-dragon-glaucus-atlanticus/  (Legend.)

question: The blue dragon (Glaucus atlanticus) is a silver-blue sea slug only about three centimeters long — smaller than a grape. It drifts belly-up on the open ocean, hunting an animal even more dangerous than itself: the Portuguese man o' war, a jellyfish-like drifter armed with venomous stinging cells. The blue dragon eats the man o' war whole and stores its stingers, still working, along its own frilly blue arms. How bad can this tiny slug then sting a swimmer?
answer: Worse than the Portuguese man o' war it ate
choices: Worse than the Portuguese man o' war it ate
About the same as a mild mosquito bite
Not at all — it has no sting of its own
Only a faint tingle you'd barely notice
context: Despite being smaller than a grape, the blue dragon can sting a human worse than the man o' war did, causing nausea, pain, and vomiting. It concentrates the venom it steals, so the thief becomes deadlier than its victim. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glaucus_atlanticus  (Legend.)

question: The blue dragon is a tiny sea slug about the size of a coin that drifts belly-up on the open tropical ocean, its arms spread out like blue wings. Its favourite meal is the Portuguese man o' war — a jellyfish-like drifter whose long tentacles bristle with venomous stinging cells that can paralyse a fish. The blue dragon bites straight into that stinging veil and swallows the cells whole, somehow without ever setting them off in its own throat. What happens to those swallowed stingers inside the slug's body?
answer: The strongest ones are moved into its own body
choices: The strongest ones are moved into its own body
They pass through and are excreted intact
They dissolve harmlessly in its gut acid
They are packed into eggs to arm its young
context: The blue dragon swallows the man o' war's stinging cells (nematocysts) undigested and moves the STRONGEST ones into its own body — a trick called kleptocnidy, meaning 'stolen stingers.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glaucus_atlanticus  (Legend.)

question: The blue dragon (Glaucus atlanticus) is a tiny sea slug only a few centimetres long that drifts upside-down at the ocean surface, carried by wind and current. It faces hungry seabirds diving from above the water and hungry fish hunting from below. How is its small drifting body actually colored to survive that double threat?
answer: Blue on one side, silver-grey on the other
choices: Blue on one side, silver-grey on the other
Bright red all over as a poison warning
See-through so light passes through it
A dull sandy brown, top and bottom alike
context: Its camouflage is counter-shaded in REVERSE: the side pointing up to the sky is brilliant blue to hide against the sea from above, and the side pointing down into the water is silver-grey to hide against the bright surface from below. Because the blue dragon floats upside down, this puts the blue on its belly. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glaucus_atlanticus  (Legend.)

question: The blue dragon (Glaucus atlanticus) is a tiny silver-blue sea slug that lives its whole life adrift at the very surface of the tropical ocean, silver belly turned up to the sky and blue back down toward the water below. It has no fins to speak of, and it can barely swim — a strong wave would drown any other snail. Yet a blue dragon never sinks from that thin sunlit layer at the top of the sea. What keeps this little slug afloat?
answer: An air bubble it holds in its stomach
choices: An air bubble it holds in its stomach
Oil-filled fins that spread like a raft
A jelly float grown on its back
Beating thousands of tiny leg-paddles
context: The blue dragon stays afloat by swallowing and holding an air bubble in its stomach — a gas-filled sac in its belly acts like a built-in life-jacket, helped by the surface tension of the water. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glaucus_atlanticus  (Legend.)

question: The blue dragon (Glaucus atlanticus) is a tiny sea slug that eats the venomous Portuguese man o' war and stores the man o' war's stinging cells in the tips of its own fingerlike body. One washes up dead and drying on a warm beach, only a few centimetres long and a beautiful electric blue. A curious child spots the pretty little shape and reaches for it. Why should they keep their hands off?
answer: Its stingers still fire on contact days after death
choices: Its stingers still fire on contact days after death
Its drying body puffs out a cloud of toxic spores
Its skin turns acidic and burns whatever touches it
Its blue pigment soaks in and poisons through the skin
context: The blue dragon's venom stays active even after the slug is DEAD — a washed-up blue dragon on the beach can still sting you, because the borrowed stinging cells fire on contact. Source: https://www.australiangeographic.com.au/fact-file/fact-file-blue-dragon-glaucus-atlanticus/  (Legend.)

question: The blue dragon (Glaucus atlanticus) is a coin-sized drifting sea slug that eats the Portuguese man o' war. It swallows the man o' war's loaded stinging cells alive and stores the strongest ones in the tips of its own arms as borrowed weapons. But no matter how carefully it swallows, a few of those stingers always misfire off inside its gut. Beyond just storing the intact survivors, how does the blue dragon's gut keep the ones that did fire from harming it?
answer: Mucus quiets the stingers, and tough chitin plates in the gut soak up the ones that fire
choices: Mucus quiets the stingers, and tough chitin plates in the gut soak up the ones that fire
Heat from its stomach denatures the stingers and makes them fall limp before they fire
It fires each stinger into a sealed water sac that then vents harmlessly to the open sea
It starves itself for days so the loaded stingers slowly discharge on their own instead
context: The disarming is a two-part trick. First, the slug's mucus suppresses nematocyst discharge (in the related aeolid Aeolidia papillosa, mucus cut prey-stinger firing by roughly 60% below control). Second, a tough chitin cuticle plus granular-chitin discs called 'spindles' line the gut and act like biological sandbags, absorbing any stinger that still goes off. So swallowing a man o' war whole is not luck: it chemically quiets the weapons, then physically shields its own insides from the ones that fire anyway. Source: PMC review 'Acquisition and Use of Nematocysts by Cnidarian Predators' (PMC2783962), citing Aeolidia papillosa mucus-suppression and buccal chitin 'spindle' data.

question: For decades marine biologists cast the blue dragon (Glaucus atlanticus) — a coin-sized, wing-armed sea slug that drifts on ocean currents — as a Portuguese man o' war specialist that killed prey with borrowed stinging cells. Then in 2025 an aquarium study filmed the little slug hunting live small fish in a tank and overturned the old story: the borrowed stings weren't its main weapon at all. How did the blue dragon actually catch a live fish in that study?
answer: It grabbed and pinned them with its long front cerata, then bit down near the gills
choices: It grabbed and pinned them with its long front cerata, then bit down near the gills
It stunned the passing fish with a sudden burst of its stored stinging cells
It lured small fish in under its belly using its bright glowing blue underside
It snared them in sticky mucus threads it spun out from its muscular foot
context: Reared in aquaria, Glaucus atlanticus used its enlarged front cerata like ARMS, pinning live whitebait (Japanese anchovy) between them and biting near the gills. Histology found a well-developed muscle-fiber layer at the base of these front cerata, which are built longer than the rest 'like an arm,' giving the grip needed to seize fast prey. It fed as a generalist on several cnidarians plus fish, not as a man o' war specialist, and the stolen stingers were NOT observed doing the killing: capture was by physical grip and biting. The frilly cerata, long thought to be purely a defensive sting-battery, turned out to be grasping limbs too. Source: Yamamoto et al. 2025, Ecology, 'Blue angels have devil hands: Predatory behavior using cerata in Glaucus atlanticus' (PMC11912302 / doi:10.1002/ecy.70062).  (Legend.)

question: A small octopus is hunting along an Australian tide pool, its skin a drab, mottled grey-brown that blends into the rocks. Then something disturbs it, and in a third of a second its skin erupts with dozens of glowing electric-blue rings. What is this sudden flash of rings?
answer: A warning display that says 'do not touch'
choices: A warning display that says 'do not touch'
A net it spreads to trap passing fish
A trail of light that lures prey closer
A glow it uses to see in dark water
context: The blue rings are aposematic — a 'do not touch' signal. When resting, the blue-ringed octopus (Hapalochlaena) is a drab grey-to-yellowish brown that camouflages into the rocks; the famous rings stay hidden until it is threatened. Source: Australian Geographic, 'Fact File: Blue-ringed octopus'; Natural History Museum (London).

question: The blue-ringed octopus is a golf-ball-sized creature that lives in shallow tide pools around Australia and Indonesia, and it carries enough venom in its bite to kill a full-grown human. Yet it would much rather scare you off than fight — its bright glowing blue rings flash on all over its skin as pure warning. What is the single thing that actually makes this tiny octopus bite a person?
answer: Being grabbed or stepped on
choices: Being grabbed or stepped on
Swimming past it in open water
Shining a bright light at it
Making a loud noise nearby
context: The rings are a warning, not an attack — the octopus flashes rather than fights, and only bites if it is grabbed or stepped on. Source: Natural History Museum (London), 'The blue-ringed octopus: small, vibrant and exceptionally deadly'.

question: You could hold a blue-ringed octopus in one open hand — including all its little arms it is only about the size of a golf ball, and it lives quietly in shallow tide pools around Australia and Indonesia. Yet a single one of these tiny creatures carries enough venom to do what to a group of grown human beings?
answer: Kill more than twenty adult humans within minutes
choices: Kill more than twenty adult humans within minutes
Dissolve a crab's shell in seconds
Stun every fish in a small tide pool
Glow brightly enough to read by
context: The blue-ringed octopus is only about 12-20 cm including its arms, yet one carries enough venom to kill over 20 adults within minutes. Source: Wikipedia, 'Blue-ringed octopus'.  (Legend.)

question: In the tide pools and coral reefs of the Pacific and Indian oceans lives the blue-ringed octopus, a tiny golf-ball-sized octopus that flashes bright electric-blue rings all over its skin when it feels threatened. It hunts by ambush, stalking small crabs and shrimp among the rocks. It is far too small to crush a crab's tough armored shell, so instead it uses one hard body part to punch through the shell and inject a paralysing venom. What is that tool?
answer: A hard, parrot-like beak
choices: A hard, parrot-like beak
A row of grinding teeth
A barbed, whip-like tail
A pair of pincer claws
context: The octopus uses a hard, parrot-like beak to pierce a crab's or shrimp's shell and inject venom, hunting small crabs, hermit crabs, and shrimp as an ambush predator. Source: Wikipedia, 'Blue-ringed octopus'; animals.net.

question: The blue-ringed octopus is a tiny cephalopod that lives in tide pools off Australia, small enough to sit in your palm. When it feels threatened, glowing blue rings flash across its skin as a warning: it carries tetrodotoxin, a poison with no known antidote. Here is the strange part — this exact toxin is not unique to the octopus. One notorious fish carries the same tetrodotoxin, and in Japan chefs must earn a special license before they are allowed to prepare it. Which fish shares this exact poison?
answer: The pufferfish
choices: The pufferfish
The stonefish
The lionfish
The electric eel
context: The venom is tetrodotoxin (TTX), the same poison found in pufferfish (and in some poison dart frogs and newts). The blue-ringed octopus was the first animal known to use tetrodotoxin as a venom. Source: Wikipedia, 'Blue-ringed octopus'; Science (1978).  (Legend.)

question: The blue-ringed octopus is a small golf-ball-sized octopus of Australian tide pools. Its saliva carries tetrodotoxin, one of the deadliest natural poisons on Earth. A tiny painless bite injects the venom straight into the bloodstream. The good news is that the human body can slowly break tetrodotoxin down over about a day — a person bitten today can walk home tomorrow. But the venom instantly paralyzes one thing that cannot wait even a few minutes. What must a rescuer do for the victim in the meantime? (LEGEND)
answer: Breathe for them with a ventilator
choices: Breathe for them with a ventilator
Warm them with heated blankets
Feed them fluids and sugar
Keep the wound above the heart
context: The venom paralyzes the breathing muscles; a victim is kept alive by artificial respiration / a ventilator until the body clears the toxin on its own. Survive the first 24 hours on breathing support and recovery is usually complete. Source: Wikipedia, 'Blue-ringed octopus'; Snopes citing Aquarium of the Pacific.  (Legend.)

question: The blue-ringed octopus is a golf-ball-sized cephalopod from Australian tide pools, and its saliva carries tetrodotoxin — a poison strong enough to stop a person breathing within minutes. Here is the twist scientists uncovered: the octopus itself doesn't manufacture the toxin at all. The chemistry that makes it happens somewhere else entirely, and the octopus just hosts and delivers the finished poison. Where does this tetrodotoxin actually come from?
answer: Symbiotic bacteria in its salivary gland
choices: Symbiotic bacteria in its salivary gland
Prey it swallows and stores unchanged
Bacteria in the seawater it filters
A dose it inherits pre-loaded from its mother
