context: The octopus does not make the tetrodotoxin itself — symbiotic bacteria living in its posterior salivary gland manufacture the toxin for it. Source: Marine Biology (Springer); Wikipedia, 'Blue-ringed octopus'.  (Legend.)

question: The blue-ringed octopus doesn't rely on a single all-purpose poison. Researchers have found it stores its venom as two distinct kinds in separate glands, each doing a different job. Besides subduing prey, what is the second job this two-venom system handles?
answer: Fighting off predators, separate from the prey venom
choices: Fighting off predators, separate from the prey venom
Digesting the crab once it is dead
Sealing the wound the beak makes
Coloring the warning rings blue
context: The blue-ringed octopus carries two different venoms in separate glands — one to subdue prey and a second used in defense against predators. Source: Great Barrier Reef Foundation, 'Blue-Ringed Octopus Facts'.

question: The blue-ringed octopus is famous for its warning display. When threatened, this tiny golf-ball-sized creature can flash roughly 60 electric-blue rings across its skin in about one-third of a second — faster than nearly any other animal can shift color at all. Ordinary octopus color-change relies on slow pigment cells the size of a grain of sand. So how does the blue-ring pull off a flash this fast?
answer: Muscle-controlled skin pouches snap open over inert mirror cells
choices: Muscle-controlled skin pouches snap open over inert mirror cells
The mirror cells suddenly light up with a glow of their own
A rippling wave of blue pigment floods across the skin
The rings rise up on the skin as tiny inflating bumps
context: The blue iridophores are physiologically inert mirrors tucked into muscle-controlled skin pouches that snap open to reveal the flash, while surrounding brown cells darken for contrast — flashing 50-60 rings in about a third of a second. Source: Journal of Experimental Biology 215(21):3752, Mäthger et al.

question: A blue-ringed octopus carries tetrodotoxin, a poison that kills by jamming the sodium channels its nerves and muscles run on. So why doesn't it paralyze itself? Researchers sequenced the gene for its own sodium channel and found the answer written into the protein.
answer: Three swapped amino acids reshape the docking site so the toxin slips off
choices: Three swapped amino acids reshape the docking site so the toxin slips off
A thick mucus layer sheathes its nerves and soaks up the toxin first
It walls the toxin off in glands its own nerves never make contact with
Its blood runs a carrier protein that ferries the toxin safely away
context: Geffeney et al. (2019) sequenced the Greater Blue-ringed Octopus sodium-channel gene HlNaV1 and found three amino-acid substitutions in the tetrodotoxin-binding site that lower the channel's affinity for the toxin. The striking part is that pufferfish, newts and salamanders, and TTX-resistant snakes independently evolved the SAME kinds of substitutions to survive the SAME poison. That is convergent evolution at its clearest: unrelated animals, facing the identical problem of not killing themselves with their own weapon, arrived at the identical molecular fix. Source: Geffeney, Williams, Rosenthal, et al., 'Convergent and parallel evolution in a voltage-gated sodium channel underlies TTX-resistance in the Greater Blue-ringed Octopus: Hapalochlaena lunulata,' Toxicon (2019), https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10148497 ; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31550451/

question: The blue-lined octopus lives off the coast of Australia and flashes electric-blue stripes when alarmed. The male is a fraction of the female's size, and she will readily grab and cannibalize any suitor that approaches her. Yet in 2025, scientists filmed something remarkable: the male manages to mate with her for 40 minutes or more without being eaten. He has one specific trick that keeps him alive throughout mating. What is his trick?
answer: He bites her aorta at the back of her head and stops her breathing
choices: He bites her aorta at the back of her head and stops her breathing
He mates at arm's length, reaching in with a single specialized arm
He darts in, deposits sperm, and flees before she can turn on him
He mimics a female's coloring to slip past her guard unnoticed
context: Chung et al. (2025, Current Biology) documented the blue-lined octopus (Hapalochlaena fasciata) as the first known animal to weaponize venom for mating. The much smaller male bites the far larger female exactly over the aorta at the back of her head and injects tetrodotoxin; her breathing slows and stops after about eight minutes and her body goes pale, immobilizing her for the 40 to 75 minutes of mating so she cannot cannibalize him. It is a targeted, non-lethal dose delivered to precisely the right spot: she recovers fully afterward, resumes eating, and lays eggs days later. Source: Chung et al., Current Biology (March 2025), reported by Smithsonian Magazine https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/these-male-octopuses-use-venom-to-subdue-female-mates-and-avoid-being-eaten-after-sex-180986208/ and CNN https://www.cnn.com/2025/03/13/science/blue-lined-octopus-venom-mating-scli-intl

question: African elephants are the biggest land animals alive today, and the largest dinosaurs — long-necked plant-eaters like Argentinosaurus — were even bigger still. But the single largest animal known to have ever lived on Earth is not extinct at all. It is alive today, swimming somewhere in the open ocean this very moment. What is it?
answer: The blue whale
choices: The blue whale
Argentinosaurus
The African elephant
The great white shark
context: A blue whale can reach about 100 feet (30 m) long and weigh up to 200 tons — bigger and far heavier than any dinosaur that ever walked. Source: NOAA Fisheries — Blue Whale species profile (fisheries.noaa.gov/species/blue-whale); Smithsonian Ocean.  (Legend.)

question: Argentinosaurus was one of the largest dinosaurs ever dug up — a long-necked, four-legged plant-eater from prehistoric South America that stretched over 30 metres long and weighed close to a hundred tons. It was the giant of the ancient world. How does the blue whale, the largest animal alive today, compare in weight to that towering ancient reptile?
answer: It weighs more than twice as much
choices: It weighs more than twice as much
It weighs about the same
It weighs a little less
It weighs roughly a tenth as much
context: A blue whale can weigh up to 200 tons — as much as about 33 elephants — so even the largest known dinosaur weighed less than half a blue whale. Source: worldatlas.com 'Why the Blue Whale Might Not Be the Largest Animal in History'; Slate 'Whales or dinosaurs' (2014).

question: A full-grown African elephant — the biggest land animal alive today — weighs about three tons. The blue whale, the largest animal ever known to have lived, is so enormous that just one single body part of it weighs as much as a whole elephant all on its own. Which single body part of the blue whale weighs about three tons?
answer: Its tongue
choices: Its tongue
Its eye
Its ear bone
Its blowhole
context: A blue whale's tongue can weigh around 3 tons (about 2.7 metric tonnes) — as heavy as a full-grown elephant. Source: AMNH Ology 'A Whale of a Tale'; howstuffworks 'This Is the Biggest Whale'.  (Legend.)

question: The blue whale is the largest animal that has ever lived on Earth, and everything about it is oversized — including its heart. At the Royal Ontario Museum in Toronto, one blue whale heart has been preserved so visitors can see it in person. Counting the aorta, the giant blood vessel above it, the heart stands nearly six and a half feet tall and weighs almost four hundred pounds. Museum staff joked it was so large it could accomplish which surprising feat?
answer: Fit a person squeezed inside a Smart car
choices: Fit a person squeezed inside a Smart car
Fill an entire swimming pool
Pump a bathtub of blood each beat
Be lifted only by a forklift
context: The preserved heart weighs nearly 400 pounds and stands roughly six and a half feet tall with the aorta — staff quipped you could 'squeeze into a Smart car.' Source: Smithsonian Magazine 'The Painstaking Process of Preserving a 400-Pound Blue Whale Heart'; Royal Ontario Museum.  (Legend.)

question: The blue whale is the biggest animal that has ever lived, larger than any dinosaur that ever walked the earth. Storybooks love to picture a child crawling right through the whale's aorta -- the huge main artery that pumps blood straight out of its heart. In real life the aorta is much narrower than that. Roughly how wide across is this biggest blood vessel in any animal?
answer: About a dinner plate
choices: About a dinner plate
About a doorway
About a manhole cover
About a dinner fork
context: The blue whale's aorta is roughly 9 inches across — about the width of a dinner plate. That is huge for a blood vessel, but far too narrow for a child to crawl through. Source: funfactz.com 'Blue Whale Aorta Size'; whalefacts.org 'The Blue Whale's Heart'; ROM specimen reporting.

question: The blue whale is longer than a basketball court and hunts tiny shrimp-like krill deep in the open ocean. It doesn't sip them politely, a few at a time. It charges straight into a dense swarm at full speed, throws its huge pleated mouth wide open, and swallows one enormous gulp before straining the water back out through its baleen. How much does that single gulp bring in?
answer: A volume of water bigger than its own body
choices: A volume of water bigger than its own body
A volume about equal to its own head and throat
A slow steady stream it sips for minutes
About a bathtub's worth at a time
context: This is called lunge feeding — one gulp engulfs about 140% of the whale's own mass in water and prey, roughly a school-bus or swimming-pool's worth. Source: Goldbogen lab / Stanford; Journal of Experimental Biology 214:131 'Mechanics, hydrodynamics and energetics of blue whale lunge feeding'; Mongabay 'Swallowing swimming pools'.  (Legend.)

question: Krill are shrimp-like sea creatures barely as long as your finger, and blue whales eat almost nothing else. A hunting blue whale strains millions of krill from mouthful after mouthful of ocean water. Even for the biggest animal that has ever lived, the daily total is astonishing. About how much krill can the largest blue whales pack away in a single day?
answer: Up to 6 tons
choices: Up to 6 tons
About 20 pounds
Roughly 200 pounds
Around half a ton
context: A big blue whale can eat up to about 6 tons of krill a day — millions of the tiny creatures. Source: NOAA Fisheries — Blue Whale species profile.

question: A blue whale's low moans are among the loudest sounds any living animal makes — reaching around 188 decibels, louder than a jet engine. Because they travel so well through water, distant whales can hear one another across a remarkable distance. How far?
answer: Up to about 1,000 miles
choices: Up to about 1,000 miles
About 10 miles
Roughly 100 yards
A few dozen miles
context: Blue whale calls can be heard by other whales up to 1,000 miles away, letting them communicate across a whole sea. Source: NOAA Fisheries — Blue Whale profile; IFAW 'loudest animals on Earth'.  (Legend.)

question: Blue whales talk to each other with deep booming moans that can travel hundreds of miles across the ocean. Yet a swimmer floating right beside a calling whale might not hear a single sound of the conversation. The calls are loud enough -- louder underwater than a jet engine on a runway -- and they still slip past human ears entirely. Why can't people hear them at all?
answer: They are too low-pitched for people to hear
choices: They are too low-pitched for people to hear
They are too quiet to detect
They only travel downward, away from the surface
They are drowned out by the whale's heartbeat
context: Blue whale calls run around 10–40 Hz, below the range of human hearing — and low sounds scatter and fade less in water, so they travel far. Source: scienceinsights.org 'How Far Can Blue Whales Communicate Underwater'; NOAA Fisheries.

question: A newborn blue whale calf is no fragile little thing. Its mother carries it inside her for nearly a full year and gives birth in warm tropical seas, and the calf slides out already bigger than most land animals a kid can name. Straight from its mother, on its very first day of life, a blue whale calf already outweighs a full-grown what?
answer: Elephant
choices: Elephant
Hippopotamus
Giraffe
Bull rhinoceros
context: A newborn blue whale calf is about 23–25 feet long and weighs up to 3 tons at birth — bigger than a full-grown elephant on day one. Source: SeaWorld 'All About Baleen Whales — Birth & Care of Young'; Marine Mammal Center 'Blue Whale'.

question: The blue whale is the biggest animal that has ever lived, and its calf grows at a nearly unbelievable pace. A human baby might gain a few ounces a day. A nursing blue whale calf, drinking hundreds of gallons of its mother's rich, creamy milk each day, adds so much weight so fast that its daily gain matches what a whole person might put on in an entire year. About how much does the calf add each day?
answer: About 200 pounds
choices: About 200 pounds
About 5 pounds
About 40 pounds
About 1,000 pounds
context: A blue whale calf gains about 200 pounds (90 kg) every day — roughly 8 to 10 pounds an hour — on milk that is 35–50% fat. Source: SeaWorld 'Birth & Care of Young'; A-Z Animals 'Baby Blue Whale Facts'.  (Legend.)

question: The blue whale is the largest animal that has ever lived, so its giant body plan must be ancient — or so it seems. When Slater, Goldbogen and Pyenson traced whale fossils across more than 30 million years, what did the record actually reveal about how this size arose?
answer: It leapt from about 10 m to 30 m only in the last few million years, on several branches at once
choices: It leapt from about 10 m to 30 m only in the last few million years, on several branches at once
It crept upward at a slow, steady pace across the whole thirty-million-year span
It was already near today’s length in the earliest baleen whales and simply held there
It shrank down from far larger ancestors and has been getting smaller ever since
context: For most of whale history the biggest baleen whales were only about 10 m long. The jump to today's ~30 m happened rapidly and independently on several branches of the family tree around 4.5 million years ago, when the first ice ages began concentrating krill into dense patches through wind-driven coastal upwelling — suddenly it paid to be a colossal filter feeder. The blue whale is the biggest animal ever, yet its body plan is evolutionarily recent and was reinvented more than once. Source: Slater, Goldbogen & Pyenson, 'Independent evolution of baleen whale gigantism linked to Plio-Pleistocene ocean dynamics,' Proceedings of the Royal Society B 284:20170546 (2017); Smithsonian Institution news release (2017).

question: A blue whale gulps a swimming-pool of water and must strain out the krill through hundreds of fringed baleen plates. The obvious picture is water pushing straight through the fringe like a kitchen sieve — but flow-tank studies showed that picture is wrong. How does the water actually move through the rack?
answer: It flows lengthwise along the inside of the plates, sweeping krill to the back of the mouth
choices: It flows lengthwise along the inside of the plates, sweeping krill to the back of the mouth
It is forced head-on through the fringe, which clogs and must be cleared between gulps
It is spat back out the same way it came in, leaving the krill stuck to the outer fringe
It is pumped through tiny pores in every plate the way a sponge draws water inward
context: This is cross-flow filtration. Instead of dead-end straining, where water pushes straight through and quickly clogs the fringe, the water slides sideways along the inner face of the baleen rack, carrying trapped krill backward to gather at the rear of the mouth for swallowing while keeping the ~0.5–2 mm bristles clear. Flow-tank experiments (first on bowhead baleen) overturned the intuitive sieve model. Source: Werth et al., 'Baleen Hydrodynamics and Morphology of Cross-Flow Filtration in Balaenid Whale Suspension Feeding,' PLOS ONE (2016) (PMC4769178); Frontiers in Marine Science, 'Dynamic filtration in baleen whales' (2024).

question: The bobbit worm is a giant sea worm that hunts in a very strange way. It burrows almost its whole long body straight down into the sandy seabed, leaving only its head poking up out of the sand. Five thin antennae stick straight up like little fingers over the buried worm. When a fish glides past, those antennae are the trigger. What are they doing for the hidden bobbit worm?
answer: Acting as tripwires that a passing fish brushes
choices: Acting as tripwires that a passing fish brushes
Filtering plankton from the passing current
Soaking up sunlight to warm its buried body
Waving to attract a mate across the sand
context: The bobbit worm buries nearly its entire body and leaves only its head exposed, waiting motionless. When a fish brushes one of the five antennae, the worm strikes. Source: BBC Science Focus, 'What is a bobbit worm?' — https://www.sciencefocus.com/nature/what-is-a-bobbit-worm  (Legend.)

question: The bobbit worm is a big undersea hunter that hides its whole body inside the sandy seabed, with only its scissor-like jaws poking above the surface. The longest bobbit worm ever measured, dug up and stretched out flat by researchers, was much longer than anyone had guessed. Fully stretched, that record-breaking worm was closest in length to which of these?
answer: A grown man lying down, nearly 10 feet
choices: A grown man lying down, nearly 10 feet
A dinner fork, about 8 inches
A garden snake, about 2 feet
A school bus, about 40 feet
context: The longest bobbit worm ever recorded measured 299 cm — nearly 10 feet — though its body averages only about 25 mm (one inch) wide, making it one of the longest worms in the ocean. Source: Wikipedia, 'Eunice aphroditois' — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eunice_aphroditois  (Legend.)

question: The bobbit worm waits buried in the seabed with only its jaws showing above the sand. When a passing fish brushes against the five thin antennae poking up around its head, the worm strikes in less than a hundredth of a second and yanks the fish down under the sand. What can its scissor-like jaws sometimes do to a fish in that single lightning strike?
answer: Slice it clean in two
choices: Slice it clean in two
Crush its skull in one bite
Tear off a chunk and let the rest flee
Pin it against the sand and swallow it whole
context: The strike is so fast the fish gets only milliseconds to flee. The worm's razor-sharp jaws can sometimes slice the prey clean in two before dragging it down into the sand. Those jaws are paired mandibles and larger serrated, hooked maxillae that snap shut like scissors. Source: BBC Science Focus, 'What is a bobbit worm?' — https://www.sciencefocus.com/nature/what-is-a-bobbit-worm  (Legend.)

question: The bobbit worm is a giant marine worm that hides buried in the sea floor with only its jaws poking out, waiting to ambush passing fish. Its jaws can grab prey far bigger than the worm itself, dragging the meal down into its burrow. But holding on to something big and thrashing is a problem. After its jaws grab the prey, what does the bobbit worm do to keep such a large meal from struggling?
answer: Injects a toxin that stuns or kills it
choices: Injects a toxin that stuns or kills it
Squeezes it until it stops moving
Drowns it by holding it under the sand
Waits days for it to tire itself out
context: After grabbing prey, the bobbit worm injects a toxin that stuns or kills it, letting the worm subdue and digest animals far larger than itself, which it drags underground to eat. Source: ScienceInsights, 'What Is a Bobbit Worm? The Ferocious Ambush Predator' — https://scienceinsights.org/what-is-a-bobbit-worm-the-ferocious-ambush-predator/

question: At the Blue Reef Aquarium in Newquay, England, staff noticed something was going wrong overnight in one of their reef tanks. The coral was being shredded, and fish kept vanishing one by one. For weeks they set baited traps, and every morning the traps came up empty. Finally the staff decided to take the whole reef display apart, rock by rock, to find the culprit. What had been living hidden in the tank?
answer: A 1.2-metre bobbit worm named 'Barry'
choices: A 1.2-metre bobbit worm named 'Barry'
An escaped moray eel from a nearby tank
A cluster of hungry crown-of-thorns starfish
A venomous stonefish buried in the gravel
context: Staff noticed coral being shredded overnight and fish vanishing, and baited traps came up empty for weeks. The culprit was a 1.2-metre bobbit worm the staff named 'Barry'. To catch him they dismantled the reef display rock by rock; when cornered, the worm bit clean through a 20-pound fishing line before they pulled him out. Source: BBC Science Focus + The Misfits Pair archive — https://themisfitspair.com/2009/04/01/barry-the-giant-sea-worm-discovered-by-aquarium-staff-after-mysterious-attacks-on-coral-reef/  (Legend.)

question: At the Blue Reef Aquarium in Newquay, England, staff kept finding fish gone missing and coral broken with no explanation. When they finally tore the tank apart to find the culprit, they discovered a four-foot bobbit worm that they had never bought, never ordered, and never seen delivered. They named him Barry. How did this monster worm actually first get into the tank where he had been quietly growing for years?
answer: He hitchhiked in as a tiny juvenile inside 'live rock'
choices: He hitchhiked in as a tiny juvenile inside 'live rock'
He crawled up a drainpipe from the sea outside
He was slipped in as a prank by a departing worker
He hatched from eggs stuck to a new fish's fins
context: Barry had hitchhiked in as a tiny juvenile hidden inside a piece of 'live rock' the aquarium had bought, then grew undetected in the tank, possibly for years — one reason a bobbit worm can go unseen for so long is that it recoils and vanishes down its burrow whenever a bright light hits it. Source: BBC Science Focus + The Misfits Pair archive — https://themisfitspair.com/2009/04/01/barry-the-giant-sea-worm-discovered-by-aquarium-staff-after-mysterious-attacks-on-coral-reef/  (Legend.)

question: Bobbit worms are soft and boneless, without a skeleton to leave behind, so their bodies almost never fossilize once they die. That seemed to mean scientists could never study prehistoric ones — until researchers in 20-million-year-old rock in Taiwan discovered 319 fossils of these ancient ambush predators. Since no worm's body was preserved, the fossils had to record something else the worms left behind. What got fossilized instead?
answer: The L-shaped burrow the worm hunted from
choices: The L-shaped burrow the worm hunted from
A cast of the worm’s serrated jaws
The mucus coating its whole body
A tangle of shed skins and molts
context: This is one of the rare cases where a predator's BEHAVIOR fossilized rather than its body. Yu-Yen Pan and colleagues named the trace fossil Pennichnus formosae from ~20-million-year-old Miocene rock (Taliao Formation) in northeast Taiwan — L-shaped burrows up to 2 m long and only 2–3 cm wide, the buried lair of an ancient bobbit-type worm. Near the top of each burrow, X-ray scans show an abrupt spike in iron: chemical residue of the worm's mucus, which fed sulfate-reducing bacteria that built iron-sulfide minerals as the worm rebuilt and reinforced its lair after each violent strike. Repeated dragging of prey down the funnel left distinctive 'feather-like' collapse structures at the mouth. (A jaw cast would seem a fair guess — bobbit-worm jaws DO survive elsewhere as fossils called scolecodonts — but here it was the burrow, not the animal, that was preserved.) Source: Pan et al., Scientific Reports 11:1174 (2021), via PMC7820589 and Nature s41598-020-79311-0.

question: A bobbit worm is a long marine worm that lies buried head-up in the sand, waiting to snatch passing fish. It strikes faster than almost any other invertebrate can move. But its jaws sit at the front of a soft, boneless body — no arm, no claw, nothing to swing them forward with. So how does the worm launch its jaws at the prey?
answer: It turns its throat inside-out, hurling the jaws forward
choices: It turns its throat inside-out, hurling the jaws forward
It coils and snaps a muscular tail like a whip
It fires the jaws on a jet of pressurized water
It rams its whole burrow upward against the fish
context: The strike is powered by pharynx eversion: the worm turns its muscular throat inside-out, flinging the jaw apparatus — interlocking mandibles plus serrated maxillae — forward like a spring-loaded gin trap, then retracts the whole thing to drag prey underground. Having no hard skeleton, the worm holds its long shape with a hydrostatic (fluid-pressure) skeleton — the same pressurized-fluid trick that powers the launch. The record wild specimen measured 299 cm (about 9.8 ft) yet was only ~25.5 mm wide, making it the longest known polychaete; despite the fearsome hunting it also scavenges algae and dead matter and lives only about 3–5 years. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eunice_aphroditois, with strike-eversion mechanics corroborated by ScienceInsights and BiologyInsights secondary summaries.

question: The female bolas spider hunts in a way no other spider does. She builds no web to trap her prey. Instead, in the dark, she dangles from a branch on a single silk thread. At the tip of that thread hangs one round, sticky glue ball. When a moth flies past, she swings the ball at it like a weapon. What is she copying with that swing?
answer: A cowboy's bolas, a weighted throwing rope
choices: A cowboy's bolas, a weighted throwing rope
A frog's tongue, flicked and retracted
A spider's usual flat orb web
A bat's wide-mouthed mid-air scoop
context: The spider swings her single glue-tipped line like a bolas — a South American throwing weapon of weights on cords — to snag moths right out of the air, which is how the spider got its name. Source: https://spiderbytes.org/2015/03/17/bolas-spiders-masters-of-deception/  (Legend.)

question: The female bolas spider dangles a sticky glue ball on a silk thread and swings it to catch flying moths. But that only works if a moth flies within reach in the first place. Rather than wait for one to blunder past by chance, the spider actively draws male moths in to her from far across the dark forest. Every time she swings, more moths keep arriving. How does the spider pull them in?
answer: It releases a chemical that mimics a female moth's perfume
choices: It releases a chemical that mimics a female moth's perfume
It glows a soft blue-green light moths drift toward
It plays a high buzz matching a female moth's wingbeat
It heats its body so moths mistake it for a warm flower
context: The spider gives off a chemical that mimics the sex pheromone of a FEMALE moth, so male moths trace the fake scent trail straight to the swinging glue ball. Source: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF00380049  (Legend.)

question: The bolas spider hunts only at night, whirling a sticky ball on a silk line to snag flying moths in mid-air. By day it cannot hunt, so it has to hide instead. It curls up motionless on a small silk mat spun across the top of a leaf, holding a shape and color that no hungry bird would ever choose to peck. What does the daytime bolas spider pretend to be?
answer: A fresh bird dropping
choices: A fresh bird dropping
A drop of morning dew
A curled dead leaf
A clump of pale fungus
context: Motionless on its silk mat, the bulbous, waxy-white spider looks exactly like a fresh bird dropping, so predators pass it by. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mastophora_hutchinsoni

question: Mastophora hutchinsoni is a species of bolas spider found in North America. It hunts by swinging a sticky glue ball on a silk line and luring moths in with a fake female-moth scent. Watch one all night and something odd shows up: the moths stuck to her glue ball before 11 p.m. and the moths caught after 11 p.m. belong to two entirely different species. She changes what she catches at that exact hour. What does she do at 11 p.m. to cause the switch?
answer: It changes the exact scent it fakes, matching a second moth species
choices: It changes the exact scent it fakes, matching a second moth species
It swings the ball faster to snag the bigger moths flying late
It creeps to a fresh leaf where the later moths gather
It brightens the glue ball so the later moths can see it
context: Mastophora hutchinsoni fakes one moth species' pheromone early in the evening, then switches to a completely different species' scent after 11 p.m., matching whichever moths are flying at that hour — so the species stuck to its glue ball changes as the night goes on. Source: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00049-002-8332-2  (Legend.)

question: The bombardier beetle is a small ground beetle only about half an inch long, common in fields and forests. Pick one up, and it fights back in a way that startles the attacker into instantly dropping it. From the tip of its abdomen, the beetle launches a defense with a loud popping bang that sounds almost like a tiny gun going off. What is that defense?
answer: A jet of boiling-hot chemical spray
choices: A jet of boiling-hot chemical spray
A cloud of sticky silk threads
A blinding flash of green light
A blast of foul-smelling gas only
context: When seized, the bombardier beetle fires a caustic spray from the rear of its abdomen with an audible pop. The spray is genuinely scalding, not just smelly. Source: Natural History Museum, London -- 'Bombardier beetles and their caustic chemical cannon' (nhm.ac.uk).

question: The bombardier beetle is a small ground beetle with a startling defense. When something grabs it, it mixes two chemicals in a special chamber inside its abdomen and shoots the boiling mixture out its rear end in a sharp popping spray. The jet isn't just an unpleasant smell -- it comes out hot enough to scald whatever it touches. About how hot is the spray as it leaves the beetle?
answer: Close to 100 C, the boiling point of water
choices: Close to 100 C, the boiling point of water
Around body temperature, about 37 C
A little above freezing, near 5 C
Hot enough to melt metal, over 1,000 C
context: The jet shoots out at close to 100 C (212 F) -- the boiling point of water -- so it scalds the mouth or feet of an attacker. Source: Wikipedia 'Bombardier beetle' citing Aneshansley & Eisner, 'Biochemistry at 100 C'; Natural History Museum, London.

question: The bombardier beetle is a small ground beetle that fires boiling-hot chemical spray from the tip of its abdomen at attackers. It carries the parts of that scalding weapon inside its own body — yet it never cooks itself. To pull that off, the beetle keeps two different chemicals in a special setup, and only combines them at the very moment it needs to fire. What setup keeps the beetle safe from its own weapon?
answer: The two chemicals are stored in separate sacs, apart
choices: The two chemicals are stored in separate sacs, apart
The two chemicals are frozen solid until needed
A thick layer of fat soaks up all the heat
The chemicals are diluted with water until harmless
context: The beetle stores hydrogen peroxide and hydroquinone in separate little reservoirs, safely apart, and only lets them meet at the instant of firing. Source: Natural History Museum, London; Wikipedia 'Bombardier beetle'.

question: When cornered, a bombardier beetle combines its two chemicals within a reinforced chamber at the back of its abdomen. Powerful enzymes there make the reaction hot enough to reach boiling temperature and explode outward. Which enzymes trigger that explosion?
answer: Catalase and peroxidase
choices: Catalase and peroxidase
Pepsin and trypsin
Amylase and lipase
Luciferase and rennin
context: The reaction chamber is lined with catalase and peroxidase; when the stored chemicals meet these enzymes the reaction is fast and hot enough to boil and blast outward. Source: Wikipedia 'Bombardier beetle'; Chemistry Steps, 'The Chemistry Behind Bombardier Beetle's Spray'.

question: When a bombardier beetle sprays boiling chemicals at an attacker, the jet does not come out as one long, steady stream. High-speed photography of the small ground beetle revealed something unexpected: the scalding spray fires in a rapid machine-gun burst of many separate blasts, about 70 of them per firing, far too fast for the human eye to separate. Roughly how fast is that pulsing?
answer: About 500 pulses per second
choices: About 500 pulses per second
About 5 pulses per second
About 20 pulses per minute
One long pulse lasting five seconds
context: The spray fires as a biological pulse jet -- roughly 70 pulses at about 500 per second. The rapid pulsing also protects the beetle: each tiny explosion is released before the next, so the reinforced chamber never overloads. Source: Wikipedia 'Bombardier beetle' citing Dean, Aneshansley, Edgerton & Eisner, 'Defensive spray of the bombardier beetle: a biological pulse jet,' Science (1990).

question: The bombardier beetle is a small ground beetle that carries boiling chemical spray inside its body. A toad flicks out its long sticky tongue and swallows one whole. Deep in the toad's dark stomach the trapped beetle fires its scalding jet — and in one lab experiment, 43% of the toads then did something surprising more than an hour later that saved the beetle's life. What did those toads do?
answer: Vomited the beetle back up alive
choices: Vomited the beetle back up alive
Grew immune and ate more beetles
Fell asleep for the rest of the day
Changed color from the beetle's dye
context: Toads that swallowed bombardier beetles heard a faint 'bu' or 'vu' pop from inside their own stomach, and 43% vomited the beetle back up -- sometimes over 90 minutes later. Beetles spent 12 to 107 minutes inside, scuttled off covered in slime, and nearly all survived; one lived at least 562 more days. Source: Sugiura & Sato, 'Successful escape of bombardier beetles from predator digestive systems,' Biology Letters (2018).  (Legend.)

question: A male satin bowerbird spends weeks weaving two neat parallel walls of twigs on the forest floor. He carefully decorates the ground between them and returns to the same spot to work on it year after year. What is this elaborate twig structure actually for?
answer: A stage for courting females
choices: A stage for courting females
A nest for the pair's eggs
A shelter from rain and heat
A store for hoarded food
context: The bower is NOT a nest. The male builds it purely as a stage to court females; the female builds a separate, plain saucer-like nest of sticks in a tree fork up to 30-35 meters high and raises the young entirely alone. Source: Australian Museum, Satin Bowerbird.

question: The satin bowerbird lives in the forests of eastern Australia. The adult male has glossy blue-black plumage and bright violet eyes. Instead of building a fancy nest to attract mates, he builds a bower — a small stage on the forest floor decorated with objects he collects. He will fly great distances and even raid other males' bowers to steal from them. He hoards objects of only one particular color, the color that matches him. Which color does he collect?
answer: Blue
choices: Blue
Red
Yellow
White
context: The satin bowerbird is obsessed with blue, decorating his bower with blue clothes pegs, drinking straws, bottle tops and blue parrot feathers, stealing objects from as far as 12 kilometers away because blue matches his own glossy blue-black plumage and violet-blue iris. Source: Australian Museum, Satin Bowerbird; Coffs Botanic Garden 'Bower Power'.  (Legend.)

question: A female satin bowerbird — an Australian forest bird whose males build decorated stages called bowers — spends days touring several rival males' bowers to inspect them carefully. She watches each male strut on his stage and quiver his blue-black wings, and finally picks the one that impresses her most. After she has mated with her chosen male, one of them heads off alone to build the nest, lay the eggs, and raise the chicks. Who does all of that work?
answer: The female, entirely on her own
choices: The female, entirely on her own
The mated pair, together at the bower
The winning male, at his bower
A group of nearby males
context: The male builds the bower purely as a courtship stage; the female builds a separate, plain saucer-like nest of sticks in a tree fork up to 30-35 meters high and raises the young entirely alone. Female bowerbirds are the judges who inspect several rival bowers before choosing. Source: Australian Museum, Satin Bowerbird; Coffs Botanic Garden 'Bower Power'.

question: A male satin bowerbird chews berries into a purple pulp mixed with spit, then daubs it along the inner walls of his bower. To spread the paint he grips a tool in his beak and works it back and forth. What does he hold as a paintbrush?
answer: A wad of bark
choices: A wad of bark
A soft green leaf
A tuft of moss
A blue feather
context: The male satin bowerbird builds two parallel walls of sticks (an 'avenue' bower), then paints the inner walls with a mixture of chewed berry pulp, vegetable matter and saliva, holding a wad of bark in his beak as a paintbrush. Source: Australian Museum, Satin Bowerbird; Coffs Botanic Garden 'Bower Power'.  (Legend.)

question: The satin bowerbird of eastern Australia has males with glossy blue-black plumage and violet eyes. But a young male looks nothing like his father at first. For years, he keeps the drab olive-green coloring of the females. During that long apprenticeship he practices building scrappy trial bowers, before he finally molts into the deep glossy blue-black plumage of an adult courter. About how long does that transformation take?
answer: Seven years
choices: Seven years
A single season
Two years
Twenty years
context: A male satin bowerbird takes a full seven years to develop his adult glossy blue-black plumage; until then young males look olive-green like females and practice building and displaying at temporary bowers. Source: Australian Museum, Satin Bowerbird; Coffs Botanic Garden 'Bower Power'.

question: In the dry woodlands of northern Australia, a male great bowerbird builds a courtship display on the forest floor. He weaves a tall arched avenue of twigs, then carefully lays out stones, snail shells, and pale bones on the open court beyond it — tiniest bits where the female will stand at the mouth of the avenue, largest at the far end. When she peers down the avenue, this careful size gradient warps what she sees. What illusion does the gradient create?
answer: He appears larger against the shrunken court
choices: He appears larger against the shrunken court
The court glitters as if wet with dew
His feathers seem a brighter blue
The avenue looks longer than it is
context: The great bowerbird arranges stones and objects in a size gradient (smallest near the avenue where the female stands, largest at the far edge), creating a forced-perspective illusion that makes the courtyard look smaller and uniform, so the displaying male appears relatively larger to the watching female. Source: National Geographic, 'Male bowerbirds create forced perspective illusions'; Endler et al., Current Biology (2010).  (Legend.)

question: The golden bowerbird lives in the tropical rainforest of northeastern Australia. Instead of the walled corridors other bowerbirds build, the male constructs two twin towers of sticks joined at the base — the tallest bowers any bird constructs, sometimes over a metre high. What is unusual is that each tower is inherited: a young male takes over an existing bower and rebuilds it on the exact same spot, generation after generation. Approximately how old is the oldest known bower?
answer: Over forty years old
choices: Over forty years old
About one year old
Over a hundred years old
Exactly ten years old
context: Golden bowerbirds build the tallest bower structures known, twin maypole towers that are inherited and rebuilt across generations, with the oldest recorded bowers over 40 years old and more than 2 meters tall. Source: Nature.org 'Kleptomaniac Love Architects'.

question: A sea creature drifts through the warm shallow waters off northern Australia. Its transparent, jelly-like bell is not the usual rounded dome shape you see on most jellyfish. Instead it has four flat sides, so the bell looks like a clear cube in the water. From each of the four corners hangs a bundle of long trailing tentacles. What is this square-shaped creature called?
answer: The box jellyfish
choices: The box jellyfish
The moon jellyfish
The sea gooseberry
The Portuguese man o' war
context: The box jellyfish is named for its body: a see-through, cube-shaped bell with four flat sides, unlike the round dome of an ordinary jellyfish. A cluster of tentacles trails from each of the four corners. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box_jellyfish

question: Most jellyfish are helpless drifters, floating blobs of jelly pushed wherever the ocean current takes them. The box jellyfish, found in the warm waters off northern Australia, is not like that at all. It squeezes its cube-shaped bell like a fist to jet through the water, and it can steer where it wants to go. How fast can it go, and how sharply can it turn?
answer: About 1.5 metres per second, whipping a 180-degree turn in a few beats of its bell
choices: About 1.5 metres per second, whipping a 180-degree turn in a few beats of its bell
About 1.5 metres per second, but it can only ever swim in a straight line
So slowly it can't beat the current, so it still just drifts like other jellyfish
Fast in bursts, but only backwards, tentacles first
context: A box jellyfish does not just drift like most jellyfish; it actively swims, reaching about 1.5 metres per second and rapidly turning up to 180 degrees in just a few contractions of its bell. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box_jellyfish  (Legend.)

question: The Australian box jellyfish, Chironex fleckeri, is a see-through cube of jelly with a deadly sting. Around the four flat sides of its bell sit four little grape-shaped sensory pods called rhopalia, and every one of these pods carries its own set of eyes. Add up every eye across every pod -- how many eyes does this brainless jellyfish have in total?
answer: 24 eyes
choices: 24 eyes
8 eyes
12 eyes
48 eyes
context: Chironex fleckeri has 24 eyes clustered on four sensory pods called rhopalia, six eyes each. Astonishingly, it has NO brain to see with, just a ring of nerves around its bell. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box_jellyfish; https://aussieanimals.com/profiles/box-jellyfish-chironex-fleckeri/  (Legend.)

question: The Australian box jellyfish has no brain at all -- just a simple ring of nerves running around the rim of its cube-shaped bell. Even so, twenty-four eyes stare out from its four little sensory pods, and not every one of them works the same way. Some are just bare pigmented patches that only sense light. But a few are surprisingly advanced. What kind of eyes are those special ones?
answer: True camera eyes with real lenses, corneas, and retinas that form an image
choices: True camera eyes with real lenses, corneas, and retinas that form an image
Bare pits that can only tell light from dark
Compound eyes, thousands of tiny units like a fly's
Mirror eyes that reflect light instead of focusing it
context: Some of the box jellyfish's 24 eyes have real lenses, corneas, and retinas, true camera-type eyes that can form an image, which is astonishing for an animal with no brain to process the picture. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box_jellyfish  (Legend.)

question: Each tentacle of the Australian box jellyfish is lined with hundreds of thousands of microscopic coiled harpoons called nematocysts, ready to shoot poisoned barbs into prey. Yet a jellyfish bumping into a piece of driftwood or a floating leaf doesn't fire even one of them. So what actually triggers a single stinging cell to explode outward and shoot its barb?
answer: Sensing the chemicals on skin, not touch alone
choices: Sensing the chemicals on skin, not touch alone
Any touch at all, driftwood or skin
A change in water temperature nearby
The shadow of prey passing overhead
context: A box jellyfish tentacle is lined with hundreds of thousands of stinging capsules called nematocysts, microscopic coiled harpoons that fire not from touch alone but when they sense the chemicals on skin, so they don't waste on driftwood. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box_jellyfish; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4379534/

question: Chironex fleckeri, the Australian box jellyfish, is among the most venomous animals alive anywhere on earth. On beaches across northern Australia, swimmers watch for its almost invisible tentacles far more carefully than they watch the water for sharks. What can a serious sting from this jellyfish do to a person if help does not come in time?
answer: Stop the heart, killing untreated victims within two to five minutes
choices: Stop the heart, killing untreated victims within two to five minutes
Cause hours of full-body paralysis while the victim stays conscious
Blind a victim, though it is almost never fatal
Only a painful welt, dangerous just to small children
context: Chironex fleckeri is among the most venomous animals alive; a serious sting can cause the heart to stop, and untreated victims have died within two to five minutes. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chironex_fleckeri; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7285912/

question: An Australian box jellyfish's clear cube-shaped bell tumbles and tilts every which way as it swims through the water, so its eyes are constantly being rolled around. Inside each of the four sensory pods hanging off the sides of the bell, a heavy crystal weight called a statolith dangles at the end of a flexible stalk. What job does that little dangling weight do for the jellyfish's vision?
answer: Pulled straight down by gravity, it keeps the eyes aimed up-and-down however the bell rolls
choices: Pulled straight down by gravity, it keeps the eyes aimed up-and-down however the bell rolls
It stores light like a battery so the eyes can still work in the dark
It adds ballast so the jellyfish can sink to the bottom to hunt
It grinds against the nerve ring to signal when prey drifts near
context: In each rhopalium a heavy crystal weight called a statolith acts like a tiny plumb bob, hanging on a flexible stalk so the eyes stay pointed up-and-down no matter how the jellyfish's bell tumbles or tilts. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box_jellyfish

question: Lift the hard bony flap on the side of a fish's head -- that flap is called the operculum -- and you find neat stacks of soft feathery red tissue tucked underneath. The tissue is packed with tiny blood vessels, and it only keeps the fish alive while it stays wet. Underwater, this is the organ the fish uses to do what?
answer: Breathe
choices: Breathe
Taste its food
Steer while swimming
Sense water pressure
context: Those red feathery stacks are the gills - a fish's underwater lungs. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fish_gill

question: A fish breathes underwater with gills — feathery rakes tucked away under a bony flap on each side of its head. Water flows in the mouth, over the gills, and out those flaps. Lift the flap of a fresh fish and peek inside, and the gills look nothing like ordinary flesh. They are a vivid red — not pink, not grey, but a deep blood-red, almost raw-looking. What makes them that startling color?
answer: Blood packed right at the surface
choices: Blood packed right at the surface
A red waxy coating that repels water
Red pigment cells for camouflage
Iron-rich slime the fish secretes
context: Each filament is crammed with tiny capillaries where blood picks up oxygen - the red you see IS the blood lying just under a wafer-thin surface. Source: https://australian.museum/learn/animals/fishes/fish-dissections/

question: A goldfish rests quietly in the middle of a fishbowl. Its fins have gone still and it isn't swimming anywhere, but the bony covers over its gills on each side of its head keep steadily fluttering open and shut, open and shut, without a pause. Even a resting goldfish never lets that flutter stop. What is that patient, endless flutter doing for the goldfish?
answer: Pumping a fresh flow of water across its gills
choices: Pumping a fresh flow of water across its gills
Cooling its blood in warm water
Shaking loose bits of trapped food
Signaling to other fish nearby
context: By opening its mouth and flaring the gill cover (buccal pumping), a resting fish drives water over its gills without swimming a stroke - which is why the covers visibly flutter. Source: https://poseidonsweb.com/how-fish-breathe-ram-ventilation-buccal-pumping/

question: A fish's water enters the mouth and exits under the gill cover, always flowing one way and never washing back. A land animal, by contrast, pulls each breath in and pushes it back out the same opening. What single advantage does the fish's one-way flow give its gills?
answer: They never bathe in water already drained of oxygen
choices: They never bathe in water already drained of oxygen
They pull oxygen across twice as fast per breath
They never touch water colder than the fish's blood
They filter out the salt before oxygen crosses
context: Lungs are a dead end - fresh and used air share one pipe, so some stale air always lingers. A fish's flow runs straight through, so its gills always face water it has not yet stripped of oxygen. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fish_gill

question: Every fish faces a breathing problem that no land animal ever has to think about. The water a fish pulls across its gills carries far less dissolved oxygen than an equal amount of air does. That is why fish gills have to be enormous, wafer-thin, and packed with blood vessels -- a fish has to work harder for every breath than any lizard or bird. Compared to the same volume of air, roughly how much less oxygen does water actually hold?
answer: Around thirty times less
choices: Around thirty times less
Around a hundred times less
Around five times less
About half as much
context: Air packs roughly 30 times more oxygen per unit volume than water - which is why a fish must pass an enormous amount of water over its gills just to get by. Source: http://www.howfishbehave.ca/pdf/oxygen.pdf

question: A tuna is a fast, powerful ocean fish that must swim non-stop across the open sea to keep water flowing over its gills. Compare a tuna's gills against those of a similar-sized bottom-dwelling fish that spends its whole life resting on the sea floor. One fish's gills are unmistakably richer, with denser comb-like red filaments crowding each gill arch. Which fish has the richer gills, and why?
answer: The tuna's - a relentless swimmer needs far more surface to feed its muscles
choices: The tuna's - a relentless swimmer needs far more surface to feed its muscles
The bottom-dweller's - lying still, it must hoard every scrap of oxygen
Neither - gill development is fixed at birth and identical in both
The tuna's - fast water flow scours its filaments larger over time
context: Bony fish carry four pairs of gill arches lined with comb-like filaments, and the more active the swimmer, the more developed those combs become - a hard-driving tuna packs far denser filaments than a fish that rests on the bottom. Source: https://australian.museum/learn/animals/fishes/fish-dissections/

question: Freshwater is famously oxygen-poor. A single liter of it holds only about eight cubic centimeters of oxygen. The same liter of air holds about two hundred and ten. To grab enough oxygen from such thin pickings, what must a fish's gills have above all?
answer: Enormous surface area
choices: Enormous surface area
A powerful pumping muscle
A way to warm the water first
Thick protective walls
context: With water holding only about a twenty-sixth of air's oxygen, gills solve it with sheer area - vast thin surfaces so more oxygen can cross into the blood at once. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fish_gill

question: Inside a single lamella, a fish's blood is driven the OPPOSITE way to the water flowing over the outside - the two run against each other along the whole plate. This one design choice is why a fish can strip far more oxygen from water than it otherwise could. How does running them against each other manage that?
answer: The blood always meets water still richer in oxygen than itself
choices: The blood always meets water still richer in oxygen than itself
The two flows cancel out and let oxygen settle at a steady midpoint
The oxygen is squeezed across faster by the blood's higher pressure
The blood loads fastest right where it enters and then coasts
context: This is countercurrent exchange: because blood and water run opposite ways, the blood never catches up to water it has already emptied - it always faces water a little richer than itself, so oxygen keeps crossing along the whole lamella instead of stopping halfway. Source: https://fishbio.com/an-efficient-exchange/

question: If a fish's blood and the passing water flowed side by side in the same direction, they would soon settle to identical oxygen levels. The fish could then extract only about half of it. Running them in opposite directions instead, how much of the water's oxygen can a fish actually strip away?
answer: Around 80 to 90 percent
choices: Around 80 to 90 percent
Around 55 percent
Around 30 percent
Around 100 percent
context: Same-direction flow equalizes at roughly 50 percent; countercurrent flow, running blood against water, lets a fish harvest about 80 to 90 percent of the oxygen present - the payoff of the whole design. Source: https://fishbio.com/an-efficient-exchange/

question: A tuna is such a relentless swimmer that it can no longer work its gill covers fast enough to pump water at speed. Its solution is drastic: it swims with its mouth gaping to force water through - and this locks it into a rule it can never break. What is that rule?
answer: It must keep swimming forever or it suffocates
choices: It must keep swimming forever or it suffocates
It can only breathe in warm surface water
It must return to shallow water each night
It can never swim faster than its own gill-pumping
context: This is ram ventilation - the tuna rams water through its gills by moving forward, so if it ever stops swimming, the flow stops and it drowns. Great white, mako, salmon, and whale sharks live under the same sentence. Source: https://poseidonsweb.com/how-fish-breathe-ram-ventilation-buccal-pumping/  (Legend.)

question: Most sharks must swim their whole lives to keep water moving over their gills. But a nurse shark lies motionless on the sea floor for hours at a stretch. With its mouth sometimes buried in sand, how does it keep breathing without moving?
answer: It pumps water in through small holes behind its eyes
choices: It pumps water in through small holes behind its eyes
It absorbs oxygen straight through its skin
It surfaces every few minutes to gulp air
It slows its heart until it barely needs oxygen
context: The nurse shark uses cheek muscles to pump water over its gills (buccal pumping), and when its mouth is buried it draws water through spiracles - small openings behind the eyes - a trick that lets it rest where ram-ventilating sharks never could. Source: https://theliquidearth.org/2025/09/meet-the-buccal-pumpers-sharks-that-mastered-the-art-of-staying-still/  (Legend.)

question: A frog begins life as a tadpole breathing underwater through feathery gills. As it grows, the tadpole loses those gills, grows lungs, and climbs out of the water to spend its adult life on land. The axolotl of Mexico and the mudpuppy of North America are amphibians too, but they break that whole script entirely. They spend their entire lives underwater and never climb out. How do they pull that off?
answer: Keep feathery external gills their whole lives
choices: Keep feathery external gills their whole lives
Grow a second set of lungs as adults
Breathe only through their moist skin
Return to the egg stage each winter
context: The axolotl and mudpuppy never trade gills for lungs - they keep the feathery external gills sprouting from the head for life, staying underwater forever. This holding-onto-youth is called neoteny. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axolotl  (Legend.)

question: A tuna drowns if it stops swimming. The African lungfish faces the mirror danger: drop it into a tank of perfectly clean, fully oxygenated water and hold it below, and it drowns anyway. Its gills alone cannot save it. Why must this fish reach the surface to survive?
answer: Its gills have shrunk so far it must gulp air into a true lung or suffocate
choices: Its gills have shrunk so far it must gulp air into a true lung or suffocate
Its gills only work while the fish is drifting slowly downward through water
Its gills seal shut in cool water and reopen only in the warm surface layer
Its gills strip salt from water and starve without the surface film of minerals
context: The African lungfish (genus Protopterus) is an 'obligate air-breather.' Its gills have reduced so far that they can no longer pull enough oxygen from water; nearly all of an adult's oxygen uptake happens across a true paired lung, while the shrunken gills mostly dump carbon dioxide. Cut off from the surface, it suffocates even in fully oxygenated water. In the dry season it goes further, burrowing into mud and sealing itself in a mucus cocoon (estivation): its gill lamellae actually collapse and it survives for months breathing air alone at a drastically lowered metabolic rate. It is a living snapshot of the evolutionary crossover from breathing water to breathing air - the mirror of the ram-ventilating tuna, which drowns if it stops swimming, while the lungfish drowns if it can't reach the top. Source: WebSearch corroborated across lungfish.info 'How Lungfish Breathe Air,' ScienceDirect 'Lungfish - an overview,' and PubMed 25499100 (Signal molecule changes in the gills and lungs of Protopterus annectens during aestivation).  (Legend.)

question: The red feathery gill grabs oxygen - but tucked among that same tissue sit special cells busy with a second job that has nothing to do with breathing. A shark in the sea and a trout in a river both carry them, each tuned to its own water. What quiet task are these cells performing?
answer: Holding the blood at the right saltiness against the water outside
choices: Holding the blood at the right saltiness against the water outside
Sensing the water temperature so the fish knows when to spawn
Storing spare oxygen for moments the fish holds still and rests
Regrowing filaments worn thin by the endless rush of water
context: The fish gill is not just a lung-underwater - it is also the animal's kidney and its acid-base buffer. Beyond gas exchange, it is the dominant site where a fish dumps its nitrogen waste (as ammonia) and controls its blood salt and pH. The work is done by mitochondrion-packed cells wedged among the respiratory tissue, historically called 'chloride cells' and now 'ionocytes.' In seawater - saltier than the fish's blood - these cells actively pump excess salt OUT; a freshwater fish, flooded by dilute water, runs the very same cells in reverse to pull scarce ions IN. So the same organ that captures oxygen is quietly excreting waste and holding the fish's internal chemistry steady. Source: Wikipedia 'Fish gill' corroborated by Evans, Piermarini & Choe (2005), 'The Multifunctional Fish Gill,' Physiological Reviews 85:97-177.

question: The American entomologist Justin Schmidt spent his career letting stinging insects sting him on purpose so he could rank the pain of each one on a four-point scale. He scored the huge black South American bullet ant a full 4 out of 4 -- the highest possible mark. In his 2016 book The Sting of the Wild, he reached for a single searing image of exactly what that pain felt like. How did he describe it?
answer: Like walking over flaming charcoal with a nail in your heel
choices: Like walking over flaming charcoal with a nail in your heel
Like a lit blowtorch held against bare skin
Like a hot iron rod driven through the wrist
Like acid poured into an open wound
context: Schmidt called it 'pure, intense, brilliant pain... like walking over flaming charcoal with a three-inch nail embedded in your heel' in The Sting of the Wild (2016). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schmidt_sting_pain_index  (Legend.)

question: A single sting from the giant black bullet ant of the South American rainforest brings waves of burning, throbbing agony that keep pounding through the victim's arm or leg long after the ant itself is gone. In Venezuela, where the ant is common, local people gave it a blunt nickname stating exactly how long the ordeal drags on. What do they call it?
answer: The 24-hour ant
choices: The 24-hour ant
The three-day ant
The one-hour ant
The all-week ant
context: The pain can continue unabated for up to a full day, which is why Venezuelans call it 'hormiga veinticuatro,' the 24-hour ant. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paraponera_clavata  (Legend.)

question: To pass into manhood, boys of the Satere-Mawe people of the Brazilian Amazon must slide a bare hand into a specially woven ceremonial glove and hold it there for about ten minutes. Enduring the pain in silence is what proves them ready to be men. They repeat this ordeal roughly twenty times over the course of their youth before the initiation is complete. What is packed inside that glove?
answer: Dozens of live bullet ants
choices: Dozens of live bullet ants
Glowing embers
Stinging nettles
Venomous spiders
context: The Satere-Mawe first sedate the ants in an herbal solution, then weave them into a glove of cashew-palm leaves with the stingers turned inward toward the wearer's hand. Source: https://whyevolutionistrue.com/2014/08/06/the-worst-pain-known-to-humans-the-bullet-ant-gloves-of-brazil/  (Legend.)

question: The bullet ant's agony doesn't come from acid burning tissue or from swelling around the wound. A single small protein in the ant's venom, called poneratoxin, sneaks in and hijacks the electrical wiring inside your own nerves. Normally, nerves send pain signals by flicking tiny channels open and shut in a controlled rhythm. What does poneratoxin do to those channels that makes the pain so unstoppable?
answer: Jams the sodium channels that carry nerve signals
choices: Jams the sodium channels that carry nerve signals
Dissolves the fatty sheath around each nerve
Floods the muscles with excess calcium
Starves the nerve endings of oxygen
context: Poneratoxin locks up the voltage-gated sodium channels nerves use to fire, scrambling the signals they send each other. There are no recorded human deaths from the sting, and the toxin fully clears the body within about a day. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paraponera_clavata

question: A long, ringed, soft-bodied animal squirms through the wet tropical soil. At first glance it looks like a giant earthworm, or maybe a small burrowing snake. But it has no legs at all, and it is really an amphibian — a cousin of frogs and salamanders, not a worm or a reptile. What is this legless creature called?
answer: A caecilian, a legless amphibian
choices: A caecilian, a legless amphibian
A slow-worm, a legless lizard
A blindworm, a burrowing snake
An amphiuma, an eel-like salamander
context: Caecilians (order Gymnophiona) are the least-known group of amphibians - true amphibians like frogs and salamanders, but with no legs and a long, segmented, worm-like body. They are not worms and not snakes. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caecilian

question: The caecilian is a legless burrowing amphibian. It spends its life hidden underground, so most people never see one. Its 220 kinds live across warm wet tropics on several continents. Yet one big continent, plenty tropical and wet, has no native caecilians. Which one?
answer: Australia
choices: Australia
Africa
South America
southern Asia
context: There are over 220 caecilian species across 10 families, found in the tropics of South and Central America, Africa, southern Asia and the Seychelles - but never in Australia. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caecilian

question: A caecilian hunts through pitch-dark soil almost blind, yet it still tracks down prey. Between each eye and nostril sits a small organ found in no other animal with a backbone, which it pushes out and pulls back as it burrows. What is this one-of-a-kind organ?
answer: A chemical-sensing tentacle
choices: A chemical-sensing tentacle
A pair of infrared pit organs
A pair of heat-tasting tongues
A set of pressure-sensing whiskers
context: The tentacle sits in a groove between eye and nostril, can be pushed out and pulled back, and connects to the animal's smell system - a sensory organ unique among all vertebrates that lets a nearly blind caecilian hunt underground. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caecilian

question: In the wet mountain forests of Kenya lives Boulengerula taitanus, a caecilian -- a legless, worm-like amphibian that spends its life burrowing through the soil. A mother caecilian rests coiled in her nest as her newly-hatched babies swarm over her body. They scrape at her skin with a special set of baby teeth found only in the young. What are those unusual baby teeth actually for?
answer: Peeling and eating her skin
choices: Peeling and eating her skin
Gripping her as she carries them
Combing parasites from her sides
Draining milk from a belly pore
context: Alexander Kupfer and his team first documented this skin-feeding (dermatophagy) in Boulengerula taitanus. The babies scrape off the fatty skin about every three days - the time a new layer takes to regrow - and can grow up to 10 times their own weight in a single week. It is a form of maternal care, not cruelty. Source: https://www.nature.com/articles/nature04403  (Legend.)

question: Caecilians are limbless, worm-like amphibians that burrow through tropical soil, so far below our notice that most people have never heard of them. In 2020, Brazilian researchers reported that the ringed caecilian, Siphonops annulatus, may share a trait long famous in snakes. If confirmed, it would be the oldest known land animal to have it, older even than snakes themselves. Which trait?
answer: An oral venom system
choices: An oral venom system
A regrowing set of fangs
A glow-in-the-dark bite
A paralyzing tail spine
context: Researchers found tiny glands at the base of the teeth that release fluid when the caecilian bites, carrying phospholipase A2 - an enzyme bees, wasps and snakes use to inflict a burning, tissue-dissolving sting. This reported finding is still under study, but if confirmed it may make caecilians the oldest land vertebrate with an oral venom system - older even than venomous snakes. Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7385905/

question: The one-hump dromedary rules the hot deserts of Arabia and North Africa. Its shaggier, two-humped cousin, the Bactrian camel, lives instead on the cold Gobi desert of central Asia. There a single year swings through a huge range of temperatures. How wide a span does the Bactrian handle?
answer: From about -20 F up to 120 F
choices: From about -20 F up to 120 F
A steady 60 F year-round
From freezing up to about 80 F
From about 40 F up to 140 F
context: The two-humped Bactrian is the cold-desert camel, handling the Gobi's brutal swing from roughly -20 F up to 120 F, while the one-humped dromedary rules the hot deserts. Source: San Diego Zoo, Camel; Britannica, Camel.

question: A one-humped Arabian camel plods calmly across open desert dunes, hardly leaving deep tracks, in country where a horse trying the same crossing would punch its narrow hooves straight down into the loose sand and bog itself. The camel's feet are built for the sand in a way a hoof simply isn't. What keeps the camel walking on top of the dunes?
answer: Broad two-toed feet
choices: Broad two-toed feet
Tiny hardened hooves
A single padded toe
Long curved climbing claws
context: Each broad, two-toed foot spreads and flattens under the camel's weight, then contracts when lifted, working like a natural snowshoe that keeps it from sinking into loose sand. Source: San Diego Zoo, Camel.

question: Almost everyone 'knows' that a camel's hump is a built-in water tank for crossing the desert -- hollow inside and full of water the camel drank days ago. That popular picture is completely wrong. A hungry camel's hump slumps sideways and shrinks as the animal uses up whatever is packed inside. What is actually stored in a camel's hump?
answer: Fat, a concentrated energy reserve
choices: Fat, a concentrated energy reserve
Water stored for the journey
A spongy sac of blood
Coiled muscle for climbing
context: The hump is a concentrated fat reserve the camel burns when food is scarce. Keeping the fat in one hump rather than spread under the skin also lets the rest of the body shed heat more easily. Source: WWF, What do camels store in their humps?

question: In the scorching Sahara desert, a camel wanders up to a fat green cactus bristling with six-inch needles. Anything else would starve rather than bite it. The camel simply opens its mouth, chomps the cactus down, spines and all, and swallows without a scratch inside its mouth. Something inside the mouth handles the needles safely on the way down. What is it?
answer: Cone-shaped mouth spikes that steer each needle point-first down
choices: Cone-shaped mouth spikes that steer each needle point-first down
A thick saliva coating that dissolves the spines before swallowing
Molars that snap each needle off cleanly at its base
A second set of lips that strips the spines away first
context: Cone-shaped keratin papillae line the camel's mouth and rotate the spines so they slide straight down the throat point-first; a vet described them as feeling almost like plastic. Source: National Geographic, Arabian Camels Eat Cacti With Hardened Mouth Structures.

question: After days of crossing hot desert sand with no water, a dangerously dehydrated camel finally reaches a stone trough at an oasis. It plunges its muzzle in and drinks nonstop for about ten minutes without ever lifting its head. Its belly swells as it drains the water down. In that single drinking session, how much water can a thirsty camel take on?
answer: Over 100 liters
choices: Over 100 liters
About 10 liters
Under 2 liters
Around 30 liters
context: A dehydrated camel can gulp well over 100 liters in about ten minutes; the San Diego Zoo cites up to 145 liters (32 gallons) in a single drink, replacing about a third of its body weight almost at once. Source: San Diego Zoo, Camel.

question: Out on the blazing desert sand, a camel faces a hard trade. Sweating would dump the heat but spend precious water it cannot spare. So through the burning day, a camel does something with its own body that most mammals never risk, because for other animals it would be dangerous. What does the camel do?
answer: Lets its body temperature climb by day and cool at night
choices: Lets its body temperature climb by day and cool at night
Slows its heartbeat to a near-standstill until dusk
Shunts blood away from its skin to trap heat inside
Shuts down its kidneys to hoard every last drop
context: Rather than sweating, a camel lets its core temperature swing widely, cooling to about 34-35 C overnight and coasting up to 41-42 C by day. Storing the heat in its own body instead of evaporating water to shed it saves enormous amounts of water. Source: Schmidt-Nielsen, 1956, Body Temperature of the Camel and Its Relation to Water Economy.

question: A South American grazer plods through a savanna near a river, chomping grass. It is four feet long, as heavy as a grown man, and about the size of a big dog. Every animal in its family is a rodent, and this is the biggest rodent alive anywhere on Earth. What is it?
answer: The capybara
choices: The capybara
The beaver
The porcupine
The muskrat
context: The capybara (Hydrochoerus hydrochaeris) is the largest living rodent — over four feet long and typically 35–66 kg (77–146 lb), about the mass of a grown man. The heaviest wild one on record was a 91 kg (201 lb) female from Brazil. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capybara

question: A capybara spends every waking hour grinding tough, gritty grass between its big front teeth. That constant scraping wears the enamel away fast — enough to file an ordinary tooth down to a useless stub. Yet an old capybara bites just as well as a young one. What trick of a rodent's front teeth beats the wear?
answer: The teeth never stop growing
choices: The teeth never stop growing
New adult teeth replace the worn ones each year
A hard enamel cap makes them wear-proof
Saliva slowly rebuilds the worn edges
context: Like all rodents, the capybara's front incisors grow continuously throughout its life, replacing exactly what constant grass-grinding wears away. That is the defining rodent trait — the word 'rodent' comes from Latin for 'to gnaw.' Source: https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/things-you-might-not-know-about-capybaras.html

question: The capybara is the world's largest rodent, a South American giant that lives near ponds and rivers. When a jaguar prowls the bank, the capybara sinks quietly into the water until only the top of its head shows above the surface. Like a hippo, it can still watch, listen, and breathe. What feature of a capybara's head lets it do all three while the rest of its body stays hidden under the water?
answer: Its eyes, ears, and nostrils all sit high on top of the head
choices: Its eyes, ears, and nostrils all sit high on top of the head
A long snorkel-like snout it lifts above the surface
A wide flat skull that keeps the whole face above water
Nostrils that pinch shut while raised eye sockets watch
context: A capybara's eyes, ears, and nostrils are all set high on the top of its head, so it can float with almost its whole body submerged and still see, hear, and breathe — the same layout a hippopotamus uses. It can even sleep in the water with just its nose poking out. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capybara  (Legend.)

question: Grass is so hard to digest that much of the protein and B vitamins a capybara's gut bacteria produce would slip away unabsorbed. To reclaim that lost nutrition, a capybara does something each morning that startles people who watch it. What does it do?
answer: It re-eats its own soft morning droppings
choices: It re-eats its own soft morning droppings
It licks mineral-rich mud from the riverbank
It chews the cud back up like a cow
It eats the droppings of the young in its group
context: The capybara is a hindgut fermenter: an enlarged cecum and colon full of bacteria break down grass cellulose its stomach cannot. Because the nutrients those bacteria make would otherwise be lost, it re-eats its soft morning droppings (coprophagy), passing the food through twice to absorb the protein and B vitamins — the same trick rabbits use. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capybara ; https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF00264639  (Legend.)

question: Deep in the rainforests of Australia and New Guinea, a shiny black bird taller than a grown man walks slowly across the forest floor. Its neck is bright electric blue, and on top of its head rises a tall bony helmet like a horn. What bird is it?
answer: The cassowary
choices: The cassowary
The greater rhea
The secretary bird
The shoebill stork
context: The southern cassowary stands up to about 2 metres (6 feet) tall, with glossy black feathers, bright blue skin on the head and fore-neck, red on the rear neck, and a tall greyish 'casque' helmet. Source: Australian Museum, Southern Cassowary.

question: Zookeepers spend their days handling huge flightless birds — the ostrich of Africa, the emu of Australia, the rhea of South America, and the cassowary of the rainforest. Ask them which one they fear most and they will not name any of the others. What title has the rainforest cassowary earned above the rest?
answer: The world's most dangerous bird
choices: The world's most dangerous bird
The world's fastest bird
The world's heaviest bird
The world's loudest bird
context: The cassowary is widely called the world's most dangerous bird. A 2019 death in Florida (its 75-year-old owner) was the first human fatality attributed to a cassowary in 93 years. Source: Guinness World Records, 'Why the cassowary is the world's most dangerous bird'.  (Legend.)

question: The cassowary is a huge flightless bird of the New Guinea and Australian rainforests. Corner one on a path and it does not run away. Instead it leaps up and drives both powerful feet forward at whatever is threatening it, like a kung fu kick. On the inner toe of each foot rides the weapon that has earned the cassowary its reputation as the world's most dangerous bird. What is that weapon?
answer: A dagger-like claw up to five inches long
choices: A dagger-like claw up to five inches long
A ring of backward-facing barbs
A gripping talon like an eagle's
A blunt spur it uses to trip
context: The inner toe on each foot ends in a dagger-like claw up to about 12 cm (5 inches) long. A threatened cassowary leaps and kicks, and the claw can slash open internal organs. Source: Wikipedia, Cassowary / Southern cassowary.  (Legend.)

question: In the dark rainforests of New Guinea and northeastern Australia lives the cassowary, a huge flightless bird with a shining blue neck and a bony helmet on its head. A baby cassowary trots behind its father, but the chick looks nothing like the black adult -- for its first months a bold striped pattern hides it against the forest floor. Field guides say the chick most resembles what?
answer: A watermelon
choices: A watermelon
A newborn fawn
A ring-tailed lemur
A rolled-up pangolin
context: Cassowary chicks hatch striped like watermelons — brown-and-cream banded down the back and thighs for camouflage — and lose the stripes at about 3 to 6 months, turning plain brown. Source: Birdfact, 'Baby Cassowaries' / San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance factsheet.

question: The cassowary is a huge flightless bird of the rainforests of New Guinea and northeastern Australia. Deep in dense foliage one of these birds makes a sound felt more than heard: a booming note near 32 hertz, right at the very floor of what human ears can pick up. Researchers think the bird uses so deep a pitch to do one thing a higher call could not. What?
answer: Carry far through thick rainforest foliage
choices: Carry far through thick rainforest foliage
Startle predators into freezing
Echo off the ground to map the forest
Mimic the calls of other animals
context: Cassowaries produce some of the lowest-frequency sounds known in any bird — deep booming notes reaching about 32 Hz — thought to carry through dense foliage where higher-pitched calls fade. The casque may act as a receiver/amplifier for these calls, though its exact function is still debated. Source: Researchgate, 'Low-Frequency Vocalizations by Cassowaries' / Rainforest Trust, 'Seven Things'.

question: A chameleon is a small, slow-moving lizard of Africa and Madagascar, famous for its turret-like eyes and its knack for changing color. Perched on a branch, one sits perfectly still, spots an insect a good distance off, and strikes without moving its body.
