context: A comb jelly has no stinging cells; its tentacles carry sticky 'glue cells' called colloblasts, mushroom-shaped cells that burst and glue prey in place. True jellyfish use venom-loaded nematocysts instead. Source: WHOI (whoi.edu/ctenophores); ScienceDirect ctenophore evo-devo review.

question: Comb jellies are soft, clear sea animals with eight glowing rows of combs running along their bodies. Most kinds catch food by dabbing at tiny plankton with long, sticky, trailing tentacles. But one kind, called Beroe, has no tentacles at all — its body is basically a huge, gaping mouth on the front of a walnut-shaped bag. So what does the tentacle-less Beroe hunt?
answer: Swallows other comb jellies whole with giant teeth in its mouth
choices: Swallows other comb jellies whole with giant teeth in its mouth
Drills into fish eggs and sucks out the yolk
Filters clouds of plankton through a fine mesh
Ambushes sleeping shrimp buried in the sand
context: Beroe hunts by swallowing other comb jellies whole, using giant 'macrocilia' teeth in its mouth. Comb jellies are voracious predators that eat each other. Source: WHOI (whoi.edu/ctenophores); Shape of Life.

question: A deep-sea comb jelly drifts through the black twilight zone as glass-clear as water, except for a single organ that glows a vivid color. That color hides the glow of the shining prey it has just swallowed, so no bigger hunter spots the meal. What color is that organ?
answer: Bright red
choices: Bright red
Pale gold
Bright white
Deep violet
context: Bathocyroe fosteri has a bright red stomach; red hides the blue-green glow of luminous prey it has swallowed, so the meal doesn't shine out and attract bigger hunters. Source: WHOI (whoi.edu/ctenophores).

question: In the 1980s a comb jelly called the sea walnut (Mnemiopsis leidyi) rode into the Black Sea in a ship's ballast water, exploded in numbers, and ate the zooplankton and fish larvae. A decade later the Black Sea was rescued from it, and the rescuer was a surprise. What knocked the invader back down?
answer: Another comb jelly that hunts and eats comb jellies
choices: Another comb jelly that hunts and eats comb jellies
A cold winter that froze the surface waters
A new fishing fleet that netted them by the ton
A virus that spread through the swarm
context: Beroe ovata, a comb-jelly-eating predator, arrived by ship in the late 1990s and knocked the sea walnut's numbers back down. Source: IUCN GISD (iucngisd.org/gisd/species.php?sc=95); NASA Earthdata 'Invasion of the Ctenophores'.

question: Sponges are usually taught as the simplest, oldest branch of the animal family tree. But some scientists studying ancient gene patterns argue a different creature, not the sponge, was the very first to split off from all other animals, making it our most distant animal cousin. Which creature do they point to?
answer: The comb jelly
choices: The comb jelly
The flatworm
The sea anemone
The tiny water bear
context: Legend/unsettled: some studies argue the comb jelly, not the sponge, was the first branch to split off from all other animals. Whether comb jellies or sponges are the 'sister to all other animals' is still a live, unsettled scientific debate. Source: Nature 2023 (nature.com/articles/s41586-023-05936-6); Nature Ecology & Evolution 2017 (Whelan et al.).

question: Sea walnuts are small oval comb jellies, only a couple of centimeters long, that drift through coastal waters. In a 2024 experiment at the Marine Biological Laboratory in Woods Hole, researchers cut two of them, placed the injured animals side by side in a dish, and watched. About nine times out of ten, something happened that no shark or human being could ever do. What became of the two animals?
answer: They fused into one animal, their nervous systems wiring together
choices: They fused into one animal, their nervous systems wiring together
They sealed their own wounds and drifted apart unharmed
They devoured each other until only the larger one was left
They cloned themselves, budding off dozens of tiny copies
context: When Kei Jokura's team cut partial lobes off two sea walnuts (Mnemiopsis leidyi) and set them together, the pair merged roughly 90% of the time. Within about two hours their two nerve nets had wired together so tightly that muscle contractions beat in near-perfect sync, and food swallowed by one mouth traveled through the shared, merged gut. This works because comb jellies lack allorecognition, the self-versus-nonself check that in most animals rejects foreign tissue. Source: sci.news coverage of Jokura et al., Current Biology, Oct 2024 (https://www.sci.news/biology/mnemiopsis-leidyi-rapid-physiological-integration-13322.html).

question: In a single drop of water squeezed from a patch of wet moss or lichen, you can find a chubby, eight-legged animal barely half a millimeter long. It waddles along in slow motion, gripping the moss with tiny claws on each of its eight feet. Under a strong microscope its rounded body and slow walk make it look like a stubby little bear. What is this tiny creature nicknamed?
answer: The water bear
choices: The water bear
The moss louse
The bog shrimp
The lichen crab
context: The tardigrade earns its nicknames 'water bear' and 'moss piglet' from its plump body and lumbering, bear-like walk across mosses and lichens. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/invertebrates/facts/tardigrades-water-bears

question: A tardigrade, sometimes called a water bear, is a microscopic eight-legged animal that lives in a drop of water on damp moss. When the moss dries out in the sun and its water vanishes, the tardigrade pulls in its head and legs and squeezes out more than 95 percent of its own body water. What shape does it curl into to wait out the drought?
answer: A shriveled barrel called a 'tun'
choices: A shriveled barrel called a 'tun'
A hard sealed sphere called a 'cyst'
A flat papery disc called a 'scute'
A coiled spring called a 'spiral'
context: Losing over 95% of its water, the tardigrade curls into a barrel-shaped 'tun' — and hours later a single drop of water swells it back up and it walks away. Source: https://www.nature.com/articles/s42003-022-04015-2  (Legend.)

question: Tardigrades, the tiny eight-legged 'water bears' that live in damp moss, can survive boiling heat, near-absolute cold, and the crushing pressure of the deep sea, so people picture them as unkillable little beasts. But a hungry mite can happily eat one, and a careless finger squeeze can pop one flat. In what state does a tardigrade actually shrug off those extremes?
answer: Only as a dried, shriveled, dormant tun
choices: Only as a dried, shriveled, dormant tun
Anytime, whether wet or dry
Only while it is actively feeding
Only when many are clustered together
context: The toughness belongs to the dried tun, not the living animal. An active, water-filled tardigrade is soft and delicate — easily crushed or eaten; only the shriveled, dormant state shrugs off boiling, freezing, and crushing. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/invertebrates/facts/tardigrades-water-bears

question: As a tardigrade dries into its dormant barrel shape, called a tun, a small amount of the sugar trehalose teams up with special tardigrade proteins named CAHS (short for cytoplasmic-abundant heat-soluble) to protect the cells from being torn apart by drying. What do these substances together do to the animal's insides?
answer: Turn them from liquid into a glass-like solid
choices: Turn them from liquid into a glass-like solid
Coat every cell in a waxy waterproof shell
Flood them with antifreeze to stop ice
Pump them full of oxygen for the wait
context: CAHS proteins and trehalose work synergistically to vitrify the tardigrade's insides — turning liquid into a glass-like solid that locks cell parts in place until water returns. Source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9526748/

question: Locked inside its dry, glassy barrel, a shape tardigrade scientists call a 'tun', a water bear can wait without food or water for years. Some reports say up to about thirty years. To pause its life that long, its metabolism drops so far that instruments can barely detect it at all. Roughly how low does it fall compared with normal?
answer: Below 0.01% of normal
choices: Below 0.01% of normal
About 10% of normal
About half of normal
About 2% of normal
context: In the tun state a tardigrade's metabolism falls below 0.01% of normal — so faint it's basically undetectable — letting it wait years, even up to about 30. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/invertebrates/facts/tardigrades-water-bears

question: In September 2007, a European experiment called Tardigrades in Space bolted a batch of dried tardigrades onto the outside of a small satellite orbiting Earth. For about ten days the tiny animals were left exposed to a place no animal had ever been shown to survive before. Where exactly were they?
answer: The open vacuum beyond the atmosphere
choices: The open vacuum beyond the atmosphere
The mouth of an undersea volcano
The heart of a nuclear reactor
The core of an Antarctic glacier
context: On the Foton-M3 capsule, dried tardigrades survived raw space vacuum for about 10–12 days — the first animal shown to endure it. Many revived on Earth; some even withstood added solar UV and later reproduced. Source: https://www.esa.int/Science_Exploration/Human_and_Robotic_Exploration/Research/Tiny_animals_survive_exposure_to_space  (Legend.)

question: In 2016, Japanese scientists sequencing the genome of the tardigrade Ramazzottius varieornatus discovered a protein they had never seen anywhere else in nature. They named it Dsup, short for 'Damage suppressor.' Startlingly, when they inserted the Dsup gene into human cells growing in a lab dish, it kept right on working there too. What does Dsup do?
answer: Wraps around DNA and shields it from radiation damage
choices: Wraps around DNA and shields it from radiation damage
Rebuilds torn muscle fibres after freezing
Digests toxins that leak in during drying
Signals nearby cells to enter dormancy together
context: Dsup binds to DNA and physically shields it from radiation-driven damage — and remarkably, it still protects DNA when inserted into human cells. Source: https://elifesciences.org/articles/47682  (Legend.)

question: Tardigrades aren't the only animals that come back from bone-dry death. One tiny crustacean is famously sold to American kids as 'Sea-Monkeys' in old comic-book ads. You buy a packet of dust, pour it into a bowl of water, and days later a tank of little swimmers appears. Its eggs can sit dried out for years before a splash of water brings them to life. What is this animal really called?
answer: The brine shrimp
choices: The brine shrimp
The pond snail
The water flea
The mud minnow
context: Brine shrimp — marketed as 'Sea-Monkeys' — hatch from cysts, dormant eggs that survive years bone-dry until water revives them. Source: https://journals.biologists.com/jeb/article/211/18/2899/17660/

question: In the seasonal ponds of central Africa lives the tiny larva of a mosquito-like insect called a midge. When its pool dries up under the hot sun, the larva shuts down completely, losing about 97 percent of its body water and stiffening on the parched ground. Splash water on it again and it revives as if nothing had happened. What is the longest a dried midge larva has still come back to life?
answer: About 17 years
choices: About 17 years
About 17 days
About 17 weeks
About 17 months
context: The sleeping chironomid larva can lose ~97% of its water, vitrify, and revive after roughly 17 years dried out — one of the toughest known cases of surviving without water. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polypedilum_vanderplanki

question: A bdelloid rotifer is a microscopic freshwater animal, smaller than a grain of sand, that whirls a ring of tiny hairs to sweep food into its mouth. In 2021, Russian scientists thawed one out of Siberian permafrost soil, then radiocarbon-dated the mud around it to see how long the animal had been frozen. When they warmed the rotifer up, it woke and began reproducing. How old was this dormant animal?
answer: About 24,000 years
choices: About 24,000 years
About 240 years
About 2,400 years
About 240,000 years
context: A bdelloid rotifer from ~24,000-year-old Arctic permafrost revived and began reproducing — one of the longest 'comebacks' ever recorded for a dormant animal. Source: https://www.cell.com/current-biology/fulltext/S0960-9822(21)00624-2  (Legend.)

question: Biologists group the tardigrade, brine shrimp, and permafrost rotifer under one survival trick: powering down so faint they seem dead until conditions improve. The same shutdown that carries them through a killing drought also carries them through two other killers. Which pair?
answer: Freezing solid or running out of oxygen
choices: Freezing solid or running out of oxygen
Blistering heat or blinding UV light
Salt so high it burns or total darkness
Crushing deep-sea pressure or acid water
context: Cryptobiosis ('hidden life') is the umbrella term for going dormant to survive drought, freezing, or lack of oxygen; the drying-out version specifically is anhydrobiosis, 'life without water.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptobiosis

question: Sea-monkey brine shrimp — those tiny freeze-dried eggs sold in kits that come back to life in water — pack their dried eggs with a protective sugar called trehalose. So it was tempting to assume water bears, the microscopic eight-legged animals also called tardigrades, rely on the same trick to survive drying out. But in 2008, one common lab tardigrade dried and revived perfectly while carrying no detectable trehalose at all. If sugar is not the water bear's rescue, what mainly does the protecting instead?
answer: Its own proteins that set the cell to glass
choices: Its own proteins that set the cell to glass
A thick waxy shell sealed over the skin
Antifreeze borrowed from Arctic fish blood
A slime coat that traps a film of water
context: For the sea-monkey (brine shrimp Artemia) and the nematode Aphelenchus avenae, trehalose really is the star — roughly 15% and 20% of dry weight. But tardigrades are the exception that breaks the rule: Hengherr et al. found they hoard at most about 2.3% trehalose, and only in one family (Macrobiotidae) does it rise on drying at all. Milnesium tardigradum has none yet dries and revives just as well. The heavy lifting is done by tardigrade-specific CAHS proteins (Cytoplasmic Abundant Heat Soluble), which vitrify the cell into a protective glass. So unlike the sea-monkey, the water bear's survival is a protein trick, not a sugar trick. Source: Hengherr et al. 2008, FEBS Journal, 'Trehalose and anhydrobiosis in tardigrades – evidence for divergence in responses to dehydration' (https://febs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1742-4658.2007.06198.x); Artemia ~15% and A. avenae ~20% trehalose corroborated in the anhydrobiosis literature.

question: A water bear tun can shrug off a brief scald, feeding its reputation for surviving 150 C. Yet Ralph Hengherr, heating nine dried species in 2009, found revival stays high up to about 80 C and then collapses — and it collapses across the exact temperature band where the tun stops working. What happens to the tun in that band that pulls the plug on survival?
answer: Its protective inner glass softens and melts
choices: Its protective inner glass softens and melts
Its outer claws snap off one by one
Its stored trehalose caramelizes to syrup
Its curled body unrolls and floods with air
context: The 'survives 150 C' headline hides a ceiling written into the very glass that protects the animal. Using calorimetry, Hengherr et al. measured each species' glass-transition temperature — the point where the solid inner glass softens back toward a liquid — at roughly 35 to 87 C depending on species. Revival stayed high up to about 80 C and then dropped steeply, and that steep drop lined up with the glass transition: once the glass un-sets, the frozen-in protection is lost and the cell is exposed. So the tun can take a quick pass through a flame, but sustained real heat melts the very thing keeping it alive — a sharper and more honest limit than the folklore number. Source: Hengherr et al. 2009, Physiological and Biochemical Zoology 82(6):749-755, 'High-Temperature Tolerance in Anhydrobiotic Tardigrades Is Limited by Glass Transition' (https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/605954; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19732016/).

question: Look closely at a dragonfly perched on a reed. Its enormous wrap-around eyes cover most of its head. Each of those eyes is not really one single eye at all — it is a bundle of up to 30,000 tiny tubes packed together, and every tube catches its own single dot of light. Together the tubes build the dragonfly's picture of the world. What are these tiny light-catching tubes called?
answer: Ommatidia
choices: Ommatidia
Feathers
Whiskers
Gills
context: A dragonfly's eye is a bundle of up to ~30,000 ommatidia — each a lens over a light-catcher (rhabdom) that sees one dot of light. The brain stitches all those dots into a mosaic, not a smooth photo. Source: grrlscientist/ScienceBlogs '30,000 Facets Give Dragonflies a Different Perspective' (2009); Britannica 'Ommatidium'.

question: Your hand swoops down to swat a housefly on the kitchen counter, and every time the fly darts away before you connect. To the fly it seems the giant hand is coming in slow motion, giving it plenty of time to move. Scientists have measured how quickly a fly's eyes and brain take in the world compared to yours. Roughly how much faster does a housefly see than a human?
answer: About four times faster
choices: About four times faster
About the same speed
About half as fast
About a hundred times faster
context: A fly sees about 250 flashes per second where a human sees about 60 — roughly four times faster — so your descending hand looks like slow motion, and the fly dodges. Compound eyes are poor at fine detail but brilliant at catching motion. Source: Big Think 'You're not fast enough to swat a fly'; ACSH 'Flicker Fusion is More Than Meets the Eye'.

question: A hunting dragonfly is one of the deadliest hunters in the animal kingdom — it catches flying prey, like mosquitoes and midges in mid-air, about 95% of the time. Experiments filming a dragonfly's head, wings and eye movement in super-slow-motion have revealed what the little insect's brain is doing during that fraction of a second before the strike. What is a dragonfly actually computing?
answer: Where the prey will be, then steering to intercept
choices: Where the prey will be, then steering to intercept
The straight path to where the prey sits right now
The prey's heartbeat, to time the grab exactly
A scent trail the prey leaves behind in the air
context: Sixteen 'target-selective descending neurons' (TSDNs) read where prey is across the full 360 degrees and steer the wings, but the brain builds an internal model of where the prey WILL be, not just where it is — then steers to intercept. This is peer-reviewed experimental science, not legend. Source: Mischiati et al. 2015 Nature 'Internal models direct dragonfly interception steering'; Gonzalez-Bellido et al. PNAS.

question: The mantis shrimp is a fierce, brightly-colored ambush predator that lurks in reef burrows on Indo-Pacific coasts, and it has the strangest compound eyes on Earth. Each eye sits on a mobile stalk driven by eight tiny muscles. When the shrimp scans its coral neighborhood for prey and rival mantis shrimp, its two eyes can do something almost no other animal's eyes can. What?
answer: Point in totally different directions at once
choices: Point in totally different directions at once
Sweep together in a locked, mirrored pair
Scan only the narrow strip straight ahead
Fuse into a single wide eye
context: Each mantis-shrimp eye sits on its own stalk and moves completely independently — left, right, up, down, even twisting — driven by eight eyecup muscles, so the two eyes can point in totally different directions at once. Source: Marshall et al. 'Stomatopod eye structure and function'; Wikipedia 'Mantis shrimp'.

question: For decades, biologists kept finding strange wounds shaped like a melon-baller's scoop on whales, tuna, orcas, and even great white sharks. Something in the deep sea was carving neat round plugs of flesh out of the biggest, fiercest animals in the ocean. When the culprit was finally caught and identified, one thing about it stunned the biologists. What?
answer: It was barely half a meter long
choices: It was barely half a meter long
It hunted in coordinated packs
It had venomous spines
It could swallow prey whole
context: The cookiecutter shark (Isistius brasiliensis) reaches only about 56 cm in females and 42 cm in males, yet it bites chunks out of whales, dolphins, orcas, tuna, swordfish, seals, and even great white sharks. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cookiecutter_shark

question: The cookiecutter shark is a small, cigar-shaped, deep-sea shark barely half a meter long. When it finds a much bigger animal — a whale, a tuna, a dolphin — it seals its thick lips onto the giant's flank, sinks its bottom teeth in, then twists its whole body in a slow spin before letting go. What does the wound it leaves behind on the giant's side look like?
answer: A near-perfect round crater
choices: A near-perfect round crater
A long ragged tear
A double row of punctures
A shallow scrape
context: The shark gouges out a neat, near-perfect round plug of flesh, leaving a crater about 5 cm across and 7 cm deep, like a cookie cutter pressed into dough. That clean circle is how the shark earned its name. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cookiecutter_shark

question: The cookiecutter shark is a small cigar-shaped deep-sea shark, about the length of a forearm, that punches round bites out of tuna, dolphins, and even whales. When a fisherman hauls one up in his net and dumps it on the boat deck at night, the shark stops moving fairly quickly. But for as much as three hours out of the water, it goes on doing one eerie thing no other shark does. What?
answer: Its belly keeps glowing green
choices: Its belly keeps glowing green
Its skin keeps changing color
Its eyes keep flashing silver
Its gills keep pulsing light
context: The cookiecutter shark's green belly light is the strongest bioluminescence known in any shark, and it can keep glowing for up to three hours after the shark is taken out of the water. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cookiecutter_shark

question: A predator prowls the black deep, looking upward for anything drifting overhead. A cookiecutter shark cruises above it, belly aglow with soft green light, yet the hunter cannot pick it out. Why does the glowing belly make the shark harder to see, not easier?
answer: Its glow matches the faint light from the surface, erasing its silhouette
choices: Its glow matches the faint light from the surface, erasing its silhouette
Its green glow matches the water color, blurring its outline
Its glow flickers fast enough to smear its shape into a haze
Its glow is too dim for deep-sea eyes to register at all
context: This is counter-illumination camouflage: lit from below, the shark's glowing belly cancels its own silhouette against the faint light above, making it nearly invisible to anything looking up from the deep. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cookiecutter_shark

question: The cookiecutter shark is a small deep-sea shark that hangs in mid-water and takes round cookie-cutter bites out of much bigger animals like tuna and dolphins. Its entire underside glows a pale green, except for one dark, non-glowing band right under its throat. Seen from far below against the bright belly, that dark patch looks exactly like the silhouette of a small fish. What does this fake shadow do for the shark?
answer: It lures big predators in to be bitten
choices: It lures big predators in to be bitten
It hides the shark's eyes from prey
It scares off rival sharks
It helps the shark find the seabed
context: The dark collar looks like the silhouette of a small fish, drawing big predators in close so the little shark can bite THEM. Scientists believe it is the only known case where the ABSENCE of glow works as a lure. Source: https://sharkangels.org/cookiecutter-sharks-use-glow-in-the-dark-ability-to-attract-prey-10x-its-own-size/  (Legend.)

question: The cookiecutter shark is a small deep-sea shark that carves neat round plugs of flesh out of whales, tuna, and other much larger animals. Unlike most sharks, which shed teeth one at a time, a cookiecutter's lower teeth are locked together into a single interlocked row. When they wear out, the entire row comes loose at once. What does the cookiecutter then do with that old set of teeth?
answer: It swallows the set whole
choices: It swallows the set whole
It spits the set onto the seabed
It keeps the set embedded for life
It grinds the set down on rocks
context: The shark's lower teeth interlock into one connected saw-like blade, and it swallows the whole old set entire, recycling the calcium. One shark shed 15 full sets growing from 14 cm to 50 cm, some 435 to 465 teeth swallowed over its life. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cookiecutter_shark

question: To core a plug from a whale, a cookiecutter shark must stay clamped to thrashing flesh while it saws and spins. Its lips form a seal, but a seal alone would peel off. What second move drops the pressure inside its mouth and locks the grip like a suction cup?
answer: It retracts its tongue to suck the pocket empty like a piston
choices: It retracts its tongue to suck the pocket empty like a piston
It pumps sticky mucus between its lips and the skin
It hooks rows of gill rakers into the wound edge
It inflates its throat to press the seal outward
context: The 'suction' is an active hydraulic trick, not just sticky lips. The shark closes its spiracles and pulls back its basihyal (the shark's tongue), dropping the pressure inside its mouth below the surrounding water while the thick suctorial lips form a gasket. Once it is vacuum-locked and anchored by the hook-like upper teeth, it drives in the lower saw and spins its whole body to core out the plug. It is the reverse of a syringe: pull the plunger back and the low pressure sucks everything tight. Source: Wikipedia, Cookiecutter shark (basihyal/spiracle-closure vacuum mechanism), corroborated by multiple secondary sources.

question: Famous for coring plugs from whales and tuna, the cookiecutter shark had its menu re-read from the chemistry of its own tissue — stable isotopes, fatty acids, and DNA traces. The nitrogen signature fell where it did not fit the whale-biter legend. What did the numbers reveal that the folklore missed?
answer: Tiny midwater fish and squid, not big surface animals, are its staple
choices: Tiny midwater fish and squid, not big surface animals, are its staple
It fasts for months between rare feasts on large prey
It scavenges dead whales far more often than it bites live ones
Its bites on whales deliver most of its yearly calories
context: Chemical-tracer detective work overturned the shark's own reputation. Carlisle et al. (2021, Scientific Reports) used stable isotopes, fatty acids, and eDNA and found that big surface victims — whales, tuna, dolphins — make up only a minor part of the diet: roughly 55% small mesopelagic fish and squid, about 39% vertically migrating midwater prey, and only around 5% large epipelagic prey. The nitrogen-isotope (delta-15N) signature sat well ABOVE that of the large prey, meaning the famous flesh-plug victims are a supplement, not the staple. The animal we picture coring whales mostly eats tiny midwater prey; the isotope mixing models beat the folklore. Source: Carlisle et al. 2021, Scientific Reports (nature.com/articles/s41598-021-89903-z; PMC8175345).  (Legend.)

question: A cuttlefish is a soft, flat, octopus-like sea animal with W-shaped eyes and eight short arms. Watch one drift just above the sandy seabed, arms fanned out, watching a shrimp on the sand below. Then, in a blink so quick your eye cannot follow, the cuttlefish strikes and the shrimp is gone. What shoots out from between the cuttlefish's arms to seize the prey?
answer: Two long feeding tentacles that uncoil in a blink
choices: Two long feeding tentacles that uncoil in a blink
A jet of scalding water from its funnel
A sticky net spun from its own slime
A ring of hooks flicked from under its arms
context: A cuttlefish is a mollusk and cephalopod, a cousin of the octopus and squid. It spreads its eight arms, then fires two long, coiled feeding tentacles so fast the strike is nearly impossible to follow with the naked eye. Source: Monterey Bay Aquarium, Common Cuttlefish (montereybayaquarium.org/animals/animals-a-to-z/common-cuttlefish).

question: During the Renaissance, artists in Italy and northern Europe prized a rich, warm brown drawing ink squeezed from the ink sac of one soft-bodied sea creature. Painters used it, mapmakers used it, and eventually the color itself took the animal's own Latin name — 'sepia,' still the word for that dusty-brown shade today. Which soft-bodied sea creature is 'sepia' named after?
answer: The cuttlefish
choices: The cuttlefish
The lugworm
The sea cucumber
The moon jellyfish
context: The cuttlefish's brown ink gave us the color 'sepia,' a prized artists' dye used in sketches since the Renaissance. The animal's genus name, Sepia, comes straight from that ink. Source: BBC Science Focus, 'Everything you wanted to know about cuttlefish'; Monterey Bay Aquarium, Common Cuttlefish.

question: Walk into almost any pet store and you will see chalky white ovals sold to clip inside a parakeet's cage. They have been sold there for more than a hundred years, so the bird can rub its beak on them and pick up calcium. But that white oval is not a rock, not a piece of coral, and not a bone from a fish. What is it really?
answer: A cuttlefish's internal shell
choices: A cuttlefish's internal shell
A dried piece of coral reef
A hardened lump of sea salt
A whale's polished ear bone
context: The 'cuttlebone' found on beaches and clipped into bird cages is the cuttlefish's internal shell. For over a hundred years it has been sold to pet birds as a beak-sharpener and calcium supplement. Source: BBC Science Focus, 'Everything you wanted to know about cuttlefish'; americansingercanary.org cuttlebone article.

question: A snail carries a hard shell on its back as armor to hide inside. A cuttlefish — the soft, flat, octopus-cousin of the sea — also has a chalky internal shell, the flat oval 'cuttlebone' you might spot in a pet store. But a cuttlebone does a completely different job than a snail shell. As the cuttlefish hovers still and level in open water, what is that porous chalky bone quietly doing for it?
answer: Working as a buoyancy tank, flooding with gas or liquid to sink or rise
choices: Working as a buoyancy tank, flooding with gas or liquid to sink or rise
Storing venom to load into its bite
Acting as a battery that powers its color changes
Growing new arms to replace lost ones
context: Unlike a snail's shell, the cuttlebone is a hard buoyancy tank stacked into tiny chambers the cuttlefish fills with gas or liquid to sink or rise, hovering like a submarine adjusting ballast. Source: AskNature, 'Layered Bone Holds Gas to Control Buoyancy'; PNAS 2020, 'Mechanical design of the highly porous cuttlebone' (pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2009531117).

question: On a tropical coral reef, a cuttlefish — a soft-bodied ocean cousin of the squid and the octopus — is the reigning champion of color-changing skin. Special cells called chromatophores let it flash stripes, spots, and rolling waves of color across its body in a heartbeat, matching sand or coral so exactly it seems to vanish. Yet when marine biologists studied the cuttlefish eye up close, they found a strange irony hidden inside it. What is it?
answer: It is colorblind, with just one kind of light-detecting cell
choices: It is colorblind, with just one kind of light-detecting cell
It has no lens and sees only blurred shadows
It cannot open its eyes in daylight
It grows a new eye each breeding season
context: The great irony of the cuttlefish, master of color, is that its eye holds only ONE type of photoreceptor, so it likely cannot see the dazzling color displays it produces the way we do. Source: Bailey-Matthews National Shell Museum, 'The Amazing Cuttlefish Eye' (shellmuseum.org); PNAS 2016 (pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1524578113).  (Legend.)

question: The broadclub cuttlefish is a big soft-bodied cousin of the octopus that hunts along Indo-Pacific coral reefs by day. When it creeps toward a crab, it does not freeze into camouflage the way an octopus might. Instead it sends dark stripes rolling downward across its head and arms, again and again, like a moving television screen. How does this 'passing-cloud' trick help it close the distance on the crab?
answer: The fake downward motion floods the prey's eyes and hides that the hunter is advancing
choices: The fake downward motion floods the prey's eyes and hides that the hunter is advancing
The rippling stripes give off a smell that lulls the crab to sleep
The moving pattern scares off larger predators nearby
The rolling bands warm the water to make the crab sluggish
context: A 2025 Bristol study found the moving stripes of the 'passing-cloud' display flood the prey's vision with fake downward motion, masking the fact that the predator is looming closer. Source: Santon & How et al., Science Advances 2025 (science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.adr3686); ScienceDaily 2025-03-26.  (Legend.)

question: Every winter the giant Australian cuttlefish, a big soft-bodied relative of the octopus, gathers in the shallow bays off South Australia to breed. Large 'guard' males win the fights and hoard the females in their arms, driving off any rival. A small male has no hope in a straight brawl, so he pulls a clever trick that fools the guard more than half the time. What does the small male do?
answer: He pales his skin and tucks his arms to pose as a female and slip past
choices: He pales his skin and tucks his arms to pose as a female and slip past
He plays dead until the guard drifts away
He blasts ink to blind the guard and dashes in
He mimics the guard's own warning pattern to bluff him off
context: A small 'sneaker' male can't win a fight, so he pales his skin, tucks his arms to fake a female's outline, and hides his male display to slip right past the guarding male to the female. The disguise works over half the time. Source: Norman/Hanlon, reported in Nature News 2005, 'Cuttlefish win mates with transvestite antics' (nature.com/news/2005/050117); ScienceDaily 2005-01-24.  (Legend.)

question: The cuttlefish has just one kind of light-detecting cell, so by the usual rules it cannot see color at all. Yet in 2016 the Stubbs father-son team proposed a way its odd W-shaped, off-center pupil turns that flaw into a tool. How could such an eye still read color?
answer: The pupil smears each wavelength to a different focus depth, and the eye reads color from how far it must refocus for a sharp image
choices: The pupil smears each wavelength to a different focus depth, and the eye reads color from how far it must refocus for a sharp image
The pupil rotates through colored filters, sampling one wavelength at a time before the brain stitches them together
The lone cell secretly holds three pigments that fatigue at different rates, mimicking three separate color receptors
The skin sends color data straight to the optic nerve, letting the body sense hues the eye alone never could
context: A covered rung already gives the paradox — the cuttlefish is a color-changing champion yet has only one photoreceptor type. This is the proposed resolution, a step deeper. Alexander and Christopher Stubbs (PNAS, 2016) argued the non-circular, off-axis W-shaped pupil deliberately MAXIMIZES chromatic aberration: the lens bends short (blue) and long (red) wavelengths to focus at different depths behind it, so no single image is ever sharp for all colors at once. By accommodating — refocusing the lens until the image snaps sharp — a single-receptor eye can infer the wavelength from the focus depth that worked. It is a color sense built from blur rather than from multiple pigments. Still a hypothesis under study, but a clever candidate answer to the puzzle. Source: Stubbs & Stubbs 2016, PNAS (pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27382180/); Berkeley News 2016-07-05; phys.org summary.

question: Cuttlefish and their kin rewrite their own genetic messages on a scale nothing else matches, recoding over 60% of the RNA transcripts in the brain where humans recode under 1%. A 2017 study by Rosenthal and Eisenberg found this flexibility came at a steep hidden price. What did these animals give up for it?
answer: The normal speed of DNA evolution, since the genome around each editing site had to freeze in place to protect it
choices: The normal speed of DNA evolution, since the genome around each editing site had to freeze in place to protect it
The ability to pass any brain traits to offspring, since the edited messages are wiped before eggs are ever formed
A working immune memory, because the busy editing machinery mistakes their own nerve proteins for foreign invaders
Half of all their protein diversity, because each new edit permanently silences the original gene it was copied from
context: Coleoid cephalopods — cuttlefish, octopus, and squid — bend biology's 'central dogma' by editing their RNA (the working copy of a gene) so heavily that one gene can yield many protein variants, especially in nerve-signaling proteins. The trade-off Joshua Rosenthal (Marine Biological Laboratory) and Eli Eisenberg (Tel Aviv) found: the editing enzymes need specific genomic structures around each editing site to do their job, so the DNA flanking those sites became evolutionarily frozen — its mutation rate is severely suppressed. In effect these animals traded the ordinary speed of DNA-based evolution for on-the-fly protein flexibility. Source: Rosenthal & Eisenberg, Cell 2017; ScienceDaily 2017-04 (sciencedaily.com/releases/2017/04/170406121601.htm); Nature news d41586-017-00612-y.

question: A hungry bird lands right beside a Darwin's frog on the forest floor, close enough to snatch it. The frog does not bolt or fight back — instead it pulls a trick that makes the bird lose all interest and move on. What is the frog doing to save itself?
answer: Playing dead — going limp and floating belly-up like a lifeless leaf
choices: Playing dead — going limp and floating belly-up like a lifeless leaf
Puffing up huge to look too big to swallow
Oozing a bitter poison from its back
Flashing bright warning colors to scare the bird
context: When a predator threatens it, Darwin's frog plays dead: it flops onto its back and lies still, and it may leap into a stream and float belly-up, motionless, until the danger passes — a leaf-shaped frog pretending to be a lifeless leaf. Source: https://www.wildlifeexplained.com/darwins-frog/

question: In most frogs, the mother's job with the eggs is finished once they are laid. But in Darwin's frog, when the developing eggs begin to twitch, the father scoops them up and holds them on his own body while the tadpoles grow. Where does the father keep his developing young?
answer: Inside his vocal sac, the balloon-like pouch in his throat
choices: Inside his vocal sac, the balloon-like pouch in his throat
Glued in a neat row along his broad back
Wrapped in a jelly ball clamped between his hind legs
Tucked into deep folds of skin on his belly
context: In Darwin's frog it is the father who broods the young: when the eggs begin to twitch, the male scoops them into his mouth and holds them inside his vocal sac — the balloon-like throat pouch he normally uses to call — where the tadpoles grow. Source: https://www.edgeofexistence.org/blog/life-within-a-vocal-sac/  (Legend.)

question: Far below the sunlit surface of the ocean, down in the cold black deep, a sperm whale — the largest toothed predator alive on Earth — dives on a single held breath. Old sailors used to bring these whales up with strange round scars crisscrossing their heads, sucker-scars left by a monster they grapple with a mile down in total darkness. What creature does the sperm whale dive down to fight?
answer: The giant squid
choices: The giant squid
The blue marlin
The leopard seal
The manta ray
context: The sperm whale (Physeter macrocephalus) dives on a single breath to hunt giant squid over a mile down. Source: Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution; Britannica (sperm whale).  (Legend.)

question: The sperm whale is the largest toothed predator alive, a huge grey square-headed whale that dives more than a mile straight down into the pitch-black deep to hunt. When one comes back up to breathe, sailors and biologists sometimes see fresh round wounds ringed across its skin, each about the size of a saucer. What left those circular scars?
answer: The suckers of a giant squid it fought
choices: The suckers of a giant squid it fought
Barnacles it scraped off a reef
The teeth of a rival whale
Lamprey mouths that clamped on
context: Sperm whales often surface bearing round sucker scars, the marks of battles fought in total darkness a mile beneath the waves. Source: American Museum of Natural History, 'Sperm Whale and Giant Squid'.  (Legend.)

question: The southern elephant seal is the biggest seal on Earth — a full-grown bull can weigh as much as a small car. Off the icy coast of Antarctica, it hunts squid far below the sunlit surface. Before every dive it fills its whole barrel of a body with one huge breath, then slips beneath the waves. On that single breath, how long can a southern elephant seal stay under before it must surface for air?
answer: Up to about two hours
choices: Up to about two hours
About ten seconds
Around four minutes
Roughly fifteen minutes
context: Southern elephant seals can occasionally dive as deep as 2,000 meters and stay under for up to about two hours on a single breath. Source: Ocean Tracks; Discover Wildlife, 'Southern elephant seal'.

question: You would expect a diving animal to gulp the biggest breath it can before plunging under. A sperm whale, the huge toothed whale that hunts giant squid a mile below the surface, does the opposite. Right before descending it blows out about 90 percent of the air in its lungs. Why on earth would it empty out on purpose?
answer: So there is almost no gas left to be crushed or dissolved dangerously
choices: So there is almost no gas left to be crushed or dissolved dangerously
So it can float higher and rest between dives
So it can call more loudly to the pod
So warm air does not chill its blood
context: By exhaling most of its air, the whale leaves little gas to be forced into its tissues under crushing pressure. Source: Biologyinsights.com, 'How Deep Can a Sperm Whale Dive?'.

question: A sperm whale hunts giant squid so deep that a mile down the ocean squeezes it with roughly 200 times the pressure at the surface, enough to crush a steel submarine. Instead of snapping under that weight, the whale's ribcage does something no human chest could possibly survive. What happens to the whale's ribs and lungs as it descends?
answer: Its ribs hinge backward and its lungs collapse on purpose
choices: Its ribs hinge backward and its lungs collapse on purpose
Its ribs lock rigid and its lungs swell with extra air
Its ribs fuse into solid bone plating
Its lungs fill with seawater to equalize
context: The sperm whale's flexible ribcage folds inward, ribs hinging toward the tail, and its lungs deflate as it dives. Source: Orca Ireland, 'Deep-diving Adaptations in the Sperm Whale'.

question: When you hold your breath, you keep the air stored in your lungs. A Weddell seal or a sperm whale doing an hour-long dive does the opposite — before going down, it actually empties most of the air out of its lungs so the deep-water pressure won't crush them. Yet it still has plenty of oxygen to burn for the whole dive. Where does a champion diver like this stash the oxygen it will live on down there?
answer: In its blood and muscle
choices: In its blood and muscle
In fat reserves under the skin
In air sacs along its spine
In its hollow bones
context: Deep divers store most of their oxygen in blood and muscle rather than the lungs, the opposite of how a human holds a breath in the chest. Source: Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution; Kooyman & Ponganis diving physiology.  (Legend.)

question: When a biologist cuts into the muscle of a deep-diving mammal — say, a Weddell seal or a sperm whale — the meat is nearly black instead of the bright red of a cow's steak. The reason the meat looks so dark is a special protein packed inside the muscle cells. It grabs and stores oxygen so the diver has an extra reserve to burn through during a long, deep dive. What protein is packed so densely into that muscle that it darkens the color?
answer: The protein myoglobin
choices: The protein myoglobin
The pigment melanin
The blood cleaner hemocyanin
The muscle sugar glycogen
context: Diving muscle is so dense with the oxygen-binding protein myoglobin that it looks nearly black. Source: Mirceta et al. 2013, Science; Discover Magazine coverage.  (Legend.)

question: A Weddell seal in Antarctica finds a breathing hole in the sea ice, takes one last gulp of air at the surface, and slips down for a dive that can last more than an hour. At the surface its heart was pounding like a normal mammal's. The moment it goes under, its body deliberately slows the heartbeat way down to stretch that one lungful of oxygen out for the long dark run below. Where does the seal's heartbeat settle during that dive?
answer: As few as 16 beats a minute
choices: As few as 16 beats a minute
Around 40 beats a minute
About 90 beats a minute
Roughly 150 beats a minute
context: As a Weddell seal dives, its heart deliberately slows (a slowdown called bradycardia) to as few as 16 beats per minute, saving oxygen. Source: Kooyman et al., 'Heart rates in freely diving Weddell seals'.

question: Deep in a dive under the Antarctic ice, a Weddell seal cannot afford to spend precious oxygen everywhere in its body — one breath has to last it up to an hour. So the seal's heart slows almost to a stop and it clamps down the blood flow to its skin, flippers, and gut, letting those parts go cold and starved. Which parts of the seal's body does it steer that saved oxygen-rich blood toward?
answer: The brain, heart, and lungs
choices: The brain, heart, and lungs
The stomach, gut, and liver
The eyes, ears, and whiskers
The muscles, joints, and blubber
context: During a dive, blood is shunted away from skin and limbs toward the brain, heart, and lungs so the organs that most need oxygen get it. Source: Journal of Experimental Biology, 'Adaptations to deep and prolonged diving in phocid seals' (2018).

question: A Weddell seal is halfway through a long dive under the Antarctic sea ice and the oxygen it stored before diving is running low. To keep going, it squeezes a special reserve organ deep inside its belly like a sponge, dumping a fresh load of oxygen-rich red blood cells straight into its bloodstream. Which organ is the seal's hidden blood reservoir?
answer: The spleen
choices: The spleen
The liver
The bladder
The pancreas
context: A diving seal squeezes its spleen to dump stored oxygen-rich red blood cells into the bloodstream mid-dive. Source: Journal of Experimental Biology, 'Adaptations to deep and prolonged diving in phocid seals' (2018).

question: In 2014 a research team off the coast of southern California, tracking a small tagged whale called Cuvier's beaked whale, watched it dive on a single held breath. The dive shattered every record ever measured for any mammal on Earth — even the giant sperm whale had never gone this far. On that one breath, how deep down did the Cuvier's beaked whale go?
answer: Nearly 3,000 meters down
choices: Nearly 3,000 meters down
About 1,500 meters down
Around 2,200 meters down
Roughly 3,400 meters down
context: Cuvier's beaked whale has been recorded plunging to nearly 3,000 meters (about 2,992 m), the deepest dive of any mammal. Beaked-whale physiology is still actively researched. Source: PLOS ONE dive-tracking study; National Geographic, 'Elusive Whales Set New Record'.  (Legend.)

question: A human scuba diver breathing pressurized air the whole way down risks the deadly 'bends' on the way up. A diving whale takes just one breath at the surface and lets its lungs collapse flat as it descends -- and it never gets the bends. What does that lung collapse prevent?
answer: Nitrogen being forced into its blood under pressure
choices: Nitrogen being forced into its blood under pressure
Its blood from cooling too fast to flow
Water from filtering in through the blowhole
Its stored oxygen from leaking back out
context: By collapsing its lungs on the way down, a diving whale keeps nitrogen from dissolving into its blood under pressure, the trap that gives human divers the deadly bends. Source: Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, 'How do marine mammals avoid the bends?'.  (Legend.)

question: A land mammal can pack only so much myoglobin into its muscle before the protein clumps and precipitates into a toxic solid. Deep divers pack in far more without that ruin. Scientists found their myoglobin is re-engineered so the molecules refuse to stick together. What trick keeps them apart?
answer: Each one carries the same positive charge, so like charges shove them apart
choices: Each one carries the same positive charge, so like charges shove them apart
A slick waxy coating seals each molecule off from its neighbors
They lock into a rigid crystal lattice that fixes their spacing
A second protein wedges between them like foam packing peanuts
context: Mirceta and colleagues (Science, 2013) found that diving mammals' myoglobin carries an unusually high net POSITIVE surface charge, from extra lysine, arginine, and histidine residues. Like charges repel, so the molecules push each other apart instead of clumping and precipitating -- that electrostatic repulsion is what lets muscle hold myoglobin at concentrations that would leave a land mammal's meat a toxic solid. Because the charge signature is written in DNA, the team reconstructed ancestral myoglobin across 130 species and read off WHEN each lineage first went deep-diving -- a molecular fossil record of diving. This goes a step beneath 'myoglobin darkens the muscle': it explains WHY the muscle can hold so much without the protein solidifying. Source: Mirceta et al. 2013, Science, 'Evolution of Mammalian Diving Capacity Traced by Myoglobin Net Surface Charge' (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23766330/); mechanism corroborated by review PMC8374505 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8374505/).

question: A whale that dives deep is supposed to be safe from the bends: its lungs collapse and stop nitrogen from dissolving into its blood. Then beaked whales that mass-stranded during naval sonar drills were examined, and their tissues carried lesions that decades of dogma said could never form in a whale. What did the examiners find?
answer: Gas bubbles scattered loose through the soft tissues all over the body
choices: Gas bubbles scattered loose through the soft tissues all over the body
Gas-filled cavities walled off inside the liver alone, and nowhere else
Fat globules clogging the fine vessels of the lungs, with no free gas
Pitted dead patches in the leg and arm bones from a lifetime of diving
context: Whether beaked whales are truly immune to the bends is a real, unsettled debate. Jepson and colleagues (Nature, 2003) found gas-bubble lesions in the tissues of beaked whales that mass-stranded during naval sonar exercises -- evidence of in-vivo bubble formation, essentially decompression sickness, in animals long assumed protected from it. The leading hypothesis is that loud mid-frequency sonar triggers a panicked change in dive behavior, surfacing too fast or altering depth profiles, so dissolved nitrogen bubbles out of blood and fat. The finding overturned the flat 'whales can't get decompression sickness' dogma and remains debated and controversial -- the counter-argument to this ladder's 'never gets the bends' payoff. Source: Jepson et al. 2003, Nature, 'Gas-bubble lesions in stranded cetaceans' (https://www.nature.com/articles/425575a); follow-up 'Whales, sonar and decompression sickness' (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15085881/).

question: A mile beneath the surface of the ocean, where sunlight never reaches, a female anglerfish hangs motionless in the pitch dark. Above her open mouth she dangles a glowing bulb on a fleshy fishing-rod spine — the only speck of light for miles in any direction. She waves it slowly back and forth. What is that little glow drawing toward her jaws?
answer: Prey coming to investigate the light
choices: Prey coming to investigate the light
A mate she is signaling
Rivals she is warning off
Her own young she is guiding
context: The rod is a modified dorsal fin ray called the illicium, and the glowing tip is the esca; it works like a fishing pole. Each species has its own uniquely shaped lure, which she waves to draw curious prey right to her mouth. Source: MBARI, 'Deep-sea anglerfish' (https://www.mbari.org/animal/deep-sea-anglerfish/).

question: Ceratioid anglerfish are the anglerfish with a glowing lure dangling on a fishing-pole spine over their heads, and mouths full of sharp teeth. They do not live anywhere near the sunlit surface where corals or tide pools are. Where in the ocean would you have to go to find one?
answer: The deep open ocean, thousands of meters down
choices: The deep open ocean, thousands of meters down
Tide pools along rocky coasts
Coral reefs in warm shallows
Rivers where they spawn each year
context: Ceratioid anglerfish live roughly 300 to 4,000 meters down in the open sea. Even after decades of deep-sea robot exploration, MBARI scientists have logged only a handful of encounters with them. Source: MBARI, 'Deep-sea anglerfish'; Live Science.

question: A mile down in the deep sea, food is desperately scarce — sometimes weeks pass with nothing edible drifting past. A female anglerfish, a fist-sized black fish with a glowing lure dangling over her mouth, cannot afford to let any meal escape once it drifts within reach. Her jaw is hinged like a trapdoor and her long, inward-curving needle teeth pin whatever she grabs. Together those weapons let her do something most other predators cannot. What can she do?
answer: Swallow prey larger than her own body
choices: Swallow prey larger than her own body
Grind through hard clam shells
Strain tiny plankton from the water
Bite a chunk and let the rest go
context: The inward-curving teeth trap anything that enters, and the hinged jaw stretches to engulf prey bigger than herself — a crucial trick where a missed meal might be the last one for a long time. Source: MBARI, 'Deep-sea anglerfish'; Live Science.

question: A female anglerfish hunts in the black deep sea by dangling a tiny glowing lure right over her mouth. But there is a problem: if her own body reflected even a little of that light, prey would spot the huge fish looming behind the bright bulb and flee. So her skin has one striking property that keeps only the lure showing, while she herself stays invisible in the dark. What is that property?
answer: It absorbs nearly all light, so her body vanishes
choices: It absorbs nearly all light, so her body vanishes
It reflects moonlight sinking from the surface
It soaks up warmth from the water around her
It flashes bright colors to startle attackers
context: This ultra-black skin absorbs nearly all light, so in the deep only the glowing esca gives her away while the rest of her body disappears into the dark. Source: MBARI, 'Deep-sea anglerfish'.

question: A mile below sunlight, in the pitch-black deep sea, a female anglerfish waves a tiny glowing bulb on a fleshy fishing-rod spine over her mouth. The bulb burns bright enough to lure passing prey. But her own body has no light-making organ at all. So the glow has to come from somewhere else, living right inside the bulb. Where does the light of the anglerfish's lure actually come from?
answer: Bioluminescent bacteria living inside the lure
choices: Bioluminescent bacteria living inside the lure
Sunlight she stored during a shallow-water youth
A chemical she secretes and swallows back
Glowing plankton she keeps trapped in her teeth
context: The light comes from symbiotic bacteria (Photobacterium and Vibrio species) living inside the esca. In some anglerfish the bacteria have grown so dependent on their host that they can no longer glow on their own either. Source: Smithsonian Ocean, 'Meet the Tiny Bacteria That Give Anglerfishes Their Spooky Glow'.

question: A mile below sunlight in the pitch-black midnight zone of the deep sea, a male anglerfish drifts alone. He is only a fraction of the size of the huge glowing female he must find to mate. She dangles a tiny lit lure from a spine on her forehead, but the black deep is enormous. For his size, the tiny male carries the largest of one body part of any animal — his ticket to finding her at all. Which body part, and why?
answer: Nostrils, to smell her species' scent in the dark
choices: Nostrils, to smell her species' scent in the dark
Eyes, to spot her faint lure from far off
Fins, to swim great distances quickly
Ears, to hear her moving through the water
context: The tiny male has the largest nostrils in proportion to head size of any animal, and uses this super-sense of smell to track a female's species-specific scent across the pitch-black deep sea. Source: Natural History Museum & Live Science, 'Animal Sex: How Anglerfish Do It'.

question: In the dark of the deep sea, male anglerfish are tiny — barely the size of a fingernail — while the females are huge, sometimes a foot long or more. Finding a mate in miles of black water is so hard that when at last a male does find a female, he does not swim away. He bites onto her side, back, or belly and holds on. Then enzymes go to work at the spot where his mouth meets her skin. What happens to the two fish?
answer: His flesh permanently fuses to hers
choices: His flesh permanently fuses to hers
He drops off and swims away after mating
He rides along, holding on by his teeth
She swallows him whole as a meal
context: Enzymes dissolve the tissue where they touch, so the male's flesh fuses permanently into the female's body — the union biologists call sexual parasitism. Source: Yale News, 'Sea of love: Behind the unusual sexual parasitism of deep-water anglerfish' (2024).  (Legend.)

question: Deep in the pitch-black midnight zone of the sea, a male anglerfish is a fraction of the size of the huge female. When he finally finds her by scent, he bites into her belly and never lets go. His mouth fuses right into her skin, and their tissues melt together until the two bodies share a single joined bloodstream. Over the days that follow, what becomes of the little male?
answer: His eyes and organs waste away to a lump of tissue
choices: His eyes and organs waste away to a lump of tissue
He grows large and dominant on her nutrients
He detaches, having passed her his genes
He develops a second lure of his own
context: He draws all his food straight from her blood, so his eyes and internal organs waste away and he shrinks to little more than a lump of sperm-supplying tissue hanging off her body. Sources: Yale News (2024); University of Washington, 'Deep-sea anglerfishes have evolved a new type of immune system' (2020).  (Legend.)

question: The American biologist Ted Pietsch examined a preserved deep-sea anglerfish of the species Photocorynus spiniceps. Fused to the back of the 46 mm female, like a barnacle riding a whale, was her tiny mate. That fused male, at just 6.2 mm long — smaller than a grain of rice — earned Pietsch's specimen a famous scientific record. What record?
answer: World's smallest known sexually mature vertebrate
choices: World's smallest known sexually mature vertebrate
First anglerfish male ever photographed alive
Only anglerfish male found without a host
Largest size gap ever measured in a fish
context: Pietsch's 6.2 mm male of Photocorynus spiniceps, fused to a 46 mm female, is the smallest known sexually mature vertebrate on record. Source: UW News, 'Small tale: Parasitic anglerfish takes size prize, prof says' (2006).  (Legend.)

question: When a fused male anglerfish shares the female's bloodstream, her body ought to attack his foreign tissue the way ours fights off an invader. Instead the merger holds. What did evolution throw away to let it work?
answer: Key parts of the adaptive immune system
choices: Key parts of the adaptive immune system
The bacteria that light their lure
Their ability to swim after birth
The bones that support the jaw
context: Permanently-attaching anglerfish have discarded the MHC genes, killer T cells, and antibodies that protect humans from disease. Lead author Thomas Boehm noted that in a human, that combined loss 'would result in fatal immunodeficiency' — yet the fish survive on a beefed-up innate immune system scientists are still working to understand. Source: Swann et al. 2020, 'The immunogenetics of sexual parasitism,' Science.

question: In the deep sea a female anglerfish is many times bigger than the male, and in some species the tiny male bites onto her side and their bodies actually grow together — his mouth becomes part of her flesh, and they share blood for the rest of their lives. Biologists don't treat this fused-male lifestyle as a single freak accident. Studying it across the eleven families of ceratioid anglerfish, they found something that makes it a repeated natural experiment. What did they find?
answer: It evolved independently several separate times
choices: It evolved independently several separate times
It appears in only one ancient species
It was inherited unchanged from a shared ancestor
It occurs only in aquarium-bred populations
context: Sexual parasitism arose independently in five of the eleven ceratioid families, which is exactly why biologists study it as a repeated natural experiment rather than a one-time fluke. Source: UW News quoting Ted Pietsch; Yale News (2024).

question: A female anglerfish's glow does not come from her body. It is made by tiny bioluminescent bacteria — living microbes that produce their own light — housed inside her fishing-rod lure. But her babies hatch with a completely dark, empty bulb. No bacteria inside yet. So somehow every new female has to get her own colony of light-makers. How does each young anglerfish come to glow?
answer: She catches fresh light-makers from the seawater
choices: She catches fresh light-makers from the seawater
She inherits the bacteria from her mother
She grows the glowing cells from her own tissue
She absorbs them from the male when he fuses
context: The glowing symbionts (Candidatus Enterovibrio luxaltus and Ca. E. escacola) are picked up fresh from the environment each generation, not passed down through the egg. The tell is in the bacteria's own genes: they still carry a complete flagellar-motility and chemotaxis toolkit that is useless inside a sealed light organ and only makes sense for a free-living swimming stage. Their DNA also shows up in ordinary seawater samples, and host and symbiont family trees do not track each other, so a single symbiont species turns up across four separate ceratioid families rather than each fish lineage having its own inherited strain. Source: Baker et al. 2019, 'Diverse deep-sea anglerfishes share a genetically reduced luminous symbiont that is acquired from the environment,' eLife 8:e47606 (https://elifesciences.org/articles/47606); PubMed 31571583.

question: Anglerfish differ in how they mate. In some deep-sea species the tiny male never attaches to the huge female, in others he grabs on for a brief encounter, and in the strangest species his body fuses onto hers for life, their skin and blood joined. Fusing to a stranger like that should trigger the immune system to attack her partner as foreign — unless the immune system has been broken. When biologists lined the different mating habits up against the immune genes each species had thrown away, what pattern emerged?
answer: The more permanent the fusion, the more immunity is lost
choices: The more permanent the fusion, the more immunity is lost
Every species had discarded the same set of genes
Only the briefly-attaching species had lost any genes
The losses appeared at random, unlinked to mating
context: The immune losses are graded, a dose-response gradient rather than one freak deletion, and this is still active research. Sequencing 31 specimens across four mating modes, Swann et al. found that species that only attach temporarily had already lost the aicda/AID gene that fine-tunes antibodies, while the species that fuse permanently went further and also lost the RAG genes (rag1 and rag2, the recombination machinery that builds antibody and T-cell receptors) along with MHC-I, CD4, and CD8. Functional CD8 was missing in all six permanent-attachment species tested. So the amount of adaptive immunity discarded scales with how committed the fusion is. Source: Swann et al. 2020, 'The immunogenetics of sexual parasitism,' Science (https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aaz9445); review 'Histocompatibility and Reproduction: Lessons from the Anglerfish,' Life 2022 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8780861/).

question: A farmer walks out to check the pasture at midday and finds one of his dairy cows standing perfectly still in the sun, eyes half shut. Her jaw is grinding steadily side to side even though there is no fresh grass in her mouth. She hasn't grabbed a new bite in a long while. What is the cow busy doing?
answer: Chewing the cud — re-chewing food it already swallowed
choices: Chewing the cud — re-chewing food it already swallowed
Scraping algae off its teeth
Grinding down grass seeds it can't swallow whole
Cooling itself by working its jaw like a pant
context: A resting cow that looks like it's doing nothing is 'chewing the cud': it swallowed grass quickly, its stomach fermented and softened it, then sent a wad back up the throat to be chewed again and re-swallowed. Source: https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Ruminant

question: Cattle, deer, and sheep all share the same trick: they swallow grass fast, then burp it back up to chew a second time. Biologists call these cud-chewers ruminants. One of these four African grazers belongs to the same club — which one re-chews its cud?
answer: The giraffe
choices: The giraffe
The elephant
The rhinoceros
The zebra
context: A giraffe is a ruminant too — one of the tallest cud-chewers alive — and the club also includes deer, sheep, goats, antelope, and cattle, all mammals of the suborder Ruminantia that regurgitate and re-chew their food. Elephants, rhinos, and zebras are not ruminants. Source: https://www.britannica.com/animal/ruminant

question: Out on the African savanna, wildebeest and gazelles graze together in huge herds, always watched by hungry lions crouched in the tall grass. These grazers evolved a strange feeding habit: they gulp down huge mouthfuls of grass barely chewing, hurry back to safety, then bring the food up as a soft cud and chew it properly much later. Why swallow first and chew carefully only afterward?
answer: To grab food in the open, then retreat somewhere safe to finish chewing
choices: To grab food in the open, then retreat somewhere safe to finish chewing
To let the grass warm to body temperature before its teeth touch it
To save its teeth, which wear down fast on gritty grass
To swallow the morning dew on the grass before it dries off
context: The whole point of eat-fast-then-chew-later: a grazer bolts down mouthfuls of grass in the open, then retreats to safety and does the careful chewing out of a predator's reach. Source: https://www.britannica.com/animal/ruminant

question: A cow's stomach has four chambers in a row. The first three ferment and squeeze the grass, working like a food-processing plant before the food moves on. Only the fourth chamber digests with acid the way a human stomach does — the animal's true stomach. What is that fourth chamber called?
answer: The abomasum
choices: The abomasum
The rumen
The reticulum
The omasum
context: A ruminant's stomach has four chambers, but only the last — the abomasum — is the 'true stomach' that works with acid like a human's. The first three prepare the food ahead of it. Source: https://extension.umn.edu/dairy-nutrition/ruminant-digestive-system

question: No cow, deer, sheep, or giraffe can actually digest grass — none of them makes cellulase, the enzyme needed to cut apart cellulose, the tough fiber grass is built from. Yet these animals thrive on grass alone. How do they pull it off?
answer: They rent trillions of gut microbes that make the enzyme and digest it for them
choices: They rent trillions of gut microbes that make the enzyme and digest it for them
Their four stomachs grind the grass so fine the fiber falls apart on its own
Their saliva contains a mineral that dissolves the tough fiber
They only absorb the sugary sap, and pass the fiber through undigested
context: A grazing mammal can't digest grass itself — it makes no cellulase. It hosts trillions of gut microbes that make the enzyme and do the digesting, then the animal lives off the products. The partnership is the real trick. Source: https://bio.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Microbiology/Microbiology_(Boundless)/16:_Microbial_Ecology/16.05:_Microbial_Symbioses/16.5B:_The_Rumen_and_Ruminant_Animals

question: A cow lives on tough grass, which she cannot break down on her own. She does the work with a huge fermenting tank in her gut called the rumen, packed with microbes that digest the grass for her. All that fermenting throws off gas, and a single cow releases 150 to 500 liters of methane every day — enough to fill hundreds of party balloons. By what route does over 80% of a cow's methane actually escape?
answer: Out the mouth, as a burp
choices: Out the mouth, as a burp
Out the back end, as flatulence
Through the skin, as it sweats
Dissolved into its milk and urine
context: A single cow burps out roughly 150 to 500 liters of methane a day, and over 80% of it leaves through the mouth by belching — not from the other end. Source: https://beef.unl.edu/understanding-and-mitigating-methane-emissions-cattle/

question: Cattle swallow nails, wire, and other metal debris along with their grass. In the reticulum, the honeycomb-lined second stomach chamber, a sharp fragment can pierce the wall and cause deadly 'hardware disease.' What object do farmers routinely place inside a calf to prevent this problem for life?
answer: A magnet that settles in the reticulum and holds metal fast
choices: A magnet that settles in the reticulum and holds metal fast
A rubber ring that filters out anything hard
A dose of clay that coats and cushions swallowed metal
A second lining grafted over the honeycomb wall
context: Because the honeycomb-lined reticulum traps swallowed metal that can pierce its wall ('hardware disease'), farmers feed cattle a magnet that sits in the reticulum for life, pinning stray nails and wire safely in place. Source: https://vivo.colostate.edu/livestock/hardware.html  (Legend.)

question: A horse and a rabbit both live on tough grass, but neither has the four-chambered stomach of a cow, and neither burps up its meal to chew again. The grass still has to be broken down by microbes somewhere along the gut, or the animal would starve. Where inside a horse or a rabbit does that microbe fermentation actually happen — the spot that plays the same role a cow's rumen does?
answer: In a big pouch called the cecum, well past the stomach
choices: In a big pouch called the cecum, well past the stomach
In the stomach itself, the very first stop
In a fifth chamber unique to grazing horses
In the mouth, mixed with fermenting saliva
context: Horses and rabbits are hindgut fermenters: they digest first and ferment later in a large cecum past the stomach, instead of fermenting up front like a cow. It's the other main solution to living on grass. Source: https://www.furrycritter.com/pages/articles/rabbits/hindgut_fermentation.htm

question: A rabbit ferments its food late, near the end of the gut, so the vitamins and protein its microbes make would be lost out the back before the rabbit could absorb them. Its solution looks strange but works: to get a second pass at all that goodness, what does the rabbit do?
answer: Eats special soft droppings straight from its bottom, then digests them again
choices: Eats special soft droppings straight from its bottom, then digests them again
Licks the nutrients off the grass a second time before swallowing
Stores the droppings in its cheek pouches to reabsorb overnight
Grinds its droppings back into the fresh grass it eats
context: A rabbit produces soft, grape-cluster droppings called cecotropes — packed with vitamins and protein its microbes made — and eats them straight from its bottom to absorb the goodness on a second pass. This is cecotrophy. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecotrope  (Legend.)

question: Picture the last ice age in America, where a wolf-shaped hunter chased huge plant-eaters. The dire wolf and the gray wolf looked alike, so a naturalist might guess they were the same size. Weigh the biggest kind of dire wolf against a big male gray wolf — how did they compare?
answer: The dire wolf was heavier, its largest kind near 68 kg to a gray wolf's 43
choices: The dire wolf was heavier, its largest kind near 68 kg to a gray wolf's 43
The dire wolf was leaner at about 30 kg, a sprinter beside the 43 kg gray wolf
The two matched almost exactly, both close to 43 kg despite the coat difference
The dire wolf was the lighter of the two, near 35 kg to a gray wolf's 43
context: The largest dire wolves averaged about 68 kg (150 lb); a big male gray wolf runs about 43 kg (95 lb) — the dire wolf was the bulkier, more powerfully built animal. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dire_wolf

question: The dire wolf's jaws were built for crushing, not just gripping. When paleontologists study which prey it brought down again and again, one particular menu of big ice-age animals keeps turning up. Which set of prey did the dire wolf actually specialize in?
answer: Ancient bison, western horses, ground sloths, and camels
choices: Ancient bison, western horses, ground sloths, and camels
Woolly mammoths, mastodons, and giant beavers
Musk oxen, caribou, and Arctic hares of the far north
Glyptodonts, giant ground sloths, and long-horned bison
context: The dire wolf hunted huge ice-age plant-eaters: ancient bison, western horses, ground sloths, and camels. When those big animals died out at the end of the ice age, the dire wolf vanished with them, while smaller, more flexible true wolves survived. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dire_wolf

question: For over a century, scientists filed the dire wolf — the massive Ice Age predator best known from the La Brea tar pits in Los Angeles — as nothing more than a bigger, beefier cousin of today's gray wolf. Then in 2021 a research team led by biologist Angela Perri managed to pull ancient DNA out of dire wolf bones and got a shock that rewrote its family tree. Which of these rewrites did the genetic answer actually confirm?
answer: It was no close cousin of wolves, distant enough to warrant its own genus, Aenocyon dirus
choices: It was no close cousin of wolves, distant enough to warrant its own genus, Aenocyon dirus
It was a hybrid, born when gray wolves crossed with coyotes deep in the ice age
It was the direct ancestor of every gray wolf and coyote alive today
It was a dog line domesticated by early Americans, then gone wild again
context: The 2021 ancient-DNA study found the dire wolf was not a close relative of the gray wolf, and it was reclassified into its own genus, Aenocyon dirus. Source: https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/dire-wolves-were-not-really-wolves-new-genetic-clues-reveal/  (Legend.)

question: The 2021 DNA study found the dire wolf lineage had split off roughly 5.7 million years ago — so long ago it couldn't interbreed with gray wolves, with no sign of mixing in its genes. Given that ancient split, which living animals turned out to be its closest relatives?
answer: African jackals
choices: African jackals
Dholes of Asia
African wild dogs
Golden jackals of Eurasia
context: Separated for millions of years, the dire wolf could not interbreed with gray wolves and the DNA showed no mixing. Its closest living relatives are African jackals, not wolves — its wolf-like look was convergent evolution. Source: https://tarpits.org/stories/our-evolving-understanding-dire-wolves  (Legend.)

question: The dire wolf, an Ice Age predator bigger and stockier than today's gray wolf, bit harder than any known wolf — and its teeth paid the price. At the La Brea tar pits in Los Angeles, where thousands of dire wolves lie preserved in the black asphalt, 5 to 17 percent of dire wolf specimens show cracked and broken teeth. In modern top predators like wolves and lions, only 0.5 to 2.7 percent do. What does all that dental damage point to?
answer: They were crunching bone during hard, competitive feeding
choices: They were crunching bone during hard, competitive feeding
They ground down their teeth chewing tough plants and roots
They were losing fights with sabertooth cats over kills
They ate abrasive sand and grit while scavenging in dunes
context: 5 to 17 percent of La Brea dire wolf specimens show cracked teeth, versus 0.5 to 2.7 percent in modern predators — evidence of crunching bone during hard, competitive feeding on big carcasses. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dire_wolf

question: At the La Brea tar pits in what is now downtown Los Angeles, sticky pools of black asphalt seeped up out of the ground and caught passing Ice Age animals. When paleontologists dug in the pits, they pulled up more dire wolves than any other predator — thousands of skeletons — far more than an odd unlucky misstep into the tar could ever explain. What kept luring so many wolves to their death in the sticky pits?
answer: A trapped plant-eater's cries drew the predators, who came to feed and got stuck too
choices: A trapped plant-eater's cries drew the predators, who came to feed and got stuck too
Whole packs deliberately denned in the warm asphalt through winter
Floods swept dead wolves from miles around into one low pit
The wolves drank from the shiny asphalt, mistaking it for water
context: A big plant-eater got mired in the asphalt, its cries drew predators and scavengers, and the dire wolves that came to grab a meal got stuck too — repeating over millennia. Source: https://tarpits.org/research-collections/tar-pits-collections/mammal-collections

question: The dire wolf, an Ice Age predator of North America, actually came in two forms spread across the continent and split by the Rocky Mountains down the middle. The eastern form ran on legs that matched a modern wolf's stride — long, lean, built for the chase. But the western form, dug up by the thousand from the La Brea tar pits in Los Angeles, carried its own quite different build. What set that western dire wolf apart as a hunter?
answer: Its hind legs ran shorter and stockier, making it the poorer sprinter of the two
choices: Its hind legs ran shorter and stockier, making it the poorer sprinter of the two
