Its skull grew longer and narrower, trading crushing force for a faster snap
Its shoulders rode higher and leaner, letting it lope for miles without tiring
Its paws spread wider and flatter, keeping it atop soft ground the other sank in
context: Bjorn Kurten named the split in 1984: Aenocyon dirus guildayi (west of the Rockies, including La Brea) averaged about 60 kg with shorter, stockier legs, its rear limbs roughly 8% shorter than a Yukon wolf's, making it a weaker runner, while the larger eastern A. d. dirus averaged about 68 kg with limbs 10 to 14% longer than guildayi and comparable to a modern wolf's. A 2019 reanalysis (Ruiz-Ramoni & Montellano-Ballesteros) even questioned whether the two are truly distinct subspecies. Source: Kurten (1984); Wikipedia 'Dire wolf' (subspecies section); Dire Wolf Project size page; 2019 Ruiz-Ramoni & Montellano-Ballesteros reanalysis.

question: A green anole is a small bright-green lizard that lives on porches and tree trunks across the southern United States. One morning a hunting bird swoops down and snatches the anole by the tail. In a heartbeat the tail comes free in the bird's beak and the anole sprints away to safety — not even bleeding. How is the anole able to part with its own tail this fast without a bloody injury?
answer: The tail is built to snap off at a weak seam
choices: The tail is built to snap off at a weak seam
The tail is soft and had no bone in it
The bird's grip crushed the tail loose
The lizard chewed through its own tail
context: This is autotomy: deliberately dropping a body part to escape a predator, then often regrowing it. The tail snaps at a built-in weak point so the lizard can run while the predator is left holding the piece. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autotomy

question: On a tropical coral reef, a hungry fish darts down and seizes a sea cucumber — a soft, sluggish, sausage-shaped animal in the class Holothuroidea that spends its life vacuuming the sand. The cucumber cannot swim away, cannot bite, cannot even close a shell. So it fights back with one of the strangest defenses in the ocean. What does the sea cucumber do to its attacker?
answer: It shoots its own internal organs out its rear at the attacker
choices: It shoots its own internal organs out its rear at the attacker
It clamps down and bites with a hidden beak
It inflates with water and floats out of reach
It sprays a cloud of black ink
context: This is called evisceration. The sea cucumber violently squeezes its body and fires its guts out the back end; the organs are sticky and distracting, and it regrows them later. A legendary bit of natural history. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evisceration_(autotomy)

question: A leopard gecko is a small spotted lizard of the dry rocky lands from Pakistan to Iran. When a hungry fox catches one, the gecko's tail snaps clean off in the fox's mouth and the gecko itself scurries away to safety. Back in the fox's jaws, though, the severed tail keeps its attacker distracted for up to half an hour. What is the dropped tail doing all that time?
answer: Thrashing and flipping on its own after it detaches
choices: Thrashing and flipping on its own after it detaches
Oozing a bitter poison that stings the predator's mouth
Screeching to warn other geckos of the danger
Clinging to the predator's teeth with tiny hooks
context: The marquee wonder of autotomy. In leopard geckos the severed tail performs acrobatic flips up to 3 cm high and jumps and lunges for as long as 30 minutes, holding the predator's attention while the gecko escapes. A genuine, well-documented feat. Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2817253/  (Legend.)

question: A shore crab is grabbed by one of its claws in the beak of a hungry gull. Rather than be held there and eaten, the crab breaks free by shedding that whole claw at a special weak joint called the basi-ischium, and scuttles off short one weapon. A crab's body is full of watery fluid instead of tidy blood vessels, so an open stump ought to bleed it dry. How does it keep from losing all its body fluid through the gap?
answer: A membrane at the break plane instantly seals the wound
choices: A membrane at the break plane instantly seals the wound
It plugs the stump with a fast-forming scab of dried mud
Its fluid is too thick to leak from the open joint
It grows a knot of new shell over the gap in seconds
context: Crabs and lobsters can shed a whole leg or claw on purpose at the pre-made break point, the basi-ischium. A membrane there seals the wound instantly so the animal doesn't lose its body fluid. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autotomy

question: A blue crab has just shed one of its claws to escape a gull and now scuttles the sea floor for weeks, short one weapon and unable to fight or feed as well. The lost claw does grow back eventually, but not right away and not on any random day. Crabs grow by climbing out of their old rigid shell whenever their body outgrows it, a process called molting. When does the new claw finally appear?
answer: When the crab molts and sheds its shell
choices: When the crab molts and sheds its shell
When the crab finds and eats enough calcium
When the crab returns to the exact spot it lost it
On the first full moon after the loss
context: A soft, folded limb bud forms at the break and stays tucked away, then unfolds and hardens into a working claw the next time the crab sheds its shell. Source: https://aquariumbreeder.com/detailed-guide-to-regeneration-in-crustaceans/

question: A skink is a small smooth-scaled lizard common in gardens and forests. If a bird grabs it by the tail, the skink can drop that tail on the spot — the loose tail keeps wriggling as a decoy while the skink escapes. Over weeks, it grows a replacement tail, but the new one is a cheap fake, not a true copy. Instead of the original chain of small bony vertebrae, what does the regrown tail contain down its length?
answer: A single stiff rod of cartilage
choices: A single stiff rod of cartilage
A hollow tube filled with fat
A string of brand-new little bones
Nothing solid at all, just skin and muscle
context: The regrown tail has no fracture planes because it is one stiff cartilage rod, not a chain of vertebrae. So if grabbed again, the tail can only break off closer to the body, above the rod. Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9054770/

question: For many lizards — skinks and geckos especially — dropping the tail to escape a predator is a last resort, never a free trick. That's because the tail is doing an important job for the whole animal, holding a store the lizard would badly miss. A leopard gecko's plump, ringed tail is the classic example: a lizard with a fat tail is a lizard in good times, and a scrawny tail means hard days ahead. Besides balance, what is a lizard's tail often used to store?
answer: Fat, the animal's main energy reserve
choices: Fat, the animal's main energy reserve
Extra water for droughts
Venom for its next strike
Spare eggs until breeding season
context: In many skinks and geckos the tail is the main fat-storage organ, so losing it burns stored reserves. A tailless lizard is also slower and often drops in social rank, losing fights and territory to rivals with intact tails. Source: https://www.mdpi.com/1424-2818/17/11/780

question: A lizard's tail snaps off in a predator's mouth and keeps wriggling. A sea cucumber vomits its own guts. A crab drops a claw. A worm splits and both halves grow back. All four are the same escape trick — biologists call it autotomy, meaning 'self-cutting' — dropping a body part to survive, then regrowing it later. Scientists have traced the deep evolutionary history of autotomy across the whole animal kingdom. What did they find about its origin?
answer: Evolution arrived at it independently many separate times
choices: Evolution arrived at it independently many separate times
It spread from one ancient sea-worm ancestor to them all
One animal taught the trick to the others
It is a single mutation carried by every animal
context: Autotomy is such a good survival trick that evolution arrived at it independently at least nine separate times across the animal kingdom, in groups as different as lizards, sea cucumbers, crabs, and worms. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autotomy

question: One European spider almost never leaves the water. It lives, hunts, and raises young among the plants of a still pond. Underwater it shines a bright silver against the dark. What makes the diving bell spider gleam like that?
answer: A film of trapped air clinging to its body
choices: A film of trapped air clinging to its body
Rows of tiny mirror-like scales on its back
A slick of oil it secretes to shed water
Silver pigment in its shell that reflects sunlight
context: Underwater the diving bell spider looks silvery because a film of trapped air clings to the water-repelling (hydrophobic) hairs on its body. This glinting bubble is behind its name Argyroneta, from Greek 'argyros' (silver) — roughly 'silver spinner.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_bell_spider  (Legend.)

question: The diving bell spider lives inside a silk air-dome anchored below the pond's surface. Its breathing gradually uses up the trapped air. Silk cannot manufacture more, so the bell must be replenished repeatedly. How does the spider actually keep its dome supplied with fresh air?
answer: Swims all the way up to the surface and ferries a bubble back down
choices: Swims all the way up to the surface and ferries a bubble back down
Filters dissolved air out of the water using strands of its silk
Lets rising marsh gas from the mud collect under the dome
Cracks the bell open to let stale water flush the old air out
context: To restock the bell, the spider swims to the surface and carries air back down trapped against a dense layer of water-repelling (hydrophobic) hairs on its abdomen and legs, ferrying the bubble down like a delivery. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_bell_spider

question: In almost every one of the world's forty-thousand-odd spider species, the female is the bigger sex, sometimes many times the male's size. The diving bell spider, a European spider that spends its whole life underwater in ponds and breathes from a bubble it carries down, breaks that rule. Here the male is the larger one, growing to about 15 mm against the female's 12 mm. What does the male do that the extra size likely helps with?
answer: Swims around actively hunting through the water
choices: Swims around actively hunting through the water
Carries the female's egg sac on his back
Spins the entire bell for the whole colony
Burrows into mud to survive the winter freeze
context: Unlike almost all other spiders, the male diving bell spider is the larger sex, likely because males swim around actively hunting and need extra strength against the water. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diving_bell_spider

question: A resting diving bell spider can stay sealed in its underwater air-dome for more than a day without surfacing — far longer than the trapped air should last. Seymour and Hetz found the bell isn't just an air tank. What lets it keep supplying the spider with oxygen?
answer: It works like a gill, pulling oxygen out of the surrounding water
choices: It works like a gill, pulling oxygen out of the surrounding water
It slowly releases oxygen frozen into the silk fibers
It captures rising oxygen from plants rooted below it
It converts the spider's own carbon dioxide back into oxygen
context: The silk bell works like a physical gill: as the spider uses up oxygen, dissolved oxygen from the surrounding water diffuses IN through the bell's surface while carbon dioxide diffuses OUT, so the bell keeps refilling itself. A resting spider only needs to surface about once every 24 hours. Source: https://journals.biologists.com/jeb/article/214/13/2175/10328/The-diving-bell-and-the-spider-the-physical-gill (Seymour & Hetz 2011)  (Legend.)

question: A resting diving bell spider's silk dome pulls oxygen straight out of the pond, so you'd think a spider could seal itself in for the whole winter. Seymour and Hetz showed it can't: no matter how much oxygen keeps flowing in, the bell steadily shrinks and collapses within a day or two, forcing the spider back to the surface. What quietly bleeds the dome away even as fresh oxygen arrives?
answer: Nitrogen slowly diffusing out of the bubble into the water
choices: Nitrogen slowly diffusing out of the bubble into the water
Carbon dioxide building up faster than it can escape
Silk dissolving under the steady pressure of the water
Oxygen leaking back out as quickly as it enters
context: The gill is not a free lunch. As the spider burns oxygen, nitrogen's share of the bubble rises (Dalton's law) and that nitrogen slowly diffuses out into the water, so the bell keeps deflating even while oxygen flows in. Seymour and Hetz's model shows a 0.5 ml bell at 100 mm depth shrinks to half its volume in about 37 hours -- exactly why the spider must still surface roughly once a day and why the bells cannot last all winter under the ice. Source: Seymour & Hetz 2011, 'The diving bell and the spider: the physical gill of Argyroneta aquatica', Journal of Experimental Biology 214(13):2175-2181 -- https://journals.biologists.com/jeb/article/214/13/2175/10328/The-diving-bell-and-the-spider-the-physical-gill

question: A dolphin off the coast rises up out of the sea, opens a single small hole on the top of its head called a blowhole, and takes a long breath before diving back under. Its body is smooth and streamlined like a fish's, but that breath through the blowhole gives away that it is not a fish at all. Even though a dolphin lives its whole life in the ocean, what kind of creature is it really?
answer: A warm-blooded mammal that must breathe air
choices: A warm-blooded mammal that must breathe air
A fish that pulls air out of the water
A shark that never needs to surface
A cold-blooded reptile like a sea turtle
context: The bottlenose dolphin (genus Tursiops) is not a fish but a small toothed whale: a warm-blooded mammal that breathes air through a blowhole on top of its head and must surface to breathe. Source: WDC / Whale and Dolphin Conservation, Tursiops biology overview.

question: A bottlenose dolphin is the big grey dolphin most people picture from aquariums and tropical beaches. In its first months of life, a young bottlenose makes up a special whistle all its own and keeps it for the rest of its life. Every other dolphin in the sea has a different one. When a dolphin calls out its whistle, other dolphins that know it recognize who is speaking. What does this personal whistle work like?
answer: Its own name, unique to just that dolphin
choices: Its own name, unique to just that dolphin
A warning siren the whole pod shares
A mating song copied from its mother
A map of the reef sung out loud
context: Every bottlenose dolphin invents its own 'signature whistle' within its first months, and it becomes a personal name for life; signature whistles make up about half of all the whistles a dolphin produces. Source: University of St Andrews (King & Janik); PNAS 2013.  (Legend.)

question: Off Shark Bay on the western coast of Australia, some wild bottlenose dolphins hunt for fish that hide down in beds of sharp, rocky rubble on the seafloor. Poking a soft, sensitive nose through those rocks would scrape it raw. So before diving down to dig, each of these dolphins tears something off the sea bottom and wears it as a protective cap. What do they wear?
answer: A cone-shaped sea sponge over the beak
choices: A cone-shaped sea sponge over the beak
A ring of seaweed around the neck
A shell cupped in the mouth
A crab claw held against the fin
context: Shark Bay 'spongers' tear a cone-shaped sea sponge off the seafloor and wear it over the beak like a glove, using it as a shield while poking through sharp rubble to flush out hidden fish (sandperch) other dolphins can't reach. Source: Whale & Dolphin Conservation USA, Meet the Shark Bay Spongers; PNAS 2005.  (Legend.)

question: A bottlenose dolphin cannot see a fish hiding in dark, muddy water, so it fires a stream of clicks out of its head and reads the returning echoes to map the world around it — a trick called echolocation. But raw clicks would spread uselessly in every direction like sound from a shouting mouth. The fatty, dome-shaped bulge in a dolphin's forehead, called the melon, fixes that problem. What does the melon do to the clicks?
answer: Bends it into a tight, aimed beam
choices: Bends it into a tight, aimed beam
Muffles it so predators can't hear
Stores it up to release all at once
Turns the echoes into a smell
context: The melon is a fatty, dome-shaped lump in the dolphin's forehead that works like an acoustic lens, bending the clicks into a narrow beam so the dolphin can 'see' prey by echo in murky, dark water. Source: biologyinsights.com, Dolphin Sonar; DolphinsPlus echolocation explainer.

question: A dolphin lives its whole life in the ocean and must keep swimming back up to the surface to breathe air. It can never sink into a full, whole-body sleep the way you do in your bed — if it did, it would stop swimming, stop breathing, and drown. Yet dolphins clearly do rest, day after day. So how does a dolphin sleep without drowning?
answer: It sleeps with only half its brain at a time
choices: It sleeps with only half its brain at a time
It floats belly-up and holds its breath for hours
It wedges into a cave and stops swimming
It naps only during the safe daylight hours
context: A dolphin uses 'unihemispheric sleep': only half its brain sleeps at a time while the other half stays awake so it never forgets to surface and breathe. It closes just one eye, the eye opposite the sleeping half. Source: Smithsonian Magazine, Dolphins Sleep With Only Half Their Brain; WDC.  (Legend.)

question: A dolphin firing its hunting clicks is not using its mouth at all, even though the sound seems to pour out ahead of it. To make each click, it snaps pressurized air past a pair of tissue flaps nicknamed monkey lips. Where in the dolphin do those flaps sit?
answer: Just below the blowhole, atop the head
choices: Just below the blowhole, atop the head
Deep in the throat behind the tongue
Inside the beak between the teeth
Down in the chest beside the lungs
context: A dolphin makes its clicks not with its mouth but with 'phonic lips' (nicknamed 'monkey lips') just below the blowhole on top of the head, snapping pressurized air past them to buzz out sound. Source: biologyinsights.com, Dolphin Sonar: How Dolphins Use Echolocation to See.

question: A dolphin has no ear-flaps sticking out of its smooth head, and only pinhole openings where you would expect ears. Yet a bottlenose dolphin hunting by echolocation — firing clicks and reading the returning echoes — catches those faint echoes with amazing precision. The returning sound doesn't come in through those tiny holes at all. It travels through a completely different, fat-filled part of the dolphin's face. Through which part of its body do those echoes travel to reach its inner ear?
answer: Its fat-filled lower jawbone
choices: Its fat-filled lower jawbone
A pair of hidden ear canals
The soft skin of its throat
The tip of its dorsal fin
context: A dolphin hears returning echoes not through ear-holes but through its lower jaw: a thin, fat-filled channel in the jawbone funnels the vibrations straight to its inner ear. Source: biologyinsights.com, Dolphin Sonar; Dolphin Communication Project FAQ.

question: Wild bottlenose dolphins each carry a personal signature whistle, essentially a name. Researcher Vincent Janik found that a dolphin will learn a close friend's whistle and repeat it back, usually after the two are apart. He called this the first known example of what, in animals other than humans?
answer: Calling each other by name
choices: Calling each other by name
Singing a shared lullaby
Passing down a family crest
Warning of a shark by rank
context: Dolphins learn a friend's signature whistle and copy it to address that specific individual, most often when separated from a close friend, as if calling out the friend's name to reunite. Janik: 'Our results present the first case of naming in mammals.' Source: University of St Andrews (King & Janik); Science.org.  (Legend.)

question: Off Shark Bay in western Australia, some female bottlenose dolphins tear a cone-shaped sea sponge off the seafloor and wear it over their beak to protect their nose while they poke through rocks for hidden fish. Most dolphins in the world never do this — only a small group of Shark Bay females do. Scientists wanted to know: is a sponging dolphin simply born knowing the trick, or does she pick it up somehow? Where does a young sponger get the skill?
answer: It learns it from its own mother
choices: It learns it from its own mother
It is hardwired into its genes at birth
It figures it out alone by trial and error
It copies whichever adults hunt nearby
context: Sponging is a taught tradition, not an instinct: calves go to 'sponge school' with mom from birth and start wearing their own mini-sponge by age two or three. Nearly every sponger shares one mitochondrial DNA marker inherited only from the mother, tracing the whole tradition back through the mother line. Source: Science News, Sponge Moms; PNAS 2005.

question: A dolphin's sonar is tested by asking it to tell two metal cylinders apart from several meters away. The cylinders look identical; they differ only in how thick their walls are. Just how tiny a difference in wall thickness can a dolphin's clicks reliably detect?
answer: Thinner than a credit card
choices: Thinner than a credit card
About the width of your hand
Roughly the length of a finger
No thinner than a coin's edge
context: Dolphin sonar can tell apart aluminum cylinders whose walls differ by just 0.23 millimeters, thinner than a credit card, from 8 meters away, and can detect targets out past 100 meters, even approaching 400. Source: biologyinsights.com, Dolphin Sonar: How Dolphins Use Echolocation to See.

question: A bottlenose dolphin plunges hundreds of meters down, far past where a human diver would be crushed or crippled by the bends. As it descends, its heart deliberately slows to a crawl and one compartment of its lungs is allowed to squeeze shut. Why would a diving dolphin let part of its own lungs collapse on purpose?
answer: To keep deadly nitrogen from dissolving into its blood
choices: To keep deadly nitrogen from dissolving into its blood
To force stale air out through the blowhole faster
To make its body less buoyant so it sinks more easily
To warm the remaining air before it reaches the gills
context: On a deep dive a dolphin's body runs a 'dive reflex': the heart slows dramatically (bradycardia) to conserve oxygen, and blood is shunted away from non-essential tissue. Under crushing pressure one lung compartment is allowed to collapse while the other stays open for gas exchange, and blood is rerouted so that very little nitrogen dissolves into the body, a built-in defense against decompression sickness, the bends, which can kill human divers who surface too fast. This is a different feat from half-brain sleep, which keeps a resting dolphin breathing; here the wonder is how the body survives the pressure of the dive itself. In 1965 a U.S. Navy-trained bottlenose named Tuffy was documented diving to about 300 m (nearly 1,000 ft). Source: WebSearch of dive-physiology literature (PMC/Nature/JEB): acetylcholine-driven bradycardia lowers oxygen use; one lung compartment collapses while the other keeps gas exchange, blood rerouted to limit nitrogen buildup; Tuffy dived ~300 m in 1965.

question: The Draco, a small lizard nicknamed the flying dragon, lives in the rainforests of Southeast Asia — places like Indonesia and the Philippines. At rest on a tree trunk it looks like an ordinary little lizard, brown and unremarkable. Then it leaps out into the air and two wide wings snap open from its sides for a long glide between trees. Those wings are thin skin stretched over what part of its body?
answer: Hugely elongated ribs that fan outward
choices: Hugely elongated ribs that fan outward
Long webbed fingers on each hand
Flaps of loose belly skin between its legs
A frame of stiffened tail spines
context: Unlike a bat's or bird's wing (built from arm and hand bones), the Draco's wing is skin (the patagium) stretched over five to seven greatly elongated ribs that swing out from the body like the sticks of a folding fan; special muscles open them and fold them flat against the flanks. Source: PLOS ONE, 'How lizards fly: A novel type of wing in animals'.  (Legend.)

question: Under his chin a male Draco lizard carries a bright yellow flap of skin. He flicks it out to warn rival males and to attract females. To make this flag blaze against his camouflaged body, what does he actually do with it?
answer: Angles it toward the sun so the flap glows
choices: Angles it toward the sun so the flap glows
Pumps it full of blood until it turns scarlet
Rattles it to make a buzzing sound
Coats it in sticky sap that catches the light
context: The throat flag is called the dewlap (or gular flag). Because it is translucent, the male holds it perpendicular to the sun so light shines through and it glows, standing out sharply against his otherwise camouflaged body. Sources: Wikipedia, Draco (lizard); A-Z Animals, Draco volans.  (Legend.)

question: Draco lizards live almost their whole lives up in the forest canopy, gliding tree to tree and eating ants and termites, and are almost never found on the forest floor. Yet one part of the population must climb all the way down to the ground. Who, and why?
answer: Females, to bury a clutch of eggs
choices: Females, to bury a clutch of eggs
Males, to gather nesting sap
The young, to drink from puddles
Old lizards, to escape rivals above
context: Only females descend to the ground: a female digs a hole, lays a clutch of about 2 to 5 eggs, fills it in, and returns to the canopy. Otherwise the lizards spend their entire lives aloft. Source: Wikipedia, Draco (lizard).

question: The Draco, a small lizard of Southeast Asian rainforests nicknamed the flying dragon, glides between trees on two wide skin-wings that fold out from its ribs. Mid-glide it does something no other gliding animal on Earth is known to do. Instead of leaving its wings to hold themselves out with air pressure alone, the Draco reaches forward with its two front hands while it is airborne. What is it doing with those hands?
answer: Gripping the front edge of each wing to hold it taut
choices: Gripping the front edge of each wing to hold it taut
Paddling the air to gain a little more speed
Clutching a leaf it tore off as a rudder
Covering its eyes against the rushing wind
context: The Draco grabs the leading edge of each wing membrane with its hands, holding it taut. Scientists call this a 'composite wing' because two different body parts (the ribs plus the forelimbs) build one wing surface, which also frees the legs to instantly climb or run the moment it lands. Source: PLOS ONE, 'How lizards fly: A novel type of wing in animals'.  (Legend.)

question: Over a summer pond, a slender four-winged insect zips low across the water on wings held straight out from its body. It stops dead in the air and hovers in place — then, faster than a blink, it darts sideways, or backward, or straight up, then holds still again. Its huge eyes almost fill its head. Which insect is this aerial acrobat of the pond?
answer: Dragonfly
choices: Dragonfly
Honeybee
Housefly
Grasshopper
context: The dragonfly's mastery of the air, including hovering and flying backward, sets it apart from most other insects. Source: Iowa DNR '6 cool things you should know about dragonflies'; Sciencenews.org 'The flap on dragonfly flight'.

question: A dragonfly is an insect that hunts over ponds, and its head is almost entirely eye. Two huge glossy domes wrap right around the top of its head, each dome made of thousands of tiny lens-cells stitched together into a single compound eye. That wraparound design gives the dragonfly a field of view most other animals could only dream about. About how much of the world can a dragonfly see at once?
answer: Nearly all the way around, a full circle
choices: Nearly all the way around, a full circle
Only straight ahead in a narrow cone
Just the ground below it
Only what is directly above it
context: A dragonfly's compound eyes wrap almost entirely around its head, giving it nearly 360-degree vision; it can see everywhere except directly behind its own head. Source: Natural History Museum 'Dragonflies: The ultimate hunters' (nhm.ac.uk); ScienceBlogs '30,000 Facets Give Dragonflies a Different Perspective'.  (Legend.)

question: A dragonfly patrolling a summer pond locks onto a hovering midge and shoots forward to strike. Scientists have filmed dragonflies hunting again and again in high-speed video and counted the hits and misses. Over many tries, dragonflies catch prey at one of the highest rates of any predator alive on Earth — higher than a lion, higher than a shark. About how often does the hunting dragonfly succeed?
answer: Around 19 times out of 20
choices: Around 19 times out of 20
Around 1 time out of 20
About half the time
Around 1 time out of 3
context: A hunting dragonfly catches prey on about 90-95% of its attempts, one of the highest success rates of any predator on Earth. Source: Nature World News 'Master Hunter Dragonflies Kill Prey 95 Percent Of The Time'; Smithsonian Magazine '14 Fun Facts About Dragonflies'.  (Legend.)

question: A dragonfly cruises the edge of a summer pond at highway speed — around 30 miles per hour, faster than most people can pedal a bike. Yet if you film it in slow motion, its four glassy wings barely blur. It moves that fast through the air, but beats those wings surprisingly slowly. About how many times each second does a dragonfly beat its wings?
answer: About 30 times
choices: About 30 times
About 600 times
About 5 times
About 200 times
context: A dragonfly beats its wings only about 30 times a second yet flies around 30 miles per hour, a striking payoff-per-beat compared to a honeybee's roughly 200. Source: Meadowia.com 'Why and How Does a Dragonfly Fly?'; Iowa DNR dragonfly facts.

question: A dragonfly darting across a summer pond can stop dead in mid-air and hold a perfect hover, or even fly backward — tricks that a honeybee or a housefly cannot manage. The secret lies in how it works its four glassy wings. Unlike most insects, which flap all their wings together in unison, the dragonfly has a different arrangement. What is unusual about a dragonfly's four wings?
answer: Each of its four wings is driven by its own muscles and moves on its own
choices: Each of its four wings is driven by its own muscles and moves on its own
All four wings are locked together and beat as one
It rides rising warm air and cannot truly flap
It folds two wings away and flies on just two
context: Each of a dragonfly's four wings is worked by its own muscles and moves independently, letting it hover, fly straight backward, and turn on a dime. Source: Sciencenews.org 'The flap on dragonfly flight'; Iowa DNR '6 cool things you should know about dragonflies'.

question: A hunting dragonfly bearing down on a fly does something strange — something a chasing hawk or a chasing dog does not. Instead of aiming right at the fly, the dragonfly aims at an empty patch of sky ahead of where the fly is right now. High-speed footage caught it again and again, and biologists were amazed at the little insect's math. Why does the dragonfly fly toward empty air?
answer: It has already calculated where the prey will be and flies to intercept it there
choices: It has already calculated where the prey will be and flies to intercept it there
It is dazzled and simply guesses a direction
It is trying to herd the prey toward the water
It flies upwind first to save energy before the chase
context: A dragonfly does not chase its prey; it predicts where the prey will BE and flies to that interception point, computing the course before the target even tries to escape. Source: UC Davis Biology, 'How Dragonflies Catch Prey in Midair' (biology.ucdavis.edu/news); Wiederman & Olberg interception research.  (Legend.)

question: The dragonfly you see darting over a summer pond has only a few weeks left to live as an adult — but the insect itself may already be several years old. Almost all of those earlier years were spent in a completely different form, in a completely different place, growing in secret while people walked right past. Where did the dragonfly spend nearly all of those earlier years?
answer: Underwater as a hunting nymph
choices: Underwater as a hunting nymph
High in the treetops
Buried in dry sand
Drifting on the open ocean
context: A dragonfly spends most of its life underwater as a fierce nymph, often for months or years, while the winged adult stage lasts only a few weeks. Source: KQED Science 'A Baby Dragonfly's Mouth Will Give You Nightmares' (kqed.org); Schlitz Audubon 'Dragonflies: Nature's Aerial Hunters'.

question: Before it grows wings and flies, a dragonfly lives underwater for years as a fierce hunting nymph — a stocky brown creature crawling along the pond floor. One nymph sits perfectly still as a tadpole drifts past. Faster than the human eye can follow, the nymph snatches the tadpole out of the water and drags it in. What does the nymph use to strike?
answer: A hinged lower jaw that shoots out and grabs, then folds back under its head
choices: A hinged lower jaw that shoots out and grabs, then folds back under its head
A sticky tongue it flicks out like a frog
A cloud of venom it puffs into the water
A net of silk it casts around the prey
context: The nymph hunts with a hinged lower jaw, the 'mask', shot out almost too fast to see to snatch mosquito larvae, tadpoles, and even small fish, then folded back under its head. Source: KQED Science 'A Baby Dragonfly's Mouth Will Give You Nightmares' (kqed.org); makeham.org 'Feeding and predation in dragonflies and damselflies'.  (Legend.)

question: On a summer morning in the countryside, a naturalist walks along the edge of a pond and finds a hollow brown husk clinging to a reed just above the water. Dragonflies spend most of their lives as underwater nymphs, breathing through gills. The husk is split open right down the back and is shaped exactly like a dragonfly nymph — but it is completely empty inside. What happened here overnight?
answer: A nymph climbed out of the water and an adult dragonfly split its skin down the back and crawled free
choices: A nymph climbed out of the water and an adult dragonfly split its skin down the back and crawled free
A dragonfly laid its eggs inside the husk to keep them warm
A hunting spider drained the nymph and left its shell
The nymph shed a layer to grow bigger and swam back down
context: When ready, the nymph climbs out onto a reed or rock, its skin splits down the back, and the adult pulls itself out, leaving behind the empty shell called an exuvia. Source: Field of Mar 'Dragonfly fact sheet' (fieldofmar-e.schools.nsw.gov.au); Schlitz Audubon.

question: Around 300 million years ago a giant dragonfly relative called Meganeura flew on wings spanning about two and a half feet, as wide as a hawk. It could grow that huge because the ancient air held something today's air does not. What did that air have far more of?
answer: Oxygen, about a third of the air instead of a fifth
choices: Oxygen, about a third of the air instead of a fifth
Water vapor, making it thick enough to float on
Carbon dioxide, which insects breathe to grow
Pollen, an endless food supply for giants
context: Carboniferous air held about 30-35% oxygen versus today's 21%, letting insects breathe enough to power giant bodies like Meganeura, the largest flying insect that ever lived. Source: Geology Page 'Meganeura: The largest insect ever existed'; A-Z Animals 'Meganeura Animal Facts'; Wikipedia 'Meganeura'/'Meganisoptera'.  (Legend.)

question: Every year the tiny globe skimmer dragonfly follows the monsoon winds on an incredible ocean journey, crossing the open Indian Ocean between India and eastern Africa with no land in sight beneath its wings. No other insect on Earth travels this far. About how long is one full round trip of the monsoon migration, which the dragonflies complete relay-style over several generations?
answer: About 11,000 miles, over several generations
choices: About 11,000 miles, over several generations
About 100 miles, in a single day
About 500 miles, along the coast
About 2,000 miles, once in a lifetime
context: The globe skimmer makes the longest migration of any insect: a multi-generation round trip of about 11,000 miles across the Indian Ocean, riding the monsoon winds. Source: Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution 'Unraveling the World's Longest Non-stop Migration: The Indian Ocean Crossing of the Globe Skimmer Dragonfly' (frontiersin.org).  (Legend.)

question: A dragonfly captures prey in mid-air nine times out of ten by aiming ahead. Researchers traced this entire feat to a shockingly small control circuit running from its brain to its wing muscles. How many nerve cells actually carry the prey-direction signal?
answer: Just sixteen cells, eight paired neurons steering the wings
choices: Just sixteen cells, eight paired neurons steering the wings
A dense web of several thousand cells across the brain
One giant command cell wired to every flight muscle
About two hundred cells lining each of the huge eyes
context: These are the target-selective descending neurons (TSDNs): eight pairs whose combined firing forms a population vector tracking prey across the full 360 degrees with a mean directional error near 1.2 degrees, firing about 30 milliseconds after the prey moves, matching the reaction time seen in real hunting flights. A 95% kill rate steered by just 16 neurons is the deep circuit behind the interception wonder. Source: Gonzalez-Bellido, Peng, Yang, Georgopoulos & Olberg, PNAS 2012, https://www.pnas.org/doi/full/10.1073/pnas.1210489109 (PMC3545807, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3545807/).

question: Textbooks say giant Meganeura flew on hawk-wide wings because Carboniferous air was about a third oxygen, which helped its tube breathing. But an even larger relative, Meganeuropsis, spanned nearly 71 cm as the biggest insect ever known. Its existence makes scientists doubt the oxygen story. What about it breaks the tidy explanation?
answer: It lived in the Permian, after oxygen had already dropped
choices: It lived in the Permian, after oxygen had already dropped
It breathed through lungs rather than the usual tubes
It was actually a hovering relative of modern mayflies
It was found in rock far older than any Carboniferous bed
context: Edouard Harle first proposed the high-oxygen idea in 1911, but the largest known insect ever, Meganeuropsis (wingspan about 71 cm, roughly 28 inches), lived in the later Permian once oxygen had already fallen, and recent work argues oxygen diffusion may not have been the real size limit at all. Proposed alternative or additional drivers include the absence of aerial predators (birds and pterosaurs had not yet evolved) and different developmental constraints. Source: Wikipedia 'Meganeura', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meganeura ; PMC2880098, 'Atmospheric oxygen level and the evolution of insect body size', https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2880098/.

question: Two miles down in the pitch-black Pacific Ocean, a pale, ghost-white octopus called the dumbo octopus moves through the water without jetting like its shallow-water cousins do. Instead it slowly beats a pair of broad, floppy paddles that stick straight out from the top of its body, one on each side. What are those two paddles?
answer: Ear-like fins
choices: Ear-like fins
Jet siphons
Sucker arms
Feathery gills
context: The dumbo octopus (Grimpoteuthis) 'flies' by flapping two big ear-like fins on its head/body, named for Disney's flying elephant Dumbo. No shallow octopus swims this way. Source: National Geographic (MBARI Davidson Seamount footage), https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/article/dumbo-octopus-monterey-seamount-news  (Legend.)

question: Deep on the pitch-dark seafloor, the dumbo octopus flaps its little ear-like fins and drifts down through cold water. Most octopuses grab prey and tear it apart with a hard beak. But the dumbo octopus meets a worm or tiny crab in a gentler way. It spreads its webbed arms around the little animal to trap it, then does something no other octopus ever does. What does it do next?
answer: Swallows it whole
choices: Swallows it whole
Bites it in half
Stings it first
Sucks it dry
context: The dumbo octopus swallows prey whole, trapping worms or tiny crustaceans in its webbed arms and gulping them down, instead of tearing them apart with a beak like most octopuses. Source: Smithsonian Ocean + DiscoverWildlife, https://www.discoverwildlife.com/animal-facts/marine-animals/dumbo-octopus-guide

question: The dumbo octopus is a small deep-sea octopus that lives thousands of metres down on the pitch-black ocean floor. It got its Disney nickname from the pair of ear-shaped fins on the top of its head that it flaps like little wings. Most shallow-water octopus mothers lay one big clutch of eggs and then die guarding it. Down where the dumbo octopus lives, the female handles her eggs in a way that surprised the scientists who studied her. How does she manage them?
answer: She carries eggs at every stage of ripeness at once
choices: She carries eggs at every stage of ripeness at once
She lays every egg together in a single spring batch
She waits years and then dies after one huge clutch
She glues her whole clutch to a rock and guards it till it hatches
context: The female dumbo octopus is a 'continuous spawner': she carries eggs at many stages of ripeness at once and lays only one or two at a time, whenever conditions suit, because the deep sea has no seasons to time breeding to. She can also store a male's sperm and fertilize her ripest eggs when she chooses. Source: Wikipedia (Grimpoteuthis, reproduction) + Smithsonian Ocean, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grimpoteuthis  (Legend.)

question: An octopus is boneless jelly, yet the dumbo octopus beats its two big ear-fins with real muscular power to fly through the water. Muscles that strong need a firm base to pull against. Inside its mantle, the dumbo octopus keeps one small piece of hard tissue for exactly that job, a part almost every other octopus has thrown away. What do its fins anchor to?
answer: A tiny saddle-shaped internal shell
choices: A tiny saddle-shaped internal shell
A ring of stiffened stomach muscle
A rod of calcium in each fin
A knot of hardened skin at the neck
context: Almost all octopuses have no shell of any kind, but Grimpoteuthis kept a small U- or V-shaped cartilaginous shell vestige, tucked in a shell sac inside the mantle. The two big fins anchor to this saddle-shaped shell, which gives the muscular fin strokes a rigid base to pull against; its shape is a genus-defining feature of the whole group. So the whimsical ear-flapping is powered by the single bit of hard skeleton the animal chose to keep. Source: Grokipedia 'Cirrina' and 'Grimpoteuthis'; corroborated by en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grimpoteuthis and marinebio.org/species/finned-deep-sea-octopuses/grimpoteuthis-spp/ (Villanueva et al. functional-morphology work on cirrate fin cartilage).

question: On the African savanna, you come across a fresh heap of animal droppings — and a stout, glossy black beetle already hard at work on it. The beetle carefully packs a wad of the dung into a neat round ball, then rolls the ball off across the ground to bury underground as food for its young. Which insect gathers manure this way?
answer: The dung beetle
choices: The dung beetle
The stag beetle
The firefly
The praying mantis
context: The dung beetle finds a fresh pile of droppings, packs some into a ball, and rolls it off to bury as buried food it can eat later. Source: Sci-News, https://www.sci.news/biology/article00844.html

question: A female dung beetle sculpts one special ball into a pear shape, tucks a single egg into its narrow end, and buries it deep underground. In most insects the mother now abandons the eggs entirely. What does this beetle mother do instead, making her unusual among insects?
answer: She stays underground tending the buried ball until her young mature
choices: She stays underground tending the buried ball until her young mature
She flies off at once and never returns to the burrow
She lays hundreds more eggs in the same ball to raise the odds
She dies on top of the ball so her body feeds the grub
context: In many dung beetle species the mother sculpts a pear-shaped brood ball, lays one egg in the narrow end, and then remains in the burrow tending and guarding the developing young — parental care that is rare among insects. Source: NCBI PMC3815100 brood-ball study + San Diego Zoo.

question: Along the Nile long ago, the ancient Egyptians watched a small black beetle push its round ball of dung across the ground, day after day. To them, the little beetle's daily labor looked like an echo of something enormous crossing the whole sky. They worshipped the beetle as the sacred scarab, and carved it onto tombs and jewels. What did they picture the beetle's rolling ball to be?
answer: The sun, pushed across the heavens each day
choices: The sun, pushed across the heavens each day
The moon, dragged through its monthly phases
A seed that would sprout the first green fields
A boulder sealing the doorway of the underworld
context: Egyptians pictured the god Khepri rolling the sun across the sky just as the beetle rolls its ball, making the scarab a symbol of rebirth and the rising sun. Legend/belief framed as such. Source: Britannica (Khepri) + Wikipedia (Scarab artifact).

question: Out on the sunlit African plains, a dung beetle rolls a ball of fresh dung faster than any rival can steal it. Before it begins the long haul home, it stops and climbs to the top of its ball, then turns a slow full circle up there -- a strange little dance in place. Scientists filmed this odd spin and found it does one crucial job for the beetle's journey. What is the beetle doing up there?
answer: Storing a snapshot of the sky to hold a straight bearing
choices: Storing a snapshot of the sky to hold a straight bearing
Scanning below for rival beetles creeping up to raid it
Softening the ball's surface so it packs tighter
Warming its wings for a quick escape flight if attacked
context: Atop the ball the beetle does a spinning 'dance,' storing a single snapshot of the sky in its brain to lock in a straight bearing before rolling. Legend-tier wonder. Source: Lund University, https://www.lunduniversity.lu.se/article/when-dung-beetles-dance-they-photograph-firmament

question: To keep its ball moving dead straight, a dung beetle steers by the Sun by day and the Moon by night. But on a black, moonless night, with no Sun and no Moon to guide it, it still rolls arrow-straight. What faint light in the sky does it lock onto — a first, for any animal on Earth?
answer: The glowing band of the Milky Way
choices: The glowing band of the Milky Way
The faint red shine of the planet Mars
The greenish shimmer of the northern lights
The dim afterglow left along the horizon
context: On moonless nights dung beetles steer by the diffuse band of the Milky Way — the only animal known to navigate by the galaxy. Marie Dacke's team confirmed it in a planetarium, where beetles rolled just as straight with only the Milky Way's band showing. Legend-tier wonder. Source: Science/AAAS on Dacke et al. 2013.

question: The male Onthophagus taurus dung beetle can pull over 1,100 times its own body weight — the strongest insect on Earth for its size, like a man dragging six double-decker buses. Researchers found this monstrous strength did not evolve to move dung at all. What is the beetle actually straining against with all that power?
answer: Rival males it wrestles in the breeding tunnel to win a mate
choices: Rival males it wrestles in the breeding tunnel to win a mate
The packed soil it must plow through to dig its burrow
The suction of wet mud gripping its buried ball
A predator's jaws it must break free from to escape
context: The male Onthophagus taurus can pull 1,141 times its own body weight, the world's strongest insect for its size. This power evolved for tunnel combat: horned males brace and shove head-to-head in the breeding burrow, and the strongest wins the female. Source: Queen Mary University of London; Knell & Simmons, Proc. Royal Society B 2010.  (Legend.)

question: About 380 million years ago, in the Late Devonian seas -- a time called the 'Age of Fishes' -- the top hunter was Dunkleosteus, a fish as long as a bus. Instead of soft skin or fine scales, its whole head and shoulders were sheathed in thick, joined plates fitted like tank armor. What was this natural armor actually made of?
answer: Bone
choices: Bone
Scales
Cartilage
Shell
context: Dunkleosteus belonged to the placoderms — 'plate-skinned' fish whose heads and front bodies were cased in thick, interlocking bony plates. Every placoderm vanished in the end-Devonian extinction ~359 million years ago. Source: fossilguy.com/gallery/vert/placoderm/dunkleosteus

question: Dunkleosteus was an armored monster fish that ruled the seas about 380 million years ago. It could shear apart even heavily armored prey with a bite twice as strong as a great white shark's. Yet when you look inside its huge open mouth, one thing every shark has today is completely missing. What did Dunkleosteus completely lack?
answer: Teeth
choices: Teeth
Scales
A tongue
Gills
context: Dunkleosteus had no teeth at all. Instead of teeth, the front of its jaws grew into self-sharpening bony blades. Source: discovermagazine.com — 'A Prehistoric Sea Monster Wielded Bone Blades'

question: A great white shark bites at roughly 4,000 newtons — bone-cracking force. When researchers Anderson and Westneat modelled Dunkleosteus in 2007, they found it concentrated an even fiercer force at the very tip of its bony blade. How hard did that blade tip bite?
answer: About 5,300 newtons
choices: About 5,300 newtons
About 4,400 newtons
About 2,500 newtons
About 8,000 newtons
context: Anderson & Westneat (2007) modelled about 4,400 N (989 lb) at the cusps and 5,300 N (1,200 lb) at the blade tip — enough to snap through armor and bone. Source: Royal Society, Biology Letters, doi:10.1098/rsbl.2006.0569

question: When paleontologists dug up the fossilized head-plates of the giant armored fish Dunkleosteus, they found some marked with deep punctures -- and those punctures fit the bladed jaw-edges of another Dunkleosteus exactly. When a top predator leaves such matching marks on the armor of its own species, what does the evidence reveal about it?
answer: It ate its own kind
choices: It ate its own kind
They locked jaws in ritual combat
They fought over shared carcasses
Mothers shielded young in their jaws
context: Hall et al. (2016) documented scrape and puncture marks on Dunkleosteus armor left by other Dunkleosteus — evidence it bit through the armor of its own kind, i.e. cannibalism. Source: fossilguy.com/gallery/vert/placoderm/dunkleosteus

question: For years Dunkleosteus was drawn as a suction feeder: a four-bar linkage of skull bones that flung its jaws open in a fiftieth of a second, whipping a vacuum in front of its mouth to inhale prey. A 2025 restudy found its skull held far more cartilage than that model assumed, and reread its cleaver-like blade jaws. What feeding style did the new work argue for instead?
answer: Biting with a wide gape and tearing prey into pieces
choices: Biting with a wide gape and tearing prey into pieces
Inhaling prey whole by suction through a fast-opening mouth
Filtering plankton through fine sieves inside the gill arches
Crushing hard shells slowly between broad flat tooth plates
context: The suction picture came from Anderson & Westneat's 2007 biomechanical model, which found the four-bar jaw could snap open in about 20 milliseconds and complete a full open-and-shut cycle in 50-60 milliseconds. Engelman and colleagues (2025) argued that model rests on anatomy that doesn't match the real skull, which held far more cartilage than assumed, and that the big slicing blades resemble predators that bite with a wide gape and actively tear prey apart (oral processing) rather than true suction feeders, which have small gapes and packed tooth patches. The feeding style of Dunkleosteus is now genuinely contested. Source: Engelman et al. (2025), 'Functional anatomy, jaw mechanisms, and feeding behavior of Dunkleosteus terrelli,' The Anatomical Record, https://anatomypubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ar.70075 ; Anderson & Westneat (2007), Biology Letters, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17443970/ ; summarized at Wikipedia 'Dunkleosteus' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunkleosteus

question: Dunkleosteus fossils keep turning up beside compact clumps of fish bones and half-broken prey remains — some even studded with the teeth of the shark-relative Orodus. Paleontologists read these clumps as something the fish produced, not something it swallowed. What do the clumps show Dunkleosteus did?
answer: It spat back up the bones it could not digest
choices: It spat back up the bones it could not digest
It stored crushed prey in a pouch for later meals
It ground shells into gravel to ballast its body
It brooded its young among piles of gathered debris
context: These compact masses are called boluses, and paleontologists interpret them as material Dunkleosteus regurgitated rather than passed through its gut, evidence that it apparently could not digest bone and other hard parts. Because some boluses contain the teeth of other fishes such as the shark-relative Orodus, they give a direct look at its menu, a rare glimpse of what an animal 360 million years dead actually ate. Source: Wikipedia 'Dunkleosteus' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunkleosteus (bolus / regurgitation and Orodus stomach-content evidence)

question: Deep inside a pitch-black barn where no moonlight or lamplight reaches, a barn owl swoops silently down from the rafters. It cannot see a thing, and it has never even glimpsed the mouse below — yet it drops straight onto the mouse and pins it on the first try. What is the one sense guiding that killing strike in total darkness?
answer: Its hearing, tracking the mouse's tiny rustle
choices: Its hearing, tracking the mouse's tiny rustle
Its sense of smell, following the mouse's scent
Its whiskers, feeling shifts in the air
Heat pits, sensing the warm mouse's body
context: In total darkness the barn owl (Tyto alba) hunts by sound alone -- the faint scratch of a mouse in leaves is enough. Owls have no heat-sensing pits (those belong to pit vipers), and their sense of smell is weak. Source: Payne 1971, J. Exp. Biol. 54:535; Wikipedia, 'Sound localization in owls'.

question: The barn owl's flat, saucer-shaped face is not just a look -- it is a working instrument. A ring of stiff feathers, the 'facial ruff,' lets the owl pinpoint a rustle so faint no other bird would even notice it. What does the ruff do for the owl's ears?
answer: Reflects faint sound toward the ear openings
choices: Reflects faint sound toward the ear openings
Blocks noise from the owl's own beating wings
Damps loud sounds so the ears are not deafened
Sweeps sideways to scan the ground like radar
context: The facial ruff works like a parabolic dish, funneling the faintest rustle to the offset ears. When Knudsen and Konishi trimmed the ruff feathers off, the owls lost the ability to tell how HIGH a sound came from. Source: MIT Press Reader, 'The Genius of the Barn Owl's Feathers'; Wikipedia, 'Sound localization in owls'.

question: The great gray owl of the northern forests carries the biggest facial disc of any owl -- a giant round dish of feathers that gathers faint sound to its ears. On a winter hunt, it does something no barn owl ever attempts: from a perch or hover, it suddenly plunges up to a foot and a half straight down through deep snow, onto prey it never sees. What is it catching under the snow?
answer: Voles it hears tunneling below the snow
choices: Voles it hears tunneling below the snow
Fish it hears splashing under thin ice
Insects it hears chewing at buried roots
Eggs it smells inside a hidden burrow
context: The great gray owl (Strix nebulosa) locates voles purely by the sound of them tunneling, then punches through roughly 18 inches of snow to grab prey it never sees. Its enormous facial disc gathers that muffled sound. Source: Cornell Lab, All About Birds / Living Bird; UC Riverside News.  (Legend.)

question: Snow bends sound like a lens, so a hunting great gray owl doesn't hear a vole quite where the vole actually is -- the little creature seems up to 5 degrees off from its true spot beneath the snow. Biologists call this an 'acoustic mirage.' Just before it dives, the great gray owl does one specific thing to defeat the illusion and line up its plunge. What is it?
answer: It hovers in place, beating its wings
choices: It hovers in place, beating its wings
It closes one ear against the snow
It calls out and waits for an echo
It presses its face flat to the snow
context: Researchers found the great gray owl hovers just before the dive, likely to lock onto the true position from the angle where the mirage error is smallest. Source: Whitchurch et al. 2022, Proc. R. Soc. B 289:20221164, 'Great Gray Owls hunting voles under snow hover to defeat an acoustic mirage.'

question: Many moths take wing at dusk and fly through the darkness, and over millions of years they evolved the simplest ear in all of nature -- just one to four nerve cells wired to a thin patch of skin. Yet this tiny ear is tuned to one deadly sound. The instant that sound arrives, the moth veers or tumbles wildly out of the sky. What is the moth listening for?
answer: The ultrasonic sonar of a hunting bat
choices: The ultrasonic sonar of a hunting bat
The wingbeat of a diving owl
The buzz of a rival moth's wings
The crackle of a spreading wildfire
context: These bare-bones ears exist for one job: hearing a bat's ultrasonic hunting calls in time to dodge. Kenneth Roeder first recorded moth ears reacting to bat calls in the early 1960s. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ultrasound avoidance'; PMC2679932; Roeder's foundational recordings.

question: The tiger moth Bertholdia trigona does not flee a hunting bat -- it fights back, firing ultrasonic clicks at about 4,500 per second. This was the first proven case of one natural trick in the wild. What does the moth's click storm actually DO to the bat?
answer: It jams the bat's sonar into useless noise
choices: It jams the bat's sonar into useless noise
It mimics a mate to lure the bat closer
It signals the moth is poisonous to eat
It bursts the bat's sensitive eardrums
context: Bertholdia trigona blankets the air with clicks so the bat's returning echoes turn to static -- the first proven case of sonar jamming in nature. Attacking big brown bats often reversed or aborted their approach. Source: Corcoran, Barber & Conner 2009, Science 325:325, 'Tiger Moth Jams Bat Sonar.'  (Legend.)

question: Bats hunt moths in the dark by firing bursts of ultrasound and listening for the tiny echo that bounces back off a moth's wings. Some moths have evolved a fuzzy coat of microscopic wing scales that quietly wins this duel almost every night -- the bat sweeps past without ever hearing them. How do the moth's scales beat the bat's sonar?
answer: They swallow the ultrasound so almost no echo returns
choices: They swallow the ultrasound so almost no echo returns
They scatter it into a confusing double echo
They retune the echo to sound like empty air
They bounce it straight back to deafen the bat
context: The wing scales act as a natural sound-absorbing 'metamaterial,' soaking up as much as 72% of the ultrasound that hits them, while fuzzy body fur absorbs about 69% -- so almost no echo returns and the moth is nearly invisible to sonar. One move in a moth-vs-bat arms race roughly 65 million years old. Source: Neil et al. 2020, PNAS 117, 'Moth wings are acoustic metamaterials' (University of Bristol).

question: A bat's shrillest hunting call tops out near 212 kHz -- already so high no human ear could ever hear it, but it is the sound most night-flying moths dread. Researchers wired up the tiny greater wax moth to test just how high a pitch its ear could still detect -- hoping to find where the moth finally goes deaf. How high did the moth's ear still respond?
answer: Up to about 300 kHz
choices: Up to about 300 kHz
Up to about 250 kHz
Up to about 150 kHz
Up to about 90 kHz
context: In this single reported study, the greater wax moth (Galleria mellonella) responded to about 300 kHz -- far past the ~212 kHz peak of even a bat's call -- described as a defense over-evolved to stay one jump ahead of bat sonar. Reported as a study finding, not a settled superlative. Source: Moir, Jackson & Windmill 2013, Biology Letters (Univ. of Strathclyde); ScienceDaily.  (Legend.)

question: A parasitic fly, Ormia ochracea, hunts down a cricket by its chirp to lay eggs on it -- but its two eardrums almost touch, half a millimeter apart. Sound hits one barely a millionth of a second before the other, a gap no nerve can measure. How does the fly still pin the chirp's direction?
answer: A stiff bridge links the eardrums so they rock like a see-saw
choices: A stiff bridge links the eardrums so they rock like a see-saw
It swivels its whole head to sweep the chirp across both ears
It floods the gap with fluid that stretches the delay tenfold
It waits for the echo off the ground to double the signal
context: The fly's eardrums sit only about 520 micrometers apart, so a male cricket's 5 kHz song reaches one just 1-2 microseconds before the other -- far too small a gap for nerves to read directly. Miles, Robert & Hoy (1995) found the fix: a stiff cuticular bridge pivoted in the middle joins the two eardrums and works like a see-saw, mechanically amplifying that microscopic time-and-loudness difference into a large motion the nervous system can sense. The result is directional hearing accurate to about plus-or-minus 2 degrees -- as good as a human's -- from ears almost touching. Engineers now copy the trick to build tiny directional microphones and hearing aids. Source: Miles, R.N., Robert, D. & Hoy, R.R. (1995), 'Mechanically coupled ears for directional hearing in the parasitoid fly Ormia ochracea,' J. Acoust. Soc. Am. -- https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8550933/ ; mechanics/520 um & MEMS mic: Nature Sci. Rep. -- https://www.nature.com/articles/srep02489

question: To prove a barn owl hunts by sound and nothing else, Roger Payne switched off every light and dragged a mouse-sized wad of dry paper across dead leaves. The owl struck it dead-on in the pitch dark. Why did that one crumpled wad settle the question for good?
answer: It gave off no body heat and could not be seen, only rustled
choices: It gave off no body heat and could not be seen, only rustled
It moved far too fast for any eye to track in the dim gloom
It carried the exact scent trail a real live mouse leaves
It warmed under the lamps to mimic a live mouse heat glow
context: Roger Payne's 1971 study (Journal of Experimental Biology) was the landmark that proved owls hunt by sound alone. In a totally dark room a trained barn owl struck not only live mice but a mouse-sized wad of paper dragged across dry leaves. Because a cold paper wad emits no body heat and cannot be seen, its successful strike ruled out both vision AND any infrared/heat-sensing, leaving only the rustling sound. Filmed under infrared, the owl's strikes landed with an error of less than 1 degree in both the horizontal and vertical planes -- and it needed sound frequencies above 5 kHz to do it. This later proved to be the smallest sound-localization error of any land animal ever tested, humans included. Source: Payne, R.S. (1971), 'Acoustic Location of Prey by Barn Owls (Tyto alba),' J. Exp. Biol. 54(3):535 -- https://journals.biologists.com/jeb/article/54/3/535/21635/ ; accuracy-vs-other-animals: Springer, J. Comp. Physiol. A -- https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF00663105

question: Nearly every mammal on Earth grows its babies inside the body and gives birth to them live. Only five living species break that rule and lay eggs instead, like a bird or a reptile. One of them is the platypus. Which of these is the OTHER egg-laying mammal?
answer: The echidna
choices: The echidna
The wombat
The pangolin
The koala
context: The echidna is one of only five living monotremes — the only mammals on Earth that lay eggs. It shares that rare club with the platypus. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Echidna  (Legend.)

question: An echidna is a small, egg-laying Australian mammal that shuffles through the leaf litter hunting ants and termites. Its back bristles with sharp spines that look just like a porcupine's quills -- but they are not quills at all. Each spine is really a stiffened, overgrown hair. What substance are those spines actually made of?
answer: Keratin
choices: Keratin
Solid bone
Horn
Chitin
context: An echidna's spines are not quills but modified hairs made of keratin — the same protein as human hair and fingernails — reaching up to about 12.7 cm long. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Echidna

question: Most people picture the echidna as the spiny little ant-eater of the Australian bush. But three larger, rarer, long-beaked cousins survive nowhere else on Earth but a single island to Australia's north. On which island do those long-beaked echidnas live?
answer: New Guinea
choices: New Guinea
Madagascar
Borneo
Tasmania
context: There are four living kinds of echidna: the common short-beaked echidna of Australia, plus three larger long-beaked echidnas found only in New Guinea. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short-beaked_echidna

question: A mother echidna lays a single leathery egg about the size of a grape and rolls it into a fold on her own belly. Roughly ten days later a tiny, pink, jellybean-shaped hatchling breaks out. What do keepers call this baby echidna?
answer: A puggle
choices: A puggle
A joey
A kit
A pup
context: A baby echidna is called a 'puggle' — a pink, jellybean-shaped hatchling that breaks out of its egg after only about 10 days inside the pouch. Source: https://sandiegozoowildlifealliance.org/story-hub/2022/09/30/two-snuggly-puggles  (Legend.)

question: An echidna is a small spiny egg-laying mammal from Australia and New Guinea, covered in stiff quills like a hedgehog. With its strong front claws it rips open the wall of an ant or termite nest, and instantly hundreds of insects come pouring out to defend the colony. The echidna has to gather them up fast — but it has no teeth in its mouth at all. How does it snatch up its swarming meal?
answer: It shoots out a long, gluey tongue
choices: It shoots out a long, gluey tongue
It sucks them up through its snout
It scoops them with cupped forepaws
It scrapes them off with sharp lips
context: The echidna flicks out a long, sticky tongue that can shoot up to about 18 cm (7 inches), coated in gluey mucus, to snatch ants and termites from a nest it has torn open. Source: https://scienceinsights.org/what-does-an-echidna-eat-its-diet-and-feeding-habits/

question: An echidna — the spiny egg-laying mammal of Australia — is caught out in the open on soft ground by a hungry dingo. A slow shuffle is the echidna's top speed, so trying to run away is hopeless. Instead of fleeing, it plants itself in the exact same spot and does something else to survive the next few seconds. What does it do?
answer: It digs straight down, leaving only its spines exposed
choices: It digs straight down, leaving only its spines exposed
It rolls into a tight armored ball
It sprays a foul musk from its tail
It freezes and plays dead until the threat leaves
context: On soft ground an echidna sinks its whole body straight down in place, until only a shield of sharp spines is left sticking out for a predator to face. Source: https://www.discoverwildlife.com/animal-facts/mammals/echidna

question: A shark hunts hidden prey by feeling the faint electric buzz that leaks from living muscle — a sixth sense almost no land animal shares. Astonishingly, the echidna’s snout does the very same thing on dry land, sensing the tiny electrical signals of prey it cannot see or smell. What does it home in on with this power?
answer: Ants and termites buried in a nest
choices: Ants and termites buried in a nest
Earthworms wriggling in wet soil
Beetle grubs tucked under tree bark
Spiders hiding in leaf litter
context: The echidna's snout carries roughly 400 electroreceptors that detect the faint electrical signals given off by the muscles of buried insect prey — a power almost unheard of in a land animal, otherwise found mainly in sharks and rays. Source: https://echidna.net.au/?p=58  (Legend.)

question: On a moonless summer night, a hunting bat swoops through the pitch-black air over a meadow. There is no starlight and no glow of any kind to help it — the bat truly cannot see the moth flying in front of it. Yet a moment later it snatches the moth right out of mid-air. How does a hunting bat find flying prey it cannot see?
answer: It screams sounds and reads the returning echoes
choices: It screams sounds and reads the returning echoes
It feels the moth's warmth from a distance
It follows the moth's scent trail on the wind
It watches for the moth against the faint sky
context: The bat fires high-pitched clicks, most of them above what humans can hear, and maps flying moths by the shape of the sound bouncing back — hunting by echo, not by sight. Source: Wikipedia 'Animal echolocation'; AAAS 'Discovering sonar in bats'.

question: A bottlenose dolphin is cruising through dark, murky water where sunlight cannot reach and its eyes are almost useless. Even so, it pinpoints a single fish swimming somewhere up ahead. It rapidly clicks with its jaws, sending out bursts of sound — but a special part of the dolphin's body focuses those clicks into a tight forward beam like a flashlight. Which body part focuses the sound?
answer: A fatty forehead organ called the melon
choices: A fatty forehead organ called the melon
A pair of clicking sacs in its throat
The blowhole flaps on top of its head
Its long snout, pointed like an antenna
context: Dolphins and toothed whales echolocate like bats. The melon, a lens of fatty tissue in the forehead, shapes their clicks into a tight forward beam. Source: Dolphins-World 'Dolphin Echolocation'; Dolphin Communication Project 'How does echolocation work?'.

question: A dolphin hunts fish in murky water by sending fast clicks out through the fatty melon on its forehead, then catching the faint echoes racing back. But the place those returning echoes actually enter its head is a surprising one -- not through its ears the way ours work. Where does the returning sound come in on a dolphin?
answer: Through its lower jawbone, filled with acoustic fat
choices: Through its lower jawbone, filled with acoustic fat
Through a soft spot in the skin near its eye
Back in through the same fatty forehead melon
Down through the open flaps of its blowhole
context: Fat inside the lower jaw carries the echo through a thin 'pan bone' up to the inner ear. Emit from the forehead, receive through the jaw. Source: SeaWorld 'All About Bottlenose Dolphins'; ResearchGate 'Behavioral evidence for hearing through the lower jaw' (Tursiops truncatus).

question: The oilbird lives deep inside pitch-black caves in northern South America. Like a bat, it navigates by clicking its tongue and listening for the echoes bouncing off the cave walls. But its clicks are much lower-pitched than a bat's ultrasound. How does that lower pitch change the picture the oilbird gets of its surroundings?
answer: It is blurrier than a bat's, missing fine detail
choices: It is blurrier than a bat's, missing fine detail
It is sharper, catching even tiny insects
It reaches only a few inches past its beak
It works only when the cave is completely silent
context: The oilbird clicks around 2,000 cycles per second — low enough for people to hear, and giving a blurrier picture than a bat's ultrasound, though it still carries well off big cave walls. Lower pitch means coarser detail. Source: Frontiers in Physiology 'Echolocation in Oilbirds and swiftlets' (2013).

question: A hunting bat has been sweeping through the night sky, giving out a slow, steady stream of clicks and listening for the faint echoes bouncing off a moth. In the very last split-second before its jaws close on the moth, that calm rhythm suddenly erupts into a machine-gun rattle — dozens of clicks in a single heartbeat. Why does the bat pour out clicks that fast right at the end?
answer: To fix the prey's exact position for the grab
choices: To fix the prey's exact position for the grab
To stun the moth with a wall of loud sound
To signal other bats to keep their distance
To warm up its throat for the coming bite
context: This 'feeding buzz' fires up to 200 clicks a second, giving the bat rapid position updates to pin the prey in the final moment of the chase. Source: Maryland DNR 'Bat Echolocation'; PMC 'Adaptive Vocal Behavior Drives Perception by Echolocation in Bats'.

question: Bats and toothed whales sit on totally separate branches of the mammal family tree -- one lineage climbed into the air, the other slid into the sea. Yet both evolved echolocation, hunting by sound. When biologists compared their Prestin gene -- a gene that helps mammal ears pick up sound -- the result surprised everyone. What did they find?
answer: The gene had changed the same way in both
choices: The gene had changed the same way in both
It had changed differently in each of them
Only the bats' version had changed at all
The change sat in a vision gene, not hearing
context: Prestin, the protein that powers the inner ear's outer hair cells, shifted in the SAME direction in echolocating bats and in toothed whales — the same molecular answer arriving twice, independently. Source: Liu et al. 2010 Current Biology; Science 'Bats and Dolphins Evolved Echolocation in Same Way'.  (Legend.)

question: After scientists learned that echolocating bats and echolocating toothed whales share the same hearing gene, they wanted to know just how deep the resemblance really went. So they zoomed all the way in on one exact position in the Prestin protein -- the tiny hearing molecule inside their ears. What did they see at that single spot in both animals?
answer: The identical building-block swap in both
choices: The identical building-block swap in both
Two different swaps that both sharpen hearing
A swap in the bat but none in the whale
A missing letter deleted from both
context: At one position an asparagine became a threonine in BOTH echolocating bats and toothed whales — the identical swap, tied to sharper high-frequency hearing. Source: Academic OUP MBE 'Parallel Sites Implicate Functional Convergence of the Hearing Gene Prestin among Echolocating Mammals' (2014).

question: A kilometre below the ocean surface, in the crushing black of the deep, a sperm whale hunts giant squid by scanning the darkness with clicks. The clicks are so powerful that scientists rank the sperm whale the loudest animal on Earth — louder than a jet engine at takeoff. Where inside the whale's blocky body is that record-breaking blast of sound actually generated?
answer: A huge spermaceti organ filling its blocky head
choices: A huge spermaceti organ filling its blocky head
A pair of oversized lungs deep in its chest
Twin sound sacs riding along its spine
A resonating chamber inside its tail flukes
context: Sperm-whale clicks reach near 230 decibels underwater, made by the enormous spermaceti organ that fills the head, used to hunt squid in total darkness a kilometre down. Source: Wikipedia 'Sperm whale'; Grokipedia 'Spermaceti organ'.  (Legend.)

question: A sperm whale hunts squid a mile below the surface using the loudest click in the animal kingdom, but it has no voice box. Instead it shoves air through a pair of lip-like flaps at the very front of its huge skull -- the flaps whalers nicknamed the 'monkey lips.' After that first pulse of sound leaves the flaps, what happens inside the whale's head before a full click finally shoots forward?
answer: It bounces between two air sacs in the head
choices: It bounces between two air sacs in the head
It is swallowed and re-fired through the throat
It splits evenly out of both sides at once
It fades out and a fresh pulse starts over
context: The pulse ricochets between two air sacs inside the head, and a slice of energy escapes forward as each click. Source: Wikipedia 'Sperm whale'; ScienceInsights 'How the Spermaceti Organ Works in a Sperm Whale'.

question: A horseshoe bat is named for the horseshoe-shaped skin flap around its nose, and it hunts by holding its call at one exact note. But as it speeds toward its target, its own motion should raise the pitch of the returning echo -- a Doppler rise that would throw off ears tuned to that single note. The bat cancels the shift out mid-chase. How does it do it?
answer: It lowers the pitch of its own outgoing call
choices: It lowers the pitch of its own outgoing call
It briefly stops flapping to slow itself down
It closes its ears until the echo settles
It fires a second call at a matching pitch
context: By shifting its call frequency down to offset its own speed, the greater horseshoe bat keeps the returning echo at the fixed pitch its ear is tuned to. Source: Wikipedia 'Doppler shift compensation'; Springer 'Control of Doppler shift compensation in the greater horseshoe bat, Rhinolophus ferrumequinum'.

question: The horseshoe bat is unusual among bats: instead of sweeping through different pitches, it locks its echolocation call to a single steady tone and listens for that exact tone to come back. A moth trying to hide silently among the leaves of a bush still gives itself away — the returning echo carries a tiny, rapid, rhythmic flicker riding on top of the steady note. What is making that flicker in the echo?
answer: The beating of the moth's wings
choices: The beating of the moth's wings
The moth's warm body cooling the air
The rustle of the leaves in the wind
The bat's own heartbeat in its ears
context: A fluttering moth's wingbeats show up as a 'glint' in the pitch-locked echo — telling the bat there's living prey ahead, even hidden in foliage. Source: Springer 'Auditory fovea and Doppler shift compensation: adaptations for flutter detection in echolocating bats using CF-FM signals'.

question: Not all moths take a bat's sonar lying down. The tiger moth Bertholdia trigona of the American deserts fights back with its own ultrasound -- firing clicks from little drum-like plates on its body thousands of times a second, the moment a bat's cries lock onto it. What does that barrage of moth-clicks do to the attacking bat?
answer: It jams the bat's sonar and spoils the strike
choices: It jams the bat's sonar and spoils the strike
It lures the bat toward a decoy target
It signals the bat that the moth is poisonous
It deafens the bat for the rest of the night
context: Bertholdia trigona fires clicks up to 4,500 times a second to jam a bat's sonar — the most effective anti-bat defense documented, cutting the bat's capture success roughly tenfold.
