context: A substance in horseshoe-crab blood clots instantly around bacterial contamination, catching it in vaccines and drugs. Source: AssayGenie, 'Horseshoe Crab Blood and Endotoxin Testing'; Natural History Museum, 'Horseshoe crab blood: the miracle vaccine ingredient'.

question: An octopus is a boneless sea animal with eight arms and blue, copper-based blood. Inside its body sit three hearts. Two of them, called branchial hearts, sit right beside the gills and handle just one job — loading fresh oxygen onto the blood as it flows through the gill tissue. Why does that loading job need its own dedicated pair of hearts?
answer: It takes a high pressure of its own
choices: It takes a high pressure of its own
It has to be kept ice-cold
It only happens while the octopus sleeps
It uses a different colored blood
context: The octopus must hold different blood pressures at the same time: high pressure at the gills to load oxygen, and a separate push from the systemic heart to send that blood to the body — so the gill-loading job gets its own dedicated pair of hearts. Source: Smithsonian Magazine; This Amazing World comparative physiology summaries.

question: The octopus is a boneless sea animal with eight sucker-lined arms and blood that runs pale blue instead of red. Blood carries oxygen with the help of a metal — human blood turns red from iron, packed into a molecule called hemoglobin. Octopus blood uses a different metal, in a molecule called hemocyanin. Which metal ferries oxygen in an octopus and turns its blood blue?
answer: Copper
choices: Copper
Gold
Zinc
Silver
context: The octopus carries oxygen with hemocyanin, a copper-based protein; copper turns blue with oxygen the way iron-based hemoglobin turns our blood red. The horseshoe crab has blue blood for the exact same reason. Source: Smithsonian Magazine octopus article.

question: An octopus is a boneless sea creature with three hearts and blue, copper-based blood that carries oxygen more weakly than our red blood. It can squirt water out of a funnel called a siphon and jet through open sea in a fast burst — but it almost always crawls slowly across the sea floor instead. What happens inside the octopus that makes a single burst of jetting so exhausting?
answer: Its main heart stops beating
choices: Its main heart stops beating
Blood pools uselessly in its arms
Its gills can't reload oxygen fast enough
Its blue pigment can't hold enough oxygen
context: The systemic (main) heart actually stops beating when the octopus jets through open water, which exhausts it, so octopuses usually prefer to crawl. Source: Smithsonian Magazine, 'Ten Wild Facts About Octopuses'.

question: The giraffe is the tallest animal alive, standing up to 5.5 metres, and it browses leaves at the top of African acacia trees. Its heart must drive blood straight up a two-metre neck to reach a brain perched high above the shoulders, fighting gravity the whole way. Compared with a human's blood pressure, how strong is the giraffe's?
answer: About double a human's
choices: About double a human's
About the same as a human's
About half a human's
Almost none at all
context: A giraffe's blood pressure reaches roughly 280/180 to 300/180 mmHg, about double a human's, to force blood up the long neck. Source: Novartis, 'Giraffes have high blood pressure. Why don't they drop dead?'; Giraffe Conservation Foundation.

question: A giraffe is the tallest animal alive — its head can stand nearly six meters above the ground. To drink at an African waterhole, it must splay its long front legs and lower that head far below its own heart. All that blood should then rush downhill and knock the giraffe out cold. But something in its neck stops the flood from ever hitting its brain. What does the trick?
answer: One-way valves in its neck veins
choices: One-way valves in its neck veins
A muscular ring inside its aorta
A valve at the exit of its heart
A clamp of muscle at the base of the skull
context: Valves in the neck veins block blood from rushing back into the skull, so the giraffe does not pass out from the sudden pressure surge when it lowers its head to drink. Source: Novartis, 'Giraffes have high blood pressure...'; Hemodynamics and Drinking in the Giraffe, PMC12012874.

question: The horseshoe crab is a helmet-shaped Atlantic sea creature older than the dinosaurs, with pale blue blood unlike any other animal's. Its blood is one of the most valuable liquids on Earth because of what happens the instant bacteria contaminate a vaccine or drug it is testing. How does horseshoe-crab blood catch that contamination?
answer: It clots into a gel around it
choices: It clots into a gel around it
It changes color to flag the batch
It binds the toxin so it can be filtered out
It triggers immune cells to swarm it
context: A substance in horseshoe-crab blood clots instantly around bacterial contamination, catching it in vaccines and drugs; the blood is worth roughly $60,000 a gallon. Source: AssayGenie; Natural History Museum, 'Horseshoe crab blood: the miracle vaccine ingredient'.

question: The Antarctic icefish is the only backboned animal on Earth with no red blood cells and no oxygen-carrying pigment. Its blood runs clear as water, so it must pump huge volumes with an oversized heart just to stay alive. What is the pigment that its blood is missing?
answer: Hemoglobin
choices: Hemoglobin
Melanin
Chlorophyll
Keratin
context: The icefish's enormous heart pumps about five times more blood than a normal fish and burns roughly 22% of the fish's energy budget (versus about 5% in ordinary fish) just to move that thin, pigment-free blood, helped by cold, oxygen-rich Antarctic water. Source: Wikipedia, 'Channichthyidae'; Scientific American icefish article.

question: Cut open an earthworm and you find no single chambered heart at all. The worm has no chest and no ribs — just a soft tube of a body slithering through wet garden soil. Instead of one big pump, a set of muscular tubes wraps around the front of its gut and squeezes rhythmically, one after another, to push its dark red blood along. How many of these pumping 'hearts' does an earthworm actually carry?
answer: Five pairs
choices: Five pairs
A single pair
Twelve pairs
One large one
context: The earthworm has no single heart; it uses five pairs of pulsing 'aortic arches' (often called pseudohearts) that squeeze rhythmically to push blood around its closed circulatory system. Source: Sciencing, 'How Many Hearts Does An Earthworm Have?'; CK-12, 'What is unique about an earthworm's heart?'.

question: The Antarctic icefish is the only backboned animal whose blood carries no hemoglobin. Biologists once assumed it had simply switched off making the protein in the cold. Reading its genome overturned that view: the explanation was more final than a switched-off gene. What had actually happened to the icefish's hemoglobin?
answer: The gene itself is physically deleted
choices: The gene itself is physically deleted
The gene is silenced but still intact
The protein misfolds and is destroyed
A cold-triggered mutation stalls it
context: In 15 of the 16 crocodile-icefish species the beta-globin gene is entirely gone and the alpha-globin gene is partly deleted — the DNA is missing, not merely switched off. The loss of myoglobin, the oxygen-store protein in muscle, happened separately and independently at least four times, so 6 of the 16 species also lack myoglobin in the heart. To move oxygen dissolved straight in watery plasma, icefish evolved blood volumes up to four times a red-blooded fish's, unusually wide capillaries, and a cardiac output about five times greater — yet their blood still carries under 20% the oxygen of their hemoglobin-bearing relatives. Source: Sidell & O'Brien, 'When bad things happen to good fish: the loss of hemoglobin and myoglobin expression in Antarctic icefishes,' Journal of Experimental Biology 209:1791 (2006); Wikipedia 'Crocodile icefish' (gene-deletion, 4x blood volume, 5x cardiac output).

question: Horseshoe-crab blood is drawn by medicine because a single kind of blood cell, the amebocyte, jams the sample into a gel the instant it meets bacterial contamination. Granules inside that cell hold one named protein that the alarm cascade converts into the clot. Which protein is it?
answer: Coagulogen
choices: Coagulogen
Hemocyanin
Fibrinogen
Thrombin
context: The crab's blood cells, called amebocytes, are packed with granules of a protein named coagulogen. When they touch bacterial endotoxin (lipopolysaccharide, LPS), a clotting-factor cascade fires and converts the coagulogen into a gel clot — this is the LAL (Limulus amebocyte lysate) test. It carries an ethical cost: bleeding is estimated to kill roughly 22-30% of the returned crabs. A synthetic drop-in replacement, recombinant Factor C (rFC), was recognized by the US Pharmacopeia (chapter <86>) in May 2025, offering a path to stop bleeding wild crabs. Source: Wikipedia 'Limulus amebocyte lysate' (amebocytes, coagulogen granules, LPS-triggered cascade; 22%/30% mortality from a 2009 Massachusetts study; recombinant Factor C and USP <86> official May 2025).

question: You are driving a country road at night when two coins of greenish-gold light flare in your headlights at the edge of the woods, then vanish as a deer turns its head. That glow comes from a layer built into the deer's eye that your own eyes lack. What is that layer?
answer: A mirror-like sheet behind the retina that bounces light back through it
choices: A mirror-like sheet behind the retina that bounces light back through it
A clear oily film spread across the front of the eyeball
A ring of tiny muscles that widens the pupil in the dark
A dense mat of blood vessels that feeds the retina from behind
context: That mirror is the tapetum lucidum, Latin for 'bright tapestry.' It sits behind the retina and reflects light that the photoreceptors missed on the way in, sending it back through them so the eye gets a second chance to catch each scrap of light. Humans and most other primates have none, so our eyes don't shine. Source: Britannica, 'tapetum lucidum'; Wikipedia, 'Tapetum lucidum.'

question: A cat's eyes blaze back at you from a dark room, but yours photograph as ordinary red 'red-eye' in a flash. The cat has a mirror behind its retina that throws light back out; you do not. So where does the plain red glow in a human flash photo actually come from?
answer: Blood in the retina at the back of the eye lighting up in the flash
choices: Blood in the retina at the back of the eye lighting up in the flash
The camera's own flash bulb reflected off the wet cornea
The colored iris reflecting the camera's light straight back
A film of tears scattering the flash across the front of the eye
context: Because humans and most primates lack a tapetum lucidum entirely, a flash reaches the back of the eye and lights up the blood-rich retina, and the camera catches that red. A cat's mirror, by contrast, retro-reflects the light straight back, so its eyes shine instead of going red. Source: Institute for Environmental Research and Education, 'What animals have a tapetum?'; Wikipedia, 'Tapetum lucidum.'

question: A house cat can pick out a moving mouse in near-total darkness — light so dim it would leave you completely blind. But that same cat cannot tell your red toy mouse from a green one the way you can. Deep in the eye, the retina is the sheet of cells that actually catches light. To be so good in the dark, a cat's retina made a trade with color. What is a cat's retina packed with?
answer: Rod cells, six to eight times as many as a human eye holds
choices: Rod cells, six to eight times as many as a human eye holds
Cone cells, packed far more densely than a human's
Extra lenses layered inside to magnify what little light there is
A second, deeper retina that switches on only after dark
context: A cat's retina packs six to eight times more rods than ours and very few cones. Rods register dim light and movement superbly but not color or fine detail, so the cat trades a rich color world for the power to see shapes and motion in near-blackness, exactly what a small ambush predator needs. Source: ScienceInsights, 'Can Cats See in the Dark?'

question: Not every glowing eye caught in headlights shines the same color. A cat's eyes flash green, a raccoon's yellow, a rabbit's red, and many dogs' eyes flash bright blue. That difference is not the color of the headlight or the angle of the beam. Deep behind the retina of a night-active animal is a mirror layer called the tapetum that bounces stray light back onto the eye. Something about that mirror decides what color you see. What actually sets it?
answer: What the mirror layer is built from, such as zinc, riboflavin, or collagen
choices: What the mirror layer is built from, such as zinc, riboflavin, or collagen
How wide the pupil happens to be opened at that moment
The color of the fur or scales surrounding the animal's eyes
How far the light source sits from the animal when it looks up
context: The tapetum lucidum can be built from crystals of zinc, riboflavin, or collagen, and each material reflects a different band of wavelengths. So the mirror's own recipe sets the glow color, which is why a fox, a cat, and a raccoon flash different hues in the same headlights. Source: scienceabc.com, 'Why Do Cats' Eyes Glow?'

question: The tarsier is a mouse-sized primate that clings to trees in the forests of Southeast Asia and hunts insects by moonlight. Most nocturnal mammals have a tapetum — a mirror layer behind the retina that bounces stray light back and roughly doubles what the eye catches. But the tarsier's daytime ancestors lost that mirror long ago, and its kind never grew it back. With no tapetum at all to help, how does the tarsier still gather enough moonlight to hunt?
answer: Each eyeball grew to the size of its own brain, the largest eyes for its body of any mammal
choices: Each eyeball grew to the size of its own brain, the largest eyes for its body of any mammal
It grew a second pair of smaller eyes above the first to double its light
Its eyes glow from within, casting their own faint light onto prey
It hunts by touch and hearing alone, its eyes nearly useless in the dark
context: A tarsier eyeball is about 16 mm across, as large as or larger than its whole brain and equal to it by volume, the biggest eyes relative to body size of any mammal. Because tarsiers lost the tapetum and never got it back, that enormous light-gathering eye is their entire compensation. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tarsier'; Collins et al. 2005, 'Overview of the visual system of Tarsius.'  (Legend.)

question: Arctic reindeer see through months of dim polar twilight, and researchers in 2013 discovered their eye-mirror does something no mammal had shown before: it changes color with the seasons, gold in summer. For the dark months it scatters more light sideways through the retina instead of reflecting it directly back. What color does it turn by winter?
answer: Deep blue
choices: Deep blue
Bright red
Silvery white
Pale green
context: Stokkan and colleagues (2013, Proc. R. Soc. B) showed the reindeer tapetum shifts from gold in summer to deep blue by winter. Blue reflects less light straight back out and scatters more of it sideways through the retina, raising sensitivity in the long Arctic twilight. It was the first seasonal color change of an eye-mirror ever shown in a mammal. Source: Stokkan et al. 2013 via ScienceDaily; National Geographic.  (Legend.)

question: In the near-black mesopelagic zone, the barreleye fish hangs motionless and stares straight up through a transparent forehead, watching for faint silhouettes drifting overhead. Its eyes are not the usual round balls. What unusual shape do they take, and why?
answer: Tube-shaped, because a tube gathers far more light than a round eye of the same width
choices: Tube-shaped, because a tube gathers far more light than a round eye of the same width
Flat and disc-shaped, to spread across the widest possible view
Mirror-backed spheres that swivel like a chameleon's independently
Split in two, one half tuned for light and the other for motion
context: The deep-sea barreleye grows tubular, barrel-shaped eyes that a tube of the same width out-gathers a round eye for light, pure light-harvesting for the dark. To beat the narrow field of view a fixed tube would give, it can swivel the eyes: it hangs with them pointed up, then rotates them forward and swims up to feed when it spots a jelly. Source: MBARI, 'Researchers solve mystery of deep-sea fish with tubular eyes and transparent head.'

question: Vision scientists studied the eye of the colossal squid, a dinner-plate orb about 27 cm across with a lens the size of an orange, and asked what payoff could be worth building the largest eye in the animal kingdom's history. Dan-Eric Nilsson and Eric Warrant argued it is tuned to catch one particular signal in the black deep. What?
answer: The faint glow a hunting sperm whale stirs up in the plankton around it
choices: The faint glow a hunting sperm whale stirs up in the plankton around it
The blue-green flashes of the bioluminescent prey it hunts
The lantern lures of anglerfish hanging in the dark below it
The glow of a passing shoal of lanternfish drifting overhead
context: Nilsson and Warrant argued the colossal and giant squid's dinner-plate eye is tuned to spot the faint bioluminescent glow a diving sperm whale, its main predator, stirs up in the plankton, an early-warning system in the black deep. At about 27 cm, it is likely the biggest eye ever to exist. Source: NCBI/PMC, 'The giant eyes of giant squid...'; Te Papa Museum, 'The eyes of the colossal squid.'  (Legend.)

question: In the pine woods and swamps of the southern United States lives the harmless scarlet kingsnake, brightly banded in red, yellow, and black. Its little jaws cannot bite hard enough to hurt a person. Yet predators still leave it alone — because it looks almost exactly like a truly deadly banded snake that lives in the same region, one whose neurotoxic bite can kill a grown man. Which venomous snake is the scarlet kingsnake imitating?
answer: The coral snake
choices: The coral snake
The copperhead
The cottonmouth
The timber rattlesnake
context: The harmless scarlet kingsnake and milk snake copy the coral snake's banded pattern so predators leave them alone. People use rhymes to tell them apart: 'red touches yellow, kill a fellow; red touches black, venom lack.' Source: Wikipedia 'Scarlet kingsnake / Milk snake'.

question: A harmless scarlet kingsnake in coral-snake colors is perfectly safe in one Florida county but gets eaten by birds in the next county over. Both counties have the same birds and the same kingsnakes. What is different about the safe county that makes the borrowed warning look actually work?
answer: Real coral snakes live there and taught predators to fear the pattern
choices: Real coral snakes live there and taught predators to fear the pattern
Kingsnakes there interbreed enough to keep their colors bright
Kingsnakes there smell like coral snakes, not just look like them
The soil there matches the color of the kingsnake's bands
context: Batesian mimicry only works where the dangerous model lives: predators near actual coral snakes have learned to fear the pattern, so a copy is protected — but the bluff fails where no coral snakes exist to teach the lesson. Source: PBS NOVA 'How the Kingsnake Is Still Fooling Predators'; UNC Endeavors 'A Striking Resemblance' (Pfennig research).

question: Look at a swarm of stinging wasps and bees and you'll notice something odd. Dozens of dangerous species all wear nearly the same black-and-yellow uniform, and none of them is a harmless faker. Why would many truly dangerous species evolve to look alike?
answer: So a predator only has to learn the one warning look once
choices: So a predator only has to learn the one warning look once
So they can recognize and swarm each other in defense
So the strongest species can hide among the weaker ones
So the pattern blends them into yellow flowers
context: This is Mullerian mimicry — several genuinely dangerous species converge on ONE warning look, so predators learn the lesson faster and every species benefits. It's different from Batesian mimicry, where a single harmless faker cheats off a dangerous model. Source: Wikipedia 'Mullerian mimicry'.

question: On the muddy bottom of a river an alligator snapping turtle sits stone-still with its mouth wide open. Something small and pink wiggles gently deep inside that gaping mouth, and a fish darts in to grab it — then the jaws slam shut. What is that wriggling pink lure?
answer: A worm-shaped part of the turtle's own tongue
choices: A worm-shaped part of the turtle's own tongue
A leech clinging to its jaw
A live minnow it caught earlier
A dangling bit of algae
context: The alligator snapping turtle wiggles a worm-shaped appendage on its tongue — a hunting trick called lingual luring, a form of aggressive mimicry, where a fake friendly signal LURES prey close instead of scaring predators off. Source: Wikipedia 'Alligator snapping turtle / Lingual luring'; HowStuffWorks.  (Legend.)

question: Off the sandy Indo-Pacific seafloor, the mimic octopus does something almost no other animal can. It does not just hide; it impersonates other animals on demand. In one of its best-known disguises, which venomous, spiny-finned fish does it pretend to be?
answer: A lionfish
choices: A lionfish
A pufferfish
A moray eel
A stonefish
context: The mimic octopus shapeshifts into several animals: arms held out radially to look like a spiny lionfish, six arms hidden and two held straight to mimic a banded sea snake, and all eight flattened behind it to glide like a flatfish. Source: Wikipedia 'Mimic octopus'.  (Legend.)

question: The mimic octopus (Thaumoctopus mimicus) can imitate a lionfish, a sea snake, or a flatfish — and researchers suspect it doesn't pick at random. Evidence suggests it changes its choice of disguise based on one thing in particular. Based on what does it seem to choose which animal to become?
answer: The specific predator it is currently facing
choices: The specific predator it is currently facing
The temperature of the surrounding water
The time of day it is hunting
How recently it last ate
context: The mimic octopus and its relative the wunderpus are the only known animals to actively impersonate several different animals on demand, and there is evidence it selects its disguise to suit the specific predator confronting it. Source: Wikipedia 'Mimic octopus'; AMNH 'The Talented Mimic Octopus'.  (Legend.)

question: On a warm summer night in North America, male fireflies drift over a meadow blinking a yellow-green light in a coded pattern that says, 'I am a male of my species — are there any females of my kind out there?' A female of his species flashes back the matching code and he lands to mate. But sometimes a male flies toward what he reads as a willing female of his own kind, she flashes back in just the right way to pull him closer — and he is grabbed and eaten. The predator is a female Photuris firefly, a different genus of firefly entirely. How did she draw him in?
answer: She fakes another firefly species' mating flash-code
choices: She fakes another firefly species' mating flash-code
She glows far brighter to blind approaching males
She releases a scent that paralyzes males mid-flight
She spins a web of light between two reeds
context: The 'femme fatale' Photuris firefly mimics the exact flash-code answer of Photinus females, luring the wrong-species males in to eat them — a form of aggressive mimicry. One female can mimic up to three different species' codes. Source: Lloyd, Science 210:669; Cornell Chronicle (1997).  (Legend.)

question: The Photuris firefly is a large firefly that lights up American summer nights. Instead of just glowing to attract her own mate, a female Photuris flashes the exact love-signal of a smaller firefly species and lures its males in — then eats them. Those males' bodies carry a bitter steroid called lucibufagin that Photuris herself cannot manufacture on her own. Once she has swallowed a male and taken his chemistry into her own body, what does that theft buy her?
answer: She becomes foul-tasting, so jumping spiders spit her out
choices: She becomes foul-tasting, so jumping spiders spit her out
Her own mating flash grows twice as bright
Her eggs hatch several days faster
She gains the ability to fly in broad daylight
context: Photinus males carry lucibufagins that Photuris can't synthesize; after eating them the female becomes distasteful, and jumping spiders spit her out. She steals her victims' chemistry as well as their bodies. Source: Eisner et al., PNAS 94:9723 (1997).  (Legend.)

question: For nearly a century, textbooks called the viceroy butterfly a cheat — a tasty look-alike copying the toxic monarch to dodge birds. In 1991, Ritland and Brower fed red-winged blackbirds just the butterflies' abdomens (no wings, so birds judged purely by taste). What did that experiment reveal about the viceroy?
answer: The viceroy is just as foul-tasting as the monarch
choices: The viceroy is just as foul-tasting as the monarch
The viceroy is even tastier than birds had thought
Birds ignore both butterflies entirely
The viceroy's toxins come from eating monarchs
context: By testing taste alone, Ritland & Brower showed the viceroy is genuinely distasteful — so the pair is really Mullerian mimicry (both defended), not the old Batesian story of a tasty viceroy cheating off the monarch. A genuine 'what we used to think' correction. Source: Ritland & Brower 1991, Nature 350:497-498.  (Legend.)

question: By 1960 the venomous coral snake had died out of the North Carolina Sandhills, so the harmless scarlet kingsnake that copied it no longer had a live model for birds to fear. Comparing museum kingsnakes across the next 50 years, biologists expected the borrowed warning-look to blur and fade. Instead the red and black bands did what?
answer: Grew ever closer to the vanished coral snake’s exact proportions
choices: Grew ever closer to the vanished coral snake’s exact proportions
Faded toward the plain brown of unrelated local snakes
Split into a brand-new pattern no coral snake ever wore
Stayed frozen at the 1960 proportions with no further change
context: This is one of the strangest results in mimicry science. Akcali & Pfennig measured red-versus-black proportions on scarlet kingsnake (Lampropeltis elapsoides) museum specimens from the 1970s through the 2010s, after the venomous coral snake (Micrurus fulvius) had already vanished locally by about 1960. Rather than decaying once the real model was gone, the mimicry got statistically MORE precise over five decades (F1,26 = 6.997; p = 0.014). They call it 'evolutionary momentum': a predator that mistook a real coral snake for a harmless mimic died, while wrongly avoiding a harmless kingsnake cost almost nothing — so that lopsided selection keeps sharpening the disguise for the few predator generations after the model disappears. Source: Akcali & Pfennig 2014, 'Rapid evolution of mimicry following local model extinction,' Biology Letters — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4090552/ ; summary https://phys.org/news/2014-06-mimicry-scarlet-kingsnake-snake-coral.html

question: The butterfly Heliconius numata wears up to seven different warning patterns, each copying a different toxic species. Every form is passed down clean, never a muddled half-and-half wing. What locks all seven disguises together and passes them on as one unit?
answer: A supergene—one chromosome block, held intact by an inversion
choices: A supergene—one chromosome block, held intact by an inversion
A gut microbe passed from the mother to each new caterpillar
The temperature the chrysalis happens to develop at
The particular Melinaea species the caterpillar feeds beside
context: Heliconius numata is nicknamed the 'jack-of-seven-trades' because it carries an entire mimicry wardrobe on one chunk of chromosome 15, a locus called P. Joron and colleagues showed that a set of chromosomal inversions — a roughly 400-kilobase inverted block holding about 21 genes — suppresses recombination there, so the whole color-pattern gene cluster is inherited as one indivisible Mendelian unit. Without the inversion those separate pattern genes would recombine and shuffle into blurred, half-and-half wings that copy no protected model and get picked off; the inversion 'freezes' each working disguise as a single allele. That is why one species can carry seven complete, distinct disguises at once. Source: Joron et al. 2011, Nature 477:203, 'Chromosomal rearrangements maintain a polymorphic supergene controlling butterfly mimicry' — https://www.nature.com/articles/nature10341 ; corroboration https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3223682/

question: A small burrowing mammal digs through cold, wet, dark soil in the wetlands of eastern North America. It cannot see a thing underground. Ringing its two nostrils is a pink crown of 22 fleshy, finger-like tentacles that it presses against the earth to feel its way, checking every crumb of dirt in a fraction of a second. Nothing else on Earth wears a face like it. Which animal is it?
answer: The star-nosed mole
choices: The star-nosed mole
The naked mole-rat
The harbor seal
The manatee
context: The star-nosed mole's 22-ray 'star' looks like a fancy nose, but it is not for smelling at all - it is a pure touch organ, the most sensitive touch organ known in any mammal. The mole hunts underground in the dark and reads the world by pressing this crown of tentacles against the soil. Source: Wikipedia, Star-nosed mole (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star-nosed_mole); Kenneth Catania research.

question: Harbor seals live along cold coasts of the North Atlantic and North Pacific, hunting fish in water often too murky to see through. In one experiment, scientists blindfolded a harbor seal in a dark tank. A live fish swam once through the water and was then lifted out. Seconds later, the blindfolded seal darted after it along the exact winding path the fish had taken, never straying a body-length off it. The water looked perfectly still. What was the seal following?
answer: The invisible wake the fish stirred up
choices: The invisible wake the fish stirred up
The faint sound of the fish breathing
A scent trail dissolved in the water
The warmth left behind by the fish
context: A swimming fish leaves a swirling trail of disturbed water - its hydrodynamic wake - and a harbor seal can feel that trail with its whiskers alone, following a fish it never saw. In Georg Dehnhardt's 2001 study the seal found the trail's end about 90% of the time, rarely straying more than a body length off the fish's path. Cover the seal's whiskers with a mask and it refuses to even begin the search - proof it is hunting by touch. Source: Dehnhardt et al. 2001, Science 293:102-104; Wiskott et al. 2007, J. Exp. Biol. 210:781.  (Legend.)

question: Hunting completely blind through wet North American soil, a star-nosed mole tunnels along in the dark using the 22 pink feelers ringing its snout. When one feeler brushes something, the mole has to check whether it is food — usually a worm — decide, and swallow it before the worm can wriggle free. This little mole holds the world record as the fastest-eating mammal on Earth. From first touch to swallowed, how long does the whole meal take?
answer: About a quarter of a second
choices: About a quarter of a second
About three seconds
About ten seconds
About half a minute
context: Its fastest recorded meal is about 120 milliseconds - roughly a quarter of a second, faster than you can blink. Guinness lists the star-nosed mole as the world's fastest forager. Packed into that tiny star are more than 25,000 microscopic touch sensors wired to over 100,000 nerve fibers, letting it identify a worm almost instantly in total darkness. Source: Wikipedia, Star-nosed mole (120 ms minimum; Guinness); Carnegie Museum, 'The Nose that Sees.'  (Legend.)

question: A manatee feeds in water so murky it can barely see, yet it feels out one water plant from another with the stiff whiskery bristles on its snout, telling them apart by touch alone. Biologists compare the fineness of that touch to one body part of another large animal. Which?
answer: An elephant feeling with its trunk tip
choices: An elephant feeling with its trunk tip
A giraffe curling its long tongue
A rhino probing with its horn
A hippo sweeping its wide lips
context: A manatee's face carries about 600 stiff bristles (and thousands more sensory hairs over its body) that it works like fingers, grasping and sorting plants it can barely see. Researchers judge this facial touch to be at least as fine as an elephant feeling with the tip of its trunk - precise enough to tell one plant from another by feel. Source: Reep et al. 2001 (~600 facial bristles); Scholarpedia, 'Tactile hair in Manatees'; asknature.org.

question: The naked mole-rat is a wrinkled, pink, buck-toothed rodent that lives in vast underground colonies beneath the deserts of East Africa. It is almost completely bald — but stiff sensory hairs run in neat rows along its flanks and tail like trip-wires. Inside its narrow, branching tunnels, those whiskers give the mole-rat one strange ability that most animals simply lack. What can a naked mole-rat do?
answer: Reverse through a tunnel as fast as it runs forward
choices: Reverse through a tunnel as fast as it runs forward
Regrow the hairs within a day if they break
Sense an intruder three tunnels away
Feel the temperature of soil to the degree
context: Those rows of body hairs act as feelers all along its sides and tail, so the naked mole-rat can move backward through its tunnels just as fast and accurately as it moves forward - handy when there is no room to turn around underground. Source: Scholarpedia, 'Tactile sensing in the naked mole rat'; ScienceDirect Topics, Naked Mole Rat.

question: Neuroscientist Kenneth Catania filmed a hunting star-nosed mole and found its star does not sweep steadily over the ground. Instead it dabs 10 to 15 separate spots every second, jumping between individual points in quick, rapid darts. What did Catania say this rapid darting was just like?
answer: The quick flicks our eyes make scanning a scene
choices: The quick flicks our eyes make scanning a scene
A dog sniffing the ground in short bursts
A snake flicking its tongue to taste the air
A bat sending out pulses of sonar
context: Catania called the star a 'tactile eye': as the mole hunts, the star jumps from spot to spot the same way primate eyes make quick darting movements called saccades. It is feeling the world in rapid glances rather than one smooth sweep. Source: Wikipedia, Star-nosed mole; Kenneth Catania, Vanderbilt (tactile eye / saccades).

question: A blue whale — the biggest animal that has ever lived on Earth — has no teeth in its mouth at all. Instead, stiff fringed plates called baleen hang down from the roof of its mouth. The whale uses them to strain tiny shrimp-like krill out of a huge gulp of seawater. That baleen turns out to be made of the exact same material as which part of your own body?
answer: Your fingernails
choices: Your fingernails
Your kneecaps
Your eardrums
Your tooth enamel
context: Baleen is keratin -- the same protein that builds your fingernails and hair. Hundreds of these plates hang like a curtain and sieve krill and small fish out of the water. Source: Natural History Museum, 'Baleen whales: Filter feeding explained'; Whale & Dolphin Conservation, 'What is baleen?'

question: The blue whale swims in every ocean and is the biggest animal that has ever lived on Earth — around 30 metres long and 150 tons, heavier than any dinosaur that ever walked. Its tongue alone weighs as much as an elephant. What does this huge creature live on almost entirely?
answer: Krill barely the size of your finger
choices: Krill barely the size of your finger
Giant squid from the deep
Schools of tuna and mackerel
Sharks and smaller whales
context: The biggest animal ever built runs almost entirely on krill -- tiny shrimp-like crustaceans -- strained from the water through baleen. The largest body eats some of the smallest food. Source: American Museum of Natural History / Smithsonian Ocean, 'The Tons that Whales Eat'; Natural History Museum, 'What do blue whales eat?'  (Legend.)

question: The whale shark cruises the warm open oceans of the world with a gentle, gaping mouth several feet across. It is the biggest fish in any sea — up to about 40 feet long and 20 tons, spotted with pale dots across a dark blue-gray back. With a mouth that enormous, what does this giant actually eat?
answer: Clouds of plankton it strains from the water
choices: Clouds of plankton it strains from the water
Seals and sea turtles
Whole dolphins in one bite
Coral snapped off the reef
context: The biggest fish alive gulps in bursts, expanding its jaws to inhale an entire cloud of plankton, then strains the tiny food through comb-like gill rakers. Source: Smithsonian Ocean, 'The Massive Filter Feeding Shark You Ought to Know'; American Oceans, '3 Species of Filter Feeding Sharks'.

question: A flamingo is a tall wading bird that stands on one thin leg in shallow salt lakes, filtering food out of the water with a curved beak held upside-down. Its chicks hatch a dull gray and stay that way for months — yet fully grown adults blaze bright pink. The color is not something the bird is born with, and it does not grow in on its own. Where does a flamingo's pink actually come from?
answer: Pigments in the shrimp and algae it eats
choices: Pigments in the shrimp and algae it eats
A dye gland under the wing
Sunlight bleaching the feathers
Minerals in the mud it stands in
context: Carotenoids -- the same kind of pigment that makes carrots orange -- come from the brine shrimp and algae the flamingo filters, and get laid down in its feathers. Take the pigment out of the diet and new feathers grow pale. Source: Smithsonian's National Zoo, 'Why Are Flamingos Pink'; webexhibits.org, 'Flamingos | Causes of Color'.  (Legend.)

question: A flamingo wades into the shallow water of a salty African or South American lake, then plunges its whole head upside-down under the surface to feed on tiny brine shrimp. Its bent, hook-shaped bill acts as a strainer. But the water does not just drift lazily through — something inside the flamingo's mouth actively pumps water in and out, over and over, driving it hard against the sieve. What does that pumping?
answer: Its thick tongue, moving like a piston
choices: Its thick tongue, moving like a piston
A muscular pouch under its chin
Rapid gulping at the back of its throat
Beats of its half-open wings
context: With its head inverted, the flamingo sweeps side to side while a piston-like tongue pumps water in and out; comb-like plates called lamellae inside the bent bill sieve out brine shrimp and algae as the water rushes back out. Source: Smithsonian's National Zoo, 'Why Are Flamingos Pink and Other Flamingo Facts'; SeaWorld, 'All About Flamingos - Diet'.  (Legend.)

question: A blue whale lunges at a school of shrimp-like krill and takes one enormous gulp — hundreds of gallons of seawater with just a scatter of krill floating in it. Hanging from the roof of its huge mouth are stiff hairy plates called baleen, the whale's food strainer. But baleen only traps the krill when water moves the right way past it. So how does the whale get rid of all that seawater and keep the food behind?
answer: It squeezes the water back out through the plates
choices: It squeezes the water back out through the plates
It pumps the water out through blowhole-like slits
It tilts head-down so water drains off the front
It filters as water rushes IN through the plates on the gulp
context: Baleen works as a one-way sieve: the whale pushes the water back out through the bristly plates, trapping krill as small as about half a millimeter on the inside, then swallows what is left. Source: AskNature, 'Hairlike Fringe Filters Food'; Natural History Museum baleen article.

question: The blue whale is the biggest animal that has ever lived, up to 30 metres long. To feed, it drives itself sideways into a swirling swarm of thumb-sized shrimp called krill, and unfolds long pleats along its throat like a giant expanding bag. In a single lunge it takes an enormous gulp of seawater to strain krill out through the baleen plates in its mouth. How much water does one lunge engulf?
answer: More than the whale's entire body weight
choices: More than the whale's entire body weight
About a bathtub's worth
Roughly a swimming pool, then a week's rest
Just enough to cover its tongue
context: One lunge engulfs around 70,000 liters -- a gulp heavier than the whale itself, holding roughly 10 kg of krill -- then the whale forces the water back out through the baleen and swallows what remains. Source: American Scientist, 'The Ultimate Mouthful: Lunge Feeding in Rorqual Whales'; Goldbogen et al., Journal of Experimental Biology 214(1):131.  (Legend.)

question: Off the coast of Alaska, a pod of humpback whales works together to hunt herring. Swimming in a tightening circle beneath a school of fish, the whales blow steadily out through their blowholes as they spiral upward. A shimmering barrier rises around the herring and fences them into a tight ball. Then all the whales lunge up through the middle of the trap with mouths wide open. What is that rising barrier made of?
answer: A rising net of bubbles
choices: A rising net of bubbles
A cloud of ink
A curtain of stinging mucus
A swirl of stirred-up sand
context: In bubble-net feeding, humpbacks blow a spiral curtain of bubbles that fences a fish school in, then all surge up through the center together. Source: National Marine Sanctuary Foundation, 'What's Bubble Net Feeding'; National Geographic, 'How humpback whales use bubbles as a tool'.  (Legend.)

question: A giant manta ray — a huge diamond-shaped fish with a wingspan of over five meters — glides through a warm-water swarm of drifting plankton off a tropical coral reef. Sticking out from either side of its mouth are two paddle-shaped fins called cephalic lobes. Rather than just letting the plankton drift into its mouth on its own, the manta puts those two head fins to a specific job. What does it do with them?
answer: Curls them into an O to funnel water into its mouth
choices: Curls them into an O to funnel water into its mouth
Beats them like wings to swim faster
Digs them into the seabed for buried prey
Snaps them shut to trap fish like jaws
context: The manta curls its two cephalic lobes into a funnel that channels water and plankton into its wide-open mouth, then strains the food through feathery gill plates; in a thick swarm it does barrel-roll somersaults to keep cycling through. Source: NOAA Fisheries, 'Giant Manta Ray'; Manta Ray Advocates Hawaii, '8 Unique Techniques Manta Rays Use for Filter-Feeding'.

question: Despite the name, the Antarctic crabeater seal eats almost nothing but krill -- and it may be the most abundant large wild mammal on Earth, numbering in the many millions. It strains krill using an unusual body part shaped into a built-in sieve, much like a whale's baleen in miniature. What does its sieve?
answer: Its bizarre interlocking lobed teeth
choices: Its bizarre interlocking lobed teeth
A fringed pouch under its jaw
Long stiff whiskers around its mouth
Ridges lining the roof of its throat
context: The crabeater seal's teeth are intricately lobed and interlock into a strainer, letting it sieve krill from the water the way baleen does for a whale. Source: whalescientists.com, 'This seal has the craziest teeth in the carnivore world'; Wikipedia, 'Crabeater seal'; Oceanwide Expeditions.  (Legend.)

question: The right whale is a slow, stocky baleen whale of the cold northern and southern oceans — once so easy for whalers to catch and float that they called it the 'right' whale to kill. It carries the longest baleen of any whale, single plates over two meters tall hanging from its upper jaw like a huge curtain. That extraordinary length matches the particular way it feeds, nothing like the fast lunging blue whale. How does a right whale gather its food?
answer: It cruises slowly with its mouth held open
choices: It cruises slowly with its mouth held open
It dives deep and ambushes prey in the dark
It herds fish into shallow bays
It filters mud from the seafloor
context: The right whale is a skim feeder: it swims steadily with mouth agape, straining tiny plankton continuously -- and that non-stop skimming is why it needs baleen plates over two meters long. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Baleen whale'; Baleines en direct, 'Teeth and Baleen'.

question: Necropsied right and bowhead whales are found with their baleen almost bare -- hardly any trapped krill jammed in the fringes, even after a lifetime of straining. Flume experiments overturned the old dead-end-strainer picture and showed why the rack never clogs. How does the water actually move through it?
answer: It runs lengthwise along the inside of the rack, sweeping prey to the back
choices: It runs lengthwise along the inside of the rack, sweeping prey to the back
It rushes straight out through the plates and cements krill into the fringes
It swirls in a slow whirlpool that spins the krill down into the throat
It is warmed and thinned so the plates can shed their catch between gulps
context: Bowhead and right whales use cross-flow filtration: water travels front-to-back ALONG the inside of the baleen rack rather than jamming straight through it, so prey is swept toward the back of the mouth to be swallowed and the filter self-cleans instead of clogging. That is why necropsied balaenid whales are found with their baleen nearly free of trapped prey. The finding upgrades the simpler squeeze-the-water-back-out picture by one mechanistic step -- the water flows parallel to the filter, not perpendicular through it. Source: Werth & Potvin, 'Baleen Hydrodynamics and Morphology of Cross-Flow Filtration in Balaenid Whale Suspension Feeding,' PLOS ONE, 2016 (https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0150106; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4769178/).

question: A blue whale never grows a single tooth -- it strains krill through baleen instead. Yet when biologists read its DNA, they found the whole set of instructions for building tooth enamel still sitting in the genome. What has become of those enamel-making genes?
answer: They have decayed into broken pseudogenes, silent leftovers of a toothed past
choices: They have decayed into broken pseudogenes, silent leftovers of a toothed past
They were copied and repurposed to grow the keratin plates of the baleen rack
They switch on only in the womb, then shut down for good before the calf is born
They now build the dense ear bones the whale uses to hear across the ocean
context: Baleen whales evolved from toothed ancestors, and the molecular ghost of those teeth is still written in their DNA. The genes for making tooth enamel -- including AMBN, ENAM, and the enamel-specific MMP20 -- have decayed into non-functional pseudogenes, broken by mutations once teeth were no longer used. So a blue whale still 'has' the instructions for teeth; they simply no longer work. This genome-level evidence matches the fossil record (forms like Aetiocetus weltoni had baleen-whale skulls but still bore teeth) and the fact that modern baleen-whale fetuses grow tooth buds in the womb that are reabsorbed before birth. Source: 'Baleen,' Wikipedia (enamel trait became a pseudogene in developing mysticetes); Meredith et al. work on cetacean enamel-gene loss (AMBN/ENAM/MMP20).

question: On a warm summer night in the American countryside, a glimmer of green-gold light drifts and blinks across the yard. The kids call the little creature a 'lightning bug' or a 'firefly.' But despite those two nicknames, this glowing insect is not actually a fly at all, and it is not a true bug either. What kind of insect is it really?
answer: A beetle
choices: A beetle
A moth
A wasp
A dragonfly
context: The firefly belongs to the beetle family Lampyridae, in the insect order Coleoptera -- about 2,000 species worldwide. 'Firefly' and 'lightning bug' are both misnomers: it is a beetle. Source: Britannica, 'Firefly | Insect'.

question: An old incandescent bulb burns your fingers because it throws away about 90% of its energy as wasted heat. A firefly glowing on your palm does the opposite -- its light is a 'cold light'. Almost all of the firefly's energy comes out as which of these?
answer: Light, with almost no heat
choices: Light, with almost no heat
Heat, with almost no light
Sound, too high to hear
A faint electric spark
context: Firefly light is nearly 100% efficient: almost all the energy leaves as visible light and only a minute amount as heat -- the reverse of a light bulb, which loses roughly 90% as heat. Source: Britannica, 'Firefly | Insect'; Firefly.org.

question: A firefly's glow is not a battery or a spark but a chemical reaction in its lower belly. A glowing molecule combines with oxygen and ATP (adenosine triphosphate) energy, sped along by a special enzyme. That enzyme even lent its name to the reaction. What is it called?
answer: Luciferase
choices: Luciferase
Chlorophyll
Hemoglobin
Keratin
context: The molecule luciferin, combined with oxygen and ATP energy and catalyzed by the enzyme luciferase, produces light with almost no heat. Source: sciencenewstoday.org, 'Why Fireflies Glow'; Bohrium sciencepedia.

question: Two fireflies of the same kind are lost in a pitch-dark field, an arm's length of black grass between them, each needing to signal 'I'm your species -- come find me' across the yard. They pull it off with a back-and-forth 'conversation' that can last more than an hour. What are they using to talk?
answer: Their flash patterns
choices: Their flash patterns
Their wing-beats
Ripples in a pond
Vibrations in the soil
context: Each species has its own signature flash code -- single, double, or multiple pulses at set intervals. A patrolling male flashes his species' code and a matching female flashes back, a light 'conversation' until they meet in the dark. Source: Firefly Atlas, 'Firefly Life History'.

question: A male Photinus firefly sees what looks like a female of his own species flashing an answer from the grass, and flies straight toward her. But the code was faked by a female of the predatory genus Photuris, a 'femme fatale'. When he lands beside her, what does she do?
answer: She catches and eats him
choices: She catches and eats him
She lays eggs on his wings
She steals his stored light
She mates and lets him go
context: A Photuris female mimics the answering flash of a Photinus female to lure the male in, then catches and eats him. A single Photuris female can imitate the answering signals of up to three different Photinus species. Source: Lloyd, 'Aggressive Mimicry in Photuris' (PubMed 17747574); phys.org 2018. LEGEND.

question: Fireflies flash coded love-signals to each other in the summer dark. A male Photinus firefly flashes his own pattern, hoping to attract a Photinus female. But a hunter — the female Photuris firefly, nicknamed the 'femme fatale' — mimics the Photinus female's answering flash, and when the male lands beside her, she eats him. She isn't just after a meal. She robs him of something she cannot make in her own body. What does devouring him give her?
answer: Toxic chemicals that guard her from predators
choices: Toxic chemicals that guard her from predators
A brighter glow for the rest of the night
The ability to fly much farther
A second set of working wings
context: Photuris cannot make the defensive steroids called lucibufagins on its own; by eating Photinus males it acquires these toxins, which then protect it from predators like birds and spiders. Source: Eisner et al., PNAS 1997; Cornell Chronicle 1997. LEGEND.

question: On specific June nights, crowds hike into the Great Smoky Mountains and sit in the dark to watch Photinus carolinus do something no other firefly in North America does. Rangers run a lottery for the parking spots. What is the wonder they come to see?
answer: The males all flash in perfect unison
choices: The males all flash in perfect unison
Each firefly glows a different color
They spell out shapes in the air
They flash only once all summer
context: Photinus carolinus males synchronize, blinking together in a series of 5-8 flashes, then a shared ~8-second pause of darkness -- whole sections of forest pulsing on and off at once. Source: firefly.org 'Synchronous Fireflies'; wate.com. LEGEND.

question: A diver watches a thumb-sized cuttlefish on a sandy reef in the warm tropical waters off northern Australia. Its skin flashes bright bands of purple, yellow, and white. Every other kind of cuttlefish jets above the sand and swims through open water. This little flamboyant one never rises up into the water at all. So how does it actually get around the seabed instead?
answer: It ambles along the bottom on two arms and two fin-flaps, like legs
choices: It ambles along the bottom on two arms and two fin-flaps, like legs
It burrows under the sand and pops up ahead of its prey
It rides the current, drifting wherever the water carries it
It anchors to a rock and waits for food to come to it
context: The flamboyant cuttlefish (Metasepia pfefferi) is one of the very few cuttlefish that WALKS rather than swims, ambling along the seabed on two of its arms plus two flaps of its lower fins that combine into leg-like appendages. Source: Monterey Bay Aquarium (montereybayaquarium.org, animals-a-to-z/flamboyant-cuttlefish).

question: A cuttlefish is a soft, boneless sea creature related to the octopus and squid, with eight arms, two extra tentacles, and a body that flickers with color. Most cuttlefish are about a forearm long. The flamboyant cuttlefish, which walks the sandy sea floor off Indonesia flashing bands of purple, yellow, and white, surprises divers the moment they see one in the wild. How big does this fully grown adult get?
answer: About 2.5 to 3 inches long, roughly half a typical cuttlefish
choices: About 2.5 to 3 inches long, roughly half a typical cuttlefish
About a foot long, the same as most reef cuttlefish
About the length of a human arm, one of the largest cuttlefish
About the size of a dinner plate across its outstretched arms
context: It is tiny, only about 2.5 to 3 inches (6-8 cm) long, roughly half the size of a typical cuttlefish. Source: Ocean Conservancy (ode-flamboyant-cuttlefish); Monterey Bay Aquarium.

question: The flamboyant cuttlefish is a small tropical Indo-Pacific cuttlefish that walks along the seabed pulsing waves of bright purple, yellow and red across its skin. Those flashy colors are not camouflage — they are a warning. When researchers analyzed its muscle tissue in the lab, they found something no other cuttlefish is known to have. What was it?
answer: A poison reportedly as lethal as a blue-ringed octopus's venom
choices: A poison reportedly as lethal as a blue-ringed octopus's venom
A store of ink far larger than any relative its size
A layer of fat that lets it survive in near-freezing deep water
A magnetic mineral it uses to navigate across the seabed
context: It is the only cuttlefish known to be toxic: a report found its muscle tissue poisonous, reportedly as lethal as blue-ringed octopus venom, making it one of only three cephalopods found to be poisonous. Its dazzling rolling color show is a warning (aposematism), the same 'don't eat me, I'm toxic' billboard a poison dart frog uses. Source: MarineBio (marinebio.org, pfeffers-flamboyant-cuttlefishes); Wikipedia (Metasepia_pfefferi).

question: Most kinds of cuttlefish carry a large gas-filled internal shell called a cuttlebone that keeps them hovering weightless in open water, so they swim easily. But the flamboyant cuttlefish of the tropical Pacific is stuck plodding along the seabed on the tips of its arms and fin-flaps instead of swimming. Its cuttlebone is different from every other cuttlefish's, and that difference is what ties it to the bottom. What is different about it?
answer: It is shrunken and lacks the outer cone the others use, so it provides too little lift
choices: It is shrunken and lacks the outer cone the others use, so it provides too little lift
It has hardened into solid calcite, adding weight the animal cannot swim off
It draws in seawater on purpose, ballasting the body down onto the sand
It has shifted back into the arms, tipping the animal toward the bottom
context: Its cuttlebone is only two-thirds to three-quarters of the mantle length and, uniquely among cuttlefish, lacks the outer cone the others rely on for buoyancy. With so little lift, it can't hover for long and is effectively tethered to the seafloor -- the walking is a consequence of a scaled-down buoyancy organ, not a lifestyle choice. Its sister species, the paintpot cuttlefish, shares the trait and is the only other cuttlefish known to walk. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ascarosepion pfefferi' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascarosepion_pfefferi), corroborated via science20.com and diving-indo.com.

question: The flamboyant cuttlefish's fame rests on one claim: that its flesh carries the same nerve poison as the blue-ringed octopus. When a second team went looking for that exact toxin in the tissue, what did they actually find, leaving the whole reputation unsettled?
answer: Only trace tetrodotoxin, far too little to harm a vertebrate, contradicting the original report
choices: Only trace tetrodotoxin, far too little to harm a vertebrate, contradicting the original report
A second, stronger toxin the first team had entirely missed in the muscle
The poison only in the ink sac, never in the muscle the first team had sampled
Tetrodotoxin at lethal levels, but produced by bacteria living in the tissue
context: Mark Norman (Museum Victoria) reported the muscle held tetrodotoxin -- the blue-ringed octopus's poison -- and called it 'highly toxic.' But teams at Georgia Southern University and Utah State University-Uintah Basin, testing directly for tetrodotoxin, found only trace amounts, too low to poison a vertebrate. Whether the 'only toxic cuttlefish' claim survives, and what the real poison even is, stays genuinely disputed -- the warning-color story rests on evidence scientists are still arguing over. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ascarosepion pfefferi' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascarosepion_pfefferi).

question: Deep down where coral reefs slope into black water, a small fish called the flashlight fish glides through the dark. It shines a bright bluish light so strong that divers can spot the beam from over a hundred feet away — brighter than any other bony fish in the sea. Where does the flashlight fish carry that light?
answer: In a pouch under each eye
choices: In a pouch under each eye
Along its bony spine
On the tip of its tail
Deep inside its mouth
context: The flashlight fish (family Anomalopidae) carries a glowing pouch beneath each eye. It is the brightest light produced by any bony fish, a bluish glow visible from over 100 feet (30 m) away in the dark ocean. Source: Georgia Aquarium, 'Flashlight Fish'.

question: The flashlight fish is a small reef fish that carries a bright bluish glow in a pouch below each eye, strong enough to spot from over a hundred feet away in dark water. But the fish itself doesn't make that light. Something living inside the pouch produces the glow, and the fish shelters and feeds it in return. What is it?
answer: Billions of glowing bacteria
choices: Billions of glowing bacteria
A colony of glowing algae
A cluster of tiny glowing shrimp
Threads of glowing fungus
context: The light comes from billions of light-making bacteria (Candidatus Photodesmus katoptron) living inside the fish's eye-pouch. It is a partnership: the fish houses and feeds the bacteria, and the bacteria give a light the fish could never make itself. Source: PLOS One / PMC5298212, 'The Flashlight Fish Anomalops katoptron Uses Bioluminescent Light to Detect Prey in the Dark'.

question: A predator is hunting a lone flashlight fish in the black water. The fish blinks its light off, and in that instant the hunter loses it. Every flashlight fish goes dark to break the chase, but Morin's team saw one move that makes the hunter strike empty water. What does the fish do the moment its light vanishes?
answer: It darts off at an angle in the dark
choices: It darts off at an angle in the dark
It sinks straight down and holds still
It doubles back the way it came
It hides motionless against the reef
context: Morin's team called it 'blink-and-run': the fish flashes, then darts off at an angle in the dark and goes dark, so the predator lunges at the spot where the light WAS. In a school they flash and zigzag so a predator cannot lock onto any single fish. Source: Morin et al. 1975, Science 190:74-76, 'Light for All Reasons: Versatility in the Behavioral Repertoire of the Flashlight Fish'.  (Legend.)

question: The flashlight fish is a small reef fish that carries a pouch of glowing bacteria under each eye. Those bacteria pump out light every single second and cannot be switched off — they glow non-stop for as long as they are alive. Yet all night long the fish blinks its light on and off, flashing coded signals into the dark. How does the fish manage to go dark when its bacteria can't stop shining?
answer: It rotates the organ down into a black-lined pocket
choices: It rotates the organ down into a black-lined pocket
It clouds the pouch with a squirt of dark ink
It rolls its eyes back into their sockets
It buries its glowing head in the reef
context: Because the bacteria glow constantly, the fish cannot dim them. To 'blink,' Anomalops rotates the whole light organ downward into a black-lined pocket, hiding the glow behind the organ's heavily pigmented back, like flipping a lamp face-down. Source: Oxford Academic, Zoological Journal of the Linnean Society 94(1):65, 'Mechanisms of light organ occlusion in flashlight fishes'.

question: The flashlight fish is a small nocturnal fish that swims the deep drop-offs of Pacific coral reefs at night. Under each eye it carries a large pouch stuffed with glowing bacteria that give off a steady bluish light. The fish can raise a black skin shutter over the pouch to hide the beam or drop it to shine. But the light that shines out is far brighter than those bacteria alone could ever manage — bright enough for a diver to spot from a hundred feet away. The back wall of the pouch does something to boost it. What lines that wall?
answer: Mirror-like crystals that reflect the light forward
choices: Mirror-like crystals that reflect the light forward
A dark velvet that soaks up stray glow
A clear lens that magnifies the glow
A ring of muscle that squeezes it brighter
context: Behind the glowing bacteria, the pouch is lined with mirror-like guanine crystals that act as reflectors, bouncing the bacterial light forward and out to make the beam even brighter, a built-in reflector cup like a real flashlight. Source: Georgia Aquarium 'Flashlight Fish' / Techtimes summary of the PLOS One study on Anomalops katoptron.

question: A flashlight fish patrols a Pacific coral reef at night, the twin pouches under its eyes full of glowing bacteria that give off a steady blue light. Most of the night the fish blinks its lights on and off in a pattern by dropping and raising a black skin shutter. But the moment it spots a cloud of tiny drifting plankton to eat, it stops the blinking and changes what the light does entirely. What does the fish do with its light to hunt the plankton down?
answer: Holds it steadily ON as a headlight
choices: Holds it steadily ON as a headlight
Blinks it faster to dazzle them
Snaps it fully off and strikes blind
Flickers it to herd them together
context: When it spots plankton, the fish stops blinking so much and holds the light ON, keeping the organ open nearly 90% of the time so it can use the beam as a headlight to spot and chase its tiny prey. At night an active fish otherwise blinks about 90 times a minute. Source: PLOS One / PMC5298212, 'The Flashlight Fish Anomalops katoptron Uses Bioluminescent Light to Detect Prey in the Dark'.

question: A colugo is a cat-sized furry mammal of Southeast Asian rainforests. It leaps from a high branch, spreads a wide flap of skin between its legs, and coasts a long way downhill before gravity puts it back on the forest floor. That is gliding — really just falling in style. Among all the mammals on Earth, only one kind actually beats its wings to climb into the air and truly fly. Which mammals are the real flyers?
answer: Bats
choices: Bats
Sugar gliders
Flying lemurs
Gliding possums
context: Bats are the only mammals capable of true powered flight. Colugos ("flying lemurs"), sugar gliders, and gliding possums only glide on a stretched skin flap and cannot gain height. Source: Smithsonian 'Bat Facts'; Wikipedia 'Flying and gliding animals'.

question: A dragonfly hovers over the edge of a pond in the summer sunshine, then darts sideways and snatches a mosquito right out of the air. It flies on four thin, see-through, hard-veined wings. Where on a dragonfly's body do those four wings actually grow out from?
answer: Straight out of the back (the body wall)
choices: Straight out of the back (the body wall)
A pair of its front legs
A pair of its middle legs
A stiffened set of antennae
context: An insect's wings are outgrowths of the body wall, not modified limbs, which is why an insect keeps all six legs AND flies at the same time. Nothing else on Earth built flight this way. Source: Wikipedia 'Insect wing'; University of Chicago News 'How insect wings evolved from the legs of an ancestral crustacean'.

question: True flapping flight — beating wings hard enough to take off from the ground and stay up on your own power — did not appear on Earth just once. Across 350 million years, completely unrelated groups of animals each invented it from scratch, with no ancestor to show them how. Every other 'flying' animal — the flying squirrels, colugos, gliding lizards, flying fish — is really just falling in style. So how many separate times did true powered flight actually evolve?
answer: Four times
choices: Four times
Two times
Nine times
Once, then it spread
context: Powered flight has been built independently only four times: insects, pterosaurs, birds, and bats. None inherited flight from a shared flying ancestor — each family solved the same problem alone. Everyone else (flying squirrels, flying fish, colugos, gliding frogs) only glides. Source: UCMP Berkeley 'Evolution of Flight'; Wikipedia 'Flying and gliding animals'.  (Legend.)

question: Roll the clock back about 400 million years, deep into the Carboniferous swamps. No bird has ever taken wing. No pterosaur has hatched. No bat has been born. And yet the humid air above the giant ferns already hums with wings — one group of small animals has been flying for tens of millions of years before any backboned creature will even try. Which group was the first ever to launch true powered flight?
answer: Insects
choices: Insects
Birds
Bats
Pterosaurs
context: Winged insects were already flying about 325 million years ago (the oldest known is Delitzschala bitterfeldensis), tens of millions of years before any backboned animal left the ground. Source: Wikipedia 'Insect wing'; Stanford Doerr School 'Insects took off when they evolved wings'.  (Legend.)

question: Insects had been ruling the air for tens of millions of years when, in the Late Triassic — over 220 million years ago — one group of backboned animals finally broke free of the ground for the very first time. They were long-jawed, leathery-winged reptiles, and they were neither birds nor bats. They were the first of any vertebrates ever to truly fly. Which group of animals was it?
answer: Pterosaurs
choices: Pterosaurs
Bats
Songbirds
Owls
context: Pterosaurs were the first vertebrates ever to truly fly, taking to the air in the Late Triassic over 220 million years ago — beating the earliest birds into the sky by more than 60 million years. Source: Natural History Museum (UK) 'The truth about pterosaurs'; UCMP Berkeley 'Pterosaurian Flight'.

question: A bat's wing is not built like a bird's wing at all. Where a bird stretches feathers over a stiff arm, a bat stretches a thin sheet of skin between long, spread-out fingers — every wing is basically its own hand. Scientists gave bats the order-name Chiroptera, built straight from two ancient Greek words that describe what that wing really is. What does Chiroptera mean?
answer: Hand-wing
choices: Hand-wing
Night-flyer
Skin-glider
Blood-drinker
context: A bat's wing is a webbed hand: skin (the patagium) stretched between four elongated finger bones. Chiroptera is Greek for 'hand-wing' (kheir 'hand' + pteron 'wing') — hold a bat's wing to the light and you see the thin finger bones running through it like the spokes of an umbrella. Source: Wikipedia 'Bat'; UCMP Berkeley bat flight page; Animal Diversity Web 'Chiroptera'.  (Legend.)

question: A pterosaur did not spread its wing across a whole hand the way a bat does. Its skin wing hung from a bony support running longer than its entire forearm, stretching from the body all the way down to the legs. Which part of its body held up the whole wing?
answer: One enormously elongated fourth finger
choices: One enormously elongated fourth finger
The full set of five fingers
The upper arm bone alone
A long spur off the ankle
context: A pterosaur flew on ONE gigantic finger: its fourth finger, stretched longer than its whole forearm, with the main skin wing (brachiopatagium) hanging off that single 'wing-finger' down to the legs. The other three fingers stayed small and clawed for walking. Source: Wikipedia 'Anatomy of pterosaurs'; Tokita 2015 'How the pterosaur got its wings'.  (Legend.)

question: In the Late Cretaceous skies over what is now North America, roughly 70 million years ago, cruised the largest flying animal that has ever lived. It stood as tall at the head as a giraffe, spread its wings wider than a small airplane — 33 to 36 feet across — and flew on a single enormously elongated wing-finger of bone and skin. Name this giant pterosaur.
answer: Quetzalcoatlus
choices: Quetzalcoatlus
Meganeuropsis
Archaeopteryx
Delitzschala
context: Quetzalcoatlus was the single biggest flying animal ever — about 12 feet tall at the head, with a wingspan of roughly 33–36 feet — yet it flew on one elongated fourth finger. Source: Britannica 'Quetzalcoatlus'; UC Berkeley News 2021.  (Legend.)

question: Down the middle of a bird's chest runs a special breastbone with a deep blade of bone sticking straight out of it, called the keel — shaped a bit like the keel that runs down the bottom of a sailboat. A strong flyer like a pigeon has a huge one. A flightless ostrich, which spends its life running on the ground, has almost none. Why does powered flight demand a big keel?
answer: It anchors the powerful flight muscles
choices: It anchors the powerful flight muscles
It stiffens the hollow wing bones
It stores the extra oxygen for flight
It shifts weight forward for balance
context: The keel is a blade jutting from a bird's breastbone, and its job is to anchor the big flight muscles — the more powerful the wingbeat, the bigger the keel. That is exactly why a flightless ostrich, which never flaps to fly, has almost no keel at all. Source: Wikipedia 'Keel (bird anatomy)'; Britannica 'Bird — Skeleton'.

question: A bird's keel anchors two big flight muscles, and oddly BOTH of them sit low on the chest, below the wing. One is the pectoralis; the other is the supracoracoideus. What job does the supracoracoideus do, and how can a muscle down on the chest manage it?
answer: Raises the wing for the recovery stroke, using a bony pulley over the shoulder
choices: Raises the wing for the recovery stroke, using a bony pulley over the shoulder
Stiffens the hollow wing bones so they don't crack in flight
Locks the wing folded flat against the body at rest
Twists the wingtip feathers to steer the bird in a turn
context: Both big flight muscles sit LOW on the chest, yet the supracoracoideus raises the wing: its tendon threads up through a tunnel of bone over the shoulder, like a rope over a pulley, so a chest muscle pulls the wing UP. The pectoralis pulls it DOWN for the power stroke — and with no keel to anchor them, flightless birds like ostriches barely have one. Source: Wikipedia 'Keel (bird anatomy)'; Britannica 'Bird — Skeleton'.

question: Pterosaurs, bats, and birds are not close cousins, yet all three built a wing out of the very same body part, inherited unchanged from a shared four-legged ancestor. Each lineage then stretched a different piece of it, ending up with three wings that look nothing alike. Which starting part did all three rebuild into a wing?
answer: The forelimb
choices: The forelimb
The rib cage
The shoulder blade
The tailbone
context: The three flying vertebrates all rebuilt the same forelimb into a wing — homologous, inherited from a common four-legged ancestor — but each stretched different bones: pterosaurs one finger, bats four, birds the whole arm. Same starting parts, three different wings. Source: Science World 'The Evolution of Flight'; Wikipedia 'Convergent evolution'.

question: A bat's wing is a webbed hand: hold it up to the light and thin bones fan out through the skin like the spokes of an umbrella. Those spokes are the bat's own finger bones, stretched out enormously. How many of the bat's finger bones does the wing skin spread between?
answer: Four finger bones
choices: Four finger bones
Three finger bones
Five finger bones
The whole hand's worth of eight
context: A bat's wing is a webbed hand: skin (the patagium) stretched between four hugely elongated finger bones, spread through the wing like umbrella spokes — the recognition mark that tells a bat wing from a pterosaur's one finger or a bird's feathered arm. Source: UCMP Berkeley 'The Three Solutions to Flight'; Wikipedia 'Bat'.

question: Bird flyers run and jump into the air, so for years nobody could explain how a giraffe-tall azhdarchid pterosaur left the ground at all -- some argued a beast that heavy barely flew. Then Michael Habib noticed its arm bone was far stronger than its leg bone, the reverse of any bird, and proposed the launch that fits that skeleton. How did the giant get airborne?
answer: It pole-vaulted off all four limbs, hurling itself up on its folded arms
choices: It pole-vaulted off all four limbs, hurling itself up on its folded arms
It sprinted across open ground until its wings caught enough lift
It climbed a cliff and dropped into a glide until the wings bit air
It hung from branches and fell free until the downstroke took hold
context: This is Habib's 'quadrupedal launch' hypothesis (Habib 2008, Zitteliana B28). A giant like Quetzalcoatlus crouched on all fours and vaulted, using its folded, super-strong forelimbs to throw its whole ~250 kg body into the air in one explosive push -- roughly 5 kilonewtons of force over about 0.6 second -- before the wings snapped open on the first downstroke. The clinching evidence: in pterosaurs the forelimb (humerus) is stronger in bending than the hindlimb (femur), the exact reverse of birds, which are bipedal hindlimb launchers. It stays a live debate -- David Unwin and others argue the very largest pterosaurs could barely fly, so the quad-launch is the mechanism that keeps them in the sky at all. Source: Scientific American 'How Pterosaurs First Took Flight'; Smithsonian Magazine; Habib 2008 'Comparative evidence for quadrupedal launch in pterosaurs', Zitteliana B28.

question: A housefly beats its wings about 200 times a second, and a mosquito faster still — quicker than any nerve can fire even one signal per wingbeat. So the fly's brain cannot possibly command each stroke by a nerve pulse, the way your brain fires a signal to move your hand. Something else must be driving the blur of a fly's wings. What actually powers each rapid wingbeat?
answer: Two muscle sheets stretch and re-fire each other, ringing the thorax like a bell
choices: Two muscle sheets stretch and re-fire each other, ringing the thorax like a bell
A single giant muscle contracts once and coasts through many strokes on momentum
One nerve fires a rapid burst that paces every downstroke in perfect lockstep
Air trapped in the chest recoils elastically to snap the wings up and down
context: These are asynchronous flight muscles. Instead of one nerve impulse per wingbeat, two antagonistic muscle sheets in the thorax pull against each other, and each one, when stretched, fires back after a tiny delay ('delayed stretch activation'), so the elastic thorax resonates like a rung bell in a self-sustaining oscillation. A single nerve pulse can drive dozens of beats -- frequencies no nerve could command one-for-one, since direct 'synchronous' muscle tops out near 100 Hz. Roughly three-quarters of flying insect species use this trick: flies, bees and wasps, and beetles are asynchronous, while dragonflies, butterflies and moths (~25 Hz), and locusts stay synchronous with one impulse per beat. Source: Nature 2023 'Bridging two insect flight modes' (PMC10599994); Science.org 'Molecular Trigger for High-Speed Wing Beats in a Bee'; JEB flight-muscle reviews.

question: High in the rainforest canopy of Southeast Asia lives a small green-and-black tree snake called the flying snake, or Chrysopelea. Instead of climbing all the way down one tree and back up the next, it travels straight from treetop to treetop through open air — with no wings, no flaps, and no limbs of any kind. How does the flying snake cross the gap?
answer: It flattens its whole body into a ribbon and glides
choices: It flattens its whole body into a ribbon and glides
It leaps and grabs the far branch with its tail
It spins a silk line and swings across
It inflates a pouch of air like a balloon
context: The flying snake has no flaps or appendages at all. It turns its own body into a wing: it flattens itself flat as a ribbon and glides tree to tree, moving through the air like a water snake crossing a pond. Source: National Wildlife Federation, 'Borneo's Wild Gliders,' via a-z-animals + NWF.

question: The flying snake, Chrysopelea, is a small tree snake of Southeast Asia that glides through the air from one treetop to another with no wings at all. Scientists set up high-speed cameras and filmed one snake launching into a glide 239 separate times. In almost every single launch it began the exact same way. What did the snake do just before it left the branch?
answer: Hung down and lifted its head into a 'J,' then sprang up and out
choices: Hung down and lifted its head into a 'J,' then sprang up and out
Coiled into a tight spiral and rolled off the edge
Dropped straight down and opened out once falling
Ran its body flat along the branch and slid off the tip
context: The snake hangs from a branch, lifts its head up into a 'J' shape, then springs upward and outward like releasing a coiled spring. This anchored J-loop takeoff was used in 74% of trials, 177 of 239. Source: Socha, 'Becoming airborne without legs,' Journal of Experimental Biology 209:3358 (2006).

question: In the tropical rainforests of Southeast Asia lives the paradise tree snake, one of a small group of serpents known as flying snakes. Along a branch it looks like an ordinary rope — round in cross-section.
