Source: Giraffe Conservation Foundation, How long is a giraffe's tongue (https://giraffeconservation.org/facts-about-giraffe/how-long-is-a-giraffes-tongue-what-color-is-it/).

question: A giraffe's tongue is a startling dark blue-black colour, not pink like yours — and while the giraffe feeds it dangles right out in the blazing African sun, hour after hour, wrapping around branch after branch. Biologists think that dark shade is doing a real job. What is that dark colour there to do?
answer: Shield the tongue from sunburn
choices: Shield the tongue from sunburn
Warn rival males to keep away
Help it taste bitter leaves
Blend in against dark bark
context: Scientists think a giraffe's tongue is dark because it hangs out in the blazing sun all day while the animal feeds; the dark pigment (melanin) protects it from sunburn — a built-in sunscreen. Source: Giraffe Conservation Foundation, How long is a giraffe's tongue (https://giraffeconservation.org/facts-about-giraffe/how-long-is-a-giraffes-tongue-what-color-is-it/).

question: On the African savanna, a giraffe reaches up with its long neck to feed on its favourite meal, the acacia tree. But acacia leaves bristle with sharp thorns that would shred a soft mouth. Yet the giraffe strips the leaves clean off the branch and swallows them without a scratch. What lets it feed on the thorny branch unharmed?
answer: A tongue armoured with tough bumps and thick sticky saliva
choices: A tongue armoured with tough bumps and thick sticky saliva
Chewing the thorns off first with its flat back teeth
Waiting for the thorns to dry out and drop away
A horny beak that snaps the twigs off cleanly
context: The giraffe's tongue is coated with tough bumps (thickened papillae) and thick, sticky saliva, so it can strip nutritious leaves right off thorny acacia branches without getting hurt. Source: Giraffe Conservation Foundation (https://giraffeconservation.org/facts-about-giraffe/how-long-is-a-giraffes-tongue-what-color-is-it/).

question: Two male giraffes settle a rivalry by swinging their long necks like sledgehammers and cracking their skulls together — one blow can land with over 2,000 pounds of force. What do biologists call this head-swinging duel?
answer: Necking
choices: Necking
Cresting
Bulling
Rutting
context: Male giraffes fight by 'necking' — swinging their long necks like sledgehammers and smashing their heads into each other. A full swing can land a blow estimated at over 2,000 pounds of force, like being hit by a small car. Source: A-Z Animals, This Is Why Giraffes Fight by Smashing Their Necks (https://a-z-animals.com/articles/this-is-why-giraffes-fight-by-smashing-their-necks-together/).

question: Two male giraffes duel by clubbing their skulls together, yet researchers watching them found the fights oddly honourable. When a rival stumbles and loses his balance mid-fight, what does the other giraffe do?
answer: Holds off and won't strike him
choices: Holds off and won't strike him
Presses in for a finishing blow
Chases him from the herd
Calls in a second bull to help
context: Researchers found giraffes fight fair: each giraffe is a 'lefty' or 'righty' when it swings, rivals respect each other's side, and they won't strike an opponent who has lost his balance. Source: CBC Radio, Giraffes fight fair when they spar, researchers find (https://www.cbc.ca/radio/asithappens/neck-to-neck-combat-giraffes-fight-fair-when-they-spar-researchers-find-1.6183914).

question: A giraffe stands eighteen feet tall on the African plains, so its heart has to shove blood up an enormous neck just to reach the brain. But to drink from a waterhole, it must splay its front legs wide and drop its head far below its heart -- and all that high-pressure blood should surge into the brain and knock it out cold. A dense net of vessels at the base of the skull saves the giraffe. How?
answer: It soaks up the sudden surge before it reaches the brain
choices: It soaks up the sudden surge before it reaches the brain
It reverses the blood flow back down the neck
It chills the blood so the brain slows down
It stores spare oxygen for the long drink
context: When a giraffe bends its head down to drink, the high-pressure blood would otherwise rush to the brain and make it faint — so a sponge-like net of blood vessels at the base of the skull (the rete mirabile) soaks up the surge and protects the brain. Source: MDPI, Rostral Epidural Rete Mirabile in Giraffe (https://www.mdpi.com/2813-0545/2/2/13); Intrepid Odyssey (https://www.intrepidodyssey.com/the-giraffes-circulatory-system-a-marvel-of-evolutionary-adaptation/).

question: A giraffe on the African plains drops its head down to a waterhole to drink, then whips it back up eighteen feet into the air in seconds. That fast a rise, and blood should pool down in the feet and drain from the brain -- yet the giraffe never crumples. The fix is the tight, inelastic skin wrapped snugly around its lower legs, squeezing the veins there. Like what everyday object does that giraffe leg-skin work?
answer: A tight compression stocking
choices: A tight compression stocking
A rigid splint or plaster cast
A hinged metal knee brace
A rubber tourniquet band
context: Tight, inelastic skin on the giraffe's lower legs works like a compression stocking so blood doesn't pool in its feet, while one-way valves in its neck veins stop blood pouring backward into the head — together they keep the animal from fainting when it stands back up. Source: Intrepid Odyssey Safaris (https://www.intrepidodyssey.com/the-giraffes-circulatory-system-a-marvel-of-evolutionary-adaptation/); Smithsonian Magazine (https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/cardiovascular-secrets-giraffes-180977785/).

question: A giraffe must drive blood two metres straight up to its brain, so people assume it packs a gigantic heart. Yet when researchers weighed it, the heart was ordinary — the same fraction of body mass as any mammal's. What lets this normal-sized heart do the job?
answer: Its left chamber is walled with dense muscle and beats fast
choices: Its left chamber is walled with dense muscle and beats fast
Its chambers are unusually roomy and hold extra blood
It sits high in the chest, closer to the head it must feed
It empties in one slow, powerful squeeze each beat
context: The 'giant giraffe heart' is a myth. A 2016 study found the heart is only about 0.5% of body mass — the same relative size as in other mammals. What is extraordinary is the left-ventricle wall, thickened to roughly 2-3.5 cm around a strikingly small cavity. That thick wall exists to generate the ~200-250 mmHg pressure needed to push blood up the long neck, but it leaves only a small cavity, so each beat pumps only about half the blood of a similar-sized mammal. The giraffe still reaches a normal cardiac output (~16 L/min) by beating fast for its size (resting ~56 bpm) — power and speed, not bulk. Source: Smerup et al., 'The thick left ventricular wall of the giraffe heart normalises wall tension, but limits stroke volume and cardiac output,' Journal of Experimental Biology 219:457 (2016).

question: For a century, the giraffe's neck was explained as a ladder to leaves no rival could reach. Then in 2022, a seventeen-million-year-old relative named Discokeryx was found in China. Its skeleton revived an old rival idea. What idea did that fossil bring back?
answer: The neck was forged as a weapon in brutal mating duels
choices: The neck was forged as a weapon in brutal mating duels
The neck lengthened to cool the blood in fierce heat
The neck grew tall to spot lions across open plains
The neck stretched to reach water in flooded ground
context: Since Darwin's day the towering neck was read as a feeding advantage — reaching foliage rivals cannot. In 2022 a fossil of the early giraffe relative Discokeryx xiezhi (~17 million years ago, China) revived a rival idea. It carried a thick helmet-like disc of bone on its head and the most reinforced, shock-absorbing head-and-neck joints known in any animal — built to survive ferocious head-butting duels over mates. This is landmark hard evidence for the 'necks for sex' hypothesis: that sexual combat, not only feeding, drove giraffe neck evolution. Both pressures may have acted together; the feeding story is no longer the only serious explanation. Source: Wang, Deng et al., 'Sexual selection promotes giraffoid head-neck evolution and ecological adaptation,' Science 376:eabl8316 (June 2022).

question: In the cloud forests of Central and South America lives a tiny lime-green tree frog called a glass frog. One perches on a leaf above a rushing mountain stream at night. Flip it gently onto its back, and the skin of its belly does something no other frog's belly does — what?
answer: It is see-through, and you look straight in at its organs
choices: It is see-through, and you look straight in at its organs
It flushes bright red as a warning to predators
It puffs into a spiny ball twice its size
It oozes a milky poison that burns the skin
context: The glass frog (family Centrolenidae, about 160 species, 3.0-7.5 cm long) has transparent skin across its abdomen -- turn one over and you can look right through it at the organs inside. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glass_frog

question: Peer through the clear belly of a Central American glass frog and you look straight in at its inner organs, plain as if the animal were a little living aquarium. Most of the organs sit quietly in place, but one of them never holds still — it keeps steadily moving the whole time you watch. Which organ is it?
answer: Its heart, beating and pumping blood
choices: Its heart, beating and pumping blood
Its lungs, drawing in air
Its kidney, filtering waste
Its stomach, churning food
context: Through a glass frog's see-through belly you can watch its actual heart beating and pumping blood -- the same beat a doctor listens for through a stethoscope -- along with its liver and looping intestines working inside its living body. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glass_frog; https://allthatsinteresting.com/glass-frog

question: In a Central American rainforest, a clutch of glass frog eggs -- tiny see-through jelly-blobs -- is stuck to the underside of a leaf that hangs out over a stream. One adult glass frog stays planted beside those eggs for days on end, driving off egg-eating wasps that come to steal them. Among glass frogs, which parent takes on this guard duty?
answer: The male
choices: The male
The female
Both parents together
Neither -- eggs are left alone
context: The male glass frog is the parent that guards the eggs, standing watch over a clutch stuck to the underside of a leaf overhanging a stream; a single male may watch several clutches at once, each at a different stage. The eggs are laid above running water so that when the tadpoles hatch (after 10-20 days, often during heavy rain) they drop straight down into the stream. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glass_frog

question: By day a glass frog sleeping on a leaf turns almost completely invisible, far clearer than when it is awake. Scientists filming it in 2022 found the trick: to lose the red tint that would give it away, the frog hides nearly 90% of its red blood cells -- packing them where?
answer: Crammed inside its liver
choices: Crammed inside its liver
Squeezed under its skin
Dissolved into its bladder
Drained down into its feet
context: A resting glass frog stashes almost 90% of its red blood cells (the cells that carry the red color) inside its liver, whose lining of reflective guanine crystals acts like a tiny mirror to hide them -- making the frog two to three times more transparent than when active. It releases the cells again at night to become active: a rare case of 'transparency on demand.' Cramming that much blood together should cause a deadly clot, yet the frog packs and unpacks it daily without clotting -- a puzzle scientists now hope to study to help prevent clots in humans. Source: Taboada, Delia et al. 2022, Science (doi:10.1126/science.abl6620); https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2022/12/221222162421.htm

question: High in a forest at night, a flying squirrel launches from one tree trunk and spreads a flap of loose skin stretched between its wrists and ankles, sailing like a paper airplane through the air. It has no beating wings to change course, yet it swerves mid-flight and lands neatly on the trunk it aimed for. Which part of its body does the squirrel use as a rudder to steer and brake?
answer: Its flattened, bushy tail
choices: Its flattened, bushy tail
Its long whiskers
Its clawed hind feet
Its round, tufted ears
context: The flying squirrel steers and brakes with its flattened, bushy tail, which acts as a rudder; it can also bank by lowering one arm to change the tension of the patagium membrane. Source: National Geographic, 'Flying squirrels'; Wikipedia 'Flying squirrel'.

question: In the rainforests of Southeast Asia lives a small lizard, only about the length of a pencil, nicknamed the 'flying dragon.' It glides from tree trunk to tree trunk on a pair of bright, fan-like wings that swing open in mid-air, then fold flat against its sides the moment it lands. What is this little glider's proper name?
answer: The Draco
choices: The Draco
The komodo dragon
The basilisk
The frilled dragon
context: The Draco lizard ('flying dragon') glides on membranes called patagia stretched over 4 to 7 greatly elongated ribs. A Draco usually glides about 10 meters between trees, but glides as long as 60 meters (200 feet) have been recorded. Source: Wikipedia 'Draco (lizard)'; Oxford Academic, 'Biology of Gliding in Flying Lizards'.

question: In a Southeast Asian rainforest, a Draco lizard steps off a branch and opens its gliding wings, which swing outward like the spokes of an umbrella and then fold flat against its sides when it lands. Unlike a flying squirrel's skin flap stretched between its legs, a Draco's wing is spread apart by a very unusual part of its skeleton. Which part is it?
answer: Greatly elongated ribs
choices: Greatly elongated ribs
An extra pair of shoulder blades
Fused, paddle-like finger bones
A rod of cartilage from the wrist
context: The Draco lizard glides on membranes stretched over 4 to 7 greatly elongated ribs; the ribs swing outward like the spokes of an umbrella to open the wings, then fold flat against the body. The same muscles that in ordinary lizards are used just for breathing (the intercostal and iliocostalis muscles) control this ribbed wing. Source: Wikipedia 'Draco (lizard)'; Oxford Academic, 'Biology of Gliding in Flying Lizards'.

question: High in the trees of a Southeast Asian rainforest, a slender tree snake called the paradise tree snake launches itself off a tall branch and glides more than 10 meters through the air to another tree. It has no limbs and no fins — no obvious wings at all. How does the 'flying' snake glide?
answer: It flares its ribs to flatten its body into a ribbon
choices: It flares its ribs to flatten its body into a ribbon
It spreads a fan of skin between its scales
It inflates its belly into a balloon shape
It trails a sticky thread that catches the wind
context: The 'flying' snake (genus Chrysopelea, such as the paradise tree snake Chrysopelea paradisi) glides by flaring its ribs to flatten its round body into a wide, concave ribbon, then keeps undulating in an S-shape while airborne to travel farther. It can cross 10 meters (33 feet) or more from a treetop. Legendary handle. Source: phys.org; Wikipedia 'Chrysopelea paradisi'.

question: Virginia Tech professor Jake Socha spent over twenty years studying the flying snake and built the first accurate 3-D model of one in flight. His virtual experiments proved that the snake's constant mid-air wriggling is not random. What does that S-shaped motion actually do for the airborne snake?
answer: It keeps the snake from tumbling and extends its glide
choices: It keeps the snake from tumbling and extends its glide
It generates thrust like a beating wing
It cools the snake's body during the fall
It scares off birds that might attack mid-glide
context: Jake Socha's virtual experiments showed the mid-air wriggling isn't random: it keeps the snake from tumbling over and increases both how far and how far down it can travel. Source: phys.org (June 2020); Sci.News, 'Biologists Offer Insights into Flight of Paradise Flying Snake'.

question: In the rainforests of Borneo, a Wallace's flying frog perches on a high branch. When danger climbs up toward it, the frog leaps into empty air and sails over 15 meters to the next tree, flashing vivid orange-and-black skin as it goes. This bright green frog was named after the Victorian naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace. What does the flying frog spread wide to turn its fall into a long glide?
answer: Its huge webbed hands and feet
choices: Its huge webbed hands and feet
Loose skin along its flanks
Its inflated throat pouches
Fan-like flaps on its hind legs
context: Wallace's flying frog (Rhacophorus nigropalmatus) glides using huge hands and feet with fully webbed, splayed fingers and toes — four little parachutes at once — plus flaps of skin along its limbs. Its webbing is vivid orange and black, and it can glide over 15 meters (50 feet). It is named for naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace, who found it in Borneo in the 1850s. Legendary handle. Source: Wikipedia "Wallace's flying frog"; National Geographic.

question: Four very different animals — the flying squirrel of North American forests, the flying fish of the open ocean, the Draco lizard of Southeast Asia, and the flying snake of Asian rainforests — can all glide long distances between treetops or across the waves. Line up how these four actually build the 'wing' that carries them. What do you find?
answer: Each uses a completely different body part for the same result
choices: Each uses a completely different body part for the same result
They all reuse the same wrist-membrane design
Each grew its wing from modified feathers
They share one gliding organ inherited from a common ancestor
context: Because each glider evolved its 'wing' independently, they solved the same problem with completely different body parts — a skin flap (squirrel, colugo), giant fins (flying fish), elongated ribs (Draco), a flattened whole body (flying snake), and webbed feet (Wallace's frog) — five different anatomies, all producing the same falling-with-style result. This repeated independent solution is called convergent evolution. Gliding has evolved over and over among tree-dwelling animals (in mammals alone at least seven separate times), whereas true powered flight has evolved only four times: insects, pterosaurs, birds, and bats. Source: Wikipedia 'Convergent evolution'; Wikipedia 'Flying and gliding animals'.

question: Among all gliding mammals, one champion has the most complete gliding membrane of any animal — webbing that runs from its neck to the very tips of its fingers and toes and on to the tip of its tail, wrapping nearly its whole body except the head. One was recorded gliding about 150 meters between trees. Which animal is it?
answer: The colugo
choices: The colugo
The flying squirrel
The sugar glider
Wallace's flying frog
context: The colugo's patagium is the most complete of any gliding animal, running from the neck to the very tips of the fingers, webbing between every finger and toe, and continuing to the tip of the tail. One colugo was recorded gliding about 150 meters (490 feet) in a single glide, barely losing altitude. A cat-sized animal, it can achieve a glide ratio better than 12 to 1. Legendary handle. Source: Wikipedia 'Colugo'; Natural History Museum, 'Colugos: expert gliders of the forest'.

question: In the rainforests of Southeast Asia lives the colugo, a cat-sized furry animal that stretches a wide flap of skin between its limbs and glides from tree to tree in the dark. It is often called the 'flying lemur' -- yet it cannot truly fly, and it is no lemur at all. When scientists finally worked out its family tree using DNA, which group turned out to be the colugo's closest living relatives, surprising those who had guessed bats?
answer: Primates, the group of monkeys and humans
choices: Primates, the group of monkeys and humans
Rodents, the group of rats and squirrels
Marsupials, the group of kangaroos
Insectivores, the group of shrews and moles
context: The colugo cannot fly and is not a lemur, so the name 'flying lemur' is wrong twice over. Its actual closest living relatives are primates (the group that includes monkeys and humans), which surprised scientists who once thought it was related to bats. The two living species are the Sunda flying lemur (Galeopterus variegatus) and the Philippine flying lemur (Cynocephalus volans). Source: Wikipedia 'Colugo'.

question: Long before the first flying squirrel or colugo, in Jurassic forests 160 million years ago, small furred creatures were already leaping from tree to tree on wing-like skin. Fossils named Maiopatagium and Vilevolodon preserve their gliding membranes. These animals were not mammals yet, but forerunners on the branch leading to them. What does their existence prove about gliding?
answer: Mammal ancestors were gliding roughly 100 million years before modern gliders
choices: Mammal ancestors were gliding roughly 100 million years before modern gliders
Gliding first appeared only after the giant dinosaurs had died out
The earliest mammals could all fly under their own power
Skin-membrane gliding evolved just once and was inherited by every glider
context: Described in 2017 from the Tiaojishan Formation near Beijing, Maiopatagium furculiferum and Vilevolodon diplomylos are haramiyidans -- an extinct branch of mammal forerunners, not crown mammals. They preserve wing-like gliding membranes, long fingers, and tree-climbing limbs, showing the gliding, tree-dwelling way of life had already evolved about 100 million years before the first modern gliding mammals. Lead author Zhe-Xi Luo called them 'the first in glide.' The 'after the dinosaurs' choice is a trap: the Jurassic is deep in the age of dinosaurs, not after it. Source: Meng, Luo et al., Nature (2017), reported by University of Chicago News, 'First winged mammals from the Jurassic period discovered' -- https://news.uchicago.edu/story/first-winged-mammals-jurassic-period-discovered

question: A flying squirrel spreads its skin flap wider than its own arm bones reach, and the very tips of the membrane curl upward instead of lying flat. A special rod of wrist cartilage swings out to hold that edge tight. Wind-study of these upturned tips revealed why they angle up rather than staying level.
answer: They cut the drag of swirling wingtip air, like the winglets on an airliner
choices: They cut the drag of swirling wingtip air, like the winglets on an airliner
They catch rain and channel it away from the gliding membrane
They flash bright color to warn off rival squirrels in the canopy
They store fat that fuels the muscles powering each long glide
context: The flying squirrel is the only gliding mammal that extends its wingtip with a styliform cartilage -- a rod of cartilage at the wrist with no equivalent in colugos, sugar gliders, or Draco lizards. The thumb's abductor muscle swings it out to spread and tension the leading edge of the patagium beyond the length of the arm bones. Thorington & Darrow showed the resulting upturned wingtips form airfoils that reduce induced drag, functioning like the winglets on a modern airplane wing. Source: Thorington & Darrow, 'Wing Tip Anatomy and Aerodynamics in Flying Squirrels,' Journal of Mammalogy 79(1):245 (1998) -- https://academic.oup.com/jmammal/article-pdf/79/1/245/2504483/79-1-245.pdf

question: During the last ice age, a plant-eating beast lumbered across the grasslands of South America. It ballooned to the size of a small Volkswagen (VW) Beetle car, its whole back vanishing under one huge bony dome. Two tons of grazing tank, shuffling the pampas on stumpy legs. Name this beast.
answer: the glyptodon
choices: the glyptodon
the giant ground sloth
the woolly rhino
the short-faced bear
context: Glyptodon was an ice-age relative of the armadillo grown to about 3 metres long; the biggest species, G. clavipes, reached roughly 2 tonnes (about 4,400 lb) with its whole back hidden under a domed shell. Source: Wikipedia, Glyptodon (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glyptodon).

question: During the last ice age in South America, the Glyptodon lumbered along the forest edge -- a two-ton armored tank of a mammal, its head capped in fused bone like a helmet and its whole back sealed under a huge bony dome. All that armor made it look like a killer. So how did this giant actually spend its days feeding?
answer: grazing low grass and plants
choices: grazing low grass and plants
cracking bones for marrow
tearing flesh from smaller mammals
trapping fish in shallow pools
context: Despite its armor and clubbed relatives, Glyptodon was a plant-eater with a wide muzzle built for bulk-feeding; it grazed and browsed low plants and grasses along the edges of forests and grasslands. Source: Wikipedia, Glyptodon (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glyptodon).

question: A modern armadillo in South America rolls into a tight ball when a predator closes in, because its shell is a set of banded, flexible plates. Its giant ice-age cousin, the Glyptodon -- a two-ton armored grazer that lumbered the pampas -- had a back-dome that worked in a completely different way from the little armadillo's. How was Glyptodon's shell built?
answer: the plates were fused solid and locked to its hips
choices: the plates were fused solid and locked to its hips
the plates overlapped like loose roof tiles
a row of soft hinges crossed its back
a thick keratin cap rode over free ribs
context: Glyptodon's shell was a single rigid dome of around 1,800 bony plates (osteoderms) fused solid and even locked onto its hip bones, so unlike a banded modern armadillo it could never roll into a ball. Source: Wikipedia, Glyptodon (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glyptodon).

question: At an ancient site in Uruguay, in South America, human spear points turned up right beside the fossils of a Glyptodon -- a two-ton, dome-backed, ice-age plant-eater. Scientists now think the early South Americans who hunted these giants made a second, surprising use of the dead animals beyond just eating the meat. What did the empty Glyptodon shells become?
answer: ready-made dome shelters from bad weather
choices: ready-made dome shelters from bad weather
canoes for crossing rivers
grinding bowls for seeds
drums for signaling
context: At the Pay Paso 1 site in Uruguay, human spear points were found together with Glyptodon fossils, and researchers think early South Americans may have sheltered under the huge empty shells during bad weather -- a ready-made dome tent left by a dead giant. Source: Wikipedia, Glyptodon (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glyptodon).

question: Glyptodon itself lacked one, but its cousin Doedicurus swung an armored tail tipped with a spiked bony club so hard it could shatter a human thigh bone. Many fossil shells carry deep dents across the dome. When scientists studied them, what did they conclude?
answer: they clubbed each other in fights
choices: they clubbed each other in fights
big cats bit down and left the marks
rockfall crushed the shells after burial
disease pitted the bone from inside
context: Doedicurus carried a tail-club that could deliver about 60 kilonewtons of force (it takes only about 4 kN to snap a human thigh bone). Some glyptodont shells carry dents that exactly match the size and shape of another glyptodont's tail club -- direct evidence these living tanks clubbed each other, likely in fights over mates or territory. Source: Prehistoric-wildlife.com, Doedicurus (https://www.prehistoric-wildlife.com/species/doedicurus/); TwilightBeasts, A home on the range (https://twilightbeasts.org/2014/09/11/a-home-on-the-range/).  (Legend.)

question: The Glyptodon's enormous back-dome, worn like a house on its shoulders during the last ice age of South America, held over a thousand bony plates. Modern armor engineers now 3D-print copies of those plates for tank and helmet designs. Fine X-ray scans called micro-CT (short for computerized tomography) revealed why one Glyptodon plate can take a heavy blow without shattering to bits. What is each plate built from?
answer: dense bone skins wrapped around a porous inner lattice
choices: dense bone skins wrapped around a porous inner lattice
a slick waxy coating that lets strikes slide off
interlocking hexagons that snap free one by one
a thick cushion of fat sealed beneath the bone
context: Each osteoderm was roughly 2.5 cm thick and built like an engineered sandwich panel: two dense outer layers of compact bone enclosing a porous inner lattice about 66% pore space, with struts only ~0.25 mm thick. That layout lets the plate soak up impact energy and stop a crack before it splits the whole plate (no catastrophic failure) -- exactly the property engineers copy for lightweight bio-inspired armor. Source: 'Analyzing nature's protective design: the glyptodont body armor,' J. Mech. Behav. Biomed. Mater. (2018), sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1751616118301656; corroborated via biomimetic-armor review literature and Glyptodon histology sources.

question: For 150 years no one knew if the car-sized glyptodon was an armadillo cousin, a turtle relative, or something odder. In 2016 scientists cracked a giant club-tailed glyptodont's mitochondrial genome and got a jolt: it sat deep INSIDE the living armadillos. Tracing the mass back down that branch to its small burrowing ancestor gave a second shock. By what factor had this lineage's body mass grown?
answer: more than 300-fold, to around two tonnes
choices: roughly 10-fold, to about 60 kilograms
roughly 50-fold, to about 300 kilograms
more than 300-fold, to around two tonnes
nearly 1,000-fold, to over five tonnes
context: Delsuc, Poinar and colleagues sequenced the complete mitochondrial genome of Doedicurus, a giant club-tailed glyptodont. It nests deep inside the living armadillos, making glyptodonts the subfamily Glyptodontinae within family Chlamyphoridae, having split from other armadillos about 35 million years ago. The kicker: the last common ancestor of glyptodonts and modern armadillos weighed only about 6 kg, yet Pleistocene glyptodonts reached roughly 2,000 kg -- a more than 300-fold increase in body mass over that lineage. Source: Delsuc, Poinar et al., Current Biology 26(4):R155-R156 (2016), corroborated via Sci-News and ScienceDaily (2016/02/160222134051.htm).

question: Japanese fishermen once pulled up a strange pale deep-sea shark from far below the waves. It had a long, flat, blade-like snout and a jaw that shot forward like a spring-loaded trap to snatch prey. They named it 'tenguzame' — 'tengu-shark' — after a long-nosed, red-faced goblin from Japanese folklore. English-speaking scientists translated the name straight over. What do we call this fish?
answer: goblin shark
choices: goblin shark
vampire squid
ghost catfish
demon stingray
context: 'Tenguzame' (天狗鮫) honors the tengu, a red-faced long-nosed goblin of Japanese folklore; 'goblin shark' is a direct translation. Source: Wikipedia 'Goblin shark' (etymology); Florida Museum of Natural History profile.

question: A young goblin shark — the deep-sea Japanese fish named after a long-nosed goblin — looks ghostly white when it is small, and its colour deepens as it grows older. But even the adult's strange pinkish tint is no trick of the light or a coating of paint from the seafloor. Something in the shark's own body is causing the colour. What actually makes this shark pink?
answer: red blood vessels showing through its thin, pale skin
choices: red blood vessels showing through its thin, pale skin
a diet of pink shrimp staining its body
glowing pigment cells that ward off rivals
a coating of pink algae from the seafloor
context: The goblin shark's skin is so thin and pale that the red blood vessels underneath show right through it, giving a real pink hue that deepens with age. Source: Florida Museum of Natural History profile; Wikipedia 'Goblin shark'.

question: The goblin shark hunts in pitch-black water hundreds of meters down, where eyes are nearly useless. Its long, flat, blade-like snout is studded with jelly-filled sensors called ampullae of Lorenzini. What do those sensors let the shark find in the dark?
answer: the faint electric fields given off by hidden animals
choices: the faint electric fields given off by hidden animals
the warmth radiating from a prey animal's body
the chemical scent trail left by wounded fish
the pressure waves of a distant tail beat
context: Ampullae of Lorenzini are jelly-filled electroreceptors; the goblin shark's blade snout sweeps them through the dark deep sea to detect the weak electric fields of buried or hidden prey. Source: Florida Museum of Natural History profile; Wikipedia 'Goblin shark'.

question: Deep in the ocean lives the goblin shark, a pale-pink deep-sea shark with a long flat snout. Its muscles are weak and its body is flabby, yet it hangs almost motionless in the black water and drifts silently toward its prey until its jaws fire out. One enormous organ, up to about a quarter of the shark's whole body weight, keeps it nearly weightless in the water. Which organ is it?
answer: its huge oil-filled liver
choices: its huge oil-filled liver
its air-filled swim bladder
its water-logged spongy skeleton
its oversized fatty brain
context: The goblin shark's oil-filled liver can reach about a quarter of its body weight; the light oil makes it nearly neutrally buoyant, so this slow ambush predator can hover in the dark and drift toward prey. Sharks have no swim bladder. Source: Wikipedia 'Goblin shark'; Smithsonian Ocean.

question: When a goblin shark catches prey, its whole mouth catapults forward out of its face, then snaps back flush against the head. High-speed footage from NHK (Japan's national broadcaster) of two wild sharks feeding, analyzed by Nakaya's team in 2016, clocked this launch at up to 3.1 meters per second. What record does that strike hold?
answer: the fastest jaw of any shark
choices: the fastest jaw of any shark
the deepest recorded shark strike
the widest gape of any deep-sea fish
the longest teeth of any predatory shark
context: At up to 3.1 m/s, the goblin shark's jaw protrusion is the fastest of any shark and the fastest jaw-protrusion speed ever recorded for a fish. LEGEND. Source: Nakaya et al. 2016, Scientific Reports 'Slingshot feeding of the goblin shark'; Hokkaido University press release.

question: The goblin shark of the deep ocean has a stunning weapon: slingshot jaws that launch forward toward prey a distance equal to about 9% of the shark's whole body length, catapulted by a double set of elastic ligaments at the jaw joints. Compared with a normal shark's jaws, which barely budge, how much more protrusible -- meaning how much farther out they can push -- are the goblin shark's?
answer: 2 to 9 times more protrusible
choices: 2 to 9 times more protrusible
only slightly, by about a tenth
exactly the same, just faster
less protrusible but far stronger
context: The jaws shoot out 8.6-9.4% of the shark's body length, and are 2.1 to 9.5 times more protrusible than a normal shark's, sprung by a double set of elastic ligaments at the jaw joints. Source: Nakaya et al. 2016, Scientific Reports; Wikipedia 'Goblin shark' (jaw protrusion figures).

question: The goblin shark is a living fossil — the only surviving member of a shark family called the Mitsukurinidae. Its lineage reaches back roughly 125 million years, to the ancient age of the dinosaurs. When scientists first studied it, what did they mistake it for?
answer: a long-extinct fossil shark, Scapanorhynchus
choices: a long-extinct fossil shark, Scapanorhynchus
a young great white that had lost its color
a hybrid of a sawfish and a deep-sea eel
an ordinary sand tiger shark with a deformity
context: The goblin shark is the sole living member of Mitsukurinidae, a lineage ~125 million years old; early scientists confused it with the extinct fossil shark Scapanorhynchus. LEGEND. Source: Florida Museum of Natural History; Wikipedia 'Goblin shark'.

question: A goblin shark fires its whole mouth out of its face like a slingshot, so scientists expected it to work like other fast-mouthed fish: yank the jaws open to create a vacuum and pull the prey in. But Nakaya's 2016 high-speed study found the opposite. The shark keeps its gill slits open and only projects the jaws AFTER the gape is fully open. What kind of feeder does that make it?
answer: a ram feeder that overtakes prey by rushing its mouth over it
choices: a ram feeder that overtakes prey by rushing its mouth over it
a suction feeder that draws prey in on an inward vacuum
a filter feeder that strains drifting plankton from the water
a bite-and-shake feeder that tears loose chunks of flesh
context: The giveaway is timing and plumbing. A suction feeder snaps its gape open first to build a vacuum and would clamp its gill slits shut to hold that low pressure. The goblin shark does neither: it fully opens its gape, keeps the gill slits open the whole time (so water flows out, not in), and only THEN catapults the jaws. Nakaya's team measured the pressure inside the mouth staying positive, pushing water outward rather than sucking prey inward. So the fastest jaws of any shark are not a vacuum gun at all; they are a ram — the mouth lunges out and swallows the prey by overtaking it. The elastic launch is stored in stretched cartilage and ligament: the basihyal (tongue-support) cartilage is hauled back and down and the palatonasal ligament stretches to its maximum around 279 ms into the strike, then that tension snaps the jaws forward. Source: Nakaya et al. 2016, 'Slingshot feeding of the goblin shark Mitsukurina owstoni', Scientific Reports (PMC PMC4901258, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4901258/).

question: A goblin shark impales soft, slippery grenadiers and squid on its long, straight, lengthwise-grooved front fangs. But near the corners of its jaws sits a second, completely different set of teeth built for a different job. What are those rear teeth shaped to do?
answer: crush hard-shelled prey like crabs
choices: crush hard-shelled prey like crabs
impale even larger slippery fish
filter tiny plankton from the water
grip the seafloor while resting
context: One shark, two toolkits. The front (anterior) teeth are long, narrow, nearly straight fangs, finely grooved lengthwise, made to punch through and hold soft, slick deep-sea prey like grenadiers (rattail fish) and squid. But the posterior teeth near the jaw corners are small and flattened for crushing hard, shelled prey like crabs and other crustaceans. A single goblin shark can carry roughly 35-53 upper and 31-62 lower tooth rows across those two jobs. Source: Wikipedia 'Goblin shark' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goblin_shark); diet corroborated by Yano et al.'s stomach-content survey of 121 specimens from Tokyo Submarine Canyon.

question: The Goliath birdeater is a tarantula from the steamy rainforests of northern South America and it is the world's heaviest spider. Its hairy body is the size of a grown man's fist, and its eight furry legs span a dinner plate. Now imagine picking a full-grown one up in both hands. Roughly what does it weigh?
answer: A young puppy
choices: A young puppy
A single grape
A pair of scissors
A garden snail
context: Theraphosa blondi tops out around 175 grams (6 oz) — the greatest mass of any spider. The giant huntsman spider has longer legs, but the Goliath wins on sheer bulk and body size. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goliath_birdeater

question: The Goliath birdeater is the largest spider on Earth by weight, a giant tarantula from the rainforests of northern South America. Its leg span is bigger than a dinner plate. It hunts on the forest floor at night, waiting silent, then pouncing on whatever creature wanders past. Its name says it eats birds, but that is mostly a myth — chicks are a rare catch. What does it drag back to its burrow most often?
answer: Earthworms and toads
choices: Earthworms and toads
Hummingbird chicks
Roosting bats
Wandering scorpions
context: On the forest floor it takes earthworms, insects, frogs, toads, lizards, and even small snakes and rodents — there are essentially no records of it regularly hunting birds. The 'birdeater' name came from Maria Sibylla Merian's 1705 engraving of a Suriname tarantula attacking a hummingbird; one famous picture stuck the myth to the whole species. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/invertebrates/facts/goliath-birdeater

question: Deep in the South American rainforest lives the Goliath birdeater, the largest spider on Earth -- a hairy tarantula the size of a dinner plate. Corner one, and its inch-long fangs are almost the last thing it reaches for. Instead the spider swivels around, scrapes its hind legs across its own belly, and aims something at your eyes and face. What does the birdeater launch?
answer: A cloud of tiny barbed itching hairs
choices: A cloud of tiny barbed itching hairs
A jet of stinging venom
A sticky net of silk
A spray of foul musk
context: The hairs are urticating setae — microscopic, harpoon-shaped barbs the spider flicks off its abdomen. They lodge in an attacker's eyes and skin and itch fiercely, a far better first defense than a bite whose venom is only mild to humans. Source: https://www.aaas.org/news/weird-wonderful-creatures-goliath-birdeater

question: Alone in the Guyana rainforest of South America at night, Harvard entomologist -- an insect scientist -- Piotr Naskrecki heard a strange sound behind him and turned to find a puppy-sized Goliath birdeater tarantula right at his heels. The huge spider was making a loud noise that almost no other spider on Earth can produce. What was making that noise?
answer: Its hard-tipped feet clicking on the ground
choices: Its hard-tipped feet clicking on the ground
Its fangs snapping open and shut
Wind rattling through its leg hairs
Air hissing from its breathing holes
context: The Goliath birdeater is essentially the only spider that makes noise as it walks: its feet carry hardened tips and claws that tap the forest floor — Naskrecki described the clicking as 'not unlike a horse's hooves.' (It can also hiss loudly by rubbing leg bristles together — stridulation — but the walking-click is what gave it away that night.) Source: https://thesmallermajority.com/2014/10/08/the-sound-of-little-hooves-in-the-night/  (Legend.)

question: Deep in the rushing rainforest rivers of Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea in West Africa lives a single frog species that holds the title of biggest frog on planet Earth — the goliath frog. Full-grown adults sit on rocks in the whitewater. About how big does one get?
answer: About the size and weight of a house cat
choices: About the size and weight of a house cat
About the size of a mouse
About the size of a large dog
About the size of a horse
context: The goliath frog (Conraua goliath) can reach about 13 inches (34 cm) long and weigh up to 7.3 pounds (about 3.3 kg) -- roughly the size and weight of a house cat. It lives in southwestern Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea. Source: Wikipedia, Goliath frog; Britannica.

question: Most male frogs court a mate by puffing up a stretchy balloon of skin on the throat, called a vocal sac, and booming a loud croak out of it across the pond. The goliath frog — a house-cat-sized frog from the fast rivers of Cameroon in West Africa, and the biggest frog on Earth — cannot do that. It has no vocal sac at all. So how does a male goliath frog attract a female?
answer: He opens his mouth and whistles
choices: He opens his mouth and whistles
He drums the water with his hind legs
He flashes a bright throat pouch
He builds a tower of stones
context: Despite being the largest frog on Earth, the goliath frog has no vocal sac and cannot make a loud croak. To attract a mate, the male opens his mouth and makes a whistling sound. Source: Animal Diversity Web; Wikipedia.

question: The goliath frog is the largest frog in the world, a five-pound giant with a body more than a foot long, living along fast rivers in Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea in West Africa. In 2019 scientists watching these giant frogs recorded something never before documented in any African frog or toad. Along the riverbank, what were the giant frogs doing?
answer: Dragging rocks to wall off little ponds as nests for their eggs
choices: Dragging rocks to wall off little ponds as nests for their eggs
Carrying their tadpoles around on their backs
Spinning ropes of slime between the reeds
Digging deep burrows to sleep through the dry season
context: In 2019 scientists discovered the goliath frog builds nests: it clears little ponds along the riverbank and shoves rocks around the edge to wall them off, then a parent guards the eggs. It was the first nest-building ever documented in an African frog or toad. Source: Schaefer et al. 2019, Journal of Natural History; Mongabay.  (Legend.)

question: In the fast rocky rivers of West Africa lives the goliath frog, the largest frog on Earth -- as big as a house cat and heavy enough to fill a dinner plate. No other frog on Earth grows anywhere near this huge, and biologists have long puzzled over what pushed this one species to swell so far past all its frog relatives. Which explanation do the scientists who study it favor?
answer: Hauling the heavy stones it needs to build its nests
choices: Hauling the heavy stones it needs to build its nests
A diet of unusually large river crabs and fish
Being a leftover giant from a cooler ancient climate
Growing big armor to survive its riverbank predators
context: To build its nests the goliath frog drags rocks weighing more than half its own body weight -- up to about 2 kg (over 4 pounds). Scientists think this heavy lifting is so demanding it may have driven the species to become the biggest frog on Earth. Source: Schaefer et al. 2019, Journal of Natural History; Mongabay.  (Legend.)

question: Watch a wild gray wolf pack lope across the winter snow. It is not a gang of unrelated fighters that teamed up, and not a squad of the toughest wolves picked from many different litters. Wolves have been studied for decades in places like Yellowstone in the American West, and researchers see the same pattern almost every time. What is a wolf pack really?
answer: A family: two parents and their pups from the last few years
choices: A family: two parents and their pups from the last few years
A crew of the strongest wolves drawn from many litters
A truce between two neighboring packs sharing a hunt
A group of females who drove off all the adult males
context: A wild pack is a breeding pair (the mother and father) plus their offspring from recent years, living and hunting together. Source: International Wolf Center, wolf.org/wolf-info/just-for-kids/wolf-families/.

question: Alone on the open Arctic tundra, a gray wolf stops in the snow, tips its head back, and lets loose a long, mournful howl. There are no trees to break the sound. It rolls out across the flat white land, a single voice searching for its scattered pack. About how far can that one howl carry across the treeless ground before it fades away?
answer: About 10 miles
choices: About 10 miles
About half a mile
About 100 miles
About 30 feet
context: A wolf howl carries roughly 10 miles (16 km) across open tundra, and about 6 miles through forest where trees muffle it. Source: Britannica, 'Why Do Wolves Howl?'; coolwoodwildlifepark.com.

question: In a snowy northern forest, a gray wolf pack scatters across miles of trees to hunt. Then a storm rolls in, the wind picks up, and the light dies. One wolf throws back its head and howls a long, rising note, and the others answer from far away. Besides finding each other again in the storm, what else does all that howling do?
answer: Warns rival packs to keep off the pack's territory
choices: Warns rival packs to keep off the pack's territory
Frightens prey into freezing so it is easier to catch
Mimics an elk call to lure curious prey closer
Echoes off hills so the pack can map the terrain
context: Wolves howl to assemble the pack before and after a hunt, to relocate one another during a storm, and to warn neighboring packs to stay off their territory. Source: Smithsonian National Zoo; Wolf Conservation Center, 'Wolves and Howling'.

question: The gray wolf is a wild dog that hunts in packs across the great northern forests of North America and Eurasia. It is no cheetah — a healthy deer can outrun a wolf in a short sprint. But a wolf's real trick is stamina. Trotting at a steady pace hour after hour, a single gray wolf tracking prey can cover an astonishing distance in one day. Roughly how far?
answer: More than 50 miles in a single day
choices: More than 50 miles in a single day
About 3 miles in a single day
About 200 miles in a single day
Less than 1 mile in a single day
context: Wolves are endurance hunters, trotting at about 5 mph for hours and covering more than 50 miles in a day while tracking prey — one wolf chased a caribou for 5 miles, another a deer for 12. Source: Wolf Conservation Center, 'How Fast Do Wolves Run?'; Wikipedia, 'Hunting behavior of gray wolves'.

question: A gray wolf pack, seven or eight strong, slips out of the pine trees and moves toward a herd of a hundred elk grazing in a Yellowstone meadow. The wolves are heavily outnumbered. A straight charge into a wall of hooves and antlers would shatter bones and end the hunt in seconds. Instead the pack fans out along the herd, testing, waiting. Before they attack, they work to do one specific thing first. What is the wolves' opening move?
answer: Split a single animal off from the rest of the herd
choices: Split a single animal off from the rest of the herd
Surround the whole herd so nothing can escape
Stampede the herd toward a cliff edge
Attack the largest and strongest bull head-on
context: Wolves try to cut one animal away from the group; if a prey animal stands its ground they often leave it and look for one that runs. Most hunts of large hoofed prey actually fail, so wolves test many animals to find a weak or slow one. Source: Wikipedia, 'Hunting behavior of gray wolves'.

question: For decades people spoke of the 'alpha wolf' — the animal that supposedly clawed its way to the top of the pack. Biologist L. David Mech, who popularized that idea in a 1970 book, later corrected himself about wild packs. In a real wild pack, who are the wolves everyone follows?
answer: Simply the parents — the breeding pair
choices: Simply the parents — the breeding pair
The oldest, most experienced wolf, kin or not
The single best hunter, who leads the chase
The mother alone, while the father ranges apart
context: The 'alpha' idea came from watching captive strangers thrown together, not wild families. Mech popularized it in 1970, then published a 1999 correction in the Canadian Journal of Zoology: in the wild the 'leaders' are just the parents. Source: Mech (1999); Scientific American, 'Is the Alpha Wolf Idea a Myth?'.  (Legend.)

question: A gray wolf pack's adult hunters have been away all morning, chasing a lame elk down a river valley. Back at the den in a hillside burrow, the pups are only weeks old, too young to have joined the chase and still too small to chew tough raw meat. The tired adults trot home successful, and the hungry pups swarm them, licking their faces and mouths. How do the returning adults actually get meat to the waiting pups?
answer: They regurgitate swallowed meat for the pups to eat
choices: They regurgitate swallowed meat for the pups to eat
They drag the whole carcass back to the den mouth
They lead the pups out to feed at the kill site
They store meat in cheek pouches and spit it out
context: Every wolf in the pack helps raise the pups: babysitters guard them while hunters are away, and returning hunters bring up swallowed meat, regurgitating it for the pups to eat. Source: International Wolf Center; Frontiers for Young Minds, 'It Takes A Pack To Raise A Pup'.

question: In 1995, gray wolves were brought back to Yellowstone National Park after about 70 years gone. Scientists watched the elk change not just their numbers but WHERE they dared to graze — and that shift set off a chain of change. As elk stopped lingering in exposed streamside valleys, what began to happen along the rivers?
answer: Browsed-down aspen and willow started growing tall again
choices: Browsed-down aspen and willow started growing tall again
The rivers dried up as plants drank the water
Elk vanished entirely from the whole park
Grass replaced every tree along the banks
context: With elk no longer lingering in open valleys, over-browsed willow and aspen recovered; taller willows let beavers return to build dams — a chain scientists call a trophic cascade. Researchers caution the effect is real but partly overstated, since drought, bears, and human hunting also thinned the elk. Source: Ripple & Beschta (2012), 'Trophic cascades in Yellowstone'; MeatEater Conservation.  (Legend.)

question: A great white shark that loses one of its long front biting teeth in a struggle — snapped off in a seal or in the flank of a rival shark — is back to a full row of biting teeth within a day or two. The empty slot fills right in. Where does the fresh replacement tooth come from?
answer: It rolls forward from a spare row waiting behind
choices: It rolls forward from a spare row waiting behind
It regrows slowly from the empty gum socket
It hardens from soft cartilage in the jaw
A neighboring tooth widens to close the gap
context: A great white's teeth are arranged in rows like a conveyor belt: when a front tooth is lost, one from the row behind rolls forward into the working position, sometimes in as little as 24 to 48 hours. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_white_shark; smartscience.blog/sharks-teeth-rows-anatomy.

question: The great white shark, the huge grey ocean predator that hunts seals along cool coastlines, carries about 300 teeth in its jaws at any one time, stacked in up to seven rows. Yet at any given moment only a small fraction of those 300 teeth are actually doing the biting into prey. Why?
answer: Most sit in reserve behind the front row until they roll forward
choices: Most sit in reserve behind the front row until they roll forward
Most stay flattened against the jaw until a big meal
Most are still buried and only erupt in old age
Most are too blunt to use and act as ballast
context: Of roughly 300 teeth in up to seven rows, most sit in reserve behind the working front row and are never used to bite until they roll forward to replace a lost tooth. Source: nationalgeographic.com/animals/fish/facts/great-white-shark; americanoceans.org/facts/how-many-rows-of-teeth-do-sharks-have.

question: A great white shark closes on a struggling seal in the cold green water off the California coast. Its upper and lower teeth do very different jobs. The broad upper teeth, backed by huge jaw muscles, carry serrated, saw-toothed edges that shear through flesh and blubber like a row of steak knives. The narrower lower teeth are a different shape entirely. What are those lower teeth built to do?
answer: Grip and hold the catch in place
choices: Grip and hold the catch in place
Crush shell and bone to powder
Comb food particles from the water
Inject a paralyzing venom
context: The upper teeth are broad triangles with serrated edges built for shearing flesh, while the lower teeth are narrower and more pointed for gripping and holding the catch in place. Source: elasmo-research.org/education/white_shark/teeth.htm; americanoceans.org/facts/shark-teeth-facts.

question: Walk any beach where old fossils weather out, from South Carolina to Morocco, and shark teeth are among the most common finds a beachcomber will pocket. They vastly outnumber fossil bones from any other animal buried in the same rocks. Shark bodies do not preserve well, but the teeth are everywhere. What about a shark's life explains why its teeth alone came to litter the ancient seabed?
answer: It sheds and replaces teeth endlessly, tens of thousands in a lifetime
choices: It sheds and replaces teeth endlessly, tens of thousands in a lifetime
Its teeth are made of near-indestructible diamond-hard enamel
It deliberately spits worn teeth onto known spawning grounds
It grows a fresh full set every single year like antlers
context: Because a shark never stops shedding and replacing teeth, it can go through tens of thousands of teeth across its lifetime, one reason fossil shark teeth are so common. Source: nhm.ac.uk/discover/what-can-shark-teeth-tell-us.html; americanoceans.org/facts/shark-teeth-facts.

question: A great white shark cruises through the dark ocean using a sense that living creatures like us do not have. Tiny jelly-filled pores on its snout, called the ampullae of Lorenzini after the 17th-century Italian anatomist who first described them, pick up the weak electric fields thrown off by every muscle twitch of nearby prey. It is one of the most sensitive electroreception systems known in any animal on Earth. How faint an electric field can it still pick up?
answer: Around five billionths of a volt per centimetre
choices: Around five billionths of a volt per centimetre
Around five thousandths of a volt per centimetre
Around five volts per centimetre
Around five hundred volts per centimetre
context: The ampullae of Lorenzini can detect electric fields as tiny as about five nanovolts per centimetre (five billionths of a volt), among the most sensitive electroreception known in any animal. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ampullae_of_Lorenzini; marinebiodiversity.ca/sharks-sixth-sense-how-electric-fields-guide-these-ocean-predators.

question: A great white shark, patrolling the murky green water off the coast of South Africa, can somehow tell a wounded seal apart from a healthy one long before its own eyes can make out the animal at all. The seal's damaged skin leaks something into the surrounding seawater, and the shark's electric sense catches on and locks in. What about the injured seal gives it away from a distance, even through cloudy water?
answer: Its leaking electrolytes make an electric field up to three times stronger
choices: Its leaking electrolytes make an electric field up to three times stronger
Its blood turns the surrounding water faintly magnetic
Its panicked heartbeat sends out a low sound only sharks hear
Its torn skin glows under the shark's ultraviolet vision
context: A wounded animal leaks charged electrolytes into the water, creating an electric field up to three times stronger than an uninjured one, so to a great white's electric sense an injured seal or fish effectively lights up. Source: elasmo-research.org/education/white_shark/electroreception.htm.

question: Most fish are cold-blooded, running at the temperature of the sea around them. A great white is not: a net of blood vessels called the rete mirabile, Latin for 'wonderful net,' does something unusual with the heat its muscles make. What does the net do with that heat?
answer: It traps the body's own heat instead of losing it at the gills
choices: It traps the body's own heat instead of losing it at the gills
It pumps the heat out fast to keep the brain from overheating
It converts the heat into a faint electric charge
It stores the heat in fatty deposits for the winter
context: Unlike most fish, the great white is partly warm-blooded (regional endothermy): a countercurrent network of blood vessels called the rete mirabile, Latin for 'wonderful net,' traps its own body heat instead of losing it at the gills. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_white_shark; biologyinsights.com/are-great-white-sharks-warm-blooded.

question: The great white shark is a huge cold-water predator that hunts seals in the chilly seas off California and South Africa. Marine biologists wondered whether its big body ran warmer than the water around it, so they slipped small temperature probes down the throats of great whites swimming in seas of about 13 to 16 degrees Celsius. The readings inside the sharks were startling next to that cold water. What did the probes show?
answer: Stomach temperatures near 25 to 27 degrees Celsius
choices: Stomach temperatures near 25 to 27 degrees Celsius
Stomach temperatures matching the water almost exactly
Stomach temperatures below freezing, kept liquid by salts
Temperatures that swung wildly with every burst of speed
context: The rete mirabile keeps a great white's swimming muscles, brain, and eyes several degrees warmer than the sea; one study measured stomach temperatures of 24.7 to 26.8 degrees Celsius in water of only about 12.9 to 16.1 degrees. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_white_shark.

question: A great white shark, unlike almost every other fish, keeps parts of its body warmer than the surrounding sea, letting its swimming muscles fire faster and its brain stay sharp in cold water. But this warm-blooded trick is not unique to the great white. It is shared with a whole family of fast, muscular ocean hunters called the mackerel sharks. Which pair of sharks are the great white's warm-bodied relatives?
answer: The shortfin mako and the salmon shark
choices: The shortfin mako and the salmon shark
The whale shark and the basking shark
The tiger shark and the bull shark
The hammerhead and the nurse shark
context: The warm-blooded trait is a family trait shared by all the mackerel sharks (family Lamnidae), including the great white's fast cousins the shortfin mako and the salmon shark. Source: sharks4kids.com/post/2019/01/31/endothermic-sharks; biologyinsights.com/are-great-white-sharks-warm-blooded.

question: At Seal Island in False Bay, South Africa, a great white waits in the dark water far below a swimming seal, then rockets straight up so hard it can launch its entire body clear of the surface. Researchers gave this vertical strike a nickname. What did they call it?
answer: The 'Polaris' breach
choices: The 'Polaris' breach
The 'Torpedo' roll
The 'Kraken' rise
The 'Thunder' lunge
context: At Seal Island, great whites hunt by lurking below and rocketing straight up at a seal, an ambush so violent the shark often launches its whole body clear of the surface. Researchers named this vertical strike the 'Polaris' breach, after the submarine-launched missile. Source: elasmo-research.org/education/white_shark/predation.htm; sharkdivingmosselbay.co.za/seal-island.  (Legend.)

question: A great white shark rises up from deep water toward an unsuspecting seal swimming near the ocean surface. Its ambush from below works partly because of a two-tone coloring shared with many ocean hunters: dark grey on the back, chalky white on the belly. Looking up from the shark's approach angle, the seal sees only the pale underside against the sun-lit surface above. How exactly does that pale belly help the shark?
answer: It blends with the bright surface so the seal never sees it coming
choices: It blends with the bright surface so the seal never sees it coming
It reflects sunlight to dazzle and blind the seal
It flashes a warning that scatters a fleeing shoal
It mimics the pale belly of a harmless fish
context: The breach works because of countershading: the shark's dark grey back hides it against the sea floor while its white belly blends with the bright surface, so a seal never sees the attacker rising from below at over 40 km/h. Source: southafrica.net; ultimate-animals.com/predatory-strategies-of-great-white-sharks-at-seal-island.

question: Watching great whites breach on seals at Seal Island year after year, researchers tracked how often the attack actually landed. For such a feared hunter, the number is humbling, and young Cape fur seals often get away. About how often does a breach attack succeed?
answer: Only about half the time, near 47 percent
choices: Only about half the time, near 47 percent
Almost always, near 95 percent
Rarely, near 5 percent
Every single time once launched
context: Long-term study at Seal Island found the success rate of a breach attack is only about 47 percent, so young Cape fur seals frequently escape. Source: sharkdivingmosselbay.co.za/seal-island; sharkresearch.earth.miami.edu.

question: Zoos and aquariums keep sharks of many kinds, but a great white almost always dies within days. Only the Monterey Bay Aquarium has ever shown one for long, and even its record run ended when the young shark was released. How long did that record last?
answer: About 198 days
choices: About 198 days
About 5 years
About 20 years
About 3 days
context: No aquarium can keep a great white for long. The Monterey Bay Aquarium is the only one ever to display one successfully, and its record was 198 days in 2004 to 2005 before the young shark was released back into the wild. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monterey_Bay_Aquarium; pbs.org/wnet/nature/oceans-in-glass.

question: Aquariums and marine parks have tried again and again to keep a great white shark in even the largest tank, and every attempt has ended in the shark's death within days or weeks. Part of the reason is how it breathes, which is unlike a goldfish that can rest quietly on the bottom of a bowl. What must a great white keep doing every hour of its life to get oxygen from the water?
answer: Keep swimming constantly to push water over its gills
choices: Keep swimming constantly to push water over its gills
Surface regularly to gulp air like a whale
Pump its cheeks to draw water while resting
Absorb oxygen through its skin when still
context: Great whites fail in tanks because they must swim constantly to push water over their gills to breathe, and they roam such distances that in a tank they injure themselves swimming into walls and often refuse to eat. Source: a-z-animals.com/animals/great-white-shark/facts; thejakartapost.com/life/2019/07/06.

question: Tagging revealed that California's great whites vanish each year on a long journey out to a barren stretch of open mid-Pacific between Baja and Hawaii, where they linger for months. Scientists gave that mysterious spot a nickname. What did they call it?
answer: The 'White Shark Cafe'
choices: The 'White Shark Cafe'
The 'Blue Desert'
The 'Shark Graveyard'
The 'Midnight Reef'
context: California's great whites make an epic open-ocean migration to a barren patch of the mid-Pacific between Baja and Hawaii that scientists nicknamed the 'White Shark Cafe,' where they linger for months before returning. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_white_shark; sharkstewards.org/sharktober.

question: For most of the 20th century, marine biologists thought great white sharks lived only a few decades, maybe twenty or thirty years at most. Then a 2014 study led by researchers at the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution counted growth bands in the sharks' vertebrae, much like counting rings in a tree stump, and pushed the true figure far higher than anyone had guessed. How long can a great white shark actually live?
answer: Over 70 years
choices: Over 70 years
About 15 years
About 200 years
About 500 years
context: Great whites are among the longest-lived cartilaginous fish: a 2014 age study estimated they can reach over 70 years old, far older than scientists once believed. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_white_shark; fisheries.noaa.gov/species/white-shark.

question: A famous female great white shark nicknamed 'Deep Blue,' filmed off Guadalupe Island near Mexico by shark researcher Mauricio Hoyos in 2013, is thought to be around 50 years old and is one of the largest great whites ever caught on camera. Divers who swam right beside her looked like small children next to the enormous fish. Roughly how long is she?
answer: About 6 metres, some 20 feet
choices: About 6 metres, some 20 feet
About 3 metres, some 10 feet
About 12 metres, some 40 feet
About 1 metre, some 3 feet
context: 'Deep Blue,' filmed off Guadalupe Island and thought to be roughly 6 m (20 ft) long and about 50 years old, is one of the biggest great whites ever caught on camera. Source: surfertoday.com/environment/who-is-the-deep-blue-shark.  (Legend.)

question: Its teeth look like shrunken versions of the giant megalodon's, so people long assumed the great white was that monster's dwindled descendant. But fossils of a transitional shark from Peru, with teeth caught mid-way through growing their serrations, point to a very different ancestor. What did the great white actually evolve from?
answer: A broad-toothed mako shark, not megalodon
choices: A broad-toothed mako shark, not megalodon
A shrunken, cold-water line of megalodon
An early hammerhead that lost its head-wings
A deep-sea goblin shark that moved to the surface
context: The great white (Carcharodon carcharias) descends not from megalodon but from a lineage of broad-toothed mako sharks (Cosmopolitodus/Carcharodon hastalis). The transitional Carcharodon hubbelli, described by Dana Ehret from Peru's Pisco Formation (about 6.5 million years old), preserves teeth mid-way through developing serrations. Megalodon sits in a separate family (Otodontidae, genus Otodus), and the tooth resemblance is now read as convergent evolution, not close kinship. One paleontologist quipped that fewer people believe the megatooth sharks are related to great whites than believe the Earth is flat. Source: Smithsonian Ocean, 'Shark Teeth Tell Great White Shark Evolution Story'; Florida Museum of Natural History (Ehret et al. 2012, Palaeontology); Wikipedia 'Great white shark' and 'Carcharodon hubbelli'.

question: Sand tiger sharks are infamous for womb cannibalism: the first embryo to develop eats its unborn siblings until a single survivor is born. Great white pups grow up in the same dark uterus over roughly a year, yet several are born together, large and strong. How do they feed in there without turning on each other?
answer: They eat unfertilised eggs, not their siblings
choices: They eat unfertilised eggs, not their siblings
They devour the weakest of their siblings
A cord ferries the mother's blood into each pup
They absorb nutrients straight through their skin
context: Great white embryos feed by oophagy, swallowing dozens of unfertilised nutrient eggs (one study counted 50 to 70 egg capsules per uterus) and drinking a lipid-rich 'uterine milk' the mother secretes, a process called lipid histotrophy documented at over 79 litres in one female. Because separate nutrient eggs are on offer, several embryos coexist and are born large and robust after roughly 12 months of gestation, rather than devouring their siblings the way sand tiger pups famously do. Source: Sato et al., 'How great white sharks nourish their embryos... lipid histotrophy in lamnoid shark reproduction' (PMC5051657, ncbi.nlm.nih.gov); Wikipedia 'Great white shark'.

question: A giant fish, sluggish and slow, haunts the pitch-black, near-freezing waters of the deep Arctic Ocean off Greenland and Iceland. It grows up to 21 feet long, weighs over 2,200 pounds, and cruises water barely above the freezing point of the sea. Colder-blooded than any other shark, it hardly ever rises anywhere near the surface. What is this cold-and-dark giant?
answer: Greenland shark
choices: Greenland shark
Bull shark
Reef manta ray
Blue marlin
context: The Greenland shark (Somniosus microcephalus) reaches about 6.4 m (21 ft) and over 1,000 kg (2,200+ lb), living in water from -1.1C to 7.4C at depths of 100 to 1,200 m. Source: Wikipedia 'Greenland shark' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenland_shark).

question: Almost every Greenland shark, the huge sluggish shark of the deep Arctic Ocean, carries a small pinkish-white parasitic copepod called Ommatokoita elongata. The parasite attaches to one specific spot on the shark's body when the shark is still young, and it clings there for years, feeding off the living shark all that time. Where on the shark does this parasite make its home?
answer: on the cornea of each eye
choices: on the cornea of each eye
in the gill slits
inside the nostrils
on the tip of the snout
context: The ~30 mm copepod anchors to the cornea of each eye and, as it feeds, scars and clouds it, leaving the shark nearly blind. Source: Wikipedia 'Ommatokoita' and 'Greenland shark'; Ocean Action Hub (oceanactionhub.org/greenland-shark-eye-parasite/).  (Legend.)

question: Greenland sharks are huge, sluggish giants of the deep Arctic Ocean, and almost every one of them carries a parasitic copepod attached to its eye. The parasite leaves the shark nearly blind. But eyes are useless anyway in the pitch-black water half a mile down, where sunlight never reaches. So how does the Greenland shark find prey it cannot see?
answer: a powerful sense of smell
choices: a powerful sense of smell
echolocation clicks
a lateral heat-sensing pit
bioluminescent lures
context: In the lightless deep the shark hunts by smell, aided by electroreceptive pores on its snout to detect prey it cannot see. Source: Wikipedia 'Greenland shark'; Institute for Environmental Research and Education (iere.org/why-do-greenland-sharks-have-parasites-in-their-eyes/).

question: The Greenland shark is a slow, giant fish that lives in the near-freezing seas of the Arctic. Its flesh is laced with high levels of urea and a chemical called trimethylamine N-oxide, or TMAO. These substances keep the shark's tissues from freezing in near-0 degree Celsius water. But when any other animal — a sled dog, a polar bear, or a person — eats the raw meat, the same chemicals do something dramatic. What?
answer: it acts as a poison
choices: it acts as a poison
it turns the blood to jelly
it triggers a deep sleep
it corrodes the stomach lining
context: The urea and TMAO act like antifreeze in near-freezing water but make the raw meat poisonous; sled dogs that eat it can become unable to stand. Source: Wikipedia 'Greenland shark'.

question: The Greenland shark, a huge slow-moving shark of the deep Arctic Ocean, is a deep-sea scavenger that will swallow almost anything that sinks past its jaws to the seafloor. Fishermen who have cut open the stomachs of caught Greenland sharks over the years have pulled out some genuinely startling meals from inside them. Which of these has actually been recovered from a Greenland shark's stomach?
answer: moose, horse, reindeer, and even polar bears
choices: moose, horse, reindeer, and even polar bears
musk oxen, walrus tusks, and caribou hides
beluga skulls, seal pups, and arctic fox pelts
sled dogs, harp seals, and narwhal ribs
context: Remains of moose, horse, reindeer, and even polar bears (thought to have died of other causes and then been scavenged) have been recovered from Greenland shark stomachs, showing this deep-sea giant will eat almost anything that sinks. Source: Wikipedia 'Greenland shark' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenland_shark).

question: The Greenland shark is a giant fish of the icy Arctic Ocean and the slowest fish in the sea for its size — creeping along at about one foot per second, under 1 mile per hour. A healthy seal in the water can swim more than ten times that fast. Yet again and again, scientists cut open Greenland shark stomachs and find fresh seal remains inside. How does the sluggish shark catch a fast seal?
answer: it creeps up on seals asleep in the water
choices: it creeps up on seals asleep in the water
it stampedes them into a wall of ice
it spits a jet of water to stun them
it waits at breathing holes to ambush them
context: Scientists think the shark sneaks up on seals dozing in the water, where they sleep to hide from polar bears, only to be caught by the silent, creeping shark. Source: Watanabe et al. 2012, J. Exp. Marine Biology and Ecology; NBC News (nbcnews.com/id/wbna47952603); Live Science.  (Legend.)

question: A Greenland shark loads its tissues with urea to keep from freezing, but urea has a nasty side effect: on its own it creeps between proteins and pries them apart, unfolding them into useless tangles. The shark survives only because a second molecule, TMAO (trimethylamine N-oxide), is always there. What does TMAO do?
answer: it holds the proteins folded and also braces them against the crushing deep-sea pressure
choices: it holds the proteins folded and also braces them against the crushing deep-sea pressure
it drives the leftover urea back out through the gills and into the surrounding seawater
it hardens into microscopic crystals that seal each protein away from the roaming urea
it seeps into the skin so that predators taste the bitter poison and spit the shark back out
context: The shark's flesh is a two-molecule pressure-armor system. Urea alone accumulates at a protein's surface and unfolds it, but TMAO (trimethylamine N-oxide) counteracts both urea's damage and the protein-crushing effect of deep-sea hydrostatic pressure, so TMAO concentration rises with depth. PNAS 2024 work shows TMAO physically strips urea out of the water shell around proteins. The same toxin that makes the raw meat deadly to humans is what keeps the shark's own proteins from unfolding in the freezing, high-pressure deep. Source: 'Trimethylamine-N-oxide depletes urea in a peptide solvation shell,' PNAS 2024 (pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2317825121); Yancey et al., 'Unusual organic osmolytes in deep-sea animals.'

question: Scientists dated these sharks using a Cold-War signature: 1950s-60s atomic bomb tests dumped a spike of carbon-14 into the ocean. When they read the eye-lens cores, that bomb-pulse spike appeared in one group of sharks but was missing from the rest, and that split cracked the puzzle. Which sharks carried the atomic mark?
answer: only the smallest sharks, meaning the giant ones were already alive before the tests
choices: only the smallest sharks, meaning the giant ones were already alive before the tests
only the largest sharks, meaning they had been feeding most recently near the surface
every shark alike, since the carbon spread evenly through the whole ocean at once
only the female sharks, since a mother passes the carbon to her pups during pregnancy
context: The 2016 Nielsen study dated 28 female sharks (81-502 cm). Only the smallest sharks (about 220 cm or under) carried the bomb-pulse spike of carbon-14, proving those individuals were born after roughly 1960, while the big ones predated the atomic age entirely. This calibration pegged sexual maturity at about 156 plus or minus 22 years and the largest 5-meter shark at roughly 392 plus or minus 120 years old. Source: Nielsen et al. 2016, Science 353:702 (science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aaf1703); ScienceDaily 2016-08-11.  (Legend.)

question: On a rocky beach, a hungry gull hammers a crab with its sharp beak in the surf. The crab is fine. Unlike you or the gull, a crab has no bones inside its body at all — no skeleton hidden under the skin. Instead, it wears its skeleton on the outside, a hard armored shell of chitin and calcium that both shields it from the beak and gives its muscles something to pull against when it walks. What is this outer skeleton called?
answer: An exoskeleton
choices: An exoskeleton
A carapace scale
A cartilage frame
A keratin plate
context: Arthropods (insects, crustaceans, arachnids) build their skeleton outward as a rigid shell of chitin. It protects the soft body and anchors the muscles, doing from the outside the job your bones do from the inside. Source: Britannica, Arthropod - Form and Function; EBSCO Exoskeletons research starter.

question: A young crab's outer shell, called its exoskeleton, is hard and stiff like a tiny suit of armor. It protects the crab from predators, but once it hardens after each growth, the shell cannot stretch even a millimeter.
