And yet crabs get much bigger as they grow up, from pea-sized babies to dinner-plate-sized adults. So how does a crab locked inside that stiff armor manage to get any bigger at all?
answer: It sheds the whole shell and swells into a new, larger one before it hardens
choices: It sheds the whole shell and swells into a new, larger one before it hardens
It slowly dissolves the shell from the inside and reabsorbs it
It grows extra shell around the seams to widen the fit
It stays the same size and simply lives longer instead
context: This shedding is called molting, or ecdysis. Because a hardened exoskeleton cannot be enlarged, the animal grows a new soft skeleton underneath, climbs out of the old one, and puffs up to a bigger size before the new shell sets. Source: Britannica, Ecdysis; EBSCO Exoskeletons ('Once formed and hardened, an exoskeleton cannot be enlarged').

question: A cicada is a stout, big-eyed insect that sings loudly from summer trees. Its young — called nymphs — spend 13 or 17 years underground drinking sap from tree roots. When their long wait ends, a nymph tunnels to the surface, climbs a tree at night, and splits open along its back, hauling itself out of its old brown skin one leg at a time. For the first few hours, before its new shell hardens and its true adult colors come in, what does the freshly emerged cicada look like?
answer: Soft and ghostly pale - often white or light green
choices: Soft and ghostly pale - often white or light green
Deep brown, the same color as the shell it just left behind
Bright red as a warning to predators
Translucent like clear glass, showing its organs
context: A freshly emerged cicada is soft and pale - often white or light green - which earns it the nickname 'ghost cicada' until its body hardens, its wings expand, and its true colors come in within a few hours. Source: a-z-animals.com cicada crawl-out article; spiderzoon.com cicada-nymph.  (Legend.)

question: After a cicada crawls out of its old skeleton, the discarded brown shell stays hooked to the bark, a hollow, perfect copy of the insect down to the empty leg-tips - a ghost of the animal that left it. Biologists don't just call it a 'shell'; they have a real name for this cast-off exoskeleton. What is it?
answer: An exuvia
choices: An exuvia
A pupa
A chrysalis
A nymph
context: The empty molted skeleton is an exuvia (plural exuviae). It is the complete discarded exoskeleton, hollow but still shaped like the insect, including the hollow legs. Source: arhfoundation.org 'What Are the Shells Cast Off From Cicada Larva Called?'; MSU Extension Cicada Exuviae newsletter.

question: A garden spider spinning its web in a hedge loses one of its eight legs to a hungry robin's beak. The spider is not stuck as a seven-legged spider forever, though. Spiders molt, shedding their whole outer skin as they grow, and at the very next molt a fresh new leg appears where the missing one used to be. What is strange, though, about how that new leg first comes back?
answer: It emerges smaller and paler, then catches up to full size across later molts
choices: It emerges smaller and paler, then catches up to full size across later molts
It comes back full-sized and fully colored right away
It grows back longer than the leg it replaced
It grows back a different color than the rest of its legs
context: A spider can regenerate a lost leg at a molt. The new leg first emerges thinner, shorter, and paler than the original, then grows toward full size over the next two to four molts. Source: academicpath.org 'Can Spiders Regrow Legs'; pestwhisperer.com Spider Molting; NCBI PMC12211592.

question: A lobster is an armored sea creature with big claws and a hard outer shell of chitin and calcium. That shell cannot stretch, but the lobster inside keeps growing. So the only way for the lobster to get bigger is to shed the old shell — a process called molting — and grow a fresh, larger one underneath. In just the first five to seven years of its life, about how many times does a young lobster shed its shell?
answer: About 25 times
choices: About 25 times
About 3 times
About 100 times
About once a year, so 5 to 7 times
context: A lobster grows by molting again and again - shedding its shell around 25 times in the first 5 to 7 years - because the hard shell simply cannot stretch with the body. Source: NOAA Fisheries 'Fun Facts About Luscious Lobsters'; lobsteranywhere.com Lobster Molt.

question: A lobster is an armored sea creature that must shed its old shell — a process called molting — in order to grow. After a molt, the lobster wriggles out of its old armor and lies beside it on the seabed, its new shell so thin it feels like wet paper. It is soft and helpless, an easy meal for any hungry fish. But before it hides, it does something startling with the empty shell it just crawled out of. What does the freshly molted lobster do with the old shell?
answer: Eats its own discarded shell
choices: Eats its own discarded shell
Buries the old shell to hide from predators
Carries the old shell on its back as armor
Leaves at once to find calcium-rich prey
context: After molting, a lobster often devours its own recently vacated shell. The old shell is rich in calcium, which the lobster reuses to harden its new, paper-thin shell faster. Source: lobsteranywhere.com Lobster Molt; parl.ns.ca American Lobster Life Cycle ('devouring their own recently vacated shells').

question: The Mexican axolotl is a favorite in biology labs for one amazing trick. If it loses a whole leg to a hunter, the leg grows back over 40 to 50 days. It comes back with bone, muscle, nerves, and blood. What is most amazing about how the new leg finishes?
answer: It grows back perfectly, with no scar at all
choices: It grows back perfectly, with no scar at all
It grows back a slightly different color
It grows back smaller and thinner
It grows back covered in protective scales
context: The axolotl regrows an entire limb — bone, muscle, nerves and blood vessels — flawlessly and scar-free in roughly 40 to 50 days. Scar-free healing is exactly what makes it so precious to researchers. Source: Biology Insights (biologyinsights.com); MDI Biological Laboratory (mdibl.org).  (Legend.)

question: In warm places all over the world — the American Southwest, southern Europe, Southeast Asia — many small lizards live with a trick their predators cannot beat. Grab a lizard by the tail and the tail simply snaps off in your hand, wriggling to distract you while the lizard sprints away. Within weeks it grows a new tail. But when scientists X-rayed the replacement, they found it is a fake copy. The original tail was built on a chain of many small linked vertebrae, real bone. What actually forms the skeleton of the regrown one?
answer: A single unsegmented tube of cartilage
choices: A single unsegmented tube of cartilage
A branching frame of cartilage rods
A chain of tiny cartilage beads
A fresh row of small new vertebrae
context: The replacement tail is not a true tail: instead of a jointed backbone of small vertebrae, its skeleton is one unsegmented tube of cartilage, with no bone at all. Dropping the tail to escape is called autotomy. Source: USC Stem Cell (stemcell.keck.usc.edu/perfect-lizard-tail/); ASU News.

question: Deer are hoofed forest mammals, and the males grow a fresh set of bony antlers on their heads every year, then shed and regrow them the next. No other mammal grows bone that fast. In the wapiti — also called the elk, one of the largest kinds of deer in North America — how much length can a single antler add in one day at peak summer growth?
answer: About 27 millimeters — roughly an inch
choices: About 27 millimeters — roughly an inch
About 3 millimeters — a pencil-tip's width
About 1 millimeter — barely visible
About 100 millimeters — a whole hand's width
context: Antler is the fastest-growing bone known in any mammal, elongating up to ~2 cm a day in big species, with wapiti hitting ~27 mm/day. A brand-new full set regrows annually. Source: NCBI PMC10733395; Alaska Dept. of Fish & Game.  (Legend.)

question: A sea cucumber is a soft, sausage-shaped animal — a slow relative of starfish — that inches along the seabed grazing on tiny scraps. When a fish or crab attacks it, the sea cucumber does something that sounds deadly to itself: it blasts a whole chunk of its own guts out through its back end. The mess tangles or scares off the attacker while the sea cucumber crawls away. But what happens to the emptied sea cucumber next?
answer: It regrows the lost organs over a few weeks
choices: It regrows the lost organs over a few weeks
It survives but can never feed again
It seals the wound and lives as an empty shell
It dies within hours from the loss
context: This defensive organ-dumping is called evisceration. Having startled or tangled a predator, the sea cucumber simply regrows the expelled organs over a few weeks. Source: Wikipedia: Evisceration (autotomy); PBS NOVA.  (Legend.)

question: Many lizards — the scaly, four-legged reptiles that skitter along walls and rocks — can drop their tail on purpose when a predator grabs it, then grow a new tail in its place. The new tail may look fine from the outside, but its skeleton is not the same inside. The old tail had a chain of jointed bones. The new one is a single stiff tube of cartilage — no joints. Compared to the old tail, the new one is:
answer: Far less flexible along its whole length
choices: Far less flexible along its whole length
Far more flexible and whip-like
Exactly as bendy as before
Able to grip branches like a hand
context: One solid cartilage tube can't bend at joints the way a segmented backbone can, so the replacement is far less flexible. The lizard trades a perfect tail for a good-enough spare. Source: ASU News — 'Researchers discover regenerated lizard tails are different from originals'.

question: Every spring a male deer grows a fresh set of antlers — branched bony horns — right out of the top of his skull. The growing antlers are not bare bone. They are wrapped in velvet, a fuzzy living skin full of nerves and blood, and they lengthen faster than almost any tissue in any animal. Then in late fall or winter, the hardened antlers drop off on their own. What change in the deer's body sets off that yearly fall?
answer: A drop in the deer's testosterone
choices: A drop in the deer's testosterone
A sudden rise in body temperature
The first heavy snowfall of winter
A shortage of calcium in the blood
context: Velvet is the nerve- and blood-vessel-rich skin that feeds fast-growing antler bone. The annual cycle restarts when a drop in testosterone makes the old antlers fall off. Source: Alaska Dept. of Fish & Game; onX Hunt.

question: Most starfish can regrow a lost arm, but they usually need part of the central disc to rebuild the whole body. Starfish of the genus Linckia break that rule: a single severed arm, with no central disc at all, can slowly rebuild an entire new animal. The lopsided shape it takes while doing so earned these starfish their nickname. What is it?
answer: A comet
choices: A comet
A pinwheel
A five-pointed disc
A curled shell
context: A lone Linckia arm can regrow a new disc and little arms, so it looks like a comet: a bright growing 'head' with the original arm fading behind like a tail — hence 'comet stars'. Source: Wikipedia: Starfish regeneration.  (Legend.)

question: The planarian is a tiny freshwater flatworm the size of a grain of rice, and it is the undisputed champion of the animal kingdom at growing back from injury. In laboratory studies, scientists have taken a single planarian and cut it into pieces, sideways or lengthwise, sometimes into more than a hundred chunks. Each individual piece then does something amazing. What does each piece do?
answer: Regrows into a complete worm, whole new head and all
choices: Regrows into a complete worm, whole new head and all
Heals over into a lifeless lump of tissue
Grows back only the tail end, never a head
Fuses back together into the original worm
context: Cut a planarian into pieces and each piece regrows into a complete worm, including a brand-new head and brain. Source: Wikipedia: Planarian; Max-Planck-Gesellschaft (mpg.de).  (Legend.)

question: The axolotl is a Mexican salamander that keeps its feathery pink gills all its life and never fully grows up. Scientists prize it — and study it hoping one day to heal human patients — because it can regrow tissues that most animals, including us, lose forever. It can even rebuild a whole missing leg. Beyond limbs and tail, what other body parts can an axolotl regrow?
answer: Parts of its heart, jaws, brain, and spinal cord
choices: Parts of its heart, jaws, brain, and spinal cord
Its lungs, kidneys, and gills
Its shell, teeth, and claws
Its scales, fins, and whiskers
context: The axolotl can regrow its tail, parts of its heart, its jaws, and even portions of its brain and spinal cord — which is why labs study it for possible human spinal-injury repair. Source: MDI Biological Laboratory (mdibl.org); Biology Insights.

question: A planarian can rebuild an entire worm from a tiny scrap of itself — because a huge share of its cells are neoblasts, adult stem cells able to become any body part. Researchers proved neoblasts are the secret with a brutal test: blast a worm with radiation to destroy them, and it loses all power to regenerate and dies. What single step restores that power?
answer: Transplanting one neoblast back into the worm
choices: Transplanting one neoblast back into the worm
Feeding it a rich diet for several weeks
Placing it in warmer, cleaner water
Cutting it again to trigger a fresh response
context: Up to 20% or more of a planarian's cells are neoblasts. Radiation wipes them out and the worm dies; transplanting a single neoblast back restores regeneration. Source: Wikipedia: Planarian; Whitehead Institute (wi.mit.edu).

question: The crown-of-thorns starfish is a big, spiny sea star, up to two feet across, that lives on coral reefs and eats live coral. In the 1960s an outbreak on Australia's Great Barrier Reef killed vast stretches of coral, so fishermen tried to wipe out the starfish. They hauled them up in boats, chopped each one into pieces with knives, and threw the pieces back into the sea. But starfish can regrow a whole body from parts. What may their effort have really done?
answer: It may have multiplied the starfish instead of killing them
choices: It may have multiplied the starfish instead of killing them
It poisoned the reef with rotting starfish
It drove the starfish into deeper water only
It had no effect on the starfish at all
context: Since some starfish regrow whole animals from pieces, chopping them up and returning them to the water may have accidentally multiplied the crown-of-thorns rather than killing them. Source: Wikipedia: Starfish regeneration.  (Legend.)

question: Planarians are little freshwater flatworms about a fingernail long, with two crossed dark eyespots on the head. Cut one clean in half and each half will regrow into a whole new worm — head, tail, and all. In the 1800s scientists called them 'immortal under the edge of a knife.' Modern labs pushed that reputation to its limit, slicing planarians into ever-smaller scraps to hunt for the tiniest piece that could still rebuild a complete worm. How tiny a fragment proved to be enough?
answer: About 1/279th of the worm
choices: About 1/279th of the worm
About one-tenth of the worm
About one-half of the worm
About one-thousandth of the worm
context: A fragment as small as 1/279th of a planarian can still rebuild a complete new animal — hence 'immortal under the edge of a knife.' Source: Wikipedia: Planarian.  (Legend.)

question: A planarian is a small freshwater flatworm that can regrow its whole body from a scrap. That regrowth is steered by a molecular signal called the Wnt pathway — the body's chemical instruction that tells a cut end which side should become a tail and which the head. In one experiment, scientists blocked the Wnt signal in a cut planarian piece as it grew back. What surprising body part grew where an ordinary tail should have formed?
answer: A second head — a two-headed worm
choices: A second head — a two-headed worm
No head at all, just a blunt stump
A body twice its normal length
A second, separate worm splitting off
context: Disrupting the Wnt/beta-catenin signal (or applying an electric field) makes a fragment grow a head where a tail should be — a two-headed planarian. Source: IFLScience; Whitehead Institute (wi.mit.edu).  (Legend.)

question: The axolotl regrows a whole leg by first building a small ball of fresh cells at the stump. About five to seven days later, that ball rebuilds cartilage, muscle, and nerve. Adult salamanders of most other kinds cannot do this. What odd fact about the axolotl's whole life do scientists tie to its regrowing power?
answer: It never fully grows up, keeping feathery gills and a larval body for life
choices: It never fully grows up, keeping feathery gills and a larval body for life
It swaps to breathing air and crawls onto land as it matures
It sheds and completely regrows its skin every few weeks
It slows its heartbeat to a near halt while a limb rebuilds
context: The axolotl (Ambystoma mexicanum) is neotenic, or paedomorphic: it never undergoes the metamorphosis that turns other salamanders into land animals, staying in a larval-like aquatic form with external feathery gills for life. That retained embryonic-like state is tied to its exceptional regenerative power. The blastema begins forming about 5–7 days after amputation, reaches an initial 1–2 mm, and peaks in cell proliferation around 14–21 days; its multipotent cells rebuild cartilage, muscle, and connective tissue while retaining positional memory. Source: Grokipedia 'Blastema' (timeline: 5–7 day onset, 1–2 mm, 14–21 day peak proliferation) and Grokipedia 'Axolotl' (neoteny).

question: A deer's velvet antler is the fastest-growing tissue any mammal makes, driven so hard by growth-factor genes that its gene-expression fingerprint reads closer to a bone tumor than to normal bone. Yet deer almost never get cancer — zoo records put their rate around five times lower than other mammals. Which built-in trio does the most to keep the racing antler from turning malignant?
answer: Beefed-up tumor-suppressor genes, mass cell suicide, and the yearly casting of the whole antler
choices: Beefed-up tumor-suppressor genes, mass cell suicide, and the yearly casting of the whole antler
A chilled antler core, a hard blood cutoff at full size, and a mineral shell that seals the tip
An immune sheath that devours mutant cells, an acidic core, and a scab coat over the beam
A frozen store of stem cells, a walled-off growth zone, and a nightly pause in cell division
context: A fast-growing antler's gene-expression profile correlates more strongly with osteosarcoma, bone cancer (r = 0.67–0.78), than with normal bone (r = 0.33–0.47). Three proto-oncogenes (FOS, FAM83A, REL) are under positive selection in deer and cancer-promoting growth-factor genes (FGF19, FGF21, PDGFD) run hot. Deer restrain this with tumor-suppressor genes under positive selection — the p53-regulator PML shows the strongest selection signal of all — plus massive apoptosis (up to ~64% of cells in the inner antler layer are programmed to die) and the annual casting of the hardened antler, which physically discards any rogue cells. Zoo records show deer get cancer roughly 5x less often than other mammals. Source: PMC10733395 'Deer antlers: the fastest growing tissue with least cancer occurrence'; genetics corroborated by Science 2019 (doi:10.1126/science.aav6335).  (Legend.)

question: Half a mile down in the black Pacific, a slim two-foot eel drifts near an empty stomach when a shrimp swims past. It has only tiny teeth and cannot chase fast prey through the dark. What lets this deep-sea eel snatch a meal from the emptiness in a single instant?
answer: Its whole head swells open like a soap bubble into a pouch bigger than its body
choices: Its whole head swells open like a soap bubble into a pouch bigger than its body
It fires a jet of venom that stuns the passing shrimp
It wraps its long tail around the prey and crushes it
It buries itself in the seafloor mud to ambush from below
context: The pelican eel (Eurypharynx pelecanoides) is famous for a mouth that balloons open into a huge pelican-like pouch, scooping up prey much larger than its own body in the empty deep. Source: Nautilus Live (nautiluslive.org/video/2018/09/20/gulper-eel-balloons-its-massive-jaws).  (Legend.)

question: The pelican eel, also called the gulper eel, is a strange fish of the deep ocean with a huge gaping pouch of a mouth that looks obviously built to swallow big fish whole, like a pelican gulping a herring. But when scientists look inside that giant mouth, they find only tiny teeth and a delicate, thin jaw. In truth, what does this monster-mouthed eel of the deep actually eat most of the time?
answer: Small crustaceans it nets from the drifting water
choices: Small crustaceans it nets from the drifting water
Other eels nearly as long as itself
Squid it drags down from shallower water
Chunks of whale carcass fallen to the seafloor
context: Despite its monstrous gape and tiny teeth, the pelican eel mostly eats small crustaceans -- the huge mouth is an all-purpose net for whatever rare meal drifts by, not a tool for swallowing big fish. Source: Wikipedia: Pelican eel (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pelican_eel).

question: The pelican eel is a strange deep-sea fish that lives more than a mile down, in the pitch dark where no sunlight ever reaches. It has a huge pouch-like mouth like a pelican's throat, and a body that tapers into a long, whip-thin tail trailing far behind the rest of the animal. Right at the very tip of that tail sits one special structure. What is it?
answer: A glowing organ that flashes pink and red
choices: A glowing organ that flashes pink and red
A cluster of taste buds that smells prey in the water
A whip-like flap it lashes to stir up drifting food
A dense knot of nerves that senses nearby movement
context: The eel's whip-thin tail is tipped with a bioluminescent organ that shines pink and gives off occasional bright red flashes -- a lure it may wave to draw prey toward its open mouth. Source: Wikipedia: Pelican eel (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pelican_eel).  (Legend.)

question: Most fish keep themselves from sinking with a gas-filled float inside their body, topping it up as they rise and dive. The pelican eel, drifting between 500 and 3,000 meters down, has no such float at all. How does its body stay buoyant instead?
answer: Jelly-filled spaces around its backbone hold it up
choices: Jelly-filled spaces around its backbone hold it up
Large gulps of swallowed air trapped in its gut
Broad oily fins that spread its weight across the water
Constant slow swimming that keeps it from sinking
context: The pelican eel has no swim bladder; instead of the gas-filled float most fish use, its body relies on gelatinous, jelly-filled spaces around the backbone to stay buoyant -- a cheap, low-energy body plan for a place where food is scarce. Source: Wikipedia: Pelican eel (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pelican_eel).

question: The hairy frog lives in the streams and forests of Cameroon in central Africa. Nicknamed the 'horror frog,' it looks like a plain, harmless, plump little frog resting on a wet leaf. Then a hunter or a hungry snake grabs it. What the hairy frog does next to fight back, no other animal on Earth is known to do. What is its bizarre defense?
answer: It deliberately snaps the bones in its own toes and shoves the sharp ends out through its skin as claws
choices: It deliberately snaps the bones in its own toes and shoves the sharp ends out through its skin as claws
It inflates its whole body until the attacker cannot get its jaws around it
It squirts a jet of foul sticky slime from glands along its spine
It sheds its entire tail, which keeps twitching to distract the predator
context: This is why it earned the nicknames 'horror frog' and 'Wolverine frog.' At rest there are no claws to see at all; the frog literally wounds itself to arm itself when threatened. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hairy_frog; Blackburn, Hanken & Jenkins 2008, 'Concealed weapons: erectile claws in African frogs,' Biology Letters.  (Legend.)

question: When the hairy frog of Cameroon in central Africa is grabbed, it drives sharp claws out through the skin of its own toes to slash at the attacker. A house cat's retractable claw and an eagle's talon both have a hard outer sheath of keratin covering a bone inside. The hairy frog's newly-made claws are strange because of what they are actually made of. What are those toe-claws?
answer: Bare bone, just the frog's own sharpened toe-bones with no covering at all
choices: Bare bone, just the frog's own sharpened toe-bones with no covering at all
A cluster of stiffened hairs matted together with dried slime
Curved spurs of thick keratin like a rooster grows on its leg
Hollow quills that snap off in the wound and grow back later
context: Unlike a cat's or a bird's claw, the hairy frog's claws have no hard outer sheath. They are simply the frog's own toe-bones, sharpened and punched out raw through the skin of the foot. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hairy_frog; Blackburn et al. 2008, Biology Letters.

question: The male hairy frog grows what looks like a coat of 'hair' along his flanks and thighs in the breeding season, made of thin fringes of skin. But it is not hair at all. What are those fringes actually for?
answer: Soaking up extra oxygen from the water so he can stay under longer
choices: Soaking up extra oxygen from the water so he can stay under longer
Trapping a warm layer of air to survive cold mountain streams
Sensing ripples in the water to detect an approaching predator
Attracting females by shimmering in the light like a lure
context: The 'hair' is really fringes of thin skin flaps (dermal papillae) packed with tiny blood vessels, working like external gills. The male grows them so he can breathe underwater for long stretches while standing guard over the clutch of eggs. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hairy_frog; iere.org/what-is-the-hairy-frog-and-why-is-it-hairy.

question: The hairy frog of Cameroon has a defense unique in the whole animal world: when grabbed, it snaps the tips of its own toe-bones and shoves the sharp broken ends out through the skin of each back foot as makeshift claws. Scientists have watched this happen under X-ray machines and filmed exactly how the claws pop out. But there is one part of the whole trick they still cannot explain. What is it?
answer: How the claw ever goes back in once the danger has passed
choices: How the claw ever goes back in once the danger has passed
Which of the toes fire their claws first when the frog is grabbed
How the frog avoids bleeding to death from the self-inflicted wound
Why only the males, and never the females, can grow the claws
context: The extension is well documented, but researchers can only hypothesize that the claw slides back passively as the torn skin heals. That 'retract-and-heal' half of the story is still unconfirmed. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hairy_frog, which states the retraction mechanism 'is not known' and is only hypothesized.

question: Hallucigenia was a tiny worm-shaped sea creature about the length of your fingernail, alive around 500 million years ago during the Cambrian explosion — the great burst of strange new animal shapes preserved in the Burgess Shale fossil beds in Canada. For decades scientists drew Hallucigenia upside down, thinking its row of stiff spines were legs. Around 1991, better fossils were carefully drilled open and revealed something that had been hidden under the surrounding rock all along. What had been buried there?
answer: A row of soft clawed walking legs
choices: A row of soft clawed walking legs
A fringe of feeding tentacles
A set of gripping suckers
A line of breathing gills
context: Flipped right-side up, Hallucigenia walked on soft clawed legs while the roughly seven pairs of stiff spines stood up along its back as protection. Researchers found the second row of walking legs by drilling out rock that had hidden it. Source: PalaeontologyOnline.com; fossilguy.com (Ramskold and Hou).  (Legend.)

question: Hallucigenia is a bizarre worm-like creature that lived in shallow tropical seas during the Cambrian period, over 500 million years ago, and is known only from thumbnail-sized fossils crushed flat in Canada's Burgess Shale. For decades scientists thought a dark blob at one end of it was its head. In 2015 a new study finally revealed what that mysterious blob actually was. What did the 'head' turn out to be?
answer: Decay fluids squeezed out of the body
choices: Decay fluids squeezed out of the body
A cluster of unhatched eggs
A bundle of grasping tentacles
A hard shell it retreated into
context: The blob was decay fluid or gut contents that had oozed from the body during fossilization; the real head was at the opposite end. So scientists had the animal not only upside down but back-to-front. Under an electron microscope the true head showed a simple face with a pair of eyes and a ring of plates around a mouth lined with tiny needle-like teeth. Source: Smith and Caron 2015, Nature; PalaeontologyOnline.com; ROM.  (Legend.)

question: Hallucigenia was a bizarre Cambrian sea creature about the length of your fingernail, alive 500 million years ago. Once scientists finally flipped its picture right-side up in the 1990s, its little clawed feet gave away its family tree. Each claw is built from three cones stacked one inside another, like paper cups nested together. That same nested-cone claw structure is found today in only one living group of animals. Which?
answer: Velvet worms
choices: Velvet worms
Sea urchins
Horseshoe crabs
Tardigrades
context: The nested-cone claws match those of today's velvet worms (onychophorans), soft caterpillar-like animals. Hallucigenia sits near the base of the lineage that also led to insects, spiders, and crustaceans. It remains the classic textbook lesson in how hard the strangest Cambrian fossils are to read. Source: Smith and Caron 2015, Nature; ROM; Wikipedia.

question: On the warm coral reefs of the Indian and Pacific Oceans, a shark cruises just above the sand. Its head has been flattened sideways into a wide, flat bar of muscle and cartilage. An eye rides at each far tip of that strange, T-shaped head, giving the shark a sweeping, almost 360-degree view. No diver who sees the silhouette ever mistakes it for another shark. Which shark is unmistakable from that shape alone?
answer: Hammerhead shark
choices: Hammerhead shark
Tiger shark
Nurse shark
Lemon shark
context: That flattened head has a real name: the cephalofoil, Greek for 'head-wing.' It is not a random shape but a sensory wing that spreads the shark's detectors far apart across its width. Source: Cape May Whale Watch & Research Center, 'The Hydrodynamic Head Of Hammerhead Sharks.'

question: Off the coasts of Florida and the Bahamas, a family of sharks cruises the warm water with heads shaped like flat, wide hammers. Most hammerheads run 5 to 10 feet long, but one kind is the giant of the group — around 15 feet, and the largest ever measured stretched close to 20 feet. Which hammerhead is the biggest?
answer: Great hammerhead
choices: Great hammerhead
Scalloped hammerhead
Bonnethead
Winghead shark
context: The great hammerhead (Sphyrna mokarran) tops the family at roughly 4.6 m on average, with the largest reaching around 6.1 m. Source: Wikipedia, 'Great hammerhead'; Florida Museum Discover Fishes.

question: A great hammerhead shark cruises just off a coral reef, swinging its wide, flat head in slow S-curves low over bare sand. Suddenly it stops, drives its snout into the seafloor, and digs out a stingray from a patch of sand where nothing was showing at all. The ray had been completely buried and motionless. What was the hammerhead's flat head sensing that let it pinpoint the hidden ray?
answer: The faint electric fields of the buried ray
choices: The faint electric fields of the buried ray
The warmth rising off the buried ray
The ray's shadow cast on the sand
Vibrations from the ray's flicking tail
context: The underside of the hammer is studded with ampullae of Lorenzini, jelly-filled pores that sense the tiny electric fields of living animals. The wide head spreads them into a broad array, so the shark sweeps the seafloor like a wide-beam metal detector, feeling for prey it cannot see. Source: Reef Check, 'Why Do Hammerheads Have Hammer Heads'; Elasmo Research, 'Sandy Plains: Great Hammerhead Shark.'

question: Hammerhead sharks have a wide, T-shaped head — called a cephalofoil — with one eye stuck out on each far end, nowhere near each other. In the 2000s, biologist Michelle McComb caught several kinds of hammerhead in nets, swept small flashing lights all around each one, and recorded the electrical response from every eye at each flash. She discovered the hammerhead has one thing no normal shark can claim. What did those tests reveal?
answer: A nearly 360-degree field of view
choices: A nearly 360-degree field of view
A pair of long-range zoom eyes
Eyes that glow to light the seabed
A blind spot it herds prey into
context: An eye on each tip gives the shark a full view up and down its own body at once, plus a stereo view straight behind it. McComb recorded the eyes' electrical response to light swept around the animal to prove the wraparound coverage. Source: Live Science, 'Hammerhead Sharks See 360 Degrees in Stereo'; McComb et al., Journal of Experimental Biology 2009.  (Legend.)

question: A hammerhead's two nostrils sit not up front but out at the very tips of its wide head, an odd place to put a nose. Kajiura's team found this wide spacing hands the shark a trick a plain-headed shark cannot do. What does the wide-set nose let it work out?
answer: Which direction a smell is coming from
choices: Which direction a smell is coming from
How far off the food still is
How big the hidden prey must be
Whether the prey is alive or dead
context: It literally smells in stereo: a scent reaches one tip-mounted nostril a split second before the other, and that tiny time gap tells it which way to turn. The scalloped hammerhead's whole brain is built around this wide nose, with its smell-processing region taking up about 7% of brain mass, roughly double the ~3% in other shark families. Source: Smithsonian Ocean, 'Do Sharks Smell in Stereo'; Kajiura research, Current Biology 2010.

question: The great hammerhead is a huge shark with a broad, flat, T-shaped head. Its favorite prey is the stingray, a flat-bodied fish that hides on the sandy seabed and stings with a barbed tail. A great hammerhead attacks by first slamming a stingray down against the sand with a hard blow from above. Then, before it bites chunks from the ray's wings, it does something no other shark does. What is its next move?
answer: Pinning the ray flat with its own head
choices: Pinning the ray flat with its own head
Wrapping the ray up in its long tail
Spinning hard to tear the ray loose
Swallowing the ray whole in one gulp
context: The head is both sensor and sledgehammer: it knocks the ray down, pins it with the flat of the hammer, then pivots to feed. The great hammerhead even eats rays whole, venomous tail-spine and all; one caught off Florida had 96 stingray spines lodged in and around its mouth and was barely bothered. Source: Wikipedia, 'Great hammerhead,' citing Strong et al. Bahamas field observations.  (Legend.)

question: Scalloped hammerheads are medium-sized hammerhead sharks with a wavy front edge on their T-shaped head. They hunt alone through the open ocean at night. So it stuns divers off Cocos Island — a rocky volcanic island in the eastern Pacific Ocean off Costa Rica — that by day hundreds of these solitary night-hunters mass together into a slow-circling wall of sharks you can swim right through. Where do the daytime crowds reliably gather?
answer: Over an underwater mountain
choices: Over an underwater mountain
Inside a coral lagoon
Along a deep-sea trench
Around a sunken shipwreck
context: These underwater mountains are called seamounts. The most famous gathering is at the Alcyone seamount off Cocos Island, Costa Rica, where from June to September divers see schools of hundreds. Cocos, the Galapagos, and Malpelo form a route divers call the 'Hammerhead Triangle.' Source: PLOS One, Cocos Island scalloped hammerhead study; Diveplanit, 'The Hammerhead Triangle.'

question: The great hammerhead is a huge shark whose famous T-shaped head — called a cephalofoil — spans only about a quarter of its body length. But one small tropical relative in the same shark family wears a cephalofoil so extreme it stretches nearly half the animal's entire length from one wingtip to the other. Which shark has the widest head, in proportion to its body, in the whole hammerhead family?
answer: The winghead shark
choices: The winghead shark
The bonnethead
The smalleye hammerhead
The scoophead
context: The winghead (Eusphyra blochii) has the most extreme cephalofoil of all, about 40-50% of its body length, versus roughly 23-27% for the great hammerhead. The wider the head, the farther apart its sensors and the wider its sensory sweep. Source: Aussie Animals, 'Winghead Shark'; Wikipedia, 'Great hammerhead.'

question: Scalloped hammerheads are warm-water sharks, yet they dive past 800 metres into water near freezing to hunt, and their swimming muscle somehow stays warm the whole way down. A shark cannot warm its blood, and the gills bleed heat straight into the sea. Mark Royer tagged them and filmed one at 1,044 metres to see the trick. What does the shark do on the way down?
answer: It clamps its gill slits shut the entire dive
choices: It clamps its gill slits shut the entire dive
It shunts warm blood inward away from the skin
It shivers its swimming muscles to make heat
It rides down inside a pocket of warmer water
context: The gills are where a fish's warm blood meets the sea across a thin membrane, so in 5C water at depth they would strip the shark's body heat away in minutes. By clamping the gill slits shut and holding its breath -- about 17 minutes per dive, with only ~4 minutes spent hunting on the bottom before it races back up to breathe -- the scalloped hammerhead seals off that heat leak, and tagged muscle temperature stays warm all the way down, cooling only as it nears the surface and opens its gills again. Source: Royer et al., 'Breath holding as a thermoregulation strategy in the deep-diving scalloped hammerhead shark,' Science (2023), DOI 10.1126/science.add4445, https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.add4445 ; ScienceDaily 2023-05-11 https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2023/05/230511164453.htm  (Legend.)

question: The bonnethead is a small, shovel-headed member of the hammerhead shark family. In 2001, at the Henry Doorly Zoo in Omaha, Nebraska, a female bonnethead who had been netted as a pup and kept in a tank for three years — with no male shark ever near her — surprised her keepers by giving birth to a healthy live pup. Scientists ran DNA tests on the newborn. How was the pup made?
answer: Her egg grew into a pup with no sperm at all
choices: Her egg grew into a pup with no sperm at all
She had stored a male's sperm for those three years
A second female in the tank had fertilised her eggs
A shred of her own body tissue budded into a pup
context: Stored sperm was the obvious suspect -- some sharks bank it for months -- but the pup's DNA held only its mother's genetic material, ruling that out and marking the first genetically confirmed virgin birth (parthenogenesis) in any shark. The mechanism is automictic parthenogenesis: the unfertilised egg fuses with a sister cell (a polar body) from its own meiosis instead of a sperm, so the pup is homozygous, essentially a half-clone of the mother. Source: Chapman, Shivji et al., 'Virgin birth in a hammerhead shark,' Biology Letters 3(4):425-427 (2007), DOI 10.1098/rsbl.2007.0189, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2390672/

question: On the cool seafloor around Tasmania, off the southern coast of Australia, lives a tiny, brightly colored fish called the handfish. It is a terrible swimmer — drop one into open water and it barely goes anywhere at all. Yet it gets around the rocky bottom just fine. How does the handfish move from one spot to the next?
answer: It walks step by step on hand-like fins
choices: It walks step by step on hand-like fins
It jets backward by squirting water
It undulates along the sand like an eel
It rides the current wherever it flows
context: The handfish is a poor swimmer that mostly crawls, a slow, sedentary bottom-dweller. It plants its splayed pectoral fins on the sand and pushes itself forward step by step. Those fins are so hand-shaped that the family name comes from the Latin 'bracchium', meaning 'arm'. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handfish  (Legend.)

question: The spotted handfish is a rare, palm-sized Tasmanian fish that walks on hand-shaped fins along the seabed. The mother lays her eggs in a small mass and stays to guard them. When an invasive Northern Pacific seastar — a hungry starfish that arrived in Tasmania on foreign ships and now hunts along that seabed — creeps toward her egg mass, the tiny mother does not flee. She wedges her body between the predator and her eggs and drives it off with one specific move. How does she shove the seastar off course?
answer: She wipes it away with her tail
choices: She wipes it away with her tail
She stabs it with venomous fin spines
She squirts ink to blind it
She bites through its arm
context: A mother spotted handfish defends her eggs from the invasive Northern Pacific seastar by wedging herself between the predator and the eggs and wiping it with her tail to shove it off course. Source: https://handfish.org.au/spawning-behaviour-of-spotted-handfish/

question: In the shallow reefs off Tasmania, in southern Australia, lives a tiny, oddly shaped fish called the handfish -- so named because it 'walks' along the seabed on stumpy, arm-like fins instead of swimming. Bomb a reef of ordinary fish and it slowly refills over the years; bomb a reef of handfish and it stays empty almost forever. Marine biologists trace that fragility to one quirk of how the handfish comes into the world. What is it?
answer: Its young hatch as tiny walkers that never drift out
choices: Its young hatch as tiny walkers that never drift out
Its larvae drift far but survive only on their birth reef
Its females spawn just one clutch in an entire lifetime
Its eggs need a warm current no other reef can supply
context: Handfish have no free-swimming larval stage: the eggs hatch directly into fully-formed miniature adults that drop onto the sand and start walking. Because no larvae drift on the current, a wiped-out reef gets no settlers from anywhere else — the very trait that makes it wondrous also makes it fragile. Handfish also spawn every year, and hatchlings can settle wherever they drop, so the other explanations do not hold. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handfish

question: Deep in the rainforests of the Amazon lives a huge, gray and black eagle strong enough to snatch a monkey or sloth right out of the treetops. Its belly is bright white against the dark leaves. On its head is a double crest of long feathers it can raise straight up when alarmed. Which powerful rainforest bird is this?
answer: The harpy eagle
choices: The harpy eagle
The bald eagle
The peregrine falcon
The snowy owl
context: The harpy eagle (Harpia harpyja) is a huge rainforest eagle of Central and South America -- slate-black above, white below, with a distinctive double crest it can raise on its head. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harpy_eagle.

question: Deep in the rainforests of South America lives the harpy eagle, the most powerful bird of prey on Earth. Of every living eagle in the world, the harpy carries by far the largest talons. Its curved rear talon reaches nearly 5 inches long -- so long it matches, almost exactly in length, the front claw of one particular animal that most people never think of alongside a bird. Whose claw does that hind talon match?
answer: A grizzly bear's front claw
choices: A grizzly bear's front claw
A house cat's front claw
A jaguar's front claw
A river otter's front claw
context: A female harpy eagle's rear (hind) talon reaches about 12.3 cm -- nearly 5 inches -- roughly the length of a grizzly bear's front claw, the largest talon of any living eagle. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harpy_eagle; Audubon '10 Fun Facts About the Harpy Eagle'.  (Legend.)

question: A wild howler monkey clings to a branch high in the canopy when a harpy eagle drops on it. Yet in one Panama study, monkeys were not the harpy's main meal at all -- a single kind of prey made up a startling 79% of everything it ate. What was on the menu most?
answer: Sloths
choices: Sloths
Snakes
Fish
Deer
context: In one study, sloths made up 79% of the harpy eagle's prey. It plucks sloths and monkeys straight off the branches, and a female can grab prey nearly her own weight and fly off without ever landing. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harpy_eagle.

question: The harpy eagle of the Amazon rainforest hunts by daylight, snatching sloths and monkeys straight out of the canopy. Yet around its face it wears a ring of feathers that it can raise flat like a shallow dish -- a feature you would normally expect only on a silent, night-hunting owl. What does raising that feather disc do for the eagle?
answer: Funnels faint sounds to its ears
choices: Funnels faint sounds to its ears
Shades its eyes from midday glare
Signals a warning to its mate
Sheds a rainforest downpour
context: Like an owl, the harpy eagle has a facial disc of feathers it can raise to funnel sound to its ears -- rare among diurnal (daytime) raptors -- helping it hear hidden prey before it sees them. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harpy_eagle; Los Angeles Zoo.

question: Most eagles around the world raise a fresh chick every year or every other year. The harpy eagle, the giant sloth-hunting eagle of the Amazon rainforest, is far rarer at it -- so much rarer that losing even one breeding pair from a patch of forest can set that whole area's harpy population back for years. How often does a harpy pair actually raise a chick?
answer: Just one chick every 2-3 years
choices: Just one chick every 2-3 years
A brood of six every spring
Several chicks every year
A new chick every single month
context: A harpy eagle pair raises just one chick every 2-3 years -- one of the slowest reproduction rates of any eagle -- which is why the species is so vulnerable to habitat loss. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harpy_eagle; Audubon.

question: In the deep-sea twilight zone, hundreds of meters below the ocean surface, there is no rock or seaweed to hide behind. A small silver fish called the hatchetfish still hides from hunters swimming below it, using a strange trick. What does the hatchetfish do so a hunter looking up cannot see its dark shape against the faint light from the sky above?
answer: Shines rows of lights along its belly
choices: Shines rows of lights along its belly
Squirts a cloud of black ink
Buries itself in the sandy bottom
Turns its skin bright coral red
context: This is called counter-illumination. Rows of light organs (photophores) along the hatchetfish's belly glow pale blue and shine downward, matching the faint sunlight from above so a predator looking up sees only background light and no dark silhouette. In the open ocean the best way to vanish isn't to be dark — it's to make your own light. Sources: https://twilightzone.whoi.edu/explore-the-otz/creature-features/hatchetfish/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_hatchetfish  (Legend.)

question: In the twilight zone of the deep ocean — hundreds of meters down, where only faint blue light filters from above — swims the marine hatchetfish. Head-on the hatchetfish looks tiny and almost impossible to see against the dim water. But when it swings sideways, it suddenly flashes a wide, mirror-bright silver flank. What about the hatchetfish's body pulls off that near-vanishing act?
answer: Its body is a thin blade, flattened side-to-side
choices: Its body is a thin blade, flattened side-to-side
Its scales fold flat like closing shutters
Its skin turns clear as glass on cue
It hollows out a see-through gap down its middle
context: The body is a thin silver blade, so compressed side-to-side that seen edge-on it is nearly two-dimensional and almost vanishes, slipping through the water 'with barely a trace.' That hatchet-blade shape is what gives the fish its name. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_hatchetfish ; https://twilightzone.whoi.edu/explore-the-otz/creature-features/hatchetfish/

question: A hatchetfish's eyes are nothing like the ordinary round domes most fish carry on the sides of their heads — their strange form is a big clue to how it makes a living in the dim twilight zone. What shape are they?
answer: Tube-shaped, pointing straight up
choices: Tube-shaped, pointing straight up
Flat, like a pair of coins
Ringed with glowing dots
Split into dozens of tiny lenses
context: The hatchetfish has huge tube-shaped eyes that point straight up, so it stares at the dim glow above and spots prey by their dark silhouettes drifting overhead — hunting for shadows against the light, the very same weakness its own glowing belly hides from below. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_hatchetfish

question: Each night, deep-sea hatchetfish ride a great daily elevator up toward the ocean surface to feed, then sink back down into the black twilight zone by dawn. The whole trip, the pale-blue belly lights they use to hide from hunters below stay glowing. What does the hatchetfish do with those belly lights on that up-and-down journey?
answer: Turns them up and down like a dimmer switch
choices: Turns them up and down like a dimmer switch
Flashes them in a fast warning pattern
Swaps their color from blue to green
Pulses them in time with its heartbeat
context: The hatchetfish rides a daily vertical migration, rising at night to feed on copepods, ostracods, and fish larvae and sinking back down by dawn. It turns its pale-blue belly lights up or down like a dimmer switch to track the changing brightness of the water, so it keeps erasing its own shadow the whole way. Being able to regulate that intensity gives it an edge over other twilight-zone fish using the same camouflage. Source: https://twilightzone.whoi.edu/explore-the-otz/creature-features/hatchetfish/

question: Down in the deep-sea twilight zone, a hunting fish sweeps a living searchlight through the black water toward a small silver hatchetfish. The hatchetfish's skin is packed with tiny crystals arranged in long parallel bundles. When the hunter's beam sweeps across those crystal bundles, what does the beam become?
answer: A soft, diffuse blur
choices: A soft, diffuse blur
A bright pinpoint glint
A mirror of the hunter's own beam
A ring of rainbow colors
context: The hatchetfish's skin doesn't just mirror light — it is packed with organized guanine crystals arranged in long parallel bundles that scatter light softly in every direction, so a predator's bioluminescent searchlight gets a diffuse blur instead of a bright flash. Penn physicist Alison Sweeney: 'nature is generally quite a bit more sophisticated in how it has evolved to manipulate light.' Source: https://www.futurity.org/hatchetfish-oceans-light-camouflage-1468942-2/

question: An emperor penguin stands barefoot on the Antarctic ice for hours in wind that howls below freezing, and its feet never freeze to the surface. Warm skin on ice would melt a puddle underneath, then freeze it back into a trap. To dodge that, the penguin's body deliberately runs its feet a very particular way — nothing like the rest of it. The feet are kept:
answer: just above freezing, cold and cheap
choices: just above freezing, cold and cheap
as warm as its chest and belly
completely numb and bloodless
warmed by a layer of fat in the sole
context: Warm arteries running down into a penguin's legs are bundled right against the cold veins coming back up, so the outgoing blood hands its heat to the returning blood before it reaches the feet. Feet kept just above freezing lose almost no heat and don't melt into the ice. Source: Britannica Blog, 'Penguin Feet: Avoiding Frostbite in the Antarctic'; CoolAntarctica.

question: A penguin stands on Antarctic sea ice for hours at a time, its bare feet pressed against a surface hardly warmer than freezing. Inside each of its legs, the arteries carrying warm blood down toward the feet are bundled tightly against the veins carrying cold blood back up toward the body. The two run side by side in opposite directions. Why does that clever arrangement help the penguin?
answer: the warm blood hands its heat to the returning blood, recycling it
choices: the warm blood hands its heat to the returning blood, recycling it
the veins keep the arteries from freezing solid
it lets the leg pump blood without a heartbeat
it warms the cold blood so the feet stay toasty
context: This is countercurrent heat exchange: warm blood flowing out runs against cold blood flowing in, and heat leaks across from one to the other, so it is recycled back into the body instead of being flushed out to the freezing feet. Herons and ducks stand for hours in near-freezing water using the same leg bundles. Source: Britannica Blog, 'Penguin Feet'; Biology Insights, 'How Do Penguins Stay Warm'.

question: A great white shark cruises the cold gray seas off California and South Africa hunting seals. Most fish are cold-blooded — as the water chills, their muscles slow and they turn sluggish. But the great white can hunt fast and hard in near-freezing water where its prey can barely move. That is because, unlike almost every other fish in the sea, it can keep its body core:
answer: 6 to 10 degrees C warmer than the water
choices: 6 to 10 degrees C warmer than the water
exactly matched to the water temperature
cooled well below the water to save energy
dry inside a sealed body cavity
context: A great white and its lamnid cousins hold their swimming muscles 6.5 to 10 degrees C above the surrounding sea, so their muscles stay powerful in cold water where a cold-blooded fish would go slow. Source: Oceans Research, 'Are sharks warm-blooded?'; GGCWiki, 'Adaptations for selective thermoregulation in large predatory fish'.

question: Tuna and the great white shark keep their swimming muscles warm in cold seas. Warm blood leaving the muscle is routed to run right alongside the cold blood coming in, handing over its heat before it can escape out the gills. Anatomists named this dense blood-vessel net with a Latin phrase meaning:
answer: wonderful net
choices: wonderful net
muscle furnace
warm heart
deep coil
context: The structure is the rete mirabile, Latin for 'wonderful net': warm blood leaving the muscle runs against cold blood coming in and hands its heat back, so the warmth is recycled rather than flushed out the gills. Source: American Scientist, 'How Tunas and Lamnid Sharks Swim'; Wikipedia, 'Rete mirabile'.

question: The swordfish is a huge, sword-nosed predator of the open ocean, chasing fast squid and fish through deep, cold water. It carries a special heater organ, built from a modified eye muscle, that warms its eyes and its brain 10 to 15 degrees C above the icy sea around it. What advantage does a warm-eyed swordfish gain over a cold-eyed fish?
answer: it detects rapid motion far better and spots darting prey
choices: it detects rapid motion far better and spots darting prey
it can see colors invisible to warm-blooded animals
its eyes glow to lure prey in the dark
it never needs to blink while hunting
context: A heated retina responds faster, so the swordfish catches quick-flitting prey a cold-eyed fish would miss. Source: Fritsches, Brill & Warrant, 'Warm Eyes Provide Superior Vision in Swordfishes', Current Biology 2005; Science AAAS, 'Hot Eyes for Cold Fish'. (Legend-tier wonder.)

question: A reindeer wandering the Arctic tundra breathes air at 40 degrees below zero, yet the air reaching its lungs arrives warmed to body temperature. Scroll-like bones inside its nose, wrapped in warm blood vessels, take care of that on the way in. On the way back out, when the reindeer exhales into the cold, those same nose-bones do a second, energy-saving job. What is it?
answer: reclaim the heat and moisture from the outgoing air
choices: reclaim the heat and moisture from the outgoing air
filter frozen dust from the airway
pump extra oxygen into the blood
seal the nostrils shut against the wind
context: The nasal scroll-bones warm every incoming breath from -40 C up to about +38 C, then recover the heat and moisture back out of the exhaled air, so almost nothing is wasted. Source: Blix et al., 'Nasal heat exchange in the reindeer', PubMed 3992062; ScienceDaily, 'The magical reindeer nose'.

question: Tunas and lamnid sharks are not close cousins, yet each evolved the same warm-blood-against-cold-blood muscle plumbing on its own, roughly 40 to 60 million years apart. A biologist looking at penguins, reindeer and these fish all landing on the identical trick would label it an example of:
answer: convergent evolution
choices: convergent evolution
genetic drift
sexual selection
adaptive radiation
context: Convergent evolution is when unrelated lineages independently arrive at the same solution; keeping warm blood next to cold blood is such a good idea that evolution stumbled onto it separately in fish, birds and mammals. Genetic drift is random allele change, sexual selection is mate-driven, and adaptive radiation is one lineage fanning into many niches. Source: American Scientist, 'How Tunas and Lamnid Sharks Swim: An Evolutionary Convergence'.

question: A whale swimming hard through cold ocean water builds up dangerous heat inside its huge working muscles. Its flippers and its tail flukes are the only parts of its body that are bare-skinned and thin, meeting the cold sea with no insulating blubber over them. When the whale starts to overheat, what does it do with those bare tail flukes to shed the extra body heat into the water?
answer: floods them with warm blood so heat pours into the water
choices: floods them with warm blood so heat pours into the water
clamps their blood vessels shut to hold warmth in
shivers them fast to burn off the extra energy
tucks them tight against the body to shed heat
context: The flippers and flukes are 'thermal windows.' Instead of routing blood through the vein bundles that normally recycle warmth, the overheating whale sends extra blood straight out to the bare skin, so the heat radiates into the sea. The very same countercurrent plumbing that saves heat can run in reverse to dump it. Source: Georgia Dolphin Ecology Program, 'Chill Out, Hot Stuff!'; SeaWorld, 'Baleen Whales - Adaptations'.

question: A fish breathing under water uses a clever gill trick to strip as much oxygen from the water as it possibly can. Water flows one way across the delicate gill filaments while blood inside the gills flows the opposite way -- a countercurrent. Because the blood always meets fresher, more oxygen-rich water on every stretch, it manages to strip out of the water about:
answer: 90% of the oxygen in the water
choices: 90% of the oxygen in the water
30% of the oxygen in the water
half the oxygen, then the rest at the tail
only what the fish can gulp at the surface
context: If blood and water flowed the SAME way they would quickly reach a stalemate; flowing opposite, the blood keeps meeting richer water and pulls out up to ~90% of its oxygen. Source: FishBIO, 'An efficient exchange: countercurrent oxygen exchange in fish'; AskNature, 'Gills Exchange Oxygen Efficiently'.

question: A tuna or a mako shark warms only patches -- the swimming muscle, the eyes, the brain -- while the heart pumps cold blood like any other fish. In 2015 the opah, a round silver fish of the deep sea, broke that pattern. Heating itself by endlessly flapping its wing-like pectoral fins and trapping that warmth with fat-wrapped vessel nets in its gills, the opah turned out to be:
answer: warm right through, heart and all
choices: warm right through, heart and all
warm only along its spine
cold except for its glowing eyes
warm only after a fast burst of swimming
context: The opah (Lampris guttatus) is the first fish shown to be whole-body endothermic -- warm all over, heart included, not just in isolated muscle, eye or brain patches like tuna and sharks. It makes heat by constantly flapping its wing-like pectoral fins, then holds that heat in with counter-current vessel nets (retia) sitting right inside its gills -- the one place warm blood would normally dump all its heat straight into the sea. Those gill retia are wrapped in a fat layer with less than half the thermal conductivity of ordinary tissue, insulating the exchanger and letting the opah stay roughly 5 degrees C warmer than the cold water it hunts in. Source: Wegner, N.C., Snodgrass, O.E., Dewar, H. & Hyde, J.R. (2015) 'Whole-body endothermy in a mesopelagic fish, the opah, Lampris guttatus', Science 348(6236):786-790 (DOI 10.1126/science.aaa8902); National Geographic, 'Meet the Comical Opah, the Only Truly Warm-Blooded Fish'.

question: A fish gill uses a paired vessel net to pull oxygen out of the water flowing past. A deep-sea fish's swim bladder uses that same net for a harder job. It has to force oxygen into the bladder even though the gas inside pushes back hard. The outgoing vein leaks its oxygen back onto the incoming artery, so that:
answer: each loop stacks onto the last, compounding the load
choices: each loop stacks onto the last, compounding the load
a molecular pump spends ATP to force gas across
the sluggish blood simply gives the gas more soak time
a vast folded surface lets more gas cross at once
context: The gill rete is a simple countercurrent EXCHANGER -- it just recovers heat or oxygen as two bloodstreams pass in opposite directions. The swim-bladder rete does something far stronger: it is a countercurrent MULTIPLIER. Oxygen unloaded on the outgoing venous side back-diffuses across onto the incoming artery, where it reloads onto hemoglobin; because that returned gas is added on top of what the artery already carries, each pass compounds the concentration, and the small single-step difference stacks up over and over along the long parallel capillaries. It is driven by the Root effect -- lactic acid from the gas gland acidifies the blood and forces its hemoglobin to dump oxygen -- and this compounding is what lets deep-sea fish secrete oxygen into the bladder against pressures up to about 380 atmospheres, starting from a partial pressure near 0.2 atmospheres in the water. No ATP pump, no extra surface, no slowed flow does this: it is pure recompounding geometry. Source: Wikipedia 'Rete mirabile' (rete pumps O2 from a partial pressure near 0.2 atm into a bladder at hundreds of atmospheres; Root effect drives back-diffusion so arterial O2 compounds until it exceeds bladder pressure); Pelster, PMC10209234 'The rete mirabile: a possible control site for swimbladder function'; PLOS One 2012, 'O2-Filled Swimbladder Employs Monocarboxylate Transporters ... Lactate-Induced Root Effect Hemoglobin'.

question: Of all the strange fossils left in the ancient seas of 270 million years ago, an old Permian sea predator called Helicoprion left the strangest signature of them all. Fossil hunters keep pulling from the Permian rock a single tight spiral, wound like a coiled clock spring, that belonged to this animal. What was that Helicoprion spiral actually made of?
answer: A whorl of saw-like teeth
choices: A whorl of saw-like teeth
A ring of armored bone plates
A coiled shell like a nautilus
A band of overlapping scales
context: Helicoprion means 'spiral saw' in Greek (helikos = spiral, prion = saw) -- a perfect name for a coil of teeth arranged like the blade of a circular saw. It swam the Permian seas roughly 290 to 270 million years ago, long before the first dinosaurs. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helicoprion

question: For over a hundred years, the only part of the ancient Permian sea predator Helicoprion that fossil hunters ever dug up was its strange buzzsaw-like spiral of teeth. Nobody could tell where on the animal's body that spiral of teeth had once sat. Then in 2013, a CT scan of a well-preserved Helicoprion fossil finally settled the argument. Where on the body did the tooth-spiral really go?
answer: Coiled inside its lower jaw
choices: Coiled inside its lower jaw
Curling off the tip of its snout
Standing up along its back fin
Trailing behind it on its tail
context: Scientists led by Leif Tapanila CT-scanned a fossil and found the whorl sat in the lower jaw. Tapanila said the teeth 'fit in the back of the mouth, right next to the back joint of the jaw.' Before that, guesses had stuck the spiral everywhere -- off the snout like an elephant's trunk, on the tail, on the back fin, even poking out of the throat. Source: https://phys.org/news/2013-02-helicoprion-scientists-mysteries-ancient-shark.html  (Legend.)

question: The ancient Permian sea predator Helicoprion stayed a puzzle to paleontologists for well over a hundred years for one simple reason. Fossil hunters almost never dug up any part of Helicoprion besides its strange coiled tooth-spiral -- no ribs, no skull, no fin bones. What made the rest of Helicoprion's body vanish before it could turn into fossilized rock?
answer: Its skeleton was cartilage, which rots away
choices: Its skeleton was cartilage, which rots away
Deep-sea scavengers stripped every carcass
Its bones were too small to leave a trace
Acidic Permian mud dissolved the buried bone
context: Like sharks and their relatives, Helicoprion had a skeleton made of cartilage rather than bone. Cartilage rots away instead of fossilizing, so the hard tooth-whorl was almost the only piece that ever survived -- which is exactly why nobody could figure out where it went for so long. Source: https://phys.org/news/2013-02-helicoprion-scientists-mysteries-ancient-shark.html

question: Helicoprion, a Permian sea predator that swam the oceans 270 million years ago, carried in its lower jaw a tooth-spiral that was a complete record of every single tooth the animal had ever grown -- it never shed one in its entire life. Fresh new teeth kept sprouting at the front of the jaw as Helicoprion aged. So where did all the older, worn-down teeth end up?
answer: Curled inward into the center of the coil
choices: Curled inward into the center of the coil
Fused into one solid slicing ridge
Dissolved and reabsorbed into the jaw
Ground flat against the toothless upper jaw
context: Instead of falling out the way most teeth do, each old tooth stayed anchored and rolled inward toward the middle of the coil as fresh teeth grew at the working front. That is why the whorl coils tighter and tighter toward its center -- the innermost teeth are the ones the animal grew as a baby. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helicoprion  (Legend.)

question: With a mouth full of saw-like coiled teeth, the ancient Permian sea predator Helicoprion was assumed for decades by paleontologists to be a kind of shark. But when a 2013 CT scan finally revealed the shape of its full skull, Helicoprion turned out to be a much closer cousin of a very different living group of fish. Which living group?
answer: The ratfishes and chimaeras
choices: The ratfishes and chimaeras
The rays and skates
The lampreys and hagfish
The coelacanths
context: Only the teeth were shark-like; as Tapanila put it, 'everything else is Holocephalan' -- the group that includes today's ratfishes and chimaeras. When it closed its jaw, the whorl rolled backward in a slicing motion; Tapanila said 'the analogy to a circular saw is almost perfect,' and it likely sawed through soft prey like squid. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/buzzsaw-jaw-helicoprion-was-a-freaky-ratfish

question: A 2015 study titled 'Eating with a saw for a jaw' worked out how the ancient Permian sea predator Helicoprion actually used its coiled spiral of teeth to feed. The paper found the whorl was not a single uniform slicer -- different stretches of the coil did different jobs as Helicoprion's lower jaw swept closed on prey. Which task fell to the teeth at the front of the whorl?
answer: Hooking and dragging prey inward
choices: Hooking and dragging prey inward
Grinding shells into fragments
Filtering plankton from seawater
Anchoring the jaw to the skull
context: Ramsay and colleagues (Journal of Morphology, 2015) modeled the whorl as a multi-tool: as the lower jaw rotated shut the anterior teeth hooked and dragged prey inward, the middle teeth pierced and cut, and the rear teeth near the jaw joint sheared and shoved the food deeper toward the throat -- the tooth paths traced arcs like curved slashing swords. The animal likely fed by opening and closing the jaw in a repeating sawing cycle that caught, cut, and swallowed in one motion. Source: Ramsay et al. 2015, Journal of Morphology 276:47-64, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25181366/

question: In the cold, fast streams of the eastern United States hides the largest salamander in North America. It is nearly two feet long, with a broad, flat head and baggy wrinkled skin hanging in ruffled folds down each side of its body. Locals along the Appalachian streams gave this river giant a whole zoo of folk nicknames over the years. Which one really stuck?
answer: Lasagna lizard
choices: Lasagna lizard
Bristle toad
Mud minnow
River newt
context: The hellbender (Cryptobranchus alleganiensis) earned a whole pile of folk names: 'lasagna lizard' for its ruffled, layered skin folds, plus 'snot otter' for its slimy skin, 'devil dog,' 'mud devil,' and 'Allegheny alligator.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellbender

question: The hellbender, a two-foot salamander that lives in the cold streams of the eastern United States, barely uses its lungs -- it pulls almost all its oxygen straight out of the stream water, right through its skin. Plenty of stream animals boost their skin-breathing in different ways: dense capillaries, mucous coatings, tiny pores. What is the hellbender's own trick?
answer: It hangs in loose, baggy wrinkles and side-folds
choices: It hangs in loose, baggy wrinkles and side-folds
It is packed with dense capillary beds just under the surface
It secretes a thin mucus film that traps dissolved oxygen
It is riddled with microscopic pores like a sponge
context: Those loose folds hugely increase the skin's surface area, so more oxygen can soak in from the water. The ruffled look is exactly why one folk name is 'lasagna lizard.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellbender

question: The hellbender is a giant salamander — up to two feet long, with slimy, wrinkled skin — that lives hidden under flat rocks in cold, fast-moving streams of the Appalachian Mountains in the eastern United States. On a still summer day when the current slows to nearly nothing, a hellbender lying under its rock will suddenly start rocking its whole body back and forth and rippling its baggy side-folds of loose skin. Why does it bother making all that motion?
answer: To sweep fresh oxygen-rich water past its skin
choices: To sweep fresh oxygen-rich water past its skin
To warn rival hellbenders off its rock
To force stale water out of its lungs
To signal a mate hiding nearby
context: By swishing fresh water past its folds, the hellbender keeps the oxygen coming even when the water goes still - the skin can only soak up what actually flows past it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellbender

question: The male Hercules beetle is a rainforest giant of Central and South America, close to seven inches long from tip to tail -- one of the largest beetles on Earth. He carries two huge horns that close on a rival male like a giant pincer during their wrestling fights. One horn is small. The other is much bigger. Where on his body does the bigger horn actually grow?
answer: His back, above the wing-covers
choices: His back, above the wing-covers
His head, between the eyes
His jaws, like a beetle's mandibles
The underside of his belly
context: Most of that seven-inch record length is horn, not body. A male grows a smaller horn jutting up from his head and a much larger one arching down from his back (the pronotum); the two meet like a giant pincer. Only males grow them. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hercules_beetle  (Legend.)

question: In the rainforests of Central and South America, the Hercules beetle grows more than six inches long, and males are armed with a huge curving horn on top of a lower horn — the pair works like a giant pincer. Two males climb a branch and clamp horns, wrestling for the right to a female nearby. Once one beetle catches his rival in the pincer, how does he actually win the fight?
answer: He pries the rival loose and hurls him off the branch
choices: He pries the rival loose and hurls him off the branch
He crushes the rival's shell until it cracks
He squeezes until the rival stops struggling
He drags the rival down into the leaf litter
context: Each beetle tries to catch the other between its upward head-horn and its downward back-horn, then pry and throw him off the branch. The horn works as a lever: muscles in the thorax rotate the head to drive the long horn upward and lift the enemy. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hercules_beetle

question: The Hercules beetle, native to the rainforests of Central and South America, is one of the largest beetles on Earth, with the males growing a huge curved horn straight out of the head. Its hard wing-covers can look olive-green or pale yellow one hour and turn near-black the next, even though the beetle itself has not moved, aged, or been hurt in any way. What flips its color back and forth like that?
answer: Rising humidity in the air around it
choices: Rising humidity in the air around it
The beetle growing older
A fresh meal of tree sap
A flash of a threat display
context: The elytra (wing-covers) shift with the weather: olive-green or yellow when the air is dry, darkening toward black as the humidity rises around the beetle. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hercules_beetle

question: The Hercules beetle of the Central and South American rainforests is famous for the enormous curved horn the adult males carry on the head. But long before it ever grows a horn, a Hercules beetle spends up to two years as a fat, C-shaped white grub, tunneling slowly through rotting logs on the forest floor and eating the soft, damp wood. How does that grub compare in size to the adult beetle it eventually becomes?
answer: It grows heavier than the adult beetle
choices: It grows heavier than the adult beetle
It is far smaller than the adult
It has tiny working horns already
It is see-through with no color
context: A Hercules beetle larva can reach about 4.5 inches (11 cm) long and weigh over 100 grams, heavier than the horned adult it becomes. The giant adult is the short chapter: after years underground it lives only about three to six months, sipping sap and fruit. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hercules_beetle

question: A two-and-a-half-tonne grey giant wallows in an African river all day, then hauls out at dusk to mow the grass on the bank. Despite eating nothing but plants, it kills more people across Africa each year than lions or sharks do. Which animal is this?
answer: The hippopotamus
choices: The hippopotamus
The Cape buffalo
The white rhinoceros
The Nile crocodile
context: Hippos (Hippopotamus amphibius) kill an estimated 500 or more people a year in Africa — deadlier to humans than lions or sharks — yet they are grazers that eat only grass. Their danger comes from aggression and sheer bulk, not from hunting. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/mammals/facts/hippopotamus

question: The hippopotamus of African rivers and lakes — from the Nile in the north to the Zambezi in the south — weighs three tons or more and spends its whole life in and around fresh water. Yet when a big bull hippo crosses a deep pool, it never paddles at the surface the way most other huge mammals do. It does not really swim at all. How does the hippo actually get across the deep water?
answer: It walks along the bottom, pushing off the riverbed
choices: It walks along the bottom, pushing off the riverbed
It floats high and dog-paddles across the top
It rolls sideways and lets the current carry it
It beats its stubby tail to scull forward
context: A hippo is too dense to float, so it can't truly swim. It walks and pushes off the riverbed in a slow-motion underwater gallop, toes barely touching the bottom. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/mammals/facts/hippopotamus

question: For a hundred years, scientists grouped the hippo with pigs based on the shape of its teeth. Then in the 1900s, blood and DNA tests told a very different story. They pointed to a group of relatives nobody had expected. What animals turned out to be the hippo's closest living relatives?
answer: Whales and dolphins
choices: Whales and dolphins
Pigs and warthogs
Rhinos and tapirs
Elephants and manatees
context: Until 1909 hippos were grouped with pigs based on their molars, but blood-protein and DNA evidence proved their closest living relatives are the cetaceans — whales, dolphins, and porpoises. The two lines are thought to have split from a shared water-loving ancestor around 55 million years ago. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hippopotamus

question: When a hippopotamus wading in an African river throws its enormous head back and gapes its jaws to nearly 150 degrees -- almost a straight line from tooth-tip to tooth-tip -- it is not yawning from boredom. It is a threat display, aimed at rival hippos. That wide-open mouth reveals the hippo's most fearsome weapons of all. What are they?
answer: Tusk-like canines that never stop growing
choices: Tusk-like canines that never stop growing
Rows of razor-edged shearing molars
A pair of horns rooted in the jaw
Backward-curving fangs full of venom
context: Inside the gaping mouth are tusk-like canine teeth that keep growing throughout life, reaching about 50 cm (20 inches) long. They stay sharp by grinding against the lower incisors as the hippo chews. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hippopotamus

question: In the flooded swamps of the Amazon rainforest lives a strange bird about the size of a crow. It has a spiky, punk-rocker red crest on its head, a bare bright-blue face, and glowing red eyes. Unlike almost any other bird, it eats only leaves from the trees along the river and ferments them in its huge crop like a tiny cow. Which South American bird is it?
answer: The hoatzin
choices: The hoatzin
The scarlet macaw
The great egret
The horned screamer
context: The hoatzin (Opisthocomus hoazin) is about 65 cm long but weighs only around 700 grams, with an unfeathered blue face, maroon eyes, and a spiky rufous crest. It lives in the swamps and riverside forests of the Amazon and Orinoco basins and eats mostly leaves. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoatzin

question: High over an Amazon river, a hoatzin — a strange, spiky-crested South American bird — builds its nest out on a slim branch. When one of its chicks hatches, the newborn already has something on each of its wings that no fully grown bird ever keeps.
