It uses this odd little tool to grip the bark and haul itself around the branches. What does the hoatzin chick have on each wing?
answer: Two working claws on each wing
choices: Two working claws on each wing
A second, hidden set of eyelids
A hooked egg-tooth on each wing
A sticky pad under each wingtip
context: Hoatzin chicks are born with two functional claws on each wing and use them to clamber through branches over the water. They are the only living birds with working wing-claws, a trait they lose as adults. Source: https://www.aip.org/inside-science/the-baby-birds-that-use-wing-claws-to-climb-through-the-amazon  (Legend.)

question: A hoatzin nest sits out on a slim branch hanging over an Amazon river. A hungry tree snake glides slowly along the branch toward it. The bald, still-flightless hoatzin chick — a young Amazon bird just growing in its feathers — is cornered, with the snake in front of it and only open air and dark river water behind. What does the chick do to escape being eaten?
answer: It flings itself off the branch and escapes underwater
choices: It flings itself off the branch and escapes underwater
It plays dead and lies limp in the nest
It shrieks without pause to summon both parents
It presses flat against the bark and holds still
context: When a predator threatens the nest, a hoatzin chick drops from the branch into the water below and swims to safety underwater — in tanks the chicks swim by moving both wings together in a breast-stroke-like motion — before later climbing back up to the nest. Source: https://www.aip.org/inside-science/the-baby-birds-that-use-wing-claws-to-climb-through-the-amazon  (Legend.)

question: The hoatzin eats mostly leaves and, alone among birds, breaks them down by fermenting them with bacteria in a huge crop — the same slow process that works in a cow's stomach. Among the people who share the Amazon with it, this leaf-eater has earned a blunt nickname. What do the locals call it?
answer: The 'stinkbird'
choices: The 'stinkbird'
The 'river ghost'
The 'leaf dragon'
The 'thunder crow'
context: The hoatzin is the only bird known to digest its leafy diet by foregut fermentation, with bacteria in an enlarged crop breaking down the leaves much as in a cow. The fermenting leaves give it a disagreeable, manure-like smell, earning it the nickname 'stinkbird'; because it smells so bad, locals only hunt it for food in times of dire need. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoatzin  (Legend.)

question: Corner an eastern hognose snake in a North American field or meadow and it puts on an amazing show. First it flops around wildly, as if in pain. Then it flips onto its back, opens its mouth, and lets its purple tongue hang out. Finally it goes completely limp and holds perfectly still, sometimes even releasing a foul stink. What is this harmless little snake pretending to be so predators leave it alone?
answer: Freshly dead and rotting
choices: Freshly dead and rotting
A venomous coral snake
A tangled clump of roots
A much larger snake
context: The hognose snake (genus Heterodon) is famous for this theatrical death-feign — belly-up, mouth agape, tongue lolling out. It is one of the animal kingdom's most committed fake-death acts. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_hognose_snake

question: A hognose snake -- a stout, upturned-snouted little snake of North American grasslands -- lies belly-up in the grass, playing 'dead': tongue lolling out of its mouth, jaws gaping, body limp. You gently reach down and flip it right-side up onto its belly, just to check. The instant its legless body settles upright, what does the hognose do?
answer: Immediately rolls straight back onto its back
choices: Immediately rolls straight back onto its back
Bolts away at full speed
Bites the hand that touched it
Freezes stiff as a stick
context: The act is so committed that a hognose insists on being 'dead': turn it belly-down and it flops right back over, as if a corpse could only possibly be lying on its back. Source: https://animals.howstuffworks.com/snakes/hognose-snake.htm

question: The hognose snake, a stout upturned-snouted snake of North American grasslands, is famous for playing dead when a predator threatens it. It does not just lie belly-up with a lolling tongue -- it works to smell and look convincingly like a real rotting corpse, not just a stunned live snake. Beyond flipping belly-up, what extra grisly step does the hognose add to really sell the death?
answer: Smears foul musk and bleeds from its mouth
choices: Smears foul musk and bleeds from its mouth
Sheds its skin in one fast piece
Puffs its whole body up like a balloon
Rattles the dry tip of its tail
context: The hognose smears foul-smelling musk from its cloaca and can even rupture blood vessels to bleed from its mouth and cloaca — making the 'corpse' look and smell genuinely rotten to a predator. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_hognose_snake

question: The eastern hognose snake, a harmless little North American snake, gets its name from an unusual scale at the very tip of its snout. This scale is hardened and curled sharply upward, like the tip of a small metal shovel. In loose, sandy soil, the snake puts this odd upturned snout to work like a real tool. What does the hognose snake dig up out of the sand with its nose?
answer: Shovels toads out of the sand
choices: Shovels toads out of the sand
Cracks open bird eggs
Scrapes bark off logs
Combs seeds from grass
context: The upturned, keeled rostral scale at the tip of the snout works like a little shovel, letting the hognose dig burrowing toads out of sandy soil. Source: https://srelherp.uga.edu/snakes/eastern-hognose-snake/

question: The eastern hognose is a stocky, upturned-nose snake of the eastern United States, and it is a toad specialist — toads make up almost everything it eats. Toads have two serious defenses. They can gulp air until they swell into a hard, round balloon too big for a snake's mouth. Their skin oozes a powerful heart-stopping poison called bufotoxin. The hognose has enlarged adrenal glands that shrug off the poison. So how does it defeat the balloon trick?
answer: Enlarged rear teeth puncture and deflate the toad
choices: Enlarged rear teeth puncture and deflate the toad
It swallows the puffed toad whole anyway
It waits days for the toad to shrink
It squeezes the toad in tight coils
context: A puffed-up toad is meant to be un-swallowable, but the hognose has enlarged rear teeth that puncture and deflate it. Enlarged adrenal glands pump out hormones to counter the toad's skin toxins, and mild rear-fang venom helps subdue it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_hognose_snake

question: This tough little African animal is about the size of a small dog — only stockier, lower to the ground, and thickly muscled. It is black on top and pale white along its back. It holds an actual world record: 'most fearless animal on Earth.' Instead of running from lions or leopards, it will stand its ground and drive them off. Name this famous little brawler of the African savanna.
answer: The honey badger
choices: The honey badger
The wolverine
The Tasmanian devil
The African civet
context: The honey badger (Mellivora capensis) is the largest land mustelid in Africa yet weighs only about 9 to 16 kg. Its reputation for standing up to far larger predators earned the Guinness listing. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honey_badger ; https://www.discoverwildlife.com/animal-facts/mammals/honey-badger-guide  (Legend.)

question: African savanna ground is baked hard as brick by the sun during the long dry season. Even so, when a honey badger is chased by a bigger predator, it can vanish into that packed earth by digging its own fresh burrow on the spot. Its front paws are armed with long claws that work like tiny picks. About how long does it take one honey badger to dig a fresh burrow in that rock-hard ground?
answer: About 10 minutes
choices: About 10 minutes
About half a day
About three days
About two weeks
context: Honey badgers are among the animal kingdom's best diggers and can tunnel a burrow into hard, sun-baked ground in about 10 minutes. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honey_badger

question: A honey badger in the African savanna rips open a wild beehive with its claws to get at the honey inside. It keeps eating even while hundreds of angry bees sting it, and it barely reacts. That same tough honey-badger hide also shrugs off porcupine quills and can even survive a machete blow from a farmer. What is a honey badger's hide actually like?
answer: Skin about 6 millimeters thick and rubbery
choices: Skin about 6 millimeters thick and rubbery
A thin skin backed by a dense pad of fat
A hide sheathed in overlapping keratin plates
A hide coated in a thick protective mucus
context: The skin on a honey badger's neck is roughly 6 mm (a quarter inch) thick and tough and rubbery enough to shrug off bee stings, quills, and machete cuts. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honey_badger

question: In the Kalahari Desert of southern Africa, the researchers Colleen and Keith Begg spent years quietly following individual honey badgers through the sand and thornbush. One day they watched a full-grown puff adder — a thick, heavy snake whose venom can kill a person — strike a hunting honey badger right in the face. The badger convulsed, collapsed on the sand, and lay as if dead for about two hours. What happened next?
answer: It woke, got up, and returned to finish eating the snake that bit it
choices: It woke, got up, and returned to finish eating the snake that bit it
It was carried off by a jackal before it could recover
It stayed down and did not survive the venom
Its mate dragged it into a burrow to sleep off the bite
context: Documented by Begg & Begg in National Geographic's 'Snake Killers: Honey Badgers of the Kalahari.' The badger passed out for about two hours, then recovered and finished its meal; full recovery came within about five hours. A legendary but observed event. Source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=chtdRCrZKuw

question: Cobra venom kills by locking onto a muscle receptor in its prey and freezing the muscles solid. But the very same cobra venom barely bothers the honey badger, a small ferocious African predator. Pigs and hedgehogs, on other continents, independently evolved the very same defensive trick against snake venoms. What is it that protects the honey badger?
answer: A charged amino acid swapped into the receptor's toxin-binding site
choices: A charged amino acid swapped into the receptor's toxin-binding site
The muscle receptor is missing from its cells entirely
It grows extra receptors so the venom spreads too thin to work
Its receptors only change shape after the venom binds, shaking it loose
context: Drabeck et al. (2015), 'Why the honey badger don't care,' found a positively charged amino acid substituted into the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor's binding site, so the venom can't attach. Pigs and hedgehogs arrived at almost the same solution separately. Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25796346/

question: A honeybee hive works like a huge, buzzing city hidden inside a hollow tree or a wooden box. Almost all of its tens of thousands of bees are females that cannot lay eggs of their own. These females do nearly every job in the hive — gathering nectar and pollen from flowers, building the wax comb, feeding the young larvae, and guarding the entrance from wasps and mice. What do we call these hardworking females?
answer: Workers
choices: Workers
Drones
Queens
Nymphs
context: A colony is overwhelmingly sterile female workers; a small hive holds about 20,000 bees, a large one can top 100,000, with one queen and a few hundred male drones. Source: https://www.mdbka.com/bee-information/ ; https://canr.udel.edu/maarec/honey-bee-biology/the-colony-and-its-organization/

question: A honeybee finds a rich patch of flowers and flies home. Back on the comb, in the crowded dark, she runs a tight figure-eight over and over: a straight dash down the middle, a fast shudder of her whole body, then a loop back to start again, while her hivemates crowd close to read her. What is this famous move called?
answer: The waggle dance
choices: The waggle dance
The swarm call
The scent trail
The nectar hum
context: The returning forager traces a figure-eight on the vertical comb, running a straight line while shaking her abdomen, then looping back to repeat it -- a symbolic message to her hivemates. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waggle_dance  (Legend.)

question: In the 1940s the Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch peered into a glass-walled beehive and saw something no one had understood. A returning forager honeybee would stomp out a strange figure-eight dance on the vertical honeycomb, wagging her body along a straight middle run in the middle of the eight. The angle of that middle run turned out to be a code — one exact piece of information the other bees needed before they flew out to find the flowers she had found. What does the angle of the run tell them?
answer: Which direction to fly, measured from the sun
choices: Which direction to fly, measured from the sun
How many bees to send out
How sweet the nectar is
Which flower species to seek
context: The angle of the waggle run relative to straight-up equals the angle to the flowers relative to the sun: waggle straight up means fly toward the sun; a run 45 degrees left means fly 45 degrees left of the sun. Source: https://www.planetbee.org/post/the-waggle-dance-bees-high-tech-navigation-system ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waggle_dance  (Legend.)

question: In her dark hive, a honeybee returning from a rich patch of clover bumps into her sisters on the honeycomb and begins the famous waggle dance first decoded by Karl von Frisch. She runs forward in a straight line, shaking her belly side to side, then loops back and does it all again. The angle of that straight run tells the hive which way to fly. But she varies one other thing too — sometimes a brief, snappy shudder, sometimes one drawn out far longer. What does the length of the waggle run encode?
answer: The distance to the flowers
choices: The distance to the flowers
The wind speed outside
The number of open blooms
The time of day to leave
context: The longer she waggles, the farther the food: a short waggle means the flowers are close, a long one means a longer flight. Direction lives in the angle, distance in the duration. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waggle_dance  (Legend.)

question: A honeybee's waggle dance points the way to flowers using the sun's angle. Yet she dances deep inside the hive, on a vertical comb, in total darkness -- she cannot see the sky at all. So what does she use in place of the sun to set the angle of her run?
answer: Gravity, treating straight-up as 'toward the sun'
choices: Gravity, treating straight-up as 'toward the sun'
The Earth's magnetic field
The warmth radiating from the hive entrance
The scent drifting in from outside
context: In the dark she substitutes 'straight up' for 'toward the sun,' using gravity as her compass since she cannot see the sky -- an abstract translation from sun-angle to gravity-angle. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waggle_dance  (Legend.)

question: In 1927 Karl von Frisch claimed the honeybee's dance was a true symbolic language, and fellow scientists scoffed -- surely an insect could not tell another insect anything in code. To settle it, he ran a test that would win him a Nobel Prize: he read a dance, then watched where the recruits went. What did the watching bees do that proved him right?
answer: Flew straight to a spot none of them had ever visited
choices: Flew straight to a spot none of them had ever visited
Circled the hive at random until they stumbled on food
Simply followed the dancer back out to the same patch
Waited for a scent trail before leaving the comb
context: Von Frisch proved the dance is a symbolic language: recruits who only watched the dance flew directly to a food source they had never been to, guided solely by the coded angle and duration. He shared the 1973 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Konrad Lorenz and Nikolaas Tinbergen. His 1927 claim of an insect 'language' was widely dismissed at first. Source: https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1973/frisch/facts/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_von_Frisch  (Legend.)

question: Inside a beehive, every ordinary worker bee and every queen begins the exact same way: as a fertilized egg laid in the same kind of wax cell, hatching into a tiny larva you could not tell apart from any of its sisters. Yet within a few days one chosen larva grows into a giant egg-laying queen while the rest become sterile workers. The whole difference comes down to one special food the workers pack into the chosen larva's cell. What are they feeding her?
answer: Royal jelly
choices: Royal jelly
Extra pollen
Crushed drones
Fermented nectar
context: A queen is made, not born: the chosen larva is fed royal jelly throughout development, while workers are cut off from it after three days. The royal-jelly larva grows into a queen. Source: https://extension.psu.edu/an-introduction-to-queen-honey-bee-development ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_jelly  (Legend.)

question: A prime honeybee queen has one overwhelming job, and she does it at a staggering pace -- each pale egg about half the size of a grain of rice, laid one after another all day long. In a single day, her total output of eggs actually outweighs her own body. About how many does she lay per day?
answer: About 2,000
choices: About 2,000
About 50
About 200
About 40,000
context: In her prime a queen lays about 2,000 eggs a day -- more than her own body weight in eggs daily, each egg about half the size of a grain of rice. Source: https://www.mdbka.com/bee-information/

question: To build the six-sided cells of her honeycomb, a worker honeybee needs wax — and she does not gather it. She manufactures it inside her own body. Tiny pale flakes of wax ooze out of eight glands on the underside of her abdomen; she scrapes them off with her legs, chews them soft in her jaws, and presses them into comb. But this little wax factory only runs if one condition is met inside the hive. What must the hive be?
answer: Warm, around 95 F
choices: Warm, around 95 F
Humid and misty
Packed with fresh pollen
Crowded shoulder to shoulder
context: Eight glands on the underside of a worker's abdomen secrete flakes of wax, which she chews and shapes -- but the hive must be warm (around 95 F / 35 C) for wax to form. Source: https://www.honeyflow.com/blogs/beekeeping-basics/how-do-bees-make-beeswax ; https://www.buddhabeeapiary.com/blog/honey-bee-wax-comb

question: Honeybee wax is enormously expensive to make: a colony eats about eight pounds of honey to produce a single pound of wax. Given that steep cost, a worker packs her precious wax into storage cells of one particular shape, repeated across the whole comb. What shape is a honeycomb cell?
answer: A hexagon
choices: A hexagon
A circle
A triangle
A square
context: Bees build hexagonal cells because the hexagon stores the most honey using the least wax and is one of the strongest shapes for the material -- and wax is costly, about 8 pounds of honey eaten per 1 pound of wax made. Source: https://www.sciencefriday.com/educational-resources/why-do-bees-build-hexagonal-honeycomb-cells/ ; https://www.vegasbees.com/post/honeybee-feats-of-strength-making-one-pound-of-beeswax

question: When a honeybee stings a person or a bear to defend her hive, it is a one-way trip — she will not survive the day. A wasp can sting again and again and fly away unharmed, but a single sting kills a honeybee within minutes. Something about her stinger, unlike a wasp's, dooms her. What is it about her sting that kills her?
answer: The stinger tears free, ripping out part of her body
choices: The stinger tears free, ripping out part of her body
Her wings lock and she cannot fly
Her venom turns inward and poisons her
She goes permanently blind
context: The honeybee's stinger is barbed like a fishhook, so it lodges in the victim's flesh; when she pulls away it tears free along with part of her abdomen and venom sac -- fatal self-sacrifice for the colony. A wasp's smooth stinger slides out cleanly, so it can sting repeatedly and survive. Source: https://www.britannica.com/science/Do-Bees-Die-After-Stinging ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bee_sting  (Legend.)

question: A honeybee flies over a meadow that looks, to us, like a scatter of plain-colored flowers. To her it is lit with glowing bull's-eyes and lines pointing straight into each bloom, guiding her to the nectar. She sees these hidden 'landing strips' because her eyes pick up a band of light ours cannot. What light is that?
answer: Ultraviolet
choices: Ultraviolet
Infrared
X-rays
Radio waves
context: Bees see ultraviolet light invisible to humans; their receptors are tuned to ultraviolet, blue, and green. Flowers like buttercups, sunflowers, and pansies reveal UV 'nectar guides' -- landing strips and bull's-eyes -- only under UV light. Source: https://apiaryproject.com/blog/honey-bee-vision-uv-compound-eyes-how-bees-see ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nectar_guide

question: Honeybees have a strange genetic system called haplodiploidy. A female worker or queen hatches from a fertilized egg and carries 32 chromosomes — half from her mother and half from the drone that mated with the queen. But a drone, a male honeybee, hatches from an unfertilized egg. His body is built from his mother's genes alone, just 16 chromosomes, and that single unfertilized egg had only one parent behind it. Because of that, one kind of blood relative that every worker and queen possesses is, for a drone, flatly impossible. Which relative can a drone never have?
answer: A father
choices: A father
A brother
A daughter
A grandfather
context: This is haplodiploidy: in honeybees a fertilized egg becomes a female, an unfertilized egg becomes a male. So a drone develops from an egg with no sperm at all -- he is haploid, carrying only his mother's 16 chromosomes, and has literally no father. Yet he still has a maternal grandfather, because his mother hatched from a fertilized egg with two parents. He can also father daughters: every one of his roughly 10 million sperm is a genetic clone of his single genome. The 'no father, but a grandfather' family tree even traces out a Fibonacci sequence of ancestors -- 1, 1, 2, 3, 5. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drone_(bee) -- drones haploid (16 chromosomes), arrhenotokous parthenogenesis, no father, maternal grandfather, Fibonacci ancestry, ~10M clonal sperm; haplodiploidy corroborated by multiple bee-genetics sources.

question: For years scientists genuinely fought over whether the waggle dance means anything -- Adrian Wenner insisted bees just sniff out food by smell and the dancing is noise. In 1989 Axel Michelsen ended the argument with one device: a small dancer of brass and beeswax, its razor-blade wing buzzing near 280 times a second, sent onto the comb. What did this thing do that settled it?
answer: Recruited real bees to a target spot only it had named
choices: Recruited real bees to a target spot only it had named
Released the exact floral scent the foragers were tracking
Out-danced the live bees until they abandoned their own runs
Proved the smell trail worked even with the dance removed
context: This was a real scientific fight, not a settled story. Von Frisch had claimed in the 1940s that the dance was a symbolic code; in 1967 Adrian Wenner mounted a serious challenge -- bees, he argued, find food by following floral and hive odors, and the dance carries no information. To test it, Axel Michelsen's team built a mechanical robot bee out of brass and beeswax, with a razor-blade wing that buzzed at about 280 cycles per second (Hz). Programmed to perform specific waggle dances, the robot successfully steered real recruits to a chosen spot in the field, proving the dance itself -- not smell -- carries the location. James Gould's manipulated-dance experiments pointed the same way. Source: link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10739-005-0552-1 (The Bee Battles: von Frisch, Wenner and the dance-language controversy); Michelsen robot-bee corroborated via link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF00166696 and the ACP Social Insects summary -- 280 Hz brass-and-beeswax robot recruited real bees to a target.

question: Deep under the deserts of Australia and the American Southwest, honeypot ants build long underground nests that snake through the packed sand. Inside, a small group of chosen workers are fed nectar and sugary droplets by their sisters, over and over, far past what any normal ant could ever eat in a meal. What happens to the body of one of these stuffed workers?
answer: Its abdomen swells into a round, translucent globe the size of a grape, full of honey
choices: Its abdomen swells into a round, translucent globe the size of a grape, full of honey
It grows a second pair of wings and flies off to start a new colony
It sprouts a hard armored shell to guard the nest entrance
It turns bright red to warn birds that it tastes bitter
context: These gorged workers are called repletes. Fed liquid nectar until their crop stretches, a replete becomes a living storage jar for the whole colony. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honeypot_ant

question: A honeypot ant that has been fed so much nectar its abdomen has swollen up to the size of a fat grape is called a replete — she has become the colony's living pantry. Her golden, glass-like belly is now far too heavy for her to carry around, and she can no longer walk anywhere at all. Where does a replete spend the coming months of her life inside the underground desert nest?
answer: Hanging motionless upside down from the ceiling of the underground nest
choices: Hanging motionless upside down from the ceiling of the underground nest
Buried in a sealed mud cell at the very bottom of the nest
Floating in a shallow pool the workers dig near the entrance
Riding on the backs of ordinary workers who carry it from room to room
context: Too swollen to move, repletes hang from the nest roof — a wall of living honey jars overhead — sometimes for months. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myrmecocystus_mexicanus

question: The Australian desert has been locked in a long, cruel dry spell, and food up on the surface has almost run out. Deep in the honeypot ant nest, a hungry worker walks up to one of the colony's repletes — a sister whose golden abdomen is swollen fat with stored nectar, hanging from the ceiling of the chamber. The hungry ant taps the replete very gently with her antennae. What does the swollen ant do in response?
answer: Regurgitates a drop of stored liquid from its crop into the hungry ant's mouth
choices: Regurgitates a drop of stored liquid from its crop into the hungry ant's mouth
Splits open along its belly so the colony can scoop the honey out
Releases a scent that calls other workers to come and share
Drops from the ceiling and rolls toward the nest entrance
context: Nestmates 'milk' the repletes this way, and the whole colony drinks from these living jars through droughts and winter famines. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honeypot_ant

question: Deep in the desert of central Australia, the Arrernte — an Aboriginal people who have lived on that land for thousands of years — call the swollen honeypot ant Yarumpa. In the dry months, the Arrernte women and children track the ants back to their nests and dig deep pits into the hard red earth to reach the repletes hanging from the ceiling inside. Why do they want these fat, honey-filled ants?
answer: To eat the swollen amber abdomens as a sweet — a rare source of sugar in the desert
choices: To eat the swollen amber abdomens as a sweet — a rare source of sugar in the desert
To collect the ants as bait for catching desert lizards
To grind the whole ants into a paste that keeps flies away
To move the colony to a wetter patch of ground before the dry season
context: Aboriginal Australians dig up the repletes of Camponotus inflatus and eat the honey-filled abdomens, a natural candy in a land with little sugar. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camponotus_inflatus

question: Across the open fields, olive groves, and orchards of Europe, North Africa, and Asia, a small pinkish-brown bird — cinnamon-fawn in color, with striking black-and-white striped wings — struts along the ground pecking for insects with its long curved beak. When it lands or is startled, it throws up a tall crest of feathers tipped in black that opens straight up like a folding fan. Which bird is it?
answer: The hoopoe
choices: The hoopoe
The bee-eater
The nightjar
The waxwing
context: The hoopoe (Upupa epops) is unmistakable: cinnamon-fawn body, black-and-white barred wings, and a fan-like crest tipped with black that pops up in alarm, courtship, or on landing, then folds sleekly flat while the bird forages. In flight it bounds along like a giant butterfly, its broad wings half-closing at the end of each beat. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurasian_hoopoe

question: A hoopoe is a striking crested bird of Europe, Africa, and Asia that nests deep inside cramped tree holes. During breeding, the mother crouches on her eggs in that tight dark space, unable to flee a predator or a slow tide of parasites creeping into the nest. So her body helps. Her preen gland, which usually just makes ordinary waterproofing oil, switches over to a thick brown brew that she paints all over her feathers and eggs. What is startling about this breeding-season brew?
answer: It reeks of rotting meat
choices: It reeks of rotting meat
It glows faintly in the dark
It hardens into a shell
It tastes bitter to the tongue
context: During nesting, the female hoopoe's uropygial (preen) gland switches to a thick brown liquid that smells of rotting meat, and she paints it over her feathers and eggs to repel predators and parasites. The stink comes largely from dimethyl sulfide, and the secretion is actually made by symbiotic Enterococcus bacteria living in her gland that also produce antibacterial chemicals shielding the eggs from harmful microbes. Sources: https://www.audubon.org/news/the-hoopoe-emissary-kings-secreter-stink ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2842625/

question: A hoopoe is a crested bird of Europe, Africa, and Asia that nests inside tight tree holes. The mother slathers the nest in stinking secretions to hold parasites off, but her chicks come armed too. From about six days old, when a predator's head appears at the hole, a hoopoe chick hisses like a snake and stabs upward with its bill. In the same moment it fires off a second, grosser weapon. What is it?
answer: Squirt streams of liquid feces
choices: Squirt streams of liquid feces
Flash a bright warning patch
Puff up to twice its size
Play dead until it leaves
context: From about six days old, hoopoe chicks add a second gross weapon to the mother's stink: they turn their tails toward an intruder and squirt streams of liquid feces at it while hissing snake-like and jabbing upward with the bill. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurasian_hoopoe

question: On the sandy beaches of the eastern United States and East Asia, a strange, ancient-looking sea animal crawls out of the surf every spring to lay its eggs by the millions. It has a hard, domed brown shell shaped like a bowl and a long, spiky tail behind it. Everyone calls it a horseshoe crab, but that name lies — it is not a true crab at all. Its closest living relatives are:
answer: spiders and scorpions
choices: spiders and scorpions
clams and oysters
true crabs and lobsters
jellyfish and corals
context: The horseshoe crab is a chelicerate, sharing a lineage with arachnids rather than crustaceans — which is why it is nicknamed the 'sea spider.' Source: Digital Atlas of Ancient Life (digitalatlasofancientlife.org); Defenders of Wildlife.

question: The horseshoe crab is a helmet-shaped sea creature that drags its dome-shaped shell across sandy beaches from Delaware to Japan, almost the same way it did 450 million years ago. Scientists call it a living fossil. The first dinosaurs did not appear until about 240 million years ago — the horseshoe crab was already ancient by then. About how much older than the earliest dinosaurs is the horseshoe crab lineage?
answer: more than 200 million years
choices: more than 200 million years
about 20 thousand years
about 5 million years
more than 2 billion years
context: Horseshoe crabs are 'living fossils' — their form has barely changed in about 450 million years, meaning they walked the shallows more than 200 million years before the first dinosaurs and survived all five great mass extinctions. Source: Defenders of Wildlife.

question: A wave dumps a horseshoe crab — an ancient armored sea creature that has scuttled the shallows since before the dinosaurs — onto its back on a Delaware beach. Its many legs kick uselessly at the sky. Left this way it will dry out in the sun or be picked off by gulls. It has no stinger, no pincer, and no venom. Yet the long spiky tail on its rear end, called the telson, is what saves it. How does the crab use the telson to right itself?
answer: stabs it into the sand and levers itself over
choices: stabs it into the sand and levers itself over
grips a rock to haul itself upright
spins in circles to dig a righting pit
pushes off a neighboring crab's shell
context: Contrary to popular belief, the telson is neither a stinger nor poisonous; the crab jabs it into the ground and uses it as a lever to flip right-side-up when stranded on its back, and to steer while swimming. Source: South Carolina DNR; Maryland DNR.

question: The horseshoe crab is a helmet-shaped sea creature that has crawled the Atlantic sea floor for 450 million years. When lab workers on the beaches of Delaware Bay nick its shell to draw a sample, the blood that wells out is not red like ours — it is a startling milky blue. Human blood carries oxygen using iron-based hemoglobin, which is why our blood turns red. The horseshoe crab uses a very different molecule. What does its blood use to carry oxygen, and why is it that shade of blue?
answer: a copper-based protein
choices: a copper-based protein
iron-rich hemoglobin
dissolved chlorophyll
liquid silver droplets
context: Instead of iron-based red hemoglobin, horseshoe crab blood uses a copper-based protein called hemocyanin to carry oxygen; the copper turns the blood blue when it meets air. Source: The Horseshoe Crab (horseshoecrab.org); Britannica.  (Legend.)

question: Every vaccine or injected drug that goes into a human body is first checked for tiny germ poisons — the leftovers of dead bacteria — that could trigger a dangerous fever. Drug companies do this by mixing a drop of the medicine with a strange blue-tinted fluid drawn from an ancient helmet-shaped sea creature that crawls up on the sand to lay eggs each spring. If germ toxins are in the sample, the fluid clots into a warning gel. That toxin-trapping blue blood comes from which animal?
answer: horseshoe crab
choices: horseshoe crab
electric eel
sea cucumber
giant clam
context: Cells in horseshoe crab blood called amebocytes instantly clot into a gel when they touch bacterial toxins, trapping the germs. This 'LAL' test checks that injectable medicines and vaccines, including COVID-19 vaccines, are free of contamination. Source: The Horseshoe Crab (horseshoecrab.org); NCBI LAL technology review.  (Legend.)

question: The horseshoe crab is a strange armored sea creature older than the dinosaurs — and it sees the world in a way no other animal alive does. Look closely at one flipped over on a beach and you find eyes almost everywhere on it. Two big compound eyes ride on top of its helmet-shell, a pair of small simple eyes sits between them, another pair hides underneath near its mouth, and light-sensing spots run all the way out along its long spiky tail. Add every one of them up. This animal has how many eyes in total?
answer: ten
choices: ten
two
five
twenty
context: A horseshoe crab has ten eyes scattered over its body — two large compound eyes (each with about 1,000 light-sensing units), several simple eyes, two on its underside near the mouth, and light sensors on its tail. Source: Florida FWC; Maryland DNR.

question: On spring high tides near the full and new moon each May, thousands of horseshoe crabs bury millions of green eggs on Delaware Bay's beaches. A threatened shorebird times a 9,000-mile Arctic migration to arrive and gorge on those eggs. In two weeks of feasting, the red knot does what to its own body?
answer: nearly doubles its body weight
choices: nearly doubles its body weight
grows an extra set of wings
turns its feathers bright green
sheds its entire skeleton
context: The fat-rich horseshoe crab eggs let the threatened red knot, mid-migration to its Arctic breeding grounds, nearly double its body weight in about two weeks — fuel it needs to finish the flight. Each female crab buries clusters of about 3,000–5,000 eggs. Source: Delaware DNREC; New Jersey DEP.

question: A hummingbird is a tiny bird of the Americas, no bigger than a person's thumb, with wings that blur into a hum as it hovers at flowers to sip nectar. Watch one at a garden feeder and you see it doing things in the air that no other bird can. What flight trick sets the hummingbird apart from every other bird on Earth?
answer: Truly hover in place and fly backward
choices: Truly hover in place and fly backward
Glide for hours without a single wingbeat
Dive faster than any other bird
Sleep in the air while still flying
context: The hummingbird is the only bird family that can truly hover and even fly backward (and briefly upside down) — no other bird can. Source: Audubon, 'Hummingbird Flight Is Like Nothing Else in the Bird World.'  (Legend.)

question: A ruby-throated hummingbird hangs motionless in front of a red trumpet-flower, its long needle beak dipping in for a sip of nectar. Its wings are a smoky gray blur — you can hear them hum in the air but you can barely see them move. That humming blur is what the whole bird is named for. About how fast are those wings actually beating in ordinary hovering flight?
answer: About 50 times every second
choices: About 50 times every second
About 5 times every second
About twice every second
About once every second
context: In ordinary hovering a hummingbird beats its wings roughly 50 times a second — the blur that makes the humming sound it's named for. Source: BBC Science Focus; Science World, 'Flight of the Hummingbird.'

question: Every other bird gets its lift only on the DOWNstroke; the upbeat is dead, wasted time. A hovering hummingbird cheats this — its wing pushes air down on the way FORWARD and again on the way back, tracing a shape in the air. What figure does the wingtip trace to make lift on both halves of the beat?
answer: A flat figure-8
choices: A flat figure-8
A tight vertical circle
A straight up-and-down line
A wide sideways oval
context: The hummingbird's wingtip traces a flat figure-8, and the wing rotates at the shoulder so both the forward and the backward stroke tilt to push air down — unlike the down-only stroke of every other bird. Source: BBC Science Focus; AskNature hummingbird hover strategy.

question: Holding yourself perfectly frozen in mid-air takes tremendous power. So a hummingbird — the smallest bird on earth — is built around its flight muscles, the big slabs of breast meat that drive its wings. Most birds carry only a small share of breast muscle for their size, maybe a tenth or so of body weight. In a hummingbird, that muscle takes up a jaw-dropping chunk of the whole bird. How much of its total weight is breast muscle?
answer: Almost a third of its body weight
choices: Almost a third of its body weight
About a tenth of its body weight
Barely a twentieth of its body weight
Roughly two-thirds of its body weight
context: A hummingbird's breast (pectoral) flight muscles make up almost a third of its body weight — twice the muscle fraction of an ordinary bird. Source: BBC Science Focus, 'Super pecs and 1,200 heartbeats per minute.'

question: Most birds barely bother with the upstroke — it makes almost no lift. A hummingbird is different: it drives a big upstroke muscle, the supracoracoideus, so the lifting UPbeat pulls real weight. About how much of a hovering hummingbird's total lift comes from that upstroke?
answer: About a quarter of its lift
choices: About a quarter of its lift
Almost none of its lift
About half of its lift
Nearly all of its lift
context: Unlike other birds, a hummingbird's big upstroke muscle (the supracoracoideus) makes the lifting upbeat supply about a quarter of its total lift — the rest of the bird world barely uses the upstroke at all. Source: BBC Science Focus; Tough Little Birds, 'hummingbird flight.'

question: To hold itself perfectly frozen in the air at a red flower, a hovering hummingbird runs its tiny engine at a rate that would kill almost any other creature. Its heart pounds so fast it becomes one nonstop hum inside the chest. A resting human heart beats about 80 times a minute, and a racing marathon runner tops out near 200. How fast does the hummingbird's heart hammer while it hovers?
answer: Around 1,200 beats a minute
choices: Around 1,200 beats a minute
Around 200 beats a minute
Around 500 beats a minute
Around 90 beats a minute
context: A hovering hummingbird's heart beats around 1,200 times a minute — versus about 80 in a human. Source: BBC Science Focus; AnimalCorner hummingbird anatomy.  (Legend.)

question: Hovering burns so much fuel that a hummingbird can't store enough to last the night, so each night, to keep from freezing before dawn, it lets its whole body go cold and lets its racing heart slow far down. That daytime heart pounds around 1,200 beats a minute. About how far down does it drop during this nightly shutdown?
answer: To as few as ~50 beats a minute
choices: To as few as ~50 beats a minute
To around 90 beats a minute
To around 130 beats a minute
To around 180 beats a minute
context: Hovering costs so much that a hummingbird cannot survive the night on its reserves, so it drops into torpor — heart falling from ~1,200 beats a minute to as few as ~50, body going cold until dawn. Source: forumscience.com; JEB, 'Flight Thermogenesis and Energy Conservation in Hovering Hummingbirds.'  (Legend.)

question: A small creature hovers at a flowerbed on a summer afternoon, wings beating so fast — about 85 times a second — that they blur into a hum, and its long tongue probes each bloom for nectar. Passersby swear a tiny hummingbird has strayed into the garden. But it is no bird at all. What kind of animal is it?
answer: A moth
choices: A moth
A bee
A hoverfly
A bat
context: The hummingbird hawkmoth (Sphingidae) hovers at flowers exactly like a hummingbird, beating its wings about 85 times a second — faster than a hummingbird's ~50 — so people mistake the insect for a tiny bird. Source: Journal of Experimental Biology jeb230920; A-Z Animals.

question: A hummingbird is a tiny bird of the Americas. A hawkmoth is a fat-bodied moth found around the world. Yet both can hang perfectly still at a flower with an almost identical figure-8 wing stroke. They are only distant relatives — a bird and an insect — and each lineage worked out this trick alone. Biologists call this kind of separate solution convergent evolution. Across all the animal kingdom, how many times has true hovering flight been invented this way?
answer: Only about four times
choices: Only about four times
Hundreds of times
In nearly every flying group
Just once, then inherited
context: True hovering evolved independently only about four times in nectar feeders — hummingbirds, some bats, hoverflies, and hawkmoths — a classic case of convergent evolution onto the same figure-8 solution. Source: Journal of Experimental Biology jeb230920; PBS Nature.

question: On a summer afternoon a small insect called a hoverfly hangs dead-still in the sunlight above a garden, its body striped bold black-and-yellow just like a wasp's. But look closer and you see only two wings, not four — this is a true fly, not a wasp at all. It has no stinger, no venom, no bite. Nothing but those borrowed colors protects it. Why do the wasp-like stripes keep the harmless hoverfly alive?
answer: Predators burned once by wasps avoid anything striped like one
choices: Predators burned once by wasps avoid anything striped like one
The stripes reflect sunlight and hide its outline in the glare
The pattern startles a bird into flinching just long enough
Wasps recognize the stripes and defend it as one of their own
context: The hoverfly wears the black-and-yellow stripes of a wasp or bee as pure bluff — Batesian mimicry — despite having no sting at all; predators that have learned to avoid stinging wasps leave the lookalike alone. Source: RHS, 'Hoverflies: Identification & Control'; Wikipedia, 'Hoverfly.'

question: A dragonfly can hang and dart with rare precision because, unlike a hummingbird's two wings, it has four — and it can steer each one on its own. It saves flapping power with a specific timing trick between its front and back pairs. What does the dragonfly do with them to cut the energy cost of hovering?
answer: Beats the front and back wings out of phase
choices: Beats the front and back wings out of phase
Beats all four wings in perfect unison
Holds the back wings still and beats only the front
Folds the front wings and glides on the back
context: A dragonfly hovers with four independently controlled wings; when its front and back wings beat out of phase (crossing near mid-stroke) it saves flapping power, letting it hang and dart precisely. Source: Royal Society Interface, Usherwood & Lehmann; Royal Society Open Science rsos.202275.

question: A kestrel — a small hunting falcon with a russet back and dark-spotted breast — appears to hover over an English hayfield. Its body hangs pinned in one spot as its head stays perfectly still, scanning the grass below for the flicker of a vole. Unlike a hummingbird, though, it isn't truly beating its wings in still air to stay put. So how does the kestrel actually hold itself in place?
answer: It faces into a headwind and flaps just enough to cancel it
choices: It faces into a headwind and flaps just enough to cancel it
It hangs on a warm updraft rising off the sunlit field
It locks its wings and glides in a tight circle
It grips the air with specially slotted feathers
context: The kestrel 'wind-hovers' by facing into a headwind and flapping just fast enough to cancel it — not truly beating in still air — which is why its old English name is the 'windhover.' Source: Birdfact, 'Kestrel Hovering'; Opposite View Wildlife.  (Legend.)

question: For 180 years textbooks said a hummingbird pumps nectar up its grooved tongue by capillary action, the way a paper towel wicks water. High-speed film of the tongue actually hitting nectar killed that idea. What is the tongue really doing when its tips touch the nectar?
answer: Its flattened grooves spring open and suck up a column of nectar
choices: Its flattened grooves spring open and suck up a column of nectar
Its outer surface wicks a thin film upward by capillary action
Its muscular walls squeeze in a slow wave to push nectar back
Its hollow core draws nectar up like a straw under suction
context: A 2015 study (Alejandro Rico-Guevara, Tai-Hsi Fan, Margaret Rubega, Proc. R. Soc. B) high-speed-filmed 18 species and falsified 180 years of capillary-action textbook claims. The tongue is squeezed flat as it extends; the instant its grooved tips touch nectar, the collapsed grooves spring back open, and that elastic re-expansion actively sucks up a column of nectar an order of magnitude faster than capillarity could. It works as an elastic micropump, not a paper towel, which is what lets a hummingbird lick a flower up to ~20 times a second. Source: Rico-Guevara, Fan & Rubega, 'Hummingbird tongues are elastic micropumps,' Proc. R. Soc. B 2015 (royalsocietypublishing.org; pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26290074).

question: All 360 living hummingbird species live only in the Americas, so the family looks purely New World. Then Gerald Mayr described 32-million-year-old hovering, nectar-feeding hummingbird fossils far outside that range. Which region turned up those oldest known hummingbird fossils?
answer: Southern Germany
choices: Southern Germany
Southern Ecuador
Southern Mexico
Southern Brazil
context: In 2004 Gerald Mayr described Eurotrochilus, a stem-group hummingbird already built for hovering and nectar-feeding, from ~32-million-year-old (early Oligocene, Rupelian) specimens at the Wiesloch-Frauenweiler clay pit in southern Germany, with more later found in France and Poland. So hummingbirds hovered over Old World flowers 30+ million years ago, then vanished from that hemisphere entirely, leaving every living species in the Americas. The family that seems quintessentially American left its oldest fossils in Europe. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurotrochilus (Mayr, 2004); corroborated en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hummingbird.

question: On the island of Cuba, deep in the forest, there darts a hummingbird so small the locals call it the zunzuncito — the little buzzer. A male weighs less than an American penny, about 1.6 grams. Nowhere on Earth does a smaller bird live. What is it?
answer: The bee hummingbird
choices: The bee hummingbird
The pygmy owl
The golden-crowned kinglet
The zebra finch
context: The bee hummingbird (Mellisuga helenae) averages about 5.5 cm (2 inches) long and under 2 grams -- lighter than a penny -- making it not only the smallest bird but the smallest warm-blooded animal on Earth. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bee_hummingbird

question: Other birds can hang in the air only by facing into a stiff wind, and every one of them can travel in just one direction: forward. A hummingbird needs no wind to hold its spot -- and it can do something no other bird on Earth can. What can it do that they cannot?
answer: Fly backward
choices: Fly backward
Sleep in flight
Breathe underwater
Glide for miles
context: A hummingbird is the only bird that can truly hover in place and fly backward. Other birds can hang briefly in a headwind, but only the hummingbird can reverse in mid-air. Source: https://www.discoverwildlife.com/animal-facts/birds/facts-about-hummingbirds

question: Most birds only make lift on the downstroke, pushing air down as they flap and losing lift when the wing comes back up. But a tiny hummingbird can hover motionless in mid-air because it sweeps its wings in a very special path — one that makes lift on both the forward stroke and the return stroke, like a swimmer's arms sculling water. What shape does the wingtip trace in the air as it does this?
answer: A figure-eight
choices: A figure-eight
A tight circle
A straight up-and-down line
A rising spiral
context: By sweeping its wings in a figure-eight, a hummingbird generates lift on both the forward stroke and the backstroke -- unlike other birds, which only get lift pushing down. This is what lets it hover and reverse. Source: https://news.oregonstate.edu/news/research-shows-hummingbird-flight-evolutionary-marvel

question: A hummingbird's tiny body burns fuel about as fast as it can take it in. It must sip flower nectar every 10 to 15 minutes just to keep from starving before dark. Imagine a person weighing 100 pounds having to eat 50 pounds of sugar in one day. About how much of its own body weight in pure sugar does a hummingbird eat in a single day of flitting from blossom to blossom?
answer: About half
choices: About half
About a tenth
About a fiftieth
About a thousandth
context: A hummingbird eats roughly half its own body weight in sugar every day and must feed every 10 to 15 minutes -- it would starve overnight if it simply slept. Source: https://birdwatchingbuzz.com/hummingbird-heart-rate/

question: A hummingbird is a tiny American bird that hovers at flowers and burns sugar as fast as any animal on Earth. To pump so much blood to its whirring wing muscles, its heart has to race far beyond anything a human could survive — a fit person's heart tops out near 200 beats per minute. Roughly how many times can a hummingbird's heart beat in one single minute?
answer: Over 1,200
choices: Over 1,200
Around 300
Around 70
Around 12
context: A hummingbird's heart can beat over 1,200 times a minute (rates up to about 1,260 bpm have been recorded), and it breathes roughly 250 times a minute even at rest. Source: https://a-z-animals.com/blog/10-incredible-hummingbird-facts/

question: The bee hummingbird lives only on the island of Cuba, and it is the smallest bird on Earth — about the length of a person's thumb, and weighing less than a paperclip. The tiny female weaves a cup nest only about an inch across and lays two eggs, the smallest eggs of any bird alive. What everyday object is each bee hummingbird egg about the size of?
answer: A coffee bean
choices: A coffee bean
A chicken egg
A golf ball
A grape
context: A bee hummingbird lays two eggs, each about the size of a coffee bean, in a cup nest only about 2.5 cm (1 inch) across. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bee_hummingbird

question: A hummingbird holds so little fuel that just sleeping through a cold night would starve it. Instead it enters a nightly near-shutdown, dropping its heart rate from over a thousand beats a minute to as few as forty. What is this survival state called?
answer: Torpor
choices: Torpor
Hibernation
Molting
Migration
context: In torpor a hummingbird's heart rate can fall from over 1,000 to as few as ~40-50 beats a minute, cutting energy use by about 95 percent -- letting it survive cold nights on its tiny fuel reserves. Source: https://www.science.org/content/article/survive-frigid-nights-hummingbirds-cool-themselves-record-low-temperatures

question: The ruby-throated hummingbird is a tiny green-and-red bird that nests in the forests of the eastern United States and southern Canada, but winters in Central America. Twice a year it faces a crossing that seems impossible for a bird weighing only 3 grams: about 500 miles of open water over the Gulf of Mexico, in a single 18-hour flight with no place to land. For weeks before takeoff, it eats and eats. What does the ruby-throated hummingbird do to fuel the trip?
answer: Nearly doubles its body weight in fat
choices: Nearly doubles its body weight in fat
Grows a second set of flight feathers
Enlarges its heart permanently
Hollows out its bones for lightness
context: A ruby-throated hummingbird crosses the Gulf of Mexico in a single nonstop flight of up to 500 miles, flying alone for 18 to 22 hours -- nearly doubling its body weight in fat beforehand to fuel the trip. Source: https://www.reconnectwithnature.org/news-events/the-buzz/5-things-about-hummingbirds

question: For the backstroke to make lift, a hummingbird has to flip its whole wing completely upside down between strokes — leading edge one way, then leading edge the other. It manages this by twisting one joint of its arm through nearly 180 degrees, the arm bone itself rotating in its socket. No other bird's flight works like this. Which joint of the hummingbird's wing does the twisting?
answer: The shoulder
choices: The shoulder
The wrist
The elbow
The knuckle
context: To flip its wing over for the lift-generating backstroke, a hummingbird rotates its wing at the shoulder nearly 180 degrees -- the humerus itself twists. Source: https://www.threads.com/@museumofscience/post/DORoQMhiO9l/

question: A diving peregrine falcon is often called the fastest animal on Earth. For its size, it covers about 200 body lengths a second. In his mating dive, a male Anna's hummingbird beats even that. How many of his own body lengths does he cover each second?
context: During his courtship dive, a male Anna's hummingbird covers 385 times its own body length every second -- the highest length-relative speed known in any vertebrate, beating even the diving peregrine falcon (about 200 body lengths per second). Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/annas-hummingbird-outflies-falcons-and-fighter-pilots  (Legend.)

question: A fighter pilot in a hard turn blacks out somewhere around 9 g -- nine times the pull of gravity. A male Anna's hummingbird yanks out of its steep courtship dive so violently that its tiny body takes a sudden jolt of g-force too. Roughly how many g's does the bird pull in that pull-up?
answer: Nearly 10 g
choices: Nearly 10 g
About 3 g
About 30 g
About 100 g
context: Pulling out of its courtship dive, an Anna's hummingbird endures nearly 10 times the force of gravity -- more than a fighter pilot endures before blacking out. Source: https://www.sciencenews.org/article/hummingbird-pulls-top-gun-stunts

question: Every other flying vertebrate that lives on nectar still stores fuel the ordinary way. But hummingbirds burn the sugar they just drank almost directly, and researchers traced this to a single change deep in their ancestry, dated to when hovering first evolved. What was that change?
answer: Their ancestor lost a muscle enzyme gene
choices: Their ancestor lost a muscle enzyme gene
Their ancestor gained a second sugar-storing organ
Their ancestor doubled its fat-making capacity
Their ancestor evolved a faster-emptying stomach
context: Osipova and colleagues found that FBP2 (fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase 2), a gluconeogenic muscle enzyme, was inactivated in the common ancestor of all living hummingbirds about 48-30 million years ago -- exactly the window when hovering flight and nectar-feeding evolved. When they knocked FBP2 out of bird cells, glycolysis rose and the cells built more mitochondria and respired harder, running more efficiently. So a gene LOSS, not a gain, helped unlock hovering flight. Source: Osipova et al. 2023, Science 379:185, "Loss of a gluconeogenic muscle enzyme contributed to adaptive metabolic traits in hummingbirds."

question: All 360 hummingbird species today live only in the Americas. Scientists long thought the family began there. Then Gerald Mayr took a fresh look at tiny long-billed skeletons in a museum drawer. Dated to 30 million years ago, the bird he named Eurotrochilus flipped that story. How?
answer: It lived in Europe, far from the Americas
choices: It lived in Europe, far from the Americas
It chased insects instead of sipping nectar
It could not hover despite a slender bill
It outweighed a present-day carrion crow
context: Mayr described Eurotrochilus in 2004 from Early Oligocene deposits (~28-34 million years ago); more fossils later turned up in Germany, France, and Poland. It already had the diagnostic long nectar bill (~15.5-20 mm, about 2.5x its skull length) and hovering wing structure -- so the nectar-hovering lineage evolved in the Old World and only later vanished there, leaving today's hummingbirds solely in the Americas. The genus name means "unexpected European version of a hummingbird." Source: Mayr 2004; Wikipedia "Eurotrochilus"; Science, "Ancient Hummingbirds Were European."

question: Off the coast of New England in the North Atlantic, a 40-ton whale surfaces beside a whale-watching boat. Its huge dark head is covered in rows of round bumps. Its side flippers are pale white and almost 5 meters long — the longest limbs of any animal on Earth. It arcs high and slaps them down with a boom. Which whale is it?
answer: The humpback whale
choices: The humpback whale
The blue whale
The sperm whale
The narwhal
context: The humpback (Megaptera novaeangliae) has the longest flippers of any whale — up to about a third of its whole body, nearly 5 meters (16 feet), the longest limbs of any animal on Earth. Source: https://gentlegiants.is/news/2025/08/03/the-pectoral-fins-of-a-humpback-whale-nature-s-marvels-of-movement-and-communication/

question: The humpback whale is a huge dark whale of the world's oceans, famous for its bumpy head and long white flippers. If a researcher in a small boat reaches down and runs a hand over that head, they feel rows of round bumps, each about the size of a golf ball. Look closely at one bump and you find something surprising growing out of it:
answer: a single hair, thought to sense the water
choices: a single hair, thought to sense the water
a tiny suction cup for grip
a glowing spot to lure prey
a venomous spine for defense
context: Each knobbly bump on a humpback's head is a tubercle, about golf-ball sized, with one hair sprouting from it — thought to help the whale sense the water flowing around it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humpback_whale

question: People love the humpback whale — a 40-ton whale of the world's oceans — for what it does at the surface. On breeding grounds near Hawaii or the Caribbean it slaps its huge flippers and its tail down on the water with booms that carry across the sea. Then it does something no crowd of whale-watchers ever forgets:
answer: hurls its whole body out of the water in a leap
choices: hurls its whole body out of the water in a leap
spins on its back for hours like an otter
walks along the seabed on its flippers
builds a floating nest of seaweed
context: Humpbacks slap their flippers and tails against the surface, and breach — hurling their whole bodies out of the water — which is why whale-watchers love them. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humpback_whale

question: The humpback whale's full scientific name is Megaptera novaeangliae — a two-word tag scientists give it in Latin. The second word, novaeangliae, means the whale was first formally described off the coast of New England in the 1780s. But the first word, Megaptera, comes from Greek and means 'great wing.' It points to the humpback's most giant body part. Which feature does the name celebrate?
answer: its enormous flippers
choices: its enormous flippers
its wide fluked tail
its arched, humped back
its fan-shaped blowhole spray
context: 'Mega-ptera' is Greek for 'giant wing' — the humpback was named for its enormous flippers, the longest limbs of any animal. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humpback_whale

question: A humpback whale is a bus-length animal — up to 17 meters and 40 tons. You would expect it to turn like an oil tanker. Instead, thanks to its giant flippers, it turns like a dolphin: it can spin around inside its own body length, and even do one thing most big whales cannot:
answer: swim backward
choices: swim backward
hold its breath for a whole day
sleep with its whole brain at once
drink seawater safely
context: The humpback's oversized flippers let a 40-ton, 17-meter animal turn inside its own body length like a dolphin, and even swim backward. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humpback_whale

question: The humpback whale is a huge whale of the world's oceans. Each winter humpbacks gather on warm breeding grounds near places like Hawaii and the Caribbean. There they fill the water with long, eerie songs — repeating melodies that can last half an hour and be heard for miles underwater. But not every humpback in the group takes part in the singing. Among the humpbacks, who actually sings?
answer: only the males
choices: only the males
only the mothers with calves
only the oldest whales
the whole pod together
context: Only male humpbacks sing, and only on the winter breeding grounds — the song is thought to be a mating display, not a message carrying a specific meaning. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humpback_whale

question: A humpback whale's song is not just random moaning. Scientists found it is built like music, with small parts joining into larger ones: 'units' join into phrases, phrases build into themes, and ordered themes make the whole song. And a male will do what with that finished song?
answer: repeat it over and over for hours
choices: repeat it over and over for hours
sing it once, then never again
teach it only to his own calf
trade it for a different male's song
context: A single humpback song runs several minutes, and a male can sing it on repeat for hours — Hawaiian recordings caught sessions lasting up to seven hours. The musical structure was first described by Payne and McVay. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humpback_whale  (Legend.)

question: When a group of humpback whales finds a school of fish, they hunt with a trap made of air. Diving below the school, the whales blow a rising spiral of bubbles — a curtain the fish will not cross — that herds the school into a tight ball. Then the whole group does what?
answer: lunges up through the middle with mouths open
choices: lunges up through the middle with mouths open
waits for the bubbles to stun the fish
drives the ball toward a second waiting pod
dives deep and lets the fish scatter
context: In bubble-net feeding, humpbacks blow a spiraling curtain of bubbles the fish won't cross, herding them into a ball, then all lunge up through the center with mouths open. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bubble-net_feeding  (Legend.)

question: Bubble-net feeding is a group hunting trick used by humpback whales off Alaska. A team of whales dives below a school of herring, and one whale spirals slowly upward blowing a rising column of bubbles that walls the fish into a shrinking ring. Then the whole team lunges up through the middle with mouths gaping wide open. It is not a skill they are born with — they learn it and pass it whale to whale, so only some pods do it at all. In one twist, a single 'caller' whale adds something that makes the group strike as one. What does the caller add?
answer: a trumpeting feeding call that signals everyone to lunge at once
choices: a trumpeting feeding call that signals everyone to lunge at once
a burst of clicks that stuns the fish
a slap of its tail to start the dive
a wall of bubbles twice as tall as the others
context: Bubble-net feeding is learned and culturally transmitted, so only some populations do it; one 'caller' whale even trumpets a feeding call to signal the group to lunge at once. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bubble-net_feeding

question: In the warm winter seas where humpback whales gather to breed, the males hang upside-down and sing haunting songs that can last twenty minutes. When Roger Payne first recorded these songs in 1967, the world was stunned. But here is the strangest thing biologists later found: across an entire population, the males don't each invent their own tune. Instead, what do all the males of a population sing — and how does it change?
answer: the same song, and when it changes they all switch together
choices: the same song, and when it changes they all switch together
a new song every night, chosen at random
their mother's song, kept unchanged for life
a fixed song that never changes over generations
context: Every male in a population sings the same song, and when the tune changes the whole population adopts the new version together — a shared culture whales learn from one another. Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9428538/  (Legend.)

question: A new hit song among humpback whales spreads like a fashion trend across the ocean. A fresh tune starts near eastern Australia and travels whale-to-whale through New Caledonia, Tonga, the Cook Islands and French Polynesia. Researchers tracked one such song moving in a striking way:
answer: eastward for 14,000 km, all the way to Ecuador
choices: eastward for 14,000 km, all the way to Ecuador
in a loop back to where it began within a season
only among whales that had met face to face
faster than the whales themselves could migrate
context: New humpback songs sweep eastward across the Pacific, tracked whale-to-whale from eastern Australia across 14,000 km all the way to Ecuador — a cultural wave moving through a whole ocean. Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9428538/  (Legend.)

question: Engineers copying the humpback whale bolted a row of bumps onto the leading edge of a flipper-shaped wing, then raced it against a smooth one in a wind tunnel. The bumps split the oncoming flow and funnel it into the grooves between them — a trick designers now borrow for turbine blades and fans. What did the bumps buy?
answer: it kept its grip on the flow far past the angle where the smooth wing stalled out
choices: it kept its grip on the flow far past the angle where the smooth wing stalled out
it shed a trailing plume of warm water that the smooth wing could never produce
it hummed a deep note that herded nearby fish straight into the path of the wing
it sprouted a fresh row of bumps to replace any that wore smooth over time
context: The humpback's leading-edge flipper bumps, called tubercles, are a stall-delaying wing device, not decoration. In a landmark 2004 Physics of Fluids study, Miklosovic, Murray, Howle and Fish tested two polycarbonate scale-model flippers — one smooth, one bumped — in a wind tunnel and found the tubercled model delayed the stall angle by about 40% while also increasing lift and cutting drag past stall. The rows of bumps split the incoming water and funnel it into the valleys between them, keeping flow attached at steep angles of attack so a 40-ton whale can bank into tight turns without its flipper stalling like a wing. This 'tubercle effect' has since been applied to wind-turbine blades, fans and airplane wings. Source: Miklosovic, Murray, Howle & Fish (2004), Physics of Fluids, 'Leading-edge tubercles delay stall on humpback whale flippers'; corroborated by Fish & Battle (1995), J. Morphology 225:51-60 (PubMed 7650744) and ScienceDaily 2004-05-12.

question: A humpback whale lunges into a bait ball and takes in a mouthful of water as big as its whole body. Inside the flexible joint between the two halves of its lower jaw sits a grape-sized organ found in 2012, present in no other creature on Earth. What does that never-before-seen organ do?
answer: it feels the jaw swing wide and the throat balloon out, timing the whole lunge
choices: it feels the jaw swing wide and the throat balloon out, timing the whole lunge
it stores a reserve of oxygen that feeds the brain through a long, deep dive
it strains the ocean salt back out of the seawater the whale gulps down
it shapes the deep booming notes the male threads all through his long song
context: Rorqual whales, including the humpback, carry a sensory organ that nothing else on Earth has, discovered only in 2012. Pyenson and colleagues, reporting in Nature, found a grape-sized organ embedded in the fibrous joint between the two unfused halves of the lower jaw. Packed with mechanoreceptors — nerve endings and papillae in a gel-like matrix derived from an ancestral tooth socket — it senses jaw rotation and throat-pouch expansion in real time and feeds that to the brain to choreograph the split-second timing of a lunge: when to open, how far the pouch has filled, and when to clamp shut. Source: Pyenson et al. (2012), Nature 485:498, 'Discovery of a sensory organ that coordinates lunge feeding in rorqual whales' (PubMed 22622577); Smithsonian Insider 2012.

question: Swim back to the age of dinosaurs and you would meet the ichthyosaur cutting through the sea: a smooth body like a dolphin or a tuna, a triangular fin on its back, flippers, and a crescent tail. But one thing set it apart from every fish around it. What was it?
answer: It had to surface to breathe air
choices: It had to surface to breathe air
It had gills like the fish it hunted
It never left the deep water
It laid its eggs on the seafloor
context: The ichthyosaur was a reptile, not a fish. It breathed air, so it rose to the surface the way a dolphin does today -- yet dolphins would not appear for another 200 million years. Source: Simple English Wikipedia, Ichthyosaur.

question: During the age of the dinosaurs, ichthyosaurs — dolphin-shaped marine reptiles — hunted the world's oceans. Some grew as long as a bus. Their fossilized skulls carry eye sockets so wide that in the biggest species each eyeball would have been nearly the size of a dinner plate — the largest eyes of any animal ever. Such colossal eyes had to be for hunting somewhere very particular. Where did they let the ichthyosaur hunt?
answer: Hunting in the black depths of the deep ocean
choices: Hunting in the black depths of the deep ocean
Watching the shore for its egg-laying beach
Spotting prey across the bright open surface
Reading the color of coral in the reef
context: Enormous eyes gather as much light as possible, letting the ichthyosaur hunt where almost no light reaches -- the deep ocean, or the surface at night. Source: Kiddle, Temnodontosaurus facts for kids.

question: Ichthyosaurs were huge dolphin-shaped reptiles that ruled the seas of the dinosaur age. Scientists measured the eye socket of the giant ichthyosaur Temnodontosaurus platyodon at about 25 centimeters — 9.8 inches — across, roughly the size of a dinner plate. It is the largest eye ever known in any animal, alive or extinct. Which living creature has an eye that comes close to that size today?
answer: The colossal squid
choices: The colossal squid
The blue whale
The great white shark
The saltwater crocodile
context: At about 25 cm across, the ichthyosaur's eye matches the colossal squid's -- among the very largest eyes nature has produced. Source: Wikipedia, Temnodontosaurus. (Legend-tier wonder.)

question: Ichthyosaurs were dolphin-shaped reptiles that ruled the oceans about 200 million years ago. Land reptiles like turtles and lizards crawl ashore and bury a clutch of leathery eggs in sand or soil. But the ichthyosaur's body — long flippers, no true feet, a fluked swimming tail — meant it could never leave the water at all. Fossils show it handled its young in a completely different way. What did the fossils reveal?
answer: It gave birth to live young in the open water
choices: It gave birth to live young in the open water
It carried its eggs in its mouth until they hatched
It glued its eggs to floating driftwood
It returned to the same beach its ancestors used
context: Some ichthyosaur fossils preserve a mother caught mid-birth, a baby half-emerged from her body -- proof these sea reptiles bore live young rather than laying eggs on land. Source: Live Science, Oldest Fossil of Reptile Live Birth Found. (Legend-tier wonder.)

question: In China, paleontologists split open a fossil of a mother Chaohusaurus, an early ichthyosaur, and found three young preserved with her -- one already born, one still inside, and one caught halfway out. That halfway pup was emerging head-first, not the tail-first way of dolphins and whales. To scientists, that head-first exit was a clue about one thing. What did it tell them?
answer: Ichthyosaurs inherited live birth from land-living ancestors
choices: Ichthyosaurs inherited live birth from land-living ancestors
Ichthyosaurs had only recently returned to land
The mother was the last of an egg-laying line
The pup had turned the wrong way and drowned
context: Head-first birth points to land ancestors that already bore live young, rather than the trait being invented for sea life. Later ichthyosaurs are found giving birth tail-first, like dolphins. Source: NPR, Fossil Shows Triassic-Era Sea Creature Gave Birth.

question: The ichthyosaur, tuna, dolphin, and lamnid shark come from four unrelated branches of the animal kingdom. Yet all four ended up with the same torpedo body, wide crescent tail, and stiff fins. What one problem drove these distant groups to the same shape?
answer: The need to swim fast for long distances in open water
choices: The need to swim fast for long distances in open water
The need to hide their color against the seafloor
The need to survive freezing polar temperatures
The need to crush hard-shelled prey with strong jaws
context: The ichthyosaur (reptile), dolphin (mammal), tuna (bony fish), and lamnid shark (shark) are four separate lineages that all evolved the same streamlined 'thunniform' shape -- the optimal body for fast, sustained swimming in open water. Source: NCBI PMC, Skeletal convergence in thunniform sharks, ichthyosaurs, whales, and tunas.

question: A stunning fossil of the ichthyosaur Stenopterygius — a dolphin-shaped marine reptile from the age of dinosaurs — was so well preserved in a German shale bed that it kept traces of the animal's actual skin. Its coloring followed a pattern you still see on sharks and dolphins in today's ocean: dark on the back, pale on the belly. Biologists call this two-tone scheme countershading. What job did it do for the ichthyosaur?
answer: Camouflage from predators looking down or up
choices: Camouflage from predators looking down or up
Warned rivals off its hunting territory
Attracted mates during the breeding season
Soaked up sunlight to warm its blood
context: Dark-above, light-below coloring -- called countershading -- hides an animal against the dark depths from above and the bright surface from below. The same fossil also preserved a layer of blubber. Source: NC State News, Soft Tissue Shows Jurassic Ichthyosaur Was Warm-Blooded. (Legend-tier preservation.)

question: In 1811 on the crumbling cliffs of Lyme Regis in Dorset, a poor family of fossil-hunters pried loose the first complete ichthyosaur skeleton ever to reach London's scientists -- a 17-foot creature. The person who dug out most of that skeleton was a surprise. Who did the digging?
answer: A twelve-year-old local girl
choices: A twelve-year-old local girl
A twelve-year-old apprentice boy
A young village schoolteacher
A young dockside fisherman
context: Mary Anning's brother Joseph spotted the skull in 1811 when Mary was just twelve; she dug out the rest of the 17-foot skeleton months later, on the Dorset cliffs. Source: Wikipedia, Mary Anning. (Legend of paleontology.)

question: When Mary Anning's dolphin-shaped sea-reptile skeleton first came out of the Dorset cliff in November 1811, no one had a name for such a creature. Reporting the strange find, the local newspaper called it something familiar but wrong. What did they call it?
answer: A crocodile
choices: A crocodile
A whale
A sea serpent
A giant fish
context: The November 1811 paper labeled it a 'crocodile' -- science had no name yet for this air-breathing, dolphin-shaped sea reptile. Source: Wikipedia, Mary Anning.

question: The giant ichthyosaur Temnodontosaurus was a dolphin-shaped marine reptile of the early dinosaur age. It stretched about 9 meters — 30 feet — long and ruled its seas as a top predator, hunting with rows of knife-sized teeth. One remarkable fossil in Britain was found with its last meal still preserved inside the stomach cavity, showing exactly what this giant had been eating just before it died. What surprising prey did the stomach contain?
answer: Other, younger ichthyosaurs
choices: Other, younger ichthyosaurs
A large sea turtle
Its own shed teeth
Chunks of driftwood
context: One Temnodontosaurus preserved three juvenile ichthyosaurs and many cephalopod hooks in its gut -- this top predator ate its own kind. Source: Wikipedia, Temnodontosaurus.

question: In 2021, workers draining a reservoir at Rutland Water in the English Midlands spotted huge bones sticking out of the mud. They had uncovered the biggest ichthyosaur — a Jurassic dolphin-shaped marine reptile — ever found in Britain, buried there for about 180 million years. The team nicknamed it the Rutland Sea Dragon. How big was this Jurassic giant?
answer: About 10 meters long, the length of a bus
choices: About 10 meters long, the length of a bus
About 6 meters long, the length of a rowboat
About 14 meters long, the length of two buses
About 8 meters long, the length of a large van
