Fig fruit
context: A koala eats almost nothing but eucalyptus (gum-tree) leaves, which carry bitter oils and cyanide-like compounds toxic to most animals. Source: https://koalainfo.com/koalas-diet-is-fully-poisonous-and-toxic

question: A koala is a slow, gray, tree-clinging marsupial of eastern Australia that eats almost nothing but eucalyptus leaves. Eucalyptus is tough, mildly poisonous, and gives back remarkably little energy. To make its meager calories last, a koala spends up to about 20 hours of every single day doing one thing. Which one?
answer: Sleeping and resting
choices: Sleeping and resting
Grooming its fur
Foraging for leaves
Climbing between trees
context: A koala's food yields so little energy that resting almost all day, up to about 20 hours, is the only way to survive on eucalyptus. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koala

question: In the eucalyptus forests of Australia, the koala spends its days chewing on gum leaves and rarely, if ever, drinks from a stream. The Aboriginal Dharug people who lived in that country long before Europeans arrived gave the animal the name we still use today. What is the Dharug word 'koala' thought to mean?
answer: No water
choices: No water
Tree sleeper
Grey climber
Gum eater
context: The word 'koala' comes from the Dharug language and is thought to mean 'no water' — koalas draw almost all their moisture from eucalyptus leaves and rarely drink. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koala

question: A koala joey lives on milk until, around six months old, it must learn to eat toxic gum leaves. To survive them, it first eats a soft, oily dropping straight from its mother — food that seeds its gut with the live microbes needed to digest eucalyptus. What is this special dropping called?
answer: Pap
choices: Pap
Curd
Whey
Silage
context: Weaning koalas eat their mother's 'pap,' described by keepers as like droppings but softer and oilier. Unlike ordinary droppings it is packed with the live gut microbes the joey needs to digest eucalyptus. Source: https://www.australiangeographic.com.au/news/2022/07/pap-not-poop-the-gift-a-mother-koala-gives-her-joey/  (Legend.)

question: The koala is a fluffy gray marsupial that spends its life clinging to the branches of Australian eucalyptus trees, eating almost nothing else. When scientists look at a koala's fingertips under a microscope, they find looping ridges and whorls so similar to a human's that fingerprint experts struggle to tell the two apart from a lifted print alone. The koala's closest marsupial cousins, the wombat and the kangaroo, have none. Why did the koala alone evolve these fingerprints?
answer: To grip branches and leaves
choices: To grip branches and leaves
To improve its sense of smell
To keep its paws from overheating
To leave scent marks on bark
context: Koala fingerprints match human ones so closely they are extremely hard to tell apart even under a microscope. Koalas are almost the only tree-climbing marsupial with them — wombats and kangaroos lack them — and they evolved the ridges to grip branches and leaves. This near-identical match to humans is a case of convergent evolution, the same trait arising independently in unrelated lineages. Source: https://www.mcgill.ca/oss/article/did-you-know/koalas-have-fingerprints-just-humans

question: On a handful of Indonesian islands — including Komodo, Rinca, and Flores — lives a monitor lizard so huge that adult males can stretch about ten feet long. The heaviest one ever weighed came in at 366 pounds. It hunts wild pigs and deer with a killing bite, and it is the largest lizard on Earth. Which giant reptile is this?
answer: The Komodo dragon
choices: The Komodo dragon
The Nile crocodile
The green iguana
The Gila monster
context: Males grow up to about 3 m (10 ft); the heaviest verified specimen reached 166 kg (366 lb). Wild Komodo dragons live only on Komodo, Rintja, Padar, and Flores in Indonesia. Source: Smithsonian's National Zoo (nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/komodo-dragon).

question: On a few dry Indonesian islands lives the Komodo dragon, the biggest lizard alive today — up to 10 feet long and 150 pounds, with dark scaly skin and a long forked tongue. It cannot chase prey for long distances. So it hides beside a game trail in the tall grass, still as a fallen log, and waits. When a deer or wild boar wanders past close enough, how does this giant lizard hunt?
answer: It ambushes from cover and lunges at the legs, belly, or throat
choices: It ambushes from cover and lunges at the legs, belly, or throat
It runs its prey down over miles of open ground
It waits underwater and drags prey below the surface
It corners prey against cliffs in cooperative packs
context: An adult Komodo dragon is an apex predator that ambushes prey from beside game trails, striking deer, wild boar, and even young water buffalo. Source: Smithsonian's National Zoo; ScienceInsights (scienceinsights.org).

question: The Komodo dragon is the biggest lizard alive today, a scaly, forked-tongued predator that hunts the dry islands of Indonesia. Because it lives on ambush and does not always find prey, it can go many weeks between meals. So when a dragon finally does kill a deer or wild boar, it gorges itself in a way that would burst most animals. In one single sitting, how much can a Komodo dragon eat?
answer: Up to 80 percent of its own body weight
choices: Up to 80 percent of its own body weight
Up to 15 percent of its own body weight
About twice its own body weight
Roughly its body weight every day
context: A Komodo dragon can gulp down up to 80 percent of its own body weight in one meal. Source: Smithsonian's National Zoo (nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/komodo-dragon).

question: As the Komodo dragon — the biggest lizard alive today — patrols the dry hills of Indonesian islands, it flicks its long, forked yellow tongue in and out of its mouth. Each of the two tips picks up scent molecules from the air. The tongue then presses those molecules into a pair of pits called the Jacobson's organ, hidden in the roof of the dragon's mouth, which reads them the way a nose reads smells. What does this two-tipped scenting system give the dragon?
answer: A 3-D sense of a scent's direction, smelling carrion up to 2.5 miles away
choices: A 3-D sense of a scent's direction, smelling carrion up to 2.5 miles away
Sharp night vision that works in near-total darkness
The ability to hear low rumbles through the ground
A taste for salt that guides it to fresh water
context: The two forked tips deliver scent molecules separately to the Jacobson's organ, giving a directional, 3-D sense of smell; a dragon can detect a rotting carcass from up to 2.5 miles (4 km) away. Source: Smithsonian's National Zoo (nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/komodo-dragon).

question: The Komodo dragon is the huge ten-foot monitor lizard of the Indonesian islands, whose bite is famous for killing prey days after the attack. For decades textbooks blamed that lethal wound on filthy, bacteria-choked saliva. Then in 2009 a team led by the venom scientist Bryan Fry at the University of Queensland dissected fresh Komodo jaws under the microscope and overturned the whole story. What did they find was the real killer inside the bite?
answer: Venom glands in the lower jaw whose toxins stop clotting and crash blood pressure
choices: Venom glands in the lower jaw whose toxins stop clotting and crash blood pressure
A crushing bite force stronger than a crocodile's
A paralyzing nerve toxin coating the teeth
Jaws that inject digestive acid into the wound
context: Fry et al. showed the Komodo has real venom glands in its lower jaw; the toxins prevent blood from clotting and drop the victim's blood pressure. A later study found the mouth bacteria are no more dangerous than any other carnivore's. Source: Fry et al., PNAS 2009 (pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0810883106); National Geographic.  (Legend.)

question: The Komodo dragon is the world's largest living lizard, a ten-foot reptile that hunts on the Indonesian island of Komodo. It lunges out of the brush, sinks its teeth into a passing water buffalo, then lets the huge animal shake free and stagger away. The dragon does not sprint after it. Its bite has already done the work — a mix of shock, deep tissue damage, and toxins in the saliva that keeps the wound bleeding. Instead of chasing, what does the dragon do?
answer: Follows at a leisurely pace for hours or days until blood loss drops the prey
choices: Follows at a leisurely pace for hours or days until blood loss drops the prey
Circles back to its burrow and waits for a fresh victim
Calls other dragons to help bring the buffalo down
Climbs a tree to watch the herd from above
context: The venom keeps the wound bleeding and lowers blood pressure; the dragon trails the weakening prey at a leisurely pace, sometimes for hours or days, then moves in when it collapses. Source: Fry et al. PNAS 2009; ScienceInsights (scienceinsights.org).

question: The Komodo dragon is a ten-foot lizard from the Indonesian island of Komodo, and inside its jaws sit about 60 curved teeth edged like tiny saws — much like the teeth of a shark. Old teeth fall out and fresh ones grow in throughout the dragon's life. When it clamps down on a struggling deer, those saw-like serrations do one crucial thing to keep the deer from getting away. What is it?
answer: They hook flesh so prey cannot pull away, opening deep wounds
choices: They hook flesh so prey cannot pull away, opening deep wounds
They grind bone into swallowable fragments
They inject venom directly through hollow grooves
They lock together to crush and hold a shell
context: The backward-curving serrations hook into flesh so prey cannot tear free, opening deep wounds the venom keeps bleeding. Like a shark, the dragon replaces its teeth throughout life. Source: Britannica; National Geographic; sciencedaily.com (2009 study).

question: At England's Chester Zoo, a female Komodo dragon named Flora lived alone in her enclosure, never once placed with a male of her kind. Yet in 2006 keepers were astonished to find that Flora had laid a clutch of 11 eggs, and every one hatched a healthy baby dragon. Since no father was ever near her, biologists asked how this could possibly happen. What made Flora's fatherless clutch possible?
answer: Parthenogenesis, a virgin birth from an unfertilized egg
choices: Parthenogenesis, a virgin birth from an unfertilized egg
Stored sperm saved from years earlier
A hormone shift that let her fertilize her own eggs
Eggs quietly swapped in by another female
context: Flora, kept with no mate, laid 11 eggs and hatched healthy young in 2006 through parthenogenesis. Source: Scientific American (scientificamerican.com); Nature 444, 1021 (2006).  (Legend.)

question: On the Indonesian islands of Komodo and Rinca prowls the world's largest lizard, the Komodo dragon. A female dragon can sometimes lay eggs and hatch a whole clutch of babies without ever mating — a rare trick called parthenogenesis, or virgin birth. When a Komodo dragon does this, every hatchling turns out to be the same sex. Which sex are they, and why?
answer: All male, because only the ZZ chromosome pairing survives
choices: All male, because only the ZZ chromosome pairing survives
All female, because eggs default to the mother's sex
All male, because heat during incubation sets sex
A random mix, just like normal fertilized clutches
context: The Komodo's sex system is the reverse of ours: females are WZ, males ZZ. When an unfertilized egg doubles its chromosomes, only the ZZ (male) combination survives, so every parthenogenetic hatchling is male. Source: Scientific American (scientificamerican.com); Nature 444, 1021 (2006).

question: The Komodo dragon is the world's biggest lizard, and it lives on a scatter of small Indonesian islands. Suppose a storm sweeps a single female across the sea and strands her, alone, on an empty island with no other dragons at all. Scientists point out that, remarkably, she could still start an entire new population by herself — no mate ever needed. How could a lone female Komodo possibly pull that off?
answer: She births sons by parthenogenesis, then breeds with them
choices: She births sons by parthenogenesis, then breeds with them
She clones exact copies of herself indefinitely
She lures males across the sea with scent
She survives centuries until castaways arrive
context: Because a lone female can produce sons on her own and then mate with them, a single female washed onto an empty island could theoretically start a whole new population by herself. Source: Scientific American (scientificamerican.com/article/strange-but-true-komodo-d).  (Legend.)

question: The Komodo dragon is the ten-foot monitor lizard of Indonesia's Lesser Sunda Islands, the largest lizard on Earth. In a 2019 study at the University of Texas at Austin, the paleontologist Jessica Maisano used a CT scan to peer underneath a Komodo dragon's tough skin and scales. She found thousands of tiny bones packed just below the surface, completely invisible to the naked eye. What role do they play?
answer: Osteoderms forming a chain-mail suit of bony armor
choices: Osteoderms forming a chain-mail suit of bony armor
Weights that anchor the dragon low against its prey
Reserves the dragon draws on to make eggshells
Buried plates that store heat soaked up while basking
context: The CT study found four osteoderm shapes (rosette, platy, dendritic, vermiform) forming a full-body 'chain mail' covering everything but the nostrils, eyes, and pineal 'third eye'. Babies hatch with no armor; it grows in with adulthood and mainly shields adults from other dragons' bites. Source: UT Austin News (news.utexas.edu/2019/09/12); The Anatomical Record, Sept 2019.  (Legend.)

question: In 2024, researchers slid a Komodo dragon's skull under high-resolution imaging to see exactly how its cutting teeth were built. On every tooth the sharp tip and the saw-like edge were stained a striking deep orange, while the rest of the enamel stayed pale. The dragon's normal food — deer, boar, buffalo — could not paint teeth that evenly on the cutting parts alone. What actually causes the orange stripe along a Komodo's tooth edges?
answer: A coating of iron concentrated along the cutting edges
choices: A coating of iron concentrated along the cutting edges
Stains from years of feeding on bloody carrion
A film of pigment-producing mouth bacteria
Enamel worn thin to expose the reddish dentin beneath
context: Many reptiles carry a trace of iron in their enamel, but the Komodo dragon is unique in lining the actual cutting edges and tips with it. The iron hardens and protects the fine serrations so the teeth stay razor-sharp and kill-ready at all times, staining them orange in the process. Researchers even suspect meat-eating dinosaurs like Tyrannosaurus rex may have kept their steak-knife teeth sharp the same way. Source: LeBlanc et al., 'Iron-coated Komodo dragon teeth and the complex dental enamel of carnivorous reptiles,' Nature Ecology & Evolution, 24 July 2024; King's College London news, 'Komodo dragons have iron-coated teeth to rip apart their prey.'

question: Textbooks long taught that the Komodo dragon — the ten-foot monitor lizard of Indonesia — ballooned into a giant on its isolated islands, evolving up from a small ancestor stranded there. Then in 2009 the paleontologist Scott Hocknull described fossils of huge Komodo-sized dragons found far outside Indonesia entirely, rewriting the story of where this species really came from. Where did the Komodo dragon actually evolve?
answer: On mainland Australia, before spreading west into Indonesia
choices: On mainland Australia, before spreading west into Indonesia
On the Indonesian islands, exactly as the old story held
In mainland Southeast Asia, then rafting south to the islands
On a since-sunken landmass between Asia and Australia
context: Komodo dragon bones dated from about 300,000 to 4 million years old, dug up in eastern Australia, are identical to living dragons. The lineage arose on the Australian mainland at least ~4 million years ago, then dispersed west across the Wallacean islands into Indonesia around a million years ago. It vanished from Australia about 50,000 years ago along with the continent's other giant beasts, so today's Indonesian dragons are the last survivors of an Australian dynasty that also produced the even larger extinct monitor Megalania. Source: Hocknull et al., 'Dragon's Paradise Lost: Palaeobiogeography, Evolution and Extinction of the Largest-Ever Terrestrial Lizards (Varanidae),' PLoS ONE, 2009.  (Legend.)

question: In a Central American rainforest, a hiker stops beside a worn path on the forest floor and sees a strange green ribbon flowing along it. Looking closer, she realizes the ribbon is alive — thousands of small dark insects marching in a long line, each one holding a bright green snip of leaf overhead like a tiny green sail. The parade keeps coming from the trees and vanishing into a hole in the ground. Which insects make this leaf parade?
answer: Leafcutter ants
choices: Leafcutter ants
Monarch butterflies
Praying mantises
Dung beetles
context: The column of green 'sails' streaming back to the nest is the classic sight of leafcutter ants -- each worker carries a leaf fragment far heavier than itself. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leafcutter_ant

question: In Central and South American rainforests, leafcutter ants march miles of fresh-cut leaf pieces down into their enormous underground nests, one snip at a time. Here is the odd part: if you dug open the deepest chambers, you would not find a single chewed-up leaf in an ant's belly. The ants aren't eating them at all. So what are the leafcutters actually doing with all those leaves underground?
answer: Chew them into mulch to grow a fungus they eat
choices: Chew them into mulch to grow a fungus they eat
Line their tunnel walls to keep out rain
Feed them straight to the newborn larvae
Pile them at the entrance to block invaders
context: Leafcutters are farmers, not leaf-eaters: they compost the leaves to cultivate a fungus and eat the fungus. Source: https://asm.org/articles/2017/september/the-leaf-cutter-ant-s-50-million-years-of-farming  (Legend.)

question: In a South American orange grove, a colony of Atta leafcutter ants — one of the biggest leafcutter species — pours out of its nest at dusk and swarms up a full-grown citrus tree. All night long the workers cut and haul leaves back underground into their fungus garden. The grove owner walks out at sunrise the next morning to see what is left of his tree. What does he find?
answer: Every leaf gone -- the whole tree bare
choices: Every leaf gone -- the whole tree bare
A few outer branches nibbled
Only the lowest leaves within reach
Just the soft new buds taken
context: Atta leafcutter ants can defoliate an entire citrus tree in under 24 hours, stripping a whole mature tree overnight. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leafcutter_ant

question: Leafcutter ants of Central and South America build enormous underground colonies with millions of workers. What is remarkable is that a single colony contains ants of wildly different sizes, each with its own job. Huge armored 'majors' stand guard at the nest entrance. Mid-sized workers march out and snip leaves from trees. But deep inside the nest, the very smallest workers — with heads under a millimetre — have another crucial job. What do these tiny workers do?
answer: Tend and weed the fungus garden
choices: Tend and weed the fungus garden
Dig every new tunnel by themselves
Lay the colony extra eggs
Carry the queen from room to room
context: The colony is a graded workforce: giant majors defend, mediae cut leaves, and the tiniest minims (heads under 1mm) care for the delicate fungus crop. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leafcutter_ant

question: In the rainforests of Central and South America, leafcutter ants march in long trails through the jungle, each big worker carrying a slice of green leaf overhead like a tiny flag. They bring the leaves home to feed a garden of underground fungus. On top of each carried leaf you can often see a much tinier ant, from the same colony, hitching a ride. That little rider has a specific job. What is it doing up there?
answer: Shooing off flies that try to lay eggs on the carrier
choices: Shooing off flies that try to lay eggs on the carrier
Resting because they are too small to walk far
Adding weight so the leaf will not blow away
Tasting each leaf to check it is safe to bring home
context: The minims act as bodyguards, driving away parasitic phorid flies that try to lay eggs in the crevices of the busy carrier's head. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leafcutter_ant  (Legend.)

question: Leafcutter ants keep vast underground gardens of a fungus they grow on chewed-up leaves — that fungus is the only food they eat. A specialized mould called Escovopsis keeps trying to invade and rot the garden. To fight off the mould, the ants don't spray anything or bite the invader. Instead they carry a tiny living partner right on their own bodies, tucked into little pits in their skin. What do the ants carry?
answer: Antibiotic-making bacteria
choices: Antibiotic-making bacteria
Poison-spraying mites
Acid-brewing yeasts
Venomous soil algae
context: The ants host living Pseudonocardia/Streptomyces bacteria as portable antimicrobials to kill the garden parasite Escovopsis; some colonies carry so much they look dusted with powdered sugar. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leafcutter_ant  (Legend.)

question: Leafcutter ants of the American tropics do something almost no other animal does. They don't actually eat the leaves they cut. Instead they carry them deep underground and feed them to a special fungus, which they cultivate, weed, and harvest as a crop, like real farmers. Humans invented agriculture roughly twelve thousand years ago. But leafcutters had already been tending their tamed fungus for a much longer time before we ever picked up a hoe. How long had they been at it?
answer: Roughly fifty million years
choices: Roughly fifty million years
A few thousand years
About one million years
Around ten million years
context: Leafcutter ants invented farming roughly 50 million years before humans, and had fully domesticated their fungus about 15 million years ago. Source: https://asm.org/articles/2017/september/the-leaf-cutter-ant-s-50-million-years-of-farming  (Legend.)

question: Drifting over a kelp reef off southern Australia, one 'leaf' of seaweed sways along with the current. It doesn't tumble loose like the rest. That is because it is really a fish, wearing long leaf-shaped skin flaps as a disguise. What is this master of seaweed camouflage?
answer: The leafy sea dragon
choices: The leafy sea dragon
The peacock flounder
The frogfish
The stonefish
context: The leafy sea dragon (Phycodurus eques) sprouts long leaf-shaped skin flaps that look exactly like drifting seaweed, and it keeps up the illusion even while moving, swaying through the water like a loose piece of floating kelp. Source: Australian Museum — australian.museum/learn/animals/fishes/leafy-seadragon-phycodurus-eques/  (Legend.)

question: A leafy sea dragon drifts across the reef looking like a motionless scrap of weed — yet it IS moving. Its big leafy lobes do nothing for swimming; those are pure camouflage. So what actually propels it so secretly that it seems to just float in place?
answer: Two tiny, nearly transparent fins fluttering almost invisibly
choices: Two tiny, nearly transparent fins fluttering almost invisibly
Slow undulating waves rippling down its whole body
A jet of water squirted from its gills
Sticky tube-feet gripping and pulling along the rocks
context: The leaf-shaped protrusions are NOT fins. The sea dragon moves with two tiny, nearly transparent fins — a pectoral fin on its 'neck' and a dorsal fin on its 'back' — that flutter so fast and faintly they are almost invisible, making it look like it is floating motionless like drifting weed. Source: Australian Museum — australian.museum/learn/animals/fishes/leafy-seadragon-phycodurus-eques/

question: The leafy sea dragon is a strange fish that drifts through the kelp forests off southern Australia, disguised as a bit of seaweed by leafy skin flaps sprouting all over its body. It has no teeth at all and no stomach either. Yet in a single day one fish can vacuum up thousands of tiny mysid shrimp. With no jaws to chew and no stomach to fill, how does it manage to eat?
answer: It sucks prey in through a long pipe-like snout, like a drinking straw
choices: It sucks prey in through a long pipe-like snout, like a drinking straw
It swallows prey whole into an expandable throat pouch
It stuns shrimp with a venomous spine, then engulfs them
It grinds prey against bony plates lining its cheeks
context: The leafy sea dragon has no teeth and no stomach. It feeds through a long, pipe-like snout that works like a drinking straw, and a single sea dragon may slurp up thousands of tiny mysid shrimp in a single day. Source: Monterey Bay Aquarium — montereybayaquarium.org/animals-the-ocean/animals-a-to-z/leafy-sea-dragon

question: The leafy sea dragon is a slow-drifting fish of southern Australian waters, wearing frilly leaf-like flaps of skin that make it look like a drifting piece of seaweed. When leafy sea dragons breed, up to about 250 bright pink eggs get pressed onto a soft spongy brood patch and carried around by one parent for weeks until they hatch. In leafy sea dragons, whose body is the one that broods the clutch?
answer: The male, on the underside of his tail
choices: The male, on the underside of his tail
The female, tucked beneath her belly
Neither — the eggs are glued to a strand of kelp
Both parents take turns holding the clutch
context: Like its seahorse relatives, it is the MALE leafy sea dragon that carries the eggs. The female presses up to about 250 eggs onto a spongy brood patch on the underside of the male's tail, where they attach and he broods them until they hatch. Source: Monterey Bay Aquarium — montereybayaquarium.org/animals-the-ocean/animals-a-to-z/leafy-sea-dragon  (Legend.)

question: A leafy sea dragon wears no ordinary scales — under its thin skin runs a jointed suit of rigid bony rings, the same armor its seahorse and pipefish cousins share. Look closer at where it breathes, and you find one more oddity setting it apart from most fish. What do its gills open through?
answer: Small round, circular holes
choices: Small round, circular holes
Long crescent-shaped slits
A single flap behind the head
Feathery tufts on the outside of the neck
context: Under its thin skin the leafy sea dragon wears a suit of rigid bony ring-plates instead of ordinary scales — a hallmark of the syngnathid family it shares with seahorses and pipefish. It even has round, circular gill openings rather than the crescent-shaped slits of most fish. Source: A-Z Animals; Wikipedia — en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leafy_seadragon

question: Off the shores of southern Australia drifts the leafy sea dragon, a slow-moving cousin of the seahorse whose body sprouts leaf-shaped flaps for camouflage. As with seahorses, it is the father who carries the eggs. A male can carry roughly 250 developing eggs on his tail, each one turning bright pink and pulling oxygen straight from his brood patch. Yet the open ocean is brutal on the tiny young. About how many of those eggs actually survive all the way to hatching?
answer: Around 5 in every 100
choices: Around 5 in every 100
Around half
Around 9 in every 10
Nearly all of them
context: The eggs the male carries turn bright pink when ripe and draw oxygen straight from the brood patch on his tail. Even so, survival is brutal — only about 5% of the eggs make it to hatch. Source: Wikipedia — en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leafy_seadragon

question: Most animals are born already knowing every call they'll ever make. But a short list of creatures must learn their sounds by listening and copying, the way a child learns to talk. Which group belongs to this exclusive club alongside whales, elephants, and humans?
answer: Songbirds and parrots
choices: Songbirds and parrots
Frogs and crickets
Wolves and coyotes
Lions and hyenas
context: The 'vocal learners' are a surprisingly short list: songbirds, parrots, hummingbirds, whales and dolphins, seals, elephants, bats, and humans. Everything else is born knowing its calls and never changes them. Source: Wikipedia 'Vocal learning'; Royal Society Phil. Trans. B 2020.0234 'Vocal learning in animals and humans'.

question: In the wet forests of southeastern Australia lives a bird so gifted at mimicry that a single male can rattle off a kookaburra's cackling laugh, a whipbird's whistle, and the babble of a whole chattering flock — the voices of twenty different birds in a row. He can even throw in a camera shutter, a chainsaw, or a car alarm he once heard from humans. Which Australian bird is this master mimic?
answer: The superb lyrebird
choices: The superb lyrebird
The common starling
The northern mockingbird
The Australian magpie
context: Australia's superb lyrebird is the animal kingdom's champion mimic, copying not only other birds but man-made sounds it has heard, including camera shutters, car alarms, and the whine of a chainsaw. Source: BBC 'Life of Birds' (Attenborough, 1998); Audubon 'The Lyrebird'; Mental Floss 653848. (Legend.)

question: The white-crowned sparrow is a small North American songbird, and its adult song has one specific tune that young males normally learn by listening to older males in the first weeks after hatching. In a classic experiment, scientists took a young white-crowned sparrow and raised it in total silence — no adult of its own kind ever sang within earshot during those critical learning weeks. When the bird finally grew up and opened its beak to sing, what came out?
answer: A broken, simplified song it never learned right
choices: A broken, simplified song it never learned right
The perfect song, note for note
No song at all, only silence
A different species' song entirely
context: A songbird learns its song during a short 'critical period' when it is too young to sing yet, by listening to an adult tutor. Raised in silence with no tune to copy, the sparrow grows up singing a broken, simplified version. Source: Springer 'Vocal learning in White-crowned Sparrows: sensitive phase and song dialects'; Nature Scitable 'The Development of Birdsong'.

question: When a young sparrow hatches, it cannot yet sing. It listens to an older tutor sparrow and memorizes the correct song note by note, storing it as a mental template in its brain. Then, before it has practiced a single note aloud, it is deafened. Months later it tries to sing, but the tune never comes out right. What did losing its hearing take away?
answer: Its ability to check its own voice against the memory
choices: Its ability to check its own voice against the memory
Its ability to sing that particular song at all
Its instinct to sing at all
The muscles that shape each note
context: A songbird needs to HEAR ITSELF, not just its tutor. Deafened after memorizing the song but before singing it, the bird still has the stored memory of the tutor's song, but it has lost the feedback loop that lets it match its own voice to the remembered tune. Source: Springer 'Critical Period for Song Learning'; Konishi white-crowned sparrow auditory-feedback studies (Caltech records).

question: At Adelaide Zoo a captive lyrebird picked up the drills and saws of construction while the panda enclosure was built next door. He could reproduce those power tools, and startled keepers by greeting them in a clear human voice. What did the bird say?
answer: 'Hello, Chook!'
choices: 'Hello, Chook!'
'Time for lunch'
'Open the gate'
'Good morning, all'
context: The most famous lyrebird footage, a bird reproducing camera clicks, a car alarm, and a chainsaw for David Attenborough, came partly from captive birds. Chook had picked up drills and saws from construction next door and even greeted keepers with 'hello, Chook!' in a human voice. Source: The Conversation 'Lyrebirds mimicking chainsaws: fact or lie?'; Atlas Obscura 'The Strange Bird That Mimics Chainsaws'.

question: Alex was an African Grey parrot who worked for 30 years with the researcher Irene Pepperberg, learning to identify colors, shapes, numbers, and simple ideas. Every night as Pepperberg left the lab, Alex called the same tender farewell after her. On the morning of September 6, 2007, he was found dead in his cage at age 31. What were his last nightly words?
answer: 'You be good. I love you. See you tomorrow.'
choices: 'You be good. I love you. See you tomorrow.'
'Goodnight now. Sleep well. See you soon.'
'Don't go yet. Please stay. I miss you.'
'Time for bed. Lights are off. Goodnight.'
context: Alex said this same phrase to Pepperberg each night as she left. He was found dead the next morning at age 31, ending a thirty-year study of a single parrot. Source: NPR 'Alex & Me: The Parrot Who Said I Love You'; Wikipedia 'Alex (parrot)'. (Legend.)

question: In 1984, at a National Marine Mammal Foundation tank in San Diego, a diver surfaced and demanded to know 'Who told me to get out?' The muffled, human-sounding words had come not from a person above the water but from a beluga whale named Noc, who had learned to lower his voice by several octaves to imitate human speech. How did Noc produce those sounds?
answer: By changing the pressure in his nasal passages
choices: By changing the pressure in his nasal passages
By vibrating his tail against the tank
By forcing air out through his blowhole slowly
By humming from deep in his throat
context: NOC dropped his voice several octaves to sound like a human, producing the speech-like sounds by altering the pressure in his nasal passages, an unusual feat for a whale. Source: National Geographic 'NOC, the white whale that tried to sound like a human'; Scientific American podcast 'Whale Mimics Human Speech'. (Legend.)

question: A single humpback whale song type doesn't just spread to the next bay; it can travel like a chain of listeners across an entire ocean. Scientists tracked one learned tune passed from population to population all the way from eastern Australia to Ecuador. Roughly how far did that one song spread?
answer: About 14,000 kilometers
choices: About 14,000 kilometers
About 140 kilometers
About 1,400 kilometers
About 140,000 kilometers
context: Humpback song spreads like a fashion sweeping an ocean, one 'hit tune' replacing the old across thousands of miles. Scientists tracked a single song type traveling roughly 14,000 km, from eastern Australia to Ecuador, passed along a chain of listeners across the whole Pacific. Source: Current Biology 'Dynamic Horizontal Cultural Transmission of Humpback Whale Song at the Ocean Basin Scale' (2011); PMC9428538.

question: A juvenile zebra finch learns its song along a brain loop that runs through a nucleus called Area X, where one gene fires hardest exactly while the bird is copying its tutor. Silence that gene during learning and the copy comes out sloppy and incomplete. It is the very same gene that shapes human speech. Which gene?
answer: FoxP2, active in the finch's Area X
choices: FoxP2, active in the finch's Area X
Myelin, wrapped around the finch's nerves
Keratin, hardening the finch's beak
Melanin, darkening the finch's feathers
context: The song system has two linked pathways: a motor pathway (nucleus HVC to RA to the vocal muscles) that produces the song, and an anterior forebrain pathway through Area X, a basal-ganglia nucleus, that is required to LEARN and fine-tune it. FoxP2 is active in Area X and spikes exactly during learning. When Sebastian Haesler's team knocked FoxP2 down in Area X of juvenile finches (about 70% reduction), their copies of the tutor's song fell from about 68% similarity in controls to about 40% -- tying one gene to the accuracy of imitation. Source: Haesler et al. 2007, 'Incomplete and Inaccurate Vocal Imitation after Knockdown of FoxP2 in Songbird Basal Ganglia Nucleus Area X,' PLOS Biology (journals.plos.org/plosbiology/article?id=10.1371/journal.pbio.0050321); song-system review, PMC5066577 and PMC2822067.

question: A young zebra finch has a few months to memorize and lock in its song; after that the tune 'crystallizes' and never changes again. Scientists found the window doesn't just fade -- it is bricked shut. Deep in the song-control circuit, a rigid matrix thickens until no new connections can form. What clamps the song in place for life?
answer: Perineuronal nets caging the neurons
choices: Perineuronal nets caging the neurons
Scar tissue sealing the old wounds
Fat deposits insulating the axons
Calcium crystals stiffening the bones
context: Perineuronal nets (PNNs) are lattice-like sheaths of extracellular matrix that build up around inhibitory neurons in the song-control nucleus HVC. In male zebra finches their density starts rising around 50-60 days after hatching, as tutor-memorization ends, and plateaus near 90 days -- exactly when the song crystallizes and stops changing. By caging the neurons in a rigid net that blocks new synapses, PNNs mechanically lock the learned song in place, and males, who must crystallize a song, grow denser nets than females. This is the mechanism one layer beneath the 'sensitive period.' Source: Cornez et al. 2018, 'Timing of perineuronal net development in the zebra finch song control system correlates with developmental song learning,' Proc. Royal Society B, PMC6083260.

question: The leatherback is the biggest sea turtle alive today. Its dark, leathery shell can stretch about 2 meters long, roughly as long as a tall grown-up lying flat on the sand. When a full-sized leatherback drags herself up a tropical beach to lay her eggs, she is a very heavy load. A big leatherback weighs about as much as which everyday object?
answer: A small car
choices: A small car
A microwave oven
A garden gnome
A house cat
context: An adult leatherback can reach roughly 500-700 kg (over 1,000 lb) - genuinely in the weight class of a small car, and the heaviest non-crocodilian reptile on Earth. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leatherback_sea_turtle

question: Run your hand down a green sea turtle's back and you feel hard bony plates locked together into a classic scaly shell. Do the same down the back of a leatherback (Dermochelys coriacea), the largest sea turtle in the world at up to 2,000 pounds, and you feel something no other sea turtle on Earth has. What covers its back instead of that hard shell?
answer: Tough rubbery leathery skin
choices: Tough rubbery leathery skin
A smooth glassy enamel
Loose overlapping feathers
A coat of coarse fur
context: Alone among sea turtles, the leatherback has no hard bony shell at all. Its back is tough, rubbery, leathery skin - which is literally its name: Dermochelys coriacea means 'leathery skin-turtle.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leatherback_sea_turtle

question: A leatherback sea turtle (Dermochelys coriacea) eats almost nothing but jellyfish, sometimes hundreds of pounds of them in a day. Jellyfish are slick and slimy, and once inside the mouth they try to slide back out on the way down. If you could safely reach a finger into a leatherback's throat, you would meet a defense no other turtle has for gripping slippery prey. What lines the leatherback's throat?
answer: Hundreds of backward-pointing spines
choices: Hundreds of backward-pointing spines
A patch of sticky glue-slime
Rows of grinding molar teeth
A ring of powerful suckers
context: A leatherback's throat is lined with hundreds of sharp, backward-pointing spines (esophageal papillae, the same keratin as fingernails). They grip slippery jellyfish so prey can't wriggle free, while letting the turtle spit out swallowed seawater without losing its meal. An adult can gulp close to its own body weight in jellyfish in a day. Legend-tier wonder. Source: https://www.floridaocean.org/blog/secret-spikes-how-sea-turtles-use-their-esophageal-papillae

question: Reptiles are famously cold-blooded, meaning their body sits at whatever temperature the water or air around them happens to be. But a leatherback sea turtle (Dermochelys coriacea) was once pulled from near-freezing Atlantic water, and a thermometer pushed into its core. For a reptile the reading was astonishingly high. How far above the sea's temperature was the turtle running?
answer: About 18 degrees C warmer
choices: About 18 degrees C warmer
About 2 degrees C warmer
About 6 degrees C warmer
About 40 degrees C warmer
context: The turtle's core ran about 18 degrees C (32 degrees F) ABOVE the surrounding water - it stays warm while swimming through near-freezing seas, extraordinary for a reptile that supposedly can't heat itself. A degree or two is what you'd expect from mere activity; 18 is the shock. Source: https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.177.4051.791

question: The leatherback is the biggest sea turtle alive, and it does not just cruise near the surface — it can plunge into the black cold of the deep ocean. In 2006 scientists off the Cape Verde islands strapped a satellite tag to a leatherback (Dermochelys coriacea) and let her go. Weeks later the tag radioed home a single plunge deeper than any reptile has ever been logged going, anywhere in the world. About how deep did that record dive reach?
answer: About 1,280 meters
choices: About 1,280 meters
About 120 meters
About 400 meters
About 3,500 meters
context: That 2006 dive reached 1,280 m (4,199 ft) - the deepest ever recorded for any reptile, deeper than most whales ever go and far past the ~200 m of a typical air-breathing diver. Legend-tier record. Source: https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/70255-deepest-dive-by-a-chelonian

question: A mayfly is famous for its brief, delicate day in the air, when the winged adults emerge from a river all at once, dance in mating clouds above the water, and die by nightfall without ever eating. But that flying adult is only the tail end of the mayfly's life. Where does a mayfly spend the long first chapter of its life, often a full year and sometimes two or three?
answer: Underwater on the riverbed as a nymph
choices: Underwater on the riverbed as a nymph
Sealed in a cocoon buried in mud
Dormant inside a tree gall
Riding wind currents high in the sky
context: For most of its life a mayfly is an aquatic nymph, crawling on the river bottom and breathing through feathery gills. The winged adult everyone pictures is the tiny tail-end of the whole life cycle. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayfly

question: A mayfly starts life as a nymph — a small crawling water insect — under stones in a river, sometimes for a year or more. One warm afternoon it finally climbs out into the air, splits its old skin down the back, and flies off as a winged adult with only about a single day of adult life ahead of it. But this rushed adult life hides a strange catch very few other animals share. What is it?
answer: Its mouthparts are shrunken and useless, so it cannot eat at all
choices: Its mouthparts are shrunken and useless, so it cannot eat at all
It must return to the water within hours or its wings dissolve
It can fly only at night and is blind in daylight
It is born already carrying a fatal parasite in its gut
context: The adult mayfly's digestive system is filled with air rather than food, and its mouthparts don't work. It emerges only to find a mate and reproduce, then dies -- eating was never part of the plan. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayfly

question: Fly fishermen tying trout flies know two mayfly stages by name. They tie one lure for the cloudy-winged mayfly they call a 'dun,' and another lure for the shinier, more elegant adult it becomes just a few hours later. To cross between those two winged stages, the mayfly does something no other winged insect on Earth ever does. What?
answer: It molts one more time, shedding its skin with the wings still attached
choices: It molts one more time, shedding its skin with the wings still attached
It swallows air to inflate its body to twice its size
It drains the color from its wings by baking in the sun
It fuses its four wings into a single broad sail
context: The mayfly is the only insect that molts one more time AFTER it already has working wings. The cloudy-winged 'dun,' or subimago, sheds its skin -- wings included -- to become the shiny final adult. No other winged insect does this. Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8463790/  (Legend.)

question: On the night of June 23, 2012, the National Weather Service's Doppler radar station near La Crosse, Wisconsin lit up in bright yellows and oranges rising off the Mississippi River, and the strange return tracked steadily from around 9 pm past 10:30. But there were no thunderstorms anywhere in the area that evening, and no rain in the forecast. What did the radar actually pick up?
answer: A gigantic swarm of hatching mayflies
choices: A gigantic swarm of hatching mayflies
A wall of hail forming over the river
A flock of migrating starlings
Smoke from a riverside grass fire
context: Mayfly hatches can be so enormous they show up on weather radar like rainfall, and forecasters tracked this one just as they would a storm. The bugs pile up so thick under bridge lights that crews have to plow them off like snow. Source: https://www.weather.gov/arx/mayfly_tracking  (Legend.)

question: The mayfly is not the only creature that pours its whole self into one breeding season. The antechinus, a mouse-sized Australian marsupial, spends two or three weeks in a frenzy -- males stop eating and sleeping, mating for sessions up to 14 hours. What does that season do to every male?
answer: His own stress hormones flood his body and trigger fatal organ failure
choices: His own stress hormones flood his body and trigger fatal organ failure
He is driven off by rivals to live and starve alone in exile
He sheds his fur and burrows deep underground to slowly recover
He guards the newborn young while the females leave to go feed
context: During the frenzy a flood of the male antechinus's own stress hormone, cortisol, triggers organ failure -- so every single male drops dead at the end of the breeding season, his whole existence spent fathering the next generation. Source: https://theconversation.com/these-fierce-tiny-marsupials-drop-dead-after-lengthy-sex-fests-and-sometimes-become-cannibals-221009  (Legend.)

question: A mayfly nymph feeds and grows underwater for a year or more, so its gut is a genuine working stomach. Yet inside the winged adult that same gut holds no food and does no digesting -- it has been remodeled for a wholly different job. What is the adult gut now doing?
answer: Sealed off and filled with air, working as a buoyancy float that lightens the weak flier
choices: Sealed off and filled with air, working as a buoyancy float that lightens the weak flier
Pumping stored fat into the wing muscles to fuel a final burst of flight
Storing water drawn from the river to keep the drying adult from shriveling
Packing the last unshed eggs so the female can drop them all at once
context: The covered ladder says the adult can't eat because its mouthparts are shrunken; the mechanism goes one step deeper. In the winged adult the entire alimentary canal is sealed off and filled with air, no longer digesting anything. It instead acts like an internal air balloon, lightening the body so the weak-flying adult can stay aloft long enough to mate -- the organ that once processed food as a nymph is repurposed into a flight-assist air bladder. Source: Wikipedia, 'Mayfly' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayfly), noting the adult digestive system is filled with air for weight reduction; corroborated by insect air-sac / weak-flight literature.

question: Across every insect ever timed, the record for the briefest adult life belongs to one mayfly of Florida sand rivers, Dolania americana. After up to two years buried as a nymph, its emerging female has just long enough to be found by a male, mate, and release her eggs before she drops. How long is that entire winged life?
answer: Under five minutes, start to finish
choices: Under five minutes, start to finish
A single night, from dusk to dawn
About one full day and its following night
Roughly three days of steady flying
context: The American sand-burrowing mayfly Dolania americana holds the shortest adult lifespan of any known insect. After up to two years as a sand-burrowing nymph, the adult female lives less than five minutes -- she emerges, is mated, lays her eggs, and dies, all within about five minutes, and the whole population dies within roughly 30 minutes of emergence. Peters & Peters (1977) timed the pre-dawn emergence on the Blackwater River in NW Florida, where males appear about 1.5 hours before sunrise and patrol a 15-20 m stretch of river. Source: Wikipedia, 'Dolania' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolania), citing Peters & Peters 1977; corroborated by Live Science, 'Which animal has the shortest life span?'

question: A camel is a big, humped desert animal that can walk for days across the Sahara or the Arabian sands without ever taking a drink. Storybooks often claim that a camel's tall back-hump is a built-in canteen — a giant water tank sloshing under the skin for the long dry crossing. Real biologists cut open a hump and found something completely different inside. What actually fills a camel's hump?
answer: Fat
choices: Fat
Water
Blood
Muscle
context: A dromedary (Camelus dromedarius) hump can hold up to about 80 pounds of fat, an energy reserve the animal burns when food is scarce. The 'water tank' idea is a myth. Source: Britannica 'Do Camels Store Water in Their Humps?'; todayifoundout.com camel humps article.  (Legend.)

question: The kangaroo rat (Dipodomys) is a small hopping rodent of the American southwestern deserts, out where puddles and streams can vanish for whole seasons. In the wild the kangaroo rat never actually drinks a drop of water, yet its body stays healthily full of moisture. It doesn't sip dew off leaves, doesn't lick damp stones, and doesn't find a hidden spring. So where does all the water in a kangaroo rat's body actually come from?
answer: It squeezes water out of the dry seeds it eats
choices: It squeezes water out of the dry seeds it eats
It absorbs moisture through its feet
It licks fog off desert plants
It swallows damp sand and filters it
context: By burning the food itself, the kangaroo rat produces 'metabolic water' from the hydrogen in the seeds it eats, making nearly all the water its body needs. Source: Schmidt-Nielsen & Schmidt-Nielsen 1951 (PubMed 14897858); OpenLearn 'Animals at the extremes'.

question: By day the North American desert bakes under the sun, and the dry air steals moisture from any small creature caught out in the open. The kangaroo rat (Dipodomys), a tiny hopping rodent barely bigger than a mouse and named for its long back legs, sidesteps the worst of the heat before the sun has even risen. What does it do all day long, from dawn until dusk?
answer: Stays underground in a cool, humid burrow
choices: Stays underground in a cool, humid burrow
Buries itself in wet riverbed mud
Floats in shaded rock pools
Shelters inside cactus flesh
context: The kangaroo rat stays in a cool, humid burrow through the heat of the day and only emerges at night, a behaviour that works alongside its body's water-saving tricks. Source: Schmidt-Nielsen & Schmidt-Nielsen 1951 (PubMed 14897858); OpenLearn 'Animals at the extremes' behavioural strategies.

question: Most mammals sweat to shed the day's heat, but sweating costs precious water — every drop lost to evaporation is a drop that has to be drunk back later. To avoid wasting that water, the Arabian camel (Camelus dromedarius) simply endures a daily internal shift that would leave a human shaking, feverish, and bedridden. What does the camel calmly allow to happen inside its body?
answer: Its body temperature to swing widely through the day
choices: Its body temperature to swing widely through the day
Its heart rate to drop until it faints
Its skin to blister and peel
Its blood to stop moving for hours
context: A camel lets its body temperature drift from about 34 C at dawn up to about 40 C by late afternoon, so it doesn't have to sweat away precious water to stay cool. Source: Britannica 'Camel'; sanjaymohindroo camel hump article.

question: A dromedary camel (Camelus dromedarius) — the tall one-humped desert camel of North Africa and the Middle East — staggers in from days out on the open sand. Its sides are visibly shrunken and it is so badly dehydrated that most large mammals in the same state would be dying. But a camel's body handles dryness in a way ours cannot. What can a parched camel safely do that would kill a horse or a cow?
answer: Gulp about 30 gallons of water in roughly ten minutes
choices: Gulp about 30 gallons of water in roughly ten minutes
Go a full month more without drinking
Sweat out half its body weight at once
Sleep for three days straight
context: A thirsty camel can drink up to about 30 gallons (100+ litres) in around ten minutes, and its cells don't burst thanks to special adaptations to sudden rehydration. Source: ScienceInsights 'Where Does a Camel Store Water?'; mannvetcorner camel humps/water article.

question: The desert tortoise (Gopherus) is a slow, dome-shelled reptile of the American Mojave and Sonoran deserts, where rain can skip a whole year. Its huge bladder normally stores months of drinking water inside its shell. When a coyote corners a desert tortoise out on the open flats, the tortoise has one panic reflex it cannot undo. Out in the dry, that reflex can end up deadlier than the coyote itself. What does the frightened tortoise do?
answer: It voids the huge water store in its oversized bladder
choices: It voids the huge water store in its oversized bladder
It sheds its whole shell and flees
It cracks its own legs to burrow faster
It bleeds out through its claws
context: The desert tortoise stores water in an oversized bladder that can hold up to about two-fifths of its body weight in fluid; if a predator frightens it into emptying that bladder, it can lose a dangerous amount of its reserve. Source: WorldAtlas 'Which Animals Can Live Without Water For Years?'; desert tortoise physiology accounts.

question: The thorny devil (Moloch horridus), a small spiky lizard of the Australian desert, is covered head to tail in sharp horn-like scales that give it its dragon nickname. Even in dry country it can stand in the faintest morning dew and take a full drink of water without ever lowering its head to a pool. How does its body pull that off?
answer: Water travels up grooves in its skin to its mouth
choices: Water travels up grooves in its skin to its mouth
It swallows dew-soaked sand and strains it
It absorbs vapour through wide-open nostrils
It presses its belly flat to soak up puddles
context: Tiny grooves between the thorny devil's scales wick up dew and puddle-water by capillary action and carry it, even uphill against gravity, all the way to the corners of its mouth. Source: Comanns et al. 2017, Royal Society Open Science (PMC5627102); AskNature 'Grooves Gather Water'.  (Legend.)

question: When a long Australian drought sets in and the outback dries hard, the water-holding frog (Ranoidea platycephala) vanishes underground for years at a time, perfectly sealed against the dry heat above. Desperate desert travellers and Aboriginal peoples have even dug them up and squeezed water from them to drink. How does the frog seal itself away underground?
answer: It wraps itself in a cocoon of its own shed skin
choices: It wraps itself in a cocoon of its own shed skin
It buries itself inside a ball of mud
It coats its body in tree sap
It fills a burrow with swallowed water
context: The water-holding frog soaks up half its body weight in water, wraps itself in a cocoon made of its own shed skin, and sleeps underground through drought for up to five years. Source: Australian Geographic 'Fact File: Water-holding frog (Cyclorana)'; Wikipedia 'Ranoidea platycephala'.  (Legend.)

question: When an Arabian camel (Camelus dromedarius) goes days without water in the desert, its blood thickens and grows sludgy from losing so much fluid. That syrupy blood would jam the tiny blood vessels — the capillaries — of nearly any other animal, and the animal would die. One quiet feature of the camel's red blood cells lets the flow keep moving through even the narrowest vessels. What is unusual about them?
answer: They are oval rather than round
choices: They are oval rather than round
They carry no oxygen at all
They are ten times larger than ours
They dissolve and reform each day
context: A camel's red blood cells are oval, not round, a shape that lets its blood keep flowing even when dehydration thickens it, so a camel can safely lose up to about 25% of its body water, where most mammals die after losing about 12%. Source: ScienceInsights 'Where Does a Camel Store Water?'; Britannica 'Camel'.

question: Every breath a warm-blooded animal exhales carries away warm, moist air — a quiet, constant water leak that a desert kangaroo rat (Dipodomys) simply cannot afford in a landscape without pools or streams. Its narrow, tightly coiled nasal passages act like a heat-and-water trap, cooling the outgoing breath and pulling moisture back inside. How much of each breath's water can the kangaroo rat recover?
answer: As much as 83%
choices: As much as 83%
About 20%
Roughly half
Nearly none
context: The kangaroo rat's cold, narrow, convoluted nose acts as a heat exchanger, condensing moisture from exhaled air and recovering as much as 83% of the water that would otherwise be lost with each breath. Source: Jackson & Schmidt-Nielsen 1964, 'Countercurrent Heat Exchange in the Respiratory Passages' (PNAS, JSTOR 72138); AskNature 'Nasal Turbinates Reduce Water Loss'.

question: The water-holding frog (Ranoidea platycephala) waits out years of Australian outback drought sealed underground in a cocoon of its own shed skin. Desperate desert travellers have dug one up, held it gently, squeezed, and drunk clean-tasting water straight from the frog's body — a trick Aboriginal peoples have known for a very long time. What that water actually is might surprise them. What is it?
answer: Dilute urine stored in a huge bladder
choices: Dilute urine stored in a huge bladder
Sap it absorbs from buried tree roots
Rainwater swallowed and held in its stomach
Fluid wrung from the fat in its thighs
context: The frog's bladder holds very dilute urine averaging about 57% of its body mass, a reserve calculated to offset water loss for two to three years underground. It doesn't just hoard the urine passively: it recycles urea (the nitrogen waste that would normally be flushed out) so it never has to spend water excreting it, and it drops its oxygen use by roughly 70% during aestivation. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Ranoidea platycephala'; Cartledge et al., 'Water balance and arginine vasotocin in the cocooning frog Cyclorana platycephala,' 2007 (pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18040971/).

question: For years, scientists watching the Australian thorny devil (Moloch horridus) assumed the little spiky lizard drank by wicking up morning dew through the microscopic grooves running between the scales of its skin. But careful experiments showed that dew, and even standing on damp sand, never wets those grooves enough to actually trigger the lizard to swallow a drop. What does the thorny devil actually do to fill its grooves and drink?
answer: It shovels damp sand onto its own back
choices: It shovels damp sand onto its own back
It licks dew straight off nearby spinifex grass
It presses its belly flat against cool wet clay
It gulps mouthfuls of moist air at first light
context: Philip Withers and colleagues found that condensation filled the skin's capillary channels to only about 0.22% of body weight, below the threshold to swallow; standing on wet sand reached just 59% and still no drink. The real trick: the lizard flicks moist sand onto its back with its legs, and gravity drives water up the grooves to its mouth (about 0.7 microliters per jaw movement). So rain and damp sand, not dew, are its water sources. Sources: Comanns et al. (with Withers), J. Exp. Biol. 219:3473, 2016 (pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27807218/); Royal Soc. Open Sci. 4:170591, 2017.

question: Lord Howe Island is a tiny forested speck of land in the Pacific Ocean, out past eastern Australia. It once crawled with an enormous flightless insect — glossy black, up to 7 inches long, and heavy enough to tip a small kitchen scale to almost an ounce, as long as a grown man's whole hand. The islanders gave this heavyweight bug an odd sea-creature nickname. What did they call it?
answer: The tree lobster
choices: The tree lobster
The bark scorpion
The giant walkingstick
The island beetle
context: Dryococelus australis grows up to about 7 inches (18 cm) long and weighs nearly an ounce (25 g) — a flightless, glossy brown-black bug whose heavy, armored bulk earned it the name 'tree lobster.' Source: San Diego Zoo Animals & Plants (animals.sandiegozoo.org).

question: By the 1920s black rats had eaten every last Lord Howe Island stick insect, and scientists wrote the species off as gone forever. Decades later, in 2001, climbers stunned the world by finding a tiny colony still alive. On what did those last survivors cling on?
answer: Ball's Pyramid, a bare ocean sea stack
choices: Ball's Pyramid, a bare ocean sea stack
A limestone cave on Lord Howe Island
A rotting log on the old rat-free islet
A coral cay far out in the lagoon
context: In 2001 climbers found a small colony of Dryococelus australis alive on Ball's Pyramid — a sheer 20-km-distant ocean rock — decades after the species was declared extinct, the rediscovery of what's been called 'the rarest insect in the world.' Source: Australian Museum blog 'VIP: Very Important Phasmid'; ecoservantsproject.org.  (Legend.)

question: For decades biologists thought the giant Lord Howe Island tree lobster — a huge flightless insect wiped out by shipwrecked rats in 1918 — was completely extinct. Then in 2001 climbers scaled a bare volcanic sea-stack called Ball's Pyramid, sticking up out of the Pacific near Lord Howe, and against all odds found the tree lobster still clinging on. Only about two dozen adults were left alive — the entire species. Where were every one of those last survivors living?
answer: On one single spindly bush
choices: On one single spindly bush
In a cave near the summit
Scattered across the whole rock
Under loose rocks by the sea
context: Roughly 24 individuals survived, all clinging to and feeding on ONE spindly tea-tree bush (Melaleuca howeana) high on a narrow ledge of the sea stack — the whole species surviving on a single plant. Source: San Diego Zoo Animals & Plants; ecoservantsproject.org.  (Legend.)

question: On tiny Lord Howe Island, a rocky volcanic dot in the sea between Australia and New Zealand, lives a giant black insect called the Lord Howe tree lobster. It looks like a stick with legs and was thought extinct for eighty years before it was rediscovered clinging to a lonely rock stack. Pairs sleep coiled up together through the day, one pressed close beside the other. What does the male do as they rest?
answer: Drapes three legs over the female beside him
choices: Drapes three legs over the female beside him
Tucks her beneath his abdomen
Interlocks his antennae with hers
Rests his head on her back
context: Dryococelus australis pairs sleep coiled together, the male draping three of his legs protectively over the female — a kind of pair-bonding almost never seen in insects. Source: San Diego Zoo Animals & Plants (animals.sandiegozoo.org).  (Legend.)

question: In the rainforests of Madagascar lives a mammal the size of a hamster. It is covered in quills like a tiny hedgehog. But it is glossy black with bright yellow stripes and a yellow streak down its snout. It weighs less than a stick of butter and eats mostly worms. What is it?
answer: The lowland streaked tenrec
choices: The lowland streaked tenrec
The greater glider
The yellow-throated marten
The pygmy slow loris
context: The lowland streaked tenrec (Hemicentetes semispinosus) weighs only about 125 to 280 grams, wears black-and-yellow spines with a yellow stripe down its snout, and feeds mostly on earthworms in Madagascar's rainforests. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lowland_streaked_tenrec

question: The lowland streaked tenrec makes a strange buzzing, clicking chatter to keep in touch with its family in the dense undergrowth. Yet it is the only mammal on Earth known to make sound with no voice, no vocal cords involved at all. How does this little Madagascan mammal produce its buzz?
answer: It rubs a patch of specialized quills on its back together
choices: It rubs a patch of specialized quills on its back together
It hums air through hollow nasal chambers
It cracks the joints in its long hind legs
It flutters loose flaps of skin along its ribs
context: This is called stridulation, the same trick crickets and grasshoppers use with their wings. The tenrec grinds together a patch of 7 to 16 specialized quills arranged in three rows on the middle of its back, producing high-frequency clicks and buzzes. A foraging mother stays in touch with her young this way, and the babies buzz back once their own quill organ develops. It is the only mammal known to communicate by stridulation. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lowland_streaked_tenrec ; https://animaldiversity.org/accounts/Hemicentetes_semispinosus/  (Legend.)

question: On Madagascar, about 31 kinds of tenrec live today. Some look like shrews, some like hedgehogs, some dig like moles. One even swims like a tiny otter. Yet all of them came from one ancestor that reached the island 30 million years ago. How did that first tenrec get there?
answer: It rafted across the sea on floating vegetation
choices: It rafted across the sea on floating vegetation
It walked over a land bridge from India
It was carried in the gut of a migrating seabird
It swam the channel from the African mainland
context: This is a textbook adaptive radiation: one ancestor that rafted from Africa on floating vegetation roughly 29 to 37 million years ago diversified into shrew-like, hedgehog-like, mole-like and otter-like forms to fill Madagascar's empty niches. Despite the resemblances, tenrecs are not related to hedgehogs, shrews or moles; that likeness is convergent evolution, and their real cousins are elephants, aardvarks and sea cows in the African group Afrotheria. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenrec  (Legend.)

question: An alligator snapping turtle, one of the largest freshwater turtles in North America and armed with a hooked beak that can slice through a stick, lies motionless on a muddy river bottom with its huge jaws gaping wide open. A hungry fish swims right into that open mouth, drawn in by something wriggling on the turtle's tongue. What clever bait did the turtle use to lure the fish in?
answer: A fake worm on its tongue
choices: A fake worm on its tongue
A flick of its bright tongue tip
A puff of scent from rotting meat
A glint off its pale mouth lining
context: The alligator snapping turtle is the only turtle with a body part built to lure prey: a pink, worm-shaped tip on its tongue. It lies still with mouth open, wiggles the fake worm, and snaps the jaws shut when a fish swims in to eat it. Source: Britannica / U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service (Macrochelys temminckii); Animal Diversity Web.

question: Deep in the black cold ocean far below where sunlight reaches, a female anglerfish hangs almost motionless in the dark. She is mostly one enormous tooth-lined mouth. Right in front of that mouth a single small point of light glows steadily, and curious little fish drift toward it as if drawn to a lantern. When they come close, she snaps them up. Where does that come-hither glow actually come from?
answer: A lure she dangles from her head
choices: A lure she dangles from her head
A glowing patch on her own belly
Prey she has swallowed and kept alight
A cloud of glowing spit she puffs out
context: The glowing tip is called the esca, dangled on a rod-like spine right in front of the anglerfish's mouth. In the lightless deep, prey drawn to the little light swim into her jaws. Source: Smithsonian Ocean (Anglerfish Lure Prey Throughout the Ocean); MBARI (deep-sea anglerfish).  (Legend.)

question: A frogfish sits perfectly still on a coral reef, disguised as a lumpy sponge-covered rock, dangling a tiny wriggling lure from a stalk on its head to draw smaller reef fish close. The instant its prey drifts into range, the frogfish lunges forward in a blur and opens its mouth to swallow the victim whole. What does the frogfish's mouth do in that fraction of a second?
answer: Balloons up to 12 times its normal size
choices: Balloons up to 12 times its normal size
Clamps shut like a steel bear trap
Fires a jet of water to stun the fish
Grows a second row of curved teeth
context: Camouflaged as a rock or sponge, the frogfish dangles a lure (the esca) on a rod-like fin spine (the illicium). It has the fastest strike of any vertebrate, and its mouth can expand up to 12 times its normal size to suck the victim in. Source: Wikipedia (Frogfish); Natural History Museum (nhm.ac.uk).

question: The bolas spider is a small hunter of warm American forests, and it builds no web at all. Instead, at night, a female hangs from one silk thread out in the open air, holding a single heavy sticky glue-ball at the end of a short line — a bit like a fisherman dangling one baited hook. Then a male moth of just the right species comes flying straight toward her out of the dark, and she swings the glue-ball and knocks him down. What lures the moth in?
answer: A scent that copies a female moth's mating perfume
choices: A scent that copies a female moth's mating perfume
A soft glow from the tip of her sticky glue-ball
A high buzz that mimics a female moth's wingbeat
A flower-like shape that draws him in to feed
context: The bolas spider releases a scent that mimics a female moth's mating pheromone; when a male flies in, she swings the glue-tipped thread like a cowboy's bolas to catch him. Source: Science 1977 (Aggressive Chemical Mimicry by a Bolas Spider); Wikipedia (Mastophora hutchinsoni).

question: A horned viper in Iran's western mountains hides among rocks and 'walks' its tail tip to lure insect-eating birds within striking range. One expert called its tail the most elaborate predatory lure known in any reptile. What is that tail tip built to look like?
answer: A crawling spider
choices: A crawling spider
A wriggling caterpillar
A fat brown beetle
A small green lizard
context: Pseudocerastes urarachnoides has a tail tip shaped and moved exactly like a spider, made entirely of soft tissue and elongated scales. It mainly fools migrating warblers; local birds seem to have learned the trick and avoid it. When a bird strikes, the snake strikes back in about 0.2 seconds. Source: National Geographic (spiders-snakes); Wikipedia (Spider-tailed horned viper).  (Legend.)

question: The anglerfish is a deep-sea predator that carries a tiny glowing bait on the end of a long fleshy 'fishing rod' rising from between its eyes. That rod did not simply appear from nowhere. Over many millions of years of evolution, one part of an ancestral fish crept forward across its head, stretched into a long stalk, and grew the glowing lure on its tip. Which body part became the rod?
answer: The front spine of its back fin
choices: The front spine of its back fin
A stiffened whisker beside its mouth
The first ray of its tail fin
A hardened tooth from its jaw
context: The rod is a modified first dorsal fin spine: over evolution the front fin ray migrated forward over the head to become the illicium (the rod), tipped by the esca (the glowing lure). Source: Wikipedia (Ceratioidei); Smithsonian Ocean.

question: Far below where any sunlight can reach, in the crushing black of the deep ocean, a fish called the anglerfish dangles a tiny lantern-like lure just in front of its mouth to draw curious prey close. The lure shines steadily in the dark, a small warm point of light in an endless night. Where does that light actually come from?
answer: Glowing bacteria living inside the lure
choices: Glowing bacteria living inside the lure
A glowing fluid the fish brews in its blood
Stored sunlight released slowly at night
Tiny crystals that shine when they are squeezed
context: Glowing bacteria live inside the tip of the lure (the esca). The fish feeds them oxygen and nutrients through its blood supply, and the bacteria produce light in return. Source: Smithsonian Ocean (Meet the Tiny Bacteria That Give Anglerfishes Their Spooky Glow); eLife 2019.

question: On a summer evening a female Photuris firefly watches a male of a different firefly species flashing his species' courtship code across the meadow — a specific rhythm of glowing pulses that his kind uses to attract females of his own species. The Photuris female is bigger and darker than his usual mates, but she flashes his species' code right back at him, perfectly copying the timing. When he lands beside her expecting a mate, what does the Photuris female do?
answer: She eats him
choices: She eats him
She lays her eggs on his back
She steals his glow for herself
She flies off with a rival male
context: The female Photuris firefly is a 'femme fatale': she flashes back the mating code of a different firefly species (Photinus) to lure the courting males, then eats them. Source: PNAS 1997 (doi 10.1073/pnas.94.18.9723); Cornell Chronicle (1997).  (Legend.)

question: A female Photuris firefly is a cunning nighttime hunter. She watches males of a different firefly species flashing their courting signals in the dark, then perfectly mimics the answering flash of one of their females. Fooled males swoop in expecting a mate, and she grabs and eats them. But she is not hunting them just for a meal — their bodies carry a defensive chemical she cannot make in her own body. What does the Photuris female actually gain by eating them?
answer: Poison to protect herself and her eggs
choices: Poison to protect herself and her eggs
A brighter flash to attract more mates
Extra body fat to lay more eggs
A scent that repels other predators
context: The Photinus males she eats carry lucibufagins, defensive steroids similar to the heart poison in foxglove. Unable to make them herself, she steals them by eating the males and passes the toxic protection on to her eggs. Source: PNAS 1997 (Firefly femmes fatales acquire defensive steroids from their firefly prey); Cornell Chronicle.  (Legend.)

question: Two Iranian vipers look nearly identical, but only one grows a spider-shaped tail tip and hunts birds; its cousins eat mammals. When researchers dripped each snake's venom into chicken blood, the bird-hunter's venom clotted that blood almost instantly while the mammal-eaters barely touched it. What specific target does the bird-hunter's venom appear chemically tuned to, given how fast it clotted the chicken blood?
answer: It is chemically tuned to the clotting system of the birds it lures in
choices: It is chemically tuned to the clotting system of the birds it lures in
It fires the same clotting trigger in any vertebrate's blood equally
It attacks a clotting protein that birds and mammals share unchanged
The fast clotting is a side effect of the lure, not the venom's design
context: The spider-tailed viper (Pseudocerastes urarachnoides) is the only Pseudocerastes that specializes in birds, and its venom evolved to match. In thromboelastography tests, its venom sped up clot formation in avian (chicken) plasma by about 96 percent, a fast, powerful procoagulant hit. Its mammal-eating relatives P. persicus and P. fieldi barely affected bird plasma, roughly a 20 percent delay in clotting, with the resulting clots no different from a no-venom control. So the bird-mimicking tail and a bird-specialized venom evolved together: the lure attracts the prey the venom is built to kill. Source: op den Brouw et al., 2021, 'Extensive Variation in the Activities of Pseudocerastes and Eristicophis Viper Venoms Suggests Divergent Envenoming Strategies Are Used for Prey Capture,' Toxins 13(2):112 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7913145/).

question: In the damp forests of southeastern Australia lives a big, brown, ground-dwelling songbird the size of a pheasant. The courting male fans a spectacular tail forward over his own head like a shimmering silvery umbrella. What is the shape of that famous tail?
answer: A small ancient harp, a lyre
choices: A small ancient harp, a lyre
A folded paper fan
A peacock's eyed wheel
A drooping willow branch
context: The superb lyrebird's ornate courtship tail spreads into the shape of a lyre, a small ancient harp. Two outer feathers curve into an 'S' shape (called 'lyrates') and frame twelve fine silvery filament feathers between them. Source: Australian Museum, 'Superb Lyrebird'; Wikipedia, 'Superb lyrebird'.

question: In an Australian eucalyptus forest, a kookaburra — a stout kingfisher famous for its wild human-sounding laughing call — perches on a branch and hears its own laughing call answer back from the bushes below. Thinking another kookaburra is talking to it, it starts calling again in reply. But when a bird-watcher creeps down to look, there is no second kookaburra there at all. What was really making the laughing sound?
answer: A superb lyrebird copying the laugh
choices: A superb lyrebird copying the laugh
An echo off a rock face
A kookaburra chick practicing
A fox imitating the bird
context: A lyrebird can imitate a kookaburra's laugh so perfectly that a nearby wild kookaburra is fooled into thinking it hears one of its own and calls back. Roughly 70-80% of a male lyrebird's song is imitation, and it can copy more than 20 other bird species accurately enough that the real birds answer. Source: Australian Museum, 'Superb Lyrebird'.  (Legend.)

question: At Adelaide Zoo, a male lyrebird named Chook lived for months next to a building site that would later become the panda house. When keepers listened close to Chook's song, they heard sounds that had nothing to do with a forest. What had he woven into his song?
answer: Hammers, power drills and saws
choices: Hammers, power drills and saws
Thunderclaps and heavy rain
Church bells across the city
Lions roaring in the next paddock
context: Captive lyrebirds copy man-made machine sounds with uncanny accuracy. Chook reproduced the hammers, power drills and saws he heard during the panda-enclosure construction beside his cage. Source: The Conversation, 'Lyrebirds mimicking chainsaws: fact or lie?'; snootypaws.com.au blog on Chook.  (Legend.)

question: The Australian lyrebird is famous in viral videos for perfectly mimicking chainsaws, camera shutters, and car alarms. The researcher Hollis Taylor spent years walking deep Australian forests searching for the bird's most famous trick and came up empty-handed. She now says no known clean recording of it comes from a truly wild bird — the celebrated feats mostly come from captive lyrebirds copying human handlers. Which crowd-pleasing feat is almost never caught from a wild lyrebird?
answer: Imitating man-made machine sounds
choices: Imitating man-made machine sounds
Copying other birds' calls
Singing loudly before dawn
Fanning its tail while it sings
context: Hollis Taylor notes 'there is no known recording of a lyrebird in the wild mimicking man-made mechanical sounds.'
