Source: Ritz et al. 2004, Nature, 'Resonance effects indicate a radical-pair mechanism for avian magnetic compass' (PubMed 15141211); 15 nT figure, Larmor formula, and 1.315 MHz value from review PMC5627152.

question: On the Pacific islands of New Caledonia lives a glossy black crow with no woodpeckers anywhere nearby to compete with. Over time this crow has taken over the woodpecker's job entirely — winkling fat grubs out of rotten holes in dead wood. Since a crow doesn't have a woodpecker's drilling beak, what does the New Caledonian crow use to yank grubs out of the wood?
answer: Tools it makes and wields
choices: Tools it makes and wields
Its extra-long barbed tongue
A drumming beak that splits bark
Sticky saliva on its feathers
context: The New Caledonian crow (Corvus moneduloides) fills the ecological niche of a woodpecker on islands that have none, and it is one of the only animals besides apes known to make its own tools. Source: Wikipedia, 'New Caledonian crow' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Caledonian_crow).

question: A New Caledonian crow doesn't just grab a handy twig — it manufactures a proper tool. It snips a twig from a fork in a branch, then trims the wood away until one specific feature is left at the tip. What has it shaped, that no other wild animal is known to make?
answer: A hook
choices: A hook
A flattened spade
A hollow straw
A forked splinter
context: The crow trims a fork down to a hook at the tip, then hooks grubs out of crevices — the only non-human animal known to manufacture hooked tools in the wild. Source: Nature, Hunt 1996, 'Manufacture and use of hook-tools by New Caledonian crows' (nature.com/articles/379249a0).

question: New Caledonian crows also work with pandanus leaves, whose edges carry rows of tiny backward-pointing barbs. A crow cuts a precise stepped strip so those barbs line up as a row of snags. Researchers compared the strip designs made by crow populations across the island, old shapes against new. What was true of how the designs changed over time?
answer: Newer strips were more refined than older ones
choices: Newer strips were more refined than older ones
Newer strips were cruder than older ones
Populations copied one identical strip
Only lone crows ever tweaked a strip
context: Different crow populations make slightly different pandanus tool designs that grew more refined generation after generation — a bird version of cumulative culture, and the only non-primate case known where each generation builds on the last. Source: Wikipedia, 'New Caledonian crow'; Hunt & Gray pandanus tool diversification research.

question: In a famous 2002 Oxford experiment, a captive crow named Betty faced a food bucket sunk deep in a tube. She was given a straight wire and a hooked wire — but her mate Abel snatched the hooked one and flew off. Left with only the straight wire, what did Betty do?
answer: Bent it into a hook herself
choices: Bent it into a hook herself
Called Abel back with the food
Dropped it and gave up
Threaded it through the tube wall
context: Betty bent the straight wire into a hook and lifted the food bucket out — a landmark moment in animal-cognition research. Source: Weir & Kacelnik 2002/2006, Oxford; Science, 'Was Betty the crow a genius—or a robot?' (science.org). (legend)

question: In 2002 at Oxford University, a captive New Caledonian crow named Betty was given a straight piece of wire and a small food bucket sitting at the bottom of a tall tube. To the scientists' amazement, she bent the wire into a neat hook with her beak and fished the bucket out — and then pulled off the same trick in nine of ten later trials. Her wire-bending was hailed as a flash of pure invention. Years later, new evidence forced scientists to revise that story of her feat. What did the new evidence show?
answer: Bending tools is a natural crow move
choices: Bending tools is a natural crow move
Crows can bend wire but never twigs
Only Betty ever managed the trick
Her wire had been pre-bent by staff
context: Wild crows were found to bend their tools the same way, so Betty's trick may be part of the species' natural repertoire rather than pure on-the-spot invention. Source: Science, AAAS; Royal Society Open Science, Rutz et al. 2016. (legend)

question: Scientists in the Pacific islands of New Caledonia set a puzzle for wild New Caledonian crows — the glossy black tool-using birds that live there. Each crow got a short stick and a scrap of meat it couldn't reach with that stick alone. A second, longer stick was locked away inside a nearby box. With no coaching and only one shot each, how did the crows crack this puzzle on their very first try?
answer: Used the short stick to fish out the long one, then reached the meat
choices: Used the short stick to fish out the long one, then reached the meat
Flung the short stick at the meat to knock it closer to the bars
Wedged the short stick into the box to pry the whole lid open
Tapped the short stick until a keeper handed over the long one
context: Six of seven crows solved this 'tool to get a tool' metatool problem on the first attempt — using the short stick to retrieve the long stick, then the long stick on the meat, a hallmark of planning. Source: Wikipedia citing metatool experiments; PubMed, 'New Caledonian Crows Use Mental Representations to Solve Metatool Problems'.

question: New Caledonian crows pass the challenge from Aesop's fable 'The Crow and the Pitcher': a treat floats out of reach in a water tube, and the crow must raise the water to reach it. Offered a mix of objects, the crows picked heavy sinking stones over floaters and solid over hollow. That grasp of cause and effect roughly matched what?
answer: A five-to-seven-year-old child
choices: A five-to-seven-year-old child
A trained laboratory rat
A newly hatched chick
An adult chimpanzee's ceiling
context: By dropping sinking stones to raise the water level, the crows displayed causal understanding roughly on par with a 5-to-7-year-old child. Source: Jelbert et al. 2014, PLOS ONE; ScienceDaily. (legend)

question: Deep in the caves of New Zealand lives a creature people call the glowworm. From the cave ceiling, hundreds of them dangle long sticky silk lines that glow blue-green in the dark, snagging any flying insect that mistakes the lights for stars. Despite its name, the glowworm is not a worm at all. What kind of animal is it?
answer: the larva of a fly
choices: the larva of a fly
a young spider
a kind of caterpillar
a small cave slug
context: The New Zealand glowworm (Arachnocampa luminosa) is really a maggot -- the larva of a fungus gnat, a fly in the order Diptera, family Keroplatidae. It glows blue-green at the tail end of its body to lure flying insects into its sticky lines. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arachnocampa_luminosa  (Legend.)

question: In New Zealand's Waitomo Caves, tourists drift on a boat through a pitch-black underground river. There are no lamps, no flashlights. They look up — and thousands of tiny blue-green glowworm lights are shining down from the cave ceiling, tiny living lamps too many to count. What does the ceiling look like?
answer: a starry night sky
choices: a starry night sky
a field of glowing mushrooms
rows of hanging lanterns
streaks of lightning
context: In the famous Waitomo Glowworm Caves, thousands of Arachnocampa luminosa larvae cover the ceiling, and their blue-green lights look exactly like a starry night sky or a galaxy overhead -- a world-famous natural spectacle visitors float beneath in the dark. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waitomo_Glowworm_Cave  (Legend.)

question: A New Zealand glowworm — really the larva of a cave fly — hangs from the ceiling of a dark cave and dangles a sticky silk fishing line below it. At the tip of its own body glows a soft blue-green light that lures flying insects into the trap. When one larva gets hungry and needs to reel in more prey, what does it do with that light?
answer: turns it brighter
choices: turns it brighter
switches it off
flashes it on and off
changes it to red
context: A hungrier Arachnocampa luminosa larva turns UP the intensity of its blue-green glow to lure more prey, then dims once it is well-fed. Its light is true bioluminescence -- a chemical light made at the end of its abdomen. Source: https://www.discoverwildlife.com/animal-facts/glow-worm-new-zealand-caves

question: In the dark limestone caves of New Zealand, the glowworm — actually the larva of a small fly — hangs from the cave ceiling and dangles glowing, sticky threads to trap insects that fly toward the light. It spends 6 to 12 whole months as this hungry, hunting larva. Then it finally transforms into an adult fly that survives only a few days before it dies. Why can the adult not live any longer?
answer: it has no mouth and cannot eat
choices: it has no mouth and cannot eat
its wings are too weak to fly
the cave cold quickly freezes it
it burns out its last light
context: The adult fly that hatches from Arachnocampa luminosa has no functional mouth -- it cannot eat at all. It lives only days (females up to about 76 hours, males up to about 96 hours) with the sole purpose of mating and laying eggs before it dies. The long larval stage exists to fund that brief adult life. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arachnocampa_luminosa  (Legend.)

question: Off the coast of Italy lives a jellyfish smaller than a pinky nail. It carries a nickname no other animal can claim: the 'immortal jellyfish.' Why are scientists watching Turritopsis dohrnii so closely?
answer: When stressed, an adult can rewind into its own younger stage and start over
choices: When stressed, an adult can rewind into its own younger stage and start over
It grows to the size of a dinner plate within a single week
It glows bright enough to read a book by on the sea floor
Its sting is the most powerful of any creature in the ocean
context: Turritopsis dohrnii's bell reaches only about 4.5 millimetres across, roughly the size of a pinky fingernail - yet a stressed adult can run its life cycle backwards, earning it the 'immortal jellyfish' name. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turritopsis_dohrnii  (Legend.)

question: Turritopsis dohrnii — the tiny 'immortal jellyfish' of the Mediterranean Sea — has a full-grown, free-swimming adult stage called a medusa. When one of these medusas is badly starved or badly injured, instead of dying it sinks to the sea floor and balls up into a featureless blob. What does that blob then become?
answer: A young polyp, the stalked seabed stage
choices: A young polyp, the stalked seabed stage
A clutch of fertilized eggs anchored to the rock
A drifting swarm of newly hatched larvae
A cloud of a hundred identical adult jellyfish
context: A polyp is the stalk-like seabed stage that jellyfish grow from before budding off as free-swimming medusae. When stressed by starvation, injury, or a sudden change in temperature or saltiness, the adult Turritopsis reverts all the way back to this young polyp - running its life cycle backwards. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turritopsis_dohrnii  (Legend.)

question: When the 'immortal jellyfish' Turritopsis dohrnii is starving or injured, it doesn't die. Instead, it rewinds into a younger polyp — its earliest stage of life. To pull this off, it doesn't just shrink. Its already-finished adult cells rebuild themselves into totally different kinds of cell. A muscle cell, for instance, can turn straight into a nerve cell. What is this cell-to-cell switch called?
answer: Transdifferentiation
choices: Transdifferentiation
Photosynthesis
Metamorphosis
Hibernation
context: Transdifferentiation is a fully specialized cell switching into a different cell type - like a muscle cell becoming a nerve cell - as the jellyfish recycles its own body into a younger form. It is the mechanism behind the reversal. Source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6893190/

question: Turritopsis dohrnii is a tiny jellyfish barely bigger than a pinhead. When it is starved or badly injured, its adult body can rewind — the medusa collapses back into a young clump of cells called a polyp, and it starts life over again. That trick has earned it headlines as the 'immortal jellyfish.' In the wild, though, most of them never live long enough to rewind at all. Why does the 'immortal jellyfish' still keep dying?
answer: Predators eat it or disease kills it while it's still an adult
choices: Predators eat it or disease kills it while it's still an adult
Its rewind only works three times before it stops
It freezes solid the first cold night of winter
It forgets how to revert once it becomes an adult
context: Myth-correction: 'immortal' only means Turritopsis dohrnii can rewind to a younger stage - it is NOT unkillable. In the wild most still die, eaten by predators or killed by disease in the medusa stage, before ever reverting. The trick is transformation, not invincibility. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turritopsis_dohrnii  (Legend.)

question: The freshwater Hydra is a tiny cousin of the jellyfish — a slim green tube with waving tentacles that lives in still ponds. For most animals, including humans, the older you get, the more likely you are to die each passing year. Scientists tracked thousands of Hydras for years to test whether that rule holds for them too. As a Hydra gets older, what does its chance of dying each year do?
answer: Stays flat - it doesn't rise as the animal ages
choices: Stays flat - it doesn't rise as the animal ages
Doubles every single month it survives
Drops to exactly zero after its first year
Climbs steeply, the way it does in most animals
context: This is called 'negligible senescence': the Hydra doesn't grow measurably more likely to die as it ages, because stem cells constantly rebuild its whole body. Source: https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1521002112

question: The freshwater Hydra is a tiny stalk-like animal, about the length of a fingernail, that clings to weeds and stems in ponds. Unlike almost every other creature, its yearly chance of dying does not climb as it gets older — an old Hydra is no more likely to die than a young one. One team ran the numbers on a whole Hydra population, assuming nothing ever ate them. How long did they calculate a few percent would still be alive?
answer: More than 1,400 years
choices: More than 1,400 years
About 40 years
Around 200 years
Roughly 60,000 years
context: With a death rate that stays flat with age, the study calculated that even after 1,400 years, a few percent of a Hydra population would still be alive - if nothing ate them first. Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4697432/  (Legend.)

question: The naked mole-rat is a wrinkled, nearly hairless rodent that digs tunnel colonies under the dry grasslands of East Africa. It is about the size of a house mouse — but where a mouse lives about three years, the naked mole-rat lives astonishingly longer. Compared with that mouse of similar size, how long can a naked mole-rat live?
answer: More than 30 years
choices: More than 30 years
About 5 years
Around 12 years
Roughly 100 years
context: The naked mole-rat is the longest-lived rodent, with some living more than 30 years - about ten times longer than a similar-sized mouse. Source: https://elifesciences.org/articles/31157  (Legend.)

question: Naked mole-rats — the wrinkled, hairless African burrowers — can live nearly thirty years underground and almost never get cancer. In their University of Rochester lab, the husband-and-wife biologists Vera Gorbunova and Andrei Seluanov opened up the mystery. They found a thick, sugary molecule called hyaluronan packed between the animal's cells. How does that molecule keep cancer away?
answer: It stops cells from crowding together and overgrowing
choices: It stops cells from crowding together and overgrowing
It poisons any tumor the moment it forms
It scrubs damaged DNA clean every single night
It starves fast-growing cells of all oxygen
context: The molecule is high-molecular-weight hyaluronan; it keeps naked mole-rat cells from crowding and overgrowing, which almost never lets cancer take hold. Discovered by Vera Gorbunova and Andrei Seluanov. Source: https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2018/02/180206115143.htm

question: A lobster is a hard-shelled sea creature that walks the ocean floor with clacking claws. Unlike most animals, a lobster doesn't slow down with age — the oldest, biggest females actually lay even more eggs than young ones do. That's because lobsters keep making telomerase, an enzyme that repairs part of every chromosome (the tightly-packed DNA bundles inside each cell). Which part of the chromosome does telomerase rebuild?
answer: The tips, which normally fray shorter each time a cell divides
choices: The tips, which normally fray shorter each time a cell divides
The centromere, the pinched waist that guides the split
The histone spools the strand winds around for storage
The replication fork where the two strands unzip
context: Lobsters keep making telomerase, an enzyme that protects the ends (tips) of their chromosomes - which is partly why they keep growing and stay fertile their whole lives. Source: https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/are-lobsters-immortal.html

question: People love to say lobsters are 'immortal' because these hard-shelled sea crawlers never stop growing — the biggest, oldest lobsters can end up as heavy as a small dog. But the very act of getting bigger is what finally kills many of them. What deadly ordeal do these old, giant lobsters have to face over and over again?
answer: Molting - shedding a huge shell exhausts them and leaves them defenseless
choices: Molting - shedding a huge shell exhausts them and leaves them defenseless
Starving because their claws grow too heavy to lift food
Sinking too deep to ever return to warm water
Freezing when their blood can no longer flow
context: Lobsters are NOT truly immortal: the older and bigger they get, the harder it is to molt their shell, and many die of exhaustion or predation during that dangerous molt. Source: https://www.mcgill.ca/oss/article/student-contributors-did-you-know/lobsters-are-not-immortal-myth-they-are-seems-be

question: The 'immortal jellyfish' Turritopsis dohrnii lives in the Mediterranean and can rewind an aging adult body back into a younger polyp when it is dying — starting its life over. Its close cousin Turritopsis rubra looks nearly the same, but lives a plain mortal life and never rewinds. In 2022, a study lined up the whole DNA of both species side by side. What did Turritopsis dohrnii carry that its mortal cousin lacked?
answer: Extra copies of genes that repair and protect its DNA
choices: Extra copies of genes that repair and protect its DNA
A second nervous system that overrides its first
Venom strong enough to paralyze its own predators
A shell it can retreat into whenever it is injured
context: In 2022, Maria Pascual-Torner, Carlos Lopez-Otin, and colleagues sequenced Turritopsis dohrnii alongside its close cousin Turritopsis rubra, which cannot rewind. The immortal one carried duplicated copies of DNA-repair genes and DNA polymerases, plus protective variants for telomere upkeep, stem-cell maintenance, and clearing damaged proteins - roughly twice as many gene-protection/repair genes as its mortal cousin. So the trick isn't magic: it's an expanded genetic toolkit for keeping its DNA clean. Source: Pascual-Torner, Lopez-Otin et al., 'Comparative genomics of mortal and immortal cnidarians unveils novel keys behind rejuvenation,' PNAS 2022, 119(36) (pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2118763119); corroborated by The Scientist.

question: A naked mole-rat cell stops dividing while its neighbors are still far apart - long before a mouse cell would quit. Researchers digested away the giant sugar molecule packed around it, and the cell promptly formed a tumor. What had that molecule been doing?
answer: Tripping the p16 brake that halts growth early
choices: Tripping the p16 brake that halts growth early
Feeding the cell so it never needed to spread
Cloaking the cell from the animal's immune patrols
Cooling the tissue below the temperature tumors need
context: In 2013, Xiao Tian, Vera Gorbunova, Andrei Seluanov, and colleagues found naked mole-rats make a giant form of hyaluronan (HMW-HA) about five times larger than a mouse's or human's (roughly 6-12 million daltons vs 0.5-3 million). It makes cells arrest at much lower densities - 'early contact inhibition' - by triggering the p16 (p16INK4a) tumor-suppressor switch, slamming the brakes before a tumor can form. When researchers digested the molecule away or knocked out the HAS2 gene that builds it, the cells could then form tumors - proving the molecule is what protects them. Source: Tian et al., 'High-molecular-mass hyaluronan mediates the cancer resistance of the naked mole rat,' Nature 2013, 499:346-349 (nature.com/articles/nature12234).

question: A numbat is a small striped pouched marsupial of Western Australia, about the size of a squirrel. It eats almost nothing but termites — it noses into their shallow underground tunnels and slurps up about 20,000 of them every single day. What body part lets a numbat pull so many termites out of those tight, narrow tunnels?
answer: A long tongue coated in sticky saliva
choices: A long tongue coated in sticky saliva
A set of powerful crushing jaws
A hollow snout it sucks air through
A mouthful of sharp shearing teeth
context: The numbat's tongue flicks out about 10 cm — nearly a third of its whole body length — and the sticky coating traps termites deep in their tunnels. It needs the reach because a small numbat can only work galleries close to the surface. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numbat

question: Nearly every marsupial — the pouched mammals of Australia like kangaroos, possums, quolls, and wombats — sleeps through the day and moves at night. The little striped numbat of Western Australia is the single exception: this small termite-eating marsupial is fully active in broad daylight. What forces the numbat onto a daytime schedule?
answer: Termites climb near the surface only in daylight
choices: Termites climb near the surface only in daylight
Its eyes are useless in total darkness
Daytime warmth keeps its small body from chilling
Night predators would easily catch it
context: The numbat is the only marsupial that is fully diurnal. A small numbat can only reach termites when they rise close to the top of their galleries, and that happens by day — so its whole schedule is set by its prey's, not by avoiding the dark. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numbat

question: In the eucalyptus forests of Western Australia lives a small striped marsupial called the numbat — an anteater roughly the size of a squirrel. A female numbat gives birth to four bean-sized young, who must spend their first months of life attached to her four teats. For a marsupial, the way she carries them is very strange. Where do these newborns actually ride?
answer: Dangling in the open from exposed teats, with no pouch
choices: Dangling in the open from exposed teats, with no pouch
Sealed inside a deep fur-lined belly pouch
Tucked into stretchy pouches in her cheeks
Gripped in the curl of her bushy tail
context: Unusually for a marsupial, the female numbat has no pouch at all. Her four teats sit on a bare patch of belly protected only by crimped golden hair, and the clinging newborns dangle in the open air for months. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numbat

question: A numbat — a small striped termite-eating marsupial of Western Australia — shelters in a hollow log or a shallow burrow it can just fit inside. When a fox or a hawk comes hunting, the numbat backs all the way to the far end. But the entrance is still open behind it. How does the little numbat stop the attacker from squeezing in after it?
answer: It jams the opening shut with its thick, tough-hided rump
choices: It jams the opening shut with its thick, tough-hided rump
It sprays a foul-smelling fluid at the entrance
It curls into a tight ball of sharp spines
It rakes the attacker back with its front claws
context: The skin over a numbat's rump is thick and tough, and it uses that hindquarter like a living door — backing in and plugging the entrance so nothing can get past it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numbat

question: For centuries sailors around the world swore they had seen sea serpents — long silver monsters writhing at the surface of the ocean before slipping back under. Marine scientists now think most of those reports were really one very strange, ribbon-shaped deep-sea fish, dying and rolling in the waves. Which animal was it?
answer: The oarfish
choices: The oarfish
The giant squid
The basking shark
The leatherback turtle
context: The giant oarfish is a scaleless ribbon of silver with a flaming red crest and fin running its whole length. A sick or dying one drifts up and rolls at the surface — a near-perfect match for the classic 'sea serpent' report. A 2016 River Monsters investigation concluded it is the most likely real-world origin of the myth. LEGEND (science-of-legend). Source: Florida Museum — Discover Fishes; Wikipedia 'Giant oarfish'.

question: On a lonely beach, a small crowd gathers around a silvery ribbon of a fish that has drifted up onto the sand. It looks like a sea serpent — a long, flat, gleaming body stretched out roughly 8 metres (26 feet) from head to tail. No other bony fish alive in the ocean grows this long. What is this record-holder?
answer: The oarfish
choices: The oarfish
The moray eel
The barracuda
The sturgeon
context: The giant oarfish (Regalecus glesne) is the longest bony fish alive, reliably reaching about 8 metres, with some reports up to 11. Sharks and rays grow longer, but their skeletons are cartilage, not bone. Old claims of 17-metre oarfish are considered exaggerations. Source: Florida Museum; Wikipedia 'Giant oarfish'.

question: The oarfish is a giant ribbon-shaped fish of the deep ocean, sometimes 8 metres long. From its head rises a tall plume of long red fin rays, spreading out like a bright crown above its polished silver body. Old fishermen who now and then hauled one up in a herring net gave it a regal folk name. What were people calling it?
answer: King of herrings
choices: King of herrings
Sea unicorn
Silver duke
Crown eel
context: A dorsal fin runs the entire length of the oarfish, tipped at the head with a tall red crest of long rays. The crownlike look earned it the folk name 'king of herrings' — giving it the appearance of a maned sea dragon. Source: Wikipedia 'Giant oarfish'; Florida Museum.

question: The oarfish is a long silver deep-sea fish that can grow as long as a bus, and it almost never comes close to shore. So when one washes up on a Japanese beach, crowds gather in wonder. In Japan they call it 'ryugu no tsukai,' meaning 'messenger from the sea dragon god's palace.' Many people believe its arrival is a warning of what?
answer: A coming earthquake
choices: A coming earthquake
A rich fishing season
A royal death
A great storm at sea
context: Because the oarfish lives deep and rarely surfaces, folklore holds that it swims up to warn of an earthquake, so a stranding draws crowds. A 2019 study of 336 sightings found no real link between oarfish and quakes — so it remains a belief, not a fact. LEGEND (folk belief, framed as belief). Source: Atlas Obscura 'The Legend of Japan's Earthquake Fish'; Logically Facts (2019 study).

question: The oarfish is a slender silver ribbon of a deep-sea fish that can grow up to 8 metres long, longer than a school bus. For a giant it is shockingly gentle — it has no real teeth at all. Instead it swims with its mouth open and feeds by straining tiny krill and plankton straight from the seawater. What in its mouth lets it filter out that swarm of tiny prey?
answer: Fine gill rakers in its mouth
choices: Fine gill rakers in its mouth
A sticky mucus net it casts out
Rows of grinding throat plates
A sucking, tube-shaped snout
context: The oarfish filters tiny krill and plankton through fine gill rakers — comblike structures in the mouth. One specimen was found with about 10,000 krill inside it. Despite its terrifying size, it is harmless. Source: Florida Museum — Discover Fishes.

question: The oarfish is a 26-foot ribbon-fish of the deep ocean. When one strands on a beach it looks as if it were forged from polished metal, flashing silver in the sun — yet unlike most fish it wears no scales at all. Its long body is completely bare skin. What coats that bare skin to give it a mirror shine?
answer: A soft layer of guanine crystals
choices: A soft layer of guanine crystals
A film of swallowed sea salt
A sheath of overlapping bony plates
A slick of reflective body oil
context: The oarfish has no scales; its body is coated in a soft, silvery layer of guanine — the same shimmering crystal that makes ordinary fish scales and mirrors flash. That is why a stranded one looks made of polished metal. Source: Florida Museum — Discover Fishes; Wikipedia 'Giant oarfish'.

question: Until 2010 nobody knew how a living oarfish actually swam — they were only ever seen dead or dying. Then Mark Benfield's team filmed one alive with a deep submersible and saw a posture that shocked them. How does the oarfish hold itself in the water?
answer: Vertically, head-up and tail-down
choices: Vertically, head-up and tail-down
Coiled in a slow rolling spiral
Belly-up, drifting with the current
Flat on the seabed like a flounder
context: Benfield et al. (2013) filmed live oarfish in the Gulf of Mexico and discovered its true posture: it hangs vertically, head-up and tail-down, rippling its long red dorsal fin to hover in the water column. Scientists think this may be a hunting trick — hanging straight up, it uses faint surface light to silhouette prey drifting above it. Source: Benfield et al. 2013, Journal of Fish Biology (doi:10.1111/jfb.12144).

question: Somewhere off a warm coast, sailors spot a fish that looks like a giant swimming head. Its body is squashed flat from the side. Tall fins jut straight up on top and straight down below. And then, oddly, it just… stops — blunt at the back, with nothing trailing behind at all. Which ocean giant is this?
answer: The ocean sunfish (mola)
choices: The ocean sunfish (mola)
The great white shark
The bluefin tuna
The manta ray
context: The ocean sunfish (Mola mola) really does look like a swimming head that ends abruptly with no real tail. Source: Monterey Bay Aquarium — Ocean sunfish.

question: The ocean sunfish, called Mola mola, is one of the strangest big fish in the sea. It has no true tail fin at all. Where a shark or a tuna would have a sweeping tail behind, the mola has a stiff blunt rudder — a scalloped fringe of muscle wrapped around its back edge. But that steering fringe isn't a shrunken tail. It's built from something else entirely on the fish. What forms it?
answer: The wrapped-around ends of its top and bottom fins
choices: The wrapped-around ends of its top and bottom fins
A stub of spine sheathed in tough skin
A fan of enlarged rear scales
A flap of cartilage grown back from the gills
context: The mola's rudder, the clavus, forms where its dorsal and anal fins wrap around and meet at the blunt rear — not a tail fin at all. Source: Wikipedia — Ocean sunfish; Monterey Bay Aquarium.

question: The ocean sunfish (Mola mola) is often seen lying flat on its side at the surface, one flank turned up to the sky and the seabirds. Scientists think this odd sunbathing pose isn't only about warmth — it also invites the birds to do something useful. What are the birds doing?
answer: Picking parasites off its exposed skin
choices: Picking parasites off its exposed skin
Guiding it away from shallow water
Warning it of approaching sharks
Cracking open its skin for food
context: Seabirds land on the basking mola and pick parasites off its skin while cleaner fish work its underside — the fish is loaded with parasites, so cleaning matters. Source: Wikipedia — Ocean sunfish; U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service.

question: The ocean sunfish, called Mola mola, is a warm-basking giant that lolls at the surface soaking up the sun. Yet when biologists tagged some, they saw something strange: as many as 40 times a day, the fish plunges into the crushing dark near 1,000 metres. Down there, in cold water where few predators follow, it hunts jellyfish. Then it labors its huge body all the way back up to the surface every single time. Why the repeated trip back up?
answer: To reheat its body chilled by the cold deep
choices: To reheat its body chilled by the cold deep
To gulp air for buoyancy control
To digest food only in bright light
To shed the pressure of the deep
context: The mola dives deep to feed in cold water, then reheats its chilled body at the warm surface like a big solar panel — earning it the nickname 'solar-powered fish.' Source: U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service — 'The Solar-Powered Fish with Jellies in Their Bellies: Molas'; Wikipedia — Ocean sunfish.

question: An octopus has eight rubbery arms and no bones in its body. Its whole head is soft and squeezable, and it can squirt itself through a hole no wider than a coin. But there is one small part of an octopus that is truly hard — the only firm piece in the entire animal. Which part is it?
answer: Its beak
choices: Its beak
Its inner shell
A plate in its gut
Its innermost sucker
context: The beak is the octopus's only hard part — everything else is pure muscle and skin. Source: Oregon Coast Aquarium DYK; sharksandco.com/the-octopus-that-can-squeeze-through-any-gap-1-7369/

question: A hungry fish corners an octopus on the reef. The octopus has no shell and no armour, but it has one hidden trick. It fills its baggy body with a big gulp of seawater, then squeezes hard and blasts the water out in one sharp push — and rockets backward through the water like a jet. Which body part does it fire that water through?
answer: Its siphon, a muscular tube
choices: Its siphon, a muscular tube
Its gills, packed with feathers
Its beak, snapped wide open
Its arms, gripping the seabed
context: The octopus fills its mantle with water and blasts it out through a muscular tube called the siphon, rocketing itself backward. Source: cimi.org/blog/octopus-jet-propulsion/; ocean.si.edu invertebrates

question: An octopus is fleeing a hungry shark. In a single instant it shoots away with a jet of water pushed out of its body. Behind it, the octopus squirts a thick dark cloud into the sea. What does that dark cloud actually do for the octopus?
answer: It hides the octopus behind a smoke screen
choices: It hides the octopus behind a smoke screen
It stuns the predator with an electric jolt
It poisons the water for a mile around
It glows to blind the predator
context: The ink is squirted into the same water jet the octopus uses to escape, making a dark screen. The ink also contains tyrosinase, which irritates a predator's eyes and garbles its smell and taste. Source: cimi.org/blog/octopus-jet-propulsion/; smithsonianmag.com ten-wild-facts-about-octopuses

question: An octopus has no bones anywhere in its body. Only one part of it is hard — its parrot-like beak, hidden at the centre of its eight arms. That means even a 50-pound giant Pacific octopus can pour its whole rubbery body through an opening no bigger than what?
answer: A two-inch coin
choices: A two-inch coin
A wedding ring
A keyhole
A walnut shell
context: With no skeleton, an octopus can squeeze through any gap its beak fits through — so a 50-pound animal can flow through a two-inch hole. Source: facebook.com/OregonCoastAquarium DYK post; sharksandco.com/the-octopus-that-can-squeeze-through-any-gap-1-7369/  (Legend.)

question: An octopus's beak sits hidden in the middle of its ring of eight arms, right at its mouth. The beak looks and works like bone, and it can crush the shells of crabs and clams. But it is not bone at all. It is made of a tough material called chitin. Where else in nature is that same chitin found?
answer: In crab claws and insect shells
choices: In crab claws and insect shells
In fish scales and shark skin
In coral reefs and clam pearls
In turtle shells and cow horns
context: Chitin is the same tough material that builds crab claws and the exoskeletons of insects. Source: theenvironmentalblog.org/2025/07/do-octopuses-have-beaks/

question: Most animals get by with a single heart pumping blood around their whole body. An octopus, though, has a surprising number of hearts, each one pushing its blue copper-based blood through a different part of the animal. How many hearts does an octopus have?
answer: Three
choices: Three
One
Two
Five
context: Two hearts pump blood only through the gills to load it with oxygen; a third pumps that blood to the rest of the body. Source: smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/ten-wild-facts-about-octopuses

question: A chameleon slowly shifts colour over many seconds by moving pigments around inside its skin cells. An octopus can flash a whole new pattern across its body in the blink of an eye. Beneath octopus skin sit thousands of tiny colour sacs called chromatophores. What makes the octopus so much faster at changing colour than the chameleon?
answer: Muscles yank its color sacs open
choices: Muscles yank its color sacs open
Sunlight warms its skin
Its blood flushes into the skin
Hormones ripple across its body
context: Under the chromatophores sit even more skin cells: iridophores that flash shimmery colors and leucophores that mirror surrounding light. Source: livescience.com/how-do-octopuses-change-color; scienceabc.com colorblind-octopuses

question: Reach out and touch something and you feel it — the ridges of a shell, the fuzz of a leaf. Now imagine getting the flavour at the same time. When an octopus lays the suckers on its arms against a rock, a crab, or a bit of food, its skin does something we cannot. What does each sucker let the octopus do?
answer: Taste whatever it touches
choices: Taste whatever it touches
See in total darkness
Hear distant sounds
Smell across the whole ocean
context: Every sucker is studded with chemoreceptors, so the octopus tastes the world with its arms. A giant Pacific octopus has about 2,000 suckers — roughly 280 per arm. Source: gizmodo.com/researchers-finally-figured-out-how-octopuses-taste; americanoceans.org giant-pacific-octopus suckers

question: An octopus is one of the smartest animals without a backbone. It has around 500 million nerve cells in its body — about the same number as a dog has. But most of those nerve cells are not packed into its head at all. Where do about two-thirds of an octopus's neurons actually live?
answer: In its arms
choices: In its arms
In its three hearts
In its skin
In its eyes
context: Each arm has its own cluster of nerve cells acting like a mini-brain, so an arm can grab food or explore a hole without waiting for orders from the central brain. Source: maketecheasier.com octopus-neurons; biologyinsights.com octopus-brain-anatomy  (Legend.)

question: An octopus is a boneless eight-armed hunter of the reef. It can vanish against any rock, coral, or patch of sand it settles on, changing its skin to match the background so perfectly that its eyes seem to miss nothing. Yet when scientists tested those eyes in the lab, they found one surprising limit. What can an octopus eye NOT do?
answer: Tell one color from another
choices: Tell one color from another
Focus a crisp, sharp image
Swivel around on its own
Close behind a proper lid
context: An octopus's eyes carry just one visual pigment, making it colorblind — yet it still matches the colors around it, and exactly how it does that remains an open puzzle. Source: scienceabc.com colorblind-octopuses; pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1524578113  (Legend.)

question: Deep in the cold Pacific, scientist Bruce Robison and his team from the Monterey Bay Aquarium sent a submersible robot down to the same rocky ledge again and again over four and a half years. Each visit they found the same female octopus — a species called Graneledone boreopacifica — curled protectively over her clutch of eggs. She never left them. She never even ate. How long did she guard her eggs?
answer: About four and a half years
choices: About four and a half years
About three weeks
About six months
About ten years
context: For 53 months she guarded her clutch of about 160 eggs and never ate once, slowly starving, and died soon after they hatched. Source: journals.plos.org PLoS ONE 10.1371/journal.pone.0103437; nationalgeographic.com octopus-cares-for-her-eggs-for-53-months  (Legend.)

question: After a female octopus lays her eggs in a rocky den, she stops eating and stays with them, cleaning them and fanning them with water. She slowly starves as she guards them, and she dies soon after they hatch — a death her own body switches on for her on purpose. In the laboratory, scientists tried a change on the mother octopus that turned the dying off and kept her alive and feeding. What did they change?
answer: They cut out two glands behind her eyes
choices: They cut out two glands behind her eyes
They fed her a steady supply of crabs
They took every egg out of her den
They chilled the water in her tank
context: After a female lays her eggs, her optic glands release self-destructive chemicals that make her stop eating; in experiments, octopuses whose optic glands were removed stopped starving and kept living. Source: smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/ten-wild-facts-about-octopuses

question: Every octopus alive today has eight arms. But the oldest known fossil on the octopus branch, Syllipsimopodi bideni, swam the seas 100 million years before the first dinosaurs and had a body plan its descendants later reduced. How many arms did that ancient ancestor have?
answer: Ten, each with a double row of suckers
choices: Ten, each with a double row of suckers
Eight, exactly like octopuses today
Six, with the front pair fused into a hood
Twelve, ringing the mouth in a single crown
context: The ~12 cm Syllipsimopodi bideni fossil comes from the Bear Gulch limestone of Montana, dated to the Mississippian (Serpukhovian), roughly 330 to 323 million years ago. That is about 100 million years before the earliest dinosaurs, and its discovery pushed the octopus lineage's fossil record back some 82 million years past the previous oldest specimen. Crucially it had ten arms, each carrying a double (biserial) row of suckers, so the familiar eight-armed body plan came LATER, by reducing one arm pair. Source: Whalen & Landman, Nature Communications 13:1107 (2022), 'Fossil coleoid cephalopod from the Mississippian Bear Gulch Lagerstatte' (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8904582/).  (Legend.)

question: Deep in a warm forest at night, a spider called the ogre-faced spider hangs head-down over a game trail on a thread of silk. Between its four front legs it holds a small stretchy web, pinched tight like a miniature fishing net. When a beetle wanders along the leaf litter beneath it, what does the ogre-faced spider do with that little web?
answer: Throws it down over the beetle like a fisherman casting a net
choices: Throws it down over the beetle like a fisherman casting a net
Drops a sticky line to reel the beetle upward
Wraps the beetle after it blunders into a hanging trap
Spits a glue thread to pin the beetle in place
context: The ogre-faced spider (genus Deinopis) is a net-caster: it holds a small stretchy net between its four front legs and plunges it down over passing prey, then snaps it shut. The net is not sticky but is made of woolly cribellate silk whose coiled threads tangle up anything that touches them, and it can stretch to two or three times its relaxed size the instant it is flung, so a small net can wrap a much bigger insect. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deinopis ; https://australian.museum/learn/animals/spiders/net-casting-spiders/  (Legend.)

question: The ogre-faced spider is a slim, long-legged spider named for the two huge, moon-round eyes that stare out of its face at night. By day it does not spin a hidden shelter or dig a burrow. Instead it survives the daylight hours right out in the open, in plain sight of birds and lizards, by doing what?
answer: Stretching its thin body and legs out straight to look like a stick
choices: Stretching its thin body and legs out straight to look like a stick
Curling into a tight ball resembling a dead bud
Wrapping itself in a papery cocoon of silk
Coating its body in bits of bark and lichen
context: By day the ogre-faced spider stretches its long thin body and legs out straight along a twig, looking exactly like a stick so predators pass it by. It only unfurls to hunt after dark. Source: https://australian.museum/learn/animals/spiders/net-casting-spiders/

question: The ogre-faced spider — also called the net-casting spider — hunts at night. It holds a small stretchy silk net between its front legs and drops it over any passing bug. The spider is named for the two huge round eyes that stare off the front of its head. Those eyes are the largest simple eyes of any spider. What do they let it do that few hunters can?
answer: Aim its throwing net in near-total darkness
choices: Aim its throwing net in near-total darkness
Spot a warm-blooded animal by its body heat
See the ultraviolet patterns painted on flowers
Snap into sharp focus on prey a meter away
context: The genus name Deinopis is Greek for 'fearful appearance' (deinos = fearful, opis = appearance), and the 'ogre face' is those two huge central eyes. They are the largest simple eyes of any spider and gather light about 2,000 times more efficiently than human eyes, giving superb night vision. Uniquely, the spider has no reflective tapetum like a cat's; instead it grows a fresh sheet of light-sensitive membrane inside each eye every night and destroys it at dawn. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deinopis  (Legend.)

question: The ogre-faced spider hunts by throwing a tiny stretchy web net down at bugs walking underneath it. To find out how it aims in the dark, scientists at Cornell University blindfolded some of these spiders. The blindfolded spiders could no longer catch bugs crawling on the ground. Yet somehow they still snatched flying insects right out of midair. In a 2020 paper the Cornell team showed the spider pulls off that midair catch by doing what?
answer: Hearing the insect's wingbeats through sensors in its legs
choices: Hearing the insect's wingbeats through sensors in its legs
Feeling the wind gusts from the wingbeats on fine body hairs
Smelling the insect through chemical pits on its feet
Tasting vibrations carried up its own silk draglines
context: In 2020 Jay Stafstrom and Ronald Hoy at Cornell discovered the ogre-faced spider can hear despite having no ears, sensing sound through metatarsal organs near the tips of its legs. When they played low tones (about 150-750 Hz, the wingbeat frequencies of moths, flies and mosquitoes), more than half the spiders lurched into a backward flip-strike, netting the imagined flying insect out of the air. The finding confirmed a hunch Cornell's Charles Walcott had proposed roughly 60 years earlier and that other scientists had dismissed. Sources: https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2020/10/buzz-kill-spiders-hear-airborne-prey-their-legs ; https://www.sciencenews.org/article/ogre-faced-spider-hearing-catch-insects-prey-air-sound-sight  (Legend.)

question: Deep inside a pitch-black cave in the mountains of South America, a big reddish-brown bird flies through the darkness between the walls. It cannot see anything down there. So it fires off fast clicking sounds and listens for the echoes bouncing back off the rock. Bats use this exact same echolocation trick. Which bird is this?
answer: The oilbird
choices: The oilbird
The barn owl
The kiwi
The nightjar
context: The oilbird (Steatornis caripensis) of northern South America is one of the very few birds on Earth that echolocates. Its clicks are pitched low enough (about 2 kHz) that a person standing in the cave can hear them, unlike a bat's ultrasonic clicks. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oilbird

question: The oilbird is the only night-flying bird in the world that lives entirely on fruit. Each night it leaves its cave in the dark and heads for oily palm and laurel fruits ripening high in the canopy. When the oilbird reaches a fruit, how does it get that fruit off the tree?
answer: Hovers and twists in mid-air to pluck each fruit off the branch
choices: Hovers and twists in mid-air to pluck each fruit off the branch
Perches on the branch and works the fruit loose with its hooked beak
Shakes the whole branch until ripe fruits rain down to gather below
Snips through the fruit's stalk and lets it drop into the leaf litter
context: The oilbird is the only nocturnal flying fruit-eating bird known. It takes each palm and laurel fruit on the wing, hovering and contorting in the dark to snatch them one by one, then flies on -- making it a champion seed-scatterer, since it swallows fruit whole and drops the seeds far across the forest. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oilbird  (Legend.)

question: Baby oilbirds gorge on oil-rich fruit until they grow fatter than their own parents -- up to about a third heavier. Long ago people climbed into the caves and made use of exactly this. What did they do with the fat chicks that gave the bird its name?
answer: Boiled them down into oil to burn in lamps and cook with
choices: Boiled them down into oil to burn in lamps and cook with
Sold their bright feathers to hat-makers in the cities
Kept them as caged singers for their echoing calls
Raised them on farms as a fast-growing meat bird
context: This rendering of the fat chicks for lamp oil is the reason the bird's scientific name Steatornis literally means 'fat bird.' Framed here as historical account of the practice that named the species. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oilbird  (Legend.)

question: A single oilbird cave can hold 15,000 birds, and in the dark they all click at once -- a deafening racket of echoes. Yet each bird can still find the return of its OWN click in the storm of sound. How does an oilbird tell its echo apart from its neighbors'?
answer: Each bird clicks at a slightly different pitch from those around it
choices: Each bird clicks at a slightly different pitch from those around it
Each bird clicks only when the others fall briefly silent
Each bird fires its clicks in a rhythm it alone can recognize
Each bird aims a tight beam of clicks and ignores echoes off to the side
context: The oilbird's clicks come in astonishingly fast bursts, and neighbors pitch theirs slightly differently, so a bird can pick its own echo out of the noise of thousands clicking together. Its clicks only switch on when a cave grows too dark even for its super-sensitive eyes. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oilbird

question: Deep in the Congo rainforest of central Africa lives a shy animal that walks alone through the shadows, quietly nibbling leaves. It has a rich chocolate-brown coat and big round radar ears. Its rump and legs are marked with bold black-and-white stripes, like a zebra's. What is this strange striped forest animal?
answer: The okapi
choices: The okapi
The bongo
The tapir
The forest buffalo
context: The okapi (Okapia johnstoni) lives only in the dense rainforests of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. So shy and solitary that it stayed hidden from Western science until 1901, it was one of the last large land mammals on the planet to be described. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okapi

question: The okapi is a shy, dark, deer-sized animal that lives deep in the Congo rainforest. Its lower legs are painted in bold black-and-white zebra stripes, so the first Europeans to hear about it guessed 'some kind of forest zebra.' But the okapi's genes tell a very different story. It is not related to zebras at all. It has just one living relative on Earth, and that animal looks very different. Which one?
answer: The giraffe
choices: The giraffe
The wild horse
The greater kudu
The bush pig
context: The okapi and the giraffe are the only two living members of the family Giraffidae, sharing a common ancestor about 11.5 million years ago. The okapi is essentially a giraffe that stayed short and hid in the forest — a short-necked forest cousin, the two the last survivors of their family. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okapi

question: The okapi is a shy forest cousin of the giraffe that lives in the Congo rainforest. It has no paws to wipe its face and no pond to splash in, yet it stays remarkably clean. Its trick is a ~30 cm blue-black prehensile tongue — long, muscular, and flexible enough to grasp like a finger. With that amazing tongue an okapi can groom two body parts almost no other mammal on Earth can even reach. Which two body parts?
answer: Its own eyes and ears
choices: Its own eyes and ears
The soles of its feet
The middle of its back
The tip of its tail
context: The okapi's tongue runs around 30 cm and has been reported up to 46 cm (18 inches) — long enough to lick clean its own eyes and even its own ears, making it one of the very few mammals on Earth able to lick its own ears. The same tongue wraps around branches to strip off leaves, just as its giraffe cousin strips an acacia. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okapi

question: Chasing rumors of a striped 'African unicorn,' the colonial official Sir Harry Johnston expected to find some kind of forest-dwelling horse. Then he examined the tracks the creature left behind — and a single detail told him this was no horse or zebra at all. What did those tracks reveal?
answer: They were cloven — split into two toes
choices: They were cloven — split into two toes
They came in a slow spiral
They were webbed like a duck's
They were clawed like a big cat's
context: Legend: locals had long known the creature, and explorer Henry Morton Stanley heard of an 'atti' in 1887. Johnston expected a forest horse, but the tracks were CLOVEN-hoofed — two toes, not the single hoof of a horse or zebra. A striped skin and a skull sent to London let zoologist Ray Lankester declare it an unknown giraffe relative, naming it Okapia johnstoni in 1901. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okapi

question: Heavy rains flooded the caves under Postojna in Slovenia. Pale, finger-sized animals came washing up from the ground. The villagers were sure they knew what these were. They thought a great beast slept below. What did they think the washed-up animals were?
answer: Baby dragons
choices: Baby dragons
Drowned salamanders
River eels
Lost fish
context: For centuries locals believed the olm (Proteus anguinus) was the young of a dragon living deep beneath the earth, flushed to the surface by floods. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olm  (Legend.)

question: The olm is a slender, pale amphibian with skin the colour of raw fish, tiny useless eyes, and feathery pink gills sticking out behind its head. It spends its whole 100-year life in the black underground rivers inside European limestone caves in places like Slovenia. Slovene speakers there gave this strange underground animal an affectionate folk name that no other creature on Earth wears. What do they call it?
answer: The human fish
choices: The human fish
The ghost eel
The cave worm
The pink serpent
context: The olm's pinkish, human-toned skin earned it the Slovene name cloveska ribica, the 'human fish.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olm

question: Most amphibians start as water-breathing larvae, then grow up and change body plan for life on land. The olm refuses to finish growing up: it stays in its baby form for its whole century in the water. What does the adult olm still wear that a grown frog has long since lost?
answer: Feathery external gills
choices: Feathery external gills
A slippery jelly coat
A sucker-tipped tail
Rows of armored scales
context: The olm keeps its larval external gills for life, a trait called neoteny that it shares with the axolotl. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olm

question: An adult olm hunts in pitch-black underground rivers where eyes are useless, and its own eyes are tiny and buried under skin. Yet it still finds the tiny animals it eats. Beyond smell and hearing, what faint signal does the olm sense to pinpoint hidden prey?
answer: The electric fields their bodies give off
choices: The electric fields their bodies give off
The warmth of their blood
The bubbles they release
The vibrations of their shells
context: The olm detects the weak electric fields of prey using special ampullary organs, letting it hunt in total darkness. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olm

question: Researchers tagged wild olms and returned to their cave rivers year after year to relocate them, expecting the animals to have wandered off. One olm astonished them: it was found in the exact same spot after an unbroken stretch of time. Roughly how long had that single olm stayed put?
answer: Over seven years
choices: Over seven years
About three months
Nearly forty years
A single winter
context: Most tracked olms moved less than 10 meters over years; one sat in the same spot for 2,569 days, over seven years. Lead researcher Gergely Balazs said 'they are hanging around, doing almost nothing' -- an energy-saving life for an animal that eats rarely and can live a century. Source: https://www.sciencealert.com/scientists-don-t-think-this-olm-bothered-to-move-much-in-7-years

question: Almost every animal alive has its eyes in a tidy matched set. Opabinia was a finger-sized swimmer from seas over 500 million years back. It had a cluster of small eyes on short stalks, plus one big eye in the middle. Count them. How many eyes did it have?
answer: Five
choices: Five
Two
Four
Six
context: A cluster of four eyes on short stalks plus one large eye set in the center gave Opabinia five eyes on top of its head, an odd number no living animal has. Source: Royal Ontario Museum, Burgess Shale.

question: In 1975 Harry Whittington finished his careful new study of Opabinia, a soft creature from ancient rock. He showed his drawing to a room of other scientists. The animal was so unlike anything alive that the meeting reacted in a way no serious talk expects. What did the audience do?
answer: Burst out laughing, sure it couldn't be real
choices: Burst out laughing, sure it couldn't be real
Voted to have his drawing withdrawn
Demanded he re-examine the fossil
Accused him of inventing the specimen
context: The reconstruction looked so bizarre that the whole audience burst out laughing, thinking such an animal couldn't possibly have existed. It had. Source: Royal Ontario Museum, Burgess Shale; corroborated by fossilguy.com. (Legendary/anecdotal.)

question: About 500 million years ago in the shallow Cambrian sea lived a five-eyed oddball animal called Opabinia. It was a soft-bodied swimmer only a few centimetres long, with no jaws and no arms of any kind. But from the very front of its head one long, flexible tube-like organ stuck out — a bit like a vacuum-cleaner hose, about four times as long as the head itself. What did the far tip of that strange front organ end in?
answer: A grasping claw studded with spines
choices: A grasping claw studded with spines
A fan of feathery breathing gills
A ring of tiny grinding teeth
A soft glowing lure for luring prey
context: At the front of its head Opabinia carried a long, flexible nozzle or hose, roughly four times longer than its head, ending in a grasping claw studded with small spines that it used to gather food. Source: Royal Ontario Museum, Burgess Shale.

question: Opabinia plucked morsels off the seafloor with the clawed hose on its head, then had to hand each scrap over to its mouth. For most animals the mouth sits up front, near where food is caught. But Opabinia's mouth sat in an unexpected spot that forced a whole extra maneuver. Where was its mouth?
answer: On the underside, opening backward
choices: On the underside, opening backward
At the very tip of the clawed hose
On the top of its head between the eyes
At the rear, flanking the tail fins
context: Opabinia's mouth sat on the underside of its body and pointed backward, so it used the claw on its hose to pluck food and pass it back and under to that rear-facing mouth. Source: Royal Ontario Museum, Burgess Shale.

question: The orca is a sleek black-and-white sea animal that hunts in tight family groups from the icy Arctic to the icy Antarctic. People often call the orca the 'killer whale,' and it can indeed kill big prey like seals and even sharks. But the famous 'whale' nickname gets its family wrong. What kind of animal is an orca really?
answer: The largest dolphin
choices: The largest dolphin
A type of small whale
A cold-water shark
A giant porpoise
context: Orcinus orca is the biggest member of the dolphin family, Delphinidae — despite the "whale" in its common name. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orca ; https://us.whales.org/whales-dolphins/facts-about-orcas/

question: The orca — also called the killer whale — is the biggest hunter in the dolphin family, a black-and-white predator that hunts fish, seals, and even other whales. Scientists divide the world's seas into five great oceans: the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Arctic, and Southern (the icy ring around Antarctica). Of those five, in how many can you find wild orcas?
answer: All five
choices: All five
Just the Pacific
The three coldest
Only two
context: Orcas live in all five of the world's oceans — they are the most widely distributed of all whales and dolphins, and one of the most widely distributed mammals on Earth. Source: https://us.whales.org/whales-dolphins/facts-about-orcas/

question: A big male orca — the black-and-white killer whale, the biggest hunter in the dolphin family — can stretch 8 metres long and weigh over 6 tonnes, as much as a truck. Inside its jaws sit more than 40 curved, interlocking teeth, built for gripping fish, seals, and even other whales. About how long is each one of those teeth?
answer: About 10 cm — the length of your finger
choices: About 10 cm — the length of your finger
About 1 cm — like a house cat's
About 30 cm — like a steak knife
About 2 mm — barely a bump
context: An orca's teeth are about 10 cm (4 inches) long and curve inward, interlocking to grip slippery prey. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orca ; https://www.britannica.com/animal/killer-whale

question: Different orca groups each lock onto one kind of prey. They pass down their own calls and hunting tricks. One rare, shy group eats only sharks. That choice shows up in the mouth. Shark skin is rough like sandpaper. What does it do to the orcas' teeth?
answer: Wears their teeth down to the gum line
choices: Wears their teeth down to the gum line
Leaves them completely toothless at birth
Turns their teeth bright orange
Makes their teeth grow back doubled
context: The elusive "offshore" ecotype eats sharks, whose rough, sandpaper-like skin grinds the orcas' teeth right down to the gum line. Source: https://www.seadocsociety.org/offshore-killer-whale-facts ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12315212/

question: On the freezing seas of Antarctica, a Weddell seal lounges safe on a floating slab of ice, well out of reach of the water below. Four orcas — the huge black-and-white dolphins we call killer whales — line up shoulder-to-shoulder just under the surface. Together they charge the floe at full speed. What are they making with that coordinated rush?
answer: A wave that sweeps the seal off the ice
choices: A wave that sweeps the seal off the ice
A loud noise to scare it into the sea
A ring of bubbles to trap it
A tunnel dug under the floe
context: Antarctic orcas hunt by "wave-washing" — charging four-abreast to push a wave over an ice floe and sweep the resting seal into the water. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/article/animals-up-close-wave-washing-killer-whales  (Legend.)

question: A pod of orcas — the giant killer whales of the polar seas — has learned an incredible hunting trick. They line up side by side and charge under an ice floe together, making a wall of water that washes a resting seal right off into the ocean. This wave-washing hunt is so tricky that only about 100 orcas in all of Antarctica know how to do it. How does a young orca come to learn this rare skill?
answer: An older female of the pod teaches it, passed down the generations
choices: An older female of the pod teaches it, passed down the generations
Every orca is born knowing it by instinct
They copy it from watching seals
They invent it fresh each hunting season
context: Wave-washing is a learned tradition held by roughly 100 Antarctic orcas, taught down the generations from the pod's matriarch. Source: https://www.discoverwildlife.com/animal-facts/marine-animals/orcas-wave-washing-seals

question: At Península Valdés in Argentina, sea lion pups splash in the shallows just off the sand, sure that no orca would follow them there. To grab a pup, the orca uses a hunting move so risky that almost no other sea animal attempts it. What does the orca do?
answer: Hurls itself right up onto the beach
choices: Hurls itself right up onto the beach
Dives to the seafloor and waits
Blows a net of bubbles around them
Lifts its head to peek above the surface
context: At Península Valdés, orcas deliberately beach themselves to grab sea lion pups, then squirm back to sea — and adults teach this risky technique to their young. Source: https://peninsulavaldes.com/wildlife/orcas  (Legend.)

question: Orcas are one of the very few animals, alongside humans, that go through menopause — females stop having calves in their 30s and 40s yet live to 80 or more. Lauren Brent's study found these old grandmother orcas do something surprising in lean salmon years. What?
answer: Swim at the front and guide the pod to food
choices: Swim at the front and guide the pod to food
Leave the pod to live alone
Stop eating so calves can feed
Sink to the seafloor to rest
context: After menopause, grandmother orcas become pod leaders; Brent's study found the oldest females lead from the front to salmon, especially when food is scarce and their memory matters most. Source: https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/killer-whale-behaviour-shows-granny-knows-best.html ; https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/after-menopause-killer-whale-moms-become-pod-leaders-180954480/  (Legend.)

question: Every orca pod speaks its own "dialect" of calls, unique to that family and unchanged for over 25 years. In 1987 an orca in Puget Sound's K-pod started a stranger fad that swept all three pods in months, then vanished — and returned in 2024. What was the fad?
answer: Balancing a dead salmon on its head like a hat
choices: Balancing a dead salmon on its head like a hat
Whistling in a brand-new tune
Slapping tails in a synchronized line
Chasing boats in circles
context: The 1987 "salmon hat" fad spread across the resident pods, disappeared, then reappeared in 2024 — still unexplained. Pod dialects, by contrast, pass down almost unchanged across decades. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salmon_hat ; https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/for-orcas-dead-salmon-hats-are-back-in-fashion/  (Legend.)

question: Off Norway, a pod of orcas circles a school of herring, blowing curtains of bubbles and flashing their white bellies to pack the fish into a tight glittering ball near the surface. Then one whale does the thing that actually kills the fish. What is it?
answer: Whips its tail into the ball, and the shockwave stuns the herring
choices: Whips its tail into the ball, and the shockwave stuns the herring
Lunges in with open jaws and swallows the whole ball at once
Bites the packed school clean in half with a snap of its teeth
Rams the ball at speed to crush the fish against the surface
context: This is carousel feeding. Norwegian orcas herd a herring school into a tight bait ball at the surface, working in shifts so it never scatters, then a whale swings its powerful flukes into the ball. The tail-slap sends out a shockwave and pressure change that stun or kill up to about 15 herring at once, and the whale picks off the stunned fish one by one. Herding and striking are traded around the pod so the ball stays packed. Source: Simon et al., acoustic behaviour of Norwegian killer whales during carousel foraging (https://www.researchgate.net/publication/240765692); National Geographic, "How Orcas Work Together to Whip Up a Meal" (https://www.nationalgeographic.com/magazine/article/orcas-feeding-cooperative-hunting-killer-whales); Wikipedia, "Carousel feeding" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carousel_feeding).

question: The mammal-hunting and the fish-eating orcas of the North Pacific never interbreed, keep entirely separate calls and diets, and split from each other hundreds of thousands of years ago. In 2024 a marine-mammal taxonomy committee finally voted on how to classify them. How did they end up officially ranked?
answer: As two subspecies of one killer-whale species
choices: As two subspecies of one killer-whale species
As two full and separate killer-whale species
As one single species with no subdivisions at all
As two distinct genera, split above species level
context: In 2024 Morin and colleagues proposed splitting these into two full species: the mammal-hunting Bigg's (transient) orca as Orcinus rectipinnus ("erect wing," for its tall pointed dorsal fin) and the fish-eating resident orca as Orcinus ater. The Society for Marine Mammalogy's Taxonomy Committee narrowly fell short of the two-thirds vote needed for full species, so it recognized them instead as subspecies -- Orcinus orca rectipinnus and Orcinus orca ater. Whether these lifelong-separate lineages are one species or several is still a live, unsettled debate. Source: Morin et al. 2024, "Revised taxonomy of eastern North Pacific killer whales," Royal Society Open Science (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10966402/); NOAA Fisheries feature (https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/feature-story/new-research-reveals-full-diversity-killer-whales-two-species-come-view-pacific-coast); Society for Marine Mammalogy 2024 annual review (https://marinemammalscience.org/smm-news/taxonomy-committee-2024-annual-review/).

question: Deep in a rain forest of Southeast Asia, a small pink-and-white insect perches on a bare green leaf. Its four legs are flared into rounded shapes that look exactly like flower petals, and bees fly straight in and try to land on it — mistaking the bug for a real blossom. What creature is this master of floral disguise?
answer: The orchid mantis
choices: The orchid mantis
A pink crab spider
A flower-mimic katydid
A blossom-shaped treehopper
context: The orchid mantis (Hymenopus coronatus) has upper leg segments flattened into heart- and petal-shapes, so its whole body reads as a pink-and-white blossom; insects fly straight toward it thinking it is a flower. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hymenopus_coronatus

question: The orchid mantis is a pink-and-white insect of Southeast Asia whose petal-shaped legs make it look like a wild orchid, tricking bees into flying right up to it. But a newly hatched baby mantis looks nothing like a flower yet. Its very first body is bright red-orange and black, and in this earliest stage it disguises itself as an entirely different kind of insect. Which one?
answer: A hard-biting, foul-tasting assassin bug
choices: A hard-biting, foul-tasting assassin bug
A stinging paper wasp on patrol
A blister beetle oozing toxic oil
A soldier ant marching in column
context: First-instar orchid mantis nymphs are red-orange and black and mimic a foul-tasting, hard-biting assassin bug (family Reduviidae), so predators leave them alone until they molt into the pink flower form. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hymenopus_coronatus

question: The orchid mantis is a small pink-and-white insect from Southeast Asia whose body mimics a flower well enough to fool bees. Biologist James O'Hanlon wanted to test just how good the trick really was. He set orchid mantises alone on plain green leaves — with no real flowers on them at all — near beds of wild blossoms, then watched where the bees and other pollinators flew. What happened?
answer: More pollinators flew to the fake mantis than to the real flowers
choices: More pollinators flew to the fake mantis than to the real flowers
The bees split about evenly between the mantis and the flowers
The bees ignored the mantis until it grew larger petal lobes
The mantis had to copy one orchid's scent to draw any bees
context: O'Hanlon's 2014 field experiments showed isolated mantises on plain leaves lured wild pollinators at a higher rate than real flowers growing nearby - the first confirmed case of an animal using floral mimicry as a lure, not just camouflage. Source: O'Hanlon, Holwell & Herberstein 2014, 'Pollinator Deception in the Orchid Mantis', The American Naturalist 183(1); https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/full/10.1086/673858  (Legend.)

question: The orchid mantis is a small pink insect from the rainforests of Southeast Asia. Its four legs are shaped and coloured like flower petals, so for years people thought those petals lured bees and flies in close for the mantis to grab. Then the biologist James O'Hanlon put that idea to the test. When he trimmed the petals off, bugs still flew in and got caught by the mantis anyway. So what does O'Hanlon now suspect those famous flower-petal legs are really for?
answer: Hiding the mantis from its own predators
choices: Hiding the mantis from its own predators
Signalling health to rival mantises
Sweeping pollen loose to eat off the leg
Cushioning the mantis when it drops off a branch
context: When O'Hanlon removed or rearranged the petal-shaped leg lobes, pollinators still approached - suggesting the famous 'petals' may not lure prey at all, but instead help hide the mantis from its own predators. Source: https://www.sciencefriday.com/articles/unraveling-the-orchid-mantis-mystery/

question: Stand on the wide African plains beside the ostrich — a flightless bird taller than a grown man, up to nine feet high and weighing past 300 pounds. Two huge feathery wings fold on its back. Yet the ostrich never once leaves the ground, all because of one deep flaw in its chest. What keeps this giant grounded for good?
answer: A breastbone too flat to anchor flight muscles
choices: A breastbone too flat to anchor flight muscles
Wings far too small for its heavy body
Bones so hollow they snap under strain
Feathers that soak up water like a sponge
context: The ostrich is the largest and heaviest living bird: males stand up to 9 feet tall and weigh 220-287 pounds, with some sources reporting 300+ lb. It is flightless because its flattened sternum (breastbone) has no keel to anchor flight muscles. Source: San Diego Zoo Animals & Plants (animals.sandiegozoo.org/animals/ostrich).

question: The ostrich is the biggest bird alive on Earth — a two-legged African giant that stands taller than a grown man and cannot fly at all. But when a predator like a lion chases one across the open savanna, the ostrich quickly leaves it behind on its huge striding legs. In a full sprint, about how fast can an ostrich run?
answer: Around 43 mph
choices: Around 43 mph
Around 15 mph
Around 25 mph
Around 60 mph
context: The ostrich is the fastest running bird in the world. It can sprint up to 43 mph (70 km/h) in short bursts and hold a steady cruising speed around 31 mph (50 km/h) over distance. Source: San Diego Zoo Animals & Plants (animals.sandiegozoo.org/animals/ostrich).

question: On the dry grasslands of Africa, an ostrich hen — the largest living bird — settles a single pale egg into her shallow ground nest. It is easily the biggest bird egg in the world. Crack one into a bowl to match it against the eggs from your fridge, and how many ordinary chicken eggs would it take to equal that one shell?
answer: About two dozen
choices: About two dozen
About three
About eight
About fifty
context: The ostrich lays the largest egg of any living bird: about 3 pounds (1,500 g) and 6 inches long, roughly the weight of 24 chicken eggs in one shell. Source: San Diego Zoo Animals & Plants (animals.sandiegozoo.org/animals/ostrich).

question: The ostrich is the largest bird alive, and it lays the largest egg on Earth — roughly the size of a small pineapple. The egg's shell is only about 3.5 millimetres thick, thinner than a stack of a few coins. That sounds fragile. Yet the curved dome shape lets an ostrich egg hold a startling amount of downward force before it cracks. About how much weight can an ostrich eggshell bear pressing straight down on it?
answer: Enough for a grown adult to stand on it
choices: Enough for a grown adult to stand on it
Barely the weight of a sparrow
No more than a stack of paper
Only the chick's own body weight
context: An ostrich eggshell is only about 3.5 mm thick but strong enough that a grown adult can stand on it without breaking it. It can bear roughly 220 kg pressing straight down. Source: Birdfact (birdfact.com/articles/largest-bird-eggs).  (Legend.)

question: The ostrich is the tallest and heaviest bird alive on Earth, sprinting across the African savanna on two long, powerful legs. Everyone has heard the old story that a frightened ostrich buries its head in the sand — but the story is not actually true. When real danger nears an ostrich on the open plain, what does the bird actually do to hide?
answer: Flattens to the ground so it looks like a low mound
choices: Flattens to the ground so it looks like a low mound
Crouches low and sprints in a zigzag for cover
Sidles behind the nearest bush and holds still
Presses flat against a termite mound and freezes
context: The head-in-sand story is a myth; an ostrich cannot breathe underground. What it really does is flop flat and press its long neck and head to the ground so its body blends into the dirt and looks like a low mound from a distance. Source: San Diego Zoo Animals & Plants (animals.sandiegozoo.org/animals/ostrich).  (Legend.)

question: The ostrich is a huge flightless bird of the African plains, built for sprinting away from lions and hyenas on long, powerful legs. Nearly every other bird alive grips the ground with three or four toes on each foot. The ostrich is the one exception — its foot pared right down for pure speed. How many toes does each ostrich foot carry?
answer: Just two
choices: Just two
Only one
Four spread wide
Three, like most birds
context: The ostrich is the ONLY bird on Earth with just two toes per foot; every other bird has three or more. One toe is huge and the smaller second toe acts as an 'outrigger' to keep balance. Source: San Diego Zoo Animals & Plants; scienceinschool.org/article/2011/ostrich.

question: The ostrich — the giant flightless bird of the African plains — carries the largest eye of any land animal on Earth. Each eye is almost two inches across, dark and glossy, rimmed in long dark lashes and set startlingly big into a small feathered head. That eye is actually so huge it outsizes one particular thing inside the ostrich itself. What?
answer: Its own brain
choices: Its own brain
Its entire foot
A grown man's fist
One of its own eggs
context: The ostrich has the largest eye of any land animal, almost 2 inches (5 cm) across. Each eyeball is actually bigger than its own brain. Source: San Diego Zoo Animals & Plants (animals.sandiegozoo.org/animals/ostrich).  (Legend.)

question: On the African plains, if a lion or a hyena corners an ostrich in the open, the big bird does not turn and flee.
