It swings around and strikes forward with a single powerful clawed foot — a two-toed foot tipped with a dagger-like claw as long as a man's finger. Zookeepers who have worked with adult ostriches warn by reputation that one such kick is strong enough to do what to even a lion?
answer: Kill it outright
choices: Kill it outright
Merely bruise it
Trip it long enough to escape
Frighten it with the noise
context: When cornered, an ostrich defends itself with a forward kick from its clawed foot said to be powerful enough to kill a lion. The claw can act like a knife; the kick is its main weapon against big predators. This lion-killing reputation is often repeated but is difficult to verify, so it is framed here as reputation rather than established fact. Source: San Diego Zoo Animals & Plants (animals.sandiegozoo.org/animals/ostrich).  (Legend.)

question: During the last ice age, tens of thousands of years ago, our own ancestors — modern humans, Homo sapiens — were not the only kind of human walking the Earth. Other species of human, close cousins of our line, roamed the same cold world alongside us. Which of these was a real, separate kind of human that shared the planet with our ancestors?
answer: The Neanderthals of Europe and western Asia
choices: The Neanderthals of Europe and western Asia
The last surviving Australopithecus troops
A tailed forest-dwelling ape-man of the Congo
The sea-dwelling merfolk of the northern coasts
context: During the last ice age at least two close cousins shared the planet with our ancestors: the Neanderthals of Europe and western Asia, and the mysterious Denisovans of Asia. Modern humans were not always the only kind of human on Earth. Source: Smithsonian Human Origins Program, humanorigins.si.edu; Max Planck Institute, mpg.de/5018269/denisovan-genome.

question: The Neanderthals (Homo neanderthalensis) were an ancient human species, cousins of our own line, who lived across Europe and western Asia during the deep cold of the last ice age. They were short and powerfully built, shaped for the frozen climate they hunted in. One feature of their face was strikingly broad and wide compared to ours. Which was it?
answer: The nose
choices: The nose
The ears
The chin
The forehead
context: A Neanderthal's big wide nose is thought to have warmed and moistened the frigid ice-age air they breathed, part of a body built for the cold. Source: Natural History Museum, 'Who were the Neanderthals?', nhm.ac.uk/discover/who-were-the-neanderthals.html.

question: The Neanderthals were an ice-age human species, cousins of our own line, who lived across Europe and western Asia. Old books and cartoons pictured them as dim, slouching 'ape-men' with tiny minds — barely thinking at all. But when scientists actually measured a Neanderthal braincase and compared it to a modern human's, what did they find?
answer: It was just as large as ours, and often a bit larger
choices: It was just as large as ours, and often a bit larger
It was roughly half the size of ours
It had no room for a frontal lobe at all
It was identical to a chimpanzee's in size
context: A Neanderthal's brain was just as large as ours, and often a bit larger, held in a long, low skull with a heavy brow ridge above the eyes. Source: Smithsonian Human Origins Program, humanorigins.si.edu/evidence/human-fossils/species/homo-neanderthalensis.  (Legend.)

question: Neanderthals were a stocky, muscular cousin of ours who lived across ice-age Europe and western Asia tens of thousands of years ago. They hunted big cold-country game — woolly mammoths, giant bison, cave bears — by thrusting long spears into the huge animals up close, again and again. Their fossil skeletons carry a strange signature of this dangerous close-in work. What do the bones of grown Neanderthal hunters show?
answer: Broken bones like the injuries of modern rodeo riders
choices: Broken bones like the injuries of modern rodeo riders
Teeth worn perfectly smooth from eating only grass
Fingers fused together into flipper-like paddles
Skulls thickened into a solid bony helmet
context: Neanderthals were skilled toolmakers and big-game hunters who thrust spears into large animals at close range, so often that their skeletons show broken bones like the injuries of modern rodeo riders. Source: Smithsonian Human Origins Program, humanorigins.si.edu/evidence/human-fossils/species/homo-neanderthalensis.  (Legend.)

question: The Denisovans are another ice-age cousin of modern humans — a lost sister population to the Neanderthals. For years scientists could barely picture them because almost nothing of a Denisovan body had ever been found. Then in 2008, in a place called Denisova Cave deep in the Siberian mountains, one tiny scrap of a body turned up. Its DNA was finally read in 2010 by geneticist Svante Paabo's team, and that reading revealed a whole new kind of human. What was that scrap?
answer: A single tiny finger bone
choices: A single tiny finger bone
A complete lower jaw
A footprint pressed in mud
A painted handprint on the wall
context: The Denisovans were discovered not from a skeleton but from a single tiny finger bone found in Denisova Cave in Siberia in 2008, whose genome was read in 2010 by Svante Paabo's team at the Max Planck Institute. Source: Max Planck Institute, mpg.de/5018269/denisovan-genome; Nobel Prize 2022 press release.  (Legend.)

question: Our own ancestors did not just live near these cousins, they met and interbred with them. When scientists sequenced the DNA of a living person whose roots lie outside Africa and searched their genome for the mark of that ancient mixing, what did they find?
answer: Roughly 1 to 4 percent Neanderthal DNA
choices: Roughly 1 to 4 percent Neanderthal DNA
Roughly 20 to 25 percent Neanderthal DNA
DNA from Homo erectus, but none from Neanderthals
No archaic trace at all, only in ancient fossils
context: Our ancestors met and interbred with both cousins, so most people alive today outside Africa carry a small slice of Neanderthal DNA, roughly 1 to 4 percent of their genome. Source: Max Planck Institute, mpg.de/5018269/denisovan-genome; Science, science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aad9416.

question: High on the Tibetan Plateau, the thin air holds far less oxygen than lowlands, yet Tibetans thrive there. Scientists traced part of their edge to a version of the EPAS1 gene inherited long ago from an extinct cousin. From which cousin did that high-altitude gene come?
answer: The Denisovans
choices: The Denisovans
The Neanderthals
Homo erectus
The Australopithecines
context: A version of the EPAS1 gene inherited from Denisovans helps Tibetans thrive in the thin high-altitude air, a gift from an extinct cousin found today only in Denisovans and Tibetans. Source: Nature, nature.com/articles/nature13408; PNAS, pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2020803118.  (Legend.)

question: Neanderthals and Denisovans were two ice-age cousins of our own species, both now long extinct. In Siberia's Denisova Cave, scientists dug up a small bone from a teenage girl who died about 90,000 years ago. When Svante Paabo's team read her DNA, they got a shock. Her mother's DNA came from a Neanderthal. Her own main DNA was almost exactly half Neanderthal and half Denisovan. What did that combination make her?
answer: A first-generation child of a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father
choices: A first-generation child of a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father
A late Neanderthal whose people had drifted north into Denisovan land
An early Denisovan carrying leftover Neanderthal genes from long ago
A modern human ancestor caught midway between the two older cousins
context: Nicknamed 'Denny,' this ~13-year-old girl was identified in 2018 from a single ~2 cm bone fragment (Denisova 11). Her mitochondrial DNA (inherited only from the mother) was Neanderthal, while her nuclear genome was almost exactly half Neanderthal and half Denisovan, meaning one parent was a Neanderthal and the other a Denisovan. She remains the only confirmed first-generation hybrid of two distinct human groups ever found, showing that when these cousins met, they could interbreed directly, not just with our own ancestors. Source: Slon, Mafessoni, Paabo et al., 'The genome of the offspring of a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father,' Nature 561:113-116 (2018), https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-018-0455-x ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denny_(hybrid_hominin)  (Legend.)

question: Most non-African people carry a small, similar slice of Neanderthal DNA. But Denisovan ancestry is spread very unevenly across the world, piling up in one region and near-absent in most others. In whose genomes does Denisovan DNA reach its highest known levels?
answer: Papuans, Aboriginal Australians and other Melanesians
choices: Papuans, Aboriginal Australians and other Melanesians
Northern Europeans descended from the first cave painters
Peoples of the Siberian plains around Denisova Cave itself
East African groups nearest our species early homeland
context: Melanesians, Papuans/New Guineans and Aboriginal Australians carry roughly 4-6% Denisovan ancestry, by far the most of any human population, and a 2021 study found the Aeta Magbukon of the Philippines carry the highest known proportion of all. Most other populations carry little or none. This is a sharp contrast to the ~1-4% Neanderthal DNA shared by most non-Africans, and it maps onto where Denisovans and our ancestors actually met in Ice Age Asia, far from the Siberian cave where the first Denisovan bones were found. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denisovan ; Larena et al. 2021 (Aeta Magbukon highest Denisovan ancestry), Current Biology; https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2405889121

question: On a moonless night in a farmer's field, a mouse rustles quietly through fallen leaves, hunting for seeds. Suddenly a round-faced night hunter with huge forward-facing eyes drops out of the black sky and snatches the mouse in silent talons. What bird is this famous nocturnal raptor?
answer: An owl
choices: An owl
A hummingbird
A pelican
A flamingo
context: Owls are the classic round-faced, forward-eyed nocturnal raptors, built to hunt in darkness. Source: Cornell Lab of Ornithology, All About Birds.

question: A mouse in a dark field has excellent ears and can usually hear a hunting bird coming from far off — the swoosh of feathered wings gives plenty of warning to bolt for cover. But when an owl attacks in the night, the mouse hears nothing at all until the talons close around it. What is uncanny about the way an owl flies?
answer: It flies almost completely silently
choices: It flies almost completely silently
It flies faster than any other bird
It glows faintly in the dark
It flies backward toward prey
context: An owl's wingbeats make so little noise that a mouse never hears it coming. Source: Audubon Magazine, 'The Silent Flight of Owls, Explained.'

question: When a duck flies overhead you can hear its wings whistling in the air, but a hunting owl swoops through the dark in near-total silence. Look closely at the very front edge of an owl's wing feathers and you can see the secret. A row of something tiny runs along the leading edge of every owl wing feather — something the front of a duck's wing feathers completely lack. What runs along those leading edges?
answer: Tiny comb-like serrations
choices: Tiny comb-like serrations
A stiff bony ridge
A coat of waterproof oil
A row of hooked claws
context: Comb-like serrations on the leading edge break up the turbulent air that would otherwise make a swooshing sound. Source: Audubon Magazine, 'The Silent Flight of Owls, Explained.'

question: An owl hunts at night, and its wing feathers have tiny comb-like edges that let it fly in near-total silence. But that silent flight isn't only useful for sneaking up on a mouse. Because its own wings barely make a sound in the air, the hunting owl gains a second big advantage that a noisy flier like a duck could never enjoy in the dark. What else does that quiet flight buy the hunting owl?
answer: Its ears stay free to track the prey's rustling
choices: Its ears stay free to track the prey's rustling
Its wings never tire on long flights
It stays invisible to other owls
It can fly through heavy rain unbothered
context: With almost no wing noise of its own, the owl's ears keep tracking the prey's faint rustling in the dark. Krista Le Piane's analysis of 70 owl species. Source: Audubon Magazine.

question: A barn owl is a white-faced night-hunting owl that finds its prey in almost total darkness, mostly by sound. It can pinpoint a mouse's tiny rustle not just to the left or the right but also whether it came from higher up or lower down, pinning the prey in three dimensions. Look at the barn owl's skull and you spot one strange feature of its head that makes this 3-D hearing possible. What is odd about a barn owl's head?
answer: Its two ear openings are offset, one higher than the other
choices: Its two ear openings are offset, one higher than the other
Its ears are hidden inside its beak
Its ears can be folded shut in the cold
Its ears glow to attract prey
context: The left ear opening sits higher and points down, the right sits lower and points up. This lopsided arrangement helps it place a sound in three dimensions. Source: Cornell Lab, All About Birds; Wikipedia, 'Sound localization in owls.'

question: A barn owl hunts by sound alone in pitch dark. Telling whether a rustle came from left or right is fairly easy — the sound reaches one ear a hair before the other. But judging whether the sound came from above or below is much harder. Barn owls solved the harder puzzle by using an unusual trick of their offset ears. What cue does a barn owl rely on to place a sound as coming from high up or low down?
answer: How much louder the sound is in one ear than the other
choices: How much louder the sound is in one ear than the other
The pitch of the sound
The delay of its echo
The gap in arrival timing
context: Left-vs-right comes from which ear a sound reaches first, by millionths of a second; up-vs-down comes from which ear it's louder in. Sounds from below are louder in the lower-pointing left ear, from above louder in the right. Two different cues, timing and loudness, working together. Source: Wikipedia, 'Sound localization in owls.'

question: An owl is a nocturnal bird of prey. Its flat, round face isn't just a wise-looking mask — it is a stiff dish of specialized feathers arranged in a shallow bowl. Owls hunt in near-total darkness and rely on their ears as much as their eyes to locate a mouse under leaves. Given that, what job does that facial disc actually do?
answer: It funnels sound waves toward the ear openings
choices: It funnels sound waves toward the ear openings
It dampens the noise of the owl's own wingbeats
It shields the eyes from bright sun
It keeps rain off the beak
context: The concave facial disc collects sound waves and funnels them to the ear openings, like a satellite dish. Source: Wikipedia, 'Facial disc'; 'Sound localization in owls.'

question: A field mouse tunnels along beneath a foot of fresh, muffling snow, completely out of sight and far from any moonlight. A barn owl glides silently overhead on wide white wings. Suddenly it folds those wings and drops, punching through the snow crust right at the exact spot the hidden mouse was running. What single sense did the barn owl use to pin down a target it could never actually see?
answer: By hearing alone
choices: By hearing alone
By its keen sense of smell
By sensing the mouse's body heat
By feeling ground vibrations
context: A barn owl can pinpoint the exact 3-D spot of a mouse under a foot of snow guided by hearing alone, with no view of its target. Legendary but documented. Source: Cornell Lab of Ornithology, All About Birds.

question: An owl's eyes are enormous — long tubes that fill most of its skull to catch every last scrap of moonlight in a dark forest. But an owl cannot glance sideways the way you can. To look off to one side, it has to swing its entire head around, sometimes almost backward. Why can't an owl simply roll its eyes to look beside it?
answer: A ring of bone locks its huge eyes in place
choices: A ring of bone locks its huge eyes in place
Its eyes are too small to aim
It sees only straight ahead by instinct
Bright light freezes its eyes open
context: An owl's eyes are so huge and tube-shaped that they're locked by a ring of bone (the sclerotic ring) and can't roll in their sockets at all, so it must turn its whole head to look around. Source: California Academy of Sciences, 'The (Bird) Eyes Have It.'

question: An owl's huge, forward-facing eyes are so big that they are wedged tightly in place inside its skull — the owl cannot roll them or swivel them the way you or a cat can. So to look around, an owl has to swing its whole head instead. About how far can an owl turn its head?
answer: About 270 degrees, three-quarters of a full circle
choices: About 270 degrees, three-quarters of a full circle
A full 360 degrees, all the way around
About 90 degrees, a quarter turn
About 45 degrees, barely to the shoulder
context: An owl rotates its head up to about 270 degrees to either side. Legendary but true; the 'full circle' myth is false. Source: Smithsonian Magazine, 'Solving the Mystery of Owls' Head-Turning Abilities' (Johns Hopkins study).

question: An owl can swivel its head about three-quarters of the way around to watch a mouse standing behind it — a turn that would pinch shut the neck arteries and starve the brain in almost any other animal. Yet the owl's arteries survive that twist just fine. When scientists finally cut into an owl's neck, they found a bit of clever bony engineering wrapped around each artery. What lets the vessels survive the twist?
answer: The bone channels around them are about ten times wider than the arteries
choices: The bone channels around them are about ten times wider than the arteries
The arteries pump blood in short bursts
A second heart sits in the neck
The blood carries built-in antifreeze
context: An owl has 14 neck vertebrae (humans have 7), and the bony holes around its neck arteries are about ten times wider than the arteries themselves, giving the vessels room to twist. Source: Smithsonian Magazine (Johns Hopkins CT/angiography study, 2013).

question: To keep an owl's brain fed with oxygen while its neck cranks nearly all the way around, evolution added a clever plumbing trick. At Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, a team of scientists ran an owl's head through a CT (computed tomography) scanner and finally saw exactly where the blood goes during the big head-twist. What did the scan reveal?
answer: Into reservoirs at the base of the skull
choices: Into reservoirs at the base of the skull
Straight back down into the heart
Out to the wingtips for storage
Into the hollow bones of the legs
context: Scientists injected dye into owls' arteries and CT-scanned them as the necks turned, finding blood pools in reservoirs at the skull base that keep the brain supplied during the twist. Source: Smithsonian Magazine; phys.org (2013).

question: An owl drops out of the night sky and seizes a struggling rat in its four sharp talons. Its foot muscles could get tired holding on for the flight home — but they don't need to. Something inside the owl's foot snaps the grip shut and keeps it clamped, almost without any effort from the bird. What clicks the talons closed and holds them there?
answer: A locking tendon that ratchets the grip shut
choices: A locking tendon that ratchets the grip shut
A sticky pad on each talon
A set of tiny hooks along the toes
A suction cup in the sole
context: When an owl grabs prey, its outer toe swings back so two talons point forward and two back, then a locking tendon ratchets the grip shut, clamping without any muscle effort. Source: The Owl Pages, 'Owl Feet & Talons.'

question: Everyone agrees an owl flies in near silence, but scientists still argue over what its velvety feather surface is actually FOR. One camp says it smooths the airflow over the wing. What does the rival camp, studying exactly where that velvet is densest, say it really does?
answer: It muffles the noise of feathers scraping against each other
choices: It muffles the noise of feathers scraping against each other
It smooths the airflow rushing over the wing surface
It traps warm air to keep the flight muscles from stiffening
It scatters the moonlight so the owl casts no moving shadow
context: How an owl's feathers actually kill the sound is still a live scientific debate. The long-dominant view (Kroeger, Lilley) holds that the leading-edge comb and downy velvet reduce AERODYNAMIC noise by smoothing airflow and keeping the boundary layer attached over the wing. A competing hypothesis (Christopher Clark, reviving Graham's 1934 idea) points out that the velvety 'pennulae' and vane fringes are best developed exactly where one feather rubs against the next, arguing they mainly muffle STRUCTURAL, frictional noise from feather-on-feather contact during flapping rather than airflow noise. The two camps disagree over what the velvet is even for. Source: PMC 'Evolution and Ecology of Silent Flight in Owls' (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7671161/) - Clark vs. Kroeger/Lilley; Graham (1934).

question: Almost every mammal alive is covered in fur or bare skin. But one shy insect-eater from the forests of Africa and Asia is different — it is armored head to tail in hard, overlapping plates that look like a walking pine cone. Those plates are made of keratin, the same stuff as your fingernails. Which animal is it?
answer: The pangolin
choices: The pangolin
The armadillo
The porcupine
The hedgehog
context: The pangolin is the only mammal covered in scales. Armadillos wear bony plates under their skin; porcupines and hedgehogs bristle with modified hairs. Only the pangolin's coat is true keratin scales. Source: https://www.savepangolins.org/what-is-a-pangolin/  (Legend.)

question: The pangolin is a shy, scale-armored mammal of Africa and Asia that eats ants and termites. When a hungry leopard closes in on one in the forest, the little animal doesn't run and it doesn't fight back. Instead it does the single thing that earned it the Malay name 'penggulung,' meaning 'the roller.' What does the pangolin do?
answer: Curls into a tight armored ball, tucking its soft belly inside
choices: Curls into a tight armored ball, tucking its soft belly inside
Freezes flat and plays dead until the danger passes
Sprays a jet of stinging venom from its snout
Puffs itself up huge with swallowed air
context: 'Penggulung' means 'one who rolls up.' The scaled back and tail wrap around the vulnerable belly and face, leaving nothing soft exposed. Source: https://www.discoverwildlife.com/animal-facts/mammals/facts-about-pangolins

question: A whole pride of African lions surrounds a pangolin — a shy, scale-covered mammal about the size of a house cat that has curled up into a tight armored ball. The lions paw at it, bat it back and forth in the dust, and try again and again to sink their teeth in through the overlapping scales. How does the standoff end?
answer: The lions give up and walk away, leaving the pangolin unharmed
choices: The lions give up and walk away, leaving the pangolin unharmed
One lion finally cracks the shell and the pride feeds
The pangolin bolts free the moment the lions tire
The pangolin is crushed under the pride's combined weight
context: A rolled pangolin's overlapping keratin scales are tough enough that even a full pride cannot bite through. Frustrated, the lions simply move on. Source: https://www.discoverwildlife.com/animal-facts/mammals/facts-about-pangolins  (Legend.)

question: The pangolin is an ant-eating mammal of Africa and Asia whose front claws are so long and curved they're wonderful for ripping open termite mounds — but they are clumsy on the ground. Walking flat-footed would drag those precious digging claws through the dirt and wear them down. To keep them safe, how does the pangolin often get around?
answer: It walks upright on its two hind legs, holding its arms and tail up for balance
choices: It walks upright on its two hind legs, holding its arms and tail up for balance
It drags itself forward on its belly like a seal
It knuckle-walks on the backs of its curled front paws
It hops with both hind feet together like a kangaroo
context: The three big digging claws on each front paw are useless for walking, so a pangolin often rears up and strides on its hind legs, tail and forelimbs raised as a counterweight. Source: https://africageographic.com/stories/fascinating-pangolin-facts/  (Legend.)

question: The pangolin — the scaly, ant-eating mammal of Africa and Asia — has no teeth at all and cannot chew a single insect. Yet ants and termites are its whole diet. To reach the bugs deep inside a nest tunnel, it uncoils an extraordinarily long tongue coated in thick sticky saliva. In a big pangolin, how far can that tongue stretch out?
answer: Up to about 40 cm (16 in), longer than its own head and body
choices: Up to about 40 cm (16 in), longer than its own head and body
Up to about 10 cm (4 in), like a house cat's
Up to about 1 m (3 ft), trailing on the ground
Just past its own lips, a few centimeters
context: A big pangolin's tongue can reach 40 cm, sometimes longer than its head and body combined, gluing ants and termites to it inside their tunnels. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pangolin  (Legend.)

question: To rip open a termite nest is to invite thousands of biting, stinging insects to swarm right at your face. Yet the pangolin — a scaly, ant-eating mammal of Africa and Asia — makes its living tearing exactly those nests apart with its long claws. Before it strikes, it protects itself in a way most other mammals simply can't. What does the pangolin do?
answer: It clamps its ears and nostrils shut with strong muscles
choices: It clamps its ears and nostrils shut with strong muscles
It coats its face in a thick layer of mud first
It attacks only at night when the insects are asleep
It smears itself with the nest's own scent to hide
context: Muscles let a pangolin seal its ears and nostrils closed, keeping swarming ants out while it laps up as many as 20,000 in a single day. Source: https://www.discoverwildlife.com/animal-facts/mammals/facts-about-pangolins

question: A pangolin is a scaly, ant-eating mammal that walks the forests and savannas of Africa and Asia. It has no teeth at all. It swallows its ants whole and toothless, yet somehow grinds up their crunchy shells inside its body. It manages this with a trick a chicken would recognize. How does a pangolin's stomach break down its food?
answer: Swallowed stones churn in a muscular gizzard-like stomach lined with keratin spines
choices: Swallowed stones churn in a muscular gizzard-like stomach lined with keratin spines
Powerful acid dissolves the shells completely within minutes
A second set of throat teeth crushes the ants on the way down
It regurgitates and re-swallows each meal to soften it
context: With no teeth, a pangolin swallows small stones (gastroliths) that collect in a muscular, keratin-spined stomach and grind the insects up, exactly the way a bird's gizzard works. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pangolin

question: The peacock spider is a tiny jumping spider that lives in Australia. It got its name from how the male shows off to a female. Facing her, he lifts his back end straight up into the air and opens up something he keeps normally tucked away against his body. Then he waves it slowly at her like a flag. What is it that the male peacock spider unfurls?
answer: A fan of brilliantly colored flaps
choices: A fan of brilliantly colored flaps
A sticky net of silk threads
A pair of transparent gliding wings
A cluster of glowing light organs
context: The male raises his abdomen and spreads a fan of vividly colored flaps, waving it like a peacock fanning its tail — which is exactly how the peacock spider got its name. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maratus_volans  (Legend.)

question: The peacock spider of Australia carries one of the most brilliantly colored displays in the entire animal kingdom — the male's flag-like back fan flashes in dazzling patterns of blue, red, and orange. Yet finding one in the wild is famously hard, and scientists only really began describing them in the 2000s. How big is a peacock spider?
answer: About the size of a grain of rice
choices: About the size of a grain of rice
About the size of a jellybean
About the size of a housefly
About the size of a ladybug
context: Both males and females are only about 5 mm long — roughly a grain of rice — yet the male packs a dazzling courtship display onto that tiny frame. Their size hid them from science for years. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maratus_volans

question: For a male peacock spider — a tiny jumping spider from Australia only a few millimeters across — the mating display is deadly serious. He raises his colorful back fan and waves it at the watching female in a careful dance. If his performance fails to impress her, this isn't just embarrassing. What may the female peacock spider do to him?
answer: Attack, kill, and eat him
choices: Attack, kill, and eat him
Trap him in her web for days
Sting him with venom to paralyze him
Chase him off her patch of ground
context: An unimpressed female may attack, kill, and eat the male — and she may even do it after mating. That deadly stakes-raising is why the dance has to be so spectacular. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maratus_volans  (Legend.)

question: In the Australian bush lives a jumping spider the size of a grain of rice, called the peacock spider. When a male finds a female, he throws his whole body into a courtship performance: he raises a bright fan of scales like a peacock's tail and waves it while dancing. Beyond the colors of his waving fan, he adds a second, private channel of communication. What is the other signal he sends her?
answer: Vibrations she feels through her legs
choices: Vibrations she feels through her legs
Puffs of scent drifting on the breeze
High-pitched chirps only she can hear
Quick flashes of light bounced off the soil
context: As he dances, the male drums the ground with his abdomen, sending vibrations through the surface that the female picks up through her legs. Scientists named the three vibration types rumble-rumps, crunch-rolls, and grind-revs. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maratus_volans

question: On a sunlit leaf in Australia, a tiny male peacock spider — no bigger than a grain of rice — fans out a colorful flap on his back and dances to court a female. Part of that fan is an 'ultra-black' patch that reflects less than half a percent of light, darker than most black paint. Surprisingly, the patch isn't made by any dark pigment at all. So what actually swallows the light on that patch?
answer: Tiny lens-like bumps on the cuticle that trap it
choices: Tiny lens-like bumps on the cuticle that trap it
A thin layer of black oil that soaks it up
Charcoal-like grains built into the scales
A living film of dark bacteria on the surface
context: The ultra-black comes from microscopic dome-shaped bumps on the cuticle, about 6 micrometers tall, that act like tiny lenses and trap incoming light — reflecting as little as 0.35% in Maratus karrie. No black pigment is involved. Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6532503/  (Legend.)

question: The peacock spider is a tiny Australian jumping spider whose male raises a brilliantly colored fan on his back to court a female. The shimmering blues on that fan can flash and shift as he moves, the same way a soap bubble or a peacock's tail feather changes color as you tilt it. There is no blue paint or blue dye on him at all. How does the spider actually produce that blue?
answer: Nanostructures on its scales that bend light
choices: Nanostructures on its scales that bend light
A dye it absorbs from the insects it eats
Blue pigment cells packed under its skin
Trapped air bubbles beneath its shell
context: The blue is structural color: microscopic nanostructures on the scales bend and reflect just the right wavelength of light — the same physics behind a soap bubble's shimmer — rather than any pigment. Source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6532503/

question: High above a cliff, a crow-sized bird spots prey below. It tucks its wings tight against its body and drops from the sky like a stone. That dive is faster than any other animal on Earth — quicker than a cheetah at full run, quicker than a race car on a track, over 200 miles per hour. Which bird makes this world-record dive?
answer: The peregrine falcon
choices: The peregrine falcon
The golden eagle
The great horned owl
The common raven
context: In its diving plunge the peregrine falcon is the fastest animal alive — faster than any cheetah or racecar. Source: Cornell Lab of Ornithology, All About Birds; Wikipedia 'Peregrine falcon'.  (Legend.)

question: The peregrine falcon, the record-setting diving bird, is one of the most widespread birds on Earth. It nests on rocky sea cliffs, tall city buildings, windy tundra, and hot desert canyons — almost every continent. Only one land has no peregrines at all. Which frozen continent does the peregrine skip?
answer: Antarctica
choices: Antarctica
Australia
South America
Africa
context: Found on every continent except Antarctica, the peregrine is the world's most widespread bird of prey. Source: Wikipedia 'Peregrine falcon'.

question: The peregrine falcon is a hunter of other birds. Its favorite prey are pigeons, ducks, gulls, and songbirds — living targets that must be caught while flying. When a hunting peregrine spots one, it climbs high above, folds its wings, and dives at hundreds of miles per hour. The kill isn't on a tree branch or on the water. Where does the peregrine's strike actually happen?
answer: In mid-air, out of the sky
choices: In mid-air, out of the sky
In shallow water
In tree branches
On open ground
context: The peregrine hunts other birds on the wing, striking them out of the sky rather than catching prey on the ground. Source: Science.org; All About Birds.

question: Peregrine falcons once nested only on remote sea cliffs and mountain crags. In the last fifty years, though, they have spread into the hearts of big cities like New York and Chicago, raising chicks on cathedrals, tall bridges, and high window ledges of skyscrapers. Something drew these wild cliff-hunters downtown. What is the pull of the city for a peregrine?
answer: Flocks of city pigeons to hunt
choices: Flocks of city pigeons to hunt
Warmth rising off the pavement
Fewer eagles competing there
Bright lights that lure insects
context: Peregrines nest on skyscraper ledges and bridges where flocks of city pigeons give them an endless food supply. Source: Wikipedia 'Peregrine falcon'; All About Birds.

question: The peregrine falcon is the fastest animal on Earth, diving through the sky at over 200 miles an hour to strike other birds in mid-air. When a peregrine lays her eggs on a high cliff ledge, she builds no twig cup and weaves nothing at all. So what exactly is a peregrine's 'nest'?
answer: A shallow scrape it scratches into gravel
choices: A shallow scrape it scratches into gravel
A borrowed old eagle nest
A burrow dug in a sandbank
A bare fork in a treetop
context: A peregrine scrapes a shallow depression in gravel or soil on a high ledge and lays its eggs right there — the whole 'nest' is just a scratched-out dip. Source: All About Birds Life History; Wikipedia.

question: In ordinary level flight, a peregrine falcon flaps along at just 25 to 34 miles per hour — no faster than a car in a school zone. Even when it flaps hard chasing prey, it barely reaches 69 mph. Yet the peregrine holds the world record as the fastest animal on Earth, over 240 mph. It doesn't get there by flapping. What trick turns this ordinary flyer into the world's fastest animal?
answer: Fold its wings and dive in a steep plunge
choices: Fold its wings and dive in a steep plunge
Beat its wings faster than a hummingbird
Ride a jet of air from its lungs
Glide on a rising column of warm air
context: The dive, called the stoop, is what makes the peregrine a rocket — in level flight it's only ordinarily fast. Source: Buffalo Bill Center of the West.

question: After World War II, farmers across North America sprayed the pesticide DDT (dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane) on their fields to kill mosquitoes and crop bugs. The chemical drifted up the food chain and built up in the peregrine falcons that ate poisoned birds and mice. It also hurt their eggs. By the 1960s, not one peregrine falcon was breeding anywhere in the eastern United States. What had DDT done to the eggs?
answer: Thinned the shells until they cracked under the parents
choices: Thinned the shells until they cracked under the parents
Turned the yolks toxic to the chicks
Made the parents abandon them cold
Kept them from ever being fertilized
context: DDT thinned peregrine eggshells until eggs cracked under the parents' weight; by the 1960s the peregrine had vanished from the whole eastern U.S. Source: Wikipedia; Audubon 'Remembering Tom Cade'.

question: A peregrine falcon dives at over 200 miles per hour, faster than any race car or jet ski. At that speed the wall of air smashing into its face should be strong enough to burst its lungs. Yet the falcon breathes easily through its beak the whole way down. Inside each nostril sits a tiny cone of bone, and engineers later copied its shape for the intakes of jet engines. What does that little cone do to the screaming rush of air?
answer: Spins it into a slowed spiral
choices: Spins it into a slowed spiral
Warms it before the lungs
Filters the dust from it
Splits it into two streams
context: The bony tubercle (a baffle) in each nostril spins the rushing air into a spiral and slows it down, so the falcon can breathe at dive speed. Some jet-engine designers study it. Source: ResearchGate; Curious Sengi summaries.  (Legend.)

question: High over a valley, a peregrine falcon spots a pigeon far below and folds its wings into a hunting dive called a 'stoop.' Hurtling downward at more than 200 miles per hour with the target locked in its sight, the falcon still needs to keep its eyes wet, clean, and in sharp focus at that killing speed. What sweeps across each eye during the plunge to protect it?
answer: A see-through third eyelid
choices: A see-through third eyelid
A clear sheet of skin from below
A slick of clear tear-fluid
A clear inner lens that slides up
context: The nictitating membrane, a transparent third eyelid, sweeps across each eye during the dive, wiping it clear while the falcon keeps its target in focus. Source: Wikipedia 'Peregrine falcon'.

question: Chasing prey flat-out in level flight, a peregrine falcon reaches only about 69 mph. But in 1999 a trained falcon named Frightful was dropped from a Cessna at 17,000 feet to chase her skydiving falconer as a lure, a chip on her back clocking the fastest bird dive ever measured. How fast did that plunge go?
answer: 242 mph
choices: 242 mph
210 mph
186 mph
273 mph
context: Frightful's 242 mph (389 km/h) dive is the fastest ever measured for a bird — more than triple her flat-out level-flight chase. Source: Guinness World Records; Smithsonian Magazine 'Falling with the Falcon'.  (Legend.)

question: Cornell professor Tom Cade set out in 1970 to bring the peregrine falcon back from near-extinction, raising captive-bred chicks in towers, fed by hidden humans so they never tamed to people, until they flew and hunted free. What proved his rescue had worked?
answer: Released falcons bred in the wild by 1980
choices: Released falcons bred in the wild by 1980
City-nesting numbers doubled by 1985
The last wild pair returned east by 1982
Wild pairs fledged three chicks by 1979
context: Cade's 'hacking' method worked: released peregrines bred in the wild by 1980, and in 1999 the bird was taken off the U.S. endangered list. Source: Audubon 'Remembering Tom Cade'; Wikipedia.  (Legend.)

question: When scientists mounted a peregrine falcon inside a wind tunnel and turned the fans up to a diving speed, they saw one of the smoothest shapes in nature — a body built for a 200-mile-per-hour hunt. But at certain spots on the falcon's back, fast air would normally tear away from the surface and drag the bird back. Instead, right there, something odd happens. What keeps the air clinging on?
answer: Tiny back feathers pop up to keep the air clinging on
choices: Tiny back feathers pop up to keep the air clinging on
It seals every feather flat into a single glassy skin
It sheds a thin film of oil that lets the air slide by
It vents warm air through its nostrils to fill the gap
context: A wind-tunnel and computer-flow study of a life-sized diving-falcon model measured a drag coefficient as low as CD around 0.094 in the full stoop — among the most streamlined shapes in nature. But the low drag is not just the teardrop body: right where the airflow would separate, small body feathers pop up during the dive and act as passive flow-control devices — the same trick as the vortex generators (turbulators) on an aircraft wing — keeping the airflow attached and drag low at extreme speed. Source: Ponitz, Schmitz, Fischer, Bleckmann & Brucker, "Diving-Flight Aerodynamics of a Peregrine Falcon (Falco peregrinus)," PLOS ONE 9(2):e86506, 2014.

question: A stooping peregrine falcon does not aim where a dodging starling IS — it curves so it turns harder the faster the line between hunter and prey swings. Physics simulations found this is the very same steering rule engineers built into one famous machine. What guides the falcon the way it guides that machine?
answer: The homing law that steers a heat-seeking missile
choices: The homing law that steers a heat-seeking missile
The autopilot loop that holds an airliner on course
The spinning gyroscope inside a ship’s compass
The braking rhythm of a train easing into a curve
context: Physics-based flight simulations (Oxford; Mills, Hildenbrandt, Taylor & Hemelrijk, PLOS Computational Biology 2018) found the peregrine steers by proportional navigation — the same guidance law used by heat-seeking, homing missiles — turning at a rate proportional to how fast the line of sight to the target rotates. The simulated navigation constant N of about 2.6 to 3.0 matched the median N of 2.6 measured in real peregrines. The study also showed why the ultra-fast stoop matters: only at high speed can the falcon out-turn an erratically dodging bird like a starling; against straight-flying prey a slow, low attack actually worked better. Source: Mills, Hildenbrandt, Taylor & Hemelrijk, PLOS Comp. Biol. 2018.  (Legend.)

question: In the sandy deserts of Argentina lives the smallest armored mammal on Earth — the pink fairy armadillo. It is smaller than a mouse, with a shell the color of soft pink candy and huge front claws almost half its body length. This tiny creature spends nearly all of its life pushing through dry sand underground. It has earned a nickname for the way it moves. What do people call the pink fairy armadillo?
answer: the 'sand-swimmer'
choices: the 'sand-swimmer'
the 'dune-jumper'
the 'sand-diver'
the 'desert-mole'
context: The pink fairy armadillo (Chlamyphorus truncatus) was long believed to burrow through loose ground almost as fast as a fish swims through water, earning the nickname 'sand-swimmer.' It is the smallest armadillo in the world, about 3.5-4.5 inches long. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pink_fairy_armadillo  (Legend.)

question: The pink fairy armadillo is a tiny, palm-sized creature that burrows through the dry sandy plains of central Argentina. Its thin shell can flush a deeper rose-pink and then fade paler again, because a dense web of blood vessels sits just beneath the surface. That color change is a clue to what the shell really does. Its main job is to:
answer: dump or hold body heat like a radiator
choices: dump or hold body heat like a radiator
shield the animal from predators' teeth
store water for the dry desert
warn rivals away with a bright signal
context: By pushing more blood into the shell the armadillo flushes pink and sheds heat; by draining blood out, the shell pales and it keeps its warmth. The shell is a thermoregulating organ, not armor. Source: https://factanimal.com/pink-fairy-armadillo/

question: Most armadillos wear a shell that wraps around their whole body like a suit of armor. But the pink fairy armadillo — a palm-sized burrower from the dry sands of Argentina — is different. It has a flat armored plate on its rear that faces straight backward, like a shield glued to its bottom. As the animal digs forward through the sand, the back plate lets it:
answer: press and pack the soil behind it, corking its tunnel
choices: press and pack the soil behind it, corking its tunnel
flip upside down to roll away downhill
scoop food up toward its mouth
reflect sunlight to stay cool underground
context: The flattened rear 'butt plate' tamps and compacts the loose soil behind the digging armadillo, shoring the tunnel against collapse and sealing (corking) the burrow entrance behind it. This flattened rear plate appears unique to this species. Source: https://www.sciencenews.org/article/pink-armadillos-aint-your-texas-critters

question: On a warm tropical reef, a small pistol shrimp hunts a passing fish without ever chasing it down. The shrimp has one oversized claw, almost half its body length. That claw slams shut with a violent snap — and the fish is stunned before the shrimp has moved an inch. So what actually reached across the water and hit the fish?
answer: A jet of water fired by the snap
choices: A jet of water fired by the snap
A sticky thread it lassoed the fish with
A cloud of ink squirted to blind it
A venom spine flicked from its tail
context: The claw itself never touches the prey — the snap shoots out a jet of water that stuns the victim from a distance. Source: Versluis et al., 'How Snapping Shrimp Snap: Through Cavitating Bubbles', Science 2000; https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2000/09/000922072104.htm

question: The pistol shrimp lives on coral reefs and carries one huge oversized claw on the front of its body. When it snaps that claw shut in a lightning-fast strike, it fires a bubble that pops with a shock wave loud enough to stun a passing fish stone dead. A weapon like that surely belongs to a giant, right? So how long is a pistol shrimp, from tip to tail?
answer: 3 to 5 cm (an adult's thumb)
choices: 3 to 5 cm (an adult's thumb)
30 to 40 cm (a forearm)
1 to 2 mm (a grain of rice)
70 to 90 cm (an arm's length)
context: Only about 3 to 5 cm (1.2 to 2 inches) long, yet it produces one of the most powerful sounds, by body size, of any animal. Source: Wikipedia 'Alpheidae'; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpheidae

question: During World War II, American submarine crews listened at their sonar sets for the sound of enemy ships. Instead, they kept hearing a loud, popping crackle across the sea floor — like a giant bowl of frying bacon. It was so noisy their sonar couldn't pick anything else out. Clever sub captains learned to park their boats right inside the loudest patches, where the racket hid the whir of their own engines. What tiny sea creatures were making all that undersea noise?
answer: Colonies of snapping shrimp
choices: Colonies of snapping shrimp
Beds of grinding sea urchins
Schools of drumming croaker fish
Currents rattling loose gravel
context: Colonies snap in such a constant din that in WWII they jammed sonar and confused submarine-detection operators — and subs hid inside shrimp beds to avoid being heard. Source: ScienceDaily, 'Snapping Shrimp Drown Out Sonar' (Science 2000); https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2000/09/000922072104.htm  (Legend.)

question: A pistol shrimp is nearly blind and lives in a burrow it digs and cleans in the sandy sea floor. It shares that burrow with a small, sharp-eyed goby fish that hovers at the entrance and stands guard. Out on the open sand, the shrimp can't see the goby's face. So how does the shrimp know the instant the goby spots danger and bolts back inside?
answer: It keeps one long antenna touching the goby
choices: It keeps one long antenna touching the goby
It watches the goby's shadow on the sand
It listens for the goby's alarm clicks
It tastes stress chemicals the goby releases
context: The shrimp keeps an antenna on the goby's body; if the goby flicks its tail and darts in, the shrimp instantly feels the signal and dives too. Source: Divers Alert Network, 'Symbiosis on the Sand'; https://dan.org/alert-diver/article/symbiosis-on-the-sand/

question: Scientists found the pistol shrimp's fired water jet alone doesn't quite explain the killing blow. The jet moves so fast it drops the water pressure and creates something behind it — and THAT is the real weapon. What forms and then destroys the prey?
answer: A collapsing bubble that unleashes a shockwave
choices: A collapsing bubble that unleashes a shockwave
A whirlpool that drags prey into the claw
A spark that electrocutes the water
A spray of jagged ice crystals
context: The low pressure forms a vapor-filled cavitation bubble; when it collapses it slams out a shockwave that stuns or kills. Source: Versluis et al., Science 2000; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7525291/  (Legend.)

question: A pistol shrimp is a small ocean shrimp with one giant snapping claw and one tiny regular claw. It snaps that big claw shut so fast it fires a bullet of hot water that can stun a small fish. Now imagine a fight goes badly and the pistol shrimp loses that big snapping claw to an attacker. Rather than simply regrowing the same weapon on the same side, what does its body do over the following molts?
answer: Its small claw becomes the new weapon; the stump regrows small
choices: Its small claw becomes the new weapon; the stump regrows small
It regrows the snapper twice as large as before
It grows a matching snapper on the other side, giving it two
It stays disarmed and switches to scavenging for life
context: The claws swap roles: the lost limb grows back as a small claw while the original small claw enlarges into a new snapping weapon. Source: Wikipedia 'Alpheidae'; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpheidae

question: When a pistol shrimp's claw slams shut, it fires a jet of water so fast that a tiny bubble collapses inside it — a moment scientists call cavitation. That collapse doesn't just make a shockwave that stuns fish. For a sliver of a second, it also emits a faint flash of light, too dim for the naked eye to catch. Researchers named this glow with a playful term. What is it called?
answer: Shrimpoluminescence
choices: Shrimpoluminescence
Bioflash cavitation
Crustaceoglow
Snapfire radiance
context: Named because it resembles sonoluminescence — light from a collapsing bubble. Source: Lohse, Schmitz & Versluis, 'Snapping shrimp make flashing bubbles', Nature 2001; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11586346/  (Legend.)

question: When a pistol shrimp's claw snaps shut, the jet it fires creates a tiny cavitation bubble — a void in the water — that collapses almost instantly. Inside that collapsing bubble, for a sliver of a second, the temperature spikes to at least about 5,000 kelvin, hotter than a blast furnace. To grasp how extreme that is, what everyday hot thing does that pinprick of heat very nearly match?
answer: The surface of the Sun
choices: The surface of the Sun
The core of a lightning bolt
Molten lava from a volcano
A blacksmith's forge fire
context: About 5,000 K (roughly 4,700 °C) — nearly the Sun's surface at about 5,772 K. Source: Wikipedia 'Alpheidae' (citing Lohse et al. 2001); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpheidae  (Legend.)

question: When British scientists in London first opened a crate from Australia in 1799, they thought it was a hoax. Inside was a stuffed animal that made no sense. It had thick brown fur and a flat beaver-like tail like a mammal, but also a rubbery duck-like bill, webbed feet, and reports said it laid eggs. The males even carried venom in their back legs. What Australian river creature was inside the crate?
answer: Platypus
choices: Platypus
Muskrat
Otter
Capybara
context: The platypus (Ornithorhynchus anatinus) of eastern Australia is one of the strangest animals alive: fur and milk like a mammal, a bill and eggs like a bird, and venom to boot. Source: Australian Museum, australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/platypus/

question: On Earth today, the duck-billed platypus of eastern Australia and four kinds of spiny echidna belong to a very small mammal club — just five species in the whole world. Every other mammal — mice, cats, whales, humans — does one thing the same way. In her riverbank burrow, a mother platypus does something no other mammal on Earth does. What sets these five apart?
answer: Lay eggs
choices: Lay eggs
Change sex
Have no bones
Breathe through skin
context: These five are the monotremes. The platypus curls around one or two leathery eggs and incubates them for about ten days before they hatch. Source: Australian Museum, australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/platypus/

question: The platypus is Australia's egg-laying mammal, with a duck-like bill and thick brown fur. A newly hatched platypus is no bigger than a jellybean, and like all mammal babies it needs milk from its mother. But here's the strange part: a platypus mother has no nipples at all — nothing for the baby to latch onto. So how does the jellybean-sized baby actually get its meal? (legend-tier oddity)
answer: Milk seeps through skin pores onto furry belly patches
choices: Milk seeps through skin pores onto furry belly patches
The mother regurgitates food into its mouth
It drinks river water rich in nutrients
It suckles milk from a slit in the mother's belly
context: The platypus's mammary glands are modified sweat glands, so milk seeps out through skin pores onto two furry patches where the young lap it up. Source: BBC Science Focus, sciencefocus.com/nature/do-platypuses-really-sweat-milk; Australian Museum  (Legend.)

question: A platypus glides along a muddy riverbed where a shrimp is buried out of sight, giving off no smell it can catch. Yet the platypus swims straight to it. Its rubbery bill is picking up something the shrimp cannot hide. What is the bill actually detecting?
answer: The faint electric currents from the prey's twitching muscles
choices: The faint electric currents from the prey's twitching muscles
The warmth of the prey's body
The vibration of the prey's heartbeat
The color of the prey against the mud
context: About 40,000 electroreceptors pack the platypus's bill, sensing the tiny electric fields thrown off by a hidden animal's moving muscles. Source: American Museum of Natural History, amnh.org/explore/news-blogs/platypus-electroreception-hunting

question: A platypus plunges into a murky, silt-clouded creek in eastern Australia. Down on the muddy bottom a small shrimp lies buried, and the platypus keeps its eyes, ears, and nostrils shut underwater — it cannot see, hear, or smell a thing. Yet its rubbery bill still locks straight onto the hidden prey and pins it. What is doing the finding down there in the dark?
answer: An electric sense and touch-sensitive push rods in its bill
choices: An electric sense and touch-sensitive push rods in its bill
A heat sense reading the prey's body warmth
A magnetic sense pointing toward the prey
Sensing the silt the prey stirs up as it moves
context: Hunting effectively blind, the platypus seals its eyes, ears, and nose and relies entirely on electroreception plus touch-sensitive 'push rods' in the bill. Source: American Museum of Natural History; Australian Platypus Conservancy, platypus.asn.au/the-platypus-bill-push-rods-and-electroreception/  (Legend.)

question: In 1986 the German biologist Henning Scheich set out to test how a platypus finds prey it cannot see or smell. He built a lifeless little 'shrimp' out of a plastic shell and wires, sank it in a tank with a platypus, and switched it on. The platypus struck the lure anyway, as if it were a living, wriggling meal. What was Scheich secretly feeding into that fake shrimp to make it strike?
answer: A tiny electric current
choices: A tiny electric current
A faint trace of warmth
A hidden wriggling motor
A low buzzing vibration
context: Scheich's platypus struck at a lure carrying only a faint electric signal, proving electroreception. The receptors respond to signals as weak as ~20 microvolts per square centimeter. Source: American Museum of Natural History  (Legend.)

question: A platypus's bill senses prey two ways at once: an electric sense and a touch sense. Underwater, electricity races ahead while the physical pressure wave lags a hair behind. Jack Pettigrew argued in 1998 the platypus uses that tiny gap between the two signals. What does timing the gap let it work out?
answer: How far away the prey is
choices: How far away the prey is
How large the prey is
Which direction the current flows
How fast the water moves
context: Because electricity travels through water faster than the mechanical wave, the delay between the two senses encodes distance, letting the platypus range its target like a stopwatch. Source: Pettigrew et al. 1998, via Australian Platypus Conservancy

question: The platypus is one of very few venomous mammals in the world. Handle one the wrong way and only half of them can hurt you — the males alone carry the weapon. Female platypuses are harmless. A male's venom is sharpest during mating season, when rival males wrestle each other over females. Where on a male platypus's body is this venomous weapon mounted?
answer: A hollow venom spur on each hind ankle
choices: A hollow venom spur on each hind ankle
A stinger at the tip of the tail
Fangs hidden inside the bill
Barbed claws on the front webbed feet
context: Each male carries a sharp hollow spur (about 12-18 mm) on each hind ankle, fed by a venom gland whose output spikes in the mating season. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platypus_venom; Australian Museum  (Legend.)

question: A male platypus carries hollow venom spurs on each hind ankle, and once in a while an Australian fisherman or bushwalker grabs one the wrong way and gets jabbed. The victim is rushed to hospital in agony. Among the small number of people this venom has actually struck, it has earned a grim reputation with doctors — worse than most snakebites in one specific way. What makes platypus venom so notorious? (legend-tier)
answer: The pain shrugs off morphine and can last weeks or months
choices: The pain shrugs off morphine and can last weeks or months
It causes the wounded limb to swell to twice its size
It leaves the victim unable to grip for months
It triggers violent, days-long fever
context: The venom is not lethal to humans but causes excruciating pain that morphine cannot relieve, persisting for weeks or months and able to incapacitate a grown adult. Source: Slate, 2015; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platypus_venom  (Legend.)

question: In 2020 American scientists were curious about the platypus — Australia's duck-billed, egg-laying mammal. They dug up old museum pelts and shone ultraviolet light on them in a dark room, expecting nothing unusual, just brown fur under a purple lamp. Instead they saw something no one had ever noticed on a platypus before. What did the fur do under UV light? (legend-tier discovery)
answer: Glows an eerie blue-green
choices: Glows an eerie blue-green
Glows a deep blood-red
Glows bright orange
Shows no reaction at all
context: Anich and colleagues reported this biofluorescence in the journal Mammalia in 2020, the first ever found in a monotreme. Source: Live Science, livescience.com/platypuses-glow-uv-light.html; ScienceDaily (Anich et al., 2020)  (Legend.)

question: An adult platypus dives to the bottom of Australian rivers to hunt crayfish, worms, and freshwater shellfish. It has no teeth in its jaws at all, yet it happily crushes hard shells to get at the meat inside. Along with each mouthful of food it also scoops up little pieces of gravel into stretchy cheek pouches. Then it paddles up to the surface to chew. Why does the platypus gather grit along with its food?
answer: It grinds food against horny pads, using the swallowed grit like millstones
choices: It grinds food against horny pads, using the swallowed grit like millstones
It uses the stones as ballast to sink while diving
It spits the grit to stun approaching prey
It stores the stones to build its riverbank burrow
context: With no teeth, the platypus mashes prey between horny keratin pads, the swallowed grit acting as millstones to crack hard shells. Source: AskNature, asknature.org/strategy/mouth-sorts-and-grinds-food/; Australian Museum

question: When the platypus genome was sequenced in 2008, its sex chromosomes stunned biologists. Most mammals settle sex with a single pair, but the platypus uses a whole chain of them, and part of that chain looks bird-like, resembling a chicken's. How many sex chromosomes does a platypus carry?
answer: Ten
choices: Ten
Two
Four
Twenty-three
context: The 2008 genome revealed 5 X and 5 Y chromosomes, and DNA blending mammal, bird, and reptile genes, with bird-like sex chromosomes echoing a chicken's. Source: WashU, source.washu.edu/2008/05/; ScienceAlert

question: The 2008 platypus genome caught the animal red-handed straddling two worlds. When placental and marsupial mammals adopted the placenta and switched to nursing, they junked one ancient gene their egg-laying ancestors had all carried. The platypus, alone among mammals, never threw its copy away — and it still switches the gene on. What does that surviving gene let the platypus do?
answer: Make egg yolk, even as it also makes milk
choices: Make egg yolk, even as it also makes milk
Grow a second, spare set of milk glands
Digest the shells of the eggs it lays
Regrow a lost venom spur within one season
context: The ancestral vertebrate had a cluster of three vitellogenin (egg-yolk protein) genes — chickens still carry all three. Placental and marsupial mammals lost every one when they swapped yolk for the placenta and milk. The platypus kept one working copy, an ortholog of the chicken's VtgI, sitting right beside its milk-casein genes. Low nonsynonymous-to-synonymous substitution ratios and almost no pseudogene decay confirm the gene is still functional, not a fossil — so the platypus is genetically half-reptile, half-mammal, making egg yolk and milk at once. Source: Warren et al. 2008 genome analysis (Nature nature06936); Wagner et al. 2008, 'Conservation of a vitellogenin gene cluster in oviparous vertebrates and identification of its traces in the platypus genome' (PubMed 18343608).  (Legend.)

question: In the fields, forests, and backyards of North America lives a slow, cat-sized animal with a bare pink tail, a long pointy snout, and beady eyes. It cannot easily fight off a fox or a dog. So when a predator corners it, it has one last trick: it flops on its side, its mouth hangs open with the tongue lolling out, and its eyes glaze over. It looks totally dead. Which animal is famous for this?
answer: The Virginia opossum
choices: The Virginia opossum
The nine-banded armadillo
The striped skunk
The North American porcupine
context: The Virginia opossum (Didelphis virginiana) is the classic death-feigner, and its cornered collapse -- eyes glazed open, tongue out -- is literally where the phrase 'playing possum' comes from. Source: https://scienceinsights.org/do-possums-actually-play-dead-the-science-explained/

question: When a possum is grabbed by a dog, it flops limp, its tongue lolls out, and its heart even slows down -- and the disgusted dog often loses interest and drops it. Faking death like this is a real trick in nature, and scientists have a name for it: thanatosis. It turns up in some surprising groups of animals. Which of these groups actually has known death-fakers?
answer: Beetles, ducks, frogs, and sharks
choices: Beetles, ducks, frogs, and sharks
Octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish
Bats, dolphins, and shrews
Corals, jellyfish, and sea anemones
context: Death-feigning shows up across an enormous range of animals -- beetles, spiders, crickets, ants, ducks, frogs, lizards, snakes, opossums, and even sharks and seahorses. It is one of nature's most widespread defenses. Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5769822/

question: A Virginia opossum cornered by a fox flops on its side and lies limp, its pink tongue hanging out on the dirt. But it isn't relying on looks alone to sell the trick. As it faints, its anal glands leak a stinking greenish fluid, and at the same moment the opossum drools, urinates, and empties its bowels, staining the ground around it. What impression does all this create for a sniffing predator?
answer: It smells like a corpse dead for days
choices: It smells like a corpse dead for days
It masks its own scent so predators lose the trail
It gives off a musk that mimics the predator's own kind
It seems to be a healthy, easy catch
context: The musky fluid reeks of rotting flesh, so the opossum doesn't just look dead -- it smells and looks DAYS-dead. Many predators avoid spoiled meat, which can be poisonous, and drop it in disgust. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/article/many-animals-play-dead-not-just-to-avoid-predators

question: To a sniffing predator, a fainted Virginia opossum doesn't just look dead — it feels and even sounds dead, thanks to real, measurable changes inside its body during the faint. Scientists have wired opossums up in the lab and watched exactly what happens to the animal's pulse in the middle of one of these 'acts.' About how far does its heart rate drop while it lies there pretending?
answer: By nearly half (about 46%)
choices: By nearly half (about 46%)
By about a tenth (roughly 10%)
It actually races faster than normal
It stops completely for minutes
context: Researchers measured the opossum's heart rate falling roughly 46%, its breathing dropping about 31%, and its body cooling slightly -- genuine physiology, not pretend, which is why the illusion is so convincing. Source: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/19169341_Physiological_responses_associated_with_feigned_death_in_the_American_opossum

question: Flip a shark upside down and it seizes up into a limp, helpless trance -- tonic immobility. Off Mexico, a pod of orcas called Moctezuma's pod learned to weaponize this against young great white sharks. Once a shark is paralyzed upside down, what do the orcas do?
answer: Rip out and eat its calorie-rich liver
choices: Rip out and eat its calorie-rich liver
Carry it to shore to eat later
Teach the trick to rival pods
Release it once it stops struggling
context: The orcas push young great whites to the surface and flip them upside down, locking them in tonic immobility, then tear out and devour the shark's huge, oil-rich liver -- a learned hunting move passed within the pod. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/orcas-in-mexico-have-learned-to-attack-young-great-white-sharks-by-flipping-them-upside-down-and-eating-their-livers-180987620/  (Legend.)

question: Along the misty shores of Scotland's Loch Ness, divers and tourists still swap stories of a huge, long-necked, small-headed creature slipping through the dark water. That classic silhouette actually comes from a real Mesozoic sea reptile that hunted the oceans in the age of the dinosaurs — a very long neck, a tiny head at the end of it, and a broad body with a paddle at each of its four corners. What was this animal?
answer: A plesiosaur
choices: A plesiosaur
A pterosaur
An ichthyosaur
A mosasaur
context: The plesiosaur was a genuine marine reptile of the Mesozoic seas, not a dinosaur and not a living lake monster; its four-flipper, long-necked shape is where the 'Loch Ness Monster' picture comes from. Ichthyosaurs were dolphin-shaped, mosasaurs were giant sea lizards, and pterosaurs flew. Source: Natural History Museum London, 'What is a plesiosaur?' (nhm.ac.uk).

question: A plesiosaur was an ocean-going reptile that swam the seas during the age of dinosaurs, roughly 200 to 66 million years ago. It had a small head on a long neck, a stout barrel body, and four wide flippers -- a shape built like almost nothing alive in the water today. When one needed to cross open sea, how did this reptile drive itself forward?
answer: It flapped all four flippers like underwater wings
choices: It flapped all four flippers like underwater wings
It sculled with a broad paddle-shaped tail
It swallowed water and jetted backward
It walked along the seafloor on its flippers
context: Almost no living animal does this. Computer simulations and a swimming robot showed the plesiosaur 'flew' through the water like a penguin, driving mostly with its two front flippers and adding a timed extra push with the back pair. Source: Muscutt et al. 2017, Royal Society Proceedings B; PBS NewsHour 'odd swimming style decoded by a robot'.

question: During the age of the dinosaurs, huge marine reptiles called plesiosaurs swam the world's oceans. A plesiosaur looked like a snake threaded through the body of a turtle, with four broad paddle-shaped flippers. It spent its entire life in the open sea and never crawled onto land. Yet like a whale today, it had to keep coming up to the surface again and again, no matter how good the hunting was down deep. What forced a plesiosaur back up?
answer: It breathed air with lungs
choices: It breathed air with lungs
It needed sunlight to warm its blood
It hunted seabirds resting on the waves
It came up to shed its old skin
context: Plesiosaurs were air-breathing reptiles, so despite living their whole lives at sea they had to surface to breathe like whales do. Because they also gave live birth in the water, they never needed to come ashore at all. Source: Natural History Museum London, 'What is a plesiosaur?'.

question: A human neck holds seven bones stacked on top of each other. A giraffe's neck stretches over six feet long, and it still holds exactly seven bones — the same count you have. Nearly every mammal on Earth sticks to that rule, no matter how long or short the neck. But an ancient sea reptile called Elasmosaurus threw that rule out entirely. About how many bones stacked up in one elasmosaur's neck?
answer: About 72, more than almost any animal ever
choices: About 72, more than almost any animal ever
About 14, just double a giraffe's seven
About 25, like a very long-necked bird
The same 7, only each bone far longer
context: A giraffe stretches seven neck bones to enormous length; elasmosaurs instead stacked up 70-plus short vertebrae, and their cousin Albertonectes had at least 75. Source: Sachs et al. 2013, PLOS ONE, 'Revised Vertebral Count in the Longest-Necked Vertebrate Elasmosaurus platyurus'; National Geographic on Albertonectes.

question: Elasmosaurus was a plesiosaur — a huge marine reptile that swam the shallow inland sea over what is now Kansas, back when the dinosaurs still ruled the land. Its body stretched about 34 feet from nose to tail, longer than a school bus. Its head was a tiny triangle at the far end, big enough only to gulp small fish and squid whole. Of that whole 34-foot body, how much was taken up by the neck alone?
answer: Around 23 feet, about two-thirds of the animal
choices: Around 23 feet, about two-thirds of the animal
A few feet, roughly the length of the head
Around half, evenly split with the tail
Almost the whole body, leaving a stub tail
context: About 23 of Elasmosaurus's 34 feet was pure neck, nearly two-thirds of its length, tipped with that small triangular head. Source: Wikipedia 'Elasmosaurus', citing Sachs 2005 and Everhart (~10.3 m long, neck ~7.1 m, about 69%).

question: Elasmosaurus was a plesiosaur that cruised the seas of what is now North America about 80 million years ago. Its neck stretched two-thirds the length of its whole body — over 20 feet of neck on a 40-foot animal. One leading idea says this strange shape solved a specific problem the elasmosaur faced whenever it closed on a passing school of fish. What was that problem?
answer: Its bulky body would scare the whole school off before it could strike
choices: Its bulky body would scare the whole school off before it could strike
Its own long shadow fell across the water and spooked the fish
It swam too slowly to chase a darting school down
Its tiny mouth could not open wide enough to engulf them
context: This is a leading hypothesis, not proven fact: the long reach may have let the plesiosaur ease its tiny head into a fish school and snatch one before its huge body spooked them. Source: Earth Archives, 'Plesiosaurs and their absurdly long necks' (eartharchives.org), flagged as a feeding hypothesis.

question: Not every plesiosaur had that spindly neck. Their cousins the pliosaurs went the other way: short neck, enormous head. The giant Pliosaurus funkei, nicknamed 'Predator X', reached 40 to 50 feet with foot-long teeth. When researchers estimated its bite force, how did it compare with the famous land king, T. rex?
answer: Even more powerful than a T. rex's bite
choices: Even more powerful than a T. rex's bite
Roughly a tenth of a T. rex's bite
About equal, but only when biting soft prey
Weaker, since its teeth were built for gripping not crushing
context: Pliosaurs were apex predators of their seas. Researchers estimated Predator X's bite as even stronger than T. rex's, though the exact figure is debated because the skull is incomplete. Source: National Geographic, 'Paleontologists Reveal the Identity of Predator X'; Britannica; Discover Wildlife on pliosaurs (~30 cm teeth).

question: For 200 years scientists argued over how plesiosaurs reproduced, since they clearly never came ashore. A single 78-million-year-old Polycotylus fossil settled it: inside the mother's body lay one large baby. What did that fossil reveal about how plesiosaurs had their young?
answer: They gave live birth at sea rather than laying eggs on land
choices: They gave live birth at sea rather than laying eggs on land
They laid a single leathery egg that hatched inside the mother
They released clouds of tiny eggs like most fish
They carried eggs in the mouth until the young hatched
context: The one large baby, rather than a litter, hints that plesiosaurs may have cared for their young like whales or dolphins do. Source: O'Keefe & Chiappe 2011, Science 333:870-873, 'Viviparity and K-selected life history in a Mesozoic marine reptile'; Natural History Museum of LA County.

question: In 1823 a young English fossil hunter named Mary Anning dug the first nearly complete plesiosaur skeleton out of the crumbling seaside cliffs at Lyme Regis on the south coast of England. Its neck was so absurdly long that the great French anatomist Baron Georges Cuvier declared the fossil a fake — the neck bones, he insisted, must have been glued on from another animal. How was the fight finally settled?
answer: A special Geological Society meeting proved it real and Cuvier admitted his error
choices: A special Geological Society meeting proved it real and Cuvier admitted his error
The skeleton was quietly reburied to end the argument
Later digs found longer-necked fossils that made it look ordinary
Cuvier's own students showed the neck bones were glued together
context: The fossil hunter was Mary Anning, whose complete plesiosaur was so long-necked that Cuvier assumed a fake, until the Geological Society examined it and he conceded he was wrong. Source: Natural History Museum London, 'Mary Anning: the unsung hero'; Geological Society online exhibition, Plesiosaurus dolichodeirus. (legend)

question: Plesiosaurs were reptiles, so you'd expect their bodies to match the temperature of the sea around them, the way a modern crocodile does — cool water, cool body. But in 2010 French scientists tested the oxygen chemistry locked inside the tooth enamel of plesiosaur fossils, and paleontologists studied the growth pattern in their fossil bones. Both lines of evidence told the same surprising story about these ancient sea reptiles. What could plesiosaurs actually do?
answer: Generate their own body heat, at a bird's metabolic rate, instead of borrowing it from the water
choices: Generate their own body heat, at a bird's metabolic rate, instead of borrowing it from the water
Simply match the cold ocean around them, exactly like a modern crocodile does
Warm up only after basking flipper-first at the sunlit surface between dives
Stay sluggish and slow-burning, coasting on sheer bulk to hold warmth in
context: Two separate lines of evidence converge on active, self-generated heat in plesiosaurs. Bernard et al. (2010, Science 328:1379-1382) measured oxygen isotopes in fossil tooth enamel and estimated elevated, regulated body temperatures well above the cold seas the animals swam in. Independently, Fleischle, Wintrich & Sander (2018, PeerJ 6:e4955; PMC5994164) modeled plesiosaur bone microstructure and recovered resting metabolic rates (~12-13 mL O2/h/g^0.67) and bone growth rates (~93-100 um/day) squarely in the BIRD range, far above any cold-blooded reptile, concluding plesiosaurs were 'truly endothermic' -- generating heat actively rather than coasting on body size. A 2024 reassessment (Reassessment of body temperature and thermoregulation strategies in Mesozoic marine reptiles, Paleobiology, biorxiv 2024.07.26.605303) refines the picture: plesiosaurs read as poikilothermic endotherms, body temperature ~27-34 C that still ran an advantage over the sea rather than holding a fixed value, while ichthyosaurs were the homeothermic ones. Across all three studies the shared, robust finding is self-produced, bird-level metabolic heat, not passive matching of the water. Sources: Bernard et al. 2010, Science (science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1187443); Fleischle, Wintrich & Sander 2018, PeerJ (peerj.com/articles/4955/; PMC5994164); 2024 Paleobiology reassessment (biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.07.26.605303v1).

question: Plesiosaurs swallowed smooth stones by the hundred, and one Styxosaurus was found with 253 in its gut. For years the tidy explanation was ballast, weight to help the reptile sink and trim. Then someone actually weighed the stones against the animal, and the ballast idea collapsed. What did the numbers force researchers toward instead?
answer: The stones ground up tough, shelled prey in the gut like a bird's gizzard
choices: The stones ground up tough, shelled prey in the gut like a bird's gizzard
The stones anchored the reptile to the seabed while it rested
The stones were swallowed by accident while snapping at fish
The stones stored minerals the reptile drew on to grow its bones
context: These swallowed stones are gastroliths; one Styxosaurus held 253, and some elasmosaurs preserve over 100. The old 'ballast for buoyancy control' idea runs into a hard quantitative wall: recovered gastrolith mass never exceeds about 0.2 percent of the animal's body mass in any plesiosaur, far too little to sink or trim a multi-ton reptile. That shortfall has shifted the leading view toward a digestive role, grinding tough prey such as shelled cephalopods in the gut the way birds use gizzard stones, though the debate is not fully closed. Sources: Everhart, 'Gastroliths Associated with Plesiosaur Remains ... Pierre Shale'; Wings & Sander on gastrolith function; corroborated by Open University 'Solving the Riddle of the Gastroliths' and PeerJ 2024 (PMC11373562), which report gastrolith mass consistently under ~0.2 percent of body mass, insufficient as ballast.
