question: In the steamy rainforests of Central and South America, tiny frogs the size of your fingernail crawl over wet leaves and mossy logs on the forest floor. They come in bright colors — fire red, sky blue, banana yellow, and neon green — with bold patterns on top. There are about 200 different kinds, and no dull brown pond frog can match them. What are these jewel-bright frogs called?
answer: Poison dart frogs
choices: Poison dart frogs
Marsh peepers
Cave newts
River toads
context: The poison dart frog family holds roughly 200 species across 16 genera, many in dazzling electric colors, on the rainforest floor of Central and South America. Source: Wikipedia, 'Poison dart frog'.

question: A poison dart frog no bigger than a thumbnail hatches its eggs on the forest floor, then faces a problem: the babies need water. One parent lets the wriggling tadpoles stick to the mucus on its back and climbs a tree trunk. Where does it carry each tadpole to grow up?
answer: A pool of rainwater trapped in a bromeliad plant
choices: A pool of rainwater trapped in a bromeliad plant
A hollow log floating in a stream
A wet burrow dug at the roots
A nest woven from leaves
context: The newly hatched tadpoles cling to the mucus on a parent's back, and the adult climbs into the canopy to deposit each one, one at a time, in a tiny pool of rainwater trapped in a bromeliad plant. Source: Wikipedia, 'Poison dart frog'; World Frog Day, 'Strawberry Poison Dart Frogs And Their Parental Care'.

question: In the rainforests of Central and South America, a tiny poison dart frog hops along the leaf litter in broad daylight. Instead of hiding, it wears blazing red, gold, or electric blue -- colors easy for any hungry bird to spot. Biologists call this bold, warning-sign display 'aposematic coloration.' What message is the frog broadcasting to every predator that sees it?
answer: 'I am deadly -- don't eat me'
choices: 'I am deadly -- don't eat me'
'This patch of forest is mine'
'I am ready to find a mate'
'Look how big and strong I am'
context: Aposematic color is an honest warning signal -- a billboard telling predators the frog is toxic. Studies show the more toxic the frog, the more conspicuous its coloring, especially to bird predators that see color well. Source: The American Naturalist, 'Poison Frog Colors Are Honest Signals of Toxicity, Particularly for Bird Predators'.  (Legend.)

question: Deep in Colombia's misty Choco rainforest lives a bright yellow frog the size of a paper clip: the golden poison frog. It is one of the most poisonous animals on Earth. A single wild frog carries only about a milligram of toxin -- roughly the weight of two grains of salt -- pooled on its skin. Roughly how much damage could that one tiny frog do?
answer: Kill 10 to 20 people
choices: Kill 10 to 20 people
Kill a single small bird
Sting like a bee
Cause a mild rash
context: One wild golden poison frog carries about a milligram of batrachotoxin on its skin -- enough to kill 10 to 20 people, or roughly 20,000 mice. Source: Wikipedia, 'Golden poison frog'; National Geographic, 'Golden Poison Frog'.  (Legend.)

question: Here is the strange secret of the poison dart frog: it is not born venomous. In the wild it eats toxic ants, mites, and tiny beetles and concentrates their poisons in its skin glands. So what happens to a poison dart frog raised in a terrarium on ordinary fruit flies?
answer: It never becomes poisonous at all
choices: It never becomes poisonous at all
It grows a weaker but still deadly poison
It makes poison faster than in the wild
It loses its bright colors within weeks
context: Because the poison comes entirely from the diet, captive-bred dart frogs fed harmless insects never accumulate the alkaloids -- no captive-bred dendrobatid frog carries them, so they are completely safe to handle. Source: Understory Enterprises, 'Toxicity of Dart Frogs'; Wikipedia, 'Poison dart frog'.

question: In the rainforests of Central and South America, indigenous hunters used to wipe their blowgun darts along the back of a living frog, letting the frog's skin toxin coat the tip -- and that is where the name 'poison dart frog' came from. The frogs most people picture, the brilliant jewel-colored Dendrobates, were never the ones the hunters actually used. Which frogs actually armed the darts?
answer: A few species of the genus Phyllobates
choices: A few species of the genus Phyllobates
The tree frogs of the genus Hyla
Toads of the genus Rhinella
The glass frogs of family Centrolenidae
context: Only about four species, all in the genus Phyllobates, were actually used to poison darts -- not the more famous brilliant Dendrobates most people imagine. Source: Wikipedia, 'Poison dart frog'; AMNH, 'Dart Poison'.

question: In the rainforests of Central America lives the strawberry poison frog — a thumb-tip-sized frog splashed bright red like a berry. When her eggs hatch into tadpoles, the mother frog carries each one on her back up into a tree, to its own private pool of water cupped inside a bromeliad leaf. She leaves each tadpole there alone. Then she keeps coming back, week after week, until it grows up. What does she bring each tadpole to eat?
answer: Her own unfertilized eggs
choices: Her own unfertilized eggs
Insects she has chewed soft
Algae she scrapes from the leaves
Ants she has drowned in the pool
context: The strawberry poison frog mother returns to each lonely tadpole in its private pool and feeds it unfertilized eggs; the tadpoles accept no other food and would starve without her. Source: World Frog Day, 'Strawberry Poison Dart Frogs And Their Parental Care'; NCBI PMC5702076, 'Induced parental care in a poison frog'.

question: The golden poison frog of Colombia carries a chemical called batrachotoxin, and a fatal dose is only the size of two grains of table salt. The poison slips into nerve and muscle cells and jams the tiny sodium gates -- which normally flick shut to let a signal reset -- wide open. Once those gates are locked open, the cells can never stop firing. What happens to the victim as the poison spreads?
answer: The muscles freeze and the heart stops
choices: The muscles freeze and the heart stops
The blood slowly thins and clots fail
The nerves go numb and pain fades
The lungs fill with fluid over days
context: Batrachotoxin jams open the sodium channels in nerve and muscle so they can never close, freezing the muscles and stopping the heart. A dose of roughly 2 to 7.5 micrograms -- about two grains of salt -- can kill an adult human. Source: McGill Office for Science and Society, 'Toxin on the Backs of Some Frogs Is Lethal to Humans'; Wikipedia, 'Batrachotoxin'.

question: The dyeing poison frog (Dendrobates tinctorius) pulls off a defense that seems to contradict itself. Up close its bold pattern screams danger to a nearby predator. But researchers found that from a distance those same markings do something unexpected. What?
answer: They blur together and blend into the background
choices: They blur together and blend into the background
They flash brighter to mimic a bigger animal
They shift color to match the leaf litter
They vanish as the frog stops moving
context: From up close the bold pattern warns predators, but from a distance the same colors blur together and merge with the background -- giving the frog warning coloration and camouflage at once. Source: PNAS, 'Distance-dependent defensive coloration in the poison frog Dendrobates tinctorius'.

question: Far up north on the frozen Arctic sea ice prowls the heaviest meat-eater that walks on land anywhere on Earth. A big male can tip the scale near 1,760 pounds — heavier than a horse — and stand ten feet tall on its hind legs. It hunts seals on the pack ice all year round. Which land carnivore holds that world-heavyweight title?
answer: The polar bear
choices: The polar bear
The Siberian tiger
The saltwater crocodile
The gray wolf
context: The polar bear (Ursus maritimus, Latin for 'sea bear') is the largest extant bear and the largest land carnivore by body mass, with adult males weighing 300-800 kg (660-1,760 lb) and standing nearly 10 feet tall on their hind legs. Source: Wikipedia, Polar bear; SeaWorld, All About Polar Bears - Characteristics.  (Legend.)

question: A polar bear crouches on the Arctic sea ice next to a small round hole in the frozen surface. It holds perfectly still — for long minutes, sometimes an hour or more. It isn't stalking anything and it isn't chasing anything. It just watches that one small hole in the ice, wind rustling its white fur. What is a polar bear waiting for at a hole like that?
answer: A seal to surface for a breath, so it can strike the moment one does
choices: A seal to surface for a breath, so it can strike the moment one does
A crack of open water where it can warm its cold paws
The wind to shift so its own scent will not carry ahead of it
Its cubs to finish nursing in a den somewhere below the ice
context: This patient technique is called 'still-hunting': the bear finds a seal's breathing hole in the ice and simply waits, frozen and patient, for a seal to surface for air, then strikes. Source: Wikipedia, Polar bear; Britannica, polar bear.

question: A polar bear weighing over a thousand pounds walks out across deep, soft Arctic snow — the kind of snow that would swallow a caribou up to its belly. Yet the huge white bear barely sinks. It pads along the surface as easily as if the snow were packed hard as a road. Some part of the bear's build is spreading that enormous weight around. What keeps a bear that heavy from breaking through the snow?
answer: Front paws up to a foot across that spread its weight like snowshoes
choices: Front paws up to a foot across that spread its weight like snowshoes
Extra-long claws that hook the crust and pull it forward
Lightweight hollow leg bones that reduce how hard it presses down
A low belly that slides it along the snow like a sled
context: A polar bear's front paws reach up to 12 inches (30 cm) across, spreading its weight so it won't sink through snow, and doubling as paddles for swimming. Source: SeaWorld characteristics; ThePrimalX polar bear paws article.

question: The polar bear of the Arctic looks snowy white from nose to tail. Its coat blends into the ice so well that seals sometimes miss it coming until it's too late. But that white color is really only in the fur — it isn't the bear itself. If you could part the thick outer coat and the fluffy undercoat and peek at the bare skin beneath, you would get a surprise. What color is a polar bear's skin?
answer: Jet black
choices: Jet black
Pale pink
Bluish gray
Snowy white, like the fur
context: A polar bear's skin is black, visible only on the nose and footpads; the dark skin soaks up the sun's warmth like a solar panel. Source: SeaWorld, All About Polar Bears - Characteristics ('A polar bear's skin, visible only on the nose and footpads, is black.').

question: Out on the open Arctic ice, a polar bear lifts its huge black nose into the wind and freezes. It has locked onto its prey — a seal's breathing hole hidden far across the ice, a spot a person walking right past would never spot or smell. The bear starts padding straight toward it. Roughly how far away can a polar bear smell a seal's breathing hole?
answer: About a mile away
choices: About a mile away
About a hundred yards away
About ten miles away
Only when nearly on top of it
context: A polar bear's nose can detect a seal's breathing hole from about a mile away, and sniff out a seal hidden under three feet of packed snow. Source: Biology Insights, 'How Far Away Can a Polar Bear Smell?'; Polar Bears International seal-detection facts.

question: A polar bear stalks a seal across the Arctic sea ice — and against that endless white, her thick coat is perfect camouflage. But when a biologist plucks a single hair and puts it under the microscope, the hair looks nothing like white paint. What is each polar bear hair actually like up close?
answer: Clear and hollow, scattering light so it only looks white
choices: Clear and hollow, scattering light so it only looks white
Coated in a fine layer of reflective white pigment
Bright white all the way through the shaft
Silver-tipped over a darker brown base
context: Each hair is translucent with an air-filled core; the fur only LOOKS white because the rough hollow hairs scatter sunlight, the same way snow looks white. Source: Britannica, Why Are Polar Bears White; SeaWorld characteristics.

question: A polar bear stands on the Arctic snow at forty degrees below zero. Inside its body, though, the bear is warm as any mammal — around 99 degrees Fahrenheit. Now point an infrared heat camera at the bear. On the screen the huge animal almost disappears, reading nearly as cold as the ice around it. It looks like a hole in the world. Why does so little of a polar bear's body heat show up on the infrared image?
answer: Its insulation is so complete that almost no body heat escapes its surface
choices: Its insulation is so complete that almost no body heat escapes its surface
Its fur reflects the camera's infrared beam straight back
It lowers its body temperature to match the surrounding snow
The white fur blends into the white background on any camera
context: Hollow fur, dense underfur, and blubber insulate the bear so well that almost no body heat reaches its surface, which reads as cold as the surrounding snow. Source: AskNature, 'See-Through Fur Traps Light and Heat'; Harvard SITN, polar-bear-inspired invisibility cloak (2018).

question: As the Arctic sea ice thins each summer, polar bears must sometimes swim across open water to reach solid ice again. Scientists in Alaska fitted one female polar bear with a GPS collar and watched her leave the ice edge in the Beaufort Sea and paddle across the freezing water -- never once hauling out to rest -- until she finally reached solid ice on the far side. How long did that single nonstop swim last?
answer: Nine days
choices: Nine days
Three days
Five days
Fourteen days
context: The tracked female swam about 426 miles (687 km) nonstop over nine days across the Beaufort Sea, losing 22% of her body weight before reaching ice. Reported from a USGS polar bear tracking study (2011). Source: USGS tracking study via Wikipedia, Polar bear, and PBS Nature Polar Bear Fact Sheet.  (Legend.)

question: The Portuguese man o' war drifts at the surface of warm oceans looking like a pale blue jellyfish. On top floats a gas-filled balloon; long stinging tentacles trail below, sometimes thirty feet down into the water. But scientists insist you should call it 'they,' not 'it.' Somebody who reaches for the creature is really reaching for a whole crowd. Why do biologists say 'they' about a Portuguese man o' war?
answer: It is a colony of many bodies
choices: It is a colony of many bodies
It changes sex through its life
It always swims in mated pairs
It splits in two when threatened
context: A Portuguese man o' war (Physalia physalis) is not a jellyfish and not even a single animal. It is a siphonophore: a floating colony of many specialized bodies called zooids, all genetically identical clones, so tightly fused that no one zooid could survive alone. That is why scientists say it is a 'they,' not an 'it.' Source: NOAA Ocean Service, oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/portuguese-man-o-war.html.  (Legend.)

question: In the warm open ocean, a Portuguese man o' war drifts along the surface. Above the water it shows a soft blue-purple bag full of gas — a float that stands up like a little balloon. It has no fins, no tail, and no way to swim. Yet somehow this creature travels for miles across the open sea. How does it move?
answer: The wind blows its bag like a sail
choices: The wind blows its bag like a sail
It jets water to shoot forward
It hitches rides on passing fish
It slowly rolls with the tide alone
context: The blue-violet-to-pink gas bag on top (the pneumatophore, or float) rises up to about six inches above the water and acts as a sail to catch the wind. The man o' war has no way to swim or steer itself; it drifts wherever wind and current carry it. Source: NOAA Ocean Service; Wikipedia, Portuguese man o' war.

question: A Portuguese man o' war looks small at the surface. Its gas-filled purple float is only about a foot long. But hanging out of sight below the waves are its stinging tentacles, thin threads packed with venom. Stretched to their full limit, those tentacles reach an astonishing distance downward. How far do those hidden threads reach?
answer: Longer than a blue whale
choices: Longer than a blue whale
Farther than a football field
About the height of a house
Roughly the length of a car
context: The stinging tentacles trail an average of about 10 meters (30 feet) below the float and can stretch as far as 30 meters (roughly 100 feet), longer than a blue whale, all hanging invisibly beneath a float only inches wide. Source: NOAA Ocean Service; Wikipedia, Portuguese man o' war.

question: A Portuguese man o' war looks like a single jellyfish, but it is really a floating colony of tiny animals called zooids that grew together and now live as one body. Each zooid has a single job. One is the float. Some sting. Others catch food or make babies. But there is a strange catch about any single body pulled from the colony. What is it?
answer: On its own it would die
choices: On its own it would die
It can regrow the whole colony
It swims off to hunt alone
It hardens into a protective shell
context: The colony is divided into jobs: one zooid type forms the gas float, dactylozooids form the stinging tentacles, gastrozooids digest, and gonozooids handle reproduction. Each body can do only its one job, and they are so dependent on one another that no single zooid could survive on its own. Source: Wikipedia, Portuguese man o' war (zooid types); NOAA Ocean Service.

question: The Portuguese man o' war looks like a jellyfish drifting on the surface of the sea, but is really a floating colony of tiny animals sharing one body. Instead of gulping ordinary air to inflate the sail-like float that holds up its long stinging tentacles, the man o' war makes its own gas from special cells inside. Startlingly, that homemade gas can be rich in the very same poison that pours from a car's exhaust pipe. What poison is it?
answer: Carbon monoxide
choices: Carbon monoxide
Chlorine
Ammonia
Methane
context: The float doesn't just hold ordinary air; the animal actively makes its own gas inside the bag, and it can be as much as 13% carbon monoxide, the same poisonous gas that comes out of a car exhaust. Source: Wikipedia, Portuguese man o' war (pneumatophore gas composition).  (Legend.)

question: The blue dragon is a tiny sea slug -- smaller than a grape -- that drifts upside-down on the surface of the open ocean. Somehow this delicate creature can eat the Portuguese man o' war, a jellyfish-like colony bristling with stinging cells that can kill fish, without being harmed at all. Stranger still is what the little slug does with the biggest, most powerful stingers after it swallows them down whole.
answer: It stores them to fire as its own weapon
choices: It stores them to fire as its own weapon
It grinds them into harmless paste
It spits them back at the colony
It uses them to build a shell
context: The blue dragon (Glaucus atlanticus) sorts out the strongest stingers, does not fire them, and stores them in the tips of its own feathery arms to reuse as a stolen weapon, a trick called kleptocnidy. Source: Wikipedia, Glaucus atlanticus; HowStuffWorks, The Blue Dragon Sea Slug Eats Venomous Prey and Saves the Stingers for Later.  (Legend.)

question: Portuguese men o' war sail with the wind, but their sails come in two mirror-image builds, so different individuals veer off to the left or the right rather than all running straight downwind. Biologists think this split helps the species in one specific way. Which?
answer: A whole fleet never all strands on one beach
choices: A whole fleet never all strands on one beach
The colonies can steer toward richer feeding grounds
Left and right builds can mate only with each other
Rivals are pushed apart to reduce competition
context: The sail comes in two mirror-image forms: some men o' war are 'left-handed' and some 'right-handed,' so they tack off at about 45 degrees to either side of the wind. This split means a whole fleet never all blows onto the same beach at once, sparing part of the population from stranding and dying together. Source: Wikipedia, Portuguese man o' war (dimorphism and drift); ScienceDirect, Relationship between dimorphism and drift in the Portuguese man-of-war.  (Legend.)

question: The potoo is a big-eyed night bird of the forests of Central and South America. In the daytime it does something bizarre to stay safe from hawks: it perches bolt upright on the stump of a broken branch, points its head and bill straight up at the sky, and freezes there for hours without so much as a twitch. What does a motionless potoo look like sitting on that broken branch?
answer: A broken-off, dead stub of the branch itself
choices: A broken-off, dead stub of the branch itself
A coiled snake draped over the wood
A clump of bright red berries
A patch of green moss on the bark
context: The potoo's daytime disguise is total: it aligns its body with a broken snag, points its bill upward, and stays motionless for hours, so it reads as a dead stub of the very tree it sits on. Its own nestlings can even resemble clumps of fungus on the wood. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_potoo ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potoo

question: A potoo -- the big-eyed night bird of the Central and South American forests -- spends the day frozen upright on a broken branch, eyes shut tight, pretending to be dead wood. Yet if a hunting hawk creeps closer, the 'sleeping' bird reacts and shifts position before the hawk can strike. Something built into its eyelids lets it track that movement without ever opening its eyes. What is it?
answer: Notched slits set into its own eyelids
choices: Notched slits set into its own eyelids
A transparent inner eyelid it peers through
Oversized eyes that shine through thin skin
A reflective backing that glows when shut
context: The potoo has two or three notches, or slits, in its eyelids that stay open even when the eyes are shut, letting it sense light and movement — so it can detect an approaching predator while sitting frozen with its eyes 'closed.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_potoo ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potoo  (Legend.)

question: The potoo is a strange night bird of the Central and South American forests. By day it sits stone-still on a broken branch and looks exactly like a chunk of dead wood. Once a season the female produces a single precious egg. She builds no nest of twigs at all. When the moment comes to lay it, where does that lone egg end up?
answer: Straight onto a bare dip on a branch or rotten stump
choices: Straight onto a bare dip on a branch or rotten stump
Inside a hole she chisels in a tree trunk
In a floating raft of reeds on the water
In a deep scrape she digs in the forest floor
context: The potoo builds nothing at all — the female lays her single egg directly into a shallow depression on a bare branch or the top of a rotten stump, and a parent hides it by perching over it like part of the wood. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potoo ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_potoo

question: After dark the common potoo lifts a strange voice across the forest — a haunting run of up to eight whistled notes that forest people once took as an omen. Track those eight whistles from the first note to the last. What does the phrase do as it goes?
answer: Steadily drop in pitch and fade to silence
choices: Steadily drop in pitch and fade to silence
Rise steadily to a piercing shriek
Hold one long flat unbroken tone
Speed up into a rattling drum-roll
context: The common potoo's song is a series of up to eight whistled notes that steadily drop in pitch and fade in volume — a sound like a distant, sorrowful human cry drifting through the dark. That eerie, sinking wail earned folk names like 'ghost bird' and 'poor-me-one,' and a Peruvian tale calls it a lost child crying for its mother. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_potoo ; https://www.iflscience.com/meet-the-great-potoo-south-americas-loud-but-elusive-ghost-bird-76689  (Legend.)

question: A red kangaroo in the Australian outback carries her baby only about 33 days inside her body before it is born. That is barely a month, far shorter than most mammals. So the newborn comes out tiny, blind, and not yet fully formed. About how big is a just-born red kangaroo?
answer: The size of a jellybean, under a gram
choices: The size of a jellybean, under a gram
The size of a house cat
The size of a rabbit
The size of a human baby
context: A newborn red kangaroo is roughly 2 cm long and weighs under a gram — about the size of a jellybean or grape — and is born blind and hairless after just ~33 days. It finishes developing outside the womb. Source: a-z-animals.com/articles/a-newborn-kangaroo-is-no-bigger-than-a-jellybean/

question: In Australia and the Americas live mammals that raise their tiny newborns inside a special belly pouch. Kangaroos, koalas, wombats, Tasmanian devils, and opossums all sit on the same branch of the mammal family tree. They are set apart from mice, monkeys, and other mammals that grow their young to term inside the mother. What is this pouch-mammal group called?
answer: Marsupials
choices: Marsupials
Rodents
Primates
Amphibians
context: Marsupials give birth to tiny, barely-formed young that complete their development in (or attached to) the mother's pouch, latched to a teat. Kangaroos, koalas, wombats and opossums are all marsupials. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marsupial

question: A newborn red kangaroo is blind and hairless, no bigger than a jellybean and lighter than a paper clip. It slips out down near its mother's tail. To survive, it must reach the pouch high up on her belly. Nobody carries it there for it. How does this tiny newborn get to the pouch?
answer: It hauls itself up through the fur on tiny clawed forelimbs
choices: It hauls itself up through the fur on tiny clawed forelimbs
Its mother lifts it in with her paws
Its mother carries it in her mouth
It is born already inside the pouch
context: The mother does not help. The newborn hauls itself up through her fur using its one well-developed feature — strong forelimbs tipped with tiny claws — while the rest of its body is still unformed. Source: a-z-animals.com/articles/a-newborn-kangaroo-is-no-bigger-than-a-jellybean/

question: A newborn red kangaroo is barely formed — blind, deaf, almost bodyless — yet the instant it is born, it must haul itself up through its mother's belly fur to reach her pouch. The whole climb is done in about three minutes, with no eyes at all to steer by. What guides this tiny newborn to find the pouch?
answer: An excellent sense of smell and direction
choices: An excellent sense of smell and direction
The mother's heartbeat
Faint warmth from the pouch
The sound of the mother's voice
context: The whole climb takes about three minutes, guided by a strong sense of smell and direction — remarkable for an animal whose body is almost entirely unformed except its grasping front limbs. Source: scienceinsights.org/how-do-kangaroos-give-birth-from-embryo-to-pouch/

question: A newborn kangaroo joey is barely the size of a jellybean, blind and hairless. After crawling on tiny arms up through its mother's fur into her warm pouch, it finally reaches a teat and latches on. In that moment something happens that locks the pair together: the joey cannot be shaken loose, even when the mother bounds across the outback at top speed. What happens where the joey meets the teat?
answer: The tip of the teat swells into a bulb inside its mouth
choices: The tip of the teat swells into a bulb inside its mouth
The joey's jaws fuse shut around the teat
The pouch fills with a sticky fluid
The joey grips the teat with its claws
context: The teat tip swells into a bulb inside the joey's mouth, fusing the two together for months — it cannot be dislodged even at full speed. Newborn marsupials also have 'oral shields' narrowing the mouth to a round hole just wide enough for the teat. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marsupial

question: In the dry red grasslands of Australia, a red kangaroo mother bounds along on her huge hind legs, sometimes leaping thirty feet in a single hop. Her pouch faces forward — the opening pointed up toward her head — with a tiny joey riding inside. It looks like every jump should fling the joey right out. Yet it never does. She controls the pouch opening like the neck of a drawstring bag. What lets her do that?
answer: A strong sphincter muscle that tightens the pouch opening
choices: A strong sphincter muscle that tightens the pouch opening
A flap of skin she folds over by hand
Sticky glands lining the pouch rim
The joey hooking its claws over the edge
context: A ring of sphincter muscle at the pouch opening lets the mother cinch it shut like a drawstring, so a joey in a forward-opening pouch can't fall out mid-leap. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pouch_(marsupial)

question: In the eucalyptus forests of Australia, a mother wombat — a stocky, badger-like marsupial — digs a deep burrow the way she always does: throwing dirt straight backward under her belly with powerful claws. All the while she has a baby riding in her pouch. If her pouch faced forward the way a kangaroo's does, she would bury her own baby alive with every scrape. Yet the baby stays perfectly clean. Why?
answer: Her pouch opens backward, toward her hind legs
choices: Her pouch opens backward, toward her hind legs
She seals the pouch shut while digging
She digs only with her front paws held high
She carries the baby in her mouth while digging
context: A wombat's pouch opens backward, toward the hind legs, so a digging mother doesn't shovel dirt onto the baby inside — the opposite orientation to a forward-opening kangaroo pouch. Source: environment.sa.gov.au/goodliving/posts/2018/10/wombat-facts

question: The Virginia opossum is the only marsupial that lives wild in North America -- a pointy-nosed, gray-furred cousin of the kangaroo. When a mother gives birth, more than twenty jellybean-sized babies come tumbling out at once, far more than she can raise. The tiny newborns must scramble blindly through her fur toward the pouch. What actually decides which of those babies survive?
answer: Only those that reach one of her ~13 teats live
choices: Only those that reach one of her ~13 teats live
The mother eats the weakest herself
The first-born pushes the rest out of the pouch
She raises whichever ones are largest at birth
context: A Virginia opossum mother has about 13 teats, so of her 20-plus newborns only those that reach and latch onto a teat survive. Her pregnancy lasts just 12–13 days, one of the shortest of any mammal. Source: sdzwildlifeexplorers.org/animals/virginia-opossum

question: On the dry plains of central Australia lives the red kangaroo, the world's largest marsupial. A female red kangaroo can pull off a trick biologists call embryonic diapause: she can mate, then simply hold the resulting embryo — a tiny ball of about 100 cells — in suspended animation, paused and ready to resume the instant her pouch is free again. What keeps that embryo on hold?
answer: Nursing the joey already in her pouch
choices: Nursing the joey already in her pouch
A drop in the season's rainfall
The mother's body temperature falling
A hormone released only after a long fast
context: This is embryonic diapause: a fertilized egg is held as a ~100-cell blastocyst, frozen and ready to develop the moment the pouch empties. Nursing the current joey is what keeps it paused. Source: ielc.libguides.com/sdzg/factsheets/westerngraykangaroo/reproduction  (Legend.)

question: In the Australian outback, a red kangaroo mother often has two children at once — a big joey almost as tall as she is, hopping along beside her, and a tiny newborn no bigger than a jellybean, latched to a teat in her pouch. Both drink from her, sometimes at the same moment, and yet each gets milk perfectly suited to its age. How does the mother kangaroo manage that?
answer: She makes two different milks from two teats at once
choices: She makes two different milks from two teats at once
She alternates one milk between the two by the hour
She feeds the newborn milk and the older one solid food
Both drink the same milk but at different times
context: From two teats simultaneously she produces fat-rich milk for the older joey 'at foot' and low-fat, immune-rich milk for the tiny newborn in the pouch — different recipes at the same time. Source: a-z-animals.com/articles/kangaroos-have-one-of-the-strangest-reproductive-systems-in-the-animal-world/  (Legend.)

question: A koala (Phascolarctos cinereus) lives on eucalyptus leaves so loaded with tannins and toxins that most animals couldn't stomach them. Around 5–6 months old, a koala joey eats a special soft dropping its mother makes, called 'pap' — not for the calories. What is it really swallowing?
answer: Live gut bacteria that let it digest eucalyptus
choices: Live gut bacteria that let it digest eucalyptus
Extra minerals stripped from the leaves
A dose of the toxins to build up tolerance
Half-digested leaves ready to eat
context: Pap comes from the caecum and is packed with live tannin-protein-degrading bacteria — far richer in microbes than ordinary droppings. The joey eats it to seed its gut before its first eucalyptus leaves. Sources: australiangeographic.com.au/news/2022/07/pap-not-poop-the-gift-a-mother-koala-gives-her-joey/ ; enviromicro-journals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/1462-2920.15858  (Legend.)

question: A female kangaroo has two uteruses, with a birth canal between them. In many kangaroos that canal only opens up at her first birth. This double plumbing was set by an accident of how the marsupial embryo grows. A pair of tubes ends up running right between the two developing reproductive tracts, blocking them from ever joining into the one system placental mammals have. Which tubes wedge in there?
answer: The ureters, draining the kidneys down to the bladder
choices: The ureters, draining the kidneys down to the bladder
The Wolffian ducts, the embryonic precursors of male plumbing
The lymphatic vessels, draining fluid back toward the heart
The urethra, draining the bladder to the outside
context: In the marsupial embryo the ureters run between the two developing reproductive tracts, so the tracts can never fuse the way they do in placental mammals — which is why marsupials keep three vaginal canals and two uteruses. The two side (lateral) canals carry sperm up to the two uteruses; a separate central 'median' canal is the road the tiny joey travels down at birth. Males match the paired lateral tracts with a two-pronged, bifurcated penis. Sources: 'Why do kangaroos have 3 vaginas?' Live Science — https://www.livescience.com/animals/land-mammals/why-do-kangaroos-have-3-vaginas ; 'Kangaroos Have Three Vaginas,' National Geographic — https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/kangaroos-have-three-vaginas ; Australian Geographic — https://www.australiangeographic.com.au/nature-wildlife/2022/12/did-you-know-kangaroos-have-three-vaginas/  (Legend.)

question: On a summer garden stem, a slender green insect sits perfectly still. Its two spiky front legs are folded up and held out before it, as though the bug were about to grasp something. It waits, motionless, for a fly or grasshopper to wander close enough to snatch. What is this ambush hunter?
answer: A praying mantis
choices: A praying mantis
A walking stick
A leaf katydid
A green lacewing
context: The praying mantis gets its name from that folded-leg posture, which looks like praying but is really a cocked spring ready to snap. Source: Live Science, high-speed video of mantis strike; My Pet Mantis hunting overview.

question: When a fly finally drifts within reach of a praying mantis, the insect explodes into motion. Its two folded, spike-lined front legs snap forward and slam shut around the prey, pinning it in place. From the very moment the mantis launches those forelegs, how long does the whole grab take?
answer: About 50 to 70 milliseconds, faster than a blink
choices: About 50 to 70 milliseconds, faster than a blink
About half a second, quicker than a hand
Two to three seconds, a slow squeeze
A tenth of a minute, deliberate and steady
context: Those raptorial forelegs snap shut like a spring-loaded trap in as little as 50 to 70 milliseconds — faster than a human can blink. Source: Live Science, high-speed video of mantis strike.

question: A praying mantis strikes only when its prey lands in a narrow window right in front of its face — the exact distance its spiked forelegs can reach. To judge that distance perfectly, it uses a visual ability found in no other insect on Earth. What is this ability?
answer: True 3D depth perception
choices: True 3D depth perception
Heat-sensing infrared sight
A 360-degree panoramic scan
X-ray sight through leaves
context: The praying mantis is the only insect known to see in true 3D depth perception (stereo vision), letting it gauge precisely when prey is in striking range. Source: Newcastle University Press Office, 'New form of 3D vision discovered in praying mantis' (2018).

question: The biggest praying mantises are strong enough to grab and eat small vertebrates alive, and researchers have collected reports from around the world of their kills — frogs, lizards, tiny fish, mice, and small birds. But one entry in those records stands out as the strangest catch ever observed, seen just once. What was it?
answer: A small bat
choices: A small bat
A small snake
A newt
A hummingbird
context: Mantises have been recorded killing and eating small frogs, lizards, salamanders, snakes, mice — and, on one remarkable occasion, a small bat. Source: phys.org, 'Praying mantises hunt down birds worldwide' (2017); Nyffeler, Maxwell & Van Remsen study.

question: The orchid mantis of Southeast Asian rainforests is pink and white with wide, petal-shaped legs. It perches on a plant, folds its body until it looks like a single blossom, and waits perfectly still to ambush the bees, wasps, and butterflies that come looking for nectar. When biologists studied wild orchid mantises in the field, they found something startling about how well its flower disguise works.
answer: It draws in more insects than the real flowers nearby
choices: It draws in more insects than the real flowers nearby
It only fools insects that are already dying
It must hide among matching blossoms to work
It works only at night when flowers are closed
context: The orchid mantis is a living flower disguise, and O'Hanlon's field study found it attracts pollinating insects even better than the real flowers around it. Source: O'Hanlon, Holwell & Herberstein, 'Pollinator Deception in the Orchid Mantis,' The American Naturalist (2014). (Legendary-sounding but real.)

question: The praying mantis is a long-legged ambush hunter that stalks other insects with folded, jackknife front legs. There's an old story about the female mantis: she always bites the head off her mate during mating. Careful laboratory experiments show the truth is more specific — she does sometimes eat him, but mainly under one particular condition. Which?
answer: When the female is hungry
choices: When the female is hungry
When the male is older than the female
When the pair mate in daylight
When the female has already mated once
context: Most matings end with the male alive; the head-biting legend is overstated. In one experiment no well-fed female ate her mate, while starved females did. Source: Snopes, 'Does a Female Praying Mantis Always Eat Her Mate's Head?'; phys.org, 'Praying mantis cannibalism explained.' (A real but overstated legend.)

question: To test whether mantises really see in true 3D, the British scientist Vivek Nityananda and his team at Newcastle University fitted each mantis with a tiny pair of blue-and-green movie glasses — like the ones humans wear for old 3D films — and then played the insects a 3D movie of prey drifting on a screen. How did the mantises react?
answer: They lunged to grab prey that was not really there
choices: They lunged to grab prey that was not really there
They ignored the screen entirely
They fled from the flickering images
They froze until the movie ended
context: Nityananda glued tiny 3D glasses onto the mantises with a drop of beeswax; when shown a 3D illusion of prey, they tried to grab it right out of the air — proving they see in 3D. Source: Live Science, 'Praying Mantises Wear Tiny 3D Glasses, for Science'; Newcastle University. (Sounds like a tall tale, but it really happened.)  (Legend.)

question: Many praying mantises carry a single 'cyclopean' ear tucked in the middle of the chest, tuned to catch ultrasound too high for human ears. On a night flight, when that one ear picks up the high-pitched hunting cries of a bat closing in from behind, the flying mantis reacts in an instant. What does the mantis suddenly do in midair?
answer: Throws itself into a spiraling power dive
choices: Throws itself into a spiraling power dive
Freezes in midair and drops straight down
Flashes bright wing spots to startle the bat
Emits its own ultrasonic clicks to jam the bat
context: On detecting a bat's ultrasonic calls, a flying mantis spirals into a steep power dive toward the ground, escaping about 80 percent of the time. Source: National Geographic, 'Praying Mantis Uses Ultrasonic Hearing to Dodge Bats'; Yager, 'The Cyclopean Ear,' Science (1986).

question: Look at the head of a wolf, an owl, a house cat, or a person. All four are hunters, and all four have both eyes pointing the same way. Because the two eyes overlap, the animal can judge exactly how far away its prey is. Where on the head do a hunter's eyes sit?
answer: on the front of the head
choices: on the front of the head
on the sides of the head
on top of the head
one on each end of a long stalk
context: Forward-facing eyes give overlapping fields of view, and that overlap is what lets a predator measure the distance to its target before it leaps. The old rhyme sums it up: 'Eyes in front, the animal hunts.' Sources: University of California / Berkeley News 'Hunter or prey? The eyes are the key' (2015-08-07); veterinaryvision.co.uk 'How animals see the World.'

question: Rabbits, horses, and deer spend their days with their heads down cropping grass, and none of them can see far in front of the nose. Even so, each one can still spot a lion or a wolf sneaking up from almost any direction around the herd. Where are a grazer's eyes placed on the skull to give it that wide, panoramic watch?
answer: on the sides of the head
choices: on the sides of the head
on the front of the head
tucked under the ears
behind a bony hood
context: Side-set eyes give up the overlap that measures distance and trade it for a nearly all-around field of view, so a hunted animal can spot danger coming from behind or the flank. The rhyme is 'Eyes on the side, the animal hides.' Sources: New Hampshire State Parks 'Reading a Skull: Predator and Prey Differences' (nhstateparks.org); Nearby Nature 'Predators and Prey Background.'

question: A horse's side-set eyes sweep almost the whole circle around it — close to 340 degrees of watch. Yet there is one spot the horse cannot see that surprises people: not just directly behind it, but a triangle a few feet long in one other place. Where is that second blind spot?
answer: right in front of its own nose
choices: right in front of its own nose
straight up above its mane
along its left flank only
under its own belly
context: The horse's panoramic side vision leaves two gaps: one directly behind the tail, and one triangle of blindness reaching a few feet straight out from the nose. A horse briefly raising or turning its head fills the front gap, which is why a grazing horse keeps bobbing its head up. Sources: Utah State University Extension 'Equine Vision and Its Effect on Behavior' (digitalcommons.usu.edu); equinehelper.com 'How Horses See.'

question: A grazing goat drops its head to the grass, and something remarkable happens inside each eye: the long, horizontal slit pupil rolls up to 50 degrees. The two eyes turn in opposite directions as the head tilts down. What is the rolling pupil actually doing?
answer: keep the pupil level with the ground
choices: keep the pupil level with the ground
seal shut against flying grit
let in far more light
point both pupils at the same blade of grass
context: This eye-roll is called cyclovergence: as the goat or sheep lowers its head to eat, each eye rotates so the wide horizontal pupil stays parallel to the horizon, keeping the whole sweep of ground in sharp focus for spotting a predator even while the animal is head-down grazing. Sources: Banks et al. 2015 'Why do animal eyes have pupils of different shapes?' (Science Advances); Berkeley News 2015-08-07; The Conversation 'Revealed: why animals' pupils come in different shapes.' (Legend-tier wonder.)

question: Martin Banks's team measured 214 land animals and found the vertical slit pupil isn't a mark of big cats at all — lions and tigers have round pupils. The slit shows up almost only in predators shorter than about knee height, like house cats and geckos. What hunting style does that low, close-to-the-ground slit belong to?
answer: an ambusher lying in wait for the pounce
choices: an ambusher lying in wait for the pounce
a runner chasing prey across open ground
a night-flying glider
a filter-feeder sifting the water
context: Banks's team found the vertical slit almost always in predators under about 42 cm at the shoulder. Down near the ground, the slit sharpens the blur and disparity cues a lying-in-wait hunter uses to time the exact moment of the strike — while tall chasers like lions keep round pupils. Sources: Banks et al. 2015 (Science Advances); Berkeley News 2015-08-07; sci.news 'New Study Reveals Why Some Animals Have Vertical Pupils.'

question: Deep in the swampy rainforests of Borneo lives a shaggy orange monkey that troops through the trees in noisy family bands. The adult male is instantly known to anyone who has seen him by a single feature on his face -- so unusual that scientists named the whole species after it. What does he sport?
answer: A drooping nose over four inches long
choices: A drooping nose over four inches long
A fan of bright blue cheek ridges
A bony crest like a rooster's comb
A mane of stiff white whiskers
context: The male proboscis monkey (Nasalis larvatus) grows the largest nose of any primate — a pendulous flap that can pass four inches (about 10 cm). Females and juveniles keep small, neat, upturned noses. Source: https://www.oneearth.org/species-of-the-week-proboscis-monkey/  (Legend.)

question: The proboscis monkey lives in the dense jungles of Borneo and has one of the strangest faces of any primate: the males grow huge, drooping noses that hang past the mouth. In thick forest the monkeys often can't see each other, so they call back and forth. A male's honking cry carries far through the trees, and that oversized nose does something to the sound that helps it travel. What does the big nose do to the honk?
answer: It acts as a resonating chamber that deepens and amplifies the honk
choices: It acts as a resonating chamber that deepens and amplifies the honk
It squeezes shut to force the honk out in sharp bursts
It funnels the honk straight up above the canopy
It filters out low tones so only the sharp notes carry
context: The nasal cavity works like a built-in loudspeaker: it resonates, deepening and amplifying the honk so it reaches monkeys the male cannot see. A bigger nose makes a deeper, louder call — so a female choosing a big-nosed male is reading his fitness off the sound, part visual banner and part megaphone. Source: https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.aaq0250

question: The proboscis monkey of Borneo has a huge round potbelly that can weigh a quarter of its whole body. It looks almost cartoonish — a skinny monkey with a giant paunch. That swollen belly holds a special kind of stomach that lets it live on a diet of tough, bitter jungle leaves. What is inside it doing the work?
answer: A chambered stomach packed with bacteria that ferment tough leaves
choices: A chambered stomach packed with bacteria that ferment tough leaves
A crop of grit and gravel that grinds the leaves to paste
A pouch of stored fat that carries it through the dry season
A tangle of extra-long coiled intestine to soak up water
context: Like a cow, the proboscis monkey has a multi-chambered stomach full of cellulose-busting bacteria that ferment tough leaves — even detoxifying poisons in near-inedible mangrove leaves. It also regurgitates and re-chews its food, the first documented rumination-like remastication in a primate. Sweet ripe fruit is dangerous: its sugars ferment inside and can bloat the monkey badly, so it eats mostly young leaves and unripe fruit. Sources: https://hakaimagazine.com/features/the-wonderful-transcendent-life-of-an-odd-nosed-monkey/ ; https://royalsocietypublishing.org/doi/full/10.1098/rsbl.2011.0197

question: The proboscis monkeys of Borneo live along muddy rivers, and they often need to cross water full of crocodiles to reach a good feeding tree. So they belly-flop straight from the branches into the river and paddle across at its narrowest point. What special body feature lets them out-swim other monkeys?
answer: Webbed hands and feet for paddling underwater
choices: Webbed hands and feet for paddling underwater
A hollow-boned tail that floats them like a cork
Oily fur that keeps water from soaking them down
Air-filled cheek pouches they gulp to stay buoyant
context: Proboscis monkeys are among the best swimmers of any monkey. Their webbed hands and feet let them dog-paddle and even swim underwater up to 20 meters (about 66 feet) to cross rivers. They slip in as silently as they can so the crocodiles don't notice them. Sources: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/mammals/facts/proboscis-monkey ; https://www.discoverwildlife.com/tv/proboscis-monkeys-leap-into-crocodile-infested-river-bbc  (Legend.)

question: Pterosaurs were huge flying creatures that ruled the skies for over 150 million years, back when dinosaurs walked the Earth. Many books and cartoons call them 'flying dinosaurs' — but that label is actually wrong. Pterosaurs were not dinosaurs at all. What kind of animal was a pterosaur really?
answer: A flying reptile, its own separate branch
choices: A flying reptile, its own separate branch
A kind of early bird
A small feathered dinosaur
A giant flying insect
context: A pterosaur is NOT a dinosaur and NOT a bird -- it is its own kind of flying reptile, though a close cousin of the dinosaurs. Calling it a 'flying dinosaur' is a common mistake. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pterosaur  (Legend.)

question: Pterosaurs first appeared roughly 230 million years ago, in the Late Triassic period. They were reptiles about the size of birds, with a long stiff finger stretching a leathery membrane along each side. Before them, no animal with a backbone had ever pulled off a certain feat in the whole history of Earth. What was pterosaurs' history-making first?
answer: The first to fly under their own power
choices: The first to fly under their own power
The first to lay eggs on land
The first to grow a bony shell
The first to breathe air on land
context: Pterosaurs were the first vertebrates ever to achieve true flapping flight, taking to the air in the Late Triassic long before birds existed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pterosaur  (Legend.)

question: Pterosaurs were flying reptiles that ruled the skies through the age of dinosaurs, from roughly 220 to 66 million years ago. A pterosaur's wing was a broad sheet of thin skin stretched taut like a kite, but almost the whole wing was held out and spread by just one part of its body. Which part?
answer: One enormously long fourth finger
choices: One enormously long fourth finger
A fan of stiff tail feathers
A row of long back ribs
A double-hinged shoulder blade
context: The wing was a sheet of skin stretched from the body all the way to the tip of one hugely elongated fourth finger -- the entire wing rode on a single giant finger. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pterosaur  (Legend.)

question: Quetzalcoatlus was a pterosaur that flew the skies of what is now Texas about 68 million years ago, at the very end of the age of dinosaurs. It was one of the largest flying animals ever to live, with a wingspan of about 10 to 11 meters. What everyday flying machine was it as wide as?
answer: A small airplane
choices: A small airplane
A hang glider
A kite
A ceiling fan
context: Quetzalcoatlus northropi spanned about 10-11 metres (33-36 feet) wingtip to wingtip -- as wide as a small airplane. It is named after Quetzalcoatl, the Aztec feathered-serpent sky god. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quetzalcoatlus  (Legend.)

question: Quetzalcoatlus, a giant Late Cretaceous pterosaur that soared over what is now Texas 68 million years ago, stretched about 11 meters from wingtip to wingtip. That is wider than a small airplane, and yet the animal still managed to leave the ground and fly. What kept such a giant light enough to fly?
answer: Hollow, air-filled bones
choices: Hollow, air-filled bones
A belly full of trapped gas
Wings lighter than paper
A body mostly made of fat
context: Pterosaur bones were hollow and air-filled, just like a bird's, which is how such huge animals stayed light enough to leave the ground. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pterosaur

question: Quetzalcoatlus was a Late Cretaceous pterosaur the size of a small airplane, with an 11-meter wingspan and a head longer than a grown man is tall. When it landed and folded its huge leathery wings away, it still had to move around on the ground to hunt and drink. How did this giant get around on land?
answer: On all fours, limbs straight under its body
choices: On all fours, limbs straight under its body
Hopping upright on two legs
Dragging itself flat on its belly
Gliding between low branches
context: On the ground it folded up its wings and walked on all fours, with its limbs held straight underneath its body like a walking animal, not sprawled out. Standing, its head reached about as high as a modern giraffe. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quetzalcoatlus

question: Quetzalcoatlus was a Late Cretaceous pterosaur the size of a small airplane, with a wingspan of about 33 feet and roughly the weight of a full-grown giraffe. It was far too heavy to sprint along the ground on two legs and flap into the air the way birds or bats get aloft. So how did this giant get itself off the ground?
answer: Vaulting straight up off its front limbs
choices: Vaulting straight up off its front limbs
Diving off a cliff to catch the wind
Flapping in place until it slowly rose
Waiting to be lifted by rising hot air
context: In this 'quad-launch,' the giant planted all four limbs and exploded upward off its powerful front limbs like a pole-vaulter. Michael Habib proposed it in 2008 from the bones themselves -- a very strong arm bone (humerus) but a comparatively weak thigh bone, the reverse of a running animal, so the arms did the launching. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quetzalcoatlus  (Legend.)

question: For decades, paleontologists have argued over how the giant pterosaur Quetzalcoatlus, an 11-meter-wingspan animal that flew over Late Cretaceous North America 68 million years ago, actually fed itself. Ideas have ranged from skimming fish on the wing to scavenging carcasses. What does today's best fossil evidence support?
answer: Striding the ground and snatching up small animals
choices: Striding the ground and snatching up small animals
Skimming low over water to snatch fish on the wing
Gliding down to feed on carcasses from above
Cropping tough plants with its long jaws
context: Rather than fishing from the air, giant Quetzalcoatlus probably stalked prey on foot, snapping up small animals on the ground much like a modern stork or ground hornbill. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quetzalcoatlus  (Legend.)

question: A pterosaur wing was a thin sheet of skin stretched from an enormously long finger down to its ankles. At full flight speed, a bare membrane like that should have flapped and rippled uselessly, the way a loose sail flaps in a gust. Yet pterosaur wings held their shape and pushed the air firmly. What kept the skin taut?
answer: Thousands of stiff internal fibers running across the membrane
choices: Thousands of stiff internal fibers running across the membrane
A hard outer shell of overlapping scales along the wing
A cushion of trapped air sealed between two layers of skin
Rows of small interlocking feathers anchored to the arm
context: The wing was not just skin. Packed inside it were thousands of thin stiffening rods called actinofibrils, each about 0.1 mm thick and crowded four to seven per millimetre, layered in criss-crossing sheets that fanned toward the long wing-finger. They worked like built-in battens or springs, spreading and tensioning the membrane so it held its shape against the air, yet still let the whole wing fold up compactly when the animal landed. Their exact material is still uncertain, most likely collagen, possibly keratin. Source: Wikipedia, 'Anatomy of pterosaurs' / 'Pterosaur', corroborating S. Christopher Bennett 2000, 'Pterosaur flight: the role of actinofibrils in wing function', Historical Biology 14:255-284.

question: For a long time scientists assumed the fuzzy coat covering pterosaurs was simple hair-like fluff — just insulation for warmth. Then in 2019 a beautifully preserved anurognathid pterosaur fossil showed something startling: some of its filaments were branched, not single strands. Branched filaments are the definition of feathers. What did that force scientists to rethink?
answer: When feathers first arose, maybe in an ancestor long before birds
choices: When feathers first arose, maybe in an ancestor long before birds
Whether the animals ran warm-blooded or stayed cold-blooded
Whether the fuzz was colored for camouflage or for display
How big pterosaur eggs were and where the parents buried them
context: The body fuzz, called pycnofibers, turned out to be more than hair. Some filaments were grouped and bilaterally branched, a feather-like structure, and preserved melanosomes even hinted at their color. Because branched filaments were thought to belong only to feathered dinosaurs, this raised a striking possibility: that true feathers, or the genetic recipe for them, first appeared in a shared archosaur ancestor tens of millions of years before birds, rather than pterosaur fuzz and dinosaur feathers being two separate inventions. The idea remains debated, but it reframes the whole origin of feathers. Source: Zixiao Yang et al. 2019, 'Pterosaur integumentary structures with complex feather-like branching', Nature Ecology & Evolution 3:24-30 (pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30568282); University of Bristol research-information page.

question: Deep in India's Western Ghats lives a bloated, dark-purple frog that spends almost its entire life buried underground. It hauls itself up to the surface only when the monsoon rains arrive. How much of the year does an adult purple frog actually spend above ground?
answer: About two weeks
choices: About two weeks
About four months
Roughly half the year
Almost all summer
context: The purple frog (Nasikabatrachus sahyadrensis) surfaces for only about two weeks a year, emerging with the monsoon to breed in temporary streams before vanishing back underground. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purple_frog  (Legend.)

question: Deep in the Western Ghats mountains of southern India lives one of the strangest frogs on Earth. Its body is glossy, dark purple, and swollen like a small balloon, and it spends almost its whole life underground, coming up only to breed. People nicknamed it the 'pignose frog' because of one especially odd feature of its face. What is that feature?
answer: A tiny, pointed pig-like snout
choices: A tiny, pointed pig-like snout
A pair of curved tusks
Bright pink cheek pouches
A flat, shovel-shaped bill
context: National Geographic describes shiny purple skin, a light-blue ring around each small eye, and a distinctive pig-like snout on the tiny pointed head. Its scientific name is Nasikabatrachus sahyadrensis. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/article/purple-frog-new-species-discovery-india-monsoon

question: The purple frog of India's Western Ghats has a squat, blimp-shaped body and a tiny, pointed head that looks glued on wrong. Unlike almost every other frog on Earth, it never surfaces to hunt: it stays buried in the wet soil for most of the year, feeding entirely underground through a fluted tongue and a special groove in its mouth. What does the purple frog eat down there in the dirt?
answer: Termites and ants
choices: Termites and ants
Earthworms and slugs
Beetle grubs
Small burrowing lizards
context: The purple frog uses a long fluted tongue and a special buccal groove to eat termites and ants entirely underground, never coming to the surface to feed. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/article/purple-frog-new-species-discovery-india-monsoon

question: The purple frog of India's Western Ghats is unlike any other frog on Earth, and its family has been evolving all on its own for a huge stretch of time. Its closest living cousins are the little Sooglossid frogs stranded on the Seychelles islands out in the Indian Ocean. When did these two frog lineages last share a common ancestor and split apart from each other?
answer: Around 100 million years ago, as Gondwana broke up
choices: Around 100 million years ago, as Gondwana broke up
Around 10 million years ago
Around 2 million years ago, in the last ice ages
Only a few hundred thousand years ago
context: The purple frog is a 'living fossil' relict. Its lineage split from the Seychelles Sooglossid frogs roughly 100 million years ago when the Gondwana supercontinent broke apart, leaving India drifting as its own island continent. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purple_frog  (Legend.)

question: On Rottnest Island off the coast of Western Australia lives a cat-sized furry marsupial called the quokka. Visitors love it because it always looks like it is grinning right at them, so quokka selfies have made the little animal famous online. What actually gives the quokka that grin?
answer: the fixed shape of its short muzzle and round cheeks
choices: the fixed shape of its short muzzle and round cheeks
a mineral stain that darkens the fur around its lips
the way it keeps leaves tucked in the sides of its mouth
loose folds of skin that curl upward as it grows older
context: The upturned mouth corners, round cheeks, short muzzle, and big dark eyes just happen to line up in the pattern humans read as a grin. It is a coincidence of anatomy, not a mood — the quokka is not actually 'happy,' and reading human emotion into an animal's face is a classic mistake. Source: Australian Geographic Fact File: Quokka; Wikipedia 'Quokka.'

question: On Rottnest Island off the coast of Western Australia lives the quokka, a small round marsupial famous for its cheerful-looking face. A fox closes in on a mother quokka carrying a joey in her belly pouch. A viral internet claim says she flings the baby at the predator to save herself — but that is a myth. What does the mother actually do to buy time to escape?
answer: loosens her pouch so the joey drops out and hisses on the ground
choices: loosens her pouch so the joey drops out and hisses on the ground
rears up and lashes at the fox with her clawed hind feet
freezes flat against the ground so the two of them go unnoticed
leads the fox on a long winding chase away from the joey
context: She relaxes her pouch muscles and the startled joey falls out and writhes and hisses on the ground, distracting the predator long enough for the mother to get away. It is a release, not a toss — the 'quokkas throw their babies' story is a myth, but the drop itself is a real anti-predator behavior. Source: Africa Check, 'No, quokkas don't throw babies at predators'; Biology Insights, 'Do Quokkas Toss Babies at Predators?'

question: Rottnest Island, off the coast of Western Australia, bakes dry for months at a time in summer, and its fresh puddles and streams all but vanish. Yet the little smiling quokkas that live there can go for roughly a month without ever taking a real drink of water. How do they keep from drying out?
answer: it pulls most of the water it needs straight from the plants it eats
choices: it pulls most of the water it needs straight from the plants it eats
it stores a water reserve in the fat of its thick tail
it soaks water through the skin of its belly from damp sand
it drinks seawater and filters the salt out through its kidneys
context: A quokka gets nearly all its water from its food, including water-storing succulents, letting it survive about a month without a drink on an island where fresh water is scarce. (Its tail does store fat, but that fuels it through lean food seasons — not thirst.) Source: The Nature Conservancy Australia, 'Meet the Quokka'; San Diego Zoo, 'Quokka.'

question: A jellyfish, a sea anemone, and a starfish all share the same body plan. Slice one down the middle from any direction and it splits into matching wedges — like a pie. Their bodies reach out in every direction at once, with no clear leading side. Because of this, what one thing do these three animals lack?
answer: A front end
choices: A front end
A stinging cell
An outer skin
A gut cavity
context: They are RADIALLY symmetric: built like a wheel around a center, with a top and a bottom but no front and no back. Cut one into wedges any way through the center and the pieces match. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symmetry_in_biology

question: A jellyfish drifts wherever the current takes it and a rooted sea anemone can never turn to face anything. Their wheel-shaped bodies, the same all the way around a center, handle danger from any side equally well. But that same plan costs them something a fish takes for granted. What can these radial animals never do?
answer: Chase or flee in one chosen direction
choices: Chase or flee in one chosen direction
Grow larger than a dinner plate
Survive in cold, deep water
Feel a touch anywhere on the body
context: A wheel-shaped body meets food or danger from any side equally well, but it has no leading point to drive toward, so it can never chase prey or flee in one committed direction. That directed speed is exactly what a bilateral, front-and-back body buys. Source: https://bio.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Introductory_and_General_Biology/General_Biology_(Boundless)/27:_Introduction_to_Animal_Diversity/27.02:_Features_Used_to_Classify_Animals/27.2A:_Animal_Characterization_Based_on_Body_Symmetry

question: Nearly every animal alive — over a million species, about 99% of them all — is built with a mirror-image left and right and a definite front and back. Three of these four animals belong to that huge club. Which one is the rare exception, built instead like a wheel around a center?
answer: A jellyfish
choices: A jellyfish
A tuna
A honeybee
An earthworm
context: You, a fish, an insect, and a worm are all bilateral — a left and a right that mirror each other, a head and a tail — and about 99% of animals are built this way. The radial jellyfish is the rare exception. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symmetry_in_biology

question: A tuna and a shark are both front-and-back animals: each one has a clear head end that leads the way and a tail that follows, unlike an animal built like a wheel spinning around a center point. A jellyfish just drifts along in whichever direction the current takes it and never needed the same shape. What does a front-to-back body plan give a swimmer like a tuna or shark that a radial drifter like a jellyfish lacks?
answer: Less drag cutting through the water
choices: Less drag cutting through the water
More powerful tail muscles
A lighter, hollow skeleton
Far larger gills for oxygen
context: A bilateral body can taper to a leading point and cut through water or air with far less drag, which is why nearly every fast pursuer or escaper is bilateral, not radial. A radial drifter never needed to be streamlined. Source: https://bio.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Introductory_and_General_Biology/General_Biology_(Boundless)/27:_Introduction_to_Animal_Diversity/27.02:_Features_Used_to_Classify_Animals/27.2A:_Animal_Characterization_Based_on_Body_Symmetry

question: A jellyfish drifting in open water and a sea star creeping on the ocean floor have barely a head to speak of -- their nerves spread out in a ring or a net rather than clustering up front. At the opposite extreme sits a group of ocean hunters that pack camera-like eyes, a sharp beak, and a large brain all crammed together at the leading end. Which sea animals are the most extreme head-havers of all?
answer: Octopuses and squid
choices: Octopuses and squid
Clams and oysters
Barnacles and limpets
Sea cucumbers and sand dollars
context: Octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish are highly cephalized — camera-like eyes and big brains packed at the front — while clams, barnacles, and sea cucumbers show little to no cephalization at all. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cephalization

question: A starfish looks like the perfect radial animal — five arms around a center, no front, no back. Yet its tiny swimming larva has a left and a right side, like you. When that larva transforms into a five-armed adult, how does the change actually happen?
answer: The left side takes over and rebuilds the body in five
choices: The left side takes over and rebuilds the body in five
It sprouts a new arm from the center each year
Its skin hardens into five plates that split apart
Both halves fuse into a single ring
context: The starfish larva is bilateral, but during metamorphosis its LEFT side grows at the expense of the right, which is absorbed and lost; the left side then rebuilds the whole body in five parts around a center. That is why echinoderms are counted as bilaterians that went radial second. Source: https://iere.org/are-starfish-larvae-bilateral/

question: A robin outside a spring window is flinging itself again and again at the glass, pecking and beating its wings against another robin on the other side of the pane. It attacks the same spot for days, but the rival never seems to fly away. The homeowner watches, puzzled. What is the robin actually attacking?
answer: Its own reflection
choices: Its own reflection
A rival male robin
A hawk hunting nearby
A mate it is courting
context: Most animals treat a mirror image as another animal. A robin will batter its reflection in a window for days, and a betta fish flares its fins at the glass, because neither realizes the 'intruder' is itself. Source: PMC/Royal Society, 'On the mirror test and the evolutionary origin of self-awareness'; aeon.co mirror-test essay.

question: In Gordon Gallup Jr.'s test, chimpanzees were anesthetized and a red dye mark was painted on one eyebrow — a spot they had no way of knowing was there. Each chimp woke and was shown a mirror. What did a chimp that recognized the reflection as itself do?
answer: Reached up and touched the mark on its own eyebrow
choices: Reached up and touched the mark on its own eyebrow
Touched the mirror where the mark appeared
Pressed its face flat against the glass
Groomed a clean, unmarked patch of fur
context: The mirror mark test hides a dye mark where the animal can only spot it in a reflection. Gallup's chimps woke, saw the mirror, and reached to touch the red marks on their own eyebrow and ear — proof they understood the reflection was themselves, not a stranger. Source: PubMed 4982211, Gallup 1970; Wikipedia, Mirror test.  (Legend.)

question: In 1970, psychologist Gordon Gallup Jr. left chimpanzees alone with a mirror for days. At first they bristled and threatened the 'stranger' in the glass. Then their behavior flipped to something no one had recorded in an animal before. What did the chimps start doing with the mirror?
answer: Grooming parts of themselves they couldn't otherwise see
choices: Grooming parts of themselves they couldn't otherwise see
Hoarding the mirror from other chimps
Smashing it to reach the intruder
Ignoring it completely and turning away
context: Gallup's 1970 study invented the mirror mark test. Once the chimps stopped treating the reflection as a rival, they used it as a tool — inspecting the insides of their mouths and other spots they could never see directly. Source: PubMed 4982211, Gallup 1970, 'Chimpanzees: self-recognition.'  (Legend.)

question: Two bottlenose dolphins named Presley and Tab, at the New York Aquarium, became the first non-primates ever shown to recognize themselves in a mirror. A dolphin has no hands to touch a mark on its skin. So how did they inspect a spot marked on their bodies?
answer: They twisted and circled to bring it in front of the mirror
choices: They twisted and circled to bring it in front of the mirror
They rubbed it against the tank floor
They called to a partner to check it
They spat a jet of water at the mark
context: With no hands, Presley and Tab contorted their bodies to maneuver the marked spot into view in the mirror and examine it — clear self-directed behavior. Source: Reiss & Marino 2001, PNAS, 'Mirror self-recognition in the bottlenose dolphin.'  (Legend.)

question: At the Bronx Zoo, an Asian elephant named Happy stood before an eight-foot mirror. Painted above one eye was a white 'X' she could only see in the reflection; a matching but invisible mark sat on the other side of her head. Happy ignored the invisible one — but what did she do about the 'X' she could see?
answer: Reached her trunk up to touch it
choices: Reached her trunk up to touch it
Splashed water over that eye
Backed away from the mirror
Trumpeted at the reflection
context: Happy repeatedly brought her trunk to the visible white mark and ignored the invisible sham mark on the other side — evidence she recognized the elephant in the glass as herself. Source: Plotnik, de Waal & Reiss 2006, PNAS; Smithsonian Magazine.  (Legend.)

question: In a 2008 study, Eurasian magpies became the first non-mammals shown to pass the mirror test — startling because birds lack the mammalian neocortex once thought necessary for self-recognition. Each bird got a small colored sticker placed where it could only be spotted in a mirror. Where on its body did the researchers stick that telltale mark?
answer: On its throat
choices: On its throat
On its tail
Under one wing
On its lower back
context: The magpies wore the sticker on the throat; those able to see it in the mirror scratched at their own throats to remove it, while birds given a sticker invisible against their dark feathers did not react. Source: Prior, Schwarz & Gunturkun 2008, PLOS Biology.  (Legend.)

question: When researchers test animals for self-awareness with the mirror test -- painting a dot on the face to see if the animal notices it in the reflection -- most wild gorillas fail. Yet gorillas raised around humans, like the famous signing gorilla Koko in California, pass it easily. The failure isn't about raw intelligence. Researchers point to a habit of normal gorilla social life that gets in the way of studying yourself in the mirror. What habit blocks a wild gorilla from passing?
answer: Avoiding a long stare, which among gorillas is a threat
choices: Avoiding a long stare, which among gorillas is a threat
Grooming each other constantly instead of alone
Deferring every action to the dominant silverback
Treating any new object as food to sample
context: Among gorillas, a hard stare is a challenge, so most avoid gazing into a mirror long enough to notice a mark — a social block, not a mental one. Koko and other human-raised gorillas, less bound by that rule, passed. Source: Wikipedia, Mirror test, gorilla section.

question: In 2019 the cleaner wrasse, a small reef fish, tried to scrape a colored mark off its own throat after seeing it in a mirror — a 'pass' no one thought a fish could manage. Rather than settling the question, the result touched off a real scientific fight, led by primatologist Frans de Waal. What did the skeptics argue?
answer: An itch worth scraping falls short of true self-recognition
choices: An itch worth scraping falls short of true self-recognition
The wrasse simply mimicked a nearby fish's movements
Only warm-blooded animals can form a self-image
The mark's color must match the fish's own for a pass
context: Primatologist Frans de Waal argued the itchy mark and ambiguous behavior fall short of true self-recognition, calling it an in-between level closer to a monkey's than an ape's. The debate over what 'passing' even means remains unsettled. Source: Kohda et al. 2019, PLOS Biology; de Waal 2019, PMC6366752.

question: A cleaner wrasse that had already recognized itself in a mirror was shown two photographs of unfamiliar rival fish: one sized a tenth larger than itself, one a tenth smaller. A mirror-naive wrasse charges both. But this fish reacted to the two photos differently. What did it do?
answer: Backed away from the larger rival but attacked the smaller one
choices: Backed away from the larger rival but attacked the smaller one
Charged the larger rival but ignored the smaller one
Fled from both rivals into the nearest crevice
Circled both rivals without striking either photo
context: In a 2024 experiment (Kobayashi, Kohda et al., Scientific Reports 14:20202), wrasse that had passed the mirror test refrained from attacking a rival photo scaled 10% LARGER than themselves while still attacking one scaled 10% smaller — as if each opponent were being measured against a stored sense of the fish’s own body size. Mirror-naive fish attacked both. The researchers argue the fish carries a mental image of how big it is. Source: Kobayashi, Kohda, Awata, Bshary, Sogawa (2024), Scientific Reports, ‘Cleaner fish...precisely realize their body size based on their mental image’ — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11390716/

question: Gordon Gallup, who invented the mirror test, holds that only chimpanzees and, weakly, orangutans truly pass it. His hardest evidence comes from a crab-eating macaque given roughly 2,400 hours in front of a mirror. After all that exposure, what had the monkey still never done?
answer: Turned the glass to inspect a mark it could not otherwise see
choices: Turned the glass to inspect a mark it could not otherwise see
Stopped threatening the reflection as a rival monkey
Learned to reach food shown only in the reflection
Groomed a companion sitting beside it at the mirror
context: For Gallup and Anderson (2020 reviews), that failure despite endless practice marks a real cognitive divide, not a matter of time at the glass: they hold no animal reliably recognizes itself in a mirror except chimpanzees and, to a lesser degree, orangutans. The macaque was given roughly 2,400 hours of mirror exposure and never developed self-directed behavior or passed the mark test. This is the strict counterweight to Frans de Waal’s gradualist view that self-awareness comes in degrees across many species.
