In the 1980s the American zoologist Brian Barnes finally settled the question. He implanted tiny radio transmitters inside the bellies of arctic ground squirrels, then did the one thing with the animals that made the experiment work. What did he do?
answer: Letting them hibernate outdoors in the wild
choices: Letting them hibernate outdoors in the wild
Freezing them in a lab chamber
Feeding them antifreeze for a year
Raising their body heat until they woke
context: Barnes, at the University of Alaska Fairbanks, let the transmitter-carrying squirrels hibernate in natural conditions and recorded their core temperature dropping below freezing, proving the supercooling. Source: https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/arctic-ground-squirrel-brain/

question: The arctic ground squirrel hibernates through the Alaskan winter, letting its body temperature plunge below freezing for months. Over that long sleep, its brain cells shrink and lose their branching connections, as if the brain were slowly wasting away. Then something surprising happens within just two hours of the squirrel waking up in spring. What?
answer: It rebuilds the connections and ends up with even more
choices: It rebuilds the connections and ends up with even more
It keeps the shrunken brain until the next summer
It sleeps another full week to recover slowly
It permanently loses a fraction of its memory
context: Within about two hours of waking, the squirrel's brain cells regrow their branching connections and end up with even more than a summer squirrel had. Source: https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/arctic-ground-squirrel-brain/

question: The North American wood frog goes further than any other cold-blooded hibernator on Earth. When autumn frost hits the forest floor, up to two-thirds of the water inside the little frog's body freezes solid into hard crystals of ice. Its heart stops beating. Its lungs stop breathing. It lies as a stiff, frozen little block in the leaf litter for months on end. What happens to the wood frog in spring?
answer: It thaws back to life
choices: It thaws back to life
It sheds its frozen skin and grows new
It stays dormant until the next winter
It leaves behind only eggs
context: The wood frog spends winter frozen solid, with no heartbeat and no breathing, then thaws and revives in spring. Source: https://www.forbes.com/sites/scotttravers/2025/12/05/meet-the-frog-that-freezes-solid-every-winter---and-thaws-back-to-life-every-spring/  (Legend.)

question: The North American wood frog can lie completely frozen for months in the leaf litter and then thaw back to life in spring. But ice growing inside a living cell would shred the cell apart, so the frog cannot let its cells freeze. Its trick is to flood the inside of each cell with a natural antifreeze so thick that the water there simply cannot crystallize — only the water outside the cells actually turns to ice. What does the wood frog flood its cells with?
answer: Sugar and urea
choices: Sugar and urea
Salt and alcohol
Fat and oil
Air and mucus
context: The wood frog packs its cells with glucose (sugar) and urea, which keep the fluid inside from freezing so that ice forms only in the spaces outside the cells. Source: https://www.discoverwildlife.com/animal-facts/amphibians/wood-frog

question: A cave full of hibernating little brown bats should sleep undisturbed all winter and wake only a few times, saving the fat they need to survive until spring. But since 2006, a cold-loving fungus called white-nose syndrome has killed millions of North American bats. The fungus does not eat the bats alive or poison their blood — it kills a different way. How does it actually kill a hibernating bat?
answer: It keeps waking them so they burn their fat too fast
choices: It keeps waking them so they burn their fat too fast
It freezes their wings to the cave wall
It clogs their lungs with spores
It drains the fat straight from their bodies
context: White-nose syndrome repeatedly rouses bats from hibernation, forcing them to burn through their winter fat too quickly, so they starve before spring arrives. Source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3380050/

question: Nearly every bird handles winter by staying active in the cold or by flying south for warmer weather. But one bird of the western North American deserts — a small ground-roosting relative of the nightjars — truly hibernates, going stiff and cold in a rock crevice for weeks or even months at a stretch. The Hopi people of the American Southwest named it 'holchoko,' meaning 'the sleeping one.' Which bird is it?
answer: The common poorwill
choices: The common poorwill
The ruby-throated hummingbird
The snowy owl
The whip-poor-will
context: The common poorwill is the only bird known to truly hibernate for long stretches, which is why the Hopi called it holchoko, 'the sleeping one.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_poorwill  (Legend.)

question: A hibernating ground squirrel doesn't stay cold all winter. Every week or so it spontaneously rewarms its whole body back to about 37 C for roughly 16 hours, then chills down again. Across the season, where does the surprising majority of its saved winter fuel actually go?
answer: Into these repeated warm-ups, not the deep cold sleep
choices: Into these repeated warm-ups, not the deep cold sleep
Into slowing its heart during the coldest weeks
Into replacing the fat lost through its skin
Into keeping its burrow above the outside air
context: Across a whole winter, the deep cold torpor itself is cheap; it is the repeated 'interbout arousals' -- rewarming to about 37 C for ~16 hours every week or so -- that burn an estimated 60-80% of all the fat the squirrel saved by hibernating. It spends most of its fuel not on sleeping cold, but on the act of waking up. WHY it does this is one of hibernation biology's great open debates: one leading idea is that the immune system shuts off entirely in the cold (a torpid squirrel injected with bacterial toxin runs no fever at all), so it must periodically rewarm to reboot its defenses; a rival theory is that torpor is not true restful sleep, so the animal wakes up carrying a 'sleep debt' and drops straight into deep slow-wave sleep -- warming up simply to sleep for real. Source: Ruf, Giroud & Geiser 2022, Frontiers in Physiology (two-process torpor-arousal model; ~60-80% of budget, ~7-day interval, ~16 h at 37 C); Prendergast, Freeman, Zucker & Nelson 2002, Am. J. Physiol. (immune response arrested in torpor); Daan, Barnes & Strijkstra 1991 / Larkin & Heller (sleep-debt slow-wave rebound).

question: A painted turtle spends months at the bottom of an ice-locked pond with almost no oxygen. It runs on oxygen-free metabolism that floods its blood with lactic acid, enough to kill most animals. To keep from being poisoned by its own acid, what does the turtle turn its shell and skeleton into?
answer: A giant antacid that dissolves to neutralize the acid
choices: A giant antacid that dissolves to neutralize the acid
A sealed tank that traps the acid away from its organs
A radiator that vents the acid out through its skin
A store of oxygen it slowly releases through winter
context: With the pond sealed under ice, a painted turtle stops using its lungs and takes up what trickle of oxygen it can straight through its skin and the lining of its cloaca. Running on oxygen-free metabolism floods it with lactic acid, so it uses its own skeleton as an antacid: the bones and shell dissolve, releasing calcium and magnesium carbonates that neutralize the acid, and the shell even soaks up and stores about 44% of the turtle's entire lactic-acid load -- the highest carbonate concentration recorded in any animal. This buffering lets it endure up to about 150-170 days with no oxygen at all. Source: Wikipedia 'Painted turtle' (shell/skeleton release carbonates to buffer lactate; shell sequesters 44% of total lactate; highest carbonate concentration among animals; cloacal/cutaneous respiration; up to ~170 days anoxia); Jackson & Ultsch, 'Hibernating without Oxygen: Physiological Adaptations of the Painted Turtle.'

question: In the steamy rainforests of Central and South America hangs a shaggy mammal so unhurried it barely seems to move at all. It spends nearly all of its life upside-down among the tree branches, hooked on by long curved claws. From the forest floor you can spot one only if it happens to blink. What is this animal?
answer: A sloth
choices: A sloth
A lemur
A koala
A gibbon
context: The sloth is a slow-moving tree mammal of Central and South American rainforests, with six species split into the three-toed sloths (Bradypus) and two-toed sloths (Choloepus). Source: https://www.slothconservation.org/blog/10-incredible-facts-about-the-sloth

question: Guinness World Records has crowned the three-toed sloth of Central and South America as the slowest mammal on Earth. On the ground, this shaggy, tree-loving animal creeps along at just 1.8 to 2.4 meters a minute — barely faster than a slow drift. Sloths are so slow they climb down from their rainforest tree only about once a week, just to poop. Which of these ways of moving across the floor would let a person out-crawl a three-toed sloth?
answer: Crawling on hands and knees
choices: Crawling on hands and knees
Wriggling forward on the belly
Scooting along seated on the hips
Rolling sideways over and over
context: The three-toed sloth holds the Guinness record for slowest mammal; a human crawling on hands and knees can out-pace its 1.8 to 2.4 meters per minute. Source: https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/70459-slowest-mammal  (Legend.)

question: A sloth moves so slowly that living things actually take root and grow in the shaggy fur along its back. In the wet rainforests of Central and South America, humidity keeps a sloth's coat damp enough for a tiny plant-like organism to colonize each hair, tinting the whole animal a leafy shade that helps it hide up in the canopy from harpy eagles. What is growing there?
answer: Green algae
choices: Green algae
Small ferns
Moss cushions
Lichen crusts
context: Green algae grows in the grooves of a sloth's fur, tinting it green so it blends into the leafy canopy like living camouflage. Source: https://www.slothconservation.org/blog/10-incredible-facts-about-the-sloth  (Legend.)

question: A three-toed sloth's shaggy fur is not just hair — it is a whole tiny ecosystem living on the animal's back. Green algae grow in grooves along each hair and tint the sloth's coat a mossy green, which hides it in the rainforest canopy. Fungi settle in. Moths and beetles live their whole lives in the fur, laying eggs there. At the extreme, how many moths and beetles has a single wild sloth been found carrying?
answer: Up to 950
choices: Up to 950
Up to 90
Up to 250
Up to 500
context: A single sloth can carry up to 950 moths and beetles living in its coat at once, alongside algae and fungi. Source: https://www.slothconservation.org/blog/10-incredible-facts-about-the-sloth  (Legend.)

question: A three-toed sloth hangs upside-down from a rainforest branch in Central America, moving so slowly its shaggy fur has become a whole tiny ecosystem. Green algae grow along each hair, and small moths live in the coat. The moths ferry nitrogen into the fur through their droppings and their decomposing bodies, and that nitrogen fertilizes the algae. Researchers who cut open the loop found the sloth completes it by doing what?
answer: Eating some of the algae
choices: Eating some of the algae
Drinking rainwater off its fur
Grooming the moths away
Rubbing the algae onto its young
context: The sloth eats some of the lipid-rich algae as a supplement to its leaf diet — researchers found the algae inside sloths' stomachs, closing the three-way sloth-moth-algae partnership. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/article/sloth-poop-moth-relationship  (Legend.)

question: A three-toed sloth spends nearly its entire life safe up in the treetops of Central and South American rainforests. High branches keep it hidden from jaguars and harpy eagles. Yet about once a week, this slow, nearly defenceless animal does something baffling: it climbs all the way down to the forest floor, one exhausting inch at a time, for a single deliberate errand. Why does it climb down?
answer: To poop
choices: To poop
To find water
To meet a mate
To gather fallen fruit
context: A sloth climbs down to the forest floor only about once a week to poop, digging a little hole at the base of a tree to bury its droppings. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/article/sloth-poop-moth-relationship  (Legend.)

question: A three-toed sloth of the South American rainforest eats a diet of tough, low-energy tree leaves that most mammals could never survive on. Its digestion is almost as slow as its climbing. A single mouthful of leaves can take about sixteen days to work all the way through the sloth's body, and a full stomach of leaves may sit fermenting for a whole month. What kind of stomach lets a sloth break tough leaves down that slowly?
answer: A four-chambered fermenting tank like a cow's
choices: A four-chambered fermenting tank like a cow's
A single acid-filled pouch like a dog's
A gizzard that grinds with swallowed stones
A stretchy crop that stores food whole
context: A sloth's four-chambered fermenting stomach, similar to a cow's, can make up as much as 30% of its body mass; digestion of a single meal averages about 16 days. Source: https://www.slothsanctuary.com/research/sloth-digestion

question: Almost every mammal alive — a mouse, a giraffe, a whale, even you — has exactly seven bones in the neck. The three-toed sloth of the Central and South American rainforest breaks that rule. It has up to nine or ten neck bones stacked in a long column. Hanging motionless upside-down from a branch, this gives the sloth a strange advantage no other mammal has. What ability does that extra bone count give it?
answer: Turning its head about 270 degrees
choices: Turning its head about 270 degrees
Stretching its neck to reach distant fruit
Bending its head back to see straight up
Tucking its head fully into its chest
context: Three-toed sloths have extra neck vertebrae — breaking the near-universal seven-bone mammal rule — letting them rotate their heads about 270 degrees to look around without moving their bodies. Source: https://www.slothconservation.org/blog/10-incredible-facts-about-the-sloth  (Legend.)

question: A three-toed sloth's legs are built for hanging from rainforest branches, not for walking. On the ground it is nearly helpless, dragging itself across the forest floor at a laughable creep of about two meters a minute. But drop that same sloth into a flooded jungle river and it surprises you — a sloth is a genuinely capable swimmer. Compared with its speed on land, how fast can a three-toed sloth go in the water?
answer: About three times faster
choices: About three times faster
About the same speed
Slightly slower
Around ten times faster
context: Sloths are surprisingly strong swimmers, moving about three times faster in water than they crawl on land; their extra neck vertebrae let them tip their nose up above the surface. Source: https://www.slothconservation.org/blog/10-incredible-facts-about-the-sloth

question: The slow loris is a shy, huge-eyed, nocturnal primate that creeps through the forests of Southeast Asia, moving hand over hand along thin branches after dark. Among all the world's primates — every monkey, every ape, and every human — this one holds a strange title held by no other member of the whole group. What is that unique title?
answer: It is the only one that carries a venomous bite
choices: It is the only one that carries a venomous bite
It is the only one that never sleeps
It is the only one that cannot climb
It is the only one born with no eyes
context: The slow loris is the only venomous primate on Earth — a toxic bite is unique among primates and rare even among mammals. It is a small, huge-eyed, slow-moving nocturnal primate of Southeast Asia's forests. Source: Wikipedia, 'Slow loris' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slow_loris).  (Legend.)

question: The slow loris, a large-eyed nocturnal primate of Southeast Asian rainforests, is the only primate on Earth with real venom — but its way of arming a bite is unlike any other animal's. It has no venom fangs and it brews nothing inside its mouth. When a snake or a rival threatens it, the loris throws both arms straight up over its head in a strange upright pose and licks them, then bites. What is it reaching for up there above its head?
answer: A gland inside its own elbow
choices: A gland inside its own elbow
A thorn snapped from a branch
A beetle crushed for its poison
A drop of sap wept by the tree
context: The loris arms itself by raising its arms above its head and licking the brachial gland on the inside of its elbow, then mixing that secretion with its saliva to make its bite toxic. Source: overview via Wikipedia, 'Slow loris' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slow_loris).  (Legend.)

question: Shine a flashlight up into a Southeast Asian rainforest at night, and the huge round eyes of a slow loris flash back at you like two glowing coins. That eerie shine — the same one you see when a cat or a raccoon crosses your headlights at night — is a side effect of a special mirror-like layer packed behind each retina of the loris's eye. What does that reflective layer do for a creature hunting in the pitch dark?
answer: Gives it a second pass at faint light
choices: Gives it a second pass at faint light
Frightens away hunting owls
Holds a reserve of water
Keeps its brain from overheating
context: The layer is the tapetum lucidum. It reflects light back through the retina, giving the eye a second chance to catch every scrap of light for keen night vision — and that reflection is what makes the eyes shine like coins when a flashlight hits them in the dark. Source: Wikipedia, 'Slow loris' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slow_loris).

question: A slow loris's bite really is venomous — the toxin rots flesh, and any animal bitten develops wounds that will not heal. Researchers tracking wild slow lorises through the forests of Java kept finding lorises with half their faces melted away, black gaping holes where skin should have been. When the researchers investigated who was inflicting the bites, the answer surprised them. Who had bitten these lorises?
answer: Other slow lorises
choices: Other slow lorises
Hunting pythons
Forest leopards
Their own mothers
context: Slow lorises use their venom mostly on EACH OTHER, in vicious territorial and mating-season fights — not on predators. Researcher Anna Nekaris called them 'adorable little furballs of death,' and her team documented wild lorises 'with half their faces melted off' from being bitten by other lorises. Source: Smithsonian Magazine, quoting K.A.I. Nekaris, Oxford Brookes (https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/adorable-little-furballs-death-slow-lorises-use-their-venomous-bites-against-each-other-180976111/).  (Legend.)

question: The slow loris of Southeast Asia is the only venomous primate. When researchers examined its strange elbow-brewed venom in the lab, they found the main protein in it oddly familiar in shape — it looks very much like a protein called Fel d 1, which millions of people meet in ordinary life every day and react to with itching, sneezing, and watery eyes. Where does Fel d 1 normally come from?
answer: The dander of cats
choices: The dander of cats
The venom of wasps
The sap of oak trees
The skin of toads
context: Fel d 1 is the protein in cat dander that makes people allergic to cats. The main protein in loris brachial-gland venom (about 17.6 kDa) structurally resembles it, hinting the loris may weaponize an allergen-like protein. This is still active research — a postulated link, not a proven identity; one structural study found only about 53% and 36% sequence similarity between the two protein chains and Fel d 1. Sources: Hagey, Fry, Fitch-Snyder 2007 / Nekaris et al., 'Mad, bad and dangerous to know' (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3852360/); Toxins 2020 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7076782/).  (Legend.)

question: It is famously called the 'saber-toothed tiger,' but this stocky Ice-age cat was not a tiger at all. It was not even a close cousin of living lions or tigers. Its own family had split from modern cats roughly 20 million years earlier. What is this fanged Ice-age hunter properly called?
answer: Smilodon
choices: Smilodon
Megalodon
Andrewsarchus
Dinofelis
context: Despite the 'saber-toothed tiger' nickname, Smilodon belonged to the subfamily Machairodontinae, a branch that split from the ancestors of today's cats around 20 million years ago. It was not closely related to any living big cat. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smilodon

question: In Los Angeles, natural pools of sticky black asphalt seeped up to the surface for thousands of years. Plant-eating animals wandered in and got stuck fast, and predators that came to feed on them got stuck too. This layered up into the world's richest saber-tooth fossil bed. What is the name of this famous fossil trap?
answer: the La Brea Tar Pits
choices: the La Brea Tar Pits
the Burgess Shale
the Olduvai Gorge
the Messel Pit
context: At the La Brea Tar Pits, natural asphalt seeps trapped plant-eaters, and the predators that came to feed on them were caught in turn, building an enormous fossil treasure trove over thousands of years. Source: https://tarpits.org/stories/here-kitty-kitty  (Legend.)

question: The biggest saber-toothed cat of all, Smilodon populator, could top 470 kg (over 1,000 lb), making it one of the largest cats that ever lived. It hunted the heaviest Ice-age plant-eaters in its range. Which enormous beast did this giant saber-tooth bring down?
answer: giant Megatherium ground sloths
choices: giant Megatherium ground sloths
armored Doedicurus glyptodonts
elephant-sized Deinotherium
shaggy Diprotodon marsupials
context: In South America, Smilodon populator preyed on huge Megatherium ground sloths and Macrauchenia. S. fatalis weighed roughly 160-280 kg, while S. populator reached up to about 470 kg. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smilodon

question: Smilodon, the saber-toothed cat that stalked Ice Age North and South America, carried two curved fangs about seven inches long — as long as a kitchen knife. They look like fearsome daggers, but paleontologists studying the fossil teeth call them surprisingly fragile. When Smilodon attacked, it had to sink its fangs into soft flesh and hold the prey still, because those long teeth had a specific mechanical weakness. What was that weakness?
answer: they snapped easily under sideways twisting
choices: they snapped easily under sideways twisting
they kept growing and never stopped
they were hollow and filled with venom
they wore down to stubs within a year
context: The long sabers were slender and could break under sideways force, so they were adapted for precise killing rather than bashing bone. Smilodon had to immobilize prey before biting to avoid snapping the fragile teeth. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smilodon

question: Many Smilodon skeletons from La Brea carry serious injuries that had fully healed over, meaning the cat lived on long after being badly hurt. One pelvis even showed crippling hip damage from a young age. What still-debated feature of Smilodon life does that survival point to?
answer: it may have lived in groups that fed the injured
choices: it may have lived in groups that fed the injured
it could regenerate broken bones quickly
it hibernated through the worst winters
it scavenged rather than hunting at all
context: Healed injuries, and a young-onset hip dysplasia that would have crippled hunting, lead some researchers to argue Smilodon lived in social groups that shared food with the hurt. This is a debated inference, not proven. Source: https://tarpits.org/stories/these-hips-dont-lie-3d-imaging-pelvis-suggests-social-care-saber-tooths

question: Finite-element modeling revealed a paradox: despite its dagger-like canines, Smilodon's jaw-muscle bite force was only about a third that of a same-sized lion, feeble for a big cat. Anatomists point to one striking skull feature this weak-jawed hunter had that no living cat comes close to matching. What was it?
answer: a jaw that could swing open past a right angle
choices: a jaw that could swing open past a right angle
a second row of shearing teeth behind the canines
a bony chin flange that shielded the long fangs
canines that retracted up into the skull when closed
context: Finite-element modeling by McHenry and colleagues (2007, PNAS) put Smilodon's muscle-driven bite at only about one-third of a comparable lion's. To clear and use its ~18 cm canines, the cat gaped to roughly 120 degrees, where a modern lion manages only about 65. That enormous, weak-jawed gape is why the real killing power came from its massive neck and forelimbs pinning prey still, not from crushing jaw pressure. Source: McHenry et al. 2007, 'Supermodeled sabercat,' PNAS 104(41):16010-15 (https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0706086104); gape figures via Wikipedia 'Smilodon' and the San Diego Zoo extinct saber-toothed cat fact sheet.  (Legend.)

question: In 2002, workers draining a Maryland pond pulled out a long fish nobody had ever seen in America before. It had a snake-patterned back, dagger-like teeth, and grew past 33 inches and 19 pounds. This was the northern snakehead, a predator from Asia that had ended up in North American waters. Reporters were horrified. What tabloid nickname did headline writers pin on it?
answer: Frankenfish
choices: Frankenfish
Razormouth
Bog demon
Mud shark
context: The northern snakehead grows past 33 inches (85 cm) and about 19 pounds, a long snake-patterned fish with dagger-like teeth that earned the tabloid nickname 'Frankenfish.' Source: National Geographic northern snakehead facts; Smithsonian's National Zoo species page.

question: Pull a northern snakehead out of the water and leave it on damp ground, and instead of dying in minutes like most fish it can last as long as four days. What lets it survive so long out of the water?
answer: It breathes air instead of relying only on gills
choices: It breathes air instead of relying only on gills
It seals its gills shut to trap moisture
It slows its heart until it seems dead
It absorbs water through its skin
context: The northern snakehead can survive out of water for up to four days as long as it stays damp, because it breathes air rather than relying only on its gills. Source: Smithsonian's National Zoo species page; National Geographic northern snakehead facts.

question: The northern snakehead is an air-breathing fish native to East Asia that has spread as an invasive species to some warm ponds in North America. Sometimes its home pond dries up or gets too crowded, so it hauls itself overland across wet grass to find a new one. How does this fish 'walk' across the ground?
answer: It makes S-shaped waves with its body while sculling with both pectoral fins
choices: It makes S-shaped waves with its body while sculling with both pectoral fins
It inflates its belly and rolls downhill like a log
It springs forward in long hops off its tail fin
It drags itself forward hand-over-hand on stiffened gill covers
context: A snakehead crawls overland by making S-shaped waves with its body while sculling with both pectoral fins at once, rolling slightly side to side and shoving its tail against the ground to push forward. Source: Integrative Organismal Biology / PMC7671134, 'Emersion and Terrestrial Locomotion of the Northern Snakehead on Multiple Substrates.'

question: The northern snakehead is a long, air-breathing freshwater fish native to eastern Asia and now an invasive troublemaker in North American rivers. Plenty of nest-guarding fish lay a modest clutch of eggs and defend it well. But a single female northern snakehead does something on another scale entirely — and her eggs hatch in barely a day or two, releasing thousands of tiny hungry predators into the water. How many eggs can she carry at once?
answer: As many as 50,000
choices: As many as 50,000
About 500
About 40
As many as 5 million
context: A single female snakehead can carry as many as 50,000 eggs, and the young hatch in only about one to two days -- part of why the fish spreads so fast once it invades. Source: USGS, 'What are snakeheads?' (usgs.gov/faqs/what-are-snakeheads).

question: A northern snakehead settles into a warm, stagnant pond where the water has so little oxygen that other fish suffocate. It keeps rising to break the surface anyway. What is it doing up there?
answer: Gulping air into a lung-like chamber above its gills
choices: Gulping air into a lung-like chamber above its gills
Skimming the oxygen-rich film off the water's surface
Cooling its blood in the thin surface layer
Flushing waste ammonia out through its mouth
context: The snakehead is an obligate air-breather -- it must come up to gulp air to survive, so unlike most fish it will actually drown if held underwater and kept from the surface. It gulps air using a suprabranchial organ, a lung-like chamber above the gills. Source: USGS Nonindigenous Aquatic Species factsheet, Channa argus (nas.er.usgs.gov/queries/factsheet.aspx?speciesid=2265); Biology Open, 'How does the snakehead Channa argus survive in air?'

question: A rat-sized night animal snuffles through leaf litter on Caribbean islands. It has a long, naked snout and tiny near-useless eyes. To find its way through a pitch-black burrow, it fires high-pitched clicks. Which animal is this?
answer: a solenodon
choices: a solenodon
an aardvark
an echidna
a pangolin
context: The solenodon is a shrew-like insectivore of Cuba and Hispaniola, about 28-32 cm (11-13 in) nose to rump and roughly 0.7-1.0 kg. It hunts at night, and because its eyes are nearly useless it produces high-pitched clicks used for echolocation inside its dark burrows. Source: https://factanimal.com/solenodon/

question: The solenodon is a rare shrew-like mammal that survives on the islands of Hispaniola and Cuba. It is one of the very few mammals that actually delivers venom when it bites -- poisonous saliva leaks into the wound. What part of its mouth carries the venom into its prey?
answer: an open channel running down a lower incisor tooth
choices: an open channel running down a lower incisor tooth
a hollow fang like a viper's
a venom spur on its ankle
a stinger in the tip of its tail
context: The solenodon injects toxic saliva through open grooves running down its second lower incisor -- a snake-like grooved-tooth delivery that is rare in mammals. Its very name means 'grooved tooth' (Greek solen 'channel' + odon 'tooth'). Only a few mammals are venomous at all: the solenodon, some shrews, the male platypus (whose venom rides an ankle spur), and the slow loris. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solenodon ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venomous_mammal

question: The solenodon is a small, shrew-like mammal that still lives in the forests of Cuba and Hispaniola. It has a long snout and a venomous bite — a rare thing in mammals. Scientists call it a living fossil because its body has barely changed in over 70 million years. That means its early ancestors shared the world with one famous group of creatures. Which group?
answer: the last of the non-bird dinosaurs
choices: the last of the non-bird dinosaurs
the woolly mammoths of the ice age
the giant ground sloths of the Americas
the saber-toothed cats
context: The solenodon's lineage split from all other living mammals about 73.6 million years ago, so its ancestors lived alongside the last non-bird dinosaurs and its family then survived the asteroid impact that ended the Age of Dinosaurs. Its form has scarcely changed since. Woolly mammoths, giant ground sloths, and saber-toothed cats all lived far more recently, in the last few million years -- long after the solenodon's line had already branched off. Source: https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2018/03/180316100638.htm

question: The solenodon is a rat-sized, night-hunting mammal that lives only on the Caribbean islands of Cuba and Hispaniola. It hunts by jamming its long, flexible snout deep into narrow rock cracks and rotten logs, sniffing and rooting out worms and beetles hidden inside. Anatomists studying the animal found that the base of its remarkable snout is built around a structure no other mammal has anywhere in its face. What sits there at the root of the solenodon's snout?
answer: a ball-and-socket joint, like a human shoulder
choices: a ball-and-socket joint, like a human shoulder
a ring of muscle with no bone, like a trunk
a plate of cartilage fused to the skull
a sheath of stiff whisker roots
context: The solenodon has a ball-and-socket joint at the base of its long, flexible snout -- structured like a human shoulder joint -- letting the snout swivel and probe into narrow cracks for prey. This joint is unique among mammals. Source: https://factanimal.com/solenodon/

question: In the deep oceans today, the largest predators with real teeth are found not on land but far below the surface. One of them is bigger and heavier than any shark, any big cat, any land predator alive. It is the reigning largest toothed hunter on Earth. Which animal holds that title?
answer: The sperm whale
choices: The sperm whale
The great white shark
The orca
The saltwater crocodile
context: A mature bull sperm whale (Physeter macrocephalus) reaches about 16 meters (52 ft) and 45 tonnes, dwarfing any shark or big cat. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sperm_whale

question: No other mammal on Earth feeds as far down as the sperm whale. It leaves the sunlit surface far behind, dives past the twilight zone, and hunts squid in the pitch-black cold where its own lungs squeeze flat under the pressure. About how deep does it plunge on a single breath?
answer: Around 2,250 meters (7,380 ft)
choices: Around 2,250 meters (7,380 ft)
Around 200 meters (660 ft)
Around 600 meters (2,000 ft)
Around 5,000 meters (16,400 ft)
context: The sperm whale dives deeper than any other mammal for its food, reaching about 2,250 m and staying under for well over an hour on one breath. Often cited as a record among diving mammals. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sperm_whale  (Legend.)

question: When a sperm whale surfaces after a long hunt in the deep, whale biologists get out their cameras and study the fresh marks on its skin. Round white scars ring its head. Long parallel scratches run down its flanks. Something down there fought back hard. What made those marks?
answer: Suckers and arms of giant squid
choices: Suckers and arms of giant squid
Barnacles it scraped off on rocks
The teeth of rival sperm whales
Bites from cookie-cutter sharks
context: Round scars from squid suckers and rake marks from squid arms are the physical record of battles fought in the crushing dark with giant squid. Source: https://thewhale.com/sperm-whale-deep-diving-giant-ocean

question: A sperm whale hunts a mile down in total blackness. No sunlight reaches this depth. Eyes are useless. And yet the whale still finds and grabs a single squid drifting through the water. It has a hunting sense most fish do not. How does it locate prey it cannot possibly see?
answer: It echolocates, reading returning echoes
choices: It echolocates, reading returning echoes
It senses the squid's electric field
It follows the squid's scent trail
It feels water currents on its skin
context: In the black cold a mile down, the whale maps its surroundings and finds squid by the returning echo of its clicks; hydrophones can pick those clicks up from up to 100 miles away. Source: https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/science-blog/diving-deep-sperm-whale-clicks

question: Whalers who cut open a sperm whale's blocky head found it packed with up to 1,900 liters of a pale, waxy oil. That oil is not fat for warmth. What job does this spermaceti do for the living whale?
answer: Focuses its clicks into a narrow beam
choices: Focuses its clicks into a narrow beam
Stores water to keep it from thirst
Cushions its brain against dive pressure
Produces venom to subdue giant squid
context: The spermaceti organ can hold up to 1,900 liters of waxy oil and works as a biological acoustic lens, focusing the whale's clicks into a narrow, powerful beam. Early whalers mistook the spermaceti for the animal's sperm, which is how it got its name. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sperm_whale

question: A sperm whale hunts nearly a mile beneath the ocean surface, in water too dark for its eyes to see. To find its favorite prey — deep-sea giant squid — it fires enormous clicks of sound out through a giant oil-filled chamber in its head. A single click can reach about 230 decibels underwater, louder than a jet engine at close range and the loudest sound any animal on Earth makes. Researchers suspect that at close range, one click may do something to the squid. What?
answer: Stun the squid
choices: Stun the squid
Boil the water around it
Crack the squid's beak
Blind the squid's eyes
context: Clicks reach a source level of about 230-236 dB underwater (a jet engine is roughly 150 dB); researchers suspect a close-range click can stun squid. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sperm_whale  (Legend.)

question: A sperm whale plunges into the deep ocean, sometimes past 3,000 feet down, where the water squeezes with hundreds of pounds of pressure per square inch. It stays under for more than an hour on a single breath. Instead of fighting that crushing pressure, the whale lets its flexible ribcage fold inward so its lungs simply cave in on the way down. What does collapsing the lungs protect the whale from?
answer: Absorbing dangerous nitrogen
choices: Absorbing dangerous nitrogen
Losing all its body heat
Filling its lungs with seawater
Bursting its eardrums
context: On a deep dive the flexible ribcage collapses the lungs, cutting nitrogen absorption, while muscles packed with oxygen-binding myoglobin supply the whale and blood shunts to brain and heart. Source: https://thewhale.com/sperm-whale-deep-diving-giant-ocean

question: Marine biologists Hal Whitehead and Shane Gero spent years listening to sperm whales click to each other in the open ocean. They found that families sharing a certain click-rhythm form 'vocal clans' that span oceans — whales born in one clan use their clan's rhythm all their lives. When a young calf picks up its clan's rhythm from the adults around it, what is that calf inheriting?
answer: A dialect passed down as culture
choices: A dialect passed down as culture
A gene coding for one fixed call
A decoded, translatable language
An instinct it was born already knowing
context: Sperm whale clicks pattern into 'codas' (usually 3-12 clicks); families sharing a coda dialect belong to the same 'vocal clan' (about seven identified across the Pacific). The dialects are learned and passed down as a form of culture documented by Whitehead and Gero, but they are NOT a decoded language. Source: https://royalsocietypublishing.org/rsos/article/11/1/231353/92647

question: The sperm whale alive today is a gentle giant that swallows squid nearly whole. Around 9 million years ago its 15-meter cousin Livyatan melvillei ruled the seas off Peru as an apex predator that bit and tore baleen whales apart. What weaponry let Livyatan rip into prey that big?
answer: Massive functional teeth in both jaws
choices: Massive functional teeth in both jaws
Blade-edged teeth that sliced like a saw
Bony crushing plates instead of teeth
A jointed jaw that unhinged like a snake
context: Livyatan melvillei is known from a roughly 3-meter skull found in Peru's Pisco Formation, laid down in the Late Miocene about 9 to 10 million years ago. Unlike the modern sperm whale, which has functional teeth only in its narrow lower jaw, Livyatan carried huge working teeth in both jaws; the largest reach about 36 cm long counting the root and 12 cm wide, among the biggest biting teeth known from any animal. Its jaw-closing muscle attachment was proportionally as large as a killer whale's, marking it as an apex predator that likely hunted baleen whales and seals. Named in 2010, its genus honors Leviathan, the biblical sea beast, and its species name melvillei honors Herman Melville, who wrote Moby-Dick. Sources: Grokipedia 'Sperm whale' (grokipedia.com/page/Sperm_whale); Wikipedia 'Livyatan'; primary description Lambert et al. 2010, Nature; A-Z Animals 'Livyatan.'  (Legend.)

question: To hold its breath for over an hour on a deep dive, a sperm whale packs its diving muscles with a red, oxygen-gripping protein called myoglobin. It crams the myoglobin in at concentrations so dense that in a cow or a human, the tightly packed molecules would clump together and turn the muscle into a useless jelly. In the whale, they somehow stay separate. What stops all that crammed-in myoglobin from clumping?
answer: Matching electric charges push them apart
choices: Matching electric charges push them apart
A fatty sheath coats and shields each one
Helper proteins pin them safely apart
A shell of bound water keeps them slick
context: Storing that much oxygen means packing muscle with myoglobin far past the point where ordinary proteins clump and precipitate, wrecking the cell. Stephen Mirceta and colleagues (2013, Science) reconstructed myoglobin across about 130 mammal species and found that the champion divers had independently evolved a strongly positive net surface charge on the molecule. Because like charges repel, the positively charged myoglobins push each other apart and refuse to gel, letting deep divers stack the protein to concentrations that would turn a land mammal's muscle into a useless mass. The charge signature is so reliable it even let the team estimate the diving ability of extinct fossil ancestors. Sources: Mirceta et al. 2013, Science, doi.org/10.1126/science.1234192, 'Evolution of Mammalian Diving Capacity Traced by Myoglobin Net Surface Charge'; ScienceDaily, 'How diving mammals evolved underwater endurance.'

question: In the rocky, sun-baked hills of western Iran, one small viper lies pressed flat against a stone. Its whole body stays perfectly still. Only the very tip of its tail wiggles and twitches across the ground in front of it. What has that tail tip evolved to look like?
answer: A scuttling spider
choices: A scuttling spider
A trickle of water
A fallen leaf
A wriggling worm
context: The spider-tailed horned viper (Pseudocerastes urarachnoides) has a tail tip shaped into a lifelike fake spider: a bulb-like 'body' fringed with long, leg-like scales. It holds its body motionless and wiggles only the tail, so the tip looks like a spider scuttling over the rock. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spider-tailed_horned_viper  (Legend.)

question: In the dusty hills of western Iran, a small insect-eating bird flying over the rocks spots something skittering across the ground. It looks like a fat spider — but it is really the tail-tip of a hidden viper called the spider-tailed viper, twitching from between two rocks. The bird swoops down to grab the 'spider.' Researchers hidden nearby caught what happened next on film. What did the camera catch the snake doing?
answer: Whipping its hidden head around to strike the bird in about 0.2 seconds
choices: Whipping its hidden head around to strike the bird in about 0.2 seconds
Coiling its tail to snare the bird's legs like a lasso
Spraying venom from the fake spider into the bird's eyes
Playing dead until the bird lost interest and flew off
context: The tail is bait; the real weapon is the head. When the bird lunges for the 'spider,' the viper's true head strikes from ambush. Researchers filmed the whole trick, and the strike takes roughly 0.2 seconds. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/article/160411-spiders-snakes-animals-science-prey-predators  (Legend.)

question: The spider-tailed viper of western Iran has a wild trick at the tip of its tail: a bulb ringed with dangling scaly threads that look exactly like a fat crawling spider. The viper hides its body among the rocks and wiggles the fake spider out in the open, and hungry birds swoop in to grab it -- and get grabbed themselves. Which birds does this fake-spider lure catch most often?
answer: Migrating shrikes and warblers
choices: Migrating shrikes and warblers
Year-round resident finches
Insect-hunting bee-eaters
Desert larks that nest among the rocks
context: The lure mostly fools migrating birds passing through the region, especially shrikes and several kinds of warblers. Local resident birds seem to have learned the trick and avoid the snake, so it is mainly the travelers who get caught. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/article/160411-spiders-snakes-animals-science-prey-predators

question: In 1968 an American couple named Smith were driving along a road in western Iran when they came across a strange dead snake — the very first spider-tailed viper ever found. Its tail ended in a bizarre, spider-shaped lump of scales and skin. For decades afterward, herpetologists paid the odd tail no serious attention. What did they first assume the fake-spider tail actually was?
answer: A tumor or parasite stuck to an ordinary snake
choices: A tumor or parasite stuck to an ordinary snake
A rare albino mutation of a known viper
A clump of eggs the snake was carrying
A wad of mud dried onto the tail
context: When the first specimen turned up in 1968, scientists thought the strange tail was just a tumor, a deformity, or a parasite clinging to the snake. It was not recognized as a genuine spider-mimicking tail, and a whole new species, until 2006. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spider-tailed_horned_viper

question: A pufferfish is a slow, chunky swimmer with no shell to hide in and no burst of speed to outrun a bigger hunter. When it spots a hungry predator closing in fast, it has only a few seconds to make itself impossible to eat. What does the pufferfish do?
answer: Gulps water and balloons into a spiky ball several times its normal size
choices: Gulps water and balloons into a spiky ball several times its normal size
Squirts a cloud of black ink and darts away into a reef crevice
Sheds its brightly colored skin and swims off pale and bare
Buries itself in the sand until only its two eyes show
context: A pufferfish (family Tetraodontidae) draws water into a stretchy stomach sac and inflates to up to three times its size, turning itself into a spiny orb far too big for a predator to swallow. Source: Seattle Aquarium, 'Pufferfish and porcupinefish' (seattleaquarium.org); a-z-animals.com/animals/pufferfish.

question: A hedgehog, caught in the open by a fox, tucks its head and feet and curls tight so that nothing shows but a bristling dome of spines. Which single part of its body is it hiding by curling this way?
answer: Its soft, unprotected belly and underside
choices: Its soft, unprotected belly and underside
Its long, sensitive whiskers
Its bright warning stripes
Its venom-tipped tail spine
context: A hedgehog (subfamily Erinaceinae) has spines only on its back and sides; curling into a ball pulls that spiny skin over the vulnerable belly. The lock is done by a special muscle described in a later rung. Source: veteriankey.com/hedgehogs-2; sciencedirect.com Erinaceidae topic page.

question: For hundreds of years, storybooks and cartoons have shown angry porcupines shooting their long quills across a clearing like a volley of tiny arrows. Wildlife biologists say this famous belief is flat wrong — a porcupine cannot throw, launch, or fire its quills at all. So what actually happens when something touches a porcupine?
answer: The loosely rooted quills detach on contact and stay stuck in whatever brushed them
choices: The loosely rooted quills detach on contact and stay stuck in whatever brushed them
The quills are flung a short distance by a flick of the tail
The porcupine sprays a fine mist of irritant from the quill tips
The quills glow and the porcupine escapes in the confusion
context: Porcupines do not shoot quills — it is a myth. The barbed quills are only loosely rooted and detach the instant a predator makes contact, staying in whatever touched them. Source: Mass Audubon, 'The truth about porcupine projectiles'; Alaska Wildlife Conservation Center, 'Porcu-LIES: Debunking the Myth of the Missile Mammal'.

question: On the plains of Africa, a hungry lion lunges at an African crested porcupine — one of the largest porcupines in the world, its back bristling with black-and-white spines. The lion pulls back yelping, with long spines driven deep into its face. Some porcupines even kill lions this way. The strange part: the porcupine never turned around to face the lion at all. How did it deliver that painful blow?
answer: Charged backwards and rammed its quill-covered rump into the lion's face
choices: Charged backwards and rammed its quill-covered rump into the lion's face
Leapt onto the lion's back and clung there with hooked claws
Rolled into a spiny ball and let the lion bat it around
Flung a spray of loose quills from its bristling tail
context: The African crested porcupine (family Hystricidae) backs into a predator, ramming its rump full of quills into the attacker; quills have been recorded penetrating more than six inches into a lion's snout, nearly reaching the brain. Source: National Geographic, 'Lions hunt porcupines' and 'Porcupines vs lions' (nationalgeographic.com).  (Legend.)

question: A porcupine quill is really just a stiff, modified hair. To an ordinary eye its tip looks smooth, but under a microscope you can see a hidden feature no bare eye can catch. That feature lets the quill drive easily into an attacker's flesh, yet fights every attempt to pull it back out — which is why a stuck quill hurts so much to remove. What covers the tip of the quill?
answer: A ring of tiny backward-pointing barbs
choices: A ring of tiny backward-pointing barbs
A coating of fast-acting venom
A hollow needle that injects air
A sticky resin that glues it in place
context: The quill is a stiff, hollow shaft tipped with microscopic backward-pointing barbs. The barbs catch the flesh, and the quill works deeper with the victim's own muscle movement, which is why it is so hard to remove. Source: Cho, Karp et al., PNAS 2012, 'Microstructured barbs on the North American porcupine quill'; Cornell vet on porcupine quill injuries.

question: When a European hedgehog senses danger, it curls into a tight prickly ball with its soft belly hidden inside. It can stay locked up like that for hours without getting tired. So it can't just be clenching every muscle the whole time. In fact, one ring-shaped muscle that wraps all around its body does the whole job almost effortlessly. How does that muscle keep the ball closed?
answer: It draws the spiny skin shut over the belly like a purse-string and holds it
choices: It draws the spiny skin shut over the belly like a purse-string and holds it
It pumps extra blood into the raised spines to keep them stiff
It seals the nostrils so the animal can hold its breath
It hooks the spines into each other so they stay latched
context: The circular 'orbicularis' muscle runs around the hedgehog's body; contracting it cinches the spiny skin closed over the soft belly and holds the ball with very little effort, so the animal can simply wait a predator out. Source: veteriankey.com/hedgehogs-2.

question: A porcupinefish resting quietly on a tropical seafloor looks almost smooth, with all its spines lying flat against its skin. When a hungry predator comes close, the fish gulps in mouthful after mouthful of seawater until it swells into a ball many times its normal size. In the same motion, its spines change too. What happens to the spines as it inflates?
answer: They stand straight out, turning it into a bristling spiky orb
choices: They stand straight out, turning it into a bristling spiky orb
They fold flatter still and lock into protective plates
They flush bright red as a warning to back off
They snap off and scatter into the water
context: The porcupinefish (family Diodontidae) usually keeps its spines — which are modified scales — flat against its body; inflating with water makes them stand straight out. Source: Seattle Aquarium, 'Pufferfish and porcupinefish'; ioa.factsanddetails.com.

question: The lionfish is a reef fish that wears bold red, white, and black stripes and drifts openly through the water column instead of hiding. Up to 18 venomous spines fan out from its back and sides — a single sting can send a diver to the hospital. Most animals in nature try hard to stay unseen. Why would a well-armed fish advertise itself so loudly to every predator around?
answer: The colors are a warning billboard telling predators the sting isn't worth it
choices: The colors are a warning billboard telling predators the sting isn't worth it
The colors mimic a harmless reef fish so predators ignore it
The colors attract small prey fish close enough to swallow
The colors let it blend into red coral and disappear
context: The lionfish (genus Pterois) has up to 18 venomous spines, each grooved to carry venom; its bold stripes are aposematism — warning coloration announcing that the sting isn't worth the meal. Source: Wikipedia 'Lionfish'; NOAA lionfish facts; hygger-online.com on warning coloration.

question: The crown-of-thorns starfish is a large, thorny starfish that lives on coral reefs across the Indo-Pacific and eats coral for a living. Its whole body is bristling with needle-sharp venomous spines. Yet unlike a snake or a wasp, it has no fangs, no stinger, no way to actively inject anything. So how does its venom get into a predator that presses against one of its spines?
answer: Venom-laced skin on the spine breaks off inside the wound
choices: Venom-laced skin on the spine breaks off inside the wound
A muscle at the spine's base pumps venom down a groove
It fires the whole spine like a dart and grows a new one
It vomits venom-soaked stomach lining over the attacker
context: The crown-of-thorns starfish (Acanthaster planci) is named for the biblical crown of thorns; its 2–3 cm venomous spines cover its upper surface but cannot inject. Instead the venom-laced skin breaks off in the wound when a spine pierces a predator. Source: Wikipedia 'Crown-of-thorns starfish'; animaldiversity.org.

question: The flower urchin lives on Indo-Pacific coral reefs and looks decorated with pretty pink-and-white 'flowers' scattered between its spines. Those flowers, not the spines, are what put it among the most venomous animals in the sea. A diver who handles one is often paralyzed for hours, sometimes needing help just to breathe. What are the flower-like petals really?
answer: Venomous jaws that snap shut and keep injecting even after breaking off
choices: Venomous jaws that snap shut and keep injecting even after breaking off
Tube feet that grip prey and drag it toward the mouth
Light-sensing spots that trigger the spines to rise
Gills that flush toxin out through the seawater
context: The flower urchin (Toxopneustes pileolus) defends itself mainly with flower-like pedicellariae — venomous pincers (tiny jaws) that snap shut on a threat, inject a paralyzing neurotoxin, and can break off and keep injecting for hours. Source: Wikipedia 'Toxopneustes pileolus'; PMC12193733.

question: When scientists finally studied porcupine quills under electron microscopes, they realized the humble quill does something no engineer had ever built. It is easy to push into flesh, yet extremely hard to pull back out — a combination human inventors had chased for centuries without success. That discovery pointed the way to a new kind of device. What did the porcupine-quill design inspire engineers to make?
answer: Better medical needles and surgical staples that grip tissue
choices: Better medical needles and surgical staples that grip tissue
Stronger fishing hooks that release on command
Self-sealing tires studded with tiny barbs
Climbing spikes that dig into ice and rock
context: The barbed quill so perfectly solves 'easy to push in, hard to pull out' — the only known structure with that dual functionality — that it inspired engineers to design better medical needles and surgical staples that grip tissue. Source: SciTechDaily, 'Barbed porcupine quills could help enhance biomedical devices'; PNAS 2012.

question: A single pufferfish carries enough of a poison called tetrodotoxin to kill several grown adults, and doctors have no antidote for it. The cruelest part is what happens to the victim. The person's body slowly goes limp, but the mind stays wide awake and fully aware right to the end — trapped, unable to move or breathe. How does tetrodotoxin actually kill?
answer: It jams the sodium gates that fire the nerves, so the breathing muscles go slack
choices: It jams the sodium gates that fire the nerves, so the breathing muscles go slack
It melts the walls of the blood vessels, so the victim slowly bleeds inward
It overloads the heart's pacemaker, so it races itself into failure
It floods the lungs with fluid, drowning the victim from within
context: Tetrodotoxin isn't the pufferfish's own invention -- it's built by marine bacteria and climbs the food chain, so the fish banks a borrowed poison in its liver, ovaries, and skin. The proof came from the tank: pufferfish reared on toxin-free food grow up completely harmless, and turn deadly again only if later fed TTX-laden prey. The toxin works by plugging the voltage-gated sodium channels that nerve and muscle cells use to fire; with the sodium inrush blocked, nerves fall silent and muscles -- including the diaphragm -- go limp, so the victim suffocates while fully conscious. Gram for gram it far outstrips cyanide (mouse LD50 about 8-10 micrograms/kg by injection), and there is still no approved antidote. Source: MDPI Marine Drugs review, 'Tetrodotoxin, an Extremely Potent Marine Neurotoxin' (2015), PMC4626696; Wikipedia, Tetrodotoxin.

question: Old World porcupines shuffle across Africa and Asia; New World porcupines climb trees in the Americas. Both bristle with quills, so you would guess a single spiny ancestor handed the trait down. DNA tells a stranger tale. What are the New World porcupine's closest kin?
answer: Guinea pigs, capybaras, and their South American rodent kin
choices: Guinea pigs, capybaras, and their South American rodent kin
Hedgehogs, Old World insect-eaters that reached the Americas
Beavers, the big gnawing rodents of northern rivers
Armadillos, whose bony shell loosened into a spiny coat
context: The two porcupine families invented their quills separately -- a textbook case of convergent evolution. New World porcupines (Erethizontidae, the tree-climbers) are caviomorph rodents, closer kin to guinea pigs and capybaras than to the Old World porcupines (Hystricidae) they resemble; the lineages split roughly 30-40 million years ago, near the Eocene-Oligocene boundary. The hardware differs to match: New World quills are round and tipped with backward-pointing barbs that dig in and resist removal, while many Old World species grow longer, grooved, largely barbless quills plus hollow 'rattle' quills on the tail that hiss a warning. Source: Voss et al., 'Phylogenetic Relationships of New World Porcupines,' American Museum Novitates 3769 (2013), BioOne; Wikipedia, Porcupine.

question: Around 95 million years ago, the shores of what is now North Africa were prowled by a giant meat-eating dinosaur about 46 to 48 feet from snout to tail. That put it a little longer than Tyrannosaurus rex, which lived a world away in North America some 30 million years later. Which predator held that length record?
answer: Spinosaurus
choices: Spinosaurus
Giganotosaurus
Carcharodontosaurus
Allosaurus
context: Spinosaurus is the longest predatory dinosaur known, reaching roughly 14 to 15 meters (about 46-48 feet) -- longer than T. rex, and edging out other giant carnivores like Giganotosaurus and Carcharodontosaurus. Source: Britannica / Live Science; Sereno 2022 via Wikipedia.

question: When the German paleontologist Ernst Stromer worked on Spinosaurus in 1915, one detail dominated his reconstruction. The dinosaur wore something so striking on its back that no other big predator carried anything like it. Whatever it was, it stood tall enough to change the animal's whole silhouette. What rose off its spine?
answer: A skin-covered 'sail'
choices: A skin-covered 'sail'
A row of bony back plates
A ridge of long spikes
A crest of stiff feathers
context: The sail was built from bony neural spines up to about 1.8 meters (6 feet) tall. Source: Live Science; Wikipedia (Spinosaurus, neural spines).

question: Spinosaurus was a huge fish-eating dinosaur that stalked North African rivers about 100 million years ago. On its back rose a giant sail. The bones holding that sail up were freakishly overbuilt — each was a long, thin blade of bone sprouting straight up from a single vertebra of its spine. Compared to the width of the vertebra it grew from, how tall did one of those spines reach?
answer: More than ten times as long
choices: More than ten times as long
About twice as long
Roughly the same length
A little shorter
context: Each neural spine reached about 1.8 meters (6 feet) -- more than ten times the width of the backbone it grew from. Source: Live Science; Wikipedia (Spinosaurus, neural spines).

question: Spinosaurus and Tyrannosaurus rex were both giant meat-eaters, but their skulls tell you they hunted totally different prey. T. rex had a short, bone-crushing skull. Spinosaurus had long, narrow jaws lined with cone-shaped teeth — the same tooth shape you see today in animals that catch slippery food. What did Spinosaurus hunt?
answer: Snatch slippery fish from the water
choices: Snatch slippery fish from the water
Crush turtles in its jaws
Pluck pterosaurs from the air
Chase down small land dinosaurs
context: Its crocodile-like snout held straight conical teeth with few or no serrations -- built to grip slippery fish like fishhooks rather than saw through flesh. Source: Wikipedia (Spinosaurus teeth); Smithsonian Magazine ('hell heron').

question: A modern crocodile can lurk in a river with almost its whole head underwater and still breathe, because of where its nostrils sit. Paleontologists studying Spinosaurus noticed the dinosaur could do the exact same trick, thanks to one feature of its skull that no other big meat-eating dinosaur shared. Where did Spinosaurus's nostrils sit?
answer: High and far back on the snout
choices: High and far back on the snout
At the very tip of the snout
On top of the skull, near the eyes
Underneath the lower jaw
context: Its retracted nostrils sat high and far back, so it could keep most of its head submerged and still breathe -- like a crocodile at the surface. Source: eLife / UChicago (Spinosaurus retracted nostrils); Wikipedia.

question: Spinosaurus was a giant Cretaceous predator that hunted along riverbanks in what is now the Sahara Desert. Compared to famous predators like T. rex or Allosaurus, its body looks strangely unbalanced. Its hind legs were startlingly short for its size, giving it a build that would have been clumsy on dry land — but it spent much of its life in the water. About how much of its total body length did those short hind legs make up?
answer: Roughly a quarter
choices: Roughly a quarter
Roughly half
Nearly two-thirds
Almost the whole length
context: Its hind legs were only about a quarter of its total body length -- awkward on land, but fitting an animal built to hunt in water. Source: Wikipedia (Spinosaurus, short legs ~25 percent of body length).

question: The paleontologist Cristiano Dal Sasso was studying the snout of Spinosaurus when he noticed a puzzle: tiny holes clustered at the tip. He had seen those very same holes before, in living crocodiles and alligators along riverbanks. In modern crocs, the pits are packed with pressure sensors. What did those same pits let Spinosaurus do?
answer: Feel prey moving in murky water
choices: Feel prey moving in murky water
Smell blood from far off
Squirt venom into wounds
Filter salt from seawater
context: The pits held pressure sensors, like a crocodile's, that detect ripples from prey -- letting Spinosaurus find fish it couldn't see. Source: Wikipedia (Spinosaurus, Dal Sasso pressure receptors); Snexplores.org.

question: To test whether Spinosaurus's paddle-shaped tail actually worked for swimming, Nizar Ibrahim's team built a flat plastic model of it. A robot clamped the model and swished it side to side in a water tank, measuring the thrust. They compared it to the tails of land dinosaurs like Allosaurus. How well did the Spinosaurus tail push?
answer: Almost as well as a living crocodile
choices: Almost as well as a living crocodile
About as well as a paddling duck
Roughly like a flapping sea turtle
Almost as well as a cruising tuna
context: The 2020 experiment, run by Nizar Ibrahim with Harvard's Stephanie Pierce and George Lauder, found the flat Spinosaurus tail model produced roughly eight times more forward thrust and was more than twice as efficient at propulsion as the tail-shapes of land theropods like Allosaurus and Coelophysis -- performing nearly as well as a crocodile's or a newt's tail. It was the strongest physical evidence yet that this dinosaur was built to swim by sweeping its tail rather than merely wade. Source: Nizar Ibrahim, Stephanie E. Pierce, George V. Lauder et al., 'Tail-propelled aquatic locomotion in a theropod dinosaur,' Nature, 29 April 2020 (PubMed 32376955).

question: Everyone agrees Spinosaurus lived in and around water; the fierce, still-unsettled fight is over how it hunted. Nizar Ibrahim's team reads its paddle-shaped tail and dense, ballast-like bones as proof it actively dove and pursued prey deep underwater. David Hone and Thomas Holtz, studying the very same fossils, reached the opposite conclusion. What did they argue instead?
answer: It waded in the shallows and snatched fish from the surface
choices: It waded in the shallows and snatched fish from the surface
It drifted at the surface and scooped up fish while afloat
It lunged from the riverbank to spear fish with its jaws
It walked along the riverbed and grabbed fish from the bottom
context: Nizar Ibrahim's team reads the 2020 paddle-tail and the dense, ballast-like bones as evidence that Spinosaurus actively dove and pursued fish underwater. David Hone and Thomas Holtz counter that it was a 'heron-like' wader that stood in the shallows and snatched fish from the surface, while Donald Henderson's 2018 buoyancy model concluded the animal was so buoyant it would bob at the surface and even roll sideways, making sustained underwater chases unlikely. Same fossils, opposite conclusions -- the active-diver-versus-shoreline-grabber question is still genuinely open. Sources: Donald M. Henderson, PeerJ, 2018; David W. E. Hone & Thomas R. Holtz Jr. (2021) shoreline/wading review; Nizar Ibrahim et al., Nature, 2020.

question: In a Central American rainforest, a boa constrictor grabs a rat that is wider than its own head. Slowly, the snake works the whole animal into its mouth head-first, swallowing it in one long piece. If you looked inside the boa's open jaws, you would find rows of sharp teeth all curved the same way. Which way do the teeth point, and what job does that shape do?
answer: Backward, so they grip and ratchet prey inward
choices: Backward, so they grip and ratchet prey inward
Forward, so they spear and pin prey in place
Sideways, so they steer prey toward the throat
Outward, so they flick prey loose to reposition
context: A snake's teeth curve backward like rows of fishhooks. They can't chew — the teeth only grip and ratchet the prey inward, so the meal goes down whole and head-first, which folds the limbs back and stops them snagging. Source: Herpetological Society of Ireland, 'Biting Off More Than They Can Chew: How Snakes Swallow Large Prey' (https://thehsi.org/2015/05/06/biting-off-more-than-they-can-chew-how-snakes-swallow-large-prey/).

question: Deep in a South American swamp lives the heaviest snake on Earth — a body so thick it is roughly a foot across, tipping the scales near 550 pounds, nearly twice a big python. Name this giant.
answer: The green anaconda
choices: The green anaconda
The king cobra
The black mamba
The Gaboon viper
context: The green anaconda (Eunectes murinus) is the heaviest snake on Earth. It can weigh up to about 250 kg (550 pounds) — nearly twice a reticulated python — because its body is so thick, roughly a foot across. Source: Britannica, 'What Is the Largest Snake in the World?' (https://www.britannica.com/science/What-Is-the-Largest-Snake-in-the-World).

question: The world's heaviest snake is one animal — the anaconda of South American swamps. But the world's longest snake is a different creature entirely, prowling the tropical rainforests of Southeast Asia, and stretching past 20 feet from head to tail. Which snake holds the length record?
answer: The reticulated python
choices: The reticulated python
The green anaconda
The boa constrictor
The Burmese python
context: The reticulated python is the longest snake in the world, not the anaconda. It can stretch past 6 meters (20+ feet), and it lives in the tropical forests of Southeast Asia. Sources: Britannica (https://www.britannica.com/science/What-Is-the-Largest-Snake-in-the-World); Natural History Museum (https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/what-is-the-biggest-snake-in-the-world.html).

question: A constrictor snake, such as a boa or python, does not crush its prey all at once with one big squeeze. Instead, once its coils are wrapped around the trapped animal, it times its grip to what the prey is doing. Every time the prey does one particular thing, the snake quietly cinches its coils one notch tighter. When does the snake tighten?
answer: Each time the prey breathes out
choices: Each time the prey breathes out
Each time the prey struggles
Each time the prey cries out
Once every few seconds on its own
context: A constrictor works with the prey's own breathing. Each time the animal exhales, the snake takes up the slack and cinches its coils a notch tighter, so the prey can never fill its lungs back up. Source: National Geographic, 'Snakes Know When to Stop Squeezing Because They Sense the Heartbeats of Their Prey' (https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/snakes-know-when-to-stop-squeezing-because-they-sense-the-heartbeats-of-their-prey).

question: For centuries people believed constrictor snakes killed their prey by crushing its bones or by slowly suffocating it in their coils. In 2015 an American biologist named Scott Boback ran careful lab experiments with boa constrictors and rats and overturned that old story. His measurements pointed to a much faster killer at work inside the coils. What actually kills the prey?
answer: The coils cut off blood flow, so it blacks out in seconds
choices: The coils cut off blood flow, so it blacks out in seconds
The coils jolt the heart into a fatal rhythm shock
The coils pinch a spinal nerve so the body seizes up
The coils spike the blood with a paralyzing stress flood
context: The old story that constrictors kill by crushing bones or suffocating prey is wrong. A 2015 study by Scott Boback showed the real, fast killer is circulatory arrest: the coils cut off blood flow, so the trapped animal blacks out and dies within seconds, long before it would run out of air. Source: Boback et al. 2015, 'Snake constriction rapidly induces circulatory arrest in rats,' Journal of Experimental Biology 218(14):2279 (https://journals.biologists.com/jeb/article/218/14/2279/14389/).  (Legend.)

question: People often say a snake 'dislocates' or 'unhinges' its jaw to swallow prey wider than its head, but that isn't quite what happens. A snake's lower jaw is really made of two completely separate bones, one on each side. Something links them at the front of the chin and lets the two halves spread apart, so the whole jaw can walk over the prey step by step. What connects the two lower-jaw bones?
answer: A stretchy ligament linking them at the chin
choices: A stretchy ligament linking them at the chin
A hinge of soft cartilage bridging the tips
A sheet of muscle fused across the gap
A flexible flap of skin webbed between them
context: A snake doesn't 'unhinge' or dislocate its jaw — that's a myth. Its lower jaw is two separate bones joined at the chin by a stretchy ligament, so the two halves spread apart and 'walk' over the prey one side at a time. Sources: Herpetological Society of Ireland (https://thehsi.org/2015/05/06/biting-off-more-than-they-can-chew-how-snakes-swallow-large-prey/); JSTOR Daily, 'How Snakes Swallow' (https://daily.jstor.org/how-snakes-swallow/).  (Legend.)

question: In Scott Boback's laboratory, a boa constrictor clamped its coils around an anesthetized rat while his team stood by with pressure probes. Just six seconds into the squeeze, they read the blood pressure inside the prey — one probe placed in the artery of the rat's leg, another in a nearby vein. What did the two readings show?
answer: Artery pressure fell to half while vein pressure jumped sixfold
choices: Artery pressure fell to half while vein pressure jumped sixfold
Artery pressure dropped a tenth while vein pressure held steady
Artery pressure doubled while vein pressure fell away to nothing
Artery pressure held firm while vein pressure slowly climbed higher
context: When a boa constricts a rat, the prey's blood pressure at the leg artery drops to HALF within just 6 seconds, while the pressure in its veins jumps sixfold in that same instant. The blood essentially stops moving almost immediately. Source: Boback et al. 2015, Journal of Experimental Biology 218(14):2279 (https://journals.biologists.com/jeb/article/218/14/2279/14389/).

question: After going months without food, a Burmese python swallows one enormous meal — sometimes a deer or a wild pig, larger around than its own head. Its ordinary gut is not built to digest something that huge. Its solution is astonishing: within about three days its own body remodels itself around the meal. What happens to the python's internal organs?
answer: The heart, liver and gut swell 40 to 100 percent bigger
choices: The heart, liver and gut swell 40 to 100 percent bigger
The stomach hardens into a rigid grinding chamber
A second stomach inflates alongside the first
The organs shut down while acid alone dissolves the meal
context: After swallowing one huge meal, a python's own organs balloon: within about 3 days the heart, liver, pancreas, kidneys and small intestine grow 40 to 100 percent bigger to handle digestion — then shrink back down once the meal is processed. Sources: ScienceDaily, 'How the Burmese python grows and shrinks after it eats' (https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2015/05/150518081447.htm); Secor & Diamond, Journal of Experimental Biology.  (Legend.)

question: In the wet marshes and dark tunnels of the northeastern United States, a hamster-sized mole snuffles through the mud in near-total darkness. Around the tip of its short pink snout sits a ring of 22 fleshy pink tentacles, spread out like a bristling burst of tiny fingers. What is this odd little animal called?
answer: The star-nosed mole
choices: The star-nosed mole
The naked mole-rat
The pygmy shrew
The European hedgehog
context: The star-nosed mole (Condylura cristata) is instantly known by that 22-tentacle 'star' around its nose. Roughly the size of a hamster, it lives in the dark, wet burrows of wetlands in northeastern North America. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star-nosed_mole

question: The star-nosed mole spends its whole life underground in pitch darkness, digging tunnels through wet soil. Its eyes are tiny, its optic nerve barely there — it can hardly see anything at all. And yet it snatches worms and insects at some of the fastest speeds ever measured in a mammal. How does it find its prey?
answer: It feels for them with its tentacled snout
choices: It feels for them with its tentacled snout
It listens for them with huge outer ears
It tracks their body heat like a pit viper
It waits for them to fall into pit traps
context: The mole is nearly blind and lives entirely underground, so it relies almost completely on its star to locate prey by touch in the dark. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star-nosed_mole

question: Everyone who first meets the star-nosed mole assumes the fleshy 22-rayed star on its face must be a super-nose for smelling prey through soil. The neuroscientist Kenneth Catania spent years studying that star with high-speed cameras and found it is nothing of the kind. What is the star actually built to do?
answer: To feel by touch, more sensitively than any other mammal's skin
choices: To feel by touch, more sensitively than any other mammal's skin
To pick up faint smells drifting through the soil
To sense electric fields given off by buried prey
To glow faintly and lure insects toward the mouth
context: Catania described the star as probably the most sensitive and acute touch organ found on any mammal. It is a touch organ, not a nose. Source: https://www.pbs.org/wnet/nature/the-beauty-of-ugly-star-nosed-moles/428/  (Legend.)

question: The star-nosed mole's 22-tentacled star is barely wider than a centimeter — smaller across than a coin. Yet biologists have counted more than 100,000 nerve fibers packed into that tiny disc. A human hand, with all its skin and fingertips, has plenty of touch nerves of its own. Compared with a whole human hand, how many touch nerves does the mole's little star carry?
answer: About five to six times as many
choices: About five to six times as many
About the same number
Roughly one-tenth as many
Roughly half as many
context: The star holds some 25,000 to 30,000 Eimer's organs feeding over 100,000 nerve fibers into a patch barely a centimeter across, versus about 17,000 in the whole human hand. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/how-the-star-nosed-mole-sees-with-its-ultra-sensitive-snout-8926067/

question: In the marshy ponds of eastern North America lives the star-nosed mole, a small mammal named for the ring of pink, finger-like feelers around its snout. It dives to the muddy pond floor and hunts in total darkness, fully submerged. Scientists once thought no mammal could smell underwater — until they filmed this mole doing it. The trick uses tiny air bubbles. What does the mole do with them?
answer: It blows bubbles onto an object, then re-inhales them to smell it
choices: It blows bubbles onto an object, then re-inhales them to smell it
It releases bubbles to scare prey out of hiding
It uses rising bubbles to steer back toward the surface
It stores bubbles in its cheeks as an oxygen supply
context: Catania showed the mole exhales tiny bubbles onto an object underwater and re-inhales them, letting the air pick up scent molecules, sniffing about 5 to 10 times a second. It is one of only two mammals known to smell underwater. Source: https://news.vanderbilt.edu/2006/12/20/scientist-discovers-some-mammals-can-smell-objects-under-water-58788/  (Legend.)

question: Kenneth Catania tested whether the star-nosed mole truly smells underwater by having moles follow a scent trail to food; they chose the right path 75 to 100 percent of the time. Then he laid a fine grid between nose and scent. Why did that grid send their success crashing down to a coin-flip 50 percent?
answer: It blocked the exhaled bubbles from ever touching the scent
choices: It blocked the exhaled bubbles from ever touching the scent
