It muffled the vibrations the prey gave off
It masked the food's faint body heat
It reflected the mole's own scent back at it
context: With the bubbles kept from reaching the scent, the mole's underwater smelling was disabled and its choices dropped to pure chance, proving the bubble-sniffing mechanism was doing the work. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/learn-to-smell-underwater-with-the-star-nosed-mole

question: A fish shovels itself down into the seabed with its side fins until only its eyes and mouth are left showing on top, then bursts upward to swallow a passing fish whole. Which fish?
answer: A stargazer
choices: A stargazer
A flounder
An anglerfish
A stonefish
context: The stargazer (family Uranoscopidae) is a true ambush-from-below specialist. It uses its pectoral (side) fins as shovels to bury itself, leaving only its upward-facing eyes and mouth exposed at the surface of the sand, then rises and gulps a passing fish whole in an instant. Flounders bury too and stonefish ambush from the bottom, but only the stargazer aims straight up. Source: Florida Museum of Natural History, Northern Stargazer species profile (https://www.floridamuseum.ufl.edu/discover-fish/species-profiles/northern-stargazer/).

question: A stargazer is a fish that ambushes prey from below. Its adult body is built for hiding on the seafloor with only its face poking up. But the baby stargazer hatches as an ordinary larva with an eye on each side of its head, like most fish. As it grows toward its ambusher form, what happens to those eyes?
answer: They migrate to the top of the head
choices: They migrate to the top of the head
They stay put on the sides
They shrink down to tiny dots
They fuse into a single central eye
context: A stargazer is not born looking upward. It hatches as an ordinary side-eyed larva, and only as it develops do the eyes travel up to the top of the head, ending in the sky-watching position that gave the family its name. Source: Florida Museum of Natural History, Northern Stargazer species profile (https://www.floridamuseum.ufl.edu/discover-fish/species-profiles/northern-stargazer/).

question: Electric eels, electric rays, and other electric fish all sense the faint electric fields of nearby animals to hunt and navigate in dark water. The northern stargazer, an ambush fish buried in the sandy sea floor, carries a shocking 50-volt organ of its own. But among electric-organ fishes, it stands apart in one strange way. What is it?
answer: It cannot sense electricity at all
choices: It cannot sense electricity at all
It jams the fields that rivals give off
It reads prey heartbeats through the sand
It stores charge for one huge final blast
context: Electric stargazers (genus Astroscopus) carry an electric organ just behind the eyes that discharges up to 50 volts of direct current. Strangely, unlike eels and other electric fish, stargazers have no electroreceptors at all, so they cannot sense electricity to find prey. The organ is purely a weapon, for stunning a meal or driving off an attacker. Source: Britannica, Electric stargazer (https://www.britannica.com/animal/electric-stargazer); Wikipedia, Stargazer (fish) (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stargazer_(fish)).

question: The stargazer is a seafloor ambush fish that carries something rare — a working electric organ that shocks prey and rivals. You might guess it was built out of spare swimming muscle, the way an electric eel's is. It was not. It was rebuilt from a surprising body part. Which one?
answer: Muscle that once moved its eyes
choices: Muscle that once moved its eyes
Muscle from its beating heart
Muscle that works its jaws
Muscle at the base of its fins
context: The stargazer's battery is a repurposed body part: the electric organ is built from modified extraocular muscle, the tissue that normally moves the eyes, rather than from ordinary swimming muscle. In the northern stargazer it is packed from roughly 200 thin stacked layers of electric tissue, like the plates in a battery. Source: Wikipedia, Astroscopus guttatus (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astroscopus_guttatus).

question: A stargazer buries itself in the sand so that only its upturned face shows on the seafloor. Its mouth gapes wide open, aimed straight up at the water above. Then, right inside its own jaws, it dangles a bit of living-looking bait to draw curious fish in close. What does that bait look like?
answer: A wriggling worm-shaped flap
choices: A wriggling worm-shaped flap
A glowing round bulb
A bright shrimp-like claw
A feathery fanned frill
context: Some stargazers grow a worm-shaped lure on the floor of the mouth and wiggle it, tricking prey into swimming right between the open jaws. Combined with the sand ambush, the electric shock, and venomous spines above the pectoral fins, it stacks several separate weapons into one buried face. Source: Wikipedia, Stargazer (fish); Discover Wildlife, Stargazer fish (https://www.discoverwildlife.com/animal-facts/marine-animals/stargazer-fish).

question: A perch hangs perfectly still in the middle of a lake — not sinking to the bottom, not rising to the surface, its fins barely twitching. Most bony fish can do this, hovering weightless at any chosen depth without swimming. What organ inside their body makes it possible?
answer: A gas-filled swim bladder
choices: A gas-filled swim bladder
A ring of stomach muscle
A pair of extra gills
A layer of belly fat
context: The swim bladder is a gas pocket the fish inflates to take up more space and displace more water (floating it up) or shrinks to sink. Puffed to the right size, the fish neither rises nor falls -- it just hangs. Source: https://biologyinsights.com/the-fish-swim-bladder-function-form-and-problems/

question: A bony fish like a tuna has a hidden gas-filled sac inside called a swim bladder, and by adjusting how much gas is in it, the tuna can hover in place with almost no effort. A shark has no swim bladder at all. That should mean a shark's dense muscle and cartilage would drag it straight to the seabed. Yet great whites and makos still cruise the open ocean. What keeps a shark from sinking?
answer: A huge liver soaked in lightweight oil
choices: A huge liver soaked in lightweight oil
Air trapped under its rough skin
Hollow, honeycombed bones
A frill of buoyant gill flaps
context: A shark's oversized liver is packed with oil lighter than seawater (about 870-880 grams per litre), and that low-density oil supplies the lift a swim bladder gives other fish. Source: https://www.wildlifeonline.me.uk/questions/answer/how-do-sharks-and-rays-control-their-buoyancy-without-a-swim-bladder

question: A shark has no gas-filled swim bladder, so instead its huge liver is its buoyancy tank. That liver can be a quarter of the animal's whole body weight, and inside it the fat vacuoles are crammed with one lightweight molecule that is even less dense than seawater. In some deep-sea shark species that single molecule fills 80% or more of the liver by volume. What is that molecule?
answer: Squalene
choices: Squalene
Lecithin
Triglyceride
Omega-3
context: The lift oil is mostly squalene, a lightweight molecule the body makes on the way to building cholesterol, and fat vacuoles packed with it can fill 80% or more of a shark's liver by volume. Source: https://www.wildlifeonline.me.uk/questions/answer/how-do-sharks-and-rays-control-their-buoyancy-without-a-swim-bladder

question: The shortfin mako is the fastest shark in the ocean, a torpedo-shaped hunter of the open Pacific and Atlantic. Sharks have no gas-filled swim bladder, so unlike a bony fish they cannot just hover in place. A mako makes lift by swimming forward, the same way an airplane's wings only work while the plane is moving. If a mako simply stopped swimming and went limp, what would happen to it?
answer: It would slowly sink
choices: It would slowly sink
It would pop to the surface
It would hold its exact depth
It would roll onto its back
context: Most sharks are slightly heavier than water and use forward motion over their fins for extra lift, so many sink if they stop swimming. A few deep-sea species, like the sixgill, carry livers so large they actually float. Source: https://www.submon.org/en/sharks-and-rays-buoyancy/

question: A cuttlefish's buoyancy tank is not a soft balloon like a regular fish's swim bladder. It is a stiff internal shell divided into chambers, the flat white oval that washes up on beaches and ends up clipped into budgie cages. What is that rigid cuttlebone mostly made of?
answer: Chalk
choices: Chalk
Cartilage
Keratin
Silica glass
context: The porous cuttlebone is the ballast tank, and it is about 95-97% aragonite -- a form of chalk (calcium carbonate). The cuttlefish floods its hundreds of tiny chambers with fluid to sink and lets gas back in to rise. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuttlebone

question: A rockfish spends its life 300 or 400 feet down along the Pacific coast, where the water pressure is many times greater than at the surface. Inside the fish is a gas-filled sac called a swim bladder that lets it hover at that depth. An angler hooks one and cranks the reel too fast. In under a minute the fish rises from the crushing dark to the sunny surface, and its stomach is pushed up into its own mouth. What went wrong inside it as the water pressure dropped?
answer: Its swim bladder swelled up like a balloon
choices: Its swim bladder swelled up like a balloon
Its blood boiled into froth
Its gills fused shut
Its heart burst from the cold
context: A rockfish's swim bladder, only thumb-sized at depth, swells to the size of a party balloon at the surface as the pressure falls -- barotrauma. Sending the fish back down re-compresses the bladder, and the injuries actually reverse. Source: https://www.mercurymarine.com/us/en/lifestyle/dockline/best-practices-for-releasing-deep-water-rockfish

question: Herring, carp, and eels are all bony fish that carry a swim bladder — a gas-filled sac inside the body that keeps the fish floating at the right depth without effort. In these three, a small open pipe called the pneumatic duct runs from the bladder straight to the gut. A perch or a bass has no such pipe; its bladder is sealed shut. What can the open-pipe fish do that a sealed-bladder fish cannot risk?
answer: Burp gas out and rise fast without bursting
choices: Burp gas out and rise fast without bursting
Breathe underwater through the stomach
Store food inside the bladder
Change color to hide from predators
context: These 'physostome' fish gulp air at the surface to inflate the bladder and can burp gas back out to descend, so they rise quickly without rupturing it. A fish with a sealed bladder cannot ascend fast or it would burst. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physostome

question: In the crushing pressure of the deep sea, thousands of metres down, many fish like the orange roughy and coelacanth quietly abandon the gas-filled swim bladder that shallow fish use. Instead their bladder is packed with light oil or wax. A gas bladder would collapse at those depths, but the oily one keeps giving steady lift. What property of oil makes it work where gas cannot?
answer: It stays the same size no matter the pressure
choices: It stays the same size no matter the pressure
It expands to give more lift as pressure rises
It absorbs gas from the surrounding water
It grows lighter the deeper the fish goes
context: A lipid is essentially incompressible -- the crushing pressure barely shrinks it -- so a fat- or wax-filled bladder holds steady lift at depths where a gas bladder would be squeezed away and fail. Source: https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-the-marine-biological-association-of-the-united-kingdom/article/abs/swimbladder-of-deepsea-fish-the-swimbladder-wall-is-a-lipidrich-barrier-to-oxygen-diffusion/52C7BC88C21569BF765FD3D597B2F2B1

question: Most ocean fish, from cod to mackerel, do not glue their eggs to the seabed the way a salmon does in a river. They release millions of tiny eggs into the open water, and those eggs drift near the sunlit surface where plankton is thickest and the newly hatched fish will have food. Each egg carries one small ingredient inside that keeps it riding the currents up top rather than sinking. What is inside each egg?
answer: A droplet of oil
choices: A droplet of oil
A pocket of gas
A jelly float ring
A cluster of salt grains
context: About 70% of ocean fish spawn floating (pelagic) eggs, and many carry an oil droplet that both nourishes the embryo and keeps the egg buoyant near the surface. Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4605736/

question: A sperm whale's huge, blocky head is famous for holding a giant reservoir of waxy spermaceti oil. One leading idea is that the whale cools this wax before a dive to help it sink and warms it to rise -- but many researchers doubt it and favor a different main job for the organ. What do those researchers think the head is really for?
answer: Echolocation -- a sonar organ
choices: Echolocation -- a sonar organ
Storing extra oxygen
Filtering food from the water
Keeping the brain warm
context: Critics of the buoyancy idea note the temperature change would barely shift the whale's buoyancy, the heat-exchange plumbing seems to be missing, and the whale stays active during dives anyway; many instead see the head as an echolocation organ. The buoyancy hypothesis is a leading-but-debated idea, not settled fact. One head can hold as much as 1,900 litres of spermaceti. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spermaceti_organ  (Legend.)

question: Down in the dim midwater layer of the deep ocean drifts the glass squid, a small cephalopod so transparent you can see straight through its body to its dark eyes and gut. It hangs perfectly still without sinking and never beats a fin to hold its depth. Something inside gives it steady, effortless lift. What fills the one huge chamber that takes up most of its body?
answer: A body-filling tank of ammonium-chloride solution
choices: A body-filling tank of ammonium-chloride solution
A rigid internal shell of gas-filled chambers
A bulky reserve of lightweight waxy oil
A soft body of near-weightless watery jelly
context: Beyond the fish's gas bladder and the shark's oily liver lies a third answer to sinking: pure chemistry. Glass squid (family Cranchiidae) and many other deep midwater squid flood a huge coelomic chamber with a watery ammonium-chloride solution. It is nearly iso-osmotic with seawater, so it does not osmotically flood the animal, yet it is distinctly less dense -- steady lift with no gas and no swimming. The scale is the shock: this low-density fluid can make up roughly 50-60% of the animal's body mass, with ammonium concentrations near 500 mM. It is also why the colossal squid's flesh is famously flabby and gelatinous. Sources: landmark discovery Denton, Gilpin-Brown & Shaw, 'A buoyancy mechanism found in cranchid squid,' Proc. R. Soc. Lond. B 174:271 (1969), royalsocietypublishing.org/doi/10.1098/rspb.1969.0093; body-mass and concentration figures from Seibel, Goffredi et al., 'Ammonium content and buoyancy in midwater cephalopods,' J. Exp. Mar. Biol. Ecol. (2004); corroborated by Wikipedia 'Teuthowenia megalops.'  (Legend.)

question: A living nautilus jets along the reef wall in a coiled shell walled off inside into a stack of sealed chambers -- the very design the extinct ammonites carried through hundreds of millions of years of ocean life. To rise, the nautilus makes one of those chambers more buoyant. Working against the crushing pressure of the sea, how does it pull that off?
answer: It slowly pumps the liquid out through a living tube
choices: It slowly pumps the liquid out through a living tube
It pumps fresh gas in from a sac in its body
It swallows seawater to drive the old gas out
It clamps the shell walls to squeeze the gas smaller
context: The chambered shell is the ancient swim bladder. A living nautilus keeps its coiled shell partitioned into gas-filled chambers (a phragmocone) and adjusts lift not by adding gas but by slowly, osmotically pumping liquid OUT of them through the siphuncle, a living tube that threads every chamber; as the liquid leaves, gas expands into the space, and that chamber gas ends up below atmospheric pressure, around 0.8 atm. The extinct ammonites and belemnites used the same septa-and-siphuncle rig for hundreds of millions of years, so paleontologists can reconstruct a fossil cephalopod's buoyancy and life depth straight from its chamber walls and siphuncle. The design carries a built-in cost: the pumping is so slow the nautilus cannot change depth quickly, and the whole shell implodes near 800 m. Sources: Wikipedia 'Nautilus' (phragmocone/siphuncle, sub-atmospheric chamber gas, implosion depth per Dunstan, Ward & Marshall); fossil application from Hoffmann et al., 'Ammonoid Buoyancy,' in Ammonoid Paleobiology (Springer, 2015), link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-94-017-9630-9_16.

question: About 150 million years ago in the late Jurassic, on a green North American floodplain, a plant-eating dinosaur the size of a city bus lumbers past a stand of ferns. Two rows of tall diamond-shaped bony plates line its back from neck to hips, and its long tail ends in four sharp spikes. Which dinosaur is it?
answer: Stegosaurus
choices: Stegosaurus
Velociraptor
Pteranodon
Ankylosaurus
context: Stegosaurus was about 6.5 to 7 meters long (over 20 feet) and weighed around 3.5 metric tons, with two rows of tall bony plates down its back, a spiked tail, and a plant-eater's diet. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stegosaurus

question: About 150 million years ago, in the Late Jurassic period, a Stegosaurus plodded across a warm floodplain in what is now Colorado. Its head hung low, only about a meter off the ground, swinging over the plants. To picture its meals, remember that Late Jurassic Earth had no grass yet and no flowering plants of any kind — those would not appear for tens of millions of years. What did the Stegosaurus actually eat?
answer: Soft, low-growing ferns and mosses
choices: Soft, low-growing ferns and mosses
Wide meadows of tall grass
Ripe fallen fruit and berries
Broad flowering shrubs and blossoms
context: Stegosaurus browsed within about a meter of the ground on soft, low-growing plants like ferns and mosses; its bite force was less than half that of a modern Labrador retriever. (Grasses had not yet spread in the Late Jurassic.) Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stegosaurus

question: A full-grown Stegosaurus lumbered across the late Jurassic floodplains weighing around 3.5 metric tons — about as heavy as a modern car. Its skull was long and narrow, ending in a beak for cropping ferns. Yet when paleontologists carefully cleaned out the braincase inside that skull, they found the organ that ran this whole huge body was startlingly small. Its whole brain was closest in size to what?
answer: A walnut
choices: A walnut
A basketball
A house cat
A grapefruit
context: Stegosaurus had a brain of only around 80 grams, about the size of a walnut, and a braincase no bigger than a dog's, despite its bus-sized body. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stegosaurus

question: Four long sharp spikes bunch at the end of a Stegosaurus's tail — the plant-eater's main weapon against Jurassic predators like Allosaurus. For decades the spikes had no formal name. Then in 1982 the cartoonist Gary Larson drew a Far Side panel showing a caveman lecturing on the tail spikes of 'the late Thag Simmons.' Paleontologists loved the joke and adopted his nickname. What do they now call that spiked tail weapon?
answer: The thagomizer
choices: The thagomizer
The tail club
The spike battery
The tail flail
context: The spikes each ran about 60 to 90 cm long (2 to 3 feet). The 'thagomizer' nickname was coined in a 1982 Gary Larson 'Far Side' cartoon and adopted scientifically by paleontologist Kenneth Carpenter starting in 1993. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thagomizer  (Legend.)

question: The two rows of tall diamond-shaped plates along a Stegosaurus's back are one of the oldest riddles in paleontology. Since the first Stegosaurus was named in 1877 by the American paleontologist Othniel Marsh, scientists have argued about what those plates were really for — some said armor, some said radiators, some said signal boards. Recent scans show the plates were criss-crossed with blood vessels and grew far too thin to stop a predator's teeth. What do most now think was their main job?
answer: Display and heat control
choices: Display and heat control
Blocking predator bites
Storing fat for lean seasons
Digging up buried roots
context: The plates did not cover the animal's vulnerable sides or belly and were laced with blood vessels, so most scientists think they served for display and thermoregulation, warming the animal in the sun or shedding heat. Source: https://dino-world.com/the-100-year-debate-about-stegosaurus-plates-display-or-thermoregulation-2-23614/

question: For a long time museums mounted Stegosaurus skeletons with the diamond plates in matching pairs, one on the left, one on the right, running down the back like buttons on a coat. But when paleontologists carefully studied specimens where the plates were still preserved in place in the rock, they found the 17 to 22 plates came out differently on the two sides. How were they really arranged?
answer: In two staggered, alternating rows
choices: In two staggered, alternating rows
In a single row along the spine
In four tight bundles near the hips
Scattered randomly across the hide
context: A Stegosaurus carried somewhere between 17 and 22 plates, and they ran in two staggered (alternating) rows down the back rather than as a mirrored pair. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stegosaurus

question: For a long time scientists doubted a Stegosaurus could really hurt a large hunter like Allosaurus with the four sharp spikes on its tail. Then in the fossil beds of the American West, paleontologists found an Allosaurus tail bone with a perfectly round hole punched clean through it — and a Stegosaurus tail spike slotted into that hole exactly. When they looked closely at the edges of the wound in the bone, what did they see?
answer: Healed, remodeled edges: the Allosaurus survived the stab
choices: Healed, remodeled edges: the Allosaurus survived the stab
A fresh, ragged break: a killing blow
No bone reaction at all: the wound came after death
Open rot that never closed: fatal infection
context: The puncture in Allosaurus specimen UMNH 10781 matches a Stegosaurus tail spike, and the edges show healed, remodeled bone, meaning the Allosaurus was stabbed but lived. Nearly 1 in 10 Stegosaurus specimens show battle damage on their tail spikes. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/watch-out-for-that-thagomizer-98891562/  (Legend.)

question: Early computer models of the Stegosaurus jaw pictured a feeble mouth that could barely snip a twig thinner than a finger. Then in 2016 Stephan Lautenschlager's team rebuilt the skull and jaw muscles of the famous 'Sophie' specimen and measured its bite for real. What did that reconstruction reveal?
answer: It bit as hard as a living sheep or cow, able to browse tougher plants
choices: It bit as hard as a living sheep or cow, able to browse tougher plants
It bit as hard as a hyena, powerful enough to crack and splinter bone
It bit even more weakly than the twig-snapping estimate had suggested
It bit hard enough to shear through wood like a beaver felling a tree
context: This is a genuine, still-unsettled scientific argument. Miriam Reichel's 2010 finite-element model of the teeth (Swiss Journal of Geosciences 103:235-240) found a very weak bite: about 140 N at the front teeth and only ~275 N at the back, enough to snip branches barely a centimeter thick. But Stephan Lautenschlager and colleagues' 2016 digital reconstruction of the whole skull (Scientific Reports, Univ. of Bristol) put the force squarely in the range of living plant-eating mammals like sheep and cows, meaning Stegosaurus could have browsed a far wider menu than just the softest ferns. Both models stand; the debate is unresolved. Sources: Reichel 2010 (link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00015-010-0025-1); Lautenschlager et al. 2016 (bristol.ac.uk/news/2016/may/stegosaurs-bite.html).

question: The tall diamond plates rose along a Stegosaurus's back, but they left the throat and underside of its neck completely bare, the very spot a low-slung predator would lunge for. Yet fossils show this browsing giant was not defenseless there. What guarded that exposed throat?
answer: A mosaic of small bony studs set right into the skin of its throat
choices: A mosaic of small bony studs set right into the skin of its throat
A curtain of overlapping horny scales, much like a pangolin's armor
A single broad shield of solid bone plated across its windpipe
A thick pad of leathery, blubber-like fat cushioning the lower jaw
context: Paleontologists call these throat studs gular ossicles: small dermal bones ('ossicles') embedded in the skin of the gula, or throat. This cobbled soft-tissue armor guarded the one soft target the showy dorsal plates could not cover, exactly where a low browser was most exposed. It is a diagnostic feature described from Stegosaurus stenops armor specimens (Kenneth Carpenter, 'Armor of Stegosaurus stenops,' Garden Park, Colorado; researchgate.net/profile/Kenneth-Carpenter-2/publication/284097770), with plate and dermal-bone histology corroborated in Hayashi et al. 2012, Palaeontology 55(1):145-161.

question: A gecko lizard dashes straight up a pane of smooth window glass and hangs there upside-down by its dry toes, leaving behind no glue, no wet mark, no scratch. There are no suction cups and no claws helping it. Something invisible, working at a scale far smaller than we can see, grips the lizard to the glass. What actually holds a gecko to smooth glass?
answer: the faint pull between molecules that touch
choices: the faint pull between molecules that touch
static electricity built up in its skin
microscopic hooks snagging the glass
a ring of suction cups on each toe
context: A gecko uses no glue at all. The bottom of each toe is packed with millions of tiny hairs (setae) that grip by van der Waals force — the faint attraction any two molecules feel when they are touching. So many hairs touch at once that the faint pulls add up to hold the whole lizard. Source: Autumn et al. 2000, Nature 405:681; Kellar Autumn 2002 review.  (Legend.)

question: In a Costa Rican rainforest at night, a red-eyed tree frog crouches on a wet, slick leaf while a downpour hammers down around it. Its round toe pads press flat against the leaf, and even as water sheets across the surface, the frog never slips. A gecko, by comparison, grips best on a bone-dry wall. This tree frog uses the opposite trick — the water is not its enemy but its ally. What lets the tree frog hold fast to the slippery leaf?
answer: a thin film of water pulling by surface tension
choices: a thin film of water pulling by surface tension
tiny claws hooking into the leaf veins
a sticky glue it makes in special glands
curling its round toes around the leaf edge
context: The tree frog uses the opposite trick from a gecko: it sticks with WATER. Its round toe-discs stay damp, and a super-thin film of fluid between the pad and the leaf grips by surface tension — the same clingy pull that makes a wet glass stick to a coaster. Dry gecko, wet frog. Source: Hanna & Barnes 1991, J. Exp. Biol. 155:103; Barnes et al. 2019 biomimetics review.

question: An octopus reaches out one arm in a pounding tidal current and presses its row of round suckers against a bare, slippery rock. It clings so firmly that even a strong wave cannot tear it loose. Each sucker on that arm is a small muscular cup that the octopus can squeeze and release on its own. How does one of those cup-shaped suckers grip smooth stone?
answer: it lowers the water pressure trapped inside the cup
choices: it lowers the water pressure trapped inside the cup
it oozes a fast-drying natural cement
it drives tiny barbs from the rim into the stone
it grows thin roots into cracks in the rock
context: An octopus grips by pure suction, not stickiness. Muscles inside each sucker pull the middle of the cup back, dropping the water pressure trapped inside; the higher pressure of the surrounding sea then presses the sucker onto the rock. Each of its hundreds of suckers works on its own. Source: Kier & Smith 1990, Biological Bulletin 178:126.

question: The Tokay gecko is a big lizard of Southeast Asia, famous for climbing walls. On the underside of each of its five toes it carries about 500,000 microscopic gripping hairs, called setae, each far too small to see with the naked eye. There are so many of these tiny hairs, all pulling at once, that the Tokay can pull off a startling feat on a vertical pane of glass. What can it do?
answer: hang from the glass by a single toe
choices: hang from the glass by a single toe
melt a shallow groove into the glass
walk across the glass upside down underwater
leap off the glass twice its body length
context: A single gecko toe carries about 500,000 of these microscopic hairs. A Tokay gecko has so many that its two front feet can hold roughly 40 times the gecko's own body weight — which is why a gecko can hang from a pane of glass by just one toe. Source: Lewis & Clark Magazine (Kellar Autumn lab); Wikipedia 'Synthetic setae' (front feet ~40x body weight).  (Legend.)

question: The common housefly (Musca domestica) walks calmly across a kitchen ceiling upside down without falling. On the last segment of each of its six legs it carries two soft pads called pulvilli, each pad covered in thousands of fine hairs. Those foot-hairs do something specific to keep the fly stuck to the plaster overhead. What do they do?
answer: each oozes a droplet of gluey fluid
choices: each oozes a droplet of gluey fluid
each spins a thread of silk to the ceiling
each inflates like a balloon against the plaster
each sparks a tiny jolt of static charge
context: On the last segment of each leg sit soft pads (pulvilli) covered in tiny hairs, and each hair oozes a droplet of gluey fluid so thin — less than a millionth of a millimeter — that the fly clings by the same molecule-touching pull the gecko uses, plus the stickiness of the fluid itself. Source: Bullock & Federle on fly pulvilli; Nature Communications 2013 (contact film <10–20 nm).

question: Under a microscope, the toe pad of a rainforest tree frog looks tiled like a tiny honeycomb: flat six-sided cells packed side by side, split by deep, straight grooves between them. The pad grips wet leaves using a paper-thin film of water squeezed between skin and leaf. Since too much water would break that thin film, what job do the deep grooves between the cells do?
answer: drain excess water out to the edges
choices: drain excess water out to the edges
store a reserve of glue for later
sharpen into tiny teeth that bite the leaf
trap air bubbles to work like suckers
context: The channels are drainage grooves — they let the water squeeze out to the edges so the pad can press close to the surface instead of just skidding on a puddle. Counterintuitively, the wet-gripping frog still needs to shed water so its pad can make close contact. Source: Hanna & Barnes 1991, J. Exp. Biol. 155:103; Federle/Barnes tree-frog pad microstructure.

question: A gecko sticks to glass because of a faint pull between molecules that touch — a grip so weak per hair that it works only because the toe carries hundreds of thousands of hairs. But that molecular pull cannot be switched off like a hand releasing a rope, and yet the gecko sprints up the pane without ever getting stuck fast. To peel each foot free instantly, the lizard changes one thing about its gripping hairs. What does it change?
answer: the angle it tilts the hairs to the surface
choices: the angle it tilts the hairs to the surface
the temperature of its toe pads
the amount of fluid it pumps into the hairs
the electric charge stored in the hairs
context: Van der Waals force can't be switched off — so the gecko changes the angle instead. When it tilts the hair's shaft to about 30 degrees from the surface, the tips peel free at the trailing edge and the grip releases instantly. That's how a gecko can run up glass without getting stuck. Source: Wikipedia 'Synthetic setae' (detach at ~30°); Autumn et al. peeling studies.

question: A limpet is a small sea snail with a low cone-shaped shell that clamps to a wave-swept rock so hard that even crashing surf cannot tear it off. To scrape a meal of algae from the stone, it grinds with a row of tiny teeth reinforced by fibers of an iron mineral called goethite. When scientists at the University of Portsmouth measured just how strong those little teeth are, what record did they set?
answer: the strongest natural material ever measured
choices: the strongest natural material ever measured
the sharpest edge found in any animal
the fastest-growing tissue known in nature
the hardest shell of any sea creature
context: The limpet's teeth are reinforced with goethite fibers ten thousand times thinner than a human hair, giving a strength up to 6.5 gigapascals — beating even spider silk, and the strongest natural material ever measured. Source: Barber, Lu & Pugno 2015, J. Royal Society Interface, 'Extreme strength observed in limpet teeth' (University of Portsmouth; 3.0–6.5 GPa).  (Legend.)

question: Inspired by the gecko's toe, engineers led by Al Crosby at the University of Massachusetts Amherst built a dry sticky pad they called Geckskin, made from cheap woven nylon and everyday bathroom caulk — no glue at all. When they pinned a piece of Geckskin only the size of an index card onto a smooth pane of glass, it could hold a shocking weight without peeling loose. How much?
answer: up to 700 pounds
choices: up to 700 pounds
up to 7 pounds
up to 70 pounds
up to 7,000 pounds
context: Geckskin, only the size of an index card, can hold up to 700 pounds pinned to a pane of glass — then peel off cleanly with a flick, just like a gecko changing the angle of its foot. It was invented by Al Crosby and Duncan Irschick out of cheap stuff like nylon and bathroom caulk. Source: University of Massachusetts Amherst (Crosby & Irschick, Geckskin); Singularity Hub 2014 (700 lbs on glass).  (Legend.)

question: Wade barefoot in shallow water on a warm Indo-Pacific reef, and one lumpy 'rock' on the sea floor may not be a rock at all. It is a fish, so still and so perfectly disguised that swimmers step right on top of it by accident. Along its back, hidden in the mottled skin, are hollow spines loaded with venom. Which fish holds the title of the most venomous fish in the world?
answer: The stonefish
choices: The stonefish
The great white shark
The electric eel
The giant clam
context: The reef stonefish (Synanceia verrucosa) is the most venomous fish in the world. Source: Australian Museum — Reef Stonefish.

question: The stonefish is the world's most venomous fish. It lives on Indo-Pacific coral reefs, sitting in one spot for hours, waiting to ambush any small fish that drifts too close. Unlike a wrasse or a shark that keeps its scales scrubbed clean, a stonefish never grooms itself at all. Because it never cleans that lumpy, warty skin, something slowly builds up on the fish and makes its rock disguise even better. What builds up?
answer: Algae and sediment
choices: Algae and sediment
A coat of slippery slime
Bright warning stripes
A shell of tiny barnacles
context: The stonefish does not clean itself, so algae and sediment accumulate on its skin, improving the camouflage the longer it sits. It ends up looking exactly like an encrusted rock or lump of coral. Sources: Australian Museum — Reef Stonefish; Oceana — Stonefish.

question: The stonefish is the world's most venomous fish, camouflaged as a lump of coral on an Indo-Pacific reef floor. Step near a bass or a grouper and it darts away in a flash. Step near a stonefish and it does the exact opposite. It holds its ground and readies its defense, trusting the venom-loaded spines that run along its back. What does a disturbed stonefish do instead of fleeing?
answer: Erects its row of dorsal spines
choices: Erects its row of dorsal spines
Puffs up into a spiny ball
Squirts a cloud of black ink
Buries itself deeper in the sand
context: When disturbed, a stonefish stays put and raises its poisonous dorsal spines. Press down on it — as a bare foot does — and the pressure squeezes the venom glands so the spines inject automatically, harder the harder they are pressed. Source: Australian Museum — Reef Stonefish.

question: The Indo-Pacific stonefish is the world's most venomous fish, and its weapons are not its jaws. Along the ridge of its back, hidden beneath thick warty skin, lie 13 stiff spikes. Each one is hollow and grooved and stays tucked in a sheath until a bare foot or a snorkeler's hand presses down. Then the spike punches through the skin and drives venom deep into the wound. What everyday medical tool are these spikes most often compared to?
answer: A row of hypodermic needles
choices: A row of hypodermic needles
A set of surgeon's scalpels
A string of stitching sutures
A row of dental drills
context: A stonefish carries 13 stout dorsal spines, each grooved and fed by a venom gland at its base and wrapped in a sheath of skin — like a row of hypodermic needles lying flat until pressed. Source: Australian Museum — Reef Stonefish.

question: Two barefoot swimmers step on the very same stonefish, yet one ends up with a far worse sting than the other. The fish injects no fixed dose — the amount of venom that enters a wound changes from one victim to the next. What controls how much venom gets pumped in?
answer: How hard the spines are pressed down
choices: How hard the spines are pressed down
The temperature of the surrounding water
The overall body size of the stonefish
The time since the fish last stung something
context: The venom is purely defensive — never used to feed — and injects automatically when the spines are pressed, in proportion to how hard they are pressed. Bear down harder and the glands deliver more venom. Sources: Australian Museum — Reef Stonefish; Fact Animal — Stonefish; NCBI PMC7232307 — Defensive Venoms.

question: The stonefish is the world's most venomous fish and one of the reef's most patient hunters. It spends most of its life statue-still on the Indo-Pacific sea floor, disguised as a lump of coral, sometimes not moving for days at a time. When a small fish or shrimp finally drifts within reach, the stonefish launches its ambush. What is remarkable about the lunge it uses to snatch that prey?
answer: It is one of the fastest strikes in the fish world
choices: It is one of the fastest strikes in the fish world
It swallows prey twice its own length
It can be aimed from several feet away
It works only at night in total darkness
context: Instead of venom, the stonefish feeds with an ambush lunge that engulfs prey in roughly 15 milliseconds — so fast that high-speed cameras are needed to film it, one of the fastest strikes among fish. Sources: Australian Museum — Reef Stonefish; TheSea.org — Stonefish Synanceia.

question: A tide goes out and leaves a stony beach behind. Hours later a barefoot walker steps on one of the 'stones' and is stung — because a stonefish can survive a surprisingly long time out of water by breathing through its moist skin. Roughly how long can it last stranded?
answer: About 24 hours
choices: About 24 hours
About 10 minutes
About three days
About one hour
context: A stonefish can survive out of water for up to about 24 hours by absorbing oxygen through its skin as long as it stays moist — so a 'rock' left by a retreating tide can still be alive and still sting. Source: Culture Trip — 7 Facts About Stonefish; Biology Insights — How Venomous Are Stonefish.

question: A stonefish antivenom has kept Australia's confirmed death count from these fish at zero since 1959, but making it is strange work. The neutralizing agent is harvested from the blood of a large farm animal that has been dosed with stonefish venom first. Which animal's blood is used?
answer: A horse's
choices: A horse's
A cow's
A sheep's
A goat's
context: Stonefish antivenom is made by injecting horses with the venom and collecting the blood fraction that neutralizes it. Made by Australia's CSL in 1959, it was the world's first widely available marine antivenom and remains the only fish antivenom commercially produced. Sources: Life Saving First Aid — How is antivenom made; Australian Museum — Reef Stonefish.

question: A human nose carries about 6 million scent receptors, and we still notice a bakery a whole block away. A bloodhound is a large, drooping-eared tracking dog bred for centuries in medieval Europe to follow the faintest trail of a person or animal. Its nose has so many more scent receptors than ours that it barely lives in the same sensory world we do. Roughly how many scent receptors line a bloodhound's nose?
answer: About 300 million
choices: About 300 million
About 30 million
About 12 million
About 800,000
context: A dog's nose carries up to 300 million scent receptors, with bloodhounds at that top end, against only about 6 million in a human nose. It doesn't just smell more, it smells in far finer detail. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dog_sense_of_smell (PBS NOVA, 'Dogs' Dazzling Sense of Smell').

question: A bloodhound's brain devotes so much of itself to processing smells that scientists estimate up to 40% of its brain is dedicated to scent. The tracking hound seems less like an animal that happens to have a nose and more like a nose that happens to have an animal. People joke that a bloodhound is really just a helper for its own nose. What is a bloodhound jokingly called?
answer: A nose with a dog attached
choices: A nose with a dog attached
A bloodhound's blessing
The four-legged detective
A tracker on paws
context: A dog dedicates a far bigger slice of its brain to smell than we do, roughly 40 times more scent-sensing tissue overall, which is why a bloodhound is sometimes called 'a nose with a dog attached.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dog_sense_of_smell; Alexandra Horowitz, 'Inside of a Dog'.

question: A dog casts its head back and forth over a trail, and it isn't just searching randomly. Because its two nostrils take in odor independently, the dog gains one navigational trick a human nose can never manage. What can the dog's nose do that ours cannot?
answer: Tell which side a scent is coming from
choices: Tell which side a scent is coming from
Detect a scent a mile off
Smell colors as well as odors
Store a smell to recall it later
context: A dog smells in stereo: its two nostrils sample independently, so it can tell which side a scent came from and use its nose like a compass to point toward the source. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dog_sense_of_smell (PBS NOVA, PetMD).

question: A dog buries its nose deep in a scent trail on the ground and keeps breathing steadily, sniffing in and puffing out about five times every second. Watch its nostrils carefully as it exhales. The spent air does not come back out the way you or I breathe out — it takes a surprising exit that a human nose never uses. When a dog breathes out mid-sniff, where does the used-up air actually leave?
answer: Through the side slits of its nose
choices: Through the side slits of its nose
Straight out the front of the nostrils
Down through the back of the throat
Out through tiny pores on the muzzle
context: When a dog exhales, the used-up air blows out through the side slits of its nose, not straight out the front, so the outgoing breath doesn't scatter the scent it's still sniffing in. This lets the dog smell continuously even while breathing out. Source: https://www.petmd.com/dog/behavior/5-dog-nose-facts-you-probably-didnt-know (PBS NOVA).

question: Alexandra Horowitz is an American cognitive scientist at Barnard College in New York who studies how dogs experience the world. In her book Being a Dog she wanted to show just how faint a smell a trained scent hound can still catch. She reached for one everyday comparison. Picture a single teaspoon of sugar dissolved into a huge amount of water. How much water?
answer: Two Olympic-sized swimming pools
choices: Two Olympic-sized swimming pools
A backyard garden pond
A single kitchen sink
A large rainwater barrel
context: A trained medical-alert dog can pick out an odor as dilute as one teaspoon of sugar dissolved in two Olympic-sized swimming pools of water, a comparison from dog-cognition researcher Alexandra Horowitz. Source: Alexandra Horowitz, 'Inside of a Dog'; med.news.am.

question: A shark hunts by sniffing with two nostrils at once, closing on prey from open water. A 2010 study on the smooth dogfish fed each nostril its own stream of squid odor to find out how the shark decides which way to turn. What does it compare between its two nostrils to steer toward the source?
answer: The timing of when the smell reaches each nostril
choices: The timing of when the smell reaches each nostril
How concentrated the smell is at each nostril
The temperature of the water at each nostril
The saltiness of the water on each side
context: Sharks steer toward prey by comparing the timing of when a smell reaches each nostril, turning toward whichever nostril the odor hits first, even when the other senses a stronger concentration. The gap can be as small as a tenth of a second. Legend/landmark study: Gardiner & Atema 2010, Current Biology; whoi.edu. Done on the smooth dogfish (Mustelus canis) with tubes feeding squid odor to each nostril separately.

question: An African elephant sorts scents in astonishing detail, sweeping its trunk over the ground and air. Its edge is written in DNA: it carries the largest known set of smell-receptor genes of any animal, roughly double a dog's. About how many olfactory-receptor genes does it have?
answer: Nearly 2,000
choices: Nearly 2,000
About 400
About 90
Around 25
context: The African elephant has the largest known set of olfactory-receptor genes of any animal, nearly 2,000, more than twice a dog's and about five times a human's, letting it sort scents in astonishing detail with its trunk. Legend/landmark finding: Niimura, Matsui & Touhara 2014, Genome Research. Source: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4158756/.

question: In the rainforest of New Guinea, a small black male bird does a strange dance. He snaps a fan of feathers open around his head into a perfect oval. The glowing blue-green marks look exactly like a floating smiley face. Which bird pulls off this trick?
answer: The superb bird-of-paradise
choices: The superb bird-of-paradise
The greater roadrunner
The Andean cock-of-the-rock
The king vulture
context: The courting male superb bird-of-paradise (Lophorina) snaps his black feather cape and iridescent blue-green breast shield open into a perfect oval that reads as a bright smiley face floating in a void. Source: birdsofparadiseproject.org (New Vogelkop superb bird-of-paradise changes up the old song and dance).  (Legend.)

question: In the mountain rainforests of New Guinea, a male superb bird-of-paradise spreads a dark cape and iridescent chest patch to form a stunning smiley-face oval — a courtship display for a watching female. He bobs and hops in tight circles around her on the forest floor. The whole time, he keeps one part of himself pointed right at her. What does he keep pointed at the female?
answer: His electric-blue breast shield
choices: His electric-blue breast shield
His long tail streamers
His hooked beak
His feathered crest
context: As he bounces around her, the male always keeps his glowing blue-green breast shield squarely aimed at the female, so she sees the full floating face throughout the dance. Source: audubon.org (New bird of paradise slides around sporting a bright blue frown).

question: The courting male superb bird-of-paradise of the New Guinea rainforest flares a bright blue-green face against his velvet-black cape, and that cape is extreme: measured head-on, it reflects back only about 0.05 percent of the light striking it -- one of the darkest surfaces known in all of nature. Why would evolution favor such a deeply black cape?
answer: With almost no light bouncing off it, the eye has nothing to judge the blue face against, so the face reads as a bright shape floating in empty space
choices: With almost no light bouncing off it, the eye has nothing to judge the blue face against, so the face reads as a bright shape floating in empty space
The dark cape soaks up sunlight, keeping the male warm through cold rainforest nights
The blackness hides the male from hawks hunting the canopy above
A wider patch of black makes the male look larger to his rivals
context: The 'super-black' cape absorbs about 99.95 percent of light striking it head-on (reflecting only 0.05-0.31 percent, versus 3-5 percent for an ordinary black feather). With almost no light returning off the cape, the eye has no reference against which to place the blue face, so it appears to float and glow against pure nothingness. Source: McCoy et al. 2018, Nature Communications, 'Structural absorption by barbule microstructures of super black bird of paradise feathers' (PMC5760687).  (Legend.)

question: The super-black cape of the superb bird-of-paradise is darker than the deepest black pigment a bird can make, yet it contains no special dark pigment at all. Researchers found the darkness comes from the shape of the tiny feather barbs. How does that shape trap the light?
answer: The barbs tilt into arrays with deep cavities, so entering light bounces around inside and never escapes
choices: The barbs tilt into arrays with deep cavities, so entering light bounces around inside and never escapes
A layer of black oil coats each feather and soaks up the light
The feathers are packed so densely no light can slip between them
The feathers chemically convert the light into heat
context: The super-black comes from structure, not pigment: the feather barbules bend upward into tilted arrays with deep cavities (200-400 micrometers deep), so light that enters bounces around inside and gets trapped instead of reflecting back out. Source: McCoy et al. 2018, Nature Communications (PMC5760687).

question: The Surinam toad is a flat, brown, wide-headed frog that lives in the muddy, sluggish rivers of the Amazon and the Guianas in South America. It lies still on the river bottom and is famously hard to spot, even in an aquarium where the keeper knows one is in there. How does the Surinam toad stay hidden from prey and predators?
answer: It looks exactly like a dead, rotting leaf lying in the litter
choices: It looks exactly like a dead, rotting leaf lying in the litter
It buries itself completely beneath the mud
It glows faintly to blend into the dim water
It clings to the underside of floating logs
context: The Surinam toad (Pipa pipa) is almost entirely flat, like a mottled brown leaf, with a broad flat triangular head. This leaf-lump shape hides it as a piece of dead leaf litter on the muddy riverbed of warm, murky, slow-moving tropical waters. Source: Wikipedia 'Common Surinam toad' + San Diego Zoo.

question: Most frogs shoot out a long sticky tongue to snap up an insect. The Surinam toad, a flat wide-mouthed frog from the muddy rivers of the Amazon in South America, has no tongue at all. And yet it still catches minnows, shrimp, and worms in open water. When prey drifts close to its huge flat mouth, how does the tongueless toad seize it?
answer: It suddenly expands its throat and vacuums in a rush of water, swallowing the prey whole
choices: It suddenly expands its throat and vacuums in a rush of water, swallowing the prey whole
It fires a jet of sticky mucus to glue the prey and reel it back
It clamps down with rows of tiny needle teeth
It lassoes the prey with its star-tipped fingers
context: The Surinam toad has no tongue and no teeth. Instead of flicking a tongue, it is a suction feeder: it rapidly expands its throat cavity to inhale a rush of water that vacuums prey whole into its large mouth. Source: San Diego Zoo + Wikipedia 'Common Surinam toad'.

question: The Surinam toad is a flat brown frog that hunts along the muddy Amazon river bottoms of South America, where the water is so dark it can barely see its own fingers in front of its face. Its front feet are unusual — each finger ends in a tiny star-shaped tip, which gives the animal its other name, the star-fingered toad. What do those odd little star tips do?
answer: Feel out hidden prey the toad cannot see and guide it to the mouth
choices: Feel out hidden prey the toad cannot see and guide it to the mouth
Anchor the toad firmly against the river current
Sift edible scraps from the mud it takes in
Churn up the riverbed to flush prey out of hiding
context: Each front finger ends in tiny star-shaped tips (four star-like appendages), the source of the alternate name 'star-fingered toad.' These sensory fingertips feel and probe through leaf litter and murky water to detect prey the toad cannot see. Source: San Diego Zoo + Wikipedia 'Common Surinam toad'.

question: A female Surinam toad releases her eggs during mating, and the male presses them onto her back. Over the next day her skin swells and grows up around each egg until they sink in and become sealed inside pockets. Three to four months later, what happens on the mother toad's back?
answer: Dozens of fully-formed baby toads erupt out through her skin and swim away
choices: Dozens of fully-formed baby toads erupt out through her skin and swim away
The eggs loosen and float up to the surface to hatch
Tadpoles wriggle free and cling to her belly to grow
She sheds her whole back skin in one piece with the eggs still attached
context: The mother's back becomes a honeycomb of skin pockets, one egg sealed in each chamber. The young develop entirely inside, skipping the free-swimming tadpole stage and transforming directly into miniature toadlets. After 3-4 months they push and squirm to loosen the skin, the pockets open, and dozens of tiny toads (about 25 mm each) erupt out through her back and swim away. Source: San Diego Zoo + Wikipedia 'Common Surinam toad'.  (Legend.)

question: On a warm tropical reef, a stinging sea anemone waves its tentacles like a poisonous flower. Nesting safely among those tentacles lives a little family of orange-and-white clownfish, five or six of them lined up by size from largest to smallest. They are all related and they never wander far from home. When it comes time to lay eggs, though, the job always falls to one particular member of that pecking order. Which fish lays the eggs?
answer: The biggest fish
choices: The biggest fish
The smallest fish
A middle-sized fish
Whichever one guards the eggs
context: Clownfish (genus Amphiprion) live in a strict size-ranked order inside one anemone: the biggest is the female, the second-biggest the breeding male, and the rest are smaller non-breeders that don't reproduce. Source: Emperor Divers (emperordivers.com/clownfish-male-female); Sequential hermaphroditism, Wikipedia.

question: On a warm damp night in the garden, two common earthworms surface partway from their burrows to mate. They line up belly-to-belly for a long, slippery exchange of sperm, but their soft, slimy bodies have nothing obvious to grip with. How does each worm keep the pair from sliding apart mid-mating?
answer: It drives dozens of tiny bristles into its partner
choices: It drives dozens of tiny bristles into its partner
It wraps its tail tightly around the other
It glues them together with sticky mucus
It bites down on the other worm's skin
context: To keep from slipping apart during the long sperm exchange, each common earthworm (Lumbricus terrestris) drives roughly 30 of its 40 tiny bristle-hairs into its partner, locking the two bodies together belly-to-belly. Source: Science News (sciencenews.org/article/battle-hermaphrodites); Koene & Schulenburg study.

question: A clownfish family lives ranked by size: the single biggest is the egg-laying female, the second-biggest her breeding mate. When that big female dies, what happens to her breeding mate?
answer: He changes into the new egg-laying female
choices: He changes into the new egg-laying female
He fights off the anemone's other fish
He leaves to find a new anemone
He shrinks back to a non-breeder
context: When the female dies, the breeding male changes sex and becomes the new female — a one-way change that cannot reverse. The largest remaining non-breeder then grows into the new breeding male. This male-first switch is called protandry, and clownfish are the classic example. Source: Emperor Divers (emperordivers.com/clownfish-male-female); Sequential hermaphroditism, Wikipedia.  (Legend.)

question: In the Pixar movie Finding Nemo, the little clownfish Nemo ends the story still a small kid fish, safe back home in his sea anemone with his father Marlin. But in real clownfish biology it would not stop there. Clownfish live in ranked groups where only the biggest female breeds. When the mother dies, the breeding male changes sex to become the new female. In that real scenario, what becomes of the tiny non-breeder like Nemo?
answer: He grows into the new breeding male
choices: He grows into the new breeding male
He is driven out of the anemone
He stays a non-breeder for life
He splits off to find his own anemone
context: In real clownfish the death of the female triggers the whole rank to shift up: the breeding male turns female, and the largest remaining non-breeder — Nemo's role — grows into the new breeding male and mates with her. The film's tidy father-and-son ending isn't how the family really works. Source: Emperor Divers (emperordivers.com/clownfish-male-female); Reader's Digest (rd.com/article/scientifically-accurate-finding-nemo).  (Legend.)

question: The common clownfish (Amphiprion ocellaris), the orange-and-white species from Finding Nemo, can switch sex when the top female in its group dies. The change is not just a switch in the ovaries — one particular body part shifts to its new female form within about six months, long before the rest of the body catches up. Which part actually leads the way?
answer: The brain
choices: The brain
The gonads
The skin
The fins
context: The change starts in the brain, not the gonads: the preoptic area grows to female size within about six months while the gonads are still male. Professor Justin Rhodes put it, 'It's got a female brain, but its gonads are male.' Some fish hold that state for over three years before the gonads finish converting. Source: news.scubatravel.co.uk (reporting on Rhodes et al., Univ. of Illinois).  (Legend.)

question: The California sheephead is a big-headed reef fish that patrols the kelp forests off the Pacific coast of North America, from Monterey Bay down to Baja. It lives in a harem — one large male, easy to spot by his bulging forehead and pink flanks, and several smaller mates gathered around him. Every fish in that group was actually born female. When the male dies or vanishes, at four to six years old the dominant female does what?
answer: Turns into the male
choices: Turns into the male
Stops feeding to guard eggs
Splits off to start a new harem
Grows a protective shell
context: The California sheephead, a wrasse, is born a pink female and turns male at about four to six years old, developing a black head and tail with a bright red band across the middle. This female-first switch is called protogyny. If the male dies, a female's ovaries degenerate and sperm develops, completing the switch in as little as five days to two weeks. Source: Catalina Island Marine Institute (cimi.org/blog/sheephead-are-protogynous-hermaphrodies).

question: A drab yellow-brown Caribbean reef wrasse (Thalassoma bifasciatum) starts life as a female. When the dominant one converts to a 'terminal-phase' male, its body turns green with black-and-white bars and its head takes on one bold color — the color that becomes its whole common name. Which color?
answer: Bright blue
choices: Bright blue
Solid black
Pale silver
Deep red
context: The terminal-phase male has a blue head, black-and-white bars, and a green body — the blue head gives the bluehead wrasse (Thalassoma bifasciatum) its name. When the dominant male is removed, a female begins acting male within minutes to hours and completes the full change in only about eight days. Source: Thalassoma bifasciatum, Wikipedia; pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24036013.  (Legend.)

question: Garden snails carry both male and female organs at once. Just before two of them mate, each snail stabs the other with a sharp calcium-carbonate 'love dart.' The dart isn't a weapon of defense — its chemical coating does something that helps the snail that fired it. What?
answer: Boosts its chances of fathering the eggs
choices: Boosts its chances of fathering the eggs
Numbs the partner's stinging cells
Dissolves the other snail's shell
Warns off rival snails nearby
context: The 'love dart' is loaded with chemicals that boost the shooter's chances of fathering the partner's eggs — and both snails are trying to do it to each other. Source: BMC blog (blogs.biomedcentral.com/bmcseriesblog/2016/05/13/love-dart-heart-sexual-conflict-snails).  (Legend.)

question: High in the Andean cloud forests of Ecuador, Colombia, and Peru lives a strange hummingbird. It feeds from long trumpet-shaped Passiflora flowers that most other hummingbirds cannot reach into. To match those deep flowers, one part of the bird's body grew unusually. It holds a world record for that feature that no other bird can match. What is special about the sword-billed hummingbird?
answer: Its bill is longer than the rest of its body
choices: Its bill is longer than the rest of its body
Its wings beat slower than any other bird's
It is the only hummingbird that cannot fly backward
Its heart stops completely every night to save energy
context: The sword-billed hummingbird (Ensifera ensifera) is the only bird in the world whose bill is longer than the rest of its body. The straight, sword-like bill runs 8 to 12 cm on a bird whose body (not counting the tail) is only about 13 to 14 cm long. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sword-billed_hummingbird  (Legend.)

question: High in the Andes cloud forests of South America flies the sword-billed hummingbird, whose slender bill is actually longer than the rest of its body. That bill is so absurdly long that the bird cannot bend it back over its own feathers the way ordinary birds preen themselves with their beaks. So how does this hummingbird keep its plumage clean and tidy?
answer: It scratches itself clean with its feet
choices: It scratches itself clean with its feet
It rubs its back against rough bark
It lets rain and mist wash the feathers
It waits for smaller birds to groom it
context: Because its bill is far too long to reach its own feathers, the sword-billed hummingbird cannot preen with its beak like other birds. Instead it grooms itself using its feet, scratching its plumage clean. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sword-billed_hummingbird  (Legend.)

question: High in the misty cloud forests of the Andes lives a tiny bird called the sword-billed hummingbird. Its whole body weighs only 10 to 15 grams, about as much as three small coins, yet its needle-like bill can stretch more than 10 cm, longer than the rest of the body put together. Carrying that enormous beak is tiring work for such a slim neck. When a sword-billed hummingbird finally lands on a twig to rest, what does it do to ease the strain?
answer: Tilts the bill almost straight up toward the sky
choices: Tilts the bill almost straight up toward the sky
Rests the bill flat along a branch
Tucks the bill under one wing
Props the bill against its own chest
context: When it lands to rest, the sword-bill tilts its heavy bill almost straight up toward the sky, leaning its head back to balance the weight and ease the strain on its neck. A perched sword-bill points its beak at the heavens. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sword-billed_hummingbird  (Legend.)

question: The high Andes cloud forests swarm with dozens of species of hummingbirds all chasing the same sweet nectar, and squabbles over flowers are common. Yet the sword-billed hummingbird, with its outrageously long bill, almost never has to fight a rival for a meal. How does it get its food while sidestepping the crowd of shorter-billed cousins?
answer: It drinks from deep tubular flowers no other bird can empty
choices: It drinks from deep tubular flowers no other bird can empty
It feeds only at dawn, before rival hummingbirds wake
It guards a patch of blossoms, chasing all other birds off
It follows blooming trees uphill as the seasons shift
context: By owning a food source no rival can reach, the sword-bill sidesteps competition entirely. Short-billed hummingbirds simply cannot get at the deep tubular flowers it drains, such as the long trumpet-shaped corolla of Passiflora mixta, so it feeds on nectar unavailable to any other bird. The bird and the flower are a matched pair. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sword-billed_hummingbird ; https://www.zmescience.com/feature-post/natural-sciences/animals/birds/the-sword-billed-hummingbird-long-beak/  (Legend.)

question: In the deserts of the American Southwest lives a big blue-black wasp with bright orange wings and a sting so painful people rank it near the worst on Earth. The females of this wasp do something wild: each one hunts a live animal much bigger than herself, stings it into paralysis, and drags it home as living baby food. What huge creature does this wasp hunt?
answer: Tarantulas
choices: Tarantulas
Scorpions
Centipedes
Praying mantises
context: The tarantula hawk (genus Pepsis) is named for its prey. A female stings a live tarantula, and her venom freezes the spider without killing it, because she needs it alive. Source: Britannica, 'Tarantula hawk'; Discover Wildlife.  (Legend.)

question: A female tarantula hawk wasp finds a tarantula spider, paralyzes it with one sting, drags it back to a burrow, and lays a single egg on its belly before sealing the tomb. The baby wasp grub hatches, burrows into the still-living spider, and slowly eats it from the inside for about three weeks. It carefully saves one group of body parts for last so the spider stays alive and fresh. Which parts does the grub eat last?
answer: The vital organs
choices: The vital organs
The eight legs
The venom glands
The silk spinnerets
context: By saving the vital organs for last, the larva keeps the paralyzed spider alive and fresh as long as possible. The tarantula only dies when the larva finally reaches those organs. Source: Discover Wildlife; Wikipedia, 'Tarantula hawk'.  (Legend.)

question: Entomologist Justin Schmidt built a pain scale by getting stung on purpose. The tarantula hawk earned a near-perfect 4.0 -- 'blinding, fierce, shockingly electric,' like a running hair dryer dropped in your bath. Asked what a person should actually DO when stung, what was Schmidt's blunt advice?
answer: Lie down and scream
choices: Lie down and scream
Run to cold water
Suck out the venom
Hold perfectly still
context: Schmidt rated it 4.0, second only to the bullet ant. The mercy: the excruciating pain fades in about five minutes. Source: Schmidt Sting Pain Index, via Natural History Museum and Britannica.  (Legend.)

question: A tarantula hawk wasp can paralyze a spider several times her own size — a fearsome hunter as a mother. Yet the adult wasp herself never hunts for her own dinner. She is a gentle sipper, and after one heavy meal on fermented juices she can even fly clumsy and drunken through the air. What does the adult wasp actually live on, day to day?
answer: Flower nectar
choices: Flower nectar
Tree sap
Aphid honeydew
Fruit-pulp juice
context: Adults are nectar-drinkers, sipping from milkweed, mesquite, and western soapberry blossoms -- and fermented nectar can leave them tipsy. The spider-hunting is done only by females, and only to feed the young. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tarantula hawk'; BeesWiki.

question: Squeeze the water out of a clump of green moss from an old wall or damp forest floor, catch the drips in a dish, and put them under a microscope. Waddling slowly across the slide on four pairs of stubby little legs comes a tiny eight-legged animal barely a millimeter long. Because of that clumsy waddle, naturalists gave the animal a two-word nickname that stuck. What did they call it?
answer: The water bear
choices: The water bear
The mud minnow
The bark beetle
The sand flea
context: The German naturalist Goeze coined the name 'Kleiner Wasserbaer' (little water bear) in 1773 for the way it lumbers along like a bear. Its other nickname is 'moss piglet.' Source: Wikipedia, Tardigrade.

question: A water bear -- scientists call it a tardigrade -- is a plump eight-legged animal you can find in the wet moss in your own yard. Its whole tiny body is made of only about a thousand cells. About how long is a normal one?
answer: Smaller than a grain of sand
choices: Smaller than a grain of sand
About the size of an ant
About the width of a coin
Longer than a fingernail
context: Most tardigrades are about half a millimetre long, smaller than a grain of sand, built from only about 1,000 cells. Source: Wikipedia, Tardigrade.

question: You do not need special gear or a faraway trip to hunt for water bears — the tiny eight-legged tardigrades that live all around us. Soak just one ordinary clump of the right green plant in tap water for a few hours, squeeze it out, and look at the drops under a microscope. Over two million water bears can pour out of a single square metre of it. What plant should you soak?
answer: Moss
choices: Moss
Seaweed
Grass clippings
Fallen leaves
context: A square metre of moss can hold over 2 million tardigrades. They also live on Himalayan mountaintops, in the deep sea, and across Antarctica. Source: Wikipedia, Tardigrade.

question: A water bear, also called a tardigrade, is a tiny eight-legged animal barely half a millimeter long. It lives in the droplets of water that cling between strands of wet moss and lichen. To something that small, a patch of moss is a tangled jungle of stems, and the water bear does not just waddle through it. It needs to grip and clamber over every strand. What does the far end of each of its eight stubby legs carry, so it can hook and hold on?
answer: A cluster of tiny claws
choices: A cluster of tiny claws
A single suction cup
A sticky pad of glue
A tuft of bristles
context: Each of a tardigrade's eight legs ends in a set of tiny claws, usually four to eight per foot, which it uses to grip and clamber through the moss it lives in. Source: Wikipedia, Tardigrade.

question: A water bear, or tardigrade, is a plump eight-legged animal barely bigger than a grain of sand, and it lives in the wet mosses that grow in your yard. When it goes on the hunt, it clamps onto a plant cell or a tiny rotifer in the moss and settles in to feed. What does it do to get its meal?
answer: Sucks out the juices inside
choices: Sucks out the juices inside
Grinds it into paste
Wraps it in sticky silk
Filters scraps from the water
context: The tardigrade stabs prey with paired stylets made of the hard mineral aragonite, then pumps out the fluids inside. Source: Wikipedia, Tardigrade.

question: When its moss dries to a crisp, a water bear pulls in its legs and shrivels into a lifeless-looking ball called a tun, its metabolism all but stopped. Two of these dried tuns and an egg were once chipped from Antarctic moss that had lain frozen since 1983. After thawing, how long a sleep had they survived?
answer: More than thirty years
choices: More than thirty years
A few weeks
About one winter
Roughly three years
context: Moss frozen at -20 C since 1983 was thawed in 2014; two tardigrades and an egg revived after 30+ years, crawled, ate, and one laid 19 eggs. Source: Tsujimoto et al., Cryobiology 2016. (Legend-tier wonder.)

question: When conditions turn deadly, a tardigrade, the tiny eight-legged water bear that lives between strands of moss, pulls in its legs and dries up into a wrinkled little barrel called a tun. Curled up inside its tun, the water bear can be baked to about 150 C and still wake up when it is soaked in water again. It has also been chilled to a shocking cold in the laboratory and revived. How cold has a water bear been chilled and lived through?
answer: To about -272 C, one degree above absolute zero
choices: To about -272 C, one degree above absolute zero
To about -40 C, a deep winter freeze
To about -90 C, the coldest Antarctic air
To about -180 C, the cold of liquid nitrogen
context: A dried tardigrade has survived roughly -272 C, a single degree above absolute zero, the coldest anything can ever be, and heating to about 149 C. Source: Wikipedia, Tardigrade. (Legend-tier.)

question: Water bears, also called tardigrades, are microscopic eight-legged animals no bigger than a grain of sand. A blast of radiation of about 5,000 gray would sterilise a whole room; just 5 to 10 gray kills a person. But a tardigrade shrugs off that same 5,000-gray dose. Scientists traced the trick to a protein they nicknamed 'damage suppressor.' What does this protein do inside the water bear's cells?
answer: Wraps around its DNA like a shield
choices: Wraps around its DNA like a shield
Rebuilds cells faster than they break
Flushes the radiation out as heat
Turns the radiation into food
context: The protein Dsup ('damage suppressor') shrouds the DNA and soaks up damage; added to human cells in the lab it made them about 40% more resistant to X-rays. Source: MIT News 2025 / Dsup, Wikipedia. (Legend-tier.)

question: In 2007, a European experiment called TARDIS strapped dried water bears to the outside of a satellite. For ten days they faced the raw vacuum of space and its cosmic rays. Back on Earth, what did the survivors go on to do?
answer: Revived and had healthy babies
choices: Revived and had healthy babies
Glowed faintly for weeks
Never moved again
Doubled in size
context: Most survived vacuum plus cosmic radiation and some even survived direct solar UV, making the tardigrade the first animal ever shown to survive open space; revived, they bred normally. Source: Jonsson et al., Current Biology 2008. (Legend-tier.)

question: A tardigrade is a microscopic 'water bear' that lives in moss, hot springs, and the ocean floor. When its puddle dries up, it curls into a barrel shape called a tun and can wait years for water to return. Many other survivors of drying — brine shrimp, some roundworms — pack their cells with the sugar trehalose so nothing collapses without water. But a tardigrade in its tun makes almost none of that sugar. Its cells still pull through unharmed. What does it flood them with instead?
answer: Its own tangled proteins, which set into glass
choices: Its own tangled proteins, which set into glass
Sticky glycerol that clings on to water
Waxy fats that seal each cell from the air
A different sugar it stockpiles in bulk
context: Those proteins are the tardigrade's own CAHS proteins — short for Cytoplasmic Abundant Heat Soluble. While the animal is wet they are 'intrinsically disordered,' floppy and shapeless, but as the water drains away they pass through a glass transition and harden into a glass-like matrix, locking the cell's membranes and enzymes in place so nothing can unfold or clump apart. When Thomas Boothby's team silenced these proteins, the tardigrades lost the ability to survive drying; the purified proteins alone shielded other creatures' enzymes right through desiccation. Brine shrimp and many roundworms lean on the sugar trehalose instead — water bears run mostly on their own protein glass. Source: Boothby et al., 'Tardigrades Use Intrinsically Disordered Proteins to Survive Desiccation,' Molecular Cell 65(6), 16 March 2017.

question: Tardigrades have trundled through the moss since long before the first dinosaurs, so for an animal famous for surviving anything you might expect them strewn all through the rocks. The truth is almost the opposite. How many tardigrade bodies have ever been found as fossils, and how were they preserved?
answer: Barely three, each locked inside amber
choices: Barely three, each locked inside amber
Many thousands, pressed flat in shale
Several hundred, turned to stone in limestone
A few dozen, frozen deep in permafrost
context: In all the world only three unmistakable tardigrade bodies have ever been dug up, and every one was sealed in amber — fossilised tree resin. The two oldest, Milnesium swolenskyi and Beorn leggi, came from Cretaceous amber roughly 72 to 90 million years old, back in the age of the dinosaurs. The third, Paradoryphoribius chronocaribbeus, was described in 2021 from 16-million-year-old Dominican amber; at just 559 micrometres — half a millimetre — it was so tiny it sat unnoticed in a corner of the amber, beside three trapped ants, for months before anyone spotted it. Called a 'once-in-a-generation' find, it let scientists study a fossil tardigrade's mouthparts for the first time. Source: Mapalo et al., Proceedings of the Royal Society B, October 2021.

question: Deep in the rainforests of Borneo, the Philippines, and other Southeast Asian islands lives a tiny nocturnal primate small enough to sit in the palm of a child's hand. It hunts insects, small lizards, and even birds at night, leaping between tree trunks. Its enormous eyeballs are so huge that one eyeball is as big as, or even bigger than, its whole brain. Which small night-hunting animal is this?
answer: The tarsier
choices: The tarsier
The slow loris
The fennec fox
The sugar glider
context: Each tarsier eyeball is about 16 mm across and equals or exceeds the size of its entire brain. No other mammal has eyes so large relative to its body. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarsier  (Legend.)

question: In the rainforests of Southeast Asia lives the tarsier, a palm-sized night-hunting primate with saucer-huge eyes and long clinging fingers. On a dark branch, a tarsier freezes and tracks a moth flitting through the canopy behind it — its perched body never shifting a muscle. To keep the moth in view, just how far can this little hunter crank its head around?
answer: Nearly 180 degrees each way, like an owl
choices: Nearly 180 degrees each way, like an owl
About 90 degrees, a quarter turn to each shoulder
Roughly 45 degrees, a small glance either side
A full 360 degrees in one continuous spin
context: A tarsier's giant eyeballs are locked in their sockets, so it turns its head roughly 180 degrees in either direction, owl-like, giving it a full 360-degree field of view without moving its body. Source: https://www.britannica.com/animal/tarsier  (Legend.)

question: Nearly every primate on Earth, from gorillas to lemurs to chimpanzees, fills its belly with fruit, leaves, and other plants. But deep in the rainforests of the Philippines, Borneo, and Sulawesi lives the palm-sized tarsier — a big-eyed night hunter that clings to tree trunks. Among all primates, the tarsier stands alone for one strange thing about its diet. What sets it apart?
answer: It is the only primate that eats nothing but meat, no plants at all
choices: It is the only primate that eats nothing but meat, no plants at all
It is the only primate that survives entirely on tree sap and gum
It is the only primate that will not drink water, only dew
It is the only primate that eats one single species of fruit
