context: The tarsier is the only entirely carnivorous primate known, eating insects like beetles, cicadas, and grasshoppers, and even snatching lizards, snakes, small birds, and bats. It eats no fruit or leaves at all. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarsier  (Legend.)

question: In the rainforests of the Philippines lives the Philippine tarsier, a palm-sized primate with saucer eyes that hunts insects at night. For years it seemed strangely silent — its mouth would open wide as if to cry out, but no sound reached human ears. In 2012, biologist Marissa Ramsier and her team pointed bat-detector microphones at the little animals and cracked the mystery. What was really happening when a tarsier 'silent-screamed'?
answer: It was calling in ultrasound, around 70 kHz, far above what we can hear
choices: It was calling in ultrasound, around 70 kHz, far above what we can hear
It was yawning as a threat display, not vocalizing at all
It was pushing air through its nose too softly to detect
It was clicking its teeth at a pitch our ears cannot register
context: The Philippine tarsier calls with a dominant pitch near 70 kHz and can hear up to about 91 kHz, far beyond the roughly 20 kHz ceiling of human hearing, so it can 'talk' in a channel we cannot detect. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarsier  (Legend.)

question: In the forests of Tasmania lives a stocky black meat-eater about the size of a dog. It screeches at night and carries its babies in a pouch. It is the biggest meat-eating marsupial left on Earth. What is it?
answer: The Tasmanian devil
choices: The Tasmanian devil
The red kangaroo
The koala
The wombat
context: The Tasmanian devil (Sarcophilus harrisii) is the largest surviving carnivorous marsupial in the world. Kangaroos, koalas, and wombats are all marsupials too, but they are plant-eaters. Source: Wikipedia 'Tasmanian devil' ('largest surviving carnivorous marsupial').

question: A Tasmanian devil is often the last scavenger to reach a dead wallaby, long after the foxes and birds have taken the easy meat and gone. Instead of just nibbling what's left, this dog-sized marsupial does something no bird or fox can. What does it do with the leftover carcass?
answer: It crunches up and swallows the whole thing — bones, fur, and teeth
choices: It crunches up and swallows the whole thing — bones, fur, and teeth
It caches the scraps in a den to eat over several days
It picks out only the rich organs and abandons the rest
It strips the last shreds of muscle and leaves the frame standing
context: Tasmanian devils consume all traces of a carcass, including bones and fur, leaving nothing for other scavengers. Source: Wikipedia 'Tasmanian devil' ('consume all traces of a carcass, including bones and fur').

question: A Tasmanian devil is no bigger than a small dog. But it is one of the noisiest animals alive. Its calls range from a soft cluck while feeding to a full scream during a fight. About how many different sounds does one devil make?
answer: At least eleven different sounds
choices: At least eleven different sounds
Just two — a growl and a scream
Around fifty separate calls
Only one, repeated at different pitches
context: Despite being small, the Tasmanian devil has one of the loudest and most complex voices of any animal, using at least eleven different sound types, from gentle clucking while feeding to screams during a fight. Source: Currumbin Sanctuary; Wikipedia 'Tasmanian devil' (eleven sound types).

question: A mother Tasmanian devil gives birth to 20 to 30 young at once, each no bigger than a grain of rice. But inside her backward-opening pouch there are only four teats to feed them all. What decides which of those newborns actually lives?
answer: Only the first four to crawl into the pouch and grab a teat survive
choices: Only the first four to crawl into the pouch and grab a teat survive
The mother carries the four strongest and abandons the rest outside
The four largest at birth push the smaller ones away from her
She feeds all of them in shifts until the weakest give out
context: A devil bears 20-30 rice-grain-sized young but has only four nipples, so the newborns race to the pouch and only the first four to latch on survive. Source: Wikipedia 'Tasmanian devil' (20-30 young, four nipples); WWF-Australia '8 Fun Facts About Tasmanian Devils'. The rice-grain newborn detail is a widely retold wonder.  (Legend.)

question: Since 1996 a disease has killed roughly 80% of wild Tasmanian devils, and it spreads in a way almost unheard of in nature: it jumps from one devil to the next when they bite each other's faces while feeding and fighting. What kind of disease behaves like that?
answer: A cancer whose living tumor cells pass directly from animal to animal
choices: A cancer whose living tumor cells pass directly from animal to animal
A virus carried in the saliva of infected devils
A bacterial infection picked up from rotting carcasses
A parasite that burrows in through bite wounds
context: Devil Facial Tumour Disease is a transmissible cancer — one of only a tiny handful ever found — in which living tumor cells themselves move between animals through facial bites, unlike a virus or bacterium. Source: Wikipedia 'Devil facial tumour disease'; The Conversation 'Tassie devil facial tumour is a transmissible cancer'; Transmissible Cancer Group, University of Cambridge.  (Legend.)

question: A channel catfish glides along the muddy, silty bottom of an American river where the water is far too dark and cloudy for eyes to be much use. Yet the moment a food pellet drifts against its long whiskers, or even just brushes against its side or belly, the catfish turns and grabs it. It seems to taste the water itself. What lets a channel catfish find its food by touch alone in the dark?
answer: Its whole skin is packed with taste buds
choices: Its whole skin is packed with taste buds
It hears the pellet strike the water
It stuns the pellet with a weak electric jolt
It traps the pellet in a sticky mucus net
context: The channel catfish is essentially a swimming tongue: its entire skin, and especially the barbel 'whiskers,' is coated in taste buds, so it tastes food the moment food brushes any part of its body. Source: AskNature, 'Fish Body Is a Swimming Tongue'; Caprio, 'The taste system of the channel catfish' (Trends in Neurosciences, 1993).

question: A human tongue holds about 10,000 taste buds, all crammed onto the tongue itself. But the channel catfish — a whiskered fish that hunts in muddy North American rivers where seeing is nearly impossible — scatters its taste buds across its whole body. Its skin, flanks, and long chin whiskers can all taste the water at once, turning the fish into a swimming tongue. Roughly how many taste buds does one big channel catfish carry?
answer: About 175,000
choices: About 175,000
About 15,000
About 2,000
About 500
context: A large catfish can carry over 100,000 taste buds — as many as 175,000 — scattered across its whole external body, versus about 10,000 crammed onto the human tongue. It tastes with its skin. Source: LiveScience, 'What Animal Has the Best Sense of Taste?'; Atema 1971 on external taste-bud distribution.

question: A female butterfly lands on a leaf and, before laying a single egg, rapidly taps the leaf with her forelegs — 'tarsal drumming.' Why does she drum the leaf with her feet before egg-laying?
answer: Her feet taste the plant to confirm it is safe for caterpillars
choices: Her feet taste the plant to confirm it is safe for caterpillars
Her feet warm the leaf so eggs will stick
Her feet scrape off rival butterflies' eggs
Her feet drum a signal to attract a mate
context: Butterflies taste with their feet: chemoreceptors on the tarsi let her read the leaf's chemistry by drumming on it, confirming the right, non-toxic host plant before she trusts it with her eggs. Source: ScienceABC, 'Do Butterflies Taste With Their Feet?'; Animals Around The Globe, 'Butterflies Taste With Their Feet.'

question: In the 1950s, the American biologist Vincent Dethier sat down to lunch when a blowfly kept landing on his liverwurst sandwich. Curious, he began touching drops of sugar water to the fly's tiny feet and watching what happened next. His work became a classic on how insects taste. Dethier found that the moment a hungry fly's foot touches sugar, it does one thing instantly and reflexively. What does the fly do?
answer: It unrolls its tongue to drink
choices: It unrolls its tongue to drink
It rubs its front legs together
It buzzes its wings in a burst
It curls its abdomen upward
context: A fly tastes with its feet too. When its foot pads touch sugar, the 'proboscis extension reflex' fires and it unrolls its tongue to feed — the reflex Dethier discovered from a blowfly on his lab-window sandwich. Source: The Wire Science, 'To Know a Fly: Vincent Dethier'; eNeuro on the gustatory system in feeding.

question: An octopus reaches an arm deep into a dark rock crevice it cannot see into and, feeling around, singles out a crab hiding there. In 2020 researchers found how each sucker does this — the suckers carry a special new family of receptors. What can those sucker receptors do?
answer: Taste prey chemicals by touch
choices: Taste prey chemicals by touch
Sense the crab's heartbeat
Detect the crab's body heat
Read faint electric fields
context: LEGEND. Van Giesen et al. (2020, Cell) found 'chemotactile receptors' in octopus suckers tuned to terpenoid chemicals leaking from prey, so the arm feels and tastes at once — the octopus tastes whatever it touches without ever seeing it. Source: van Giesen et al. 2020, Cell; Harvard Gazette, 'Octopus suction cups hold its taste and touch sensors.'

question: A snake flicks its forked tongue, catching scent particles from the air, then pulls it back inside. The tongue does not carry those particles to the nose. Where inside the snake does the flicking tongue deliver its scent load?
answer: To a paired sensor in the roof of its mouth
choices: To a paired sensor in the roof of its mouth
To glands behind its fangs
To sacs deep in its throat
To pits below its eyes
context: A snake 'smells with its mouth': flicking collects scent particles and delivers them to the two-pronged vomeronasal (Jacobson's) organ in the palate. Source: ScienceTimes, 'Snakes Use Their Forked Tongues to Smell'; on the Jacobson's organ.

question: Kurt Schwenk reported in Science in 1994 the real reason a snake's tongue forks rather than ending in a single point. As a snake works along a scent trail, what does the fork let it do that one tip could not?
answer: Sense which side the scent is stronger on, and steer toward it
choices: Sense which side the scent is stronger on, and steer toward it
Smell a wider slice of air in a single flick
Refresh its Jacobson's organ twice as fast
Tell an old, cold trail from a fresh one
context: LEGEND. Schwenk (1994, Science) showed the fork gives the snake a stereo, left-versus-right reading of a scent trail: each tip samples a slightly different spot, so the snake can tell which side the scent is stronger on and steer to follow the trail — smelling in stereo. Source: Schwenk 1994 (Science); UConn Today, 'Smelling in Stereo.'

question: A shark bites down on a seal, and a front tooth snaps off and sinks into the deep. In most animals that gap would be permanent, but the shark simply keeps hunting. Where does its next tooth come from?
answer: A fresh row waiting stacked behind it rotates forward into place
choices: A fresh row waiting stacked behind it rotates forward into place
The broken piece slowly regrows from the same empty socket
A neighboring tooth drifts sideways to fill the open gap
The jaw stays gap-toothed until the whole set is replaced at once
context: A shark's teeth sit in rows stacked like a conveyor belt; when a front tooth breaks off, the one behind rotates forward to replace it, sometimes within a day or two. Source: Scientific American, Sharks Never Run Out of Teeth; sharkcagediving.net.

question: Pull back the lips of a wolf and a cow at the same time and look at their cheek teeth, the big teeth well back inside the jaw. The wolf's cheek teeth are thin, blade-shaped edges that meet like a pair of scissors. The cow's cheek teeth are broad, flat slabs with hard ridges running across the top. From just those cheek teeth, what can you tell about what each animal eats?
answer: The wolf slices meat; the cow grinds tough plants
choices: The wolf slices meat; the cow grinds tough plants
The wolf grinds plants; the cow slices meat
Both slice meat, but the wolf's blades are simply larger
Both grind plants, but the cow's slabs are simply harder
context: A carnivore has bladelike shearing teeth for slicing meat; a herbivore has broad, flat, ridged molars for grinding tough plants. You can read the diet from the shape: a slicer versus a grinder. Source: Britannica, Carnivore (Form and function); Berkeley Morphology of the Vertebrate Skeleton.

question: A pet rat is given a small block of wood, and day after day it gnaws the block down to a pile of splinters. This is not just play or boredom. For a rat, chewing on something hard every day is a matter of survival. If a rat stops gnawing, its own mouth eventually becomes a danger to itself. Why must a rat keep gnawing constantly?
answer: Its front incisors never stop growing and must be worn down
choices: Its front incisors never stop growing and must be worn down
Its molars fall out and gnawing helps new ones erupt
Chewing wood is the only way it can digest hard seeds
Wood shavings are the main source of its drinking water
context: A rodent's front incisors never stop growing; a squirrel's grow about half an inch a month. The animal must gnaw constantly just to keep them in check. Source: Naturally Curious with Mary Holland, Rodent Incisors; ScienceDirect.

question: A great white shark cruises the coast for decades, and every broken or lost tooth is instantly replaced. Add up all the teeth one great white sheds and regrows across its whole life. The total is closer to:
answer: More than twenty thousand
choices: More than twenty thousand
About five hundred
About three thousand
About one million
context: A great white keeps about 300 teeth in five-plus rows and can shed and regrow more than 20,000 (some say up to 30,000) across its lifetime. Source: sharkcagediving.net; A-Z Animals, Great White Shark Teeth.

question: A horse crops grass with its wide biting front teeth and then grinds it up with big flat cheek teeth farther back in the jaw. Between those two sets, along the side of the jaw, is a long bare stretch of gum with no teeth at all. Scientists call it the diastema, and the horse's tongue uses it to shuffle grass sideways to the grinders. In a meat-eating animal like a wolf or lion, what fills that same spot in the jaw instead?
answer: Long stabbing canines for seizing prey
choices: Long stabbing canines for seizing prey
A second row of grinding molars
A bony ridge that anchors the jaw muscle
An extra pair of biting front teeth
context: The toothless gap in a horse or cow is called a diastema, the empty space where a meat-eater's slashing canines would be. The tongue uses that gap to shuffle grass back to the grinding molars. Source: Berkeley Morphology of the Vertebrate Skeleton; BW Equine Vets, Equine Dentistry.

question: A cat's back cheek teeth have no flat grinding surface, and the uppers and lowers never quite meet. Even so, a cat works clean through hide, tendon, and bone. What everyday tool do these teeth work like?
answer: A pair of scissors
choices: A pair of scissors
A hammer driven onto an anvil
A pestle crushing in a bowl
A rasp dragged across a surface
context: These specialized cheek teeth are called carnassials (the upper fourth premolar and lower first molar). Their blade edges slide past each other like scissor blades, shearing meat and cracking bone. Cats, wolves, and hyenas have them. Source: Wikipedia, Carnassial; Britannica.

question: An elephant chews rough vegetation all day, and each grinding molar can be a foot long and weigh about eleven pounds. Rather than losing a tooth here and there, how does an elephant's jaw handle the constant wear?
answer: Worn molars ride forward and crumble off the front as new ones push in from behind
choices: Worn molars ride forward and crumble off the front as new ones push in from behind
A single molar keeps growing taller from its root all life long
The elephant swallows worn teeth and grows softer replacements
Both jaws rotate the same four molars end over end to spread the wear
context: An elephant carries only four huge molars at a time, riding forward on a conveyor belt: worn ones crumble off the front in wafer-like sheets as new ones push in from the back. Source: globalelephants.org, EleFact Friday: Elephant Molars are Unique.

question: A rodent's incisor grows without stop, so what happens if it can never grind against an opposing tooth? One documented woodchuck showed the grim answer. Its unchecked upper incisor kept curving until it:
answer: Grew up through the roof of its mouth into its own brain
choices: Grew up through the roof of its mouth into its own brain
Locked its jaw permanently shut so it could not eat
Split down the middle and fell harmlessly out
Curled outward into a useless spiral past its lips
context: If a rodent can't gnaw, the tooth keeps growing in a curve until it spirals into the animal's own skull. A woodchuck's upper incisor once grew through its palate and into its brain, killing it. Source: Naturally Curious with Mary Holland, Rodent Incisors (documented case).  (Legend.)

question: During the last Ice Age, the saber-toothed cat Smilodon prowled the grasslands and tar pits of the Americas, ambushing bison, camels, and giant ground sloths. Its upper canines were curved blades that grew up to about eight inches long, longer than a kitchen knife. But those famous fangs were surprisingly fragile and would snap if they hit bone the wrong way. They were not built for crunching. What were Smilodon's saber fangs actually built to do?
answer: Deliver one precise stab to the throat of pinned prey
choices: Deliver one precise stab to the throat of pinned prey
Rake and slash at fleeing prey on the run
Dig burrowing animals out of packed earth
Lock with a rival male's fangs in mating duels
context: Smilodon's upper canines grew up to about 8 inches (roughly 11 in the biggest), used not for crunching but for a single precise stab to a pinned prey's throat, like an assassin's stiletto rather than a chewing tool. Source: Britannica, Sabre-toothed cat; Smithsonian Magazine.  (Legend.)

question: An elephant gets a fixed number of molar sets, and when the last one wears smooth around its forties, it can no longer grind plants and slowly starves. Because of this, how many sets does one elephant get in its whole life?
answer: Six sets, and no more
choices: Six sets, and no more
A new set every single year
Two sets, like most mammals
An unlimited supply for as long as it lives
context: An elephant gets only six sets of molars in its whole life; the last erupt around its early 40s. When that final set wears smooth, the elephant can no longer grind plants and slowly starves. Its own teeth are its life clock. Source: globalelephants.org; Save the Elephants.  (Legend.)

question: Along the rivers and streams of North America, a beaver spends its whole life gnawing down hardwood trees, felling trunks as thick as a person's leg to build its dams and lodges. Its four orange chisel-shaped front teeth, called incisors, take a beating every single day for years, yet they stay razor-sharp and never need a whetstone. The secret is not new growth alone but the way the tooth itself is built. How does the simple act of gnawing keep the beaver's front teeth sharp?
answer: Hard enamel coats the front and softer dentine the back, so wear leaves a chisel edge
choices: Hard enamel coats the front and softer dentine the back, so wear leaves a chisel edge
A wax coating slides down the tooth and re-hones it each night
New enamel grows only along the cutting edge as the tip wears
The two front teeth grind against each other like a strop
context: A rodent's incisor sharpens itself: the front face is hard enamel and the back is softer dentine, so gnawing wears the back away faster and leaves a chisel edge, like a self-honing knife. Source: Naturally Curious with Mary Holland; ACS PressPac.

question: The front of a beaver's or rat's incisor is a striking rusty orange, not white like ours. Recent chemistry credits that face's hardness and acid resistance to one added ingredient worked into the enamel. What is it?
answer: Iron, worked into the enamel
choices: Iron, worked into the enamel
Fluoride, absorbed from river water
Silica, ground in from chewing sand
Calcium, layered on far thicker than normal
context: The orange front is iron-toughened enamel; the iron makes it hard and acid-resistant so the tooth can gnaw wood without wearing to a nub. 2024 research found the iron gives the strength, while the orange color likely comes from amino acids in the enamel, not the iron itself. Source: American Chemical Society PressPac, April 2024; Chemistry World.

question: The saber-tooth cat Smilodon carried eight-inch upper canines, so you would expect a crushing bite behind them. Instead, biomechanical models put its jaw force at only about a third of a lion's, feeble for a cat its size. With such a weak jaw, how did it force those long blades deep into pinned prey?
answer: Powerful neck muscles hauled its skull down to sink them in
choices: Powerful neck muscles hauled its skull down to sink them in
The full weight of its pouncing body dropped onto the fangs
A fast side-to-side sawing of its whole head worked them in
The prey drove itself onto the fixed fangs as it thrashed
context: Its sabers looked built for a monstrous bite, but the opposite was true. Biomechanical modeling estimates a canine bite force around 1,283 N, roughly a third of a modern lion's and close to the much smaller jaguar. So Smilodon used a 'canine shear-bite': the forelimbs pinned the prey motionless first, then the massive neck muscles pulled the skull downward to drive the blades home, doing the work the jaw could not. The killing power came from the neck, not the jaw. Source: Wikipedia 'Smilodon' (bite force ~1/3 of a lion, ~1,283.74 N at the canine; 'canine shear-bite' via neck flexion / skull rotation), from biomechanical modeling by Wroe et al. 2007/2008, corroborated by a 2018 comparative skull study.

question: Cow molars grind hard, and elephants' do too. But the best grinding teeth ever belonged to a duck-billed dinosaur like Edmontosaurus. Hundreds of its teeth were cemented into one slab called a dental battery. Each tooth wove six kinds of tissue, where a horse molar uses four. As it chewed gritty plants year after year, what did the wear keep doing to the grinding surface?
answer: It kept re-cutting fresh, self-sharpening ridges
choices: It kept re-cutting fresh, self-sharpening ridges
It wore the surface flat and glassy, like a tile
It cracked and pitted the surface under the grit
It buffed the surface smoother and harder each bite
context: Duck-billed dinosaurs had the most sophisticated grinding teeth ever evolved. Each tooth was built from six distinct dental tissues, versus four in a horse or bison molar and just two in most other dinosaurs. Because those six tissues wore away at different rates, ordinary chewing constantly re-carved fresh ridges and hollows into the surface, so the teeth kept sharpening themselves as they wore. Source: Erickson, Krick, Hamilton, Bourne, Norell, Lilleodden et al., 'Complex Dental Structure and Wear Biomechanics in Hadrosaurid Dinosaurs,' Science 2012;338:98-101 (six tissue types vs four in mammals, two in most dinosaurs), corroborated by a 2017 Scientific Reports dynamic-dental-battery histology study.  (Legend.)

question: Long before saber-toothed cats and dire wolves arrived, ice-age South America had almost no large mammal hunters at all. The top predator of big prey on foot was not a mammal. It was a huge flightless bird nearly 10 feet tall, with powerful running legs, a massive hooked beak, and tiny useless wings. Fossils of it have been dug up all across the pampas of Argentina. What are these vanished giant hunter-birds called?
answer: a terror bird
choices: a terror bird
a thunderbird
a war eagle
a dread crane
context: The 'terror birds' (phorusrhacids) stood up to about 3 meters (nearly 10 feet) tall and reigned as the top land predators of South America for millions of years, long before and into the ice age. Source: Wikipedia, Phorusrhacidae (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phorusrhacidae).  (Legend.)

question: In ice-age South America the top hunter on foot was the terror bird, a 10-foot flightless predator with a huge hooked beak and long powerful running legs. When a terror bird caught up with a smaller mammal, it did not clamp on and thrash the prey back and forth the way a lion or a wolf does. It killed with the beak in a very different way. Instead of biting and shaking, how did the terror bird actually use that massive hooked beak?
answer: it struck straight down like a swinging pickaxe
choices: it struck straight down like a swinging pickaxe
it clamped shut and dragged prey underwater
it sprayed venom through a groove in the tip
it filtered small prey from mud like a spoon
context: Its most fearsome weapon was a huge hatchet-shaped beak with a hooked tip; instead of biting and shaking, it struck straight DOWN at prey like swinging a pickaxe to break the neck or skull. Source: PMC 2923598, Mechanical Analysis of Feeding Behavior in Andalgalornis (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2923598/).  (Legend.)

question: The terror bird was a towering predator of ice-age South America, standing nearly 10 feet tall on long, muscular running legs and armed with an enormous hooked beak. Its whole body was built for chasing prey across open pampas on foot, not for taking to the air the way an eagle or a hawk does. So what were the wings of a terror bird actually like?
answer: tiny and nearly useless
choices: tiny and nearly useless
large and clawed for grappling
tucked spurs it used to slash
paddle-shaped for pushing through brush
context: Terror birds had almost useless tiny wings but long, powerful running legs, and were built to chase prey down on foot rather than fly. Source: Wikipedia, Phorusrhacidae (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phorusrhacidae).

question: In 2006, in the fossil-rich cliffs of Patagonia in southern Argentina, someone unearthed the biggest bird skull ever found — a 28-inch skull of Kelenken, an extinct 'terror bird' that stood about 10 feet tall and hunted mammals across ancient South America. The finder was no seasoned professor. Who was Guillermo Aguirre-Zabala?
answer: a high-school student
choices: a high-school student
a retired sea captain
a museum night guard
a visiting oil surveyor
context: The largest terror bird skull known belongs to Kelenken, found in Patagonia in 2006 by high-school student Guillermo Aguirre-Zabala; at about 71 cm (28 inches) it is the biggest bird skull known, with a hooked beak roughly 46 cm long. Source: Wikipedia, Kelenken (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelenken).  (Legend.)

question: Terror birds were huge extinct flightless predators of South America — some stood 10 feet tall with hooked beaks the size of a horse's head. Scientists put a fossil terror bird's fused, rigid skull through a computer stress test to see how it handled the forces of hunting. The skull held up beautifully under some attacks, but one kind of head motion would have risked snapping it in two. Which motion was the skull's weak point?
answer: twisting prey side to side
choices: twisting prey side to side
a hard downward blow
a forward jab at prey
a straight backward pull
context: Finite element analysis showed the skull was strong for straight downward strikes but weak against side-to-side twisting, so the bird could NOT thrash prey like a mammal; its skull bones were fused rigid (loss of cranial kinesis), turning the head into a solid pickaxe built to survive a hard downward blow. Source: PMC 2923598, Mechanical Analysis of Feeding Behavior in Andalgalornis steulleti (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2923598/).

question: In 2024, a single fossil shin bone from Colombia revealed a terror bird that may be the largest ever found -- an apex hunter from twelve million years ago. Yet that same bone is scarred with deep bite marks, showing that even this ultimate land predator became prey itself. Whose bite left the marks?
answer: a giant caiman as long as a bus
choices: a giant caiman as long as a bus
a saber-toothed marsupial as big as a bear
a pack of wolf-sized marsupial hunters
a rival terror bird ten feet tall
context: This is the 2024 La Venta discovery from Colombia's Tatacoa Desert (Degrange et al., Papers in Palaeontology). The bird -- the northernmost terror bird known and possibly the biggest, roughly 5-20% larger than any before it -- survives as a single left shin bone (tibiotarsus) about 12 million years old. The bite marks on it match Purussaurus, an extinct caiman that grew to about 10 m (30 ft), longer than a school bus. So even the age's ultimate land hunter could be dragged down by a colossal crocodilian at the water's edge. Source: Degrange et al. 2024, Papers in Palaeontology 10(6):e1601, DOI 10.1002/spp2.1601; reported by Sci.News and Johns Hopkins Medicine, November 2024.

question: The most complete terror bird skeleton ever found preserved even the fragile, coiled bones deep inside its ear. When researchers ran CT scans through that ear, its shape revealed the kind of sound this hunter was tuned to catch. What was its hearing built for?
answer: deep, low sounds that carry for miles, like an elephant
choices: deep, low sounds that carry for miles, like an elephant
faint, high squeaks up close, like an owl hunting mice
its own echoes bouncing back, like a cave-nesting bird
a wide band of chirps and trills, like a songbird
context: This is Llallawavis scagliai, described in 2015 from Argentina -- about 95% complete, the finest terror bird fossil known (Degrange et al., Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology). CT scans of its inner ear showed its hearing was tuned unusually low for a bird, with mean sensitivity around 2,300 Hz, below the average for living birds. Low-pitched sound fades slowly and travels far, so the bird could likely hear prey moving out of sight -- footsteps in the grass -- and probably answered with its own deep, booming calls over long distances. Source: Degrange et al. 2015, Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology; reported via National Geographic ('The Call of the Terror Bird') and the Florida Museum (FLMNH) fossil-project research page.

question: A tide pool is full of no-backbone animals. A little crab scuttles across the rocks on legs that each bend at a joint like a knee, its whole body wrapped in a hard shell on the OUTSIDE. Which big invertebrate group does the crab belong to?
answer: Arthropods
choices: Arthropods
Cnidarians
Echinoderms
Sponges
context: Jointed legs plus a hard external skeleton (an exoskeleton made of chitin) is the give-away trait of the arthropods — insects, spiders, scorpions, crabs, lobsters, centipedes and millipedes all share this one body plan. Source: https://www.britannica.com/animal/arthropod

question: A see-through bell drifts through the sea trailing tentacles. Any small fish that brushes them gets zapped and paralyzed. Jellyfish, corals, and sea anemones all fight with these stinging cells. Which big invertebrate group is this?
answer: Cnidarians
choices: Cnidarians
Arthropods
Annelids
Mollusks
context: Cnidarians are the stingers: they carry stinging cells (cnidocytes holding harpoon-like nematocysts), have radial bodies, and a single opening that serves as both mouth and anus. Jellyfish, corals, and sea anemones are all cnidarians. Source: https://www.britannica.com/animal/cnidarian

question: You flip over a starfish on the rocks and see its body is built like a wheel — five identical arms spoking out from the center, no left or right, no front or back. Sea urchins and sea cucumbers are built the same way. Which big group is this?
answer: Echinoderms
choices: Echinoderms
Cnidarians
Arthropods
Sponges
context: Echinoderms are built on five-fold (pentaradial) symmetry and move on hundreds of tiny tube feet powered by a water-vascular system. Starfish, sea urchins, and sea cucumbers are echinoderms. Source: https://www.britannica.com/animal/echinoderm

question: Take every animal on Earth, every insect and worm and jellyfish and snail and fish and bird and mammal, and sort them all by body plan into a handful of big groups called phyla. One of those groups turns out to be so enormous that it holds more species than all the other animal groups on the planet put together. About four out of every five known animal species belong to it. Which group is that big?
answer: Arthropods
choices: Arthropods
Mollusks
Cnidarians
Annelids
context: Arthropods are the biggest animal group by far: roughly 80–84% of all known animal species are arthropods (insects, spiders, crabs). Source: https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/anatomy-and-physiology/arthropods

question: An earthworm's body is one long tube divided into a row of little repeating rings, each ring a segment stacked on the next. Leeches share this ringed, segmented plan. Which big invertebrate group does the earthworm belong to?
answer: Annelids
choices: Annelids
Echinoderms
Cnidarians
Arthropods
context: Annelids are the segmented (ringed) worms: their bodies are divided into repeating segments by transverse rings, and most bear tiny bristles called setae. Earthworms and leeches are annelids. Source: https://www.britannica.com/animal/annelid

question: A garden snail creeping across a wet leaf has no bones at all inside its soft body, not even a tiny one, yet it hauls around a hard spiral shell that it grew itself. Snails belong to a group of animals called mollusks, which also includes clams, oysters, and octopuses. Without any inner skeleton to build from, how does a snail actually manufacture that hard shell on its back?
answer: A sheet of tissue over its body lays down shell material layer by layer
choices: A sheet of tissue over its body lays down shell material layer by layer
Tiny bristles along its foot weave the shell like a basket
It hardens a patch of its skin into bone from the inside out
It glues sand grains together with slime into a crust
context: Mollusks have a soft body, often a shell, and a muscular 'foot' plus a tissue fold called the mantle that secretes the shell layer by layer. Snails, clams, and octopuses are all mollusks. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mollusca

question: On a coral reef, you brush against a bright, blob-like sponge and find a strange kind of animal. A sponge has no head, no gut, no nerves, and no muscles. Of all the big animal groups, it alone never forms true tissues or organs. It is really just a loose colony of cells strung together, filtering seawater that flows through its holes. Which big invertebrate group does this simple reef dweller belong to?
answer: Sponges
choices: Sponges
Cnidarians
Annelids
Echinoderms
context: Sponges (Porifera, 'pore-bearers') are the simplest animals: no true tissues, no organs — just a body full of pores. Collar cells (choanocytes) beat tiny whips to pump water through and strain out food. Source: https://shapeoflife.org/phylum-porifera

question: Hold two long, damp worms in your hand — an earthworm from the garden and a leech from a pond. Both have ringed, segmented bodies, so you can tell them apart just by counting rings. A common earthworm has well over a hundred body segments, sometimes 150 or more. A leech, no matter how big or small, always stops at the exact same tidy number. How many segments does every leech have?
answer: 34 segments
choices: 34 segments
12 segments
100 segments
6 segments
context: Segment-counting sorts the worms: an earthworm has over a hundred segments (8 tiny bristles each), while every leech has exactly 34 segments and no bristles at all. Source: https://www.britannica.com/animal/annelid/Form-and-function

question: An octopus is a genius hunter — big-brained, jet-propelled, with eight grabbing arms tipped in suction cups. A garden snail is nothing like that: it creeps along on a slimy foot, hauling a coiled shell on its back. They look nothing alike, yet biologists file them in the very same enormous invertebrate group, together with clams, oysters, and slugs. Which group's soft body plan do all these creatures secretly share?
answer: Mollusks
choices: Mollusks
Cnidarians
Arthropods
Echinoderms
context: An octopus and a snail are cousins — both mollusks. The snail's muscular foot creeps along rocks; in the octopus that same 'foot' is divided into the arms that catch prey. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mollusca  (Legend.)

question: An arthropod's shell is like a suit of armor: hard as bone and unable to stretch as the animal grows. So a crab that wants to get bigger must literally haul itself out of the very armor protecting it and leave the empty old shell behind — a risky maneuver biologists call molting. In the hours right after a crab wriggles free of its old shell, what state is the crab in?
answer: Its new shell is soft and pale, leaving it briefly defenseless
choices: Its new shell is soft and pale, leaving it briefly defenseless
Its new shell is already rock-hard and battle-ready
It has no shell for weeks until a new one grows
It borrows an empty shell from another animal
context: Because the hard shell can't stretch, the animal climbs out of its old exoskeleton to grow — shedding called molting (ecdysis). Right after, the new shell is soft and pale, leaving the animal briefly defenseless until it hardens. Source: https://www.britannica.com/science/ecdysis

question: A grown starfish sitting on the seafloor is a five-armed wheel with no front and no back — you can turn it any way and it still looks the same. But its tiny drifting larva, floating in the plankton before it settles down, is built on a completely different kind of symmetry, one it will abandon and reorganize away from as it becomes the adult wheel. What kind of symmetry does an echinoderm larva start life with?
answer: Bilateral
choices: Bilateral
Five-fold (pentaradial)
No symmetry at all
Radial
context: Echinoderm larvae start out with bilateral (mirror-image) symmetry — a distinct left, right, front and back — and only become five-fold as adults. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Echinoderm

question: An octopus is a mollusk, the same broad group of soft-bodied animals as snails and clams, but its inner plumbing is far stranger than either of its cousins. It does not have one heart pumping its blood but three. Two of those hearts push blood through the gills, and a third pushes the returning blood around the rest of the body. Its blood does not carry oxygen on iron the way human blood does, but on a metal called copper. Because of that copper, when an octopus bleeds, what color is its blood?
answer: Blue
choices: Blue
Red
Green
Clear
context: An octopus has three hearts and blue blood: its blood uses copper-based hemocyanin, not iron-based hemoglobin, so it runs blue. The central heart even stops when it swims, which is why octopuses prefer to crawl. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/ten-wild-facts-about-octopuses  (Legend.)

question: A hungry starfish humps over a clam sitting on the tide-pool floor. The clam has slammed its two heavy shells shut so tightly that no jaw, no beak, and no claw could ever pry it open. The starfish just clings to the top and pulls, very slowly, for hours. Then, all at once, the clam is an empty shell — and the starfish never cracked the shells apart. How did the starfish eat the meat sealed inside?
answer: It pushed its stomach out through the gap and digested the clam outside its body
choices: It pushed its stomach out through the gap and digested the clam outside its body
It injected a venom that dissolved the clam from within
It swallowed the clam whole and crushed the shell in its gut
It drilled a hidden hole and sucked the meat out
context: A starfish pushes its cardiac stomach out through its own mouth, slips it into the gap between a clam's shells, digests the animal outside its body, then slurps the liquefied meal back in. Source: https://ocean.si.edu/ocean-life/invertebrates/sea-stars-urchins-and-relatives  (Legend.)

question: In 1907 the biologist H.V. Wilson pushed a whole living sponge through a fine mesh, mashing it into a soup of separate loose cells — a fate that would kill almost any animal. Because a sponge has no true tissues binding its cells, what did those scattered cells then do?
answer: Crawled back together and rebuilt the sponge
choices: Crawled back together and rebuilt the sponge
Died apart as separated single cells
Grew into many tiny new sponges
Turned into free-swimming larvae
context: In H.V. Wilson's 1907 experiment the cells crawled back together and rebuilt themselves into a working sponge — possible because a sponge's cells are loners with no true tissues. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Van_Peters_Wilson  (Legend.)

question: Around 1950, scientists worked out how a nerve fires — sodium ions rushing in, then potassium flowing back out. They did it by threading fine wires down a single giant nerve fiber up to a thousand times thicker than one of ours. Which animal held that giant fiber?
answer: A squid
choices: A squid
A frog
A cat
An octopus
context: That fat fiber is the squid's 'giant axon' — a single nerve up to about a millimeter across, roughly a thousand times wider than a human nerve fiber, which fires the squid's escape jet. Because it was big enough to poke electrodes into, Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley used it in the late 1940s and early 1950s to show exactly how a nerve impulse works: a fast inward rush of sodium ions followed by an outward flow of potassium. That squid work won the 1963 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine and underpins essentially all of modern neuroscience — how your own brain sends its signals was first cracked open in a mollusk. Source: NobelPrize.org, 1963 Physiology or Medicine, 'Speed read: Signal to charge' (https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1963/speedread/); The Physiological Society, 'Hodgkin and Huxley's modelling of the action potential' (https://www.physoc.org/about-us/history-archives/historicalhighlights/hodgkin-and-huxleys-modelling-of-the-action-potential/).  (Legend.)

question: In a developing embryo, the very first opening usually becomes the mouth. In one small camp of animals it becomes the OTHER end — the anus — and the mouth forms only later, the same back-to-front way your own body was built. Which of these tide-pool animals develops that way too, making it a closer developmental cousin to you than the rest?
answer: A sea urchin
choices: A sea urchin
A giant octopus
A horseshoe crab
A blue mussel
context: Biologists split most animals into two great camps by this embryo tell. Protostomes ('mouth first') build the mouth from the embryo's first opening — arthropods (insects, crabs, horseshoe crabs), mollusks like the octopus, mussel, and snail, and segmented worms all belong here. Deuterostomes ('mouth second') form the anus first and the mouth later; the echinoderms — sea urchins, sea stars, and their kin — sit in this camp right alongside the chordates, the group that includes fish, frogs, and us. So the spiny sea urchin in a tide pool is a closer developmental cousin to you than the sharp-eyed octopus beside it — even though the octopus carries the big brain and the urchin has none. (Frontier note: the protostome/deuterostome split itself is textbook-solid, but a 2021 genomic study questioned exactly how tight the echinoderm-chordate grouping is, so the finest branching is still being worked out.) Source: OpenStax Biology 2e, 'Superphylum Deuterostomia' (https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/28-7-superphylum-deuterostomia); UCL News, 'Are we more closely related to starfish or insects?' 2021 (https://www.ucl.ac.uk/news/2021/mar/analysis-are-we-more-closely-related-starfish-or-insects).  (Legend.)

question: Out on the open savanna of Africa, a slender spotted cat with a small round head spots a gazelle at the edge of the herd. It drops low in the tall grass, creeps forward, and then explodes into a sprint that is a blur of legs and dust, faster than any other animal that runs on land. Which spotted African cat is the fastest land animal on Earth?
answer: The cheetah
choices: The cheetah
The leopard
The lion
The jaguar
context: The cheetah (Acinonyx jubatus) is the fastest land animal, hitting about 100-120 km/h (roughly 70-75 mph). No other land animal comes close in a flat-out sprint. Source: Britannica, How Fast Are Cheetahs; SeaWorld cheetah adaptations.  (Legend.)

question: On the wide dry plains of Africa lives an enormous flightless bird taller than a grown man, with a long bare neck and two very long, powerful legs. When something spooks it, the bird bursts into a sprint that can hit about 70 kilometers per hour, roughly 43 miles per hour, faster than any other creature that runs on two legs. Which African bird is the fastest two-legged runner on Earth?
answer: The ostrich
choices: The ostrich
The emu
The flamingo
The pelican
context: The common ostrich (Struthio camelus) is the fastest two-legged runner, cruising near 55 km/h and sprinting to 70 km/h with strides up to 5 meters. Its foot has just TWO toes, the big one tipped with a hoof-like claw for grip. Source: Common ostrich, Wikipedia; Biology Insights, How Fast Is an Ostrich.

question: Of every dog breed you would meet on a leash — poodles, retrievers, sheepdogs, huskies — one is built for pure speed. It has long legs, a deep chest, and a whip-thin body. Trainers have clocked one running close to 45 miles per hour on the track, faster than any other dog on Earth. Which breed holds the canine speed record?
answer: The greyhound
choices: The greyhound
The Doberman
The Dalmatian
The husky
context: The greyhound is the domestic echo of the cheetah's build: it runs the same double-suspension gallop, with two airborne phases per stride, powered by a flexible spine and a disproportionately large heart. Source: Greyhound, Wikipedia; RevealingPaws, Double Suspension Gallop.

question: A cheetah sprinting across the African plains has the longest, bendiest spine of any big cat. On every single stride, that spine coils up like a drawn bow and then springs open, hurling the cheetah's shoulders far forward through the air. In one leap the cat crosses a shocking amount of ground before its paws touch down again. About how far does a single cheetah bound cover?
answer: 6-7 meters (about 21-23 feet)
choices: 6-7 meters (about 21-23 feet)
1-2 meters (about 3-6 feet)
10-12 meters (about 33-39 feet)
Just under 1 meter (about 2 feet)
context: The cheetah's spring-spine throws the shoulder blades so far forward that a single bound covers 6-7 meters, roughly the length of a small car and a half. Source: SeaWorld cheetah adaptations; Cheetah Conservation Fund.

question: A cheetah in full sprint uses its long, springy backbone like a giant steel coil. As the cat runs down a gazelle across the African savanna, the spine bunches up and then snaps straight again, flinging the whole body forward. In the middle of that drive, something happens to the cheetah's feet that almost no other running animal on Earth manages, and it happens twice on every single stride. What is it that its feet do?
answer: All four paws leave the ground at once
choices: All four paws leave the ground at once
One paw always stays planted
Only the front paws touch down
The paws never fully leave the ground
context: This is the double-suspension gallop: once with the legs stretched fully out and once with them bunched under the body, all four paws are airborne twice per stride. The greyhound is the only common animal that runs the same way. Source: Cheetah Conservation Fund; Biology Insights, How Can a Cheetah Run So Fast.

question: A cheetah chasing a gazelle across the African plains can carve a razor-sharp corner at full sprint without ever tumbling head over heels. The secret is the long, heavy tail streaming out behind it, which the cat uses much the way a tightrope walker uses a balancing pole. As a cheetah swerves hard to one side to follow its prey, what does that long tail do to keep the cat from flipping?
answer: Counter-swings to throw its weight the other way
choices: Counter-swings to throw its weight the other way
Coils tight around a back leg
Digs into the ground like an anchor
Beats up and down like a wing
context: The cheetah's tail works like a boat's rudder: it counter-swings side to side, throwing the cat's weight opposite the turn so the animal keeps its balance through a sharp cut. Source: SeaWorld cheetah adaptations; Cheetah Conservation Fund.

question: A cheetah can crouch perfectly still in the grass, then explode into a full sprint faster off the line than most supercars. In just a few strides it hits its top running speed of roughly 70 mph — quicker than most Ferraris can reach 60. About how long does it take a cheetah, starting from a standstill, to reach that 70 mph top speed?
answer: About 3 seconds
choices: About 3 seconds
About 15 seconds
About half a second
About 30 seconds
context: A cheetah reaches its top speed of about 70 mph in only around three seconds, out-accelerating most supercars off the line. That explosive launch is what its whole race-engine body is built for. Source: Britannica, How Fast Are Cheetahs; SeaWorld cheetah adaptations.

question: In 2012, an 11-year-old cheetah named Sarah at the Cincinnati Zoo was clocked on a certified 100-meter track built just for her. She tore down the lane at 61 mph and finished so fast that Usain Bolt's 9.58-second human world record looked slow by comparison. What was Sarah the cheetah's time for the 100-meter dash?
answer: 5.95 seconds
choices: 5.95 seconds
8.10 seconds
3.20 seconds
9.40 seconds
context: Sarah ran the fastest 100 meters ever recorded by anything on Earth: 5.95 seconds, more than three and a half seconds quicker than Usain Bolt's human world record. Source: National Geographic 2012, Cheetah Breaks Speed Record.  (Legend.)

question: The pronghorn of the American West runs far faster than any hunter alive today needs it to. Biologist John Byers thinks it got that speed to escape the American cheetah, which died out about 10,000 years ago. He gave that vanished hunter a haunting nickname. What did Byers call it?
answer: The ghost of predators past
choices: The ghost of predators past
The king of the old plains
The shadow on the mountain
The last of the fast cats
context: Byers calls the extinct American cheetah 'the ghost of predators past': it vanished roughly 10,000 years ago, but the pronghorn still runs full-tilt from it. Source: John A. Byers, Built for Speed / American Pronghorn; National Geographic, Did False Cheetahs Give Pronghorn a Need for Speed?  (Legend.)

question: An ostrich sprints about twice as fast as a person yet burns only about half the energy per step, a bargain no human runner can match. When biologists compared ostrich and human running, they found what makes it so fast and so cheap at once. What is it?
answer: Long tendons that recoil like springs each stride
choices: Long tendons that recoil like springs each stride
Oversized lungs that flood the muscles with oxygen
Hollow bird bones that lighten every single step
Two clawed toes that grip the ground like cleats
context: Studies led by Jonas Rubenson (around 2010-2011) compared mass-matched ostriches and humans and found the ostrich stores and returns roughly DOUBLE the elastic strain energy per step that a person does. Long tendons running down the leg and foot stretch as the foot lands and snap back on push-off, recycling much of each stride's energy instead of burning it in muscle, a biological pogo stick. The payoff: an ostrich runs about twice as fast as a human while spending only about half the metabolic energy. Source: Rubenson et al., 'Adaptations for economical bipedal running,' J. R. Soc. Interface / PMC3061092 (2011); phys.org, 'Ostriches run fast because of springy tendons' (2010).

question: The pronghorn's absurd speed was forged running from a long-legged, short-faced Ice Age sprinter of the American plains, nicknamed the 'American cheetah' (Miracinonyx) and extinct for about 10,000 years. Its cheetah-like build made its family seem obvious, until ancient DNA pinned its true closest living relative. Which cat is it?
answer: The mountain lion
choices: The mountain lion
The African cheetah
The American jaguar
The Eurasian lynx
context: A 2005 study reading mitochondrial DNA from Miracinonyx fossils, backed by a fresh look at its bones, placed it firmly inside the Puma lineage, closer to today's mountain lion (cougar) than to the Old World cheetah (Acinonyx). Its long legs and shortened, flattened face were not inherited from a cheetah at all but evolved independently, a textbook case of convergent evolution: two different cats invented the same sprinter's body to chase fast prey across open country. So the pronghorn's ghost predator was really a sprinting cousin of the cougar, not a true cheetah, a genuine and still-discussed paleobiology finding. Source: Wikipedia 'Miracinonyx' summarizing Barnett et al. (2005) mtDNA/morphology study; Encyclopedia MDPI 'Acinonychini'.

question: Run your hand over this animal and you feel a covering no other class of vertebrate on Earth grows. Light, branching vanes zip together into a smooth, insulating sheet — soft to the touch, and strong enough to hold up in flight. In the classic five-class lineup of vertebrates (fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals), that one trait settles which class you are touching. Which class of animal is it?
answer: A bird
choices: A bird
A reptile
A mammal
A fish
context: Feathers are the one trait no other living animal grows - a just-skinned creature wearing them is a bird, full stop. Birds are characterized by feathers, toothless beaked jaws, and hard-shelled eggs. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bird

question: This animal is covered in a coat of fine hair, and its young press close against its underside to feed on their mother's milk. That combination points to one class - which?
answer: A mammal
choices: A mammal
A bird
A reptile
An amphibian
context: Fur or hair plus milk-making mammary glands is a double tell no other class shares. Those young pressed to the body are nursing on milk - the milk gland, the mamma, is literally what the word 'mammal' is named after. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mammal

question: A snake wriggles slowly out of its old, dry outer skin, sliding forward like a foot pulling out of a sock. When the snake is finished, its whole old skin is left behind on the ground as one long, turned-inside-out tube. That trick of shedding the entire hide at once, along with having dry scales all over the body and laying eggs on land, belongs to which class of animals?
answer: A reptile
choices: A reptile
An amphibian
A mammal
A fish
context: A reptile's tell is dry keratin scales or scutes - snakes, lizards, turtles and crocodiles all wear them, and the skin is dry rather than slimy. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reptile

question: A brook trout hovers in a clear, cold mountain stream, opening and closing its mouth as water flows past. It is pulling the oxygen it needs straight out of the water through feathery organs tucked behind its head called gills. If the trout is lifted into the open air, it cannot breathe at all and will suffocate. Which class of animals does the brook trout belong to?
answer: A fish
choices: A fish
An amphibian
A reptile
A bird
context: A fish's tell is gills - comb-like filaments on the sides of the throat that pull oxygen straight out of the water - plus fins and a life lived underwater. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fish

question: Under a rotten log in a damp Appalachian forest lives a small, slippery salamander called a lungless salamander. As its name says, this salamander has no lungs at all, not even a tiny sac, yet it lives its whole life breathing perfectly well. Since a lungless salamander cannot use lungs, what does it take in oxygen through instead?
answer: Its skin
choices: Its skin
Its gills
Its bloodstream directly
The lining of its mouth
context: An amphibian's tell is wet, permeable skin it actually breathes through - some small salamanders and frogs lack lungs and rely entirely on their skin to take in oxygen. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amphibian

question: A hunter standing at the edge of a woodland pond sees something wriggling in the weeds and swears it is a small lizard. But this creature has damp, permeable skin instead of dry scales, and it spent its youth as a gilled tadpole swimming underwater before growing legs and crawling out onto land. This animal is a newt. Since it starts life in water and later breathes on land, what class of animals does a newt actually belong to?
answer: An amphibian
choices: An amphibian
A reptile
A fish
A bird
context: A newt is an amphibian, not a lizard: newts are salamanders (family Salamandridae), with wet skin and a water-bound youth. The dry-scaled lizard only looks similar. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amphibian

question: A blue whale glides through the open ocean the way a fish does and is often called one, but the whale must rise to the surface every so often to breathe air through a blowhole on top of its head. Its body grows a scattering of hair, its blood is warm, and a mother whale nurses her baby calf on rich, fatty milk. Given all of that, which class of animals does a whale actually belong to?
answer: A mammal
choices: A mammal
A fish
A reptile
An amphibian
context: A whale is a mammal, not a fish: cetaceans breathe air, have hair, and nurse their offspring with milk rather than laying eggs the way fish do. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mammal

question: On the Antarctic ice, a colony of emperor penguins waddles and dives, but not one of them can fly a single inch. A kid watching a nature show guesses they must not really be birds at all. Scientists say penguins are true birds anyway, and one body feature settles it. Not flight, not the beak — one trait shared by every bird alive proves it. What makes a penguin a genuine bird?
answer: Its feathers
choices: Its feathers
Its flight
Its beak
Its scales
context: Feathers, not flight, define the class - penguins and ostriches remain genuine birds because both possess feathers. A flightless bird is still every bit a bird. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bird

question: A frog must hop back to a pond every spring, because its soft jelly eggs would dry out on land. But a desert lizard can lay its eggs on baking sand and walk away, and the young still develop fully inside the shell. Reptile eggs, unlike amphibian eggs, seal the embryo inside a private water world. What structure inside the reptile's shell lets the embryo grow up out of any pond?
answer: A sealed amniotic sac around the embryo
choices: A sealed amniotic sac around the embryo
A soft jelly coating
A yolk twice the usual size
A pocket of stored air
context: The shelled amniotic egg freed vertebrates from water: its membranes retain water, so reptiles could reproduce on dry land even in extreme, arid habitats. Amphibians still must lay their shell-less eggs in water. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reptile

question: Almost every mammal on Earth — dogs, whales, mice, humans — grows its young inside the mother and gives birth to live babies. Fur and milk feed and warm this whole class of animals. But in Australia and New Guinea, five odd species break the pattern outright: the duck-billed platypus and four kinds of spiny echidna. What do those five do instead?
answer: Lay eggs
choices: Lay eggs
Carry their young in a pouch from birth
Give birth to swimming larvae
Split off buds of themselves
context: Almost all mammals give birth to live young - the lone exceptions are the five monotreme species, like the platypus and echidnas, the only mammals that lay eggs. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mammal  (Legend.)

question: Four furry, milk-fed animals are all famous for taking to the air: the bat, the flying squirrel, the sugar glider, and the colugo. But three of them are cheating. They leap from a high branch and coast on stretched flaps of skin like living kites, only gliding downward. Just one flaps real wings and truly flies with its own muscle power. Which is the only mammal that really flies?
answer: The bat
choices: The bat
The flying squirrel
The sugar glider
The colugo
context: Bats are the only mammal that truly flies - a fur-and-milk creature powering itself on the wing. The flying squirrel, sugar glider, and colugo only glide, coasting on flaps of skin. The earliest known bat is about 50 million years old. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mammal

question: Line a bird feather up beside a lizard's dry, overlapping body covering. They look nothing alike, but under a microscope both are built from the very same tough protein — beta-keratin — just folded into different shapes. Birds evolved from feathered dinosaurs, and their showy feathers started as a made-over reptile body part. Which reptile body part is a feather a reshaped form of?
answer: A scale
choices: A scale
A claw
A tooth
A belly scute
context: Feathers are made of the very same beta-keratin as reptile claws, scales and shells - a bird's feather and a lizard's scale are the same protein, reshaped. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feather

question: Here is the twist hidden in the neat five-class portrait of vertebrates. Scientists tracing the fossil record have shown that one whole class alive today is directly descended from small, feathered theropod dinosaurs — the same fossil family as Tyrannosaurus rex and Velociraptor. That class is the only branch of Dinosauria still walking the Earth. Which 'class' of vertebrate animal is really a living dinosaur?
answer: The birds
choices: The birds
The reptiles
The mammals
The amphibians
context: Birds ARE living dinosaurs: Aves is the only surviving group of Dinosauria, descended from theropod dinosaurs - so the 'five classes' is hiding a dinosaur among them. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bird  (Legend.)

question: For a long time, kids learned that reptiles (crocodiles, snakes, lizards) and birds were separate groups. But when scientists trace the animal family tree by shared traits and DNA, a crocodile turns out to be closer kin to a sparrow than to a lizard. Crocodiles and birds share the clade Archosauria — the 'ruling reptiles.' Where does that place the birds on the tree of life?
answer: Deep inside the reptile branch, as one twig of it
choices: Deep inside the reptile branch, as one twig of it
As the reptiles' nearest outside cousins
As a fresh branch grown from the mammal line
As a lone trunk with no living relatives
context: Cladistically a crocodile is closer kin to a sparrow than to a lizard: birds are more closely related to crocodilians than to other living reptiles, both nested in the clade Archosauria - so birds sit inside the reptiles. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reptile  (Legend.)

question: A bird's lung works like no mammal's: fresh air sweeps one way across it in a continuous loop, so oxygen keeps flowing even as the bird breathes out. Scientists long chalked this up to flight machinery unique to birds - until 2010, when the very same one-way airflow turned up in the lungs of a living animal with no air sacs at all. Which animal?
answer: The American alligator
choices: The American alligator
The fruit bat
The bottlenose dolphin
The giant tortoise
context: Birds move air one direction through their lungs - a continuous fresh stream even during exhale - and this was long assumed to be a specialization for the huge oxygen demand of flight. In 2010, Colleen Farmer and Kent Sanders of the University of Utah reported in Science that American alligators, which have no air sacs at all, also route air unidirectionally through their lungs, steered by aerodynamic 'valve' branch-points. Because crocodilians and birds sit on opposite sides of the archosaur family tree, the shared one-way lung is most simply explained as ancestral to all Archosauria - meaning the non-avian dinosaurs were already breathing this way. A 2013-14 follow-up found similar one-way flow in monitor lizards, hinting the trait may reach back roughly 270 million years. Source: Farmer & Sanders 2010, Science 327:338 (science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1180219); peerj.com/articles/60/.

question: Four sail-backed beasts loom out of the deep past, and those sails invite one easy guess: dinosaur. But one of the four is no reptile at all. Behind each eye socket it carries a single opening - the synapsid mark - that lands it on the branch leading to mammals. Which sail-back is really a stem-mammal, a closer cousin to a cow than to a lizard?
answer: Dimetrodon
choices: Dimetrodon
Spinosaurus
Ouranosaurus
Amargasaurus
context: Around 320-315 million years ago, in the late Carboniferous, the amniotes (backboned animals that lay waterproof eggs on land) split into two sister branches: Synapsida, which led to mammals, and Sauropsida, which led to every reptile and bird. Mammals never descended from reptiles - the two lines are cousins. The give-away is in the skull: synapsids carry a single opening (one temporal fenestra) behind each eye socket. Dimetrodon, the sail-backed Permian predator forever shelved with the dinosaurs, has that single hole, which makes it a synapsid - more closely related to you and to a cow than to any living lizard or crocodile. The other three sails all belong to genuine dinosaurs on the reptile (sauropsid) side: Spinosaurus, a spinosaurid theropod with a tall dorsal sail; Ouranosaurus, an iguanodontian ornithopod whose long back spines are usually restored as a sail; and Amargasaurus, a dicraeosaurid sauropod whose neck bore tall paired spines that may have carried sails. It is the mirror-image of the bird twist: just as a dinosaur hides among the 'reptiles,' a stem-mammal hides among the 'prehistoric reptiles.' Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synapsida; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sauropsida; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimetrodon; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spinosaurus; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ouranosaurus; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amargasaurus.  (Legend.)

question: One small white seabird breeds during the endless daylight of the Arctic summer. When autumn comes, it does not stop at a warm coast. It flies all the way south to Antarctica for a second summer there, then turns around and flies back. Every year. That round trip is the longest journey any animal on Earth makes. Which bird is it?
answer: The Arctic tern
choices: The Arctic tern
The bald eagle
The snowy owl
The wandering albatross
context: Geolocator-tracked Arctic terns averaged about 70,900 km (44,000 miles) a year, with some individuals topping 81,600 km - no animal migrates farther. Source: Audubon, 'How a Tern Broke the Record for the Longest Known Migration'; PMC6745660 (tern tracking study).

question: Across the vast, treeless Arctic tundra of Alaska and northern Canada, one shaggy brown deer walks farther in a single year than any other land animal on the planet. The herds cross frozen rivers, mountains, and endless plains in loops of about 3,000 miles, chasing lichen and fresh grass. Which hoofed animal makes the longest land trip on Earth?
answer: The caribou
choices: The caribou
The bison
The gray wolf
The moose
context: Caribou hold the record for the longest land migration of any animal, with some Arctic herds traveling on the order of 3,000 miles a year across the tundra. Source: NPS, 'Confirmed! Caribou have the longest land migration in the world'; Earth.com, 'Largest On Earth: Caribou Migration'.

question: Every year on the African Serengeti grasslands, up to 1.5 million of these tough hoofed grazers, joined by nearly a million zebras, sweep in one vast Great Migration. Each animal covers 800 to 1,000 kilometers as the huge herd chases the seasonal rains that push fresh grass up out of the dry plains. Which African animal forms this million-strong migrating herd?
answer: The wildebeest
choices: The wildebeest
The impala
The Cape buffalo
The springbok
context: Each year up to 1.5 million wildebeest, joined by nearly a million zebras, move as a single vast herd around the Serengeti-Mara ecosystem, each animal covering 800 to 1,000 km following the rains. Source: masaimara.travel, 'Wildebeest Migration'; Go2Africa, 'Guide to a Wildebeest Migration Safari'.

question: On the Serengeti plains of Tanzania and Kenya, more than a million wildebeest — hoofed grazers that look like scruffy short-horned cattle — travel together in one enormous herd, chasing fresh grass in a giant loop around East Africa. They aren't just wandering. Somehow, they know which faraway plains will turn green next. How do they find fresh grass hundreds of miles away?
answer: They watch for distant rain clouds and move toward them
choices: They watch for distant rain clouds and move toward them
They follow the scent of new grass carried on the wind
They retrace the exact path they walked the year before
They trail the zebra herds grazing just ahead of them
context: Wildebeest track the rain: they spot distant storm clouds and head toward them, because heavy rain means fresh grass will soon sprout where it falls. Source: serengeti.com, 'The great migration'; masaimara.travel.

question: The scariest part of the great wildebeest migration is one river crossing in East Africa. To reach fresh grass on the far bank of the Mara River between Kenya and Tanzania, over a million wildebeest have to plunge into deep, muddy water — where more than 3,000 huge reptiles wait. The herd panics, splashes, and hundreds are seized. What lurks below the Mara River's surface?
answer: Crocodiles
choices: Crocodiles
Hippos
Piranhas
Snapping turtles
context: At the Mara River crossing, more than 3,000 crocodiles wait in the water while big cats wait on the far bank, together picking off the weakest of the herd - the deadliest stretch of the whole migration. Source: masaimara.com, 'The Great Migration in Masai Mara'; Discover Wildlife.  (Legend.)

question: A salmon is born in one small freshwater stream high in the mountains. As a young fish it swims down the rivers to the sea, spends years hunting in the open Pacific, and then, years later, turns around and swims all the way back — returning to spawn in the very same little stream where it first hatched. How does a returning salmon find that one exact stream again out of thousands?
answer: By smelling the unique odor of its home water
choices: By smelling the unique odor of its home water
By following the position of the sun overhead
By sensing the pull of the Earth's magnetic field
By memorizing landmarks along the coastline
context: As juveniles, salmon imprint on the specific smell of their home water - the dissolved amino acids that give it a unique odor - and follow that memory back to the exact stream years later. Source: NOAA Fisheries, 'Fish Olfaction and Homing Research'; Nature Scientific Reports srep36393.

question: Pacific salmon — sockeye, chinook, coho — spend most of their lives fattening in the open ocean. Then they turn homeward and swim thousands of miles back into the very stream where they were born. They fight their way upstream against the current, leaping waterfalls and dodging bears, to reach the exact spawning gravel of their birth. Within days of finally breeding there, what happens to them?
answer: They all die, spent by that one single breeding effort
choices: They all die, spent by that one single breeding effort
They rest for weeks, then drift back downstream to the sea
They stay behind to guard the eggs until the young hatch
They lose their bright colors and quietly return to feed
context: Pacific salmon pour everything into one breeding effort - a strategy called semelparity. A surge of reproductive and stress hormones triggers rapid aging and organ failure, and the fish die within days of spawning. Source: Britannica, 'Why Do Salmon Die After Spawning?'; Bay Nature.

question: The Arctic tern is a small, gull-like seabird that lives an almost impossible life. Every year it nests near the North Pole from May to August, when the Arctic sun barely sets. Then it flies all the way to the other end of the planet, arriving near the South Pole just in time for the polar summer down there. By always chasing the sunny season, the tern gets more of what than any other creature on Earth?
answer: Daylight
choices: Daylight
Meals
Sleep
Rainfall
context: By chasing summer at both ends of the planet, the Arctic tern lives almost year-round in the endless daylight of the polar summer - so it sees more daylight in a year than any other animal alive. Source: Smithsonian Ocean, 'Arctic Tern'; carstenegevang.com.  (Legend.)

question: In 2022, biologists in Alaska fitted a young bar-tailed godwit — a long-legged shorebird — with a tiny satellite tag labeled 'B6.' In autumn B6 lifted off, flew south across the open Pacific Ocean, and did not touch down until it reached Tasmania, off Australia. No landing. No eating. No drinking. Just wing-beating over empty sea, day and night. How long was that nonstop flight?
answer: 11 days straight
choices: 11 days straight
About 30 hours
About 3 days
Nearly 6 weeks
context: B6 flew about 13,560 km (8,425 miles) in 11 days and 1 hour without a single stop - the longest documented nonstop flight by any animal. To do it, the bird had fattened up until it was nearly half fat. Source: USGS Alaska Science Center, 'Juvenile bar-tailed godwit B6 Sets World Record'.  (Legend.)

question: Every year one kind of whale swims a round trip of some 10,000 to 12,000 miles along the Pacific coast — between its cold Arctic feeding grounds off Alaska and the warm, shallow lagoons of Baja California in Mexico, where it gives birth to its calves. That is the longest migration of any mammal on Earth. Which mottled, barnacle-crusted whale?
answer: The gray whale
choices: The gray whale
The blue whale
The orca
The sperm whale
context: The gray whale holds the mammal migration record at roughly 16,000-20,000 km round trip; one tracked female, Varvara, logged about 22,500 km (nearly 14,000 miles) in a single round trip. Source: NOAA Ocean Today, 'Gray Whale Migration'; Mate et al., Biology Letters (2015).  (Legend.)

question: You might picture one bright orange monarch butterfly flying all the way from Canada down to Mexico and back again for the winter — but no single monarch ever does the whole round trip. The journey gets passed along like a relay baton: each butterfly flies part of the way, lays eggs, dies, and its children hatch and continue the migration. About how many generations of butterflies does the full round trip take?
answer: Three to five generations
choices: Three to five generations
Two generations
A single generation
Dozens of generations
context: The monarch's annual round trip takes three to five generations - the butterflies that reach Mexico are the great-great-grandchildren of the ones that set out the previous spring. Source: Nat Hab, 'The Migration' (Mexico's Monarchs Guide); Monarch butterfly migration - Wikipedia.  (Legend.)

question: Every autumn, orange-and-black monarch butterflies born in Canada and the northern United States fly south — up to 3,000 miles — until they reach central Mexico. Amazingly, they settle in the very same groves of oyamel fir trees on the very same mountains where their great-great-grandparents overwintered generations ago. What makes this so hard to explain?
answer: Not one of them has ever seen the place before
choices: Not one of them has ever seen the place before
They must be led there by the older butterflies
They leave a scent trail across the whole continent
They can spot the mountains from thousands of miles off
context: The monarchs return to the exact same oyamel fir groves in Mexico's Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt that their ancestors left generations earlier - even though not one of them has ever been there. Source: Nature.org, 'Monarch Butterflies Bring Together Conservation and Culture'; A Closer Look Tours.  (Legend.)

question: Most monarch butterflies live only about a month. But the single autumn generation that must fly all the way to Mexico and survive the whole winter before starting back lives about eight times longer than its own parents. It manages this by holding off on one thing. What does this 'super generation' delay?
answer: Making the hormone that ages its body
choices: Making the hormone that ages its body
Growing its full-sized wings
Feeding on milkweed as a caterpillar
Developing its sense of direction
context: The southbound 'super generation' (sometimes called the Methuselah generation) lives about eight times longer than its parents because it holds off producing an aging hormone - letting it survive the whole winter and start the trip back north. Source: Green Bay Botanical Garden, 'The Magnificent Migration of Monarch Butterflies'.  (Legend.)

question: Migrating monarchs steer by a sun compass, which only works if the butterfly also keeps an accurate internal clock to allow for the sun sliding across the sky. Scientists were surprised to find the master clock keeping this compass on course is not in the monarch's brain at all. Where is it?
answer: In its antennae
choices: In its antennae
On its wingtips
Behind its eyes
In its legs
context: Steven Reppert's lab found the clock that keeps a monarch's sun compass accurate sits in its antennae, not just its brain; painting the antennae black disrupts the butterfly's ability to hold a course. Source: Merlin et al., Science 325:1700 (2009); pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19779201.

question: A bar-tailed godwit flies eleven days over open ocean without a single bite of food, carrying all its fuel as fat piled on until fat is more than half its whole body weight. To avoid being too heavy to ever leave the ground, in the days before takeoff its body destroys part of itself. Which part?
answer: Its digestive organs, shrunk down and absorbed into the body
choices: Its digestive organs, shrunk down and absorbed into the body
Its tail feathers, molted away to trim weight and drag
Its leg muscles, wasted away over the long ocean crossing
Its blood, thinned into a lighter and more watery plasma
context: The classic study is literally titled 'Guts Don't Fly: Small Digestive Organs in Obese Bar-tailed Godwits' (Piersma & Gill 1998). Before the nonstop crossing the godwit shrinks its gut, liver, kidneys, and gizzard - organs useless in the air - and reabsorbs the tissue, while fat swells to about 55% of body mass (among the highest fat loads ever recorded in a bird) and the flight muscles and heart enlarge. The record juvenile, tagged B6, flew roughly 13,560 km from Alaska to Tasmania. Sources: Piersma & Gill 1998, 'Guts Don't Fly'; Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution 2021 physiomorphic review (fevo.2021.685764); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bar-tailed_godwit.  (Legend.)

question: A salmon can smell out its home stream, but only within a few km of the coast. Yet for two years it roams thousands of km across the open Gulf of Alaska, far from any scent of home, then still returns to the right river.
