The leading, and still debated, explanation is that as a young smolt it memorized one feature of its home river. Which one?
answer: The magnetic field's strength and tilt at its river mouth
choices: The magnetic field's strength and tilt at its river mouth
The star patterns above the coast on the night it swam out
The temperature and saltiness of the water at the river mouth
The arc the sun traces across the sky at that latitude
context: Homing looks like a two-stage act: a magnetic map for the open ocean, then smell for the final stream. As smolts, salmon appear to imprint on the geomagnetic 'signature' - field intensity and inclination angle - at their river mouth, then years later seek that same value across the featureless sea. The landmark evidence is Putman et al. 2013 (Current Biology), which mined a 56-year Fraser River sockeye fishery record: as Earth's field slowly drifted, the fish shifted which side of Vancouver Island they used, and the more a passage's field diverged from the river-mouth value, the fewer fish chose it. The magnetic-map role remains an active scientific debate. Source: Putman et al. 2013, 'Evidence for Geomagnetic Imprinting as a Homing Mechanism in Pacific Salmon,' cell.com/current-biology; follow-up PMC4233730.  (Legend.)

question: Look closely at a goldfish drifting in a tank and you will spot a faint dotted line running along each flank, from behind its gills all the way to its tail. It is easy to mistake for a color stripe, but every dot is a tiny pore opening in the skin. Together they form a working sense organ, called the lateral line, that no land animal has. What does that line of pores let the fish do?
answer: Feel the water moving against its body
choices: Feel the water moving against its body
Taste chemicals dissolved in the water
Glow faintly to signal other fish
Filter oxygen straight from the current
context: That line is the lateral line — a row of sense organs, not a stripe of pigment. It gives a fish a kind of touch that works at a distance, feeling currents and ripples push against its skin. Source: Wikipedia, 'Lateral line' (faint lines of pores running along each side; pored scales visible on a goldfish).

question: A fish swimming in muddy pond water can somehow sense a wall, a hidden hunter, or a passing neighbor even when its eyes can't see them. It reads the world by feeling how they push the water around. This job is done by its lateral line — the row of tiny pores running along each side of its body. What kind of water movement is the lateral line especially tuned to feel?
answer: Slow, large ripples in the water
choices: Slow, large ripples in the water
Fast, tiny high-pitched vibrations
Sudden sharp jolts like a slammed door
A steady one-way current, nothing else
context: The lateral line answers to slow, large water movements — currents, ripples, and the push of an object gliding by (below about 100 cycles per second). Faster pressure wiggles get picked up by the ear instead. Source: Wikipedia, 'Lateral line' (detects frequencies below 100 Hz; determines direction and rate of water movement).

question: A fish's lateral line — the dotted stripe of pores running along each side of its body — holds thousands of tiny sensors called neuromasts. Each neuromast is a little cluster of hair-like bristles buried inside a soft blob of clear jelly. When a passing current pushes on the jelly and bends the hairs sideways, what happens next to turn that moving water into a feeling the fish's brain can read?
answer: The bent hairs fire a nerve signal
choices: The bent hairs fire a nerve signal
The jelly changes color to warn the brain
The scales lift to catch more current
A muscle squeezes water back out
context: Flowing water shoves the jelly blob (the cupula), the jelly bends the hair bundles, and the bent hairs fire nerve signals — that's how moving water becomes a sensation. Source: scienceinsights.org and Wikipedia, 'Lateral line' (neuromast = hair cells capped by a gelatinous cupula).

question: Scientists blinded a predatory fish and it still struck its prey dead-on in the dark. Then they switched off its lateral line with cobalt ions — and the same blind hunter suddenly couldn't find a thing. What had the predator really been 'seeing' all along?
answer: The water the prey disturbed
choices: The water the prey disturbed
The prey's faint body heat
A scent cloud trailing the prey
The prey's shadow on the bottom
context: Blinded predators hunted fine, but not once cobalt ions shut down the lateral line — proof they were tracking the water their prey stirred up, not any image of it. Source: Wikipedia, 'Lateral line' (blinded predatory fishes remain able to hunt, but not when lateral line function is inhibited by cobalt ions).

question: In a classic experiment, Tony Pitcher and Brian Partridge blindfolded saithe and the fish still slotted perfectly into their school, turning as one. Only when the researchers also cut the lateral line nerve did the school fall apart. How does a leaderless school stay in formation in the dark?
answer: Each fish feels its neighbors' pressure waves
choices: Each fish feels its neighbors' pressure waves
One elder fish calls the turns with sound
They follow a scent the leader releases
They lock onto the seabed's magnetic field
context: Every fish feels the pressure waves its neighbors push against its flank and matches them — vision alone or the lateral line alone is enough, but knocking out both breaks the school. Source: Partridge & Pitcher 1980; journals.biologists.com/jeb (blinded saithe still school; both senses must be ablated for schooling to cease).  (Legend.)

question: The blind Mexican cave fish, Astyanax mexicanus, spends its whole life in lightless caves — yet it swims straight toward a tiny food-vibration in total darkness. Its river-dwelling cousins can't. What did evolution give the cave fish to pull that off?
answer: Neuromasts crowding its empty eye sockets
choices: Neuromasts crowding its empty eye sockets
A second lateral line down its belly
Neuromasts that fire only in the dark
A ring of stiff whiskers on its snout
context: Living in the dark, the cave fish evolved more and larger neuromasts — even in the empty sockets where its useless eyes shrank away — and homes in on faint vibrations (peak sensitivity around 35 cycles per second), a behavior called vibration attraction. Source: Yoshizawa et al., Current Biology 2010.  (Legend.)

question: A fish's lateral line and your own ears run on the very same kind of sensor: hair cells that fire when they are bent. Evolution took that sensor, sealed it inside the head, and built what out of it in every backboned animal — fish, frog, bird, and you?
answer: The inner ear
choices: The inner ear
The eye's lens
The taste buds
The sense of smell
context: That same hair-cell sensor, moved inside the head, became the inner ear of every vertebrate — so both your hearing AND your balance descend from a fish's lateral line. Scientists even group the two systems together as the 'octavolateralis' system. Source: Wikipedia, 'Lateral line'; Springer, 'Functional Evolution of Lateral Line and Inner Ear Sensory Systems' (homologous hair cells).  (Legend.)

question: Sharks and rays hunt by feeling the faint electric crackle of prey buried in sand, using pit-sensors called the ampullae of Lorenzini -- which grow from the very same embryonic tissue as the mechanical lateral line, its electric twin. Follow that electric sense back through fish history, though, and you hit a real puzzle. What does the fossil-and-gene trail actually show?
answer: It was lost in the bony-fish line, then re-evolved more than once
choices: It was lost in the bony-fish line, then re-evolved more than once
It has run unbroken from the earliest jawed fishes to today
It arose late and stayed unique to sharks and their kin
It passed into bony fish from one shared ancestor, just once
context: Both senses belong to one embryonic system, the octavolateralis system, and both grow from the same lateral-line placodes (thickenings of embryonic skin). Ancestral jawed vertebrates had both the mechanical line and the electric one. The electric sense was then lost in the lineage leading to the neopterygian bony fish -- gars, bowfin, and the teleosts -- and in frogs, and then independently re-evolved at least twice within teleosts, most likely by re-tuning ordinary neuromast hair cells into electroreceptors. So electroreception is an old lateral-line trick that has been dropped and reinvented across fish history -- a genuine, still-debated pattern of repeated loss and convergent regain. Source: Wikipedia 'Lateral line' and 'Ampullae of Lorenzini'; Baker, Modrell & Gillis, 'The evolution and development of vertebrate lateral line electroreceptors', J. Exp. Biol. (PMC4988487); eLife 2016, 'Insights into electrosensory organ development... from a lateral line-enriched transcriptome' (elifesciences.org/articles/24197).

question: A human eye sees color using just three kinds of receptor — one for red, one green, one blue. The mantis shrimp's eye is famous for packing many more. That gap alone started an internet legend that it must see a wild rainbow. How many kinds of color receptor does its eye have?
answer: Twelve
choices: Five
Seven
Twelve
Three
context: Twelve of the mantis shrimp's roughly 16 photoreceptor types are tuned for color, spanning deep ultraviolet to far red (about 300 to 720 nanometers), against a human's three. That 12-versus-3 gap is exactly what launched the internet legend of super color vision — a legend the actual experiments would later puncture. Source: Thoen, How, Chiou & Marshall 2014, Science 343:411 ('A Different Form of Color Vision in Mantis Shrimp'); Mapping Ignorance (mappingignorance.org, 2014-03-24).

question: Scientists at Queensland trained mantis shrimp to pick a colored light for a food reward. Then they slid two colors closer and closer until the shrimp could not tell them apart. A trained human can still tell colors just 1 to 5 nanometers apart. How close could the mantis shrimp still tell them apart?
answer: Down to about 12 to 25 nanometers apart
choices: Down to about 1 to 2 nanometers apart
Down to about 4 to 6 nanometers apart
Down to about 12 to 25 nanometers apart
Down to less than 1 nanometer apart
context: The shrimp fell apart when two colors sat only about 12 to 25 nanometers apart; a human can split colors as close as 1 to 5 nanometers. The animal with twelve color channels is actually worse at telling similar hues apart than a human with three — the opposite of the legend. Source: Thoen, How, Chiou & Marshall 2014, Science 343:411; sci-news.com/biology/science-color-vision-mantis-shrimp-01719.html.

question: The 2014 result left a deep puzzle: a mantis shrimp with twelve color channels told similar colors apart far more coarsely than the math said twelve channels should allow. The study's answer was that the eye reads color in a way no textbook had described. How did it propose the mantis shrimp eye pins down a color?
answer: It sweeps its eye stripe across the object and reads the spectral signature like a barcode
choices: It sweeps its eye stripe across the object and reads the spectral signature like a barcode
It bends each color onto its own sharp point in a central pit and compares them
It runs each pair of channels against each other and averages the result
It pipes all twelve signals into one nerve that blends them into a master hue
context: Eye muscles sweep the color-sensing 'mid-band' stripe across an object in one fast pass, and the brain recognizes the object's spectral signature like a barcode rather than finely discriminating it — trading precision for near-instant, low-brain-cost speed. Lead author Hanne Thoen called it 'another way of color processing,' the first genuinely new category of seeing described since the 1800s; it is treated as an active reinterpretation, not a closed case. Source: Thoen et al. 2014, Science 343:411; sci-news.com; Mapping Ignorance (mappingignorance.org, 2014-03-24).  (Legend.)

question: A light wave can spiral as it travels, twisting like a corkscrew — physicists call this circular polarization — and almost no eye on Earth reacts to it. The mantis shrimp is the only animal known to detect the spiraling light, and the whole trick happens inside a single cell in each unit of its eye. What does that one cell do to the incoming spiral?
answer: It untwists the spiral into flat light, handing an easy signal to the cells below it
choices: It untwists the spiral into flat light, handing an easy signal to the cells below it
It absorbs the left-hand spiral and passes only the right-hand spiral to the cells below it
It spins to match the spiral's rotation, then relays a steady beam to the cells below it
It scatters the spiral into a soft blur that the broad cells below it can average out
context: This is real, and it made headlines: the mantis shrimp is the only animal known to detect circularly polarized light — light whose wave spirals like a corkscrew. In rows 5 and 6 of the eye's midband, one photoreceptor, the R8 cell, acts as a 'quarter-wave plate': an optical part that converts spiraling (circular) light into flat (linear) light. The deeper receptors can only read flat light, so R8 performs the conversion first. Chiou, Kleinlogel, Cronin, Caldwell, Loeffler, Siddiqi, Goldizen & Marshall, 'Circular Polarization Vision in a Stomatopod Crustacean,' Current Biology 18 (2008).

question: Ultraviolet light is invisible to us, yet the mantis shrimp eye splits it into six separate channels — which ought to demand six different UV-catching pigments. The eye carries only two. It conjures the other four channels by stacking colored filters ahead of the pigments, each one shaving a slice off the band before the light arrives. The strange part is what those filters are built from. What does the eye repurpose to make them?
answer: The same sunscreen molecules that other reef animals grow to guard their bodies from the sun
choices: The same sunscreen molecules that other reef animals grow to guard their bodies from the sun
The red carotenoid pigments that flamingos and salmon pull straight out of their daily food
The clear crystal proteins that shape the transparent lens set at the very front of the eye
The dark melanin grains that line the back of a human retina and soak up the stray glare
context: The mantis shrimp builds six distinct ultraviolet receptor classes from only two UV visual pigments by placing four different colored filters in front of them. Those filters are made of mycosporine-like amino acids (MAAs) — the same 'biological sunscreen' compounds many reef animals use to shield their tissues from UV damage — here repurposed to carve the ultraviolet band into six channels instead of blocking it out. Bok, Porter, Place & Cronin, 'Biological Sunscreens Tune Polychromatic Ultraviolet Vision in Mantis Shrimp,' Current Biology 24 (2014).

question: In the freezing black water beneath Arctic sea ice, a slow, sluggish shark cruises the deep. Fishermen sometimes haul one up beside their boat, silver-gray and often blind from a parasite dangling off its eye. No backboned animal on Earth is proven to outlive this fish — some individuals may push past 400 years. Which cold-water shark holds the record as the longest-lived vertebrate known?
answer: The Greenland shark
choices: The Greenland shark
The great white shark
The whale shark
The rougheye rockfish
context: The Greenland shark is the longest-lived vertebrate known on Earth — no backboned animal is proven to live longer. Source: ScienceDaily, on Nielsen et al. 2016, Science (https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2016/08/160811143218.htm).

question: On the tiny, remote British island of Saint Helena in the South Atlantic Ocean — the same island where the emperor Napoleon was exiled after Waterloo — a giant Seychelles tortoise named Jonathan grazes slowly across the governor's lawn every day. Jonathan is the oldest known living creature on land anywhere on Earth. Roughly how old is Jonathan?
answer: Over 190 years
choices: Over 190 years
About 40 years
Over 500 years
About 90 years
context: Jonathan, a Seychelles giant tortoise on Saint Helena, is over 190 years old — the oldest known living land animal, hatched around 1832, before the camera or the telephone was invented. Source: Wikipedia; Smithsonian (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_(tortoise)).  (Legend.)

question: Scientists date Greenland sharks — the giant, slow-moving sharks that cruise deep Arctic water — by measuring chemicals in the lenses of their eyes. They estimate the biggest ones can live around 250 to 400 years, and possibly longer. That means one of these sharks cruising the icy deep right now was probably alive when your great-great-great-grandparents were kids. What almost-unbelievable fact does that make true of a Greenland shark swimming in the deep today?
answer: It may have been born in the 1600s
choices: It may have been born in the 1600s
It stops growing after age fifty
It must return to shore to breed
It glows to lure deep-sea prey
context: Age estimates run roughly 250–400+ years; the two largest studied sharks were estimated at about 335 and 392 years — so one alive today may have been born before the United States existed. Source: ScienceDaily, on Nielsen et al. 2016 (https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2016/08/160811143218.htm).  (Legend.)

question: Off the coast of Iceland in 2006, marine biologists dredged up a small ocean quahog clam from the seabed and brought it back to the lab. They cracked open its shell, counted its layers, and got a shock: this clam had been alive since around the year 1499 — back when the Ming dynasty ruled China. They nicknamed the clam 'Ming' after that dynasty. At roughly 507 years old, what record did Ming set?
answer: Oldest individual animal ever found
choices: Oldest individual animal ever found
Largest clam ever measured
Deepest-dwelling shellfish known
First clam ever raised in a lab
context: Ming lived about 507 years — the oldest individual animal ever found. It was dredged up off Iceland in 2006; the scientists accidentally killed it by prying open its shell to study it. Source: Wikipedia; Guinness World Records (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ming_(clam)).  (Legend.)

question: Ming the ocean quahog — the little Iceland clam alive since around the year 1499 — had no bones, no teeth, no skeleton, and no rings around any trunk to give away its age. Yet marine biologists pinned Ming at 507 years old by studying one single part of its body under a microscope. What did they count?
answer: Growth rings layered in its shell
choices: Growth rings layered in its shell
Chemicals dissolved in its blood
The length of its muscular foot
Barnacles clustered on its outside
context: Ming's age was counted from growth rings in its shell, just like counting rings in a tree trunk. Source: National Museum Wales; Wikipedia (https://museum.wales/blog/2122/Meet-Ming-the-clam---the-oldest-animal-in-the-world/).

question: A Greenland shark is a huge, slow, cold-blooded predator that prowls the icy deep water of the North Atlantic. It grows so slowly that it stays a youngster for a shockingly long time before it can ever have babies of its own. Scientists tagging and studying wild Greenland sharks have measured exactly when they finally reach adulthood. At about what age does a Greenland shark first become an adult able to reproduce?
answer: Around 150 years old
choices: Around 150 years old
Around 15 years old
Around 40 years old
Around 300 years old
context: A Greenland shark doesn't become an adult able to reproduce until it is at least about 150 years old — older than most countries. Source: ScienceDaily, on Nielsen et al. 2016 (https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2016/08/160811143218.htm).

question: A Greenland shark has almost none of the hard, layered body parts — like ear bones or annual scale rings — that scientists usually count like tree rings to age a fish. Yet one soft tissue in its head holds a chemical record that has been locked away, untouched by later years, since before the shark ever hatched. Which tissue do scientists carefully cut open to read a Greenland shark's true age?
answer: The lens of its eye
choices: The lens of its eye
The tip of its dorsal fin
The cartilage of its jaw
The scales along its back
context: The center of the eye lens forms before the shark is born and is never replaced, preserving a chemical record of its birth that scientists read to estimate age. Source: Nielsen et al., Science (https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aaf1703).

question: Greenland sharks have no reliable rings to count, so dating them seemed almost hopeless. Then scientists realized one strange 20th-century event had left a chemical timestamp inside the sharks' bodies. What leftover signal let them date the youngest sharks?
answer: Radioactive carbon from 1950s bomb tests
choices: Radioactive carbon from 1950s bomb tests
Plastic microbeads from ocean pollution
Mercury built up from eating deep prey
Oil residue from Arctic drilling rigs
context: Scientists dated Greenland sharks using leftover radioactive carbon from 1950s–60s nuclear bomb tests: only the smallest, youngest sharks carried that 'bomb pulse' marker, proving the big ones were born long before the atomic age. Source: Science News, on Nielsen et al. 2016 (https://www.sciencenews.org/article/study-ranks-greenland-shark-longest-lived-vertebrate).

question: A rougheye rockfish pulled up by scientists off Alaska turned out to be 205 years old, yet from the outside it showed no clue at all to its great age. To read the answer, researchers reached deep inside the fish's skull, near the inner ear, and lifted out a pair of tiny hard stones. They sliced them open and counted the growth layers stacked inside, exactly like counting tree rings. What are these age-keeping stones inside a fish's skull called?
answer: Otoliths
choices: Otoliths
Scutes
Denticles
Ossicles
context: The rougheye rockfish is one of the longest-lived fish, reaching about 205 years, aged by counting yearly rings in its otoliths — tiny 'ear stones' inside the head. Source: Wikipedia; Alaska Dept. of Fish and Game (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rougheye_rockfish).

question: In 2007, Alaskan hunters landed a living bowhead whale — the huge, thick-blubbered whale that swims among the Arctic ice — and found something extraordinary embedded in its shoulder. A rusty fragment of an old exploding harpoon was still lodged there, and researchers traced that weapon to a factory in the whaling town of New Bedford, Massachusetts, that had made it around 1879. What did the stuck fragment prove about the whale?
answer: The whale had swum for over 100 years
choices: The whale had swum for over 100 years
The whale had been raised in captivity
The harpoon had been fired that season
The whale was younger than first believed
context: The New Bedford harpoon fragment, made around 1879–80, meant that whale had been swimming for well over 100 years — the kind of embedded old harpoon tip that first revealed how long bowheads live. Source: Forbes (https://www.forbes.com/sites/scotttravers/2024/09/19/meet-the-longest-living-mammal-hint-its-been-found-alive-with-an-1880s-era-harpoon-in-its-side/).

question: In 2013, an enormous rockfish was pulled from deep Alaskan water, and, judging just by its huge size, biologists at first guessed it might be around 200 years old — nearly a record for its kind. Then they carefully removed its otoliths — the tiny growth-ringed ear stones inside its skull — split them open, and counted the rings under a microscope. The rings told a very different story. How old was the fish really?
answer: Only 64 years
choices: Only 64 years
Exactly 200 years
Over 400 years
Just 12 years
context: Otolith testing showed the record rockfish was really only 64 — a reminder that scientists must measure age carefully, not just eyeball a big animal. Source: The Spokesman-Review (https://www.spokesman.com/stories/2013/jul/06/record-rockfish-was-64-years-old-not-200-tests-sho/).

question: Ming the clam and the Greenland shark get crowned as the oldest animals alive. But off Hawaii, scientists radiocarbon-dated a slow-growing animal on the deep seafloor — already alive when Egypt's pyramids were new, and roughly eight times older than Ming. What holds the true record?
answer: A deep-sea black coral
choices: A deep-sea black coral
A deep-sea tube worm
A deep-sea sea anemone
A deep-sea feather star
context: A single colony of the deep-sea black coral Leiopathes glaberrima, collected off Hawaii, was radiocarbon-dated along its growth axis to about 4,265 years old — roughly eight times the age of Ming the clam and more than ten times a Greenland shark's. A black coral is not one creature but a colony of tiny cnidarian polyps that slowly build a shared protein skeleton, so the true oldest animals alive are ones most people would never call animals at all. A companion 'gold coral' (Gerardia) from the same waters came in near 2,700 years. Source: Roark, Guilderson, Dunbar, Fallon & Mucciarone (2009), 'Extreme longevity in proteinaceous deep-sea corals,' PNAS; corroborated by Wikipedia (Black coral; List of longest-living organisms).  (Legend.)

question: A bowhead whale lives past 200 years and carries thousands of times more cells than a person. By pure odds, that many dividing cells should make cancer almost certain — yet bowheads almost never get it. When scientists sequenced the whale's genome, what did they find shielding it?
answer: A knack for repairing its own DNA
choices: A knack for repairing its own DNA
A body kept too cold for tumors
Blood that hunts down cancer cells
An immune system that never sleeps
context: A bowhead's huge, long-lived body should be riddled with cancer — the puzzle biologists call Peto's paradox — yet the whales almost never get it despite carrying thousands of times more cells than a human. When the bowhead genome was sequenced in 2015, researchers found distinctive variants in DNA-repair and cell-cycle genes, notably ERCC1 (which helps fix damaged DNA) and PCNA (a hub of DNA replication and repair). Better damage repair is thought to head off the cancers that should overwhelm so many cells — a clue to not just how old bowheads get, but how. Source: Keane, de Magalhaes et al. (2015), 'Insights into the Evolution of Longevity from the Bowhead Whale Genome,' Cell Reports; corroborated by Wikipedia (Bowhead whale).

question: Nearly every mammal on Earth — from mice to elephants to humans — is born live from its mother's body, warm and wriggling. But one tiny group of furry, milk-feeding animals in Australia and New Guinea breaks that rule outright. Instead of giving birth, they lay leathery eggs and hatch tiny, jelly-bean-sized babies that lap up milk oozing through the mother's skin. What are these strange egg-laying mammals called as a group?
answer: Monotremes
choices: Monotremes
Marsupials
Cetaceans
Placentals
context: Monotremes are the only mammals that lay eggs rather than giving live birth, yet they still nurse their young with milk. Source: npj Biodiversity (nature.com/articles/s44185-025-00086-6), 'one of only five modern egg-laying mammals'.

question: The entire family of egg-laying mammals — the monotremes — is astonishingly tiny. Count them and there is one lone duck-billed platypus, plus four kinds of spiny, ant-eating cousins called echidnas, all living in Australia and New Guinea. How many kinds of egg-laying mammal live in the world today?
answer: Exactly five
choices: Exactly five
Around forty
Just one
Over two hundred
context: The five living monotremes are the platypus plus four echidnas: the short-beaked echidna and three long-beaked echidnas. Source: npj Biodiversity (nature.com/articles/s44185-025-00086-6), 'one of only five modern egg-laying mammals'; Wikipedia 'Echidna'.

question: When a kangaroo mother in the Australian outback has a baby, the joey that eventually pokes its head out of her pouch is not what she actually gives birth to. The creature that is actually born, right at the moment of birth, is blind, hairless, and shockingly tiny — it has to crawl up through her fur on its own to reach the safety of the pouch. About how big is a newborn kangaroo the moment it is born?
answer: About the size of a jellybean
choices: About the size of a jellybean
About the size of a house cat
About the size of a rabbit
About the size of a loaf of bread
context: A newborn joey is born blind, hairless, and about 2 cm long, weighing under a gram. It must then crawl unaided up its mother's fur to the pouch using surprisingly strong, clawed forelimbs. Source: A-Z Animals; Ask A Biologist (askabiologist.asu.edu/kangaroo-joey).  (Legend.)

question: An egg-laying mammal mother still feeds her babies milk, but she has a strange problem: her body has no nipples at all. How do her babies get their milk?
answer: The milk oozes out through pores in her skin and they lap it from her fur
choices: The milk oozes out through pores in her skin and they lap it from her fur
She regurgitates a milky paste into their open mouths
They chew special milk-filled sacs that grow on her belly
She soaks leaves in milk for them to suck
context: With no teats, a monotreme's milk is released through pores and patches in the skin, and the young lap it up from her fur. Source: Wikipedia 'Platypus', 'with no teats, the milk is released through pores in the skin from which the young lap it up in her fur'.  (Legend.)

question: A platypus is a strange, duck-billed, egg-laying mammal that lives in the rivers and creeks of Australia. When it dives to hunt, it seals its eyes, ears, and nostrils shut against the muddy water, yet it still finds shrimp, insects, and worms hidden in the river gloom. Its rubbery, flat bill is packed with about 40,000 special sensors that let it 'see' in the dark. What do those bill sensors actually detect?
answer: The faint electricity of prey's moving muscles
choices: The faint electricity of prey's moving muscles
The warmth given off by hidden prey
Ripples in the water made by prey
The scent trails prey leave in mud
context: The platypus bill holds about 40,000 electroreceptors arranged in rows, detecting the tiny electric fields made when prey muscles move. Source: Wikipedia 'Platypus', '40,000 electroreceptors arranged in rows in the skin of the bill'.  (Legend.)

question: In Australia lives the wombat, a stocky burrowing marsupial that spends its life digging long underground tunnels. It scoops out earth with its front paws and kicks the loose dirt and sticks out behind it as it works. Like other marsupials, a mother wombat carries her tiny baby, called a joey, in a body pouch on her belly. That pouch has one odd feature that keeps her joey clean and safe while all that debris flies. What is unusual about a wombat's pouch?
answer: Its opening points toward the mother's rear, away from the flying dirt
choices: Its opening points toward the mother's rear, away from the flying dirt
Its opening can be sealed shut like a zip-lock bag
Its opening is lined with waterproof waxy skin
Its opening splits into two separate mouths
context: A wombat's pouch opens toward its rear so that when the mother digs, dirt and sticks don't fall in on the joey. Source: Cool Green Science (blog.nature.org) / National Geographic, 'a wombat's pouch faces backwards... to protect their joeys from dirt'.  (Legend.)

question: North America has just one native pouched mammal — a marsupial whose babies grow up inside a body pouch on the mother's belly. It is called the Virginia opossum. Its newborns are each about the size of a honeybee, and the pouch holds only 13 teats for them to nurse from. When a mother has more than 13 babies in a litter, what decides which of them survive?
answer: Only the babies that reach and latch onto a teat survive
choices: Only the babies that reach and latch onto a teat survive
The mother nudges the weakest ones out first
The largest babies push the others off the teats
The mother splits them between two litters
context: The Virginia opossum is the only marsupial native to North America. With exactly 13 teats, only the newborns that reach a teat survive. Source: Alabama Cooperative Extension; Opossum Society US.

question: The platypus is a strange furry mammal from the rivers of Australia. It lays eggs, has a duck-like bill, and hunts underwater. Only the male platypus carries a weapon: a sharp spur on the heel of each hind leg that delivers venom when he stabs. The venom will not kill a grown person, but anyone jabbed learns to respect it fast. What does a male platypus's venom do to a human?
answer: Causes excruciating pain that can last for months
choices: Causes excruciating pain that can last for months
Makes the wound glow faintly for hours
Paralyzes the arm for a full day
Triggers uncontrollable sleepiness
context: The male platypus's spur venom is not lethal to humans but causes excruciating pain, a hyperalgesia that can last as long as months. Source: Wikipedia 'Platypus'.  (Legend.)

question: The platypus (Ornithorhynchus anatinus) piles oddity on oddity. Along with laying eggs and a venomous spur, it has one more secret revealed only in the dark: shine an ultraviolet light on its fur and something surprising happens. What does its fur do under UV light?
answer: It glows cyan and green
choices: It glows cyan and green
It turns jet black
It becomes completely transparent
It sheds a fine glowing powder
context: The platypus's fur biofluoresces, glowing cyan and green under ultraviolet light. The animal also lacks a functional stomach entirely, having lost the genes to make one. Source: Wikipedia 'Platypus', 'glows cyan and green when under ultraviolet light'.  (Legend.)

question: Both the platypus and the echidna are odd egg-laying mammals from Australia and New Guinea. Both can sense the faint electricity given off by their prey — the platypus in muddy river bottoms, the echidna nosing through leaf litter — through the tip of their snouts. But the two are not equipped to the same degree. The platypus bill carries about 40,000 electric sensors. Roughly how many does the echidna's beak carry?
answer: Only about 400 to 2,000
choices: Only about 400 to 2,000
Roughly 30,000
About 15,000
Around 8,000
context: A baby echidna is called a puggle, and the echidna does have electroreceptors in its beak, but only 400 to 2,000 of them compared with the platypus's 40,000. Source: Discover Wildlife (discoverwildlife.com echidna).

question: The echidna is a spiny Australian mammal that lays a single leathery egg and rolls it directly into a temporary pouch on her belly. When the egg hatches, out comes a tiny hairless baby called a puggle, which rides in the pouch and suckles milk from patches on her skin. But the puggle soon grows something that forces her to evict it and dig it a burrow instead. What makes her move the puggle out?
answer: It grows spines and becomes too prickly to carry
choices: It grows spines and becomes too prickly to carry
It grows too heavy for her to walk
It starts trying to eat her own food
It grows a long tail that won't fit
context: Once the puggle develops spines and becomes too prickly, the mother removes it from her pouch and builds a burrow for it, where it keeps suckling for about six months. Source: Australian Museum, Short-beaked Echidna.

question: Attenborough's long-beaked echidna is one of the five egg-laying mammals. Science had no record of it for 62 years. In 2023 a team set camera traps deep in the Cyclops Mountains of New Guinea. When they finally checked the footage, what had the cameras caught?
answer: The living animal itself, snuffling past on camera
choices: The living animal itself, snuffling past on camera
Only a set of fresh claw-marks in the mud
A distant call recorded but never seen
A single blurry shape too dark to identify
context: Attenborough's long-beaked echidna (Zaglossus attenboroughi) was rediscovered alive in 2023 after 62 years unrecorded by science, filmed on camera traps in the Cyclops Mountains. Source: npj Biodiversity (nature.com/articles/s44185-025-00086-6); Sci.News.  (Legend.)

question: In 1799 a preserved specimen of a strange furry animal from Australia — with a broad duck-like bill, webbed feet, thick brown fur, and a flat beaver-like tail — reached naturalists at the British Museum in London. They stared at the platypus, poked at the seams between the bill and the skull, and refused outright to believe it was one real animal at all. What did they suspect had happened?
answer: That a duck's bill had been sewn onto a beaver-like body as a hoax
choices: That a duck's bill had been sewn onto a beaver-like body as a hoax
That it was a diseased, deformed otter
That two shipped animals had been mixed up in one crate
That it was a clever wax model, not a real creature
context: The platypus so baffled European scientists that some suspected the duck bill had been stitched onto a beaver-like body as a taxidermy hoax. Source: Natural History Museum, 'The platypus puzzle' (nhm.ac.uk/discover/the-platypus-puzzle.html).  (Legend.)

question: A wombat marks its ground by placing its droppings on top of rocks and logs. They sit there without rolling away — because a wombat is the only animal on Earth whose droppings come out as neat, flat-faced cubes. How does a wombat shape its droppings into cubes?
answer: Its intestine wall alternates stiff and stretchy zones that mould them.
choices: Its intestine wall alternates stiff and stretchy zones that mould them.
The dry outback heat bakes each soft pellet until it cracks into blocks.
It tamps each one flat against a rock with its broad, stumpy tail.
A ring of bony plates just inside its rear stamps square corners in.
context: When researchers inflated preserved wombat intestines, they found the wall wasn't uniform — it had alternating stiff and stretchy regions. In the final roughly 8% of the intestine, those uneven contractions slowly mould the drying droppings into flat-faced cubes. The wombat then stacks the cubes to scent-mark its territory, and because they're square they resist rolling off rocks. The work won the 2019 Ig Nobel Prize in Physics. Source: Yang, Lee, Chan, Martin, Edwards, Carver & Hu — 2019 Ig Nobel Prize in Physics (improbable.com/2019/09/12); Soft Matter / APS study on wombat cube feces; Georgia Tech Quantitative Biosciences (qbios.gatech.edu).

question: Egg-laying mammals barely hang on today — worldwide, only the platypus and a few echidna species are left. But at one opal field near Lightning Ridge in New South Wales, fossils about 100 million years old, some preserved as solid opal, capture a very different Cretaceous world. What did that single site hold?
answer: At least six egg-laying mammal species living there side by side.
choices: At least six egg-laying mammal species living there side by side.
Two platypus lineages already split between river and seashore.
Three egg-laying species that each dwarfed any alive today.
A dozen individuals of one burrowing species denning together.
context: The site is Lightning Ridge in New South Wales, famous for opal — and here the monotreme bones themselves survive as gem opal, so rare they're described as roughly one monotreme fragment per million opal pieces. Dated to the Cenomanian, about 100 million years ago, the deposit held at least six egg-laying-mammal species at once, more monotreme diversity in one place than exists on the whole planet today. The 2024 star is a creature nicknamed the 'echidnapus,' Opalios splendens, whose skull blends platypus and echidna features. Source: Flannery, Helgen, McCurry et al. 2024, Alcheringa: An Australasian Journal of Palaeontology (sci.news/paleontology/lightning-ridge-monotremes-12964.html; ScienceDaily 2024-05-27); Opalios, Wikipedia.

question: A scallop is a hinged shellfish, cousin to clams and oysters, that rests on the seabed with its two fan-ridged shells cracked open to filter water. Peer between the halves of one as it sits open on the sand and, staring back at you along the frilly edge of its mantle, you find a row of tiny, glinting blue dots. What are they?
answer: Up to 200 tiny eyes
choices: Up to 200 tiny eyes
Filter-feeding gills
Rows of stinging cells
Grip pads for the sand
context: A scallop can have up to 200 tiny blue eyes lining the edge of its mantle, peering out between the two halves of its shell. Source: C&EN, 'Reflective guanine crystals lend sight to scallops' (cen.acs.org/articles/95/i48); Palmer et al., Science 2017.

question: A human eye and a camera work the same way: a curved lens at the front bends incoming light and focuses it to a sharp point at the back. A scallop, a hinged shellfish sitting on the seabed, has around 200 tiny blue eyes strung along the frilly edge of its shell. Each of those little eyes throws away the lens trick entirely and focuses light a different way. How?
answer: It bounces light off a curved mirror
choices: It bounces light off a curved mirror
It funnels light down a narrow tube
It splits light through a crystal prism
It soaks up light with a dark pit
context: Instead of a lens, each scallop eye focuses light using a curved mirror built from tiles of guanine crystal behind the retina. Source: Palmer et al., 'The image-forming mirror in the eye of the scallop', Science 2017 (science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aam9506).

question: Behind each scallop eye sits a curved mirror built from thousands of tiny guanine crystals in 20-30 stacked layers. For the reflected image to stay sharp rather than blurred, the crystals themselves must have one particular shape. What shape are they?
answer: Perfectly square, flat plates
choices: Perfectly square, flat plates
Round like tiny marbles
Long and needle-like
Six-sided like honeycomb
context: The scallop's mirror is made of 20-30 stacked layers of tiny square guanine plates, fitted edge-to-edge like bathroom tiles so the reflected image stays sharp. Source: C&EN (cen.acs.org/articles/95/i48); Science News, 'Scallops' amazing eyes use millions of tiny, square crystals to see'.

question: Anableps, nicknamed the 'four-eyed fish', is a small fish that lives in the rivers and shallow lagoons of Central America. Despite the name, it actually has only two eyes — but they are built in a very odd way. It hangs at the water's surface all day with the waterline resting exactly across the middle of each eye, cutting each one into an upper half and a lower half. Why does that eye-line matter?
answer: Each eye's top half sees in air while its bottom half sees underwater
choices: Each eye's top half sees in air while its bottom half sees underwater
Each eye stores sunlight above and releases the glow below
The line marks where the eye must be kept wet to survive
The upper half is blind and only the lower half truly sees
context: The four-eyed fish (Anableps) has only two eyes, but each eye is split by a band of tissue into an upper half that sees in air and a lower half that sees in water at the same time. Source: Four-eyed fish, Wikipedia (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four-eyed_fish); California Academy of Sciences.

question: Each eye of the four-eyed fish Anableps must send a sharp image to two retinas at once, catching light coming through air above the waterline and light coming through water below. Light bends by different amounts in air and water, yet the eye holds just ONE lens. How does that single lens cope?
answer: The lens is egg-shaped, so its two directions bend light differently
choices: The lens is egg-shaped, so its two directions bend light differently
The lens flips rapidly between two focal settings
A second clear lens slides in only underwater
The lens is filled with two liquids of different density
context: Each Anableps eye has two pupils but only one lens, and that single egg-shaped lens bends light from both air and water correctly onto its two retinas. Source: Four-eyed fish, Wikipedia (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four-eyed_fish).

question: Deep beneath the Pacific Ocean, in cold black water where sunlight barely reaches, drifts a strange fish called the barreleye. The strangest thing about a barreleye is its forehead: a see-through, fluid-filled dome you can look right into, like a soft glass window on the top of its head. What are you actually looking at inside that clear head?
answer: Its two glowing green eyes, tucked inside the skull
choices: Its two glowing green eyes, tucked inside the skull
Its brain, lit up as it thinks
A pocket of swallowed jellyfish
A gas bladder that keeps it afloat
context: The barreleye fish has a see-through, fluid-filled dome for a forehead, and you can look straight through its transparent head at its two glowing green eyes inside. This one is a legend of the deep. Source: MBARI (mbari.org/barreleye-fish-with-tubular-eyes-and-transparent-head).

question: For 70 years scientists thought the barreleye fish's tube-shaped eyes were locked staring straight up. In 2008 the MBARI team kept a live one at the surface. They filmed something inside its clear dome that overturned decades of belief. What did the eyes do?
answer: They swivelled forward to aim at food
choices: They swivelled forward to aim at food
They blinked shut and reopened
They glowed brighter to signal
They retracted deeper into the skull
context: The barreleye's tubular green eyes rotate up to watch for prey overhead, then swivel forward to aim at food as it eats; MBARI first filmed this in 2008 after decades of assuming the eyes were fixed. Source: MBARI, Robison & Reisenbichler 2008; ScienceDaily 2009.

question: The brownsnout spookfish is a small deep-sea fish that hunts in near-total darkness thousands of feet below the ocean surface, where sunlight has almost run out. It builds an image inside its eyes in a way no other backboned animal on Earth does. Each of its eyes is split into two halves. One half still uses a normal curved lens like ours to focus the light. How does the other half focus its image?
answer: With a curved mirror of stacked crystals
choices: With a curved mirror of stacked crystals
With an extra-thick bulging lens
By glowing to light up its own prey
With a heat-sensing pit instead of light
context: The brownsnout spookfish is the only vertebrate known to focus an image with a mirror of stacked guanine crystals, doing so in one half of its divided eye while the other half still uses a lens. A legendary find. Source: University of Bristol news 2009 (bristol.ac.uk/news/2009/6086.html); Wagner et al., Current Biology 2009.

question: The ogre-faced spider — also known as the net-casting spider — is a nocturnal hunter of warm forests that stalks its prey in almost total darkness. It has two huge staring lenses, about 2000 times more light-sensitive than a human's eyes. To squeeze every last photon out of the night, it does something drastic to those enormous eyes on a strict daily cycle. What?
answer: It grows a fresh light-catching membrane each night and destroys it by dawn
choices: It grows a fresh light-catching membrane each night and destroys it by dawn
It seals the lenses shut through the bright daylight hours
It coats the lenses in reflective silk before hunting
It regrows entirely new lenses after every kill
context: The ogre-faced spider's eyes are so light-hungry that it builds a fresh light-sensitive membrane inside them every night and chemically destroys it again at dawn. A legend among spiders. Source: Smithsonian Magazine; Gil Wizen, 'Little Transformers: Deinopis'; biologyinsights.com.

question: A bluefin tuna, a mako shark, and a bottlenose dolphin are three totally unrelated animals — a bony fish, a cartilage fish, and an air-breathing mammal — that all cruise fast through the open ocean chasing prey. Even though evolution built them separately from different ancestors, all three ended up with almost exactly the same overall body shape. What is that shape?
answer: A stiff, torpedo-shaped body that knifes through the water
choices: A stiff, torpedo-shaped body that knifes through the water
A flat, ribbon-like body for hiding on the seafloor
A round, balloon-like body that drifts with the current
A long, eel-like body that wriggles head to tail
context: This is the thunniform (tuna-like) body plan: a stiff, streamlined torso, a narrow tail-base, and a crescent tail. Fast open-ocean swimmers keep re-inventing it. Source: Nature Scientific Reports, 'Skeletal convergence in thunniform sharks, ichthyosaurs, whales, and tunas' (2023), https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-023-41812-z

question: A tuna is a huge fish that hunts in the open ocean. A dolphin is an ocean mammal that must come up to breathe air. Watch a tuna and a dolphin swim past and both look like sleek grey torpedoes shaped by the same water. But look at how each one is actually moving through the water — one clue instantly tells you the dolphin is a mammal, not a fish. What is that clue?
answer: Its tail beats up and down, not side to side
choices: Its tail beats up and down, not side to side
Its tail glows a faint blue as it swims
It has no tail fin at all, just a smooth stump
Its tail spins in a full circle like a propeller
context: A fish's or shark's tail sweeps side to side; a dolphin's or whale's tail beats up and down. The direction of the tail-beat tells you instantly whether you are looking at a mammal or a fish. Source: Whale and Dolphin Conservation, 'Why do whale and dolphin tails go up and down?', https://uk.whales.org/whales-dolphins/why-do-whale-and-dolphin-tails-go-up-and-down/

question: A tuna is a big open-ocean fish that can cruise for days without stopping. Watch one glide by and its whole silvery body seems almost stiff — barely a wiggle from head to shoulder. Yet almost every bit of the power that shoves it forward is happening in just one small place along its body. Where on the tuna is nearly all the swimming motion coming from?
answer: At the narrow tail-base and the crescent tail
choices: At the narrow tail-base and the crescent tail
Along its whole body, rippling head to tail
In its wide, fanned-out pectoral fins
In its puffed-out gill covers on each side
context: A tuna's body barely bends when it swims. The stiff front knifes through the water while almost all the movement is isolated to the very tip. Source: American Scientist, 'How Tunas and Lamnid Sharks Swim: An Evolutionary Convergence', https://www.americanscientist.org/article/how-tunas-and-lamnid-sharks-swim-an-evolutionary-convergence

question: A bluefin tuna is a big ocean fish that hunts by chasing prey at incredible speed — over 40 miles per hour through open sea. As it accelerates, its body shape suddenly changes. The tall dorsal fin on its back and the wide pectoral fins on its sides seem to disappear, leaving a smooth torpedo with nothing sticking out to slow it down. Where did those fins go?
answer: They folded flat into grooves and slots in its body
choices: They folded flat into grooves and slots in its body
They dissolved and will regrow after the sprint
They were shed like a lizard dropping its tail
They pulled inward and turned into extra muscle
context: The first dorsal fin drops flush into a groove along the back and the pectoral fins tuck into slots on the sides, cutting drag. The tuna pops the fins back up for tight turns. Source: ResearchGate, 'Slot for storage of dorsal fin in a Pacific bluefin tuna (Thunnus orientalis)', https://www.researchgate.net/figure/Slot-for-storage-of-dorsal-fin-in-a-Pacific-bluefin-tuna_fig1_321700630; AskNature, 'Fins Provide Streamlined Shape', https://asknature.org/strategy/fins-provide-streamlined-shape/

question: A tuna's tail isn't the flat rowing paddle you see on a goldfish. It is a stiff, thin, crescent-moon curve, held out like a scythe blade behind a narrow ankle of muscle. If you sliced straight across that crescent and looked at the cut end, the shape of the slice would explain why so little of the tuna's swimming effort is wasted in useless swirl and drag. What shape is that cross-section?
answer: A curved airplane wing, an airfoil
choices: A curved airplane wing, an airfoil
A flat, thin blade like a butter knife
A round tube like a drinking straw
A jagged saw-edge for cutting water
context: The tuna's crescent tail is taller, narrower, and stiffer than an ordinary fish tail. Shaped like an airfoil, it makes thrust the same way a wing makes lift, turning each tail-beat into forward push instead of wasted motion. Source: American Scientist, 'How Tunas and Lamnid Sharks Swim'; Nature/PMC thunniform convergence review, https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10550938/

question: Most fish are as cold as the sea water around them, but the bluefin tuna is different. This huge torpedo-shaped ocean predator races across the open Atlantic and Pacific chasing schools of smaller fish. Grip a freshly caught bluefin near the spine and the deep red swimming muscle there is startlingly warm to the touch — much hotter than the surrounding water. What does keeping that muscle warm do for the tuna?
answer: It fires faster and harder, driving the tuna's blazing speed
choices: It fires faster and harder, driving the tuna's blazing speed
It makes the muscle glow to attract mates in the dark
It lets the tuna survive on almost no oxygen
It replaces the swim bladder and keeps the tuna afloat
context: A big Pacific bluefin tuna holds its red swimming muscle about 11 C (roughly 20 F) hotter than the water. Warm muscles fire faster and harder, part of why tuna are so fast. It only warms certain regions, not the whole body, so it is called 'regional endothermy,' not fully warm-blooded. Source: Springer, 'Ontogeny of regional endothermy in Pacific bluefin tuna (Thunnus orientalis)', https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00227-020-03753-3

question: Bluefin tuna are among the fastest fish in the sea, built like a smooth torpedo with a curved crescent tail for pure speed. Millions of years later, the mako shark and the great white shark — both part of a family called lamnid sharks — independently evolved the exact same torpedo body and crescent tail shape, even though they are not closely related to tuna. A few of these lamnid sharks even copied one more of the tuna's tricks. What was it?
answer: They keep their muscles warmer than the sea
choices: They keep their muscles warmer than the sea
They lay eggs in neat rows on the seafloor
They glow in the dark to lure in prey
They breathe air at the surface like whales
context: Like tuna, a few lamnid (mackerel) sharks are warm-bodied, holding their muscles about 7-10 F above the surrounding ocean. The shortfin mako is the fastest shark, with burst speeds around 46 mph (74 km/h). Source: Smithsonian Ocean, 'Shortfin Mako Shark', https://ocean.si.edu/ocean-life/sharks-rays/shortfin-mako-shark; Wikipedia (sourced), 'Shortfin mako shark'

question: A bluefin tuna's red swimming muscle runs hot, giving this huge ocean predator its explosive speed. But here is the danger for any fish: all its warm blood eventually flows out to the gills, where fish breathe by pushing water across thin membranes. In cold sea water the heat should pour right out through those gills. Yet the tuna hangs on to its warmth. What lets it keep the heat inside its body?
answer: A tangle of arteries and veins called the rete mirabile
choices: A tangle of arteries and veins called the rete mirabile
A layer of insulating blubber wrapped around its gills
A swim bladder that stores the warmth like a hot pack
A dark groove along its back that soaks up the heat
context: The rete mirabile means 'wonderful net': bundles of intertwined arteries and veins that trap the muscle's heat before it can leak out the gills. It is a countercurrent heat exchanger. Source: ScienceDirect, 'Heat and oxygen exchange in the rete mirabile of the bluefin tuna', https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/0300962983906126

question: The bluefin tuna's body is a masterpiece of speed — a smooth torpedo shape ending in a crescent-shaped tail. Dolphins later evolved the same body plan, even though they are mammals. But long before dolphins existed, back in the age of the dinosaurs, an extinct sea reptile had already worked out the same design. It swam the ancient Jurassic oceans looking uncannily like a modern tuna, with the same torpedo body and crescent tail. What was this reptile called?
answer: The ichthyosaur
choices: The ichthyosaur
The pterosaur
The plesiosaur
The mosasaur
context: Ichthyosaurs already had the tuna body plan, first appearing about 248 million years ago at the start of the Triassic. One superbly preserved Jurassic Stenopterygius even shows a crescent tail fin, porpoise-like blubber, and dark-on-top, pale-below countershading. Being a reptile, it beat that crescent tail side to side like a fish, not up and down like a dolphin. Source: Capeia, 'The Evolutionary History of Ichthyosaurs'; Lindgren et al., Nature (2018), via Earth Archives, https://eartharchives.org/articles/dolphin-like-marine-reptiles-were-more-dolphin-like-than-previously-thought/index.html  (Legend.)

question: Tuna are fish, sharks split from fish long ago, ichthyosaurs were reptiles, and dolphins are mammals. These four groups are barely related — their last common ancestor lived hundreds of millions of years ago. Yet each one, on its own, evolved into a torpedo-shaped swimmer with a crescent-shaped tail. Something about the ocean itself keeps forcing every fast swimmer toward the exact same design. What is it about seawater that does this?
answer: Seawater is dense and sticky, so speed demands one best shape
choices: Seawater is dense and sticky, so speed demands one best shape
The ocean is too dark for any other body to survive
Salt in the water slowly reshapes any animal that enters
Ocean currents physically bend every swimmer the same way
context: Seawater is dense and sticky, so pushing through it fast is hard. Those strong physical demands force fast open-ocean cruisers toward one high-performance design, no matter what ancestors they started from. This is why so many lineages converge on the tuna shape. Source: Nature/PMC, 'Skeletal convergence in thunniform sharks, ichthyosaurs, whales, and tunas', https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10550938/

question: Bluefin tuna (a fast bony fish), mako sharks (cartilaginous fish), ichthyosaurs (extinct sea-going reptiles from the dinosaur age), and dolphins and whales (ocean mammals) all look strikingly alike on the outside — sleek, torpedo-shaped bodies with pointed snouts and crescent tails. Their skeletons show the copying runs even deeper: all four groups evolved the same hidden internal engineering. What did they build inside their bodies?
answer: A thick, reinforced backbone and a stiffened tail-stem
choices: A thick, reinforced backbone and a stiffened tail-stem
A see-through skull to let in more light
Hollow, air-filled bones like a bird's
A second spine running along the belly
context: Shared skeletons show the convergence is real, not skin-deep: an unusually thick, reinforced backbone and a stiffened tail-stem are the internal engineering needed to concentrate the swimming motion at the very back of the body. (The vertebral analysis behind this is rated medium-confidence in the source.) Source: Nature Scientific Reports (2023), vertebral analysis, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-023-41812-z

question: In most fish, swimming muscle bends whatever flank it lies against. But a tuna's deep red muscle sits buried near the backbone at mid-body, while nearly all the visible motion is back at the tail. How does that muscle move a tail it doesn't even touch?
answer: It hauls on long tendons that reach all the way back to the tail
choices: It hauls on long tendons that reach all the way back to the tail
It squeezes fluid through a channel that stiffens the whole tail-stem
It fires nerve signals to a second muscle packed inside the tail
It winds up the backbone like a spring that recoils at the tail
context: A tuna's red aerobic muscle is decoupled from the body wall beside it. Sitting deep against the backbone, it doesn't bend the nearby flank; instead it pulls on long tendons -- the posterior oblique and great lateral tendons -- that thread backward through the white muscle to the tail-base, driving the tail remotely. Because of this, the muscle's shortening and the body's local bending are out of phase, which is the mechanical secret behind the stiff-torso, all-the-motion-at-the-tail thunniform style. Source: Cromie Lear, Millard, Gleiss, Dale, Block et al., 'Biomechanical Analysis of the Slow-Twitch (Red) Muscle Force Transmission Pathways in Tunas,' Physiological & Biochemical Zoology 93(3):185-198, 2020 -- https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32196408/  (Legend.)

question: An ichthyosaur was a dolphin-shaped reptile that hunted the Jurassic seas around 180 million years ago. One Early Jurassic ichthyosaur fossil is so beautifully preserved that its very skin survived across the ages — and just beneath that skin, scientists found something that proved this ancient sea reptile ran warm-bodied, not cold like a modern lizard. What did they find under its skin?
answer: A thick, smooth layer of blubber packed under the skin
choices: A thick, smooth layer of blubber packed under the skin
A dense net of blood vessels coiled around the muscle
A honeycomb of tiny air pockets sealed below the skin
A pad of packed brown fat that burns to make heat
context: Lindgren et al. (2018, Nature) chemically analyzed a superbly preserved Stenopterygius and found flexible skin over a layer of blubber -- the first direct evidence an ichthyosaur was warm-blooded (homeothermic), the same insulating solution whales and dolphins would re-invent tens of millions of years later. Preserved melanophores even revealed countershading: a dark back and pale belly, the classic open-ocean camouflage of living dolphins and sharks. So the tuna body plan arrived already bundled with warm-blooded, dolphin-like biology roughly 90 million years before dolphins existed. Source: Lindgren et al., 'Soft-tissue evidence for homeothermy and crypsis in a Jurassic ichthyosaur,' Nature 564:359-365, 2018 -- https://news.ncsu.edu/2018/12/ichthyosaur-blubber/  (Legend.)

question: On a cold morning a small lizard climbs up onto a big sunny rock and flattens its body against the warm stone. It sits like that for a long time, soaking in the heat. When the sun finally makes it too hot, it slips off into the shade. A little later it moves right back into the sun. Where does a lizard get the warmth that its body runs on?
answer: From the sun and hot rock outside its body
choices: From the sun and hot rock outside its body
From burning the food in its stomach
From shivering its leg muscles
From a warm nest it built overnight
context: This shuttling between sun and shade is called behavioral thermoregulation: a cold-blooded animal takes its heat from the world around it rather than making its own, so it steers its body toward warmth or shade like moving between rooms. Source: https://southernxreptiles.com/how-do-lizards-regulate-body-temperature/

question: At dawn a snake lies stretched out across the cool ground while a mouse the same size scurries past it in the same chilly air. The mouse must keep eating almost nonstop just to stay alive, but the snake can lie perfectly still for days on end without a meal. What is the deep difference in how these two little animals run their bodies?
answer: The snake takes its warmth from outside; the mouse burns food to make its own
choices: The snake takes its warmth from outside; the mouse burns food to make its own
The snake burns twice the food to stay hotter than the mouse
The mouse takes its warmth from the sun the way the snake does
Both make their own heat, but the mouse makes far less of it
context: This is the fundamental split. Warm-blooded animals (mammals and birds) make their own heat by burning food; cold-blooded animals (reptiles, amphibians, fish, insects) take theirs from the world around them. The whole rest of the story is the trade-off that follows: the mouse can move in the cold but must eat constantly, while the snake is cheap to run but at the mercy of the weather. Source: comparative physiology (Hill, Wyse & Anderson framing).

question: A pet mouse and a pet lizard sit in the same cool room, both doing nothing at all. Within a couple of hours the mouse is frantic to find food, squeaking and scrabbling in its cage. The lizard, meanwhile, can sit still and eat nothing for weeks and be perfectly fine. What is the mouse constantly paying an energy price for that the lizard is not?
answer: Keeping its inner furnace lit at a steady temperature
choices: Keeping its inner furnace lit at a steady temperature
Growing a new coat of winter fur
Storing fat for a coming hibernation
Rebuilding muscle worn out by shivering
context: Warm-blooded is the more expensive engine: size for size a mammal or bird must eat far more than a same-sized reptile because so much of its food is burned just to keep its temperature steady. That is exactly why a lizard can rest quietly for weeks while a mouse hunts for food almost constantly. Source: https://www.open.edu/openlearn/nature-environment/natural-history/studying-mammals-the-insect-hunters/content-section-5.2

question: The ball python is a chunky West African snake that hunts small rodents in the grasslands at night. Because it is cold-blooded — its body just matches the temperature of the air around it — it does not have to burn food to stay warm. That means it can go a shockingly long time between meals without wasting away. For a healthy adult ball python, how long can that fast stretch?
answer: At least six months without a single meal
choices: At least six months without a single meal
About two weeks before it weakens
Three or four days at most
Right through a whole decade
context: A healthy adult ball python can survive at least six months without eating, and the longest fast ever recorded in any snake was 21 months, also by a ball python. A big African rock python can be kept going for up to two years on one very large kill. Not paying to heat yourself is what makes such long fasting possible. Source: https://www.terrariumquest.com/ball-python/how-long-without-eating/

question: The Etruscan shrew is the world's smallest mammal — a tiny mouse-like creature of Europe and North Africa that weighs less than a paperclip. Because it is warm-blooded and so small, its little body leaks heat into the air at an alarming speed. To keep from freezing it must hunt insects and worms almost nonstop, all day and all night. If a shrew stops finding food, how fast can it starve to death?
answer: In as little as two to three hours
choices: In as little as two to three hours
In about two or three days
In roughly a week
In a month, like most small mammals
context: The Etruscan shrew, the world's smallest mammal by weight, must eat 1.5 to 2 times its own body weight in food every single day, and its heart beats up to about 1,500 times a minute, the fastest of any mammal. That runaway furnace means it can starve in as little as two to three hours. Source: https://smart.columbus.gov/columbus-news/meet-the-worlds-smallest-mammal-the-etruscan-shrew-1764805785 ; https://www.mpg.de/14755962/shrews-metabolism-winter

question: A hummingbird burns fuel so furiously that it eats about 80 percent of its body weight in nectar every day. On a cold night it perches alone in the dark, hours from its next sip of nectar. How does a hummingbird keep from burning through its whole body overnight?
answer: It drops into torpor, cooling its body and slowing its engine tenfold
choices: It drops into torpor, cooling its body and slowing its engine tenfold
It fattens up at dusk so it has fuel to burn all night
It lets its heart slow only slightly and simply rides the night out
It roosts deep in a warm tree cavity to slow its heat loss
context: A hummingbird has one of the highest metabolic rates known of any animal. To survive the nightly stretch when it cannot feed, it drops into torpor, cutting its resting metabolism about tenfold and letting its own body cool, then rewarms at dawn. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/uncovering-the-secrets-behind-hummingbirds-extreme-lifestyle-180985186/

question: Honeybees are insects, and insects are usually cold-blooded — they cannot heat themselves the way a mammal can. Yet inside a beehive full of honeybees, the center of the colony stays close to 85°F all winter long, even while snow piles up and freezing wind blows outside. Thousands of bees pack into a tight ball called a winter cluster and somehow generate real body heat. How do the bees produce that warmth?
answer: They contract their flight muscles hard without flapping their wings
choices: They contract their flight muscles hard without flapping their wings
They burn stored honey inside special heating glands
They pant warm air over the cluster in shifts
They press against the sun-warmed hive walls
context: When it turns cold the colony packs into a tight cluster and the bees shiver, contracting their big flight muscles against each other without flapping, generating heat instead of motion. They rotate from the warm center to the chilly edge and back, like huddling penguins, keeping the core near 85°F and rising toward 95°F when the queen starts laying. Source: https://www.betterbee.com/instructions-and-resources/what-your-honey-bees-do-in-the-winter.asp

question: A bluefin tuna is a fish, so its blood should chill to sea temperature at the gills. Instead a mesh of vessels called the rete mirabile, the 'wonderful net,' captures its own muscle heat, running warm outgoing blood right beside the cold incoming blood. Just how much warmer than the sea can this hold the tuna's swimming muscles?
answer: As much as around 20°C warmer
choices: As much as around 20°C warmer
About 3 to 4°C warmer
Around 50°C warmer
Just under 1°C warmer
context: This is called regional endothermy. The rete mirabile captures the muscle's own heat instead of losing it at the gills, up to 99 percent efficiently, so a bluefin tuna can hold its swimming muscles as much as around 20°C warmer than the water it swims in. Warm muscle is faster, more powerful muscle. Source: https://biologyinsights.com/are-tuna-warm-blooded-the-science-of-regional-endothermy/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rete_mirabile  (Legend.)

question: Most sharks are cold-blooded — their body temperature just matches the sea water around them. But one big ocean-hunting shark uses a special network called a countercurrent 'wonderful net' of blood vessels to trap the heat its swimming muscles make. Because of that net, it can hold its body as much as 25°F above the surrounding water, giving it the warmest body of any shark alive. Which shark is this?
answer: The great white shark
choices: The great white shark
The whale shark
The hammerhead shark
The nurse shark
context: The great white is a fish that runs warm. Keeping its body up to about 14°C above the sea gives its muscles more speed and power for the hunt, which is a big part of why it is such a formidable ambush predator. Source: http://www.elasmo-research.org/education/white_shark/p_body_temp.htm  (Legend.)

question: The leatherback is the largest sea turtle on Earth — a huge black-shelled reptile that can grow over 6 feet long. Even though it is a cold-blooded reptile, it swims all the way from the warm tropics up to near the Arctic Circle. Even in polar seas as cold as 7.5°C (about 46°F), it holds its body around 18°C warmer than the water. It has no furnace and it does not shiver. What keeps a leatherback that warm?
answer: Its sheer enormous size holding heat in
choices: Its sheer enormous size holding heat in
A thick layer of blubber like a whale's
Warm blood pumped from a special gland
Basking at the surface between dives
context: This trick is called gigantothermy. As one of the largest living reptiles, over 900 kg, the leatherback's huge body, insulating outer tissues, and heat-exchanger flippers let it hold heat that a smaller reptile would lose, giving it the widest temperature range of any reptile. Source: https://www.nature.com/articles/344858a0 ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2978089/  (Legend.)

question: Whether the giant dinosaurs ran warm like a bird or cold like a lizard is a genuinely open scientific question. In 2014 a team led by John Grady reasoned from how fast the giant dinosaurs grew as they matured and reached a startling verdict about their inner engine. What did that study conclude the giants actually were?
answer: An in-between engine that could raise its heat but not hold it steady, like a tuna
choices: An in-between engine that could raise its heat but not hold it steady, like a tuna
Fully warm-blooded, running as hot and steady as any living bird
Fully cold-blooded, no warmer than the swamps they waded in
Cold-blooded as hatchlings but turning warm-blooded once grown
context: The 2014 study (Grady et al., Science) argued from growth rates that big dinosaurs were mesothermic, neither warm- nor cold-blooded but able to raise their body heat without holding it at a fixed level, like tuna and the echidna today. Other scientists soon published formal comments challenging the statistics, so the debate is far from closed. This is honestly unsettled science, not a settled fact. Source: https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1253143 ; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26023130/

question: For a Burmese python, fasting for months is cheap but digesting is violent. Within days of swallowing large prey its heart, liver, and intestines swell by 40 percent to double their size before shrinking back. How much does its metabolism speed up to power that meal?
answer: Ten to forty-four times its resting rate
choices: Ten to forty-four times its resting rate
About double its resting rate
Roughly a quarter faster
Around a hundred times its resting rate
context: Within days of a big meal a Burmese python's metabolism runs 10 to 44 times faster, and its organs balloon in size, then shrink back to normal once the meal is digested by about the tenth day. The digestive burst is so extreme that sitting still and fasting for months is cheap by comparison, which is the whole cold-blooded bargain. Source: https://journals.biologists.com/jeb/article/211/24/3767/18007/Digestive-physiology-of-the-Burmese-python-broad

question: A fossil skeleton keeps no soft tissue, so it cannot record the body heat that warm-bloodedness makes. Yet a 2022 team led by Ricardo Araújo read the inner temperature of long-dead mammal ancestors from bone alone, and pinned the birth of mammalian warm blood to the Late Triassic. Which fossil clue let them take a dead animal's temperature?
answer: The shape of the fluid-filled canals of the inner ear
choices: The shape of the fluid-filled canals of the inner ear
The scroll-like nasal bones that warm each breath drawn in
The dense growth rings banded through the limb bones
The slope of the long leg bones set beneath the hips
context: Warm blood thins the fluid inside the ear's looping semicircular canals — the organ of balance — the way heat loosens honey, so a hot-running animal needs narrower ducts to keep that fluid reading motion sharply. Reading canal shape across the mammal lineage, Ricardo Araújo's team (Nature, 2022) found endothermy appeared abruptly in the Late Triassic, about 233 million years ago — before true mammals arose (~200 Ma) — alongside a sharp 5–9°C jump in body temperature. Exactly when the warm engine first switched on remains an open, active research question. Source: Araújo et al. 2022, Nature, 'Inner ear biomechanics reveals a Late Triassic origin for mammalian endothermy.'

question: A ground squirrel ends its winter hibernation chilled almost to freezing, then floods itself with heat to wake without a single shiver or twitch of muscle. All that warmth wells up from a special tissue, brown fat, whose cells are crammed with mitochondria. How does brown fat make heat with no movement at all?
answer: Its cells let their fuel's energy leak out as heat instead of banking it as usable power
choices: Its cells let their fuel's energy leak out as heat instead of banking it as usable power
Its cells pack in far more mitochondria and drive them to burn their fuel much faster
Its cells release a hormone that speeds every reaction inside the tissue at once
Its cells snap their stored fat apart in a rapid, self-feeding chemical cascade
context: Normally a cell's mitochondria pump protons across a membrane, then let them flow back through a turbine that banks the energy as ATP, the cell's usable fuel. Brown fat carries a protein called UCP1 (thermogenin) that punches an open hole in that membrane, so the protons rush back with no turbine and no ATP — the fuel's energy escapes purely as heat. This 'non-shivering thermogenesis,' switched on by the sympathetic nervous system, lets hibernating mammals (and brown-fat-rich newborns) rewarm without the muscular shivering that a winter honeybee cluster relies on. Source: 'Thermogenin (UCP1)'; Nicholls & Locke on brown adipose tissue.

question: A honeybee scout is a worker bee whose job is to fly out and search for food. One scout finds a rich patch of clover flowers full of nectar and pollen, then flies straight home into the pitch-dark inside of her hive. Alone in the dark, standing on the vertical wall of the honeycomb, what does she do next to tell her hivemates where she found the flowers?
answer: Dances across the comb in a coded pattern
choices: Dances across the comb in a coded pattern
Leaves a trail of scent leading to the flowers
Buzzes a rising and falling musical tone
Nudges each bee toward the hive entrance
context: The waggle dance: a scout who has found good flowers returns to the dark hive and dances on the vertical comb to tell the others where to fly. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waggle_dance

question: When a honeybee finds a rich patch of flowers, she flies home and performs a special dance on the dark honeycomb inside the hive to tell her sisters where the food is. This is called the waggle dance, and it traces a figure-eight path she runs over and over. But the coded message about the flowers is packed into just one part of that path. Which part of the figure-eight carries the message?
answer: The straight, waggling middle run
choices: The straight, waggling middle run
The wide curving sweep of each loop
The moment she circles back to the top
The pause where she meets a follower bee
context: The figure-eight has two curved return loops, but only the straight 'waggle run' down the middle carries the coded information; the loops just bring her back to start it again. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waggle_dance

question: A honeybee that has found a good flower patch flies home and dances on the vertical honeycomb inside the dark hive to send other bees to the food. This is her waggle dance — a figure-eight with a straight middle stretch called the waggle run. The angle at which she runs that stretch on the vertical comb is a code for direction. If a bee waggles her run straight up the comb, what direction outside is she telling her hivemates to fly?
answer: Straight toward the sun
choices: Straight toward the sun
Straight into the wind
Toward the nearest tall landmark
Back the way the last forager came
