context: The angle of the waggle run relative to straight-up encodes direction relative to the sun. Straight up means 'fly toward the sun'; a run tilted left or right of vertical means that same angle left or right of the sun. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waggle_dance

question: A honeybee returning to the hive with news of flowers dances a figure-eight on the honeycomb. The straight middle stretch — the waggle run — carries the coded message for the other bees. The angle of that run tells them which direction to fly, but the length of the run codes another piece of information. As a foraging bee waggles her middle run longer and longer, what is she telling her hivemates?
answer: That the food lies farther away
choices: That the food lies farther away
That it is a poorer patch
That the wind is against the trip
That more bees should stay behind
context: Duration encodes distance: the longer the waggle run, the farther the food. Roughly one second of waggling means the flowers are about one kilometre off. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waggle_dance

question: Honeybees have two different dances for reporting where food is. When flowers are far from the hive, a scout does a long 'waggle dance' on the comb that codes both the direction and the distance. But when the flowers are very close — under about 50 meters, roughly a school hallway away — she skips that fancy waggle dance and does a much simpler little routine instead. What does that near-food dance look like?
answer: Just circling one way, then the other
choices: Just circling one way, then the other
A single sharp jab toward the door
Trembling in place without moving
Climbing straight up and freezing
context: For food closer than about 50 metres a bee does the 'round dance' - simply circling one direction then reversing - instead of the full waggle dance with its angle and duration code. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Round_dance_(honey_bee)

question: When a honeybee finds flowers, she flies home and dances on the vertical honeycomb to tell her hivemates where to fly. The angle of her dance codes the direction to the food relative to the sun outside. But the inside of a hive is completely dark — she cannot see the sun she is supposedly pointing to, and neither can any of the watching bees. Yet the direction code still works. How does the dancer encode a sun-direction she cannot see?
answer: She uses straight-up, felt through gravity, to stand in for the sun
choices: She uses straight-up, felt through gravity, to stand in for the sun
She remembers the sun's glare on the comb
She points using the warmth of the hive entrance
She copies the angle from the bee who danced before her
context: Inside the pitch-dark hive the bee can't see the sun, so she substitutes 'up' on the vertical comb - sensed through gravity - for the sun's direction. Up on the wall means toward the sun. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waggle_dance

question: When a honeybee scout returns to her dark hive after finding flowers, she does a 'waggle dance' on the comb. The angle at which she waggles tells her hivemates the direction to the food, measured against where the sun is in the sky. But the sun creeps across the sky all afternoon, so a bee dancing for a long stretch has a real problem: the same patch of flowers now sits at a different angle from the sun than it did an hour ago. How does she keep her dance pointing true?
answer: An internal clock slowly shifts her dance angle
choices: An internal clock slowly shifts her dance angle
She stops and re-scouts the flowers
Other bees correct her by touch
She waits for the sun to hold still
context: A bee dancing for a while gradually changes her dance angle to track the moving sun - her internal biological clock corrects for it, so the instruction stays accurate as the sun travels. Source: https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/frisch-discovers-bees-communicate-through-body-movements

question: In the 1940s the Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch was trying to crack the mystery of how honeybees tell each other where flowers are. To follow the movements of one single bee through a crowd of thousands of near-identical workers, he built a special 'observation hive' with glass walls and watched them work. But every bee looked exactly like every other bee. What clever trick let von Frisch pick out one marked forager from all the rest?
answer: Tiny dots of red paint on the thorax
choices: Tiny dots of red paint on the thorax
A numbered tag glued to each wing
Clipping one antenna short
A dab of scent only he could smell
context: Von Frisch marked his foragers with tiny dots of red paint on the thorax and watched them in a glass-walled observation hive by a window, so he could track individual bees through the crowd. He later shared the 1973 Nobel Prize for decoding the dance. Source: https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/frisch-discovers-bees-communicate-through-body-movements  (Legend.)

question: The Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch had watched honeybees do a strange little 'waggle dance' on the honeycomb after coming home from a flower patch, and he suspected the dance was actually a coded map to the food — not just excited wiggling. To prove it, he set out a small dish of sugar water at a known spot in the meadow, let a marked bee find it and fly home to dance, then watched what the audience of watching bees did next. What settled that the dance really was a set of instructions?
answer: The watchers flew straight out to the exact dish
choices: The watchers flew straight out to the exact dish
The watchers copied her dance in turn
The dish emptied faster than any control
The dancer led them there in a swarm
context: After a marked bee danced, the bees that had watched left the hive and flew straight to the exact feeding dish von Frisch had placed - proof they had read the coded run as directions, not merely caught excitement. Source: https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/frisch-discovers-bees-communicate-through-body-movements

question: Inside a honeybee hive it is pitch dark — no light gets in through the wax walls. A scout bee still dances her coded 'waggle dance' on the vertical honeycomb after finding flowers, and afterward the follower bees who attended fly straight out to the exact right patch of flowers. But the dancer's whole run is invisible in the darkness — the followers cannot possibly see it. So what does each follower rely on to pick up the message?
answer: She reaches out with her antennae and keeps touching the dancer
choices: She reaches out with her antennae and keeps touching the dancer
She feels the comb shudder under her feet
She tracks the heat rising off the dancer's body
She listens for the rhythm of the dancer's buzz
context: Follower bees crowd the dancer and keep in contact with her body using their antennae, reading the coded run by touch in the hive's total darkness. Source: https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/frisch-discovers-bees-communicate-through-body-movements

question: In the hot dry deserts of central Australia lives a small spiky lizard called the thorny devil, covered head to tail in sharp cone-shaped spikes. Water is scarce out on the sand, and the thorny devil never bends its head down to drink from a puddle. Instead it just stands still on damp sand, and water somehow climbs up its legs and body all the way to its mouth. What part of the thorny devil actually pulls in the water?
answer: Its skin
choices: Its skin
Its tail
Its eyes
Its front feet
context: Tiny grooves between the thorny devil's spines wick water up to its mouth by capillary action -- so it can drink just by standing in a puddle or damp sand, the water crawling uphill against gravity across its whole body to its jaws. Source: Animal Diversity Web (animaldiversity.org/accounts/Moloch_horridus/); JEB 2016 'Cutaneous water collection by a moisture-harvesting lizard'.  (Legend.)

question: A hungry predator — maybe a hawk or a goanna — closes in on a thorny devil, the spiky little Australian desert lizard also known by its scientific name Moloch horridus. Instead of running, the lizard tucks its real head down low between its front legs and holds perfectly still. Something on top of its body fools the attacker into striking the wrong target. What defensive trick foils the predator?
answer: A knobby fake head
choices: A knobby fake head
A cloud of foul spray
A rattling tail
A pair of glowing eyespots
context: The thorny devil has a decoy 'false head' -- a knobby, spiny lump on the back of its neck. When threatened it hides its real head between its front legs and shows the soft decoy, which can heal if it gets bitten. Source: Animal Diversity Web (animaldiversity.org/accounts/Moloch_horridus/); Wikipedia 'Thorny devil'.  (Legend.)

question: The thorny devil is a small Australian desert lizard covered in hard cone-shaped spikes that make it look like a walking pincushion. Even with such a fierce appearance, it eats just one kind of tiny creature — and only that kind — all day long. It sits beside a busy trail and flicks its dinner up one at a time with a sticky tongue, as fast as 45 a minute. What does this lizard eat?
answer: Ants
choices: Ants
Beetles
Termites
Small spiders
context: The thorny devil eats nothing but ants, taking them one tiny ant at a time off ant trails -- records of about one ant per second and estimates around 750 ants in a single day. Source: Animal Diversity Web (animaldiversity.org, ~750/day); Bush Heritage Australia.

question: A thorny devil (Moloch horridus) crosses open desert in broad daylight with hawks circling overhead. Instead of bolting for cover, it does something odd with the way it walks that keeps a bird of prey from locking onto it. How does the thorny devil move across the open?
answer: Rocks and freezes like a wind-blown leaf
choices: Rocks and freezes like a wind-blown leaf
In a fast zig-zag sprint
By burrowing forward under the sand
In long bounding hops
context: The thorny devil walks with a slow, jerky, rocking motion -- freezing and rocking back and forth as it goes -- thought to make it look like a wind-blown leaf and confuse birds of prey watching from above. Source: Animal Diversity Web (animaldiversity.org); Parks Australia / Uluru-Kata Tjuta (uluru.gov.au).

question: Water in the deep desert is often locked away as damp grains rather than open pools. A thorny devil (Moloch horridus) has a way to squeeze even that hidden moisture out to a drink. What does it do with its legs to pull water from damp ground into its skin grooves?
answer: Shovels moist sand onto its own back
choices: Shovels moist sand onto its own back
Digs a deep well and waits
Presses its belly flat against wet clay
Kicks sand into a rain-catching pit
context: In the desert the thorny devil shovels moist sand up onto its back with its legs, pressing damp grains against its skin so the grooves can wick even more water out of the sand and up to its mouth. Source: Journal of Experimental Biology 219:3473 (2016); asknature.org 'Grooves Gather Water'.

question: Deep in Australia's dry outback lives a small, spiky lizard called the thorny devil. When rare drops of dew land anywhere on its body, water climbs up its legs and moves across its skin toward its mouth -- even flowing uphill against gravity. Tiny grooves running all over its skin do the pulling. About how wide is each of those water-carrying channels?
answer: About 200 micrometres -- thinner than a hair
choices: About 200 micrometres -- thinner than a hair
About 2 millimetres -- like a pencil lead
About 1 centimetre -- like a finger
About 5 millimetres -- like a straw
context: The skin channels that carry water to the thorny devil's mouth are microscopic -- roughly 200 micrometres wide and 100 micrometres tall (thinner than a human hair is wide), running in a network all over its body up to the corners of its mouth. Source: Journal of Experimental Biology 219:3473 (2016), journals.biologists.com/jeb/article/219/21/3473.

question: The thresher shark is a slim ocean shark that cuts through the sea trailing a huge curved upper tail behind it like a whip. No other shark on Earth is built quite like this — the thresher swings that long tail to slap and stun fish before eating them. Compared to the rest of the thresher's body, how long is that whip-like upper tail?
answer: As long as its entire body
choices: As long as its entire body
About the length of one fin
Barely longer than its head
Roughly a third of its length
context: The upper lobe of a thresher shark's tail can equal the length of the shark's entire body, extending in a long sickle-like arc — no other shark has a tail like it. Source: Britannica Kids / Florida Museum of Natural History (thresher shark species profile).

question: Most sharks hunt the same way -- chase a fish down and bite it. But the thresher shark, a long-tailed hunter of the open ocean, does something almost no other predator on Earth does. It kills its prey with a body part almost nothing else hunts with. Which part does the thresher use to strike?
answer: Its tail
choices: Its tail
Its jaws
Its snout
Its fins
context: The thresher is one of the only sharks that hunts with its tail: it whips the giant upper tail lobe overhead like a bullwhip to stun and kill fish, rather than biting them first. Researchers called it 'extraordinarily rare in the animal kingdom to see animals hunt with their tails.' Source: National Geographic, 'Thresher Sharks Hunt With Huge Weaponised Tails' (quoting Simon Oliver).  (Legend.)

question: A thresher shark -- a long-tailed hunter of the open ocean -- charges straight into a swirling ball of sardines. Just before impact it suddenly snaps its wide pectoral fins inward to slam on the brakes. Hitting the brakes tips its back end upward. What does that sudden lift let the thresher do next with its enormous whip-like tail?
answer: Fling it overhead like a trebuchet
choices: Fling it overhead like a trebuchet
Curl it beneath its belly for balance
Lock it stiff to glide silently
Fan it sideways to change direction
context: To wind up the strike, the thresher charges a ball of sardines, then snaps its pectoral fins inward to brake hard — lifting its back end and slinging its tail forward 'over its head like a trebuchet.' Source: National Geographic, 'Thresher Sharks Hunt With Huge Weaponised Tails.'

question: A thresher shark is an ocean shark with a tail longer than the rest of its whole body — a whip of muscle it snaps in the water like a bullwhip when it feeds. Marine biologists off the Philippines filmed thresher sharks hunting a packed shoal of sardines, and slowed the video down to see what one single overhead tail-slap actually did to the fish. What did one slap accomplish?
answer: Killed several fish at once
choices: Killed several fish at once
Herded the shoal into a cave
Startled the fish into scattering
Stripped scales off one fish
context: A single overhead tail-slap can kill several fish at once without a chase: successful strikes averaged 3.6 sardines each, and one strike killed 7 sardines in one blow. Source: Oliver et al. 2013, PLOS ONE 8(7):e67380 (via PMC3707734).

question: The thresher shark, a long-tailed hunter of the open ocean, whips its huge tail through the sea at astonishing speed. High-speed underwater film caught tiny plumes fizzing off the tail-tip -- the very same shockwave trick a mantis shrimp uses to stun prey with a punch. What actually makes those tiny plumes appear along the thresher's tail?
answer: The tail-tip moving fast enough to boil the water
choices: The tail-tip moving fast enough to boil the water
A gland releasing ink to hide the strike
Trapped air escaping the shark's gills
Salt crystallizing in the cold water
context: The tail moves so fast it makes the water boil: filmmakers caught bubble plumes (cavitation) at the tail tip — the same shockwave trick the mantis shrimp uses. Oliver: 'I think the shark's causing a shockwave that's strong enough to debilitate small prey.' Source: National Geographic (quoting Simon Oliver); Oliver et al. 2013 PLOS ONE.  (Legend.)

question: A scuba diver drifts along a reef off the Philippines and meets a big thresher shark -- the same long-tailed open-ocean hunter whose whip-crack tail can kill several sardines in a single blow. Given a tail that powerful, how does the thresher actually treat a human diver it encounters underwater?
answer: It stays shy, with no recorded attack on a person
choices: It stays shy, with no recorded attack on a person
It circles in tight and rams the diver's flank
It lashes its tail toward the diver as a warning
It charges the moment the diver comes near
context: Despite being a fearsome hunter, the thresher is shy and harmless to people: the International Shark Attack File records no unprovoked attacks and no fatal attack by a thresher on a human. Source: Florida Museum of Natural History / International Shark Attack File; Britannica.

question: Three thresher shark species swim the world's oceans, and from the outside they look almost identical -- huge scythe-like tail, big eyes, streamlined body. But only the common thresher's swimming muscle runs warm, many degrees above the seawater around it. Its two cousins stay at sea temperature. What sets the warm-muscled common thresher apart on the inside?
answer: Its red muscle sits deep by the spine, wrapped in heat-trapping vessel nets
choices: Its red muscle sits deep by the spine, wrapped in heat-trapping vessel nets
Its oily liver slowly ferments as it swims, shedding warmth into the core
Its gills reclaim heat from outgoing blood before it meets the open sea
It basks belly-up at the surface between deep dives to soak up the sun
context: This is regional endothermy - the same trick tunas and makos use to power fast, sustained swimming. In the common thresher (Alopias vulpinus) the red swimming muscle is shifted deep and forward, right against the backbone, and sheathed in retia mirabilia: dense 'wonder nets' of blood vessels that work as a counter-current heat exchanger, catching warmth from outgoing blood before it can bleed away at the gills. The muscle averages about 2.3 C above the sea (measured up to 5.4 C above ambient, and as much as 7.6 C above the shark's own white muscle). Its cousins the bigeye (A. superciliosus) and pelagic (A. pelagicus) threshers lack this and run at water temperature. Source: Sepulveda & Bernal, 'The vascular morphology and in vivo muscle temperatures of thresher sharks (Alopiidae)' (PubMed 21688299); Bernal & Sepulveda, 'The red muscle morphology of the thresher sharks,' J. Exp. Biol. 208:4255 (2005).  (Legend.)

question: Threshers are slender fish-flingers today, but roughly 15 million years ago cousins the size of a great white shark prowled the sea, known only from teeth that wash out of Maryland's Calvert Cliffs. When scientists formally named one such giant, Alopias palatasi, in 2023, a single feature of its big teeth stunned them. What was it?
answer: They were serrated - steak-knife edges, unheard of in a thresher
choices: They were serrated - steak-knife edges, unheard of in a thresher
They were grooved to inject venom, unmatched in any living shark
They curved back into hooks like a deep-sea viperfish's fangs
They fused edge to edge into one long continuous sawing plate
context: Almost every thresher tooth ever found - living species or fossil - has a smooth cutting edge, which is exactly why the serrations on Alopias palatasi (nicknamed the 'serrated giant thresher') were such a shock. It and its relative A. grandis reached roughly great-white size, with teeth topping 4 cm, and both lived about 20 to 13 million years ago in the Oligocene-Miocene. A. palatasi was described as a brand-new species only in 2023 by Kent & Ward, from teeth collected at the Calvert Cliffs of Maryland - a giant shark scientists know entirely from its teeth. Source: Kent & Ward 2023, 'A New Species of Giant Thresher Shark (Family Alopiidae) with serrated teeth' (Calvert Cliffs monograph); Wikipedia 'Alopias palatasi' and 'Alopias grandis'.  (Legend.)

question: In 2004, on Ellesmere Island in Canada's frozen Arctic, the American paleontologist Neil Shubin and his team chipped a strange 375-million-year-old creature out of the rock. It was half fish and half four-legged animal -- scales and fins at one end, the start of a land body at the other. Shubin nicknamed the fossil the:
answer: fishapod
choices: fishapod
lungfish
mudskipper
coelacanth
context: Tiktaalik lived in the Late Devonian, roughly 375 million years ago. Because it mixes fish traits and land-animal traits in one body, Shubin coined the nickname 'fishapod' — fish plus tetrapod. It sits right on the road from water to land. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiktaalik  (Legend.)

question: When Neil Shubin's team pulled the half-fish, half-four-legged fossil out of the Nunavut Arctic in 2004, they asked the local Inuit elders to help name it. The elders chose an Inuktitut word from their own daily world -- not from science -- and that is why paleontologists today call the animal Tiktaalik. What does that Inuktitut word actually mean?
answer: large freshwater fish
choices: large freshwater fish
big-mouthed river seal
rock that walks
shallow-water crawler
context: 'Tiktaalik' is an Inuktitut word meaning 'large freshwater fish,' suggested by Inuit elders of Nunavut, where the fossil was found. It was indeed a big freshwater animal. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiktaalik

question: Tiktaalik was an ancient creature that lived about 375 million years ago in warm swampy shallows. It already had a flat crocodile-shaped head, a neck, wrist bones, and lungs — a fish that was halfway to becoming the first four-legged land animals. Its fossils, dug from the frozen rocks of Arctic Canada, run 4 to 9 feet long. But its back still carried one very fishy holdover from its water-only ancestors. Covering that body were:
answer: diamond-shaped scales
choices: diamond-shaped scales
feathery down
armored plates
slimy bare skin
context: Tiktaalik reached about 4 to 9 feet (1.25–2.75 meters) long, and its body was still covered in diamond-shaped fish scales — a reminder that this in-between animal was still very much a fish in many ways. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiktaalik

question: Tiktaalik was a strange extinct animal from about 375 million years ago — a fish that was starting to become a land animal, and one of the earliest known ancestors of everything with four legs, including us. It had a low, flat head unlike any modern fish's rounded snout, and it hunted in shallow Devonian swamps thick with plants and prey. Its two eyes sat in a spot strange for a fish. Where were they placed on its head?
answer: on top of its head
choices: on top of its head
wide-set to the sides
close to the snout tip
on short stalks
context: Tiktaalik's flat, crocodile-like head carried its eyes on TOP — perfect for peering up above the water's surface while the rest of its body stayed hidden below, exactly like a crocodile lurking at the waterline. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiktaalik

question: Tiktaalik was a 375-million-year-old creature, half fish and half four-legged animal, dug from the Canadian Arctic by Neil Shubin's team. In a normal fish, bony gill plates bolt the skull straight onto the shoulders, so the head and body move as one stiff block. Tiktaalik shed those plates, gaining something no fish before it had ever had. What was it?
answer: a neck
choices: a neck
a hinged jaw joint
a rotating eye socket
a flexible spine
context: By losing the bony gill plates that fasten a normal fish's head to its body, Tiktaalik gained a real NECK — the first fish that could turn its head to snap at prey. Source: https://evolution.berkeley.edu/evo-news/what-has-the-head-of-a-crocodile-and-the-gills-of-a-fish/  (Legend.)

question: Tiktaalik was a strange fish-with-legs from about 375 million years ago, one of the earliest ancestors of every four-legged animal alive today. It lived at the surface of shallow Devonian swamps where the warm water often ran low in oxygen. To survive, Tiktaalik could take in oxygen two different ways — one that no purely water-bound fish could rely on. Besides its ordinary gills, what else did Tiktaalik have?
answer: lungs to gulp air
choices: lungs to gulp air
a spare set of gills
a blowhole
gill-filtering barbels
context: Tiktaalik carried BOTH gills and lungs, so it could breathe water and also gulp air at the surface — a body caught right between two worlds. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiktaalik

question: Tiktaalik -- the 375-million-year-old half-fish, half-four-legged creature Neil Shubin's team dug from the Canadian Arctic -- still had thin fish fin-rays for paddling on the outside of its front fins. But cut one of those fins open and, past a shoulder and an elbow, you'd find bones we humans still use today to bend our own hand. What were they?
answer: a wrist
choices: a wrist
finger bones
a collarbone
a thumb
context: Inside Tiktaalik's front fins were the bones of a shoulder, an elbow, and a wrist — the very bones that would become our arms — while the outside still carried thin fish fin-rays for paddling. Source: https://www.nature.com/articles/nature04637  (Legend.)

question: Tiktaalik is famous partly because Neil Shubin's team went looking for it BEFORE anyone had seen it. Reasoning from when fish first walked, they targeted rocks of the right age — and after five expeditions struck the fossil in 2004. Where did they dig?
answer: the Canadian High Arctic
choices: the Canadian High Arctic
the Australian outback
a Gobi Desert cliff
a South African cave
context: Reasoning about when fish moved onto land, Shubin's team deliberately searched rocks of the right age in the Canadian Arctic — and found Tiktaalik on Ellesmere Island in 2004, a rare case of paleontology 'calling its shot.' Tetrapod expert Jennifer Clack said of it: 'It's one of those things you can point to and say, I told you this would exist, and there it is.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiktaalik  (Legend.)

question: Tiktaalik is famous for the shoulder-elbow-wrist bones in its front fins. But in 2014 Shubin's team finally described its back half, and got a shock: in most fish the pelvis is a tiny, simple bone, yet Tiktaalik's was huge — nearly the size of its shoulder girdle — with a hind fin as long and complex as the famous front one. In that powerful back end sat one joint you'd expect only in a four-legged walker. Which joint?
answer: a ball-and-socket hip
choices: a ball-and-socket hip
a hinge-jointed knee
a pivoting, rolling ankle
a socketed, clawed toe
context: The 2014 description of Tiktaalik's pelvis overturned the old 'front-wheel drive fish becomes four-wheel drive tetrapod' story. Its pelvis was nearly as large as its shoulder girdle and carried a true ball-and-socket hip joint with a mobile femur, and its hind fin was at least as long and complex as the celebrated front one. The upshot: powerful, weight-bearing hind limbs began evolving while the animal was still a fish — before anything walked on land. Source: Shubin, Daeschler & Jenkins, 'Pelvic girdle and fin of Tiktaalik roseae,' PNAS 111:893-899 (2014), pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3903263; sciencedaily.com/releases/2014/01/140113154211.htm; Grokipedia (grokipedia.com/page/Tiktaalik).

question: Two enlarged holes sat on top of Tiktaalik's flat skull — spiracles, leftover slits from its gill-breathing past. In its warm, oxygen-poor swamp, they likely let it gulp air at the surface. In its land-living descendants, that very passage was never abandoned; it was rebuilt into a different organ entirely. Which one?
answer: the middle ear
choices: the middle ear
the voice box
the tear ducts
the nasal passage
context: On top of Tiktaalik's flat skull sat enlarged spiracles — relics of a gill slit. Devonian swamp water was warm, and warm water holds less dissolved oxygen, so these top-of-head openings likely helped it gulp air at the surface. In more derived, land-living descendants that same spiracular passage was not lost but repurposed: the space and bones once used to breathe became the machinery of the middle ear, the apparatus of hearing on land. Source: Grokipedia (grokipedia.com/page/Tiktaalik) — spiracle/otic notch 'that in more derived animals became an ear'; corroborated by general Devonian tetrapod evo-devo (spiracle to stapes/middle ear).

question: The sea otter is a small furry ocean mammal that lives in the kelp forests along the North Pacific coast. It floats on its back at the surface of the sea, using its own belly like a little dinner table. There it works to crack open a tough clam, but instead of biting through the shell with its teeth it presses one hard object down against its chest and smashes the clam onto it. What does the otter use as its anvil?
answer: A flat rock it kept from an earlier dive
choices: A flat rock it kept from an earlier dive
A stiff strand of kelp it wound tight
A second clam with a harder shell
A crab claw it snapped off first
context: The sea otter is one of the few animals that keeps and reuses the SAME single tool across many meals. It carries a favorite rock between dives, tucked into a loose pouch of skin under its forearm, and lies on its back to use it as an anvil on its chest. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tool use by sea otters'; ZME Science.

question: The sea otter is a North Pacific mammal that floats on its back and smashes clams and mussels open on a rock resting on its chest. Otters do not just grab any pebble off the seafloor — they are fussy, hunting the bottom for one particular kind of rock, and once they find a good one they tuck it into a loose fold of skin under the armpit and keep it for meal after meal. What trait makes a rock a keeper for a picky otter?
answer: A flat side and a weight of about half a pound
choices: A flat side and a weight of about half a pound
A jagged edge sharp enough to pierce shell
A hollow center it can grip with one paw
A porous surface that traps and holds bait
context: The sea otter becomes picky about a rock's exact shape and weight — roughly half a pound to a pound, with a flat side that works as a good anvil. It tucks that favorite into a pouch of loose skin under its forearm to carry between dives. Source: Silicon Canals; Animals Around The Globe.

question: The Egyptian vulture is a small white scavenger that hunts across the African savanna. It comes across an ostrich egg lying in the grass — the biggest bird egg on Earth, its shell thick as the rim of a coffee mug. The vulture's own beak is nowhere near strong enough to crack that shell open. To get at the rich meal sloshing inside, what does the vulture do?
answer: Picks up a stone in its bill and hurls it down at the shell
choices: Picks up a stone in its bill and hurls it down at the shell
Rolls the egg off a cliff onto the rocks below
Sits on the egg until the heat cracks it open
Pecks a single weak spot for hours until it caves
context: The Egyptian vulture holds a stone in its bill and throws it down at the egg by swinging its neck, repeating until the shell cracks. An ostrich shell is too tough for the vulture's beak, so the thrown stone does what the beak cannot. Source: Wikipedia, 'Egyptian vulture'; National Geographic.

question: The Egyptian vulture is a small white scavenger bird of Africa and southern Europe with a bare yellow face. When it comes across an ostrich egg — a shell so thick and tough a lion cannot bite through it — the vulture picks up a stone in its bill and stands over the egg. But a bird's neck is short, and it has no arm to wind up a real throw. Where does the force to crack that huge shell actually come from?
answer: It swings its whole neck to drive the stone down
choices: It swings its whole neck to drive the stone down
It flaps hard and dives, adding its body weight
It jerks the stone with a snap of its beak alone
It drops the stone from as high as it can jump
context: With no arm to throw, the Egyptian vulture generates its force by swinging its whole neck, hurling the held stone down at the egg and repeating until the shell cracks. This stone-throwing was famously filmed in 1966 near Olduvai Gorge and reported in the journal Nature. Source: Wikipedia, 'Egyptian vulture'; Thouless et al. 1989, Ibis.

question: In 1960, at Gombe Stream in Tanzania, the young English researcher Jane Goodall watched a wild chimpanzee she had named David Greybeard strip the leaves off a grass stem, then poke that trimmed stem down into a termite mound to pull out termites to eat. Why did this one quiet moment shake all of science?
answer: It was the first recorded case of an animal MAKING a tool
choices: It was the first recorded case of an animal MAKING a tool
It proved chimpanzees eat insects for most of their diet
It showed chimps teaching each other by imitation
It was the first chimp ever seen standing fully upright
context: Stripping the leaves off the stem was manufacture, not just use — the first recorded case of an animal making a tool. Until then, toolmaking was thought to be uniquely human. Source: History.com; Leakey Foundation.  (Legend.)

question: In 1960 the young English researcher Jane Goodall was living among wild chimpanzees in Gombe, Tanzania, watching them from close up. She saw a chimp strip the leaves off a twig, poke it into a termite mound, and pull it out covered in termites to eat — the chimp had made a tool. At the time, most scientists believed only humans made tools. When Goodall reported the sighting to her mentor, the famous paleontologist Louis Leakey, he wrote back that the discovery forced a hard choice. What three options did Leakey say science now faced?
answer: Redefine tool, redefine man, or accept chimpanzees as humans
choices: Redefine tool, redefine man, or accept chimpanzees as humans
Rewrite evolution, rewrite the fossils, or start again
Ignore the finding, repeat it, or bury the report
Study apes, study man, or abandon both fields
context: Leakey's exact reply: 'Now we must redefine tool, redefine man, or accept chimpanzees as humans.' The termite-fishing chimp had erased a line long thought to separate humans from every other animal. Source: History.com; National Geographic.  (Legend.)

question: In the Tai Forest of Ivory Coast in West Africa, wild chimpanzees have learned a trick that takes years to master — cracking open the rock-hard Panda nut. They set the nut down on a hard tree root that works like an anvil, then swing a heavy stone hammer down on it with both hands, over and over, until the shell splits. How heavy can the hammer stone that a Tai Forest chimp wields actually get?
answer: Up to about 15 kilograms
choices: Up to about 15 kilograms
About the weight of a golf ball
No more than a single kilogram
Around 50 kilograms, needing two chimps
context: Tai Forest chimpanzees use stone hammers weighing from 3 up to 15 kilograms — a heavy rock swung with real force — to smash the very hard Panda nut against a tree-root anvil. Source: Boesch & Boesch 1984; Royal Society Open Science.

question: Chimpanzee nut-cracking with heavy stones is no recent trick. In the Tai Forest, a rainforest on the Ivory Coast of West Africa, archaeologists digging under a modern chimp nut-cracking site uncovered ancient stone hammers and nut fragments far older than anyone expected -- a real 'chimpanzee Stone Age.' About how old were the tools they found?
answer: About 4,300 years old
choices: About 4,300 years old
About 200 years old
About 500 years old
About 40,000 years old
context: Excavators found a 4,300-year-old chimpanzee nut-cracking site in the Tai Forest — evidence that chimps have used stone tools for thousands of years. Source: Mercader et al. 2002, via National Geographic; ScienceDirect.

question: The Galapagos Islands lie in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of Ecuador, and their strange collection of birds is what famously inspired Charles Darwin. No true woodpeckers live on those islands — but one small brown finch, the woodpecker finch, fills the same job of digging insect grubs out of tree bark. Since it lacks the true woodpecker's long tongue and hammering skull, how does the woodpecker finch pry the grubs out from under the bark?
answer: It holds a cactus spine in its beak to pry them out
choices: It holds a cactus spine in its beak to pry them out
It hammers the bark loose with a reinforced skull
It licks them up with an extra-long barbed tongue
It waits for the grubs to crawl out at dusk
context: The woodpecker finch holds a cactus spine or twig in its beak to pry grubs out of bark — and will even snap the spine shorter to make it easier to handle. With no woodpecker to compete with, it took over that job using a tool. Source: Wikipedia, 'Woodpecker finch'; Earth Life.

question: On the tropical Pacific island of New Caledonia lives a crow that behaves more like a small engineer than a bird. Where two twigs meet at a branching fork on a tree, the crow snaps off the joint and starts shaping it in its beak — nibbling, stripping, working the wood into just the right form. It isn't just poking about. It is building something. What does the New Caledonian crow craft at that twig fork?
answer: A hooked tool it whittles down to snag prey
choices: A hooked tool it whittles down to snag prey
A whistle it uses to call other crows
A nest lining woven from split bark
A blunt club for smashing snail shells
context: The New Caledonian crow trims the fork where two twigs meet into a tick shape and whittles it down into a working hooked tool — genuine manufacture, not just grabbing a stick. Source: Wikipedia, 'New Caledonian crow'; Oxford Behavioural Ecology Research Group.  (Legend.)

question: On the Pacific island of New Caledonia lives a famously clever crow that makes tools. New Caledonian crows tear cutting tools out of the long, saw-toothed edges of Pandanus leaves, in three neat, repeated designs -- wide, narrow, and stepped. Across the whole species, which edge of a Pandanus leaf do most of these crows tear their tool from?
answer: The left edge
choices: The left edge
The right edge
The pointed tip
The base near the stem
context: When making stepped Pandanus tools, most New Caledonian crows tear from the LEFT edge of the leaf — a population-wide 'handedness,' or laterality, seen across the species. The stepped design also takes the most steps to make of the three. Source: Hunt et al., Nature 414:707.

question: On the Pacific island of New Caledonia lives a crow famous among biologists for making tools out of twigs. In one lab experiment, researchers put a piece of food inside a box out of the crow's reach and handed the bird a short stick that couldn't quite touch it — with other objects scattered around the enclosure. Six of seven New Caledonian crows solved the puzzle on their very first try. What did they figure out to do?
answer: Use the short stick to fish out a longer stick, then reach the food
choices: Use the short stick to fish out a longer stick, then reach the food
Snap the short stick to make a sharper point
Wait for a second crow to bring a longer stick
Bend the short stick into a hook to extend its reach
context: This is the 'metatool' problem — using one tool to obtain another. Six of seven crows used the short stick to retrieve a longer stick, then used the long stick to get the food, most on their very first try. Source: Taylor et al., via Wikipedia, 'New Caledonian crow'.

question: The New Caledonian crow is a jet-black tropical bird that scientists think is one of the smartest tool-users on Earth. In one famous experiment, researchers gave a crow named 007 a puzzle box with eight linked stages — a short stick locked behind a door, a longer stick reachable only with the short one, and finally a piece of meat trapped in a tube at the end. Each stage needed the tool from the last stage to unlock the next. Roughly how fast did 007 work through the whole eight-stage sequence?
answer: About two and a half minutes
choices: About two and a half minutes
About half a second
About two full hours
About three days of attempts
context: The crow named 007 solved the eight-stage puzzle in about two and a half minutes, using tools in sequence — one tool to fetch the next — to reach the meat. Source: Alex Taylor, University of Auckland, via BBC 'Inside the Animal Mind'; Gizmodo.  (Legend.)

question: A New Caledonian crow snips a twig, strips the bark, and bends one end into a barb to fish grubs from a rotting log. It then guards that favorite tool between uses. Besides humans and great apes, this crow is the only known animal to do what in the wild?
answer: Craft hooked tools
choices: Craft hooked tools
Farm insects
Weave hanging nests
Use fire
context: New Caledonian crows safekeep their hand-made hooked tools about 95% of the time, trapping them underfoot or tucking them behind bark — behavior that suggests they value a good tool. Source: Klump et al. 2021, eLife.

question: Off the coast of Indonesia, divers filmed the small soft-bodied veined octopus doing something no octopus was believed to do. She had gathered two matching halves of a coconut shell that people had thrown overboard, and she was hauling them slowly across the open sandy sea floor, walking stiffly on her arms like a creature on stilts for up to 20 meters. Why would an octopus go to all that trouble to carry two empty coconut shells across the sea floor?
answer: To reassemble them later as a hideout
choices: To reassemble them later as a hideout
To trap small fish between the shells as bait
To use the shells as paddles for faster swimming
To scrape algae off the shells for food
context: The veined (coconut) octopus carries shell halves — sometimes as far as about 20 meters — to reassemble later as a shelter. Carrying a tool for FUTURE use, when it gives no benefit in the moment, is a rare sign of planning. This was a documented observation by Julian Finn and Mark Norman off Sulawesi and Bali, not a legend. Source: Finn & Norman 2009, Current Biology, via CBC News; National Geographic.

question: In Shark Bay, a bottlenose dolphin tears a cone-shaped sponge loose and wedges it over her beak before jabbing into the rocky seafloor to flush out fish. Other dolphins share the same bay but never take this particular prey. What puts these fish beyond every other dolphin's reach?
answer: The fish have no swim bladder, so the dolphin's sonar can't spot them
choices: The fish have no swim bladder, so the dolphin's sonar can't spot them
The fish burrow so deep in sand that sonar echoes never reach them
The fish hide in rock crevices too tight for an unguarded beak
The fish carry sharp spines that only a padded beak can brave
context: In Shark Bay, Western Australia, a subgroup of Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphins (Tursiops aduncus) called 'spongers' break off a cone-shaped marine sponge and wear it like a glove over the rostrum, then plough the rocky seabed to root out bottom-dwelling fish. Those prey lack a gas-filled swim bladder -- the very structure a dolphin's echolocation normally pings off -- so they are effectively invisible to sonar and can only be flushed out by physical probing; the sponge saves the beak from the sharp rocks, opening a hunting niche no other dolphin can exploit. Krutzen and colleagues (PNAS, 2005) sequenced mitochondrial DNA and found the skill passes almost entirely down the female line, mother to daughter, tracing back to one recent founder nicknamed 'Sponging Eve' -- making it a learned tradition, not a gene or a quirk of habitat. It remains the only documented case of material culture in a marine mammal. Source: Krutzen et al., 'Cultural transmission of tool use in bottlenose dolphins,' PNAS 2005 (pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0500232102).

question: For a century, a sharp stone flake with a shell-like fracture was read as a fingerprint of early humans -- proof someone had knapped a cutting edge. Then wild capuchins in Brazil's Serra da Capivara were filmed hammering cobbles and flinging off nearly identical flakes, yet never cutting a thing with them. What are the monkeys actually after?
answer: The quartz dust they lick off the shattered stone
choices: The quartz dust they lick off the shattered stone
Insects the hammering flushes out of the rocks
Nuts they have wedged against the anvil to crack
A hammer stone they will carry off and reuse
context: At Serra da Capivara, Brazil, bearded capuchins (Sapajus libidinosus) pound rounded quartzite cobbles against embedded anvil stones. Proffitt and colleagues (Nature, 2016) analysed 111 of the resulting artefacts and found sharp-edged flakes bearing conchoidal (shell-like) fractures nearly indistinguishable from the Oldowan cutting flakes long treated as a hallmark of early hominins. The twist: the capuchins ignore the cutting edges entirely -- they pound to lick the quartz dust and grit off the smashed cobble (likely for minerals, or to scrape away lichen). Because a wild monkey mass-produces 'stone tools' with no interest in a blade, the find complicates how archaeologists read the earliest human stone record -- as the Oxford team put it, humans may be 'not unique after all.' Source: Proffitt et al., 'Wild monkeys flake stone tools,' Nature 2016 (nature.com/articles/nature20112).

question: Deep in the South American rainforest, a big black-and-white bird perches on a mossy branch. Its body would just about fit under your arm — but the beak alone stretches on and on in front of it, bright orange or yellow, and about a third of the bird's whole length from tip to tail. Which rainforest bird is famous for that ridiculous, over-sized, brightly colored beak?
answer: Toucan
choices: Toucan
Flamingo
Pelican
Ostrich
context: The toucan is famous for a bill that can run up to four times the size of its own head and nearly as long as the rest of its body. Source: San Diego Zoo Animals & Plants — Toucan (animals.sandiegozoo.org/animals/toucan).

question: The toucan is a big tropical rainforest bird of Central and South America with a huge colorful bill nearly as long as its whole body. When a toucan feeds on rainforest berries, it can only pinch a berry at the very tip of that long bill — far out past its real mouth — and there is no way to just swallow the fruit from way out there. How does a toucan get a berry from the tip of its bill down into its throat?
answer: It jerks its head back and tosses the berry up, then catches it dropping straight down its throat
choices: It jerks its head back and tosses the berry up, then catches it dropping straight down its throat
It works the berry inward along the bill, then rolls it back to the mouth with its tongue
It clamps down to crush the berry open, then laps the sweet juice off the bill
It grips the berry against a branch, then shears off bites small enough to swallow
context: A toucan grabs fruit at the tip of its bill, then jerks its head back and flicks the food into the air so it drops straight down the throat — it eats by throwing its food and catching it. Source: HowStuffWorks — The Toucan (animals.howstuffworks.com/birds/toucan.htm); San Diego Zoo — Toucan.

question: The toucan is a colorful rainforest bird of Central and South America whose beak is nearly as long as the rest of its body — a huge orange banana shape jutting out of a small black bird. You would expect such a beak to weigh the toucan down and tire it out in flight, but the bird flies with ease and barely seems to feel it. What keeps that enormous bill so astonishingly light?
answer: A crisscross scaffold of thin bony struts wrapped in keratin, mostly hollow inside
choices: A crisscross scaffold of thin bony struts wrapped in keratin, mostly hollow inside
Solid bone that grows lighter as the bird ages
A core of soft cartilage like a shark's skeleton
Air sacs the bird inflates before takeoff
context: The bill is a natural foam sandwich — an outer sheath of keratin (the stuff of hair and fingernails) over an airy inner core of bony struts and closed air-filled cells, so it weighs only a tiny fraction of the bird's body. Source: SeaWorld — Toco Toucan Facts (seaworld.org/animals/facts/birds/toco-toucan/); San Diego Zoo — Toucan.

question: A toucan of the South American rainforest -- a black bird with an enormous, brightly colored bill nearly as long as its body -- roasts through a sweltering afternoon, then shivers through a chilly tropical night with that same giant bill still attached. Scientists using thermal cameras found the bird uses its bill to manage its body temperature in both directions. What's the trick?
answer: It ramps blood flow into the bill to dump warmth on hot days, then throttles the flow back to trap it on cold nights
choices: It ramps blood flow into the bill to dump warmth on hot days, then throttles the flow back to trap it on cold nights
It faces the bill into the breeze when hot and tucks it under a wing when cold
It grows a thicker keratin layer for winter and molts it thinner for summer
It pants with the bill wide open to cool, then clamps it shut to stay warm
context: The bill is a controllable radiator: the toucan adjusts blood flow to dump 30–60% of its total heat loss through the beak, one of the largest heat-exchange 'thermal windows' relative to body size of any animal, rivaling an elephant's ears. Source: Tattersall, Andrade & Abe (2009), 'Heat Exchange from the Toucan Bill Reveals a Controllable Vascular Thermal Radiator,' Science 325:468–470.  (Legend.)

question: A tiny hunter of the tropical leaf litter walks the forest floor holding its two long jaws locked wide open, like a spring-loaded trap. When its trigger hairs feel prey, it snaps those jaws shut faster than almost any other move in the animal world — over 60 meters per second, faster than a bullet leaves a pellet gun. Which creature is this?
answer: The trap-jaw ant
choices: The trap-jaw ant
The bombardier beetle
The tiger beetle
The whip spider
context: The trap-jaw ant (genus Odontomachus) cocks its huge straight mandibles wide open at a full 180 degrees, then snaps them shut in about 0.13 milliseconds -- roughly 35 to 64 m/s, over 60 m/s at the top end, one of the fastest movements known in any animal. Source: Patek, Baio, Fisher & Suarez 2006, PNAS 'Ballistic jaw propulsion in trap-jaw ants'; Patek Lab, Duke.  (Legend.)

question: Trap-jaw ants (Odontomachus) live in tropical forests and hunt with jaws that snap shut faster than almost anything else in the animal world. When one is cornered on the forest floor by a bigger predator, it does something startling with those very same jaws: it aims them straight down at the ground and fires them shut. What does this do for the ant?
answer: The recoil catapults its whole body backflipping into the air
choices: The recoil catapults its whole body backflipping into the air
It burrows into the soil to hide
It sprays a jet of stinging acid
It clamps onto the predator and holds on
context: The trap-jaw ant uses one structure two ways: a lethal snap-trap on prey and an ejector seat for itself. Firing the jaws against the ground, the recoil flings the ant about 8.3 cm (3.3 inches) up and backward -- over 20 times its body length, like a five-foot-six adult leaping 44 feet with a snap of the jaw. Source: Patek et al. 2006, PNAS; Larabee & Suarez, PLOS ONE 2015; National Geographic Kids 'Fastest jaw on the draw'.  (Legend.)

question: A trap-jaw ant -- a tropical hunter whose jaws snap shut faster than almost any other animal movement on Earth -- creeps forward with its jaws locked open at 180 degrees. The instant a prey insect wanders between them, the latch fires on its own and the ant never has to aim. What on the inside of each open jaw tells the ant that prey has arrived?
answer: Rows of sensitive trigger hairs
choices: Rows of sensitive trigger hairs
A ring of tiny suction cups
A patch of light-sensing cells
A coating of sticky glue
context: Fine sensory hairs line the inside face of each open mandible and wire directly to the nerves that release the catch -- so the jaws fire the moment prey brushes them, no aiming required. Source: Wikipedia 'Odontomachus'; Patek Lab, Duke.

question: A trap-jaw ant, a tropical hunter named for its snapping jaws, closes those jaws in about a tenth of a millisecond -- one of the fastest movements ever measured in an animal. That is far faster than any muscle inside the ant could ever pull them shut on its own. Muscle alone is simply too slow. How does the ant move those jaws at such impossible speed?
answer: It pre-loads spring energy behind a latch, then releases it all at once
choices: It pre-loads spring energy behind a latch, then releases it all at once
It grows the jaws lighter so they fall shut on their own
It uses jets of pressurized fluid to fling them
It relies on a whip-like flick of its antennae
context: The trap-jaw ant works like a loaded crossbow: it locks the open jaws with an internal latch, builds up spring energy in advance, and releases it in an instant. That stored-and-released spring energy lets the strike accelerate at roughly 100,000 times gravity -- a snap no muscle could ever match. Source: Patek Lab, Duke; Sheila Patek in NBC News 'Trap-jaw ant has world's fastest bite'.

question: A treehopper is a tiny plant-sap-sucking insect that clings to stems in fields and forests. One part of its body -- the plate that would be an ordinary bug's neck shield -- swells up huge and grows into thorns, antlers, spikes, or a horned helmet arching over its back. What is that overgrown part called?
answer: the pronotum
choices: the pronotum
the mandible
the ovipositor
the abdomen
context: In treehoppers (family Membracidae), the pronotum -- normally a small plate on the top of the thorax -- balloons into an ornate helmet sculpted into thorns, antlers, horns, or spiky shapes, giving each species its own alien-looking headgear. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treehopper

question: A hungry songbird patrols a plant stem, hunting for the soft, juicy insects it likes to eat. Right in the open on that stem sits a whole cluster of treehoppers -- tiny sap-sucking bugs with strange bumpy shells. Yet the bird's gaze slides straight over them. What is it about how these treehoppers hold themselves that lets a bird look right past them?
answer: they line up in a row so they resemble the plant's own thorns
choices: they line up in a row so they resemble the plant's own thorns
their bodies are transparent, letting the green stem show through
they flatten against the bark and match its mottled brown color
they hang motionless underneath leaves like tiny curled buds
context: Many treehoppers are thorn mimics: lined up along a stem, a row of them looks exactly like the plant's own spines, hiding the insects in plain sight from birds. Source: https://biologyinsights.com/membracidae-a-look-at-bizarre-thorn-mimicking-insects/

question: A treehopper is a tiny sap-sucking insect the size of a raisin, clinging in groups to plant stems. Ants swarm around a colony of treehoppers like paid bodyguards, biting and chasing off ladybird beetles and other predators that would happily eat them. The ants are not there for nothing, though. The treehoppers hand something over in return for the protection. What do the treehoppers give the ants?
answer: honeydew, a sweet liquid waste they dribble out
choices: honeydew, a sweet liquid waste they dribble out
tiny eggs the ants carry back to feed their grubs
shed skins the ants use to line their nest
a scent trail that guides the ants to new plants
context: Treehoppers suck sugary sap and excrete a sweet waste called honeydew. Ants farm them for it -- guarding the treehoppers from predators in exchange for the sugar, a classic mutualism. Sources: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2627810/ and https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0960982208007409

question: A treehopper's spiky helmet is part of its thorax, so biologist Cera Fisher expected thorax-building genes to switch on as it grows. Instead hundreds of genes lit up that build a structure found nowhere near the helmet. Which structure's genes turned out to grow it?
answer: the wings
choices: the wings
the legs
the eyes
the antennae
context: The treehopper's helmet is part of the thorax, but researcher Cera Fisher found hundreds of genes giving off a wing-like pattern as it grows, prompting her reaction: 'Oh my god, how did something like that evolve?' Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/treehoppers-bizarre-wondrous-helmets-use-wing-genes-grow-180973713/

question: About 68 million years ago, near the end of the age of dinosaurs, a rhino-sized plant-eater roamed the plains of what is now North America. It carried a short horn on its nose, two long horns above its eyes, and a huge bony frill fanning out behind its head. What dinosaur was it?
answer: Triceratops
choices: Triceratops
Stegosaurus
Ankylosaurus
Iguanodon
context: Triceratops means 'three-horned face' -- a short nose horn plus two long brow horns on a big bony frill. Source: AMNH (amnh.org/exhibitions/permanent/ornithischian-dinosaurs/triceratops).

question: Triceratops was a hulking four-legged plant-eater that lived in North America about 68 million years ago. It stretched 26 to 30 feet long from beak to tail and walked on stout, elephant-like legs built low and broad. Roughly how heavy did the biggest ones get?
answer: 6 to 10 tons
choices: 6 to 10 tons
1 to 2 tons
20 to 30 tons
40 to 50 tons
context: Triceratops was rhino-shaped and built low and heavy, weighing 6-10 tons in Late Cretaceous North America. Source: National Geographic (nationalgeographic.com/animals/facts/triceratops-horridus).

question: Triceratops bones are famous for turning up in the very last layer of rock before the worldwide dinosaur die-off begins, right at the top of its range 66 million years ago. Scientists point to a single catastrophe that ended the world Triceratops lived in. What was it?
answer: A city-sized asteroid slammed into what is now Mexico
choices: A city-sized asteroid slammed into what is now Mexico
A slow ice age froze the plains over ten thousand years
Rising seas drowned the continents in one vast flood
A supernova exploded a few light-years from Earth
context: Triceratops lived right up to 66 million years ago, one of the very last dinosaurs, wiped out in the extinction after the Chicxulub asteroid struck what is now Mexico. Source: Wikipedia Triceratops; NatGeo.

question: Triceratops, the three-horned, frilled plant-eating dinosaur of Late Cretaceous North America, snipped tough leaves off with a sharp parrot-like beak, then ground the mouthful down using columns of teeth stacked one behind another inside its jaws. When a tooth on top wore out, a fresh one was always rising up to replace it from below. How many teeth did this grinding system hold at once?
answer: Up to 800
choices: Up to 800
About 60
Exactly 32
About a dozen
context: These stacked columns are called 'dental batteries' -- roughly 36-40 columns of 3-5 teeth each, up to 800 total, for grinding tough plants. Source: Wikipedia Triceratops; Animalia.bio.

question: Triceratops, the three-horned plant-eater of late-Cretaceous North America, carried the largest skull known from any land animal that has ever lived. Its bony frill fanned out behind the head, and the whole heavy skull -- horns, beak, and frill together -- made up nearly a third of the animal from beak-tip to tail. About how long was that famous skull?
answer: About 8 feet
choices: About 8 feet
About 8 inches
About 30 feet
About 2 feet
context: The Triceratops skull reached about 8 feet, the largest of any land animal ever, nearly a third of its body length. Source: Wikipedia Triceratops; AMNH.  (Legend.)

question: Paleontologists compared healed scars on the skulls of two horned dinosaurs from Late Cretaceous North America -- Triceratops, with its pair of long forehead horns, and its cousin Centrosaurus, which carried only a single nose horn. The two-horned Triceratops skulls turned out to carry far more frill wounds than Centrosaurus skulls did. What best explains why Triceratops had so many more frill scars?
answer: Triceratops regularly fought each other with their horns
choices: Triceratops regularly fought each other with their horns
The scars were T. rex bites, not horn wounds
The frill marks were birth deformities, not injuries
Triceratops horns were too soft to wound anything
context: Two-horned Triceratops racked up far more squamosal wounds than one-horned Centrosaurus -- the tell-tale sign of Triceratops jousting rivals of their own kind. Source: Farke, Wolff & Tanke 2009, PLoS ONE (PMC2617760).

question: A microprobe crawling across a fossil Triceratops tooth mapped five different tissues -- one of them a soft, blood-vessel-riddled dentine you would not expect in a grinding tooth. That soft strip turned out to be the whole trick. What did it do as the tooth wore down?
answer: It wore down faster than the rest, carving a groove that kept the tooth self-sharpening
choices: It wore down faster than the rest, carving a groove that kept the tooth self-sharpening
It flexed under the load, cushioning the tooth against gritty sand and stone
It funneled fresh blood to the crown to sense which plants were the toughest
It swelled with fluid to shove the next replacement tooth up into place
context: Erickson and colleagues (2015, Science Advances) dragged a diamond-tipped microprobe across Triceratops teeth and found FIVE distinct tissues -- enamel, hard mantle dentine, orthodentine, soft vasodentine, and coronal cementum -- one more than the four-tissue teeth of horses and bison, until then thought the most complex teeth evolution had ever produced. The blood-vessel-filled vasodentine wore about 1.6 times faster than the orthodentine beside it, so grinding gritty Cretaceous plants hollowed a recessed central channel -- a 'fuller,' the very same blood-groove ground into a sword or knife blade -- that kept a sharp slicing edge instead of grinding to a blunt nub. It is an actual mechanism for how the tooth batteries stayed sharp. Source: Erickson et al. 2015, Science Advances (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4640618/); Live Science summary (https://www.livescience.com/51108-triceratops-teeth.html).

question: The classic adult Triceratops carries two long brow horns that sweep forward over its beak. But when paleontologists lined up a growth series from a 38-centimeter hatchling skull to two-meter adults, they found the brow horns rebuilt themselves as the animal aged. On a young juvenile, which way did those brow horns point?
answer: Backward toward the frill, only recurving forward once it reached adulthood
choices: Backward toward the frill, only recurving forward once it reached adulthood
Straight upward at first, then folding flat against the skull with age
Forward already, just shorter and blunter than the adult pair
Downward past the beak, then lifting and lengthening as it grew
context: Horner and Goodwin (2006, Proceedings of the Royal Society B) assembled a growth series of ten skulls, from a 38-cm baby to roughly 2-m adults, and traced how the head remodeled through life. The postorbital (brow) horns began as straight little stubs, curved BACKWARD in juveniles, straightened out in subadults, then recurved FORWARD in adults. Meanwhile the frill margin, deeply scalloped in babies, sprouted 17-19 delta-shaped triangular bones (epoccipitals) that later flattened, elongated, and fused smoothly into its edge -- so a juvenile Triceratops looked strikingly unlike the forward-horned adult everyone pictures. Source: Horner & Goodwin 2006, Proc. R. Soc. B (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC1635501/).

question: A trilobite crawls across the ocean floor 500 million years ago, in a stretch of prehistoric time called the Cambrian period, when the seas were first filling with animal life. Its body is covered in jointed armor over soft flesh, and it has many legs like a modern woodlouse. Trilobites are long extinct now, but what great group of animals did they belong to?
answer: Arthropods
choices: Arthropods
Mollusks
Corals
Sponges
context: Trilobites were arthropods — the same great group as today's insects, crabs, and spiders. Hard-shelled, jointed-limbed sea creatures, they crawled, burrowed, and swam across the ancient ocean floor for hundreds of millions of years. Source: Natural History Museum, London — 'How trilobites conquered prehistoric oceans' (nhm.ac.uk).

question: Trilobites were small hard-shelled sea creatures that scuttled across the ocean floor hundreds of millions of years ago. Many were not smooth, armored ovals. Their shells grew strange features that may have kept predators from biting them, or kept them from sinking into the soft sea mud. What did these trilobites grow all over their shells?
answer: Long, sharp spines
choices: Long, sharp spines
A thick coat of fur
Rows of suction cups
A pair of grasping claws
context: Many trilobites, especially in the Ordovician, grew elaborate spines all over their shells — long spikes for defense, or possibly to keep from sinking into soft mud — turning the armored crawler into a walking pincushion. Source: Wikipedia 'Trilobite' (Lichida and spinose forms, Ordovician–Devonian).

question: A trilobite -- a small hard-shelled sea creature of the ancient oceans -- is scuttling across the seafloor when a predator looms above it. Its back is all hard armored shell, but its belly and jointed legs are soft and completely exposed underneath. With no hope of outrunning the attacker, what did many kinds of trilobite do when they were threatened?
answer: Curled into a tight armored ball
choices: Curled into a tight armored ball
Buried straight down into the sand
Squirted a cloud of ink
Shed its legs to escape
context: When threatened, many trilobites rolled up into a tight ball — bending the thorax and tucking the tail beneath the head — exactly like a modern pillbug or woodlouse, hiding the soft underside behind the armored shell. Source: Natural History Museum, London (nhm.ac.uk); Oxford UMNH.

question: Trilobites, the hard-shelled sea creatures that dominated the ancient oceans for nearly 300 million years, came in wildly different sizes. The biggest known one, Isotelus rex, stretched over two feet from head to tail. The tiniest one ever found, called Acanthopleurella stipulae, sat at the far opposite end of that scale. About how big was that smallest trilobite?
answer: About 1.5 millimeters, smaller than a grain of rice
choices: About 1.5 millimeters, smaller than a grain of rice
About 2 centimeters, like a coin
About 10 centimeters, like a hand
About 30 centimeters, like a ruler
context: Trilobites ranged from giant to tiny: the largest known, Isotelus rex, reached about 72 cm (over 2 feet), while the smallest, Acanthopleurella stipulae, was just 1.5 mm — smaller than a grain of rice. Source: Wikipedia 'Trilobite' (Isotelus rex; Acanthopleurella stipulae).

question: Trilobites, small hard-shelled sea creatures that lived for nearly 300 million years, were a huge evolutionary success -- more than 22,000 different kinds have been named from the fossils they left behind. But paleontologists warn that those fossils are actually far more common than the animals themselves ever were. Why do so many trilobite fossils exist for each trilobite that lived?
answer: Each one shed many empty shells while alive
choices: Each one shed many empty shells while alive
They laid thousands of hard-shelled eggs
Their shells split into pieces after death
They lived crowded together in vast reefs
context: Like all arthropods, a trilobite grew by molting — splitting its old shell open along built-in weak lines (facial sutures) and crawling out. Because one animal shed many times in a lifetime, a huge number of trilobite 'fossils' are actually just empty cast-off shells, not dead animals. Source: NHM London; Oxford UMNH; PMC review on trilobite moulting.

question: Trilobites carried some of the first true complex eyes in the whole fossil record — the same mosaic, many-lensed design a bee or dragonfly uses today. But one thing those trilobite lenses were made of has no match in any animal alive. What were the lenses made of?
answer: Calcite — clear crystal, actual stone
choices: Calcite — clear crystal, actual stone
A soft transparent jelly
Thin sheets of chitin shell
A ring of tiny water droplets
context: Astonishingly, trilobite eye lenses were made of the mineral calcite — actual clear crystal, a stone lens set right in the head. They are the only animals known to have made their eyes out of rock. Their compound eyes stitched many separate lens units, called ommatidia, into a mosaic picture. Source: Beaty Biodiversity Museum, UBC — 'Trilobite Eyes Are Hard'; ScienceAlert.  (Legend.)

question: Trilobites first appear deep in the Cambrian and vanish at the end of the Permian. Their run was so long that, set beside it, our own genus Homo — barely 2 million years old — is little more than a blink. Roughly how long did trilobites rule the seas?
answer: Almost 270 million years
choices: Almost 270 million years
About 40 million years
About 90 million years
About 900 million years
context: Trilobites ruled the seas for almost 270 million years — from about 521 million years ago in the Cambrian until roughly 251 million years ago. For comparison, our own genus Homo is only about 2 million years old. Source: Wikipedia 'Trilobite'; Oxford University Museum of Natural History.

question: One Devonian trilobite, Erbenochile, carried a towering eye packed with hundreds of stone lenses in dozens of vertical rows, giving it a near-360-degree view around itself. Perched right on top of that eye-tower sat one more small structure. What was it?
answer: A shell rim shading the eye from above
choices: A shell rim shading the eye from above
A second eye facing backward
A pair of long feeler-antennae
A hollow snorkel-like tube
context: Erbenochile's tall eye held roughly 560 calcite lenses in 33-36 vertical rows, giving it a nearly 360-degree view at eye level — and a rim of shell projected over the top to block glare from light overhead. It was a fossil animal wearing its own visor. Source: Fortey & Chatterton, 'A Devonian Trilobite with an Eyeshade,' Science (2003).  (Legend.)

question: After ruling the oceans for 270 million years, every last trilobite disappeared about 251 million years ago in the end-Permian catastrophe, the 'Great Dying.' This was no ordinary die-off. Of every kind of living thing in the sea and on land, how much did this single event erase?
answer: More than 90% of all species
choices: More than 90% of all species
About 10% of all species
About one-third of all species
About half of all species
context: After 270 million years, trilobites vanished completely in the end-Permian 'Great Dying' — the largest mass extinction in Earth's history, which killed more than 90% of all species on the planet. Not a single trilobite survived it. Source: Oxford University Museum of Natural History; Wikipedia 'Trilobite' (end-Permian extinction).  (Legend.)

question: A phacopid trilobite's calcite eye lens looks like a single crystal blob, but 3-D modeling revealed it as two stacked units meeting at a curved inner surface. That surface matched a lens design Descartes and Huygens would work out on paper only 400 million years later. What optical feat did the trilobite's built-in surface pull off?
answer: Focused every ray to one crisp point
choices: Focused every ray to one crisp point
Split white light into rainbow bands
Filtered out the sea's dim blue glow
Polarized the light to cut the glare
context: Those two designs are the only aberration-correcting lens shapes humans ever derived on paper — René Descartes in 1637 and Christiaan Huygens in 1690 — yet a phacopid grew the same aspherical calcite interface some 400 million years earlier, cancelling the blur (spherical aberration) that plagues a simple lens and driving light to a single sharp focus. Clarkson & Levi-Setti first matched the geometry (Nature 261:130, 1975, 'Trilobite eyes and the optics of Des Cartes and Huygens'); Lee, Torney & Owen later measured a real magnesium-concentration contrast between the two calcite units, chemical proof the doublet was genuine (Palaeontology 50:1031, 2007).  (Legend.)

question: Millions of trilobite shells sit in collections, yet no one had ever seen what a trilobite actually ate — the soft gut never survives. Then in 2023 a synchrotron scan looked inside a 465-million-year-old Bohemolichas and found its gut packed solid. What was crammed in there?
answer: Crushed shells of clams, ostracods, and shelled seafloor prey
choices: Crushed shells of clams, ostracods, and shelled seafloor prey
A soupy mush of filtered plankton and free-drifting algae
Soft marine worms tugged live from their muddy burrows
Films of bacteria scraped off the muddy seafloor bottom
context: It was the first trilobite ever found with its gut contents preserved — 3-D imaged by high-resolution synchrotron microtomography at the ESRF — despite the millions of trilobite fossils already known. The crushed shells mark Bohemolichas incola as an opportunistic durophage: a shell-crusher and scavenger that bolted small seafloor animals whole or in fragments. Tellingly, the swallowed shells were not etched by acid, so the team inferred a neutral-to-alkaline gut like a modern horseshoe crab or crustacean, not the acidic stomach of a vertebrate. Kraft, Vaškaninová, Mergl, Budil, Fatka & Ahlberg, Nature 622:545 (2023), 'Uniquely preserved gut contents illuminate trilobite palaeophysiology'.  (Legend.)

question: Back in the Jurassic, over 150 million years ago, the tuatara's spiny reptile relatives scurried among the dinosaurs on nearly every continent. Then the whole group vanished -- except for the tuatara itself, a lizard-shaped reptile that today survives only on a few small islands off New Zealand. What nickname has it earned because of that long survival?
answer: A living fossil, its lineage older than lizards
choices: A living fossil, its lineage older than lizards
A missing link, caught mid-change to a snake
A living rainbow, for its shifting colors
A living compass, for its unerring homing
context: The tuatara is the sole surviving member of an order that flourished 200 million years ago. Its lineage split off before lizards and snakes even existed. Source: Wikipedia (Tuatara); NZ Geographic, 'Tuatara — A survivor from the dinosaur age'.  (Legend.)

question: The tuatara is a rare reptile of New Zealand that looks like a lizard but belongs to its own ancient order -- the last surviving member of a group older than the first dinosaurs. A ridge of tall, pointed spines called the crest runs down its back, standing tallest on the males. When a male tuatara squares off against a rival on his patch of rock, what does he do with that crest?
answer: Flares it and inflates his body dark
choices: Flares it and inflates his body dark
Sheds it in a startling spray of spines
Snaps it flat and plays dead
Lights it up with glowing tips
context: The Māori name 'tuatara' means 'peaks on the back', describing the spiny crest down its spine — largest in males, who erect the crest and darken as they inflate the body during territorial display. Source: Wikipedia (Tuatara).

question: The tuatara is a lizard-shaped reptile that survives only on a few small islands off New Zealand -- the last of an ancient line older than lizards. On the crown of a tuatara hatchling's head sits a small pale patch, ringed by scales that slowly grow over it as the animal matures. Almost no other living reptile carries anything like the organ beneath that patch. What is it?
answer: A working third eye, with its own lens and retina
choices: A working third eye, with its own lens and retina
A heat-sensing pit that maps warm prey
A pressure gland that reads coming storms
A scent organ that tastes the air
context: The tuatara's parietal eye is a genuine third eye, complete with lens and light-sensitive retina, visible in hatchlings before scales cover it. Source: Wikipedia (Tuatara); Animal Diversity Web (Sphenodon punctatus).  (Legend.)

question: The tuatara's third eye, perched on the crown of its head, cannot form a picture of the world. Yet it earns its keep. Researchers think this organ works as a kind of natural compass the animal uses to set its inner clock and body temperature through the changing seasons. What kind of compass is it?
answer: A sun-compass, reading daylight
choices: A sun-compass, reading daylight
A magnetic compass, reading Earth's field
A star-compass, reading the night sky
A wind-compass, reading the breeze
context: The parietal eye is thought to act as a light sensor and sun-compass, tracking daylight to regulate the tuatara's circadian rhythms and temperature rather than forming images. Source: Wikipedia (Tuatara); 'The lonely eye', PMC/NIH.

question: Nearly every reptile basks in the sun to warm its body, and most thrive in real heat. The tuatara is the strange exception: it stays active in near-freezing cold and can barely tolerate a warm afternoon. Its preferred body temperature — the lowest of any reptile — sits at just what?
context: The tuatara prefers a body temperature of about 16–21°C — the lowest of any reptile — and stays active down to 5°C, overheating and dying above about 28°C. Source: Wikipedia (Tuatara); Animal Diversity Web (Sphenodon punctatus).  (Legend.)

question: A tuatara grows slowly for its first 35 years, then keeps going for decade after decade. At the Southland Museum, a captive male named Henry stunned his keepers not merely by surviving to a great age, but by doing something no one expects of so ancient an animal. What was Henry still doing past the age of 100?
answer: Fathering new offspring
choices: Fathering new offspring
Growing a fresh set of teeth
Regrowing a lost tail
Shedding his skin whole
context: Tuatara can live past 100. Henry, a captive male at the Southland Museum, was reported still breeding — fathering offspring — at age 111. Source: Wikipedia (Tuatara); Animal Diversity Web (Sphenodon punctatus).  (Legend.)

question: A two-legged meat-eating dinosaur about 40 feet long stalked western North America 66 million years ago -- the very last days of the Late Cretaceous, right before an asteroid strike ended the age of dinosaurs. It stood 13 feet tall at the hip and weighed up to 8 tons. Which famous dinosaur was it?
answer: Tyrannosaurus rex
choices: Tyrannosaurus rex
Triceratops horridus
Stegosaurus ungulatus
Brachiosaurus altithorax
context: Tyrannosaurus rex means 'tyrant lizard king.' It stood roughly 13 feet tall at the hip and could weigh up to about 8 tons, living at the very end of the age of dinosaurs, 68 to 66 million years ago. Source: Australian Museum fact sheet, https://australian.museum/learn/dinosaurs/fact-sheets/tyrannosaurus-rex/

question: Tyrannosaurus rex, the giant meat-eater of late-Cretaceous North America, had a huge boxy skull built for crushing bone. Inside it sat roughly 60 curved teeth and the massive jaw muscles that powered its bite. Roughly how long was that whole skull, measured from the snout tip to the back of the head?
answer: About 5 feet (1.5 m)
choices: About 5 feet (1.5 m)
About 1 foot (0.3 m)
About 15 feet (4.5 m)
About 2 inches (5 cm)
context: A T. rex skull was about 1.5 meters (5 feet) long, roughly as long as a grown person is tall, and carried around 60 teeth. A head that size gave the animal room for the bone-crushing jaw muscles that made it such a fearsome predator.
