Source: Australian Museum fact sheet, https://australian.museum/learn/dinosaurs/fact-sheets/tyrannosaurus-rex/

question: Tyrannosaurus rex hunted through the swamps and forests of North America about 68 million years ago. People today picture a giant meat-eater with thin, knife-like teeth for slicing flesh, the way a shark or a movie dinosaur is drawn. But the back teeth of T. rex broke that expectation completely -- they were built for a very different job. What were those back teeth shaped like?
answer: Thick and banana-shaped
choices: Thick and banana-shaped
Flat and shovel-shaped
Long and needle-thin
Curved like a comb
context: The back teeth of T. rex were thick and banana-shaped, not thin blades. The largest reached about 20 to 30 cm (8 to 12 inches) long including the root, and were built to withstand struggling prey and crush bone. Source: Extinct Atlas T. rex skull guide, https://extinctatlas.org/species-guide/tyrannosaurus-rex-skull-and-teeth/

question: Tyrannosaurus rex, the great meat-eating dinosaur of late-Cretaceous North America, gripped its prey with about 60 curved teeth. Every time it bit down hard on a struggling Triceratops or duck-billed hadrosaur, one of those teeth might snap off deep in the wound. Unlike a modern human, T. rex did not lose that tooth for life. What happened to the gap left behind in the jaw?
answer: A fresh tooth grew in to replace it
choices: A fresh tooth grew in to replace it
The jaw sealed the socket shut for good
A neighboring tooth slid over to fill it
The gum hardened into a bony ridge
context: T. rex replaced its teeth throughout its life. If a tooth broke off while feeding, a new tooth grew in to take its place, so the animal never ran short of weapons. Source: Australian Museum / Extinct Atlas, https://extinctatlas.org/species-guide/tyrannosaurus-rex-skull-and-teeth/

question: When Tyrannosaurus rex, the giant meat-eater of late-Cretaceous North America, clamped its jaws around a Triceratops, its bite drove down with tremendous force. Scientists later reconstructed how strong that bite was by measuring the tooth marks left in fossil bones and modeling the massive jaw muscles that packed the back of the T. rex skull. Roughly how much force did those jaws deliver?
answer: About 8,000 pounds
choices: About 8,000 pounds
About 3,000 pounds
About 5,500 pounds
About 12,000 pounds
context: T. rex bit with a force of about 8,000 pounds, nearly 3.6 tonnes, the strongest bite of any known land animal. The pointed tips of its teeth could focus pressures up to about 431,000 pounds per square inch, enough to pulverize bone. Source: Gignac & Erickson, Scientific Reports 2017, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-017-02161-w

question: In 1998 the American paleontologist Karen Chin, a scientist who studies the fossils that many of her colleagues walk right past, published a paper describing a strange 15-pound lump of rock dug up in Saskatchewan, Canada. It had been left behind by a Tyrannosaurus rex more than 65 million years ago, and it was the largest specimen of its kind ever found. What was this famous find?
answer: Fossilized dung packed with crushed bone
choices: Fossilized dung packed with crushed bone
A jawbone with a tooth still lodged in it
A footprint pressed deep into old mud
A nest of eggs with unhatched young
context: The 15-pound (7 kg) T. rex coprolite, or fossilized dung, from Saskatchewan was packed with crushed fragments of a young plant-eating dinosaur's bones, proving T. rex swallowed bone. It is the largest meat-eater dropping ever found. Source: Karen Chin et al., Nature 1998, 'A king-sized theropod coprolite', https://www.nature.com/articles/31461

question: Paleontologists poured latex or plaster into the empty inside of Tyrannosaurus rex skulls to make casts of the brain that once sat there. Those casts revealed that one region devoted to a single sense was proportionally among the largest of any known dinosaur -- larger than the parts for sight or hearing. Which sense was T. rex especially built for?
answer: Smell
choices: Smell
Hearing
Touch
Taste
context: The olfactory bulbs, the part of the brain handling smell, were proportionally enormous in T. rex, among the largest of any known dinosaur. It likely could detect carcasses or blood from far away. Source: AMNH, 'How Superior Senses Helped T. rex Hunt', https://www.amnh.org/explore/news-blogs/t-rex-super-senses

question: Tyrannosaurus rex weighed as much as a modern school bus and stood over a dozen feet tall at the hip, yet it is famous for the wild mismatch between that huge body and its stubby, almost comical front arms. Each little arm was barely three feet long and ended in an odd number of clawed fingers. How many fingers did each tiny arm have?
answer: Two
choices: Two
Three
Five
Four
context: Each T. rex arm ended in just two fingers, while most of its relatives had three. The arm bones show the limbs were thick and muscular, but what T. rex actually used them for, pushing up off the ground, gripping prey, or mating, is still debated. Source: Natural History Museum, https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/how-did-tyrannosaurus-use-its-arms.html

question: About 66 million years ago in what is now western North America, a young Tyrannosaurus rex was living through a stage of its life scientists can now read like a book. Deep inside a rex's leg bone, growth rings stack up the way tree rings do — one line for every year lived. When paleontologists sliced open the bones of teenage rexes, the rings from about age 14 to age 18 revealed something dramatic. What did those years record?
answer: A teenage growth spurt packing on pounds daily
choices: A teenage growth spurt packing on pounds daily
A long stretch of near-starvation and shrinking
A slow, steady gain across its whole lifespan
A sudden stop in growth in its earliest years
context: Growth rings show T. rex bulked up in a teenage growth spurt from about age 14 to 18, packing on roughly 4.6 pounds (about 2 kg) a day at its peak and adding most of its adult weight in just a few years. Source: Erickson et al.; Science News 'Growth Spurt', https://www.sciencenews.org/article/growth-spurt-teenage-tyrannosaurs-packed-pounds

question: Tyrannosaurus rex had a 30-foot tyrant cousin named Yutyrannus, announced in 2012, whose fossils preserved a soft-tissue feature that hints parts of T. rex may have looked different from the bare-scaled giant people usually picture. What did Yutyrannus preserve?
answer: Down-like feathery filaments
choices: Down-like feathery filaments
A fleshy throat pouch
A brightly color-banded skin patch
A dangling skin wattle
context: Yutyrannus, a roughly 30-foot feathered tyrannosaur, was found with down-like filaments, which is why scientists suspect parts of T. rex may have had a sparse feathery covering. Direct T. rex skin impressions found so far show scales, so full feathering is not settled. Source: AMNH Yutyrannus, https://www.amnh.org/explore/news-blogs/yutyrannus-huali-feathered-tyrannosaur  (Legend.)

question: In 1990 the American fossil hunter Sue Hendrickson spotted bones sticking out of a cliff near Faith, South Dakota. She had stumbled onto a Tyrannosaurus rex skeleton, and the specimen was later nicknamed Sue in her honor. Sue now stands mounted in the Field Museum in Chicago and is one of the most-studied dinosaur skeletons in the world. What makes Sue so prized by scientists?
answer: It is about 90 percent complete
choices: It is about 90 percent complete
It is the smallest T. rex on record
It was the first ever dug up
It still had skin covering the bones
context: SUE, nicknamed after fossil hunter Sue Hendrickson, is about 90 percent complete and over 40 feet long, one of the most complete T. rex skeletons ever found. SUE sold at auction in 1997 for $8.3 million and is now displayed at the Field Museum in Chicago. Source: Field Museum, https://www.fieldmuseum.org/blog/sue-t-rex  (Legend.)

question: In 2005 Mary Schweitzer found soft, still-bendy tissue inside a 68-million-year-old Tyrannosaurus rex thigh bone. Two years later she and John Asara pulled collagen protein from it and compared it to living animals. Which creature's protein turned out to be the closest match?
answer: A chicken
choices: A chicken
A crocodile
An ostrich
An iguana
context: That 2007 result, published in Science, was the first time anyone had read a dinosaur's actual protein rather than just its bone shape -- and the recovered amino-acid sequence lined up with birds, matching chicken most closely of all. It was molecular confirmation of what the skeletons already suggested: birds are living theropod dinosaurs, so T. rex is far nearer kin to a barnyard hen than to any crocodile or lizard. The femur was specimen MOR 1125, nicknamed 'B-rex.' Sources: Schweitzer, Asara et al., Science 316:277-280 (2007), https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1138709 ; summary https://phys.org/news/2007-04-soft-tissue-million-year-old-tyrannosaurus-rex.html  (Legend.)

question: A small bat of Latin American cattle country is a strict, single-food specialist. It is one of only three mammals on Earth that eats nothing else for its entire life -- never fruit, never insects, never nectar. What is the only thing on this bat's menu?
answer: Blood
choices: Blood
Fruit
Insects
Nectar
context: The common vampire bat (Desmodus rotundus) is one of just three mammal species that live entirely on blood. It doesn't suck it like the movies show -- it presses its grooved lower lip and tongue to a small cut and laps, like a cat at a bowl of milk. Source: Wikipedia, Vampire bat; HowStuffWorks 'Meet the Real Vampires of the Animal Kingdom'.

question: A common vampire bat glides out of the Latin American night and lands near a sleeping cow. In total darkness, the bat needs to find the one spot on the cow's body where blood runs closest under the skin, so its meal will be easy to lap. Three tiny pit organs set around its nose let the bat locate that spot without ever seeing it. What do those pit organs sense?
answer: The heat radiating off the animal
choices: The heat radiating off the animal
The animal's heartbeat vibrations
The smell of the blood vessels
The faint sound of blood flowing
context: Three pit organs around the nose, called leaf pits, sense warmth radiating off a warm-blooded animal from as far as 20 centimeters away, letting the bat aim for the exact spot where blood runs closest to the surface. Source: Nature news 2011; National Geographic 'Vampire Bats Have Vein Sensors'; Wikipedia, Infrared sensing in vampire bats.

question: A common vampire bat lands lightly on a sleeping tapir in the Latin American forest and slices a small nick in the animal's shoulder. The tapir never even stirs. The bat's two upper incisors -- the front teeth on the top jaw -- cut so cleanly because those teeth carry an unusual trait that no other mammal shares. What makes them so keen?
answer: They lack enamel and stay razor-sharp
choices: They lack enamel and stay razor-sharp
They inject a numbing venom first
They are coated in a slick oil
They vibrate rapidly like a saw
context: The upper incisors are so sharp and lack enamel that they slice a tiny cut without waking the animal, and they're self-sharpening. Museum workers have cut themselves just handling vampire-bat skulls. Source: Wikipedia, Vampire bat; DentisX 'The Specialized Teeth of Vampire Bats for Blood Feeding'.

question: A common vampire bat, a small blood-drinking bat of Latin America, laps at a tiny nick it has cut in a sleeping cow's leg. It keeps feeding there for a full 20 minutes -- and unlike an ordinary scratch on your knee, the little wound refuses to seal. Something the bat is leaving behind in the cut is holding the meal open. What in the bat lets a single meal last that long?
answer: A chemical in its saliva that blocks the blood from clotting
choices: A chemical in its saliva that blocks the blood from clotting
A grip that keeps the two teeth wedged in the skin
A tongue that scrapes away each new clot
A body heat that keeps the blood warm and thin
context: The bat's saliva holds an anticoagulant nicknamed 'draculin' that blocks clotting, so the little cut keeps bleeding while the bat laps for up to 20 minutes. Source: Wikipedia, Draculin; MDPI Toxins 'Vampire Venom' (PMC6356263).  (Legend.)

question: There are more than 1,300 kinds of bat in the world, and almost every one of them is helpless on the ground -- if a bat falls off a branch or a cave ceiling, it can only crawl awkwardly, dragging its wings, until it can climb up and take off again. The common vampire bat of Latin America is the great exception. On solid ground, what can this one bat uniquely do that no other bat can?
answer: Run, galloping along the ground
choices: Run, galloping along the ground
Swim across small streams
Dig burrows to hide in
Leap straight up ten times its height
context: Out of more than 1,300 bat species, only the common vampire bat can run. It gallops with a bounding gait that uses its powerful wings, not its legs, to push off the ground -- one scientist called it 'kind of like running push-ups.' Source: Riskin & Hermanson, Nature (2005); Science 'Vampires Run'.  (Legend.)

question: Scientists at Cornell University in New York wanted to know whether the tiny vampire bat of Central America truly runs on the ground or only shuffles quickly. They set several vampire bats down on a laboratory treadmill and slowly cranked up the belt speed while high-speed cameras rolled. On the film, the vampire bat did something no other bat on Earth is known to do. What was it?
answer: Leave the ground completely between strides
choices: Leave the ground completely between strides
Fold its wings and sprint on its hind legs
Grip the moving belt with hooked thumbs
Somersault forward to keep up the pace
context: On a treadmill vampire bats walk on all fours at slow speeds, but at about 1.8 km/h they break into a true run, leaving the ground completely between strides. Cornell researchers filmed them in a plexiglass cage to prove it. Source: Riskin & Hermanson, Nature (2005); Cornell Daily Sun (2005).

question: A vampire bat is a tiny animal — only about 40 grams, lighter than a slice of bread. In one nighttime meal it can gulp down more than 20 grams of blood from a sleeping cow, a full third of its own body weight. Loaded with that much liquid, it would be too heavy to fly back to its roost. Yet within two minutes of feeding, the bat lightens itself. How does it dump the extra load so fast?
answer: It pees out the watery part right at the wound
choices: It pees out the watery part right at the wound
It coughs up the extra to a waiting roost-mate
It rests until the meal digests down
It clings to the prey and waits till dawn
context: A gorged bat would be too heavy to fly, so it starts peeing out the watery part of the blood within two minutes of feeding, right there at the wound. Source: Wikipedia, Vampire bat; Bohn et al., kidney physiology (PMC/PubMed 12010738).

question: Common vampire bats have such a fast body clock that missing just three nights of feeding in a row will kill them of starvation. When one bat comes back to the cave roost hungry, having failed to find any animal to feed on, another well-fed bat in the group can save its life. The full bat does something surprising to keep the hungry one alive. What does it do?
answer: Throwing up part of its own blood meal into the hungry bat's mouth
choices: Throwing up part of its own blood meal into the hungry bat's mouth
Leading the hungry bat back to a fresh wound
Wrapping its wings around it to keep it warm
Sharing the warmest sleeping spot in the roost
context: A vampire bat dies after about 70 hours without a meal -- roughly three missed nights. A bat that fed well will regurgitate part of its meal into the mouth of a hungry roost-mate, giving up a little to save a friend's life. Source: Wilkinson (1984); Scientific American 'Blood Sisters'; Carter & Wilkinson (PMC3574350).  (Legend.)

question: The American biologist Gerald Wilkinson set up cages of common vampire bats and watched, night after night, as one bat gave up part of its own hard-earned blood meal to feed a hungry neighbor. He recorded 950 sharing bouts in all, trying to figure out what actually decides who a full bat will feed. One factor stood out far above the rest. Which one?
answer: Whether that bat had fed IT before
choices: Whether that bat had fed IT before
How closely the two bats were related
Which bat was physically largest
How loudly the hungry bat begged
context: Across 950 sharing bouts, the best predictor of which bat a hungry bat fed was who had fed it before -- 8.5 times more important than relatedness. Vampire bats keep score, remembering who shared and paying it back. Source: Carter & Wilkinson (PMC3574350).  (Legend.)

question: Deep in the ocean drifts a small, dark, jelly-like animal called the vampire squid. Its eight arms are joined by a webbed cloak of skin, its body is a deep blood-red, and its scientific name — Vampyroteuthis infernalis — literally means 'vampire squid from hell.' The name sounds terrifying, as if it must be a fierce hunter. But what does this creature actually feed on?
answer: Drifting flakes of dead matter it collects while floating
choices: Drifting flakes of dead matter it collects while floating
Live fish it chases down and drains of blood
Warm mammal blood, like the bat it is named for
Coral polyps it scrapes off the reef with its beak
context: The vampire squid (Vampyroteuthis infernalis) is the only cephalopod that does not chase living prey. It drifts in the deep and collects 'marine snow' — drifting flakes of dead matter. The scary name comes from its blood-red skin and cloak-like webbing, not its gentle habits. Source: Hoving & Robison 2012, MBARI news release (mbari.org).

question: The vampire squid is a small deep-sea animal, only about 15 centimeters long — roughly the length of a kid's hand. One part of its body, though, sets a world record: in proportion to its body size, this feature is the biggest of any animal on Earth. Which body part is it?
answer: Its globe-shaped eyes, each about 2.5 cm across
choices: Its globe-shaped eyes, each about 2.5 cm across
Its beak, sharp enough to crack open shellfish
Its brain, unusually large for a sea creature
Its webbed cloak, which can span a full meter
context: In a squid only about 6 inches long, the globe-shaped eyes are roughly 2.5 cm (1 inch) across — proportionately the largest eyes in the animal kingdom. They are huge to catch the faintest glimmer of deep-sea light. Source: Wikipedia: Vampire squid.  (Legend.)

question: When a predator closes in on a vampire squid, the squid flips its webbed arms up and back over its own head. It turns almost inside out into a spiny ball that hides the soft body and points fleshy spines out at the attacker. What do scientists call this defensive shape?
answer: The 'pineapple posture'
choices: The 'pineapple posture'
The 'artichoke fold'
The 'acorn ball'
The 'walnut curl'
context: Turning inside out into this spiny defensive shape — also called the 'pumpkin posture' — hides the vampire squid's vulnerable body and points its fleshy spines (cirri) outward at the attacker. It is the animal's signature move. Source: MBARI Animals of the Deep; Wikipedia: Vampire squid.  (Legend.)

question: Most squids that live in sunlit water escape a predator by firing a black cloud of ink and darting away behind the cloud. But the vampire squid lives 600 to 900 meters down in permanent darkness, where a black cloud in black water would do absolutely nothing. So when a hungry predator lunges at a vampire squid in the deep, what does it shoot out instead of ordinary ink?
answer: A glowing cloud of bioluminescent mucus
choices: A glowing cloud of bioluminescent mucus
A jet of icy water to numb the attacker
A spray of stinging venom from its arm tips
A burst of bubbles that blinds the hunter
context: The vampire squid has no ink sac at all — ink is useless in its lightless world. Instead it squirts a glowing cloud of bioluminescent mucus full of blue light orbs to dazzle predators, a dazzling display that can last nearly 10 minutes. Source: Wikipedia: Vampire squid; MBARI.  (Legend.)

question: The vampire squid never swims after food. It hangs motionless and pays out two thin, sticky fishing threads to catch drifting scraps. A diver might expect these threads to reach an arm's length or so — but each one unspools far past that. How far can a single feeding thread stretch?
answer: Up to eight times the length of its own body
choices: Up to eight times the length of its own body
About half the length of its own body
Roughly the same length as its own body
Up to twice the length of its own body
context: It catches food on two long, sticky, retractable filaments that can stretch up to eight times its body length, then wipes the loaded thread back through its arms to eat. Source: MBARI news release on Hoving & Robison 2012 (mbari.org).

question: Deep in the ocean, far below where sunlight reaches, the vampire squid feeds on a slow, drifting rain of specks that scientists call marine snow. The name sounds pretty, but the flakes are really the leftovers of everything living in the water above. Scientists describe this drifting food, bluntly, as a mixture of three things. Which three?
answer: Dead bodies, poop, and snot
choices: Dead bodies, poop, and snot
Salt crystals, sand, and foam
Live plankton, eggs, and larvae
Seaweed, shells, and pebbles
context: Marine snow is remains of tiny algae and animals, fecal pellets from copepods and krill, and mucus debris from gelatinous larvaceans — dead bodies, poop, and snot. Source: MBARI / Hoving & Robison 2012 (mbari.org).

question: In 1903 the German zoologist Carl Chun, leader of the first deep-sea expedition to trawl the Atlantic, hauled a strange soft creature up from thousands of feet down. It was small, dark, and covered in a webbed cloak of skin between its arms. He gave it the Latin name Vampyroteuthis infernalis -- literally 'the vampire squid from hell.' What features of the animal did he base that dramatic name on?
answer: Its blood-red skin and cloak-like webbing
choices: Its blood-red skin and cloak-like webbing
Its habit of draining blood from fish
The bat-shaped fins on its head
The way it shrieks when pulled from the water
context: Vampyroteuthis infernalis literally means 'vampire squid from hell.' The teuthologist Carl Chun named it in 1903 for its dark blood-red skin and cloak-like webbing — not for its habits, which are gentle. Source: Wikipedia: Vampire squid.

question: The vampire squid makes its home in a very strange band of the deep ocean, 600 to 900 meters below the surface. Almost no other predator can survive there — not because of the cold or the crushing pressure, but because of a chemistry problem that suffocates most animals. What deadly condition of this deep band does the vampire squid tolerate that its rivals cannot?
answer: Oxygen drops as low as 3 percent saturation
choices: Oxygen drops as low as 3 percent saturation
The water pressure crushes bone instantly
Freezing temperatures turn the water to slush
Toxic gas bubbles up from vents on the seafloor
context: This band is called the 'oxygen minimum zone.' The vampire squid lives there permanently, surviving where oxygen saturation drops as low as 3 percent — an environment so hostile that few predators can follow it there. Source: Wikipedia: Vampire squid; MBARI (Hoving).

question: The vampire squid is a small dark cephalopod that drifts in the deep ocean, a thousand meters down where sunlight never reaches. When a hungry predator lunges at it, the squid detaches the glowing tip of one of its arms — and the attacker swims off with the flashing morsel, thinking it has caught a meal. The squid itself glides away nearly unhurt. Why is the bitten-off arm tip such a clever loss?
answer: It keeps flashing as a decoy while the tip regrows
choices: It keeps flashing as a decoy while the tip regrows
It releases venom into the predator's mouth
It was already dead tissue the squid was shedding
It signals nearby squid to swarm the attacker
context: The vampire squid's body is dotted with light organs (photophores). If a predator bites off a glowing arm tip, the tip keeps flashing as a decoy while the squid escapes — and the arm tip grows back. Source: Wikipedia: Vampire squid; Animal Diversity Web.

question: The vampire squid drifts through the low-oxygen midwater of the deep ocean, a soft dark body no bigger than a football. It is the last member of an ancient cephalopod order called Vampyromorphida, whose other species vanished millions of years ago. Biologists call it a 'living fossil' because it survives almost unchanged from a much older world. What makes its place on the cephalopod family tree so strange?
answer: It shares traits with octopuses and squids but is neither
choices: It shares traits with octopuses and squids but is neither
It is the direct ancestor of the modern octopus
It is the only cephalopod without a beak or arms
It evolved from a fish that lost its bones
context: The vampire squid is the only surviving member of the order Vampyromorphida, an ancient cephalopod lineage. It shares traits with both octopuses and squids while being neither — a true living fossil. Source: Wikipedia: Vampire squid; marine-biology sources.  (Legend.)

question: The modern vampire squid chases nothing — it drifts and dabs up marine snow. But its 164-million-year-old Jurassic ancestor, scanned in 3D by a synchrotron X-ray, left behind two elongated arms whose fine detail revealed a very different way of life. What did those arms carry?
answer: Rows of muscular suckers for gripping live prey
choices: Rows of muscular suckers for gripping live prey
Sticky threads for gathering drifting flakes of food
Rows of glowing organs to lure prey closer
Curved hooks for snagging small passing fish
context: The fossil is Vampyronassa rhodanica, a roughly 10-cm cephalopod from the 164-million-year-old La Voulte-sur-Rhône deposit in France. Rowe and colleagues (Scientific Reports, 2022) used synchrotron X-ray microtomography on its exceptionally 3D-preserved soft tissue, revealing robust muscular suckers on two elongated dorsal arms — forming a watertight suction seal — plus sensory appendages for detecting prey. That marks it as an active hunter, in sharp contrast to the modern vampire squid's low-energy life scavenging marine snow. Source: Rowe et al., Scientific Reports (2022), nature.com/articles/s41598-022-12269-3; via Sci.News (sci.news/paleontology/vampyronassa-rhodanica-10934.html) and ScienceDaily.

question: The vampire squid is a small deep-sea cephalopod whose tube-shaped body — the mantle — carries a pair of fins on the sides for gentle steering. Early scientists netted these animals at different growth stages and were so confused by the way they changed shape that they catalogued the same species several times. As the young squid's mantle grows past about two centimeters, its fins do something no other cephalopod does. How do the fins change?
answer: A new pair sprouts up front and the old pair is absorbed
choices: A new pair sprouts up front and the old pair is absorbed
The single pair splits lengthwise, leaving it with four
The fins fuse into one broad fin ringing the mantle
The fins are pulled inside and it jets like a young squid
context: Juvenile vampire squid have a single pair of fins and swim by jet propulsion. When the mantle reaches about 15–25 mm long, a second pair of fins develops farther forward (anterior); once the new pair matures, the original pair is reabsorbed, and the animal switches to swimming by flapping its fins. Because it looks so different at each stage, early naturalists mistakenly described the life stages as separate species. Source: Animal Diversity Web (animaldiversity.org/accounts/Vampyroteuthis_infernalis); corroborated by Wikipedia, 'Vampire squid'.

question: A stick insect — an insect of the order Phasmatodea — is long, thin, and brown, and it hides in plain sight among the twigs of a bush. Birds and lizards walk right past without spotting it. But the insect adds one extra trick: it copies something a real twig would do on a gentle breezy day. What is it?
answer: It rocks and sways gently from side to side
choices: It rocks and sways gently from side to side
It curls up tightly into a hard ball
It buries itself in the loose soil below
It spins a sticky web between two leaves
context: Many stick insects sway as they walk or rest, mimicking a real twig or leaf trembling in the breeze — so even their MOVEMENT doesn't give them away. Source: Wikipedia, Phasmatodea ('swaying' behavioural crypsis).

question: A ptarmigan is a plump mountain grouse that lives where deep snow buries the ground for half the year. In winter its feathers are pure snowy white; in summer they turn mottled brown. What flips the switch between the two coats each year, right on schedule?
answer: The number of daylight hours
choices: The number of daylight hours
The temperature of the air
The first snowfall of the season
The food it finds to eat
context: The change is triggered by DAY LENGTH, not temperature — so the timing is the same every year even when snow comes early or late, which can leave a half-turned bird briefly mismatched. Source: Audubon Field Guide, Rock Ptarmigan; Alaska Dept. Fish & Game.

question: A leaf insect is a bug of the Southeast Asian rainforest that survives by looking exactly like a leaf. Its flat green body has fake veins running through it and ragged brown edges, so a bird gliding past sees only foliage. The leaf insect even wears one extra detail that makes its 'leaf' look old and used rather than fresh and perfect. What is that finishing touch?
answer: Fake chewed-out bite marks and blemishes
choices: Fake chewed-out bite marks and blemishes
A row of bright warning eyespots
A dusting of glittering silver scales
A pair of long trailing feelers
context: The insect mimics a leaf a caterpillar already chewed on — a perfect, unblemished leaf would actually look MORE suspicious than a battered one. Source: Australian Museum, Leaf and Stick Insects (Phasmatodea).

question: An octopus resting on a coral reef can make its normally smooth skin suddenly erupt into a bumpy, ragged surface — matching the seaweed, sponges, and coral around it. When the octopus wants to swim off, it flattens right back out again. Biologists call the little muscle bumps papillae. Roughly how fast can the octopus throw up those bumps?
answer: In about a fifth of a second
choices: In about a fifth of a second
In about ten minutes
Over the course of a full day
Only once, permanently, as it grows up
context: The bumps are muscle-driven skin projections called papillae; the octopus pushes them up in about 0.2 seconds and can hold them or drop them at will. Source: Scientific American, octopus 3-D camouflage; PMC6059360, Neural Control of Dynamic 3-D Skin Papillae.

question: A decorator crab, from the crab family Majidae, lives on coral reefs and does more than just match its surroundings — it actually builds its disguise onto its own back. Its shell is covered in tiny hooked bristles that grab like Velcro. Instead of hiding under things, the crab plants a living garden on itself and walks around wearing it. What does it stick onto those hooks?
answer: Living sponges, algae, and stinging anemones
choices: Living sponges, algae, and stinging anemones
Flat pebbles it glues down with mucus
Shed scales borrowed from passing fish
A hard crust of dried salt and sand
context: The crab plucks bits of the reef and presses them onto its hooked bristles — anemones even add stinging defense — and can swap the decorations out as it moves to new ground. Source: Smithsonian Ocean, Decorator Crab; Wikipedia, Decorator crab.

question: A stonefish is a chunky, slow-moving fish of tropical Indo-Pacific reefs. It lies on the seafloor looking exactly like an algae-covered rock, and stays so still that real algae actually grows over its back and it disappears completely. A swimmer or a hungry predator can easily step right on top of it. What happens the instant a foot lands on the fish?
answer: Thirteen back spines fire venom automatically
choices: Thirteen back spines fire venom automatically
It inflates into a spiky ball of armor
It bites down with rows of curved fangs
It squirts a cloud of blinding black ink
context: The stonefish is the world's most venomous fish: 13 hollow dorsal spines inject venom driven purely by the pressure of the foot pressing down — no decision needed. Source: Wikipedia, Synanceia; HowStuffWorks, Stonefish.

question: In a cuttlefish's skin, every tiny pigment sac is its own miniature machine. A ring of muscles yanks it open, and a private nerve line runs directly back to the brain. Given that each sac needs all that equipment, how many are crammed into a single patch of skin one millimeter square?
answer: Around 200 of them
choices: Around 200 of them
Around 5 of them
Around 20 of them
Just a single large one
context: These pigment sacs are called chromatophores, and they're packed up to about 200 per square millimeter — each with its own muscles and its own nerve line — which is how a cuttlefish can 'paint' finely detailed patterns across its skin. Source: Roger Hanlon, National Geographic; PMC3403426, chromatophore density.

question: A flounder is a flatfish that spends its life lying flat on the seabed, changing its skin color to match the sand or gravel underneath. In one famous laboratory test, scientists dropped a flounder onto a black-and-white checkerboard floor to see how it would react to a pattern that doesn't exist in nature. Cameras watched its skin. About a minute later, what had happened to the flounder?
answer: It broke into dark and light blotches copying the squares
choices: It broke into dark and light blotches copying the squares
It settled on a single grey average of the whole board
It flashed rippling stripes across its back
It darkened uniformly to a flat solid tone
context: The flounder's skin broke into dark and light blotches roughly matching the checkerboard — a striking demonstration of background-matching against an unnatural pattern, rather than just averaging or flashing. Source: American Museum of Natural History; Royal Society Open Science, flounder background-matching study.

question: Look at a shark, a deer, or a penguin: dark on the back, pale on the belly. Sunlight pours down from ABOVE, so a rounded animal casts a dark shadow across its own underside that betrays its solid 3-D shape. How does painting the belly paler defeat that shadow?
answer: The paler belly reflects light back to fill the shadow to an even tone
choices: The paler belly reflects light back to fill the shadow to an even tone
The dark back soaks up the sunlight before it can cast a shadow
The dark-pale boundary sits where a predator's eye locks, pulling the gaze off
The pale belly matches the bright surface above, erasing it from below
context: This is countershading: the naturally-shaded belly is painted paler so it reflects light back and fills in its own shadow, leaving the body one even tone that reads as flat and un-solid instead of a spottable 3-D shape. The other options are real tricks other animals use — heat-absorbing dark backs, disruptive edge patterns, mirror-belly matching the surface from below — but none is how countershading works. Source: Wikipedia, Countershading ('Thayer's law'); The Conversation, dark backs and pale bellies.

question: The satanic leaf-tailed gecko (Uroplatus phantasticus) of Madagascar looks like a dead leaf come to life. Its flat tail is notched, fake-veined, and ragged like something half-rotted. But one more feature erases the tell-tale line where a body meets the ground. What does the gecko have that blurs its outline?
answer: Fringes of skin along its edges
choices: Fringes of skin along its edges
A coat of loose downy fur
A shell of overlapping hard plates
A trailing cloud of fine bubbles
context: Skin fringes break up the gecko's silhouette against the forest floor, so predators can't find the crisp edge that would betray an animal. Source: Wikipedia, Uroplatus phantasticus; Smithsonian National Zoo, Phantastic Leaf-tailed Gecko.

question: The mimic octopus lives on the sandy seafloor of the Indo-Pacific, from Indonesia to New Guinea. It does more than blend in — it impersonates other animals to scare predators away. In one famous trick, it tucks six of its arms down into a burrow and waves only two of them, one out each side. That striped, wavy shape mimics a deadly banded reef animal. Which one is it copying?
answer: A banded sea snake
choices: A banded sea snake
A stinging box jellyfish
A bristling stonefish
A venomous cone snail
context: By tucking six arms and trailing two, the octopus mimics a banded sea snake — all four choices name genuinely venomous reef animals, but the two-armed, striped display copies the snake. It also splays its arms to imitate a spiny lionfish and flattens all eight to glide like a flatfish, swapping impersonations to match whatever predator is near. Source: Wikipedia, Mimic octopus; ScienceDaily, flatfish mimicry study.

question: A cuttlefish's pigment sacs can only make a limited palette — there are shades they simply can't mix. Yet the animal still matches those colors, using a hidden second layer of skin beneath the pigment. What trick does that under-layer use to fill in a shade the pigments can't make?
answer: Mirror-like cells bounce back whatever light is around
choices: Mirror-like cells bounce back whatever light is around
It slowly grows fresh pigment to order over minutes
It borrows dye absorbed from the food it eats
It bends its whole body to catch a different angle
context: By pulling the top pigment sacs aside, the cuttlefish lets reflective under-layer cells — iridophores and white leucophores — throw back the surrounding light, filling in colors the pigments alone can't produce, and matching a shade it may not even be able to see. Source: Nature Scitable, Cephalopod Camouflage.

question: Here is the deep puzzle of the cuttlefish: with just ONE kind of light-sensor in its eye it should be colorblind, yet it matches the colors around it in about a second. Scientists haven't settled how — so what is one leading explanation they are actively testing?
answer: It reads color from how its oddly-shaped pupil blurs the light
choices: It reads color from how its oddly-shaped pupil blurs the light
It memorizes a fixed color from one bright dawn each day
It was found to grow a second light-sensor as an adult
It simply copies the nearest cuttlefish's color guess
context: Genuinely unsettled research: with one sensor the cuttlefish should be colorblind, so scientists debate whether it matches BRIGHTNESS instead of hue, or 'reads' color from the way its oddly-shaped pupil blurs different wavelengths (chromatic aberration) — the question is still open. Source: PNAS 2016, Spectral discrimination in color blind animals via chromatic aberration and pupil shape; PNAS 2011, hyperspectral imaging of cuttlefish camouflage.  (Legend.)

question: Everyone assumes a chameleon changes color by shuffling pigment through its skin. But a panther chameleon (Furcifer pardalis) gets its calm green from a deep layer of cells holding tiny guanine crystals in a tidy lattice. When an excited male flushes yellow-orange in seconds, no new pigment appears at all. What did 2015 imaging catch it doing to that crystal lattice?
answer: It stretches the lattice so its crystals sit farther apart
choices: It stretches the lattice so its crystals sit farther apart
It grinds the crystals down into a much finer, denser powder
It swivels each crystal to face straight into the bright sun
It dissolves the crystals and regrows them in a fresh new shape
context: The 2015 study (Teyssier, Saenko, van der Marel & Milinkovitch, 'Photonic crystals cause active colour change in chameleons,' Nature Communications 6:6368) overturned the old 'pigment disperses' story. In a calm chameleon the guanine nanocrystals sit packed close together, and the lattice reflects short blue-green wavelengths, so the skin looks green. When the animal gets excited it actively spreads that lattice apart -- crystal-to-crystal spacing widens by about 30% -- which shifts the reflected light to long yellow/orange/red wavelengths and turns the skin orange in seconds. So the color change is a living photonic crystal being tuned, not a pigment shuffle. Corroborated by the University of Geneva press release (unige.ch) and Science news; open-access via PMC4366488. (Grokipedia checked first, returned HTTP 403.)  (Legend.)

question: A glass frog (Hyalinobatrachium fleischmanni) has see-through skin -- superb camouflage, except its blood is bright red and ought to glow through like a warning light. Yet when the frog settles onto a leaf to sleep by day, it turns two to three times MORE transparent than when awake. How does it hide its telltale red blood?
answer: It packs most of its red blood cells into its mirror-lined liver
choices: It packs most of its red blood cells into its mirror-lined liver
It swaps the red pigment in its blood for a clear, colorless kind
It drains its blood down into its dark and opaque hind legs
It floods its body with clear fluid to dilute the red away
context: The 2022 study (Taboada et al., 'Glassfrogs conceal blood in their liver to maintain transparency,' Science 378:1315-1320) found that a sleeping glass frog pulls roughly 89% of its red blood cells out of circulation and packs them into its liver, whose mirror-like reflective coating keeps the stashed blood from showing. Emptying the red out of its see-through parts makes the frog two to three times more transparent; when it wakes and needs to move, it sends the red cells back into the bloodstream. Researchers mapped where the hidden blood went using photoacoustic imaging -- a green laser makes the packed red cells emit ultrasound. Corroborated by the NIH/NIBIB newsroom and Duke Pratt School of Engineering news. (Grokipedia checked first, returned HTTP 403.)  (Legend.)

question: In the movie Jurassic Park, Velociraptor is a scaly monster taller than a grown-up, stalking kids through the kitchen. But the real Velociraptor, whose bones came out of the sandy Gobi Desert in Mongolia in the 1920s, was actually about the size of what farm bird?
answer: A turkey
choices: A turkey
An ostrich
A chicken
A goose
context: The real Velociraptor stood only about 0.5 m (1.6 ft) at the hip and ran 1.5–2 m long — turkey-sized, far smaller than the man-sized monsters of the films. Source: Natural History Museum, nhm.ac.uk/discover/velociraptor-facts.html; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velociraptor.

question: Most kids picture Velociraptor as a bare, scaly killer — that is how the Jurassic Park movies drew it. But since those movies came out, paleontologists digging Velociraptor bones in the Gobi Desert have found that its arms and body weren't scaly at all. The little dinosaur had the same body covering modern birds wear. What was really covering Velociraptor?
answer: Feathers
choices: Feathers
Fur
Bony scales
Slimy skin
context: Velociraptor was a feathered dinosaur — it just couldn't fly. Feathers on non-flying dinosaurs likely helped with warmth and display before flight ever evolved. Source: Turner et al. 2007, Science; nationalgeographic.com/science/article/evidence-that-velociraptor-had-feathers.

question: In 1924 the American paleontologist Henry Fairfield Osborn wrote up a small, sharp-toothed dinosaur newly dug out of the Gobi Desert of Mongolia — a fast little meat-eater about the size of a turkey, with a big curved claw on each foot. He gave it a Latin name that has stuck in every kid's dinosaur book ever since. What does the name Velociraptor mean?
answer: Swift robber
choices: Swift robber
Terrible claw
Feathered thief
Desert hunter
context: From Latin velox ('swift') and raptor ('robber' or 'plunderer'). Osborn named it in 1924 for a small, fast, meat-eating dinosaur. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velociraptor.

question: Velociraptor was a small feathered predator that hunted across what is now Mongolia around 75 million years ago. The Jurassic Park films made it famous as a huge scaly monster, but the real animal was closer to the size of a turkey and surprisingly clever. Fossil braincases — the bony shells that once held its brain — show paleontologists what its head really did. Which of these did its skull actually give it?
answer: A relatively large brain for its size
choices: A relatively large brain for its size
Heat-sensing pits like a pit viper
A second jaw joint for a wider gape
A bony crest for booming calls
context: For its size Velociraptor was smart and sharp-sensed, with a relatively large brain, keen eyes and a good sense of smell — a small, clever hunter that chased small prey, not the giant creatures of the films. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velociraptor; ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7542195/ (endocranium and trophic ecology of Velociraptor).

question: The famous raptors that stalk the kids through the kitchen in Jurassic Park are actually much too big for the real thing — the real Velociraptor from Mongolia was only turkey-sized. To make raptors scary on screen, the filmmakers modeled their monsters on a bigger North American cousin: a 10-foot meat-eating dinosaur named for the huge curved killing claw on each of its feet. Which cousin was that?
answer: Deinonychus
choices: Deinonychus
Tyrannosaurus
Spinosaurus
Allosaurus
context: The film's 'Velociraptors' were sized after Deinonychus, a larger raptor cousin — which is why the movie monsters dwarf the real turkey-sized, feathered Velociraptor of Mongolia. Source: nhm.ac.uk/discover/velociraptor-facts.html; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velociraptor.

question: Velociraptor was a small, fast, meat-eating dinosaur with a huge curved sickle-shaped claw on the second toe of each foot — bigger than the other toe claws around it. Fossil footprints of raptors like it show no drag mark from that big claw at all. Only the two outer toes ever touched the ground. Somehow the animal walked and ran with that one giant claw always held up in the air. Why did Velociraptor keep it raised?
answer: To keep it sharp like a switchblade
choices: To keep it sharp like a switchblade
To grip slippery rocks
To signal to other raptors
Because it was broken
context: The sickle claw curved over 6.5 cm (2.6 in) around its arc. Held up off the ground, it stayed unworn and razor-sharp — raised and ready like a switchblade. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velociraptor; nhm.ac.uk/discover/velociraptor-facts.html.

question: Velociraptor was a small predatory dinosaur that raced across the deserts of ancient Mongolia around 75 million years ago. In 2007 the paleontologist Alan Turner and his team examined a well-preserved forearm bone from one of these animals and spotted something startling: a neat row of six evenly spaced bumps running along the bone's rear edge. On modern birds, this exact pattern has a well-known meaning. What did those bumps turn out to be?
answer: Quill knobs where feathers anchored
choices: Quill knobs where feathers anchored
Scars from an old bite wound
Growth rings marking its age
Attachment points for venom glands
context: The six 'quill knobs' on specimen IGM 100/981 are the same anchor points where wing feathers attach in living birds — direct proof of feathered arms, even though Velociraptor could not fly. Source: Turner et al. 2007, Science, science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1145076.

question: Velociraptor was a small feathered dinosaur that hunted in the deserts of ancient Mongolia, sprinting after lizards and baby dinosaurs. Its long tail did not swish loosely like a lizard's — instead, bundles of hardened tendons called ossified tendons ran through it, turning the tail into a stiff, springy rod almost like a broomstick. That rigidity gave the running hunter a special advantage. What did the rigid tail let the animal do?
answer: Turn on a dime while chasing prey
choices: Turn on a dime while chasing prey
Whip it like a club in defense
Prop itself upright to rest
Rattle it to warn rivals
context: Ossified tendons — bundles of bony rods — stiffened the long tail into a counterbalance, helping Velociraptor turn and change direction quickly at a run. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velociraptor.

question: According to new research, Velociraptor hunted much like a modern eagle. It leapt onto smaller prey, pinned it under its body weight, and hooked the big sickle claw in to hold it fast. In this 'raptor prey restraint' model, what actually dispatched the pinned prey?
answer: Its jaws
choices: Its jaws
The sickle claw
Its stiff tail
Its front arms
context: This is the 'raptor prey restraint' model: the sickle claw gripped and pinned rather than slashed, while the jaws did the killing — just as a hawk or eagle holds prey with its talons and dispatches it with the beak. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velociraptor; livescience.com/deinonychus-dinosaur-claw-pin-grasp.

question: A famous 1971 fossil from Mongolia preserves a Velociraptor and a plant-eating Protoceratops locked in mid-battle, its sickle claw at the throat while the plant-eater bit down. Scientists believe both animals were suddenly buried alive together. What killed them?
answer: A collapsing sand dune
choices: A collapsing sand dune
A rising flood
A lava flow
A tar pit
context: The 'Fighting Dinosaurs' specimen froze a real dinosaur fight in stone — the raptor's claw at the Protoceratops's throat, the plant-eater's bite snapping the raptor's right arm — when a sudden sandstorm or collapsing dune buried them mid-struggle. It is now a national treasure of Mongolia. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_Dinosaurs; amnh.org/explore/ology/ology-cards/038-fighting-dinosaurs.  (Legend.)

question: Velociraptor prowled the deserts of ancient Mongolia around 75 million years ago. In 2012 the paleontologist David Hone and his team examined a beautifully preserved fossil of one of these predators and peered inside its rib cage — the same spot in the body where its last meal would have been. Tucked in there they found a long, thin limb bone from another animal, the leftovers of dinner. That bone belonged to what kind of creature?
answer: A large flying reptile.
choices: A large flying reptile.
A young horned dinosaur.
A small burrowing mammal.
A slow shelled turtle.
context: The bone came from an azhdarchid pterosaur, a flying reptile with a wingspan near two metres, an animal far too large and formidable for a turkey-sized raptor to have pulled from the air alive. David Hone's team read it instead as a scavenged meal: the raptor fed on the carcass after the pterosaur was already dead. A second clue points the same way. In 2010 Hone described shed Velociraptor teeth scattered beside a tooth-marked Protoceratops jaw, read as late-stage carcass consumption, the raptor gnawing bony scraps from a head after the good meat was gone. Together they show an opportunistic carnivore that took carrion as readily as it took live prey. (Hone et al. 2012, azhdarchid gut content; Hone et al. 2010, Protoceratops jaw. https://www.ucd.ie/news/2012/03MAR12/080312-Preserved-bone-of-Pterosaur-in--stomach-of-Velociraptor.html ; https://archosaurmusings.wordpress.com/2012/03/04/velociraptor-scavenging-azhdarchid/ )  (Legend.)

question: To learn if a fossil predator was active by day or by night, scientists measure a bony ring inside its eye socket. Its size matches that habit in modern animals. When Schmitz and Motani measured this ring in Velociraptor in 2011, what did they find about its active hours?
answer: It prowled through the dark of night.
choices: It prowled through the dark of night.
It hunted under the bright midday sun.
It stirred only at dawn and dusk.
It stayed active around the clock.
context: Schmitz and Motani measured the scleral ring, a bony circlet inside the eye socket, across 164 living species and found its shape tracks activity: a wide opening gathers faint light in night-active animals, while a thick narrow ring suits daylight hunters. Applied to fossils, Velociraptor came out nocturnal, while the plant-eater Protoceratops looked cathemeral (active by day or night), hinting the famous 'Fighting Dinosaurs' clash may have happened at twilight. It remains a genuine debate: later work questioned whether eye shape alone can cleanly separate day-active from night-active animals. (Schmitz & Motani 2011, 'Nocturnality in Dinosaurs Inferred from Scleral Ring and Orbit Morphology.' https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21493820/ ; https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/dinosaurs-around-the-clock-or-how-we-know-velociraptor-hunted-by-night )  (Legend.)

question: A gardener in the U.S. state of Georgia is weeding a flower bed when a fuzzy bug the size of a fingernail scurries across the bare dirt. It is bright orange and black, covered in soft velvet-like hair, and it looks a lot like a very fancy ant. Locals call it a 'velvet ant.' But look closely — no bent antennae, no ant waist — and it is not an ant at all. What is this creature actually?
answer: A wingless female wasp
choices: A wingless female wasp
A furry moth caterpillar
A flightless beetle
A ground-dwelling spider
context: The velvet ant belongs to the wasp family Mutillidae. Every female is flightless and fuzzy, while the males have dark translucent wings — they look so unlike each other that the two sexes are easily mistaken for different species. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velvet_ant

question: The velvet ant is not really an ant at all — it is a wingless female wasp that runs across bare sunny ground looking like a bright orange-and-black fuzzball. Farmers gave it a scary nickname, 'cow killer,' because its sting hurts so badly that a grown adult can scream. But hurt and poison are not the same thing. If a lab measured its actual venom side by side with an ordinary honeybee's, how would the velvet ant's compare?
answer: Far less toxic than a honeybee's
choices: Far less toxic than a honeybee's
More toxic than any other insect
Roughly ten times as toxic
About the same as a honeybee's
context: The screaming pain comes from overwhelming the nerves, not from poisoning the body: the venom is actually far less toxic than a honeybee's. No cow — and no human — has ever died from the sting; the 'cow killer' name is pure pain-reputation. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velvet_ant  (Legend.)

question: The velvet ant is really a wingless female wasp that scurries across sunny dirt in bright orange fuzz. Grab one gently between two fingers and it does something no true ant would ever do — it rubs a pair of rough ridges on its abdomen together, like a cricket rubs its wings, and fires off a rapid, high-pitched chirp you can actually hear. What is this tiny squeak for?
answer: To warn a predator to let go
choices: To warn a predator to let go
To call a mate over
To echolocate in the dark
To cool its body by vibrating
context: This chirping is called stridulation, made by scraping ridged patches on the abdominal segments together. Both males and females do it — a sound warning to back up the insect's other defenses when it is grabbed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velvet_ant

question: A velvet ant is not actually an ant — it is a fuzzy, brightly colored wingless wasp of the American deserts. An insect collector working at his display board tries to pin a velvet ant next to an ordinary honeybee. The bee's shell gives easily. But when the collector presses the steel pin against the velvet ant, the pin will not go in — sometimes he has to reach for a small hand drill to bore a hole first. Why is this little insect so hard to pin?
answer: Its exoskeleton is armored many times harder to crush
choices: Its exoskeleton is armored many times harder to crush
Its body is coated in a slippery wax
It curls into a spiny defensive ball
Its shell is hollow and shatters the pin
context: A velvet ant's exoskeleton takes roughly eleven times more crushing force to break than a honeybee's. This tank-like armor is also what lets a female raid another wasp's nest and stay 'impervious to the stings' of the furious owners. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velvet_ant

question: A velvet ant isn't actually an ant — she is a wingless female wasp covered in bright fuzzy hair, roaming sunny fields in search of a nursery to raid. A female velvet ant does not build a nest of her own. Instead she creeps down into the underground burrow of a ground-nesting bee, hunting for the owner's helpless young. Once she finds a bee larva, what does she do to it?
answer: Lays an egg on it so her own young can devour it
choices: Lays an egg on it so her own young can devour it
Carries it back to her own burrow
Stings it to store as paralyzed food
Eats it whole on the spot
context: The velvet ant is an ectoparasitoid: her larva feeds on the host from the OUTSIDE. Eastern cow killers (Dasymutilla occidentalis) target big diggers like cicada killers, laying an egg in the pupal case of the host's young. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velvet_ant

question: In the dark leaf litter of the forest floor, a velvet worm creeps up on a cricket far too fast to catch by chasing. From a few centimetres away it launches a surprise attack that pins the cricket to the ground before it can hop. What does the velvet worm fire at its prey?
answer: Two jets of sticky glue from nozzles beside its mouth
choices: Two jets of sticky glue from nozzles beside its mouth
A cloud of choking gas from vents along its back
A cluster of barbed harpoons from its clawed feet
A jolt of electricity through the damp soil
context: The velvet worm has a pair of nozzles (oral papillae) on either side of its mouth. It sprays two jets of slime that fling a net of glue over prey from a short distance, sticking the animal to the ground before the velvet worm moves in to eat it. Source: eartharchives.org/articles/velvet-worms-the-voracious-snipers-of-the-undergrowth/  (Legend.)

question: A velvet worm's two slime nozzles are tiny, yet a single squirt lays down a wide zig-zag net of glue that blankets far more ground than a straight shot could. As the slime fires, the nozzles blur back and forth 30 to 60 times a second. Astonishingly, the animal has no muscle anywhere near fast enough to wave them. So what makes the nozzles whip that fast?
answer: The force of the fluid firing through the floppy nozzle whips it on its own
choices: The force of the fluid firing through the floppy nozzle whips it on its own
A ring of super-fast muscle unique to the mouth region
A spinning valve that flicks the stream side to side
Rapid puffs of air that buffet the jet mid-flight
context: This is an elastohydrodynamic instability: the fast fluid passing through the flexible nozzle makes it flail on its own, with no fast muscle involved. The worm's quickest real muscle is about 25 times too slow to move the nozzle that fast. Source: Concha et al., Nature Communications 2015, PMC4382676.

question: The velvet worm looks like a soft, stubby-legged worm oozing through the leaf litter, but that soft body plan is over 500 million years old, tracing back to the Cambrian seas. It is not a true worm, not an insect, and not an arthropod. Where does biology actually place it?
answer: In its own phylum, Onychophora, the 'claw-bearers'
choices: In its own phylum, Onychophora, the 'claw-bearers'
Among the segmented annelid worms, like earthworms
Among the myriapods, alongside centipedes
Among the soft-bodied molluscs, like slugs
context: The velvet worm is its own phylum, Onychophora ('claw-bearers') - a soft-bodied survivor of a Cambrian-era body plan over 500 million years old. Its closest living relatives are the tiny tardigrades (water bears). Source: Burgess Shale (Royal Ontario Museum); bmcecolevol.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12862-014-0222-z.  (Legend.)

question: An Australian velvet worm, Euperipatoides rowelli, lives in a family group of up to fifteen that hunts together to bring down prey too big for one alone. When the catch is glued down, though, the group does not share it evenly - one member feeds for up to an hour and bites any who try to sneak in early. Who gets to eat first?
answer: The dominant female, usually the largest and most aggressive
choices: The dominant female, usually the largest and most aggressive
The oldest male, who leads the group on the hunt
Whichever animal landed the first slime shot
The smallest youngsters, fed before the adults
context: These velvet worm families are ruled by a single dominant 'alpha female,' usually the biggest and most aggressive, who keeps order by biting and shoving. She feeds first and alone for up to an hour before the other females, then the males and young, take their turn. Source: Reinhard & Rowell, Journal of Zoology 2005; eartharchives.org.  (Legend.)

question: Toxic animals do their damage in two different ways. A poison-dart frog of the Central American rainforest oozes deadly chemicals from its skin — one lick is enough to kill a person. A rattlesnake of the American deserts stores just as deadly a chemical inside its head, but you could actually drink it from a cup and be fine. The difference is delivery. Which of these two animals injects its toxin through a wound as venom?
answer: The rattlesnake
choices: The rattlesnake
The poison-dart frog
Both of them
Neither of them
context: Venom must be INJECTED through a bite, sting, or spine; poison harms on eating, touching, or inhaling. The rattlesnake injects venom through its bite, which is why swallowing that venom is harmless — it is made of proteins too large to cross the gut wall into your blood. The poison-dart frog's toxin sits on its skin and harms on contact or if eaten. Source: Natural History Museum, 'Bite or be bitten' (nhm.ac.uk/discover/bite-or-be-bitten.html).

question: In the rivers and streams of eastern Australia lives a strange four-legged, egg-laying mammal with soft brown fur and a wide, rubbery, duck-like bill. It looks harmless enough — until you flip a male over. Only the males grow a sharp spur on each hind ankle, and each spur is wired to a real venom gland tucked in the thigh. Which animal is this?
answer: The platypus
choices: The platypus
The echidna
The wombat
The quokka
context: The platypus is one of the very few venomous mammals. Only the male carries the spur (a calcar) on each hind ankle, and it produces venom mainly during the breeding season — the weapon is for fighting rival males, not hunting. Source: Platypus venom, Wikipedia; Australian Platypus Conservancy (platypus.asn.au). LEGEND.

question: Of all the snakes on Earth, one African viper of the deep rainforest holds the record for the longest fangs. Its needle-like teeth grow up to about 5 centimeters — 2 inches — and fold flat against the roof of its mouth when they aren't in use. When the snake lunges, they swing forward like switchblades. Which African snake carries these record-breaking fangs?
answer: The Gaboon viper
choices: The Gaboon viper
The king cobra
The black mamba
The reticulated python
context: The Gaboon viper (Bitis gabonica) holds the record for the longest fangs of any snake, and also the highest venom yield of any snake. The folding fangs let a short-faced viper carry blades far longer than its own mouth. Source: Guinness World Records; Smithsonian's National Zoo (nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/gaboon-viper).

question: Vipers and cobras kill in very different ways. A viper's bite delivers a haemotoxic venom that breaks down tissue — the leg it strikes swells, bruises purple, and starts bleeding under the skin. A cobra's venom is neurotoxic instead: it blocks the electrical signals that travel from nerve to muscle. That is why a cobra bite can kill a victim faster. It works by quietly shutting down which part of the body?
answer: The breathing muscles
choices: The breathing muscles
The blood-clotting system
The heart's valves
The digestive tract
context: Neurotoxic venom (typical of cobras) blocks the nerve signals that command the muscles, so the breathing muscles fail and the victim cannot draw breath. Hemotoxic venom (typical of vipers) instead destroys blood cells, prevents clotting, and rots tissue — hence the swelling and bruising. Real venoms usually mix both; the clean cobra-vs-viper split is a teaching simplification. Source: Zoo Atlanta, 'Snake venoms and myths'; Snake venom, Wikipedia.

question: The spitting cobra of Africa doesn't wait to be cornered before it fights. When a threat gets close, it rears up and sprays venom through tiny holes in its fangs, aiming a fine stream up to 3 meters away. Even more amazing, it tracks the threat's movements while it spits. About 90 percent of the time, the venom hits one particular part of the threat's body. Which part is it aiming for?
answer: The eyes
choices: The eyes
The mouth
The nose
The hands
context: A 'spitting' cobra sprays venom out of forward-facing holes in its fangs, aiming for the eyes of a threat up to about 3 metres away; roughly 90% of spits hit the eyes, and the snake predicts where the threat's head will move. This is defense, not hunting. Source: Live Science, 'Secret to Spitting Cobra's Deadly Accurate Aim Revealed'; Britannica, 'Spitting cobra.'

question: In the shallow reefs of the Pacific and Indian Oceans lives a tiny octopus no bigger than a golf ball. Cornered by a curious diver, it suddenly lights up — about 60 electric-blue rings flash bright across its yellow skin as a warning. If the diver keeps pressing in, it bites with a small beak loaded with tetrodotoxin, one of the most powerful nerve poisons known in the animal world. Which animal is this?
answer: The blue-ringed octopus
choices: The blue-ringed octopus
The mimic octopus
The vampire squid
The reef cuttlefish
context: The blue-ringed octopus flashes roughly 60 iridescent blue rings as an aposematic (warning) display before biting. Its tetrodotoxin is one of the deadliest nerve toxins known — far more potent than cyanide — and there is no antivenom. Source: Britannica, 'Blue-ringed octopus'; Natural History Museum (nhm.ac.uk). LEGEND.

question: On a coral reef in the tropics, a slow, thumb-sized sea snail called the cone snail somehow hunts fast little fish. It extends a fleshy tube from its shell, fires a single hollow, harpoon-like structure on a tether, stabs the fish, injects venom, and reels the paralyzed meal back in. But what is that harpoon actually made from — because the cone snail has no metal to work with?
answer: A modified tooth
choices: A modified tooth
A sharpened claw
A hardened tentacle
A stinging hair
context: The geography cone snail (Conus geographus) fires a single hollow, barbed radular TOOTH — a modified tooth on a tether — from an extendable proboscis, then reels the speared fish back to swallow it. Source: Conus geographus, Wikipedia (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conus_geographus).

question: A jellyfish's trailing tentacles carry thousands of microscopic sting-capsules called nematocysts. When one is triggered by a brush of fish skin, a tightly coiled tube unrolls and drives a barb into the victim in about 3 milliseconds, injecting venom before the fish even feels the touch. Compared with every movement biologists have measured in living animals, how does this firing speed rank?
answer: One of the fastest movements known
choices: One of the fastest movements known
About as fast as a human blink
A typical nerve-reflex speed
The fastest a muscle can contract
context: On contact a nematocyst fires in roughly 3 milliseconds, driving a spined tube into the skin to inject venom — one of the fastest movements known in all of biology, far quicker than a reflex, a blink, or a muscle twitch. Each is a pre-loaded microscopic harpoon. Source: University of Melbourne AVRU, 'Venomous marine animals — jellyfish'; Firing the Sting, PMC4379534.

question: A cone snail is a slow-moving sea snail with a beautifully patterned shell, and some species hunt fast-swimming fish. A few of these fish-hunters don't bother with a harpoon at all. They release a cloud of a chemical the fish's own body already makes inside itself. It drifts in through the fish's gills and drops it into a helpless stupor, and the slow snail then swallows the fish whole. Which of the fish's own hormones has the cone snail turned into a weapon?
answer: Insulin
choices: Insulin
Adrenaline
Melatonin
Testosterone
context: Certain cone snails release a specialized INSULIN into the water; through the gills it drives the fish into hypoglycemic shock, sedating it — chemistry out-drugging a faster animal. Researchers nicknamed this sedating blend the 'nirvana cabal.' Source: PNAS 2015, 'Specialized insulin is used for chemical warfare by fish-hunting cone snails.' LEGEND.

question: The blue-ringed octopus is a tiny golf-ball-sized octopus of Pacific tide pools whose bite carries tetrodotoxin, one of the deadliest poisons on Earth — enough to kill a human in minutes. Yet when biologists read the octopus's DNA looking for the recipe, they found no gene anywhere that could build tetrodotoxin. The octopus itself is not making the poison. So where does the toxin actually come from?
answer: Bacteria living in its salivary glands
choices: Bacteria living in its salivary glands
A gland behind each blue ring
The venom of prey it eats
Sunlight stored in its skin
context: The octopus does not make its own toxin — symbiotic bacteria in its salivary glands produce the tetrodotoxin. That also makes it BOTH venomous (its bite injects the toxin) and poisonous (harmful if eaten). Source: Britannica, 'Blue-ringed octopus'; Natural History Museum, 'Bite or be bitten' (nhm.ac.uk).

question: The box jellyfish carries one of the deadliest venoms in the sea, but for decades nobody knew how it wrecked a cell. In 2019 a gene-editing screen finally cracked it: the venom cannot harm a cell unless the cell hands it one particular molecule, and a drug that strips that molecule away works as an antidote. What does the venom depend on?
answer: Cholesterol built into the cell membrane
choices: Cholesterol built into the cell membrane
Iron carried in the red blood cells
Calcium stored inside the muscle fibers
Sugar coating the cell's outer surface
context: Chironex fleckeri is often called the most venomous animal in the sea: a single individual carries roughly enough venom to kill about 60 adults, and a severe sting can stop the heart in 2-5 minutes. The venom works through pore-forming proteins (porins) that punch holes in cell membranes; potassium floods out, and the resulting spike in blood potassium (hyperkalemia) drives cardiovascular collapse. In 2019 a University of Sydney team (Greg Neely and Raymond Lau) ran a genome-wide CRISPR knockout screen and found the venom requires membrane cholesterol to act. Common cholesterol-stripping drugs called cyclodextrins block the damage and, in mice, still worked as an antidote up to about 15 minutes after the sting. Sources: Nature Communications 2019, 'Molecular dissection of box jellyfish venom cytotoxicity highlights an effective venom antidote' (s41467-019-09681-1); University of Sydney news, 1 May 2019; Wikipedia, 'Chironex fleckeri'.

question: Long before any snake existed, a Late Triassic reptile on the crocodile-and-dinosaur branch already delivered venom. Today it survives only as fossilized teeth in the rock. Laid out in order, those teeth are prized because they preserve which rare record?
answer: A step-by-step shift from an open surface groove to a fully enclosed internal tube
choices: A step-by-step shift from an open surface groove to a fully enclosed internal tube
A step-by-step shift from a crushing molar into a sharp slicing blade
The earliest known bite marks left by one predator upon another
A single fang regrown and resharpened dozens of times in one lifetime
context: The animal is Uatchitodon, a Late Triassic archosauriform (a reptile on the crocodile-and-dinosaur branch, roughly 220-237 million years ago), known only from its teeth. Those teeth are extraordinary because, across different specimens, they capture a complete transition series: from a shallow open groove on the tooth surface to a fully enclosed, tube-like internal canal for conducting venom, with some teeth carrying two canals apiece. This 'grooves to tubes' sequence shows the very pathway by which a venom-delivery system evolves, it predates venomous snakes by well over 100 million years, and it happened on a completely separate reptile lineage. Sources: Mitchell, Heckert & Sues 2010, Naturwissenschaften (The Science of Nature), 'Grooves to tubes: evolution of the venom delivery system in a Late Triassic reptile' (doi 10.1007/s00114-010-0729-0); Wikipedia, 'Uatchitodon'.

question: Deep in the western Pacific Ocean, about a kilometer down in the cold black water, a slender white vase sits on the muddy seafloor. It is a Venus flower basket, a kind of sponge, and its whole cage-like skeleton is woven from a lattice of long, thin spikes called spicules. What are those spikes made of?
answer: Silica — the same stuff as glass
choices: Silica — the same stuff as glass
Coral limestone
Woven seaweed fiber
Hardened tree resin
context: The Venus's flower basket (Euplectella aspergillum) is a deep-sea glass sponge whose entire skeleton is woven from silica, the same material as glass, built into a delicate white latticework cage shaped like a vase or basket, roughly 10 to 30 cm (4 to 12 inches) tall. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus'_flower_basket

question: The Venus flower basket is a deep-sea sponge shaped like a slender hollow vase, and its cage-like walls are woven from a lattice of glass spikes with tiny openings between them. A pair of baby shrimp squeeze through those openings, settle inside, and start life in this glass cage — feeding on scraps that drift in and cleaning its inner walls. As the shrimp keep growing, something happens that they never planned for. What is it?
answer: They grow too big to ever get back out
choices: They grow too big to ever get back out
They eat their way through the glass
They turn transparent like the sponge
They stop growing to stay small
context: A breeding pair of tiny shrimp (Spongicola venusta) swims into the sponge as babies, then grows too big to ever get back out through the glass lattice — so the pair spends its whole life imprisoned together inside the glass cage, cleaning it in exchange for food and shelter. Their own babies are born small enough to slip out through the lattice and find a sponge of their own. Source: https://schmidtocean.org/cruise-log-post/a-deep-sea-love-story/  (Legend.)

question: A Venus flower basket sponge holds a pair of grown shrimp locked inside its glass cage for their entire lives. Yet the species keeps colonizing fresh sponges across the seafloor. At what point in a shrimp's life can it move into a brand-new sponge home?
answer: Only as a newborn, small enough to slip the lattice
choices: Only as a newborn, small enough to slip the lattice
Only after molting its shell to shrink down
Only once the parent sponge dies and opens up
Only by burrowing through the sponge's soft base
context: The shrimp pair's babies are born small enough to slip out through the glass lattice and swim off to find their own sponge home — so only the parents stay imprisoned, and each new sponge gets its own captive couple. Source: https://schmidtocean.org/cruise-log-post/a-deep-sea-love-story/

question: The Venus flower basket is a deep-sea sponge whose delicate glass skeleton grows into a slender vase-shaped cage. It lives about a kilometer down, where a slow, steady bottom current filters food past it — but only if the sponge stays upright, mouth into the flow. And the seafloor there is soft mud with no rocks or reef to grip. How does it hold itself up?
answer: A tuft of hair-thin glass threads driven into the mud
choices: A tuft of hair-thin glass threads driven into the mud
Suckers that clamp onto passing fish
A heavy stone it swallows for ballast
Long muscular roots that dig downward
context: The sponge anchors to the muddy deep seafloor with a tuft of glass threads — spun-glass fibers about 5 to 20 cm long and as thin as a human hair — that hold it upright in the current like a base of spun glass. Source: https://www.pnas.org/content/101/10/3358.full

question: The hair-thin glass threads that anchor a Venus flower basket in the deep-sea mud stunned materials researchers: grown in cold seawater with no furnace, they already pull off a high-tech trick the researchers' own factories struggle to match. What do these threads do?
answer: Pipe light along their length like fiber-optic cables
choices: Pipe light along their length like fiber-optic cables
Spin a trickle of electricity from the passing current
Flex toward drifting food and grip it like tiny fingers
Ring with sound to scare off circling deep-sea hunters
context: Each thread is a natural fibre-optic cable: a core of pure silica about two micrometres across, wrapped around a central organic filament and sheathed in a finely layered shell that works just like the optical cladding of a telecom cable -- and it carries light just as well. Because the sponge grows the thread in cold seawater instead of a furnace, it can lace the glass with impurities such as sodium that IMPROVE light transmission but get destroyed in high-temperature factory glass. And unlike brittle manufactured fibre, you can tie the sponge's thread in a knot without snapping it. Source: Sundar, Yablon, Grazul, Ilan & Aizenberg, 'Fibre-optical features of a glass sponge,' Nature vol. 424, pp. 899-900 (2003), https://www.nature.com/articles/424899a ; Scientific American, 'Sea Sponge Inspires Better Fiber-Optic Cables.'

question: A Venus flower basket's glass skeleton was 3D-printed beside the criss-cross lattice that human engineers have braced bridges and towers with since the 1820s, then both were loaded until they buckled -- same material, same amount. How did the sponge's design do?
answer: It carried over 20% more load before buckling
choices: It carried over 20% more load before buckling
It matched the human grid almost exactly
It gave way first but sprang back unharmed
It held less, though it bent much further
context: The sponge's cage is no plain grid: a square lattice is overlaid with a DOUBLE set of parallel diagonal struts fused across it in a checkerboard pattern. Harvard engineers Matheus Fernandes, James Weaver and Katia Bertoldi 3D-printed rival lattice shapes and ran finite-element buckling tests, and found the paired-diagonal design is over 20% stronger -- higher buckling resistance for the same amount of material -- than the criss-cross lattice humans have braced bridges and towers with since Ithiel Town patented it in the 1820s. The sponge quietly solved a load-bearing problem better than 200 years of human engineering. Source: Fernandes, Weaver, Bertoldi et al., 'Mechanically robust lattices inspired by deep-sea glass sponges,' Nature Materials vol. 20 (2021), https://www.nature.com/articles/s41563-020-0798-1 ; Harvard SEAS news, https://seas.harvard.edu/news/marine-sponges-inspire-next-generation-skyscrapers-and-bridges.

question: A small desert arachnid called the vinegaroon — also known as a whip scorpion — lives in the American Southwest and has no stinger and no venom anywhere in its body. When a predator like a lizard lunges at it, the vinegaroon swings its rear end up toward the attacker's face and fires a fine spray. What ordinary kitchen smell does that spray smell strongly of?
answer: Vinegar
